11982-eighty-years-and-more-reminiscence:
Elizabeth Cady Stanton's Eighty Years and More, covering 1815 to 1897, opens with an epigraph that woman's place in society marks the level of civilization. Stanton dedicates the volume to Susan B. Anthony, her steadfast friend for half a century, and the contents run from childhood and school days through a long public life.

The reminiscences trace Stanton from a girlhood in a judge's household to the women's rights movement she helped lead, with friendships, campaigns, and family life woven together. Written late in life, the book is both autobiography and argument: a record of what one woman saw change, and what, in her view, still needed changing.
12288-the-witchcraft-delusion-in-colonia:
This study of the witchcraft delusion in colonial Connecticut, 1647 to 1697, draws on court records and grand jury presentments from the Connecticut Historical Society. A presentment from Fairfield charges the widow Mary Staple, Mary Harvey, and Hannah Harvey with suspicion of witchcraft, abominable in the sight of God and man.

The book traces trials, testimony, and acquittals, with depositions like Goodwife Seager account of prayer against Satan and gossip about who was no witch. It shows how fear, neighbor quarrels, and legal forms combined in a small colony. The study is documentary rather than sensational, letting records speak. It remains a key source for New England witchcraft beyond Salem, where fewer died but suspicion ran deep.
22806-the-bronze-hand-1897:
The Bronze Hand is a mystery story dated 1897, built around a woman's voice that arrests its listener with sudden, extraordinary emotion. The catalog record names no author. Tales of the 1890s loved an object with a secret, and a bronze hand promises one: a relic, a clue, or a token from a buried past.

Any words from those lips, the narrator says, would have drawn my attention. But this utterance carried such marked emotion that curiosity woke in me at once, and interest with it. Curiosity is the detective story's true engine, and this one starts it early. The story proceeds in the era's manner: respectable people, a strange inheritance or summons, and the past reaching, literally, into the present.
25622-beatrice-d-este-duchess-of-milan-1:
Julia Cartwright, Mrs. Henry Ady, writes this study of Beatrice d'Este, Duchess of Milan from 1475 to 1497, as a study of the Renaissance, published by Dent in London and Dutton in New York. The first edition came in November 1899, with a sixth in May 1910. Bianca Sforza, painted by Ambrogio de Predis, fronts the book.

Chapters follow the Este house at Ferrara, Lodovico Sforza called Il Moro, wars of Venice and Ferrara, and Isabella d'Este. Beatrice, Duchess of Bari, wins popularity at court in 1491, and Cartwright sets her brief life among artists, courts, and Italian power politics.
25769-more-cargoes-1897:
W. W. Jacobs writes More Cargoes, published by Frederick A. Stokes in 1897, a set of sea tales told in the voice of Thames watermen and sailors. Contents list Smoked Skipper, A Safety Match, A Rash Experiment, The Cabin Passenger, Choice Spirits, and A Disciplinarian.

Brother Hutchins, The Disbursement Sheet, Rule of Three, Pickled Herring, Two of a Trade, An Intervention, and The Grey Parrot follow. Money changers, the lost ship, and smoked skipper close the run. Smoked Skipper opens at Wapping Old Stairs, where a rough man with a new sea chest trots off with a small lad of fourteen in tow.
25874-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
This April 1897 number of Birds Illustrated by Color Photography offers short bird lives told in the birds' own voices, with color plates to match. A woodpecker explains how its sharp bill pecks holes to store acorns, cracks nuts in tree crevices for breakfast, and guards its hoard from thieves while keeping friends by a mild temper. Its nest, dug as hall and living room inside a tree, gets a plain, fond account.

Letters up front praise the new magazine, with the New York schools chief and the head of the National Teachers' Association both signing on as pleased readers. Rail ads for the Monon Route fill the back pages, touting parlor cars and fast trains to the Nashville Centennial and the health resorts. The number aims at homes and schools keen to know birds by sight and habit.
25983-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
The May 1897 number of Birds Illustrated by Color Photography continues the magazine's bird lives in plain words with color plates. Letters up front repeat the praise of the New York schools chief and the teachers' president for the first numbers, calling the magazine beautiful and interesting. Rail ads for the Monon Route fill the back pages, promising parlor cars by day and palace sleeping cars by night.

Bird notes describe nests with care. One nest, built in a stump cavity three feet high, took the stump's irregular shape and was packed with leaves, grass bits, stems, moss, and decayed wood, lined with hair. Another nest sat in a mill brace hole, where watchers saw birds carry in materials unafraid. The number teaches young readers to know birds by home and habit.
30081-the-arena-volume-18-no-92-july-189:
Volume 18 of The Arena, July to December 1897, edited by John Clark Ridpath and published in Boston, gathers a half year of reform debate. Henry Clews and Ridpath open on the citadel of the money power and the true inwardness of Wall Street. A symposium on honest money hears William Jennings Bryan, Wharton Barker, and others. Credit and prices, the American and French constitutions, and Japan's new civil code follow.

Later pages add John Ruskin as a type of twentieth-century manhood, the single tax in operation, natural and social selection, psychic forces, and an industrial fable, with poems closing the run. The volume shows a progressive monthly at full stretch, arguing money, morals, and science in one place. Readers of Gilded Age reform will find its hopes and quarrels intact.
30103-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
Birds Illustrated by Color Photography, volume one, number three, is dated March 1897. The issue opens with a letter from the State of New York's Department of Public Instruction, dated Albany, December 26, 1896. It thanks the publisher for the first publication of Birds and asks to be entered as a regular subscriber. The superintendent calls it one of the most beautiful and interesting publications yet attempted in this direction, and wishes the handsome little magazine abundant prosperity.

 The bird writing itself speaks in the bluebird's own voice: when it sings, buds and flowers whisper that springtime is coming. The bluebird nests in a box the farmer puts up near his barn, or in a hole in an old tree. It raises four or five little ones before going south again when winter breathes.
30523-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
Birds, a monthly serial illustrated by color photography, volume two, copyrighted in Chicago in 1897, aims to promote knowledge of bird life. Its introduction describes a series in accurate colored portraiture and popular, juvenile biographical text, covering a considerable portion of common North American birds.

Many more interesting specimens from other countries also appear, in a form the editors claim superior to rival bird publications and far cheaper. Monthly parts won a warm public reception for volume one, for which the editors give grateful thanks. The serial suits families, schools, and young bird lovers who learn best from pictures and plain text.
30666-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
Birds Illustrated by Color Photography, volume one, number six, for June 1897, closes the first half year of the serial, with volume one, January to June, now ready as a book. The bound volume runs two hundred twenty-four pages, with sixty full-page illustrations made by the new process of color photography.

Suited to old and young, in a neat, durable binding, it sells through newsdealers and booksellers and by subscription. Cloth costs one dollar twenty-five, half morocco one seventy-five, and morocco two twenty-five, with mail orders to Nature Study Publishing in Chicago. Three annual subscriptions earn a cloth binding, four a half morocco, and five a full morocco.
33646-the-arena-volume-18-no-93-august-1:
The Arena for August 1897, volume eighteen, number ninety-three, opens with David Starr Jordan, president of Leland Stanford Junior University, on evolution. He asks what it is and what it is not. Jordan, addressing the Starr King Fraternity of Oakland, observes that the word evolution is used by many in many senses, and often in no sense at all. Some dread it as the downfall of religion and social stability, while others hail it as if progress were secured by uttering the name.

Further articles in the issue include John Clark Ridpath on the segregation and permanent isolation of criminals, Norman Robinson, Emily Dickey Beery, Stinson Jarvis, Miles Menander Dawson, and Coates Kinney. The Arena was a leading progressive monthly, and this number shows its range: science, reform, economics, and literature in one lively volume.
35922-victorian-ode-for-jubilee-day-1897:
Victorian Ode for Jubilee Day, 1897 is a ceremonial poem by Francis Thompson, printed for private circulation at the Westminster Press in 1897. The occasion was Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee. Thompson imagines the night street before the festival as a corpse beneath the moon, waiting for its soul.

Through the dark street passes a long procession of the Victorian dead. First go the holy poets, two on two, while music buds like flowers along the ground. The phantom pageant reviews the reign's glories before the real celebrations begin. Thompson, a poet of Catholic mysticism and opium-shadowed years, writes the ode in high ceremonial style. Private circulation kept the poem a keepsake rather than a public broadsheet. It survives as a strange, dreamlike footnote to the Jubilee's official rejoicing.
37470-the-great-war-in-england-in-1897:
The Great War in England in 1897, by William Le Queux, first came out in July 1894 and ran through eight editions by December of that year. The hosted text is the eleventh edition, printed in London in 1895. Le Queux gives the book to Alfred Charles Harmsworth.

A plate shows the bombardment of London, with an awful scene in Ludgate Hill. Lord Roberts wrote in praise of the forecast, and warned of the loss of sea power. Le Queux shows a foe war on England at home, with towns struck and armies in the field. He calls the book a forecast of the coming war. Readers of the day got a scare tale meant to wake the land to its weak guard.
40531-a-century-in-the-comptroller-s-off:
A Century in the Comptroller's Office is a record of that office in the State of New York from 1797 to 1897. It was written by James A. Roberts, the Comptroller of the day. The book came out at Albany in 1897 from James B. Lyon, printer, with a picture of State Hall. A note states that old and varied spellings have been kept as printed, as far as could be done.

The book opens with a date. On 17 February 1897 fell the one hundredth year of the setting up of the office of Comptroller of the State of New York. The man who then held the office trusts, he says, that no charge of vain pride will be laid on him for what follows. He has gathered and set down, in honor of that hundredth birthday, the chief facts that bear on the office and its past.
41144-the-fishguard-invasion-by-the-fren:
The Fishguard Invasion by the French in 1797 was published in London in 1892. Fisher Unwin issued the narrative. Passages come from the diary of the late Reverend Daniel Rowlands. Rowlands had been vicar of a Welsh parish near the scene. The book is given, by permission, to the Earl of Cawdor. Contents divide the tale by days. Wednesday brings three frigates, the landing, and the fate of the clock. Thursday adds Welsh wives and General Tate's letter. Friday closes with the gathering at Goodwich and the capitulation. A sequel treats the golden prison at Pembroke.

The introduction owns that the affair reads like improbable fiction. Its authorities are named: eye-witnesses who recalled the landing. The last of them, Nelly Phillips, died in February 1891 aged 103. She was nine in 1797, driving cows when the frigates appeared.
60288-harper-s-round-table-january-5-189:
Harper's Round Table for Tuesday, January 5, 1897, is the Harper brothers' weekly paper for young readers, volume 18, number 897, at five cents a copy. The number leads with The Little Bishop, a story by Kate Douglas Wiggin. Its hero is Phillips Brooks Sanderson, called Phil by the village and the Little Bishop by the narrator.

Phil is spending the summer at Pleasant River while his mother is ill. The narrator watches the aunt shake her Welcome rug into the sunshine and longs to know the boy. Uncle Abner, red-bearded and gruff, has no children of his own to smooth his temper. The tale begins the morning a tiny boy comes down the grass-grown road leading a huge cow by a rope. The paper mixed story, sport, and fact for boys and girls each week.
60423-harper-s-round-table-january-12-18:
Harper's Round Table for 12 January 1897 is a weekly magazine number, volume eighteen, number 898, printed at New York for five cents a copy. Its leading article is Famous Cavalry Charges, by Richard Barry. The piece opens with Cooke's cavalry at Gaines's Mill. All day long the Union and Confederate batteries had been replying to one another.

Barry argues that those in authority at Washington did not early in the war recognize the immense importance of a well-organized cavalry. The mounted troops were used as orderly messengers, on patrol duty, and as advance outposts. Those duties were onerous and brought little chance for glory. The lesson in the uses of mounted troops was gained from battle experience. Against the Union troopers stood the quickly moving, impetuous horsemen of Stuart and the younger Lees. The Round Table was Harper's magazine for young readers.
60470-harper-s-round-table-january-19-18:
Harper Round Table, volume eighteen, number eight hundred ninety nine, for Tuesday, January nineteenth, eighteen ninety seven, cost five cents a copy or two dollars a year. Harper and Brothers in New York published the weekly. Hon Theodore Roosevelt leads the number with A Christmas Buck, a ranch hunting piece. Plates and tales for young readers fill the rest.

Roosevelt treats two kinds of deer in ranch country, the black tail and the white tail. The white tail, he says, is the deer of the East, light and graceful, and loves thick timber. The black tail is larger, with a stiff legged bounding gait, all four feet striking at once. It is bolder and fonder of open country, he notes. Fifteen years past it was far more plentiful, but is more easily killed out. Boys and girls got sport, nature, and stories in one weekly.
60509-harper-s-round-table-january-26-18:
Harper's Round Table of Tuesday, January 26, 1897, is one weekly number of Harper's magazine for boys. It cost five cents a copy, or two dollars a year, and this is number nine hundred of volume eighteen. The lead piece, Boys at Sea by Clark Russell, recalls the exciting story of the ship Aberfoyle. Her captain drank himself into delirium and poisoned himself, and her crew mutinied.

Russell tells also of young Shotten, an apprentice left alone when fever killed his officers. Charged with a desperate, reckless crew who refused his rule, the boy carried his ship to Sydney in safety. Russell calls it a true romance of the deep. He scorns sea tales that boys know could never be true, full of blunders in seamanship. This number shows its standard: fact told with a storyteller's fire.
60620-harper-s-round-table-february-2-18:
Harper Round Table for February second 1897 is a weekly boys paper, number 901. Harper and Brothers sold the issue at five cents, two dollars a year. Crying Tommy, a sea story by Molly Elliot Seawell, leads the number. Jenks, the master at arms called Jimmylegs, opens the tale on the training ship Spitfire.

Jimmylegs face is usually as stolid as a mummy, his voice steady as the Sphinx. He would announce the magazine on fire in the same tone as a broken liberty. A rudimentary grin on that face stops the first lieutenant mid shave in wonder. Naval training life for boys fills this number of Harper youth weekly.
60755-harper-s-round-table-february-16-1:
An issue of Harper's Round Table dated February 16, 1897. Harper and Brothers published the weekly for young readers. It cost five cents a copy, or two dollars a year. This is number 903 of volume eighteen. Frank R Stockton leads the number with a reminiscence. His piece recalls a boyhood archery company.

The boys named themselves the Ringgold Archers. Major Ringgold, a Mexican War cavalry hero, inspired them. His long hair, worn after a crossed love affair, supplied the romance. Green blouses and belts formed their cheap uniform. Straw hats with optional feathers completed it. Stockton wrote Ruthless tales for adults and droll stories for youth. The Round Table carried fiction, sport, and science to American teenagers weekly.
60764-harper-s-round-table-february-23-1:
Harper's Round Table for Tuesday, February 23, 1897, is number 904 of volume eighteen. Five cents bought it, or two dollars a year. A tale of northern Arizona by Kirk Munroe leads the number in full colour of words.

The Painted Desert opens on a land of wonders. As far as the eye could see, the tale says, a strange landscape spread on all sides. Castles with towers, Greek temples, thin spires, columns, arches, and walled cities rose tier above tier. Their hues ran from red and crimson through orange and buff, with greens, purples, pinks, white, and brown. Munroe wrote of the seal fisheries and the Mate series; here the desert itself is the hero.
60823-harper-s-round-table-march-2-1897:
Harper's Round Table for March 2, 1897, is a weekly number. Harper published it at New York on that Tuesday. Five cents bought a copy; the year cost two dollars. Volume eighteen, number 905, stands on the masthead. Richard Barry's battle piece leads the issue. The Battle of Opequan Creek is its title. Sheridan, Barry writes, was a cautious commander at heart. Dashing bravery had made his name, yet he distrusted forced marches. Fresh men and surprise won charges, in his view. Early in September 1864 his army camped above the Opequan. Early's Confederates held the far bank in a strong trench line. The creek ran crooked, four miles from Winchester.

For ten days the armies faced each other. By the afternoon of the eighteenth, Sheridan's plan stood perfected.
60887-harper-s-round-table-march-9-1897:
Harper's Round Table for Tuesday, March 9, 1897, is number 906 of volume eighteen. Harper and Brothers published the weekly at New York at five cents a copy, two dollars a year. Poultney Bigelow's story, How Tom Rodman Joined the German Army, leads the number. Tom, fifteen years old, is living in 1870 with Professor Schinkel at Slaugenstein on the Rhine. The French emperor has declared war on the Germans.

Soldiers march from every village toward the frontier. At supper the professor sends Tom down to learn the noise in the street. The street stands full of troops in black leather helmets, brown and strong from a day's march. A big corporal chalks the door: one corporal and seven men. The whole town is to be night quarters for the army.
61154-harper-s-round-table-march-23-1897:
Harper's Round Table for March 23, 1897, was a weekly for youth. Harper sold the New York paper at five cents a copy. Sir Walter Besant Old Portsmouth opens the number as life story. Besant recalls the town of 1844 to 1850 as most lively.

Portsmouth had no industry but the dock yard and fleecing sailors. Sailors enjoyed the game and lost their money with good cheer. The Common Hard stood as the true centre of town life. Gabled timber houses had vanished long before his boyhood years there. Gates in the walls and the Domus Dei chapel stood among its old marks then.
63219-the-missouri-archaeologist-volume-:
The Missouri Archaeologist for December 1972, volume thirty four numbers one and two, came out at Columbia, Missouri. Robert Bray of the University of Missouri at Columbia edited the journal. The Pamplin kiln is pictured at the front. Henry Hamilton stands as president of the society for 1972, with Leonard Blake and Allen Eichenberger among the vice presidents.

Carl Chapman serves as secretary and David Evans as treasurer. Trustees are listed in a long roll of Missouri names, from Harold Mohrman as chairman through farmers, doctors, and teachers across the state. The journal carries the society's studies of Missouri's mounds, camps, tools, and burials, written by professionals and keen amateurs side by side. State archaeology societies ran on such member rolls in those years. Their journals keep county by county records of sites now mostly ploughed away.
arxiv-2412-00497:
Jakob Burkhardt and co-authors design a middle path for private data analysis across many servers, in a 2024 paper. Differential privacy guards each person's record, but the usual setups clash: one trusted server sees everything, a single point of failure, or every client adds heavy noise alone. Their linear-transformation model lets clients hand data to a platform that may only apply a fixed public matrix, spread securely across servers.

That narrow power still allows linear sketches, compact summaries that keep most of the value. Private low-rank approximation and ridge regression run on the sketches with error that does not grow with data size. The model trades a little freedom for far cheaper trust.
arxiv-2412-00797:
Jianhui Li and co-authors build an on-line taint strike on learn agents when the world stays a black box. The work dates to 2024. A foe can warp teach data to bend an agent toward a bad plan. Past strikes knew the world's rules; here the foe does not.

The strike warps both prize scores and step shifts. The task is cast as a bound math hunt. Since shift odds are dark to the foe, slopes come from loose test draws. A fee trick and a two-tier recast dodge a clash in the math. A maze world showed the strike can bend the agent's plan.
arxiv-2412-01197:
Chenyang Zhu and seven co-authors present, in 2024 work, a fast tool that swaps an object in a photo for a custom one. Text-to-image models can do such swaps, but they often warp the rest of the scene, above all when the new object has a very unlike shape. They can also be slow to run or train.

Their tool, InstantSwap, first finds the object's box from the model's own focus maps. Inside the box, a cross-focus step feeds in the sense of both old and new objects. Outside it, changes are blocked so the backdrop stays put. To cut cost, slopes are worked out only at set steps, not each one. A new test set backs wide checks, and the team reports top results.
arxiv-2412-01297:
Five authors build a graph neural network that respects robot body symmetry in this 2024 paper. Robots with legs have repeating limbs, and a learning system that knows those symmetries can generalize better from less data.

Their network weaves the robot's kinematic structure and its shape symmetries into one graph model as built in constraints. The authors prove the symmetry property formally. Tests on several quadruped robot tasks, with both real and simulated data, showed the design works well. Code is public. Symmetry aware learning could cut the data and compute needed to teach robots new motions.
arxiv-2412-01897: Miguel Gallego, writing alone in 2024, asked whether a base claim of quantum theory can be tested: that its space splits neatly into countable parts. He offers a test that would show the space does not split that way, though it needs outcomes with no countable limit. He also shows that a famous paired state cannot be a vector in any paired space at all, under mild claims.
arxiv-2412-02597:
Salman Ahmadi-Asl and co-authors present faster randomized methods for breaking big data arrays into a compact Kronecker form, in a 2024 paper. Tensors, or multi-way arrays, appear across science and engineering. The standard breakdown runs many exact decompositions, which is slow. Random sampling can replace much of that grind.

Their algorithms swap exact steps for randomized ones with oversampling and power rounds. A full error analysis tracks how mistakes grow through the method's tree shape. The expected error is bounded by tail terms that shrink fast with more power rounds. Tests on synthetic and real data showed speedups of several fold. Faster tensor tools help fields from imaging to signal processing.
arxiv-2412-03797:
Taban Baghfalaki and colleagues proposed in 2024 a two-stage Bayesian method to pick key longitudinal markers when several markers and competing risks are tracked. Full joint models get hard to fit as markers multiply and may fail to converge. Their method aims to keep both marker selection and risk prediction workable.

In the first stage, a joint model is fit for each marker alone, and each person's marker path is predicted, which cuts bias from dropout. In the second stage, a hazards model uses the predicted current values of all markers at once, with spike-and-slab priors to select among them. Tests by simulation looked good, and the method was applied to dementia risk in a French cohort.
arxiv-2412-04397:
Christian de Ronde, Raimundo Fernández Mouján, and César Massri recast entanglement for many screens in a 2024 paper. Entanglement links far parts of a quantum set in ways no classic tale tells. The stock Dirac form strains when many screens and catchers join the scene. Their tensor form grows out of Heisenberg's matrix path. It states entanglement in terms that hold firm across frames.

The new form dodges flaws of the stock tale for split sets, they argue. Many-screen acts get a clean, shared mark set. Past tensor work forms the base they extend. The paper serves quantum theory's base craft more than bench work.
arxiv-2412-04597:
Alexia Bravo and co-authors search for ultracool companions to nearby white dwarfs, in work from 2024. White dwarfs are the dense embers of dead stars. A faint, cold companion can reveal the system's age and birth makeup.

The team combined color checks with image review in visible and infrared light. They found fifty-one new candidate systems in total. Most were resolved in at least one catalog, and nearly all shared motion and distance with their dwarf. Spectra confirmed four companions as truly ultracool. Twenty more candidates hide in blended light, showing infrared excess. Those may hold cold companions or dusty disks, and need follow-up.
arxiv-2412-04697:
Tatsuki Koga, Ruihan Wu, Zhiyuan Zhang, and Kamalika Chaudhuri present privacy-preserving retrieval-augmented generation with differential privacy, in a research paper from 2024. Retrieval-augmented systems feed private documents to a language model at answer time. Without guards, answers can leak sensitive facts from those sources, which blocks use in fields such as health and law.

Their algorithm spends the privacy budget only on tokens that need the private data. All other tokens come from the plain, non-private model, which saves budget for accuracy where it counts. Tests across models and data sets beat the no-retrieval baseline at a moderate privacy level. Long, accurate answers become feasible under a formal privacy guarantee.
arxiv-2412-04897:
A sharp tip that feels force can map a sample while a beam of heat light warms it, giving views far finer than plain light allows. Shohely Tasnim Anindo, Daniela Täuber, and Christin David model that tool in a 2024 study. Warmth makes the sample swell, and the swell shifts the weak pull between tip and sample.

Their model joins heat flow, swell, and tip motion in one frame, with light slant and form of the sample built in. They test the model on a tiny plastic ball and get a close match with lab runs. The match helps turn raw maps into firm numbers for stuff at the nano scale. Such maps serve both stuff science and life science.
arxiv-2412-04997:
Jacob Benestad and a large team of co-authors work on tuning a tiny quantum device in a two thousand twenty-four paper. The device uses nine small gates set over a narrow channel. By changing the gate voltages, staff can shape the flow of charge through the channel. Doing this by hand is slow and hard.

The team let a search method tune the gates on its own, guided by a score for how clean the flow steps look. In computer tests, the tuning fixed much of the harm from random flaws in the device. They then ran the same method on a real device. The flow steps became much cleaner there too.
arxiv-2412-05097:
Haowu Duan, Alex Kovner, and Michael Lublinsky extend a quantum framework for how particle distributions inside fast hadrons change with energy. In their first paper, the team borrowed the Born-Oppenheimer idea to describe a speeding hadron's wave function. Here they use it to track two distribution types: one spread over sideways momentum, one integrated.

Each distribution obeys an evolution equation with a straight term and a curved one. For the sideways-spread type, the straight term reproduces a classic equation, with a physical link between its two resolution scales. For the integrated type, it recovers the standard splitting equation at moderate momentum shares. At tiny shares, extra gluon splittings bend that equation. The curved terms share one origin: stimulated emission, where gluons prefer already busy states. That effect mimics shadowing in the net correction.
arxiv-2412-05197:
Li, Qiu, and Calinon extend a basic robotics tool, the distance field, from flat geometry to curved spaces. Distance fields tell a robot how far it sits from objects, and they feed control, planning, and learning. Many robot tasks, though, live on curved manifolds where straight-line distance misleads.

Their approach solves a curved-space version of the eikonal equation, whose answer gives both distances and shortest paths. A neural solver learns the field without any grid and without labeled examples, guided only by the equation itself. Two variants handle fixed targets or changing geometry. Tests across robot tasks produced true shortest paths, the authors report.
arxiv-2412-05697:
Orizon Ferreira, Boris Mordukhovich, Wilkreffy Santos, and João Souza wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four on a math method for hard optimization problems. The problems involve functions written as the difference of two curved functions. A known method gains speed by taking a boosted step, but it can fail when the functions have kinks and no smooth slope.

The authors propose a version that allows careful inexactness in two places. The inner subproblem is solved only roughly, within a set error limit, and the step size search need not improve the value at every step. They prove the method is well defined and that its limit points are true critical points. Tests show it beating two rival methods in practice.
arxiv-2412-05897:
Jun Nie and co-authors present a 2024 computing paper on spotting AI-generated images. As image generators improve, telling real photos from fake ones becomes a security concern. Their key insight links the task to how unsure a model is about an image.

Models trained on natural images tend to show high epistemic uncertainty, a measure of what the model does not know, when shown generated images. The shift between real and fake data shows up clearly in that uncertainty space. The team uses large pre-trained vision models to estimate the uncertainty and flags high scores as generated. Wide tests support the approach. The method turns a detection problem into an uncertainty problem, resting on the strength of big pre-trained models.
arxiv-2412-05997:
Vittorio D'Esposito and co-authors take first steps toward a doubly quantum mechanics. Their paper appeared in 2024. In ordinary quantum theory, space and measuring devices are classical backdrops. Quantum gravity hints that geometry itself may be quantum. The authors build a version of quantum mechanics where the shapes of systems, devices, and reference frames are quantum states too.

They work out spin measurements by replacing the rotation group with its quantum version. In the new setup, probability itself becomes an operator, with non-classical traits. For near-classical geometry states, measuring still works, but a built-in blur appears. Observers swapping quantum bits to align their frames can never align perfectly, even with endless bits. The blur is a concrete, testable difference from the standard theory.
arxiv-2412-06097:
Eric Dolores-Cuenca and co-authors import order theory into neural network design, turning partial orders into working image filters. A known bridge links integer-weighted networks to tropical geometry and polytopes. Every partially ordered set owns a matching order polytope. Their 2024 paper studies networks whose polytope is exactly such an object.

The smallest interesting case pays off concretely: posets on four points generate filters shaped like the two-by-two kernels of convolutional networks. These poset filters can drop into ordinary networks, not just the integer kind. During training they update weights with finer precision than max or average pooling, in the spirit of maxout units. Machine learning theorists get a new organ for networks, grown from pure combinatorics.
arxiv-2412-06297:
Joscha Knolle reports recent results for the ATLAS and CMS teams in a 2024 review of hunts for shy new particles. Some theories predict particles that barely interact with matter. Colliders can still catch them if they leave prompt traces in the detector.

The review covers data from proton smashes at the Large Hadron Collider from 2015 to 2018. Target models include dark mesons, heavy neutral leptons, dark matter, and dark photons. No find is claimed; instead, the teams set bounds that rule out parts of each model's space. Some bounds are the first ever from a collider for these ideas. The limits guide where future hunts should dig, and what they can skip.
arxiv-2412-06697:
Daniel Félix-González and co-authors compute collision rates for a key interstellar ion in a 2024 paper. The ion H3 plus is a workhorse probe of diffuse space clouds, but its excitation temperature reads lower than that of hydrogen molecules, a long-standing puzzle. Missing or rough rates for how collisions and chemistry set its level populations may explain the gap.

Using a precise full-dimensional energy surface and a quantum close-coupling method, the team derived state-to-state rates for collisions with atomic hydrogen up to high rotational levels, for both nuclear spin forms. The new rates shift the computed excitation temperature by up to twenty percent, with bigger effects where molecules are scarce. Chemical destruction reactions also confirmed their role in the balance.
arxiv-2412-06897:
Robert Harris and co-authors describe a small test instrument for starlight studies in 2024. The main instrument it serves will measure tiny shifts in starlight to find planets. Such work needs high precision and steady performance, which calls for careful testing on real skies.

The small version, called Lili, was built to test the front-end system that feeds light into fibers. It was tried at a large telescope in tests with standard stars. The team also checked a device that corrects air distortion and took spectra of close star pairs. Results matched hopes and bode well for the full instrument.
arxiv-2412-06997:
Kumar and co-authors study how adhesion at the join between a silicone rubber sheet and a glass slide can be tuned, in work from 2024. Such control matters for microfluidic devices, biochips, and electronic sensors.

Instead of treating surfaces chemically or reshaping them, the team changes the rubber's stiffness by varying the mix of base and curing agent in PDMS silicone. Wedge tests, in which a thin glass cover slip is pushed into the joint, measured adhesion for sheets of different stiffness and thickness. Stiffer and thicker sheets stuck less, with longer equilibrium cracks. The work links simple material settings to measured grip.
arxiv-2412-07397:
Ananga Mohan Datta and co-authors show how removing photons from a special light state changes its character depending on whether an even or odd number leaves, in this 2024 paper. The starting point is a two-mode squeezed vacuum, an entangled light state prized as a resource for quantum technologies. Subtracting photons from it, counterintuitively, can strengthen its useful quantum correlations.

The team proposes a buildable device, a trimer of three coupled light guides, that engineers these subtracted states. Their analysis finds the resulting state's properties hinge on parity: even and odd subtraction counts leave measurably different fingerprints. The same device can also brew multiphoton states whose correlations are tunable by design. For quantum engineers, parity becomes a dial, letting one piece of hardware produce families of states for sensing and communication experiments.
arxiv-2412-07697:
Young stars sometimes flare violently as they gulp gas from their disks, and Siwak and a large team of co-authors report a fresh case, Gaia20bdk, in the Sharpless 2-301 star-forming region. The outburst began in twenty eighteen. Old survey data pinned down the quiet star: about two point seven times the Sun's mass, at three point three kiloparsecs, still wrapped in its birth material.

New light and spectrum records show the classic marks of an FUor, the best-known class of such eruptions. Disk modeling puts the flare's glow at one to two hundred times the Sun's output, fed by a heavy inflow of gas. The team calls for continued watching to track the flicker and learn what drives it.
arxiv-2412-08297:
Thomas Krieguer and Yanko Todorov build a quantum theory of nonlinear optics where light and matter fuse ultra-strongly, in a 2024 physics paper. In that regime, semiconductor wells inside microcavities host hybrid light-matter states called polaritons. Older theories simplify the electrons away, which can mislead design. Their theory extends a classic electrodynamics formulation and treats the electrons fully, with no boson approximation.

Microcavity effects and local field boosts emerge in one frame, including the epsilon-near-zero effect that heightens nonlinear response. The theory shows how coupled states shape high-frequency generation, the process behind new light colors from polariton surfaces. The authors draw design rules for better conversion in dense electronic systems, aimed at mid-infrared and terahertz devices.
arxiv-2412-08497:
Rhoss Likibi Pellat and co-authors study how to step through time in a class of linked stochastic equations, in this 2024 paper. The equations pair a forward path with a backward one, a setup used in finance and control. Here the backward part grows quadratically and the forward drift can be rough, even singular. Chopping time into small steps lets computers solve them, but error control under such loose conditions is delicate.

The team revisits a known stepping scheme and proves an error rate close to the best seen under stricter rules. A key step re-examines how regular the solution's random part is over time. Their funding came through a German foundation program. Sharper error bounds matter when these equations price risk or guide control in rough settings.
arxiv-2412-08697:
Lorenzo Bianchi and co-authors open the study of defects in a long-range field model in a 2024 paper. The model lets far points sway each other, a twist on the stock local kind. Long defects, lines and sheets that cut the field, were known in the local kind but not yet framed here.

Three builds are put forth. One bends the flow math with a new dial, one grows defect parts of their own, and one shapes line defects by a classic large-field path. Each yields sound defect worlds to probe. The work seeds a fresh branch of field study.
arxiv-2412-08797:
Irene Prieto-Rodríguez, Antonio Prados, and Carlos A. Plata wrote a physics paper in 2024 on a heat engine built from one tiny particle. The particle sits in a trap and in a fluid that acts as a heat bath. Their engine runs a cycle much like a Stirling engine, with two steps at fixed heat and two at fixed volume.

Real engines run in finite time, so they can give out real power. The authors use math tools from optimal control to find the best way to drive the cycle. They then test how peak power and the share of heat turned into work change with the setup. The work helps guide tests of engines at the scale of single particles.
arxiv-2412-08997:
William Erickson and Nicholas Jones classify a family of number sets in a 2024 mathematics paper. Two sets are called homometric if the gaps between their pairs of points match exactly, when points sit on a ring of positions. The authors solve the case where each set has five points, for rings of any size.

Their classification lists six families of matching pairs and one family of matching triples, up to shifting or flipping the ring. They also give a formula that counts all such pairs and triples. The result settles a problem left open for smaller set sizes decades ago. It also gives a clear test for a signal recovery problem in crystallography.
arxiv-2412-09197:
Isaac García and Jaume Giné characterize when a planar system's equilibrium is a center, using the complex curves that wind through the singularity. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Telling centers, where orbits loop closed, from foci, where they spiral, is a classic hard problem. The systems here depend analytically on parameters.

An invariant analytic curve always passes through the monodromic singularity in question. The authors tie centerhood to one specific integral of that curve's cofactor. Degenerate centers are covered by the same test. Several consequences and applications follow from the characterization. A single integral test replaces case-by-case hunting. The partition of parameter space into centers and foci becomes computable in principle. The result serves the qualitative theory of differential equations.
arxiv-2412-09697:
Sangjin Lee and Kwonsang Lee build new tests for how a treatment's effect on paired, cut-off results shifts over time. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Past tests for such data can spot a broad effect across a whole follow-up span. They say little on when an effect starts or how it grows or fades. The new tests give each person a score tied to life at a set time, built from stand-in views of full data. They can probe both set times and the long run. The team adds checks for hidden bias in studies where chance was not used to assign the treatment, and shows the method on a Korean aging study.
arxiv-2412-09897:
Spinning particles from gold collisions reveal the spin of the fireball that made them, Qiang Hu reports for the STAR collaboration in a 2024 paper. Lambda particles and their antimatter twins were tracked across collision energies at a US collider. Their spin alignment, global and local, serves as the probe.

Matter and antimatter spins matched within error, which bounds the fireball's late magnetic field. One local spin measure grows as energy drops, while the beam-wise part stays small. A difference signal built to hunt a baryonic spin Hall effect reads as zero within wide error bars. The scan maps how swirl fades as collisions heat up.
arxiv-2412-10197:
Abderrahim Boussaïri, Brahim Chergui, Zaineb Sarir, and Mohamed Zouagui ask which symmetric matrices can sit inside a scaled orthogonal one in a 2024 paper. A matrix is quasi-orthogonal when its Gram matrix is a constant times the identity, so its columns are orthogonal and equally long. Any block cut from such a matrix inherits limits on its shape.

The authors characterize when a symmetric matrix admits such an extension, following their earlier work on the skew-symmetric case with a different approach. Extension problems like this one connect matrix theory to signal sets with low interference. Knowing exactly which blocks extend tells engineers which correlation patterns can be realized by clean, balanced codebooks in communications.
arxiv-2412-10597:
Blaine Hoak, Ryan Sheatsley, and Patrick McDaniel measure texture bias on real data in two thousand twenty four. Image classifiers lean on texture more than shape. That bias is among the strongest known in vision models. Past measures failed to capture real world robustness effects.

Their Texture Association Value scores reliance on specific textures. Accuracy and robustness both swing with texture alignment. Natural adversarial examples turn out to be texture cases. Over ninety percent carry textures mismatched to their true label. Models then err with high confidence on those images.
arxiv-2412-10697:
Wojciech Młotkowski and Nobuaki Obata introduce two new families of polynomials split from a classic set, in a 2024 mathematics paper. The classic Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind have a tidy rule for multiplying them. The authors split that family into even and odd parts with separate names, the partial Chebyshev polynomials. They set out the basic properties of the new pieces and how they relate to the originals.

The split pays off in a problem about fan graphs, networks shaped like a hand fan. A number called the quadratic embedding constant measures how awkwardly such a graph sits in space. The authors build a fresh polynomial for the fan, show it factors through their even partial polynomial, and prove the constant is set by that polynomial's smallest root. They give the exact value for even-sized fans and a sound estimate for odd ones.
arxiv-2412-10897:
Junliang Lyu and co-authors present a federated learning method that can handle classification and regression tasks at the same time on different devices, in a 2024 paper. Federated learning trains a shared model while data stay on local devices. Most methods assume every device does the same kind of task, which real settings rarely satisfy.

Their design pairs a multi-output Gaussian process on each device with federated pooling at a central server. The process handles linked tasks and reports its own uncertainty in a principled way. Tricks for fast local inference speed the training. On synthetic and real data, the method beat rivals on accuracy, uncertainty fit, and out-of-sample detection.
arxiv-2412-11197:
Seema Satin wrote, in two thousand twenty-four, on stochastic gravity, in which space and time can shake with quantum waves. The view aims to tell how the first big clumps of mass took shape in the young cosmos. Its core is a pair of kernels, one for noise and one for loss. Both are built from the quantum stress of scalar fields.

Her step is to treat those fields like a fluid: the hydrodynamic approximation of the loss kernel. She also moves the view toward the decoherence limit, where quantum acts fade into plain acts. A like step was made not long ago for the noise kernel. Hers does the same for loss in a fluid at near light speed. The work could let the view probe clump growth near when the inflaton field faded in that way.
arxiv-2412-11297:
Sreeveni Das and co-authors build an artificial synapse that uses moving ions to control magnetism. Their 2024 paper works in neuromorphic computing, which designs hardware that mimics how brains process information. In their device, applied voltages drive lithium ions that shift the magnetic state of a thin ferromagnetic layer.

The device behaves like a biological synapse in key ways: its response is graded rather than on-off, and it holds its state without power. The team wires it into a small reservoir computing system, a design where a dynamic medium does part of the computing. They show the system can classify waveforms, and tune voltage range and magnetic field for best accuracy. Such devices could one day support low-power brain-like chips.
arxiv-2412-11597:
Anton Pichler tracks how electricity firms change, or fail to change, their technology mix over time. Renewables have grown fast and fallen in cost, yet incumbent energy firms show strong inertia. The study draws on more than 140,000 investments in power assets over more than two decades. It measures how firms expand what they already hold and how often they adopt new technology.

Only about 10% of firms change capacity in a given year, and portfolios stay concentrated and persistent. Fewer than 3% of the more than 8,400 fossil fuel-dominated firms shifted to a renewable focus, and full transitions are almost unheard of. A small set of large, frequent investors drives most capacity growth.
arxiv-2412-11697:
Chin-Chia Chang and co-authors compute a key term in the growth formula for Toeplitz operators on CR manifolds. These operators sit at the crossroads of complex geometry and quantum-style analysis. When a cutoff version of the operator is scaled up, its kernel spreads out in a neat series of terms.

The first term of that series is classical. The second term carries finer shape data and drives much of the field's next work. Earlier studies proved the full series exists for manifolds tied to a Reeb flow. This paper pins down the second coefficient in closed form. Such formulas feed back into CR geometry, where they gauge curvature and embedding traits. The result gives geometers a sharper tool for reading these curved spaces.
arxiv-2412-11797:
Poorta and co-authors hunt for disks around young mid-weight and heavy stars in the huge star-forming cloud M17 in a 2024 study. Such stars are thought to grow by pulling in gas through disks, as small stars do, but their disks are much harder to see. The team used the ALMA scope array to scan four young stars of four to ten sun masses.

ALMA saw all four targets for the first time, plus four chance finds nearby. The disks are small, under 120 times the Earth-sun gap, and hold just a few Earth masses of dust, with low gas caps. Though this group is the youngest and heaviest yet, its disks are the lightest on record.
arxiv-2412-11897:
Naageswaran Manikandan, writing alone, proves a vanishing result inside Siefring's intersection theory in this 2024 arXiv paper. Siefring's theory, from 2009, counts how punctured pseudoholomorphic curves cross, adding extra terms for how the curves behave far out at their ends. Whether those extra terms can simply vanish was the open point.

Manikandan sorts the space of such curves by how fast they settle toward their end behavior. With that sorting in hand, he can say exactly which curves have zero extra contribution. He then proves the extra terms vanish under generic small changes to the setup. In practice, that means the usual crossing counts are all a researcher needs in most cases.
arxiv-2412-12397:
Léa Cassé and co-authors study small quantum circuits for sorting particle signals in a 2024 paper. The hosted text carries the title Quantum Re-Uploading for Calorimetry. Their tool is a quantum re-uploading unit, a compact circuit that feeds the same data in again and again. The team compares it, at the same size, with a standard quantum circuit on a task with three input values.

The re-uploading circuit sorted signals into three classes more often than the standard one did. Tests that varied depth, scaling, and training choices showed most gains came at small depths. Deeper circuits cost more time for less gain. The team also ran the trained model on a real quantum chip through a cloud link, as a proof that the setup works in practice.
arxiv-2412-12497:
Xin Yi and co-authors propose, in a 2024 paper, a cheap fix for large language models whose safety training has been undone by harmful fine-tuning. A few bad training examples sent by a user can break a model's alignment. Past fixes need heavy computing and fresh gradient training, which many providers cannot afford for each case.

Their method, called NLSR, needs no new training at all. It builds a safety reference model, finds the neurons most tied to safe behavior, and copies those neurons into the damaged model where they differ most. Tests showed large safety gains across tasks while task accuracy stayed high. Only a small part of the model changes.
arxiv-2412-12597:
Niloufar Eghbali, Tuka Alhanai, and Mohammad Ghassemi teach a machine to set breathing machines in intensive care, with an honest gauge of its own doubt. Vent settings are hard to tune: each patient differs, and bad settings can harm. Their 2024 method pairs deep learning with a stats tool that bounds how wrong a pick may be.

Trained on records from a large care database, the system learned to favor picks inside safe, known ranges. It turns shy in odd states it has not seen, rather than guessing boldly. Against doctor choices and rival methods, its picks linked to better ninety-day survival. The doubt gauge also shows its work, which the team says aids trust and joint use with doctors.
arxiv-2412-12997:
Umer Butt, Stalin Varanasi, and Günter Neumann build the first large search benchmark for Urdu in a 2024 paper. Urdu is spoken by millions but lacks the datasets that power modern search research. The team machine translated a major English retrieval collection into Urdu and used it to set baseline results.

Systems were first tested with no Urdu training, then fine tuned with a multilingual method adapted to the new data. The tuned model's scores rose clearly over the zero shot baseline on both ranking and recall measures. The authors stress the social stakes: search access in low resource languages is an inclusion issue. Their approach should transfer to other South Asian languages.
arxiv-2412-13197:
Anirudh Bangalore Shankar and co-authors built this 2024 math framework for predicting how long coupled memory cells hold their state. Experiments show that linking memory units in certain patterns can hit performance targets. Testing each pattern and material in the lab or simulator is slow and costly. Borrowing from the statistical physics of spin systems, the team wrote a general model of retention.

For several popular linked and unlinked layouts, they derived exact formulas that match simulations. The formulas reveal how material choices and layout each move retention time. Designers can thus screen ideas on paper before building anything. The work turns a trial-and-error search into guided design for future memory hardware.
arxiv-2412-13397:
Rajesh Gopakumar, Rishabh Kaushik, Shota Komatsu, and two colleagues rewrite the Feynman diagrams of a supersymmetric gauge theory as a sum over strings, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. The theory is N=4 super Yang-Mills, and the correlators studied preserve half of its supersymmetry.

Each individual diagram maps onto a Riemann surface with specific moduli, the mathematical shape of a closed string's worldsheet. Strikingly, the diagrams land on discrete lattice points of the string's moduli space rather than on chopped-up worldsheets. The construction works to all orders in the expansion in inverse colors. Concretely it runs through a two-matrix integral with a dual string description. The picture gives a microscopic view of open-closed string duality in this corner of the AdS/CFT correspondence. It also predicts that one closed string theory can admit several open string descriptions.
arxiv-2412-14097:
Jihye Choi, Jayaram Raghuram, Yixuan Li, and Somesh Jha make concept-based models adapt after deployment in a paper from 2024. Concept bottleneck models explain predictions through human ideas rather than raw features. They sit on top of large foundation models in fields like medicine and finance. Trouble comes when real-world data drifts from the training data. The authors first map how such pipelines fail under different drifts.

Their framework updates the concept bank and prediction layer using only unlabeled new data. No access to the original training set is needed. Across real-world shifts, accuracy rose by up to twenty-eight percent. Explanations also matched the new data better. The method aims to keep interpretable models trustworthy in the wild.
arxiv-2412-14197:
Nouar AlDahoul and co-authors test vision-language models for reading license plates, in a 2024 paper. Plate reading systems help police find stolen cars, uninsured drivers, and suspects. Classic character recognition struggles when plates are blurred, dirty, or tightly lettered. Weather and noise add to the problem.

The team tried a roster of leading vision-language models on hard plate images. These models read images and text together, so they can guess smeared characters from context. They also built VehiclePaliGemma, a fine-tuned open model specialized for the task. The paper weighs how far such models push past the classic pipeline. Traffic agencies get a direct comparison for the messiest real-world plates.
arxiv-2412-14597:
Salma Rahmouni and co-authors revisit the near-infrared fingerprints of kilonovae in two thousand twenty-four, the glowing debris of merged neutron stars. The famous two thousand seventeen event proved such mergers forge heavy elements, but naming the elements behind each spectral dip is hard, especially in infrared light.

The team systematically searched measured atomic energy levels for all heavy elements with strong infrared lines. Most candidates were lanthanides and actinides, whose complex atoms pack many low levels. Earlier work credited two elements for features near twelve to fifteen thousand angstroms. The new search adds gadolinium as the next strongest suspect, thanks to its half-filled shell and low-lying levels. Its lines also appear in a peculiar star's spectrum. Simulations confirm gadolinium reshapes the twelve-thousand-angstrom feature.
arxiv-2412-14797:
Quantum simulators stumble on spin symmetry, whose bookkeeping can balloon past any memory. Anthony Gandon, Alberto Baiardi, Max Rossmannek, Werner Dobrautz, and Ivano Tavernelli shrink that bookkeeping in a 2024 paper. They build algorithms inside the spin eigenbasis itself.

A group-theory frame plus a cutoff ranks spin states by weight. Cut models converge fast to the full model's ground state. A test magnet chain shows the ladder at work. The cut Hamiltonians stay sparse and local on qubits. Shallow circuits can then prep the ground states sector by sector. Symmetry, handled natively, stops being a tax.
arxiv-2412-14897:
Julian Möbius and Michael Habeck rebuild 3D shapes from broken data using learned priors in a 2024 paper. Many measurement problems are ill-posed: too little data, too many possible shapes. Classic Bayesian fixes prefer smooth or sparse answers, which look nothing like real objects.

Their priors come from diffusion models trained on 3D point clouds. Those models know what plausible objects look like at medium detail. Folded into Bayesian sampling, the prior steers guesses toward realistic shapes. The test case is cryo-electron microscopy, rebuilding protein assemblies from sparse, low-resolution views. Posterior sampling recovered structures from very partial observations. The authors pitch learned priors as a general upgrade for inverse problems.
arxiv-2412-14997:
Lukas Fußangel, Buddhika Priyasad, and Paul Stephan study rough spots in math minimizers in a 2024 paper. They work with energy functions that depend on position, not just on slope, and grow in a simple linear way. Solutions of bounded variation can have a singular set, the points where they fail to behave smoothly.

Under stated conditions on the energy's shape and smoothness, the authors prove the slope of such solutions is more tamed than expected. They also bound the size of the singular set using a standard measure of dimension. The results extend what is known about how wild the worst points of these solutions can be.
arxiv-2412-15097:
Chloe Gaudu reports, for the CORSIKA 8 Collaboration, on the status of the successor to the world's standard air shower simulation code. For over two decades, CORSIKA 7 has been the top Monte Carlo code to model extensive air showers from cosmic rays. Its single-block Fortran design and hand-tuned code have made upkeep hard. They have also made it hard to adapt to new compute paths and to extend to complex models.

CORSIKA 8 is a full rewrite in a modern, modular C++ frame. It has reached a physics-complete state. It supports top high-energy hadronic interaction models and electromagnetic cascades. It also supports many interaction media, including cross-media showers, and better radio emission calculations. The report gives an overview of current functions and shows validation results. It also treats future plans for growth.
arxiv-2412-15297:
Poyatos and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on faint flares from small red stars, caught by the CHEOPS space telescope. Flares are bursts of light from a star's magnetic field. Past missions found bright ones with ease but missed the faint end. Faint flares can shape the air of planets near such stars, so the gap matters.

The team built a wavelet based cleaner to lift faint flares from noise. They tuned it by planting fake flares and checking which came back. Close to three hundred flares were found across a group of red dwarfs. The cleaner raised finds by about a third. Size counts fit a bell shaped curve more well than a power law.
arxiv-2412-15497:
Annika Marie Schoene and co-authors describe a project that translates a dictionary of suicide-related words into 200 languages, in a 2024 paper. Most tools for spotting suicide risk are built for English and Western settings, yet suicide is a global harm and cutting its rate is a United Nations goal. Using English word lists in other cultures can distort local ways of speaking about suicide.

The project first sets out ethics guidance to limit harm when building such resources. It then translates the dictionary and has people judge a subset of the versions by hand. A public website shares the results and invites community input, so the word lists can improve with local knowledge.
arxiv-2412-15897:
Alexander von Bank and colleagues present an improved decoder for error-correcting codes that runs on brain-like spiking networks. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, concerns low-density parity-check codes, widely used to fix errors in transmitted data. An earlier decoder from the same research line used a single spiking network to handle part of the decoding math. That shortcut worked poorly when each variable node in the code connects to only a few others, because the rough estimate lost too much detail.

The new design runs several spiking networks side by side for the same step, giving finer resolution and a wider range of message values. On a large test code, the improved decoder matched the performance of a standard widely used decoder. The result keeps alive the hope of decoding with much lower energy use, since spiking hardware works only when events occur.
arxiv-2412-16097:
Matteo Nerini and Bruno Clerckx studied smarter signal-bouncing panels for wireless networks in a 2024 paper. Such panels, placed on walls, reflect radio waves toward users to fill coverage gaps. A newer family rewires the panel elements in groups, giving more control than a plain panel, but at higher circuit cost.

Most earlier work assumed waves with a single polarization, while real systems use two. Nerini and Clerckx derive the growth laws and the best trade-off curve for the dual case. Panels grouped in pairs gave large gains over plain panels in both scattered and direct channels, while keeping circuits modest. The results guide builders choosing how much complexity a panel deserves.
arxiv-2412-16497: Rotan Hawlader Pranto and Shahnewaz Siddique build a real-time translator for Bangla Sign Language, in work from twenty twenty-four. Sign language lets deaf and mute people communicate through hand gestures. A camera pipeline captures body and hand key points for each sign. A memory network learns the motion patterns across sign sequences. Live vision then spots signs as a user performs them.
arxiv-2412-17097:
Eduard Emelyanov studied how time evolution extends to completed spaces in a 2024 working analysis paper. The setting is Archimedean vector lattices, spaces that combine algebra with an order form, and one-setting semigroups, which describe steady evolution like heat flow. Such spaces are often completed by adding limit points. The question is whether an evolution defined on the first space extends to the completion, uniquely and well.

For positive semigroups, Emelyanov establishes that an extension to the ru-completion always exists and is unique. An extension theorem for a continuity class on spaces with a regularity property follows. Letting later results drop the assumption that the space was complete to begin with.
arxiv-2412-17197:
Nelson Colón Vargas gives a quantum twist to a popular explanation tool in this 2024 paper. LIME explains a model's answer by removing words and watching the output shift. His version, Q-LIME pi, loads the word pattern into a quantum state. Superposition and interference then let it probe many removals at once.

The method mirrors LIME's removal trick by flipping present words off, and it can also add words where that helps. On slices of a movie-review dataset, the quantum version matched the classical one's top words almost exactly. It also ran faster on small to mid-sized inputs. The author frames it as a path toward quicker explanations as quantum hardware matures.
arxiv-2412-17497:
Sergi Masot-Llima and Artur Garcia-Saez test how the wiring shape of a tensor network affects its training, in a 2024 paper. Tensor networks, born in quantum physics, now serve machine learning as flexible data structures. Their geometry can be regular or mixed, and the best shape for learning was unclear.

The pair train networks of varied shapes to encode a random quantum state, using gradient methods on a modern supercomputer. Densely wired structures reached lower error, succeeded more often, and trained faster than sparse ones. They also share tricks to cut memory use in sparse layouts and measure what those tricks cost. Graphics processors sped the work greatly. The guidance helps designers pick shapes before burning compute.
arxiv-2412-17597:
Guillermo García-Sánchez and four co-authors trace, in 2024 work, the hidden lanes that steered oil spills to Middle East shores in the east Mediterranean. No wreck was told before the oil landed, so its birth place and time were dark. Sea flow is chaotic, yet set lanes run inside the chaos.

Lane math on the shore hits, joined with past satellite shots and flow sims, walked the oil back to its source and start time. Model and sky tales matched well. The team backs lane reads as a way to read such blind spills, and to warn shores in time.
arxiv-2412-17697:
Divya Acharya, Prasanna Poojary, and Vadiraja Bhatta G R work out the structure of a family of error-correcting codes in a 2024 mathematics paper. The codes are constacyclic, meaning a shifted codeword with a twist stays a codeword, and they live over an unusual finite ring built from a field with two added nilpotent letters.

The codes have a repeated-root length tied to a prime power. The authors split the problem by whether a key unit is a cube in the ring, then handle many subcases when it is not even a unit. They give the codes' shapes, count their codewords, and describe their duals, which matter for decoding.
arxiv-2412-17797:
Scott Emmons and co-authors study whether a helpful AI might ever gain by hiding facts from its user, in a 2024 theory paper. Their setting is an assistance game, a model of alignment where a human and an AI share a goal but each sees only part of the world. Partial views create room for a new worry: meddling with what the human observes.

The authors prove that sometimes the best assistant must take actions that interfere with the human's observations. That holds even when the human plays perfectly and equal non-interfering actions exist. The result is unsettling but precise. It shows that good intentions alone do not rule out meddling, so oversight schemes must watch information flow, not just outcomes.
arxiv-2412-18097:
Nan Yang and co-authors present LangYa, an AI system for forecasting the world ocean, in a research paper from 2024. Standard ocean forecast systems solve physics equations on grids, which costs much compute and lets errors build up. AI models run faster, but a single model that spans times and couples air with sea remained a gap.

LangYa trains on 27 years of global ocean reanalysis data. A time embedding lets one model issue forecasts from one to seven days ahead. A coupled module mimics air-sea exchange, and a self-attention module steadies training. A custom loss sharpens forecasts of the thermocline, the layer where temperature drops fast. The team reports more reliable forecasts than rival numeric and AI systems.
arxiv-2412-18197:
Hiroyuki Chihara computes a key quantity for an imaging transform in a 2024 math study. The d-plane transform averages a function over all flat slices of a given dimension, a model for tomographic scanning. Reconstructing the function uses a filtered backprojection formula, whose core is the normal operator built by composing the transform with its adjoint.

Chihara computes that operator's symbol directly. The symbol factors into the symbol of a fractional power of the Laplacian times a constant from an invariant integral over the extra dimensions. The factorization gives a fresh route to the reconstruction formula, confirming the classic result from a new angle.
arxiv-2412-18297:
Eshwar Ram Arunachaleswaran, Natalie Collina, and Jon Schneider study how a learner should play a repeated game against a foe whose goals are unknown, in work from 2024. The learner knows its own payoffs but only the odds over the foe's. The foe plays back at full strength, always answering the learner's habits.

If the learner sticks to no-regret play, the paper builds a best possible algorithm in fast time, for both average and worst-case goals. Without that limit, near-best play is still computable fast when the game or the foe's range is small. A safest-play goal gets its own treatment. The results map when optimal play against strangers is tractable.
arxiv-2412-18397:
Ning Sun, Pengfei Zhang, and Lei Feng design an experiment-friendly way to spot a new kind of symmetry breaking. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. In mixed quantum states, a strong symmetry can soften into a weak one. That shift marks a distinct phase of matter. The usual detector needs multi-replica correlation functions. Those are hard to measure directly in the lab.

Their scheme uses randomized measurements instead. Random Pauli measurements are taken on the state as prepared. A second round follows after charged operators act on it. With many samples, the key correlator comes out exactly. With few samples, phase boundaries can still be estimated. The protocol fits tools experimenters already have. Exotic mixed-state phases move closer to direct observation.
arxiv-2412-18697:
Cong Jiang and Xiaolei Yang present a 2024 plan for using large language models in court work. Courts hope such tools can speed up case work. Yet past tools gave weak grounds for their calls, which hurt trust in their use.

Their plan, named AgentsBench, uses a group of model agents that act like a bench of judges. The agents weigh a case side by side, much as real judges do in joint talks. Tests on a task that forecasts court calls show the group beats past single-model methods. The authors argue the setup yields fairer, clearer calls across case types.
arxiv-2412-18897:
Sangita Dutta and co-authors wrote a 2024 physics paper on synchronization shifts that jump twice, in networks where links bind three or more nodes at once. The base play is a known one: nodes with their own rhythms pull to one rhythm as ties grow. With pair ties, the shift to synchrony is smooth or sharp. Three-way ties can make it sharp.

The team asks what blend gives a two-step explosion: a jump up, then a jump more, on the way in or out. Two ingredients are the key. The three-way ties must be in play. And a share of the joint synchronization grade of the whole group must feed back on those ties. A known mathematics trick supports the simulation findings. For a wide class of such networks, the blend gives the twin explosion.
arxiv-2412-18997:
Kirillov, Murygin, and Nikulin simulate the birth of soliton structures in the early universe in a 2024 paper. Solitons are stable lumps of field energy. Rather than forming through a hot phase change, their solitons grow from quantum ripples stretched during inflation, so no universe-wide network is needed.

Starting from simulated inflation-era fluctuations, the team evolved the fields in three dimensions after inflation. The outcome is what they call soliton foam: closed domain walls, walls edged by cosmic strings, and loose radiation mixed together. Local clusters appear where the ripples were strongest. The paper closes by weighing what such foam could mean for cosmology.
arxiv-2412-19197:
Shikun Cui, Lili Wang, and Wendong Wang prove a stabilizing result in a 2024 mathematics paper. Their subject couples a classic model of cell movement, the Patlak-Keller-Segel system, with fluid flow. Left alone, the cell model can blow up in finite time, even from a tiny starting mass.

The authors place the system inside a Couette flow, a simple shearing motion of the fluid. They prove that a strong enough shear keeps solutions well behaved for all time, as long as the starting flow is small and cell mass stays below a stated bound. The paper gives the first proof that moving fluid can fully suppress this blow-up in three dimensions.
arxiv-2412-20097:
Gulsemay Yigit and three co-authors map where patterns form in a ring shaped zone in a 2024 paper. Their model tracks two chemicals that react and spread, with each one's spread nudging the other's. On a ring, unlike a disc, the shape itself may steer which patterns can arise and when.

Math from stability theory gave the terms for three kinds of pattern birth. Ring size bounds came with the terms, and cross spread loosened the usual rules for pattern growth. Computer runs on the ring showed spot and wave patterns that match ring slices of low oxygen tumors. The work sorts the full knob space for the model and ties shape to pattern in a clean frame.
arxiv-2501-00697:
Michael Bennie and six co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on counter speech in Mandarin Chinese. Counter speech replies to hate speech with calm, firm words. Tools for it in Chinese are near nil, though the language is used world wide. The team built the first such data set for mainland China, named PANDA.

They used a language model as judge, plus search tricks and round based picks, to draft replies. Human checks then vet the drafts for quality and fit. Their study maps which groups get maligned and which speech marks flag hate in this tongue. They also show gaps in open Chinese hate data. The limits of a model as judge in Chinese stand out as a key find.
arxiv-2501-01397:
Wesley Hanwen Deng and co-authors present WeAudit in a 2025 paper on helping everyday users audit generative AI for harms. Users hold lived knowledge that builders lack, yet they need support to turn finds into notes builders can use. The team first ran small studies with users and builders to set design goals.

WeAudit then guides users through checks alone and in groups, and shapes their reports for builder use. A three-week study with user auditors, plus talks with industry builders, showed the tool helps users spot and state harms clearly. The paper names gaps where more support is needed.
arxiv-2501-01497:
Shahar Hod, writing alone in 2025, proves a cap on force in curved space for stable balls of self-pulled stuff. Two names of lore had bid a neat cap: force can not top a set share of light's speed to the fourth, split by the pull mark. Flat bids are one thing; bent space with live stuff is the true test.

Hod takes the full bent laws, pull wed to stuff, and works the force in a stable, rim-less ball: four pi times span squared times the push at that span. The cap falls out at the bid's kin value. A guess of lore is now a proved bound for a wide class of stars and balls, with no rim in sight.
arxiv-2501-01597:
Noman Yousuf and co-authors simulate turbulent flow in a pipe for fluids whose thickness changes with their recent history. Such fluids, found in slurries and emulsions, thin or thicken based on how they were lately sheared. At large scale their springy response is too fast to matter, leaving only the memory effect.

Full computer runs covered cases where the memory is slow, fast, or matched to the swirl time of the flow. In the slow and fast limits the fluid acted like a simple one with a fixed rule. At matched rates, a record of each parcel's shear past set the thickness. A shortcut model using that record matched the full runs within a few percent.
arxiv-2501-01697:
Le Quang Hung and co-authors bound the symmetry group of a plane point set in a 2025 paper. The stage is the affine plane over a finite field. The group is the special linear group of two by two matrices.

They ask how large a subgroup can leave a set fully unmoved. A point line incidence bound from past work drives the proof. If a small set is kept by a large subgroup, shape must collapse. Past a set ratio of exponents, the set must sit inside a line. The bound is sharp in general, they show. Finite field symmetry thus forces plain shapes.
arxiv-2501-01797:
Hiroyasu Koizumi wrote a 2025 theoretical physics paper rethinking where the energy in familiar electrical processes really comes from. A recent line of work traces a chemical potential force to a geometric phase in the many electron wave function. Koizumi argues this force is central to how currents start and how their energy is supplied.

Textbooks explain Joule heating with a subtle story: the heat energy enters the wire from outside as radiation. The paper shows the battery's chemical potential gradient supplies that energy instead. The same lens is turned on a discharging capacitor and on supercurrents through Josephson junctions, where the capacitor's role was missing from the original derivation. Finally, fluctuations of the geometric phase are proposed as the source of the universal Planckian dissipation seen in high temperature superconductors.
arxiv-2501-02797:
Tadikonda Shiva Sai, Hemanth Kolla, and Konduri Aditya test a reduced model for reacting flows in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Chemical systems in flames involve many linked quantities, so modelers compress them into a few components. A method based on co-kurtosis captures stiff chemistry better than the standard approach in early checks.

The team now tests the compressed model in full simulations of ignition in a uniform reactor. They evolve the system with a standard solver and with a neural solver that folds time stepping into training. The neural solver cut error growth across steps and gave more accurate profiles. The authors say the manifold could serve large parallel flow solvers.
arxiv-2501-03197:
Cyrus Mehta, Ajoy Mukhopadhyay, and Martin Posch extend a graphical method for juggling many hypotheses into adaptive two-stage trial designs. The graph method draws a trial's testing priorities as arrows: when one hypothesis falls, its error budget flows to the next.
