Adaptive designs complicate the picture, since treatments may be dropped, sample sizes re-estimated, and even the hierarchy revised after stage one. Family-wise error must survive all that freedom.

Two preservation strategies compete: combining p-values across stages, and conditioning the stage-two error rate on stage one. The paper lays out each method's statistical machinery. A large simulation experiment then compares their operating characteristics head to head. Multi-arm, multi-endpoint trials, common in modern drug development, are the beneficiaries. Adaptivity without error control is just optimism; this work prices it honestly.
arxiv-2501-03397:
Xuyang Wang and co-authors paint surface skins for 3D mesh models in a fresh way. Most past tools paint flat views of a model first, then bake those views onto the mesh. Seams, hid faces, and bake flaws creep in at that step. Their 2025 method, DoubleDiffusion, grows the skin right on the mesh face, with no flat step in between.

Heat spread gives the trick: warmth flows on a mesh face in a smooth way that ignores how the wire frame is laid out. That flow is set as the spread rule inside a learned paint tool. Side by side with past tools, the new path paints skins at a much faster pace. The team frames mesh-born skin as the fix for seam and shade flaws.
arxiv-2501-04797: Karlo Lelas and Nikola Poljak took a fresh look at a classic setup in 2025: a driven spring system that loses energy as it moves. They derived an exact formula for the drive rate at which the mean energy over time peaks. That rate is well matched by a simple mean of two known peak rates, one for swing size and one for speed. They argue the swing-size peak also serves well as the energy peak.
arxiv-2501-04897:
Seyed Amir Bidaki and co-authors give the first full review of online continual learning in the field today. That field trains models on live data streams. Models must learn new tasks fast yet not forget old ones, a hard trade off.

The review sorts many past methods, pulls out their parts and tasks, and lists test sets for images, objects, and mixed media. Key pains are high compute cost and poor fit to tight devices. The authors urge work on self taught learning, smarter memory, and robust tools for noisy real world use.
arxiv-2501-04997:
Sara Sameer and co-authors proposed GiNet in 2025, a model for predicting how much capacity a battery has left. Good capacity estimates are central to battery management, and they must be drawn from past readings of how the battery behaved. Batteries act in complex ways over both short and long spans.

GiNet blends a gated recurrent design with an Informer network to capture both stepwise patterns and long-range links. On a public data set, it predicted capacity in future slots without being told past capacity values. Its error was low, and it beat the plain Informer model by a wide margin on average. The authors stress that tailoring the model to battery knowledge drove the gain.
arxiv-2501-05097:
Van Thien Nguyen, William Guicquero, and Gilles Sicard build a tiny neural encoder chip in a 2025 paper. Specialized circuits bring neural inference to edge devices, but each chip usually serves one task. The authors show one application-specific design can handle two tasks of different levels, image classification and patch-based compression, with very limited hardware.

The key component is a reconfigurable encoder using mixed precision, three, two, or one bit, for weights and activations. Careful quantization keeps accuracy while shrinking the memory budget to about one megabit. Multi-task edge chips lower cost for cameras and sensors.
arxiv-2501-05197:
Drago Plečko and a team of co-authors build a causal frame for health equity in twenty twenty-five. Big data now lets researchers trace why health outcomes differ between groups. Their framework analyzes disparities with causal inference rather than plain statistics. They apply it to intensive care outcomes by race and ethnicity.

Cases come from Australia, comparing Indigenous and non-Indigenous patients, and from the United States. There, African-American and White patients are compared. The authors show common statistical measures of inequity are not enough. Instead, a disparity should be attributed to the mechanisms that generate it. Among their findings, minority patients tended to be younger at admission with worse chronic health. Readers get a method for moving from gap-watching to cause-finding.
arxiv-2501-05297:
Kuzucan and co-authors ask how a planet's air shifts the habitable zone and whether microbes could grow at its hot edge. The habitable zone marks where liquid water can persist on a surface. Air makeup moves those edges, and water alone does not promise life. The team used a 3D climate model for planets near the inner edge. They refined that edge for hydrogen-rich and carbon dioxide air for the first time.

In parallel, lab tests grew E. coli under the modeled conditions. Growth and survival were tracked across the settings. Pairing climate math with live microbes grounds habitability claims. The study tests more than where water stays liquid.
arxiv-2501-05597:
The Casimir force pulls two uncharged plates together from empty-space fluctuations, and changing the rules of gravity changes the force. Byron Droguett and Claudio Bórquez compute that force in 2025 inside Hořava-Lifshitz gravity, with rough plates and a magnetic field in play.

A charged scalar field with an uneven ticking of time and space lives between the plates. To handle roughness, the authors mathematically flatten the plates and treat what remains as a small disturbance, then extract the spectrum with perturbation theory and tame the infinities with the zeta-function method. Their example uses plates with periodic edges. The work shows how exotic gravity, surface texture, and magnetism would each leave fingerprints on a tabletop force.
arxiv-2501-05697:
Fusheng Deng, Gang Huang, and Xiangsen Qin estimate the Green kernel for a twisted geometric operator on domains with boundary. Their 2025 paper studies the Dolbeault Laplacian acting on forms that take values in a bundle, over a region inside a Kähler manifold. Such kernels are the building blocks for solving the associated equations.

The authors prove global bounds that hold uniformly up to the boundary, including versions with one or two boundary factors. They also bound the kernel's derivatives in both natural directions. From these bounds flow Sobolev-style inequalities that keep boundary terms visible. In the lowest dimension the first-order bound pays a logarithmic price. In top degree they gain quantitative solvability without assuming the domain bulges the usual way.
arxiv-2501-05997:
Sanjay Kumar and co-authors study dirty camera lenses on self-driving cars in a 2025 paper. Dirt, dust, rain, and fog can block car cameras and harm tasks such as spotting objects and lanes. The team asks how such blocks spread when camera views are merged into a bird's-eye view. They use the nuScenes data set for the test.

To fight the loss, they add lidar and radar data to the camera feed. That sensor mix raised the accuracy and strength of vehicle segmentation in their tests. The work fills a gap on how camera blocks affect bird's-eye systems, they say, and points to safer driving setups.
arxiv-2501-06097:
Chinnarasu leads a team of eight on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It runs a classic nuclear model, the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model, on a neutral atom quantum computer with a variational solver.

Ground state energies are found for spin systems of up to fifteen spins. Two encodings are tried. In one, each spin takes its own qubit. In the other, a Gray code packs the spins into far fewer qubits, a count that grows with the log of the spin count. The lean code, plus a noise stretch trick that cleans the read, lands much closer to the exact energies. The work shows a small quantum machine can host a real physics model with care.
arxiv-2501-06297:
Galaxies die by stopping star birth, and many studies say the shutdown starts in the center and spreads outward. Alexander de la Vega and co-authors show that conclusion depends on how you fit the light. Standard fits assume a fixed dust law and flat assumptions about history. Their improved fits let dust behave flexibly and favor drawn-out star formation. The new assumptions match observed colors better.

They re-fit more than fourteen hundred galaxies seen by the Hubble telescope. Star formation and dust profiles from the new method agree with spectroscopic checks. At earlier cosmic times, galaxies quench at all radii at once. The inside-out pattern appears later, at lower redshift. Part of a popular story about galaxy death, it turns out, was an artifact of the fitting recipe.
arxiv-2501-06397:
Ilham Variansyah, Ryan McClarren, and Todd Palmer present a 2025 paper on computing sensitivities in particle transport. Monte Carlo codes simulate neutrons or photons wandering through materials. Engineers often need to know how results shift when a material's density or a part's size changes a little.

Their derivative source method takes derivatives of the transport equation and solves them in the same random walk as the main problem. One run then yields sensitivities to many sizes and densities at once. They tested it on a slab lattice of fuel, moderator, and absorber. Results matched the classic finite difference approach. A combined score of speed and error showed the new method wins in most cases, since good difference setups are hard to find.
arxiv-2501-06497:
Tushar Aggarwal and Aarohi Bhand automate the whole presentation, slides and speech alike, in this 2025 paper. Building a good deck eats hours: digging out key points, shaping slides, then rehearsing the talk. Past tools mostly turned research papers into slides and left the delivery to the human.

Their pipeline starts from ordinary Word documents instead. It pulls the document's structure apart, drafts a dynamic slide set, and writes a narration that a synthetic voice performs, so the talk itself is delivered too. To judge the output they built a grading scheme run by a language model, scoring each deck on relevance, coherence, and lack of repetition. The authors present the system as a way to hand routine presenting to software, with data and code released for others to test.
arxiv-2501-06597:
Shireesh Reddy Pyreddy and Tarannum Shaila Zaman compare the tone of human posts and AI replies in a 2025 study. People online voice strong and mixed feelings about tools like ChatGPT. The pair asked how the feelings in human tweets differ from the feelings in the replies ChatGPT gives to those same posts.

They built a framework called EmoXpt to score the tone on both sides. Human posts about the new tools ranged widely in mood. The model's replies came out more even, more joined up, and far more often upbeat in tone. The authors read that gap as a sign of how the model handles feeling, and they note it shapes how users judge the tool.
arxiv-2501-06897:
Chen and co-authors present ActiveGAMER, a system that maps a space by choosing where to look next, in this 2025 paper. It builds scenes with 3D Gaussian splatting, a fast rendering method using soft blobs. Older neural field methods were too slow for active exploration.

A rendering-based module scores which new viewpoint would teach the system most. The planner mixes broad exploration with fine detail passes and picks keyframes at two scales. The robot then moves on its own, filling gaps as it goes. On the Replica and MP3D benchmarks the system beat earlier approaches in both shape accuracy and visual fidelity. Complete, faithful maps help robots plan and people inspect spaces remotely.
arxiv-2501-06997:
Wenhan Jiang, Tingting Chai, Hongri Liu, Kai Wang, and co-authors present TFLAG, a system to detect advanced persistent threats in computer networks. Their 2025 paper works with temporal provenance graphs, which record how files, processes, and other items link over time.

Past graph methods often missed slow, subtle changes in graph shape that can mark a hidden attack. TFLAG joins a temporal graph model, which tracks how structure shifts, with a deviation network that flags odd behavior. The mix is self-supervised and aims to point to covert attack steps with fine detail. For security teams, the goal is more practical detection of long, stealthy intrusions.
arxiv-2501-07497:
Christopher Chiu, Alessandro Danelon, and Jan Draisma prove a fact about rough points in tensor spaces in their 2025 paper. Tensor spaces sort arrays of numbers, and each space can be seen across all sizes of input at once. Rough points are spots where the space is not smooth, and they matter for later work on smoothing such spaces.

The proof shows the rough spots form a smaller closed space of the same kind. Past work then means those spots can be set out with a finite list of rules. Early steps toward a full smoothing method are also given for cases where size grows in a straight line. The result gives tensor work a firmer base.
arxiv-2501-07997:
Davide Ricci and co-authors describe running a telescope in northern Italy from across the world through a web browser, in work from 2025. Older telescope software often feels stuck in a past era, with slow screens and tangled scripts. A browser tool works on any system and is born for remote use.

The team applied that approach to a one-meter class telescope while fitting it for remote work. The web software runs all parts of the scope in one place and can also be scripted for set routines. Two recent cases show the range. Skilled users tracked a planet crossing a star. A Japanese high school class ran the scope in their daytime to view star clusters on their own.
arxiv-2501-08097:
Sarfati and co-authors guide a computer diagnosis of liver cancer from three-dimensional CT scans, in a 2025 paper. This cancer is the most common primary liver tumour worldwide. Biopsy is the gold standard, but in practice radiologists read scans against a standard protocol that weighs five features in a decision tree. The authors aim to cut the variation between readers with an automatic method.

Plain deep learning, they show, reads these scans poorly on their hard data set. Their two-step approach instead mimics the radiologists protocol: it joins learned features with hand-crafted ones that match the criteria doctors use. Accuracy rose by six to eighteen points over deep learning baselines of several designs. In clinical validation, the method beat non-expert radiologists and matched experts. The authors present it as decision support grounded in how diagnosis is already done.
arxiv-2501-08197:
Yijiong Yu and five colleagues release a family of Chinese text datasets built for training large language models, in a 2025 paper. Chinese models lag partly because high-quality Chinese training text is scarce. Scraped web text is plentiful but noisy, and filtering decides model quality.

The OpenCSG corpus bundles four datasets with distinct roles. Two education-focused sets filter Chinese web content for quality, one in a revised second version. A third offers synthetic, textbook-style text for knowledge-heavy training. A fourth supplies chat-format data with varied style for fine-tuning. The team documents scalable, reproducible curation pipelines for all of them. Tests on smaller models showed clear gains, including on a Chinese evaluation benchmark. The authors present the corpus as open infrastructure for the Chinese language model community.
arxiv-2501-08297:
Karine Chubarian, Johnny Joyce, and Gyorgy Turan study a spare way to write yes-no rules in a 2025 paper. A rule can be cast as the sign of a number formula, plus or minus. When the formula's web of terms stays narrow, like a thin tree, hard tasks can turn easy to solve.

The team asks which yes-no rules fit that spare form, and what the form costs to find and read. Two uses land on Bayes net classifiers, a known tool that sorts cases by chance. Both uses serve clear AI, where users must see why a model chose as it did.
arxiv-2501-08397:
Jayadratha Gayen, Himanshu Pal, Naresh Manwani, and Charu Sharma teach graph learning models to say 'not sure' when a guess would be risky, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Many real systems are graphs that change over time, from social ties to transactions. Models that track them are used where a wrong call is costly, yet they always answer, even when unsure.

The authors add a reject option to temporal graph networks, a first for this setting. A coverage rule lets the model answer only on the share of cases it trusts, aiming for the best score inside that share. On six datasets covering link guessing and node sorting, scores and reliability rose together. The method can also weight rare classes more heavily, a common need in skewed real data.
arxiv-2501-08497:
Myles Joshua Toledo Tan and Panayiotis Benos answer a call to put accuracy first in AI diagnosis by urging a wider lens, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Accuracy matters, they grant, but fairness, privacy, and layered identity can be flattened into mere scores. Their rebuttal asks for work across social science, ethics, and public health.

Clear explanations must sit at the core of design so users can trust and check the tools. Layered traits, like race plus sex plus income, can stack harms that single marks miss. The authors propose a frame that holds accuracy beside fairness, privacy, and inclusion. Readers get a plea for diagnosis tools that serve mixed publics well.
arxiv-2501-09197:
Miguel Sánchez Sánchez, José González, and Tobias Stauber study twisted bilayer graphene, two sheets of carbon one atom thick, rotated by a tiny 'magic' angle. At that angle the electron bands flatten, and odd quantum states appear. The authors build a model of the interacting electrons and simplify it by folding high-energy effects into an effective theory around the neutral state.

In their effective picture, the flat bands widen notably, which suggests the true magic angle shifts once interactions are counted. The electron wave patterns also drift toward a symmetric ideal form that theorists call the chiral limit. The team then rewrites the bands in a new basis named for swirling patterns in the waves. They discuss what the flatness and the near-symmetry mean for the broken-symmetry states seen at neutrality. The paper is a theory study aimed at researchers in quantum materials.
arxiv-2501-09497:
Yun Chen, Yuqi Wang, Jingjun You, Yingqi Liu, Su Yi, and Yuangang Deng propose making molecules inside a light cavity so atoms and molecules radiate together, in a 2025 paper. Ultracold atoms in optical cavities are a prized testbed for many-body physics. Their scheme uses the cavity to help bind atom pairs into molecules, which creates long-range three-way interactions among cavity light, atoms, and molecules.

Past a threshold pump strength, the molecules settle into a self-organized square lattice. That marks a joint atom-molecule superradiance, with a broken symmetry. Unlike earlier atomic versions, the light output grows with the cube of the atom count, a bosonic boost. Strong entanglement between light and matter flags the transition. The authors say the setup opens fresh ground in quantum superchemistry.
arxiv-2501-09697: Valentio Iverson, Gian Cordana Sanjaya, and Xiaoheng Wang count special polynomials in a 2025 math paper. They look at polynomials whose coefficients are all prime numbers, in two families: those with a fixed leading term and those without. Each polynomial carries a derived number, its discriminant, which tells whether its roots are distinct. The team counts exactly how many in each family have a discriminant with no repeated prime factor. They also count how many yield the largest possible ring of algebraic integers in their number field.
arxiv-2501-09797:
Karan Tiwana, Edoardo Lauria, and Antoine Tilloy set out a new way to compute mean values in field theories that have a line flaw. Their paper appeared in twenty twenty-five. The theories live in one space plus one time dimension and describe bulk matter with mass. A line flaw breaks the clean case and makes direct sums hard.

The trick is to run time across the flaw, not along it. Sums with the flaw then turn into mean values in the clean case, which a smooth matrix state can handle well. The team tests the plan on a known theory with a field flaw. It works in weak, strong, and border cases alike.
arxiv-2501-09997:
Qiang Liu and co-authors present a 2025 paper on catching false statements made by large language models. Such errors, called hallucinations, are a major barrier to trusting these systems. Their method uses the model's own attention patterns to judge whether an answer is trustworthy, without any labeled training data.

Each question is classed as attentive or not, based on attention measures, and the model answers it two ways. Consistency scores from the two runs are compared, and the gap serves as the hallucination signal. The method needs only three passes through the model. Tests on four models and three benchmarks beat prior zero-shot detectors while cutting compute cost.
arxiv-2501-10197:
Xi Yang, Haoyuan Shi, Zihan Wang, Nannan Wang, and Xinbo Gao present CSHNet in 2025 for translating images across domains with uneven detail. Tasks like radar-to-photo conversion must invent rich content from sparse input. Standard networks catch fine detail but lose global shape, merging regions that should stay apart.

Their hybrid network braids two designs: one strong on detail, one strong on structure. Cross links let the two halves trade information as they work, and a special loss guards edges during conversion. On scene-level and object-level data sets, the method beat prior tools in both looks and scores. Code is shared in public.
arxiv-2501-10297:
Simone Daniotti, Matte Hartog, and Frank Neffke measure how coherent the economies of United States cities are, in work from 2025. A city's coherence is the typical distance between the skills its activities need. Diverse economies support growth but force cities to build many unrelated skills, which is costly.

The team tracked the urban system from 1850 to today. They used census records covering over six hundred million people for the early period, plus patent and job data for recent decades. Despite huge shifts in where activity sits, average coherence barely changed over 170 years. Coherence also falls with city size at the same rate in every era and dataset. The authors read this as a universal constraint on how cities diversify, set by size itself.
arxiv-2501-10497:
Rijken built a quark-level model of baryons in two thousand twenty-five. Baryons, like the proton, are made of three constituent quarks. The model holds quarks with a harmonic confining force. That force grows like a spring as quarks separate. Exchange of mesons between quarks adds further pull. Smooth bell-shaped quark wave forms make the math tractable.

The notes derive soft two-body forces between the quarks. They convert the forces into momentum space for use. Set parameters from a known interaction model fix the strength. That leaves the quark forces with no free tuning. Three-body forces between quark groups also emerge. The model was applied to the baryon octet and a key resonance. Results gave a satisfactory picture of the mass splitting.
arxiv-2501-11097:
Huichao Zhang, Pengyu Wang, Manyi Li, Zuojun Li, and Yaguang Wu encode floorplans as latent codes over adaptive unit regions, in a representation meant to serve many tasks at once. Their paper from twenty twenty-five contrasts the offer with raster images, which over-segment, and room graphs, which throw away geometry. A geometry-aware density map is clustered into boundary-hugging unit regions. A trained network then reads density and semantic maps into compact codes per region.

Interior planning, floorplan metric learning, and generation all run on the same encoding. Experiments beat state-of-the-art rivals in accuracy and visual quality across those tasks. Ablations show the slicing choices matter. Architecture tools gain one representation where three formats used to compete.
arxiv-2501-11197:
Udekwe and co-authors present Q-RESTORE, a framework for rebuilding road networks after disasters with fairness built in. Fast recovery matters most in underserved areas, where isolation deepens harm. Classic methods prize raw function and speed of planning over equity. Low-income areas often lose out under those rules. The new frame pairs quantum computing with equity goals. A hybrid quantum solver picks which road links to restore within budget.

The solver weighs the needs of low-, middle-, and high-income communities side by side. Priority goes to keeping all groups connected to vital services. Compute speed is treated as a means, not the end. The authors frame fair recovery as a design constraint, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2501-11597:
Verya Monjezi and co-authors test, in a 2025 paper, whether software fairness tools miss the worst harms hiding in the tails. Past fairness work mostly guards the average case. Extreme outcomes, though, can mark deep shifts in how groups fare.

Their gauge, extreme counterfactual discrimination, uses extreme value statistics to size the worst disadvantage tied to group membership alone. A randomized search with generative AI draws enough tail samples even when the raw data lacks them. In tests on four model types across ten social tasks, the generators fed valid tail fits in 95 percent of cases. A sharp pattern emerged: common bias fixes cut average discrimination yet raised worst-case discrimination. Averages, the authors warn, can hide growing harm at the edge.
arxiv-2501-11797:
Ashot Aleksian and Stéphane Villeneuve study how long a noisy process stays inside a safe region. Their 2025 math paper treats diffusions whose rules change with time. The question is the exit time: how long until the process first leaves a bounded region. They focus on the small-noise limit, where escapes are rare.

When the changing rules stay close to fixed ones, the exit time grows at an exponential rate as noise shrinks. That growth holds both in chance and on average. They also pin down where on the boundary the process tends to leave. Loosening the closeness condition changes the picture, and they trace how. A final part extends the results to interacting McKean-Vlasov processes.
arxiv-2501-12497:
Toluwani Okunola, Mirjeta Pasha, Misha Kilmer, and Melina Freitag tackle the rebuilding of moving images from limited data, in a 2025 paper. Dynamic scans, such as heart or lung imaging, must recover a sharp picture for each moment from sparse measurements. Motion between frames is both a problem and a clue. The authors add a motion model, based on optical flow, that estimates how objects move while also guessing the images.

That motion estimate becomes an extra rule guiding the reconstruction over time. Edge-keeping rules sharpen spatial detail at the same time. The team solves the combined problem with an efficient subspace method built for large problems. Tests on varied examples show cleaner sequences, a step toward faster scans that patients can tolerate more easily.
arxiv-2501-12997:
Pablo Barceló, Alexander Kozachinskiy, and Tomasz Steifer tie a classic learning rank to transformer reasoning in a 2025 paper. The rank of a Boolean function anchors PAC learning theory. It yields fast learning for small decision trees. The team reframe rank through the Transformer architecture.

Rank equals the fewest chain-of-thought steps a one-layer Transformer needs. That count applies to a single-layer net with hard attention. Composing a function with itself sets an exact step price. Hunting the k-th one in a bit string also costs k steps. A multi-head rank extends the idea to richer models. Bounded rank classes get fresh learnability results.
arxiv-2501-13297:
Yang Bai, Christan Grant, and Daisy Wang fuse learned ranking with generative ranking to answer questions from text and images. Mixed questions need documents and images pulled and ranked, yet small encoder rankers clash with big generative models. Their 2025 frame, RAMQA, first trains a mixed pointwise ranker on a vision-text base. Then a generative model learns to re-rank the top items and produce both the item IDs and the reply.

The model runs through item orders in turns, so order bias can be read and cut. On two benchmark sets of mixed questions the frame beat strong bases by a firm step. One frame for pulling, ranking, and replying is the pitch. Code and data are free.
arxiv-2501-13597:
Spectral clustering groups data by the structure of a similarity graph, which makes the graph itself the make-or-break step. Kamal Berahmand and co-authors survey how graph structure learning feeds this clustering family. They cover graph building by pairs, by anchors, and by hypergraphs, in both fixed and adaptive flavors.

The survey sorts clustering into single-view and multi-view camps, and into one-step and two-step pipelines. It also reviews how multi-view methods fuse their information. Open challenges and future directions close the tour. The 2025 paper argues that learning the graph, not just using it, is where spectral clustering now wins or loses on big, high-dimensional data.
arxiv-2501-14097:
Raphael Morsomme and six co-authors build a faster engine for judging treatments when the key events are only glimpsed between tests. Their 2025 paper models illness as movement among states over time, where patients are checked at scattered visits, so exact transition times stay hidden. Their target case is a household trial of an antibody combination given to prevent Covid infection in exposed contacts.

The method blends symptom records, swab tests, and blood antibody results into one model. A Monte Carlo fitting routine with importance sampling makes the math tractable and far faster than older routes. Applied to the trial, the drug cut the risk of silent infection, shortened the time patients shed virus, and lowered later antibody conversion among those infected without symptoms. The authors offer the approach for any study where endpoints arrive as fragments.
arxiv-2501-14297:
Mendoza Tavera and co-authors caged a hydrogen atom in a tube in two thousand twenty-five. The cylinder is infinite and impenetrable. A magnetic field runs along its axis. The nucleus sits anchored at the center. Squeezing plus field reshapes the atom's ground state. A trial wave function with three parameters models it.

The function respects the problem's symmetries exactly. It also captures the key limiting behaviors. Neither the electric pull nor magnetism is treated as small. A new variational cut-off factor is the advance. It bends smoothly to zero at the wall. Earlier cut-offs lacked that variational freedom. Energies from the model improve on past estimates.
arxiv-2501-14397:
Jonas Primbs and co-authors simplify how electric cars prove they may charge in a 2025 paper. The standing plug and charge scheme works, but its setup is uneven, rests on a heavy trust chain, and gives drivers little say over limits.

Their fix borrows web login tools built for phones and apps. Setup shrinks, and drivers can set time or cost caps as part of the grant. A test build runs the flow, timed checks gauge its speed, and a formal proof tool vets the protocol's safety. The blueprint could serve other cross device grants beyond car charging.
arxiv-2501-14597:
Samuel Escribano and three co-authors wrote a 2025 paper that puts forth a nanodevice to create and detect Majorana-like modes with no magnets. Such modes are prized as building blocks for fault-tolerant quantum computers. The smallest recipe is a Kitaev chain of just two sites, which hosts so-called poor man's Majorana modes. Magnetic fields usually complicate the setup.

The device joins two three-terminal Josephson junctions in a flat semiconductor. Tuning the superconducting phases of the ends and the link between the junctions builds the two-site chain. Runs with disorder mixed in, in a wider layout, show the modes hold up. Conductance readings give a workable way to show the modes are there. With no magnet, more materials can be used, germanium-based ones among them, and energy levels read more sharply. The design brings this kind of Majorana work within easier reach.
arxiv-2501-14897:
Filandri and co-authors model two light atomic nuclei as clusters of alpha particles in a 2025 physics paper. Carbon-12 is treated as three such clusters, and oxygen-16 as four. These nuclei matter far beyond the lab, since their making in stars lies at the root of heavy element building and of life on Earth.

The team works in a short range effective field theory, which captures the key forces without tracking every detail. They solve for the ground and excited states with a math method built for cluster systems. With a two body force plus a tuned three body force, carbon-12 came out matching data well. Oxygen-16 did not, until a four body force was added. The contrast shows how cluster forces change as the system grows by one unit.
arxiv-2501-14997:
Bao Duong, Sunil Gupta, and Thin Nguyen propose a new way to learn causal graphs from observational data. Score-based methods search over directed acyclic graphs for the one that best fits the data, but the search is slow and often inaccurate. Their framework, called DrBO, hands the search to Bayesian optimization, a method that picks the most promising candidates to try next.

Standard Bayesian optimization does not scale to this problem, so the team replaced its usual Gaussian process model with dropout neural networks trained continuously. The swap lets the model track uncertainty in graph scores without overfitting, and it grows gracefully with the number of trials. In wide tests on synthetic and real data, DrBO found the correct graph in fewer trials and less time than leading methods. The authors have released their code publicly. The work aims to make causal discovery practical on harder problems.
arxiv-2501-15197:
Sharpening a satellite image by fusing a detailed but colour-poor picture with a colourful but blurry one is a workhorse trick in remote sensing. Xi-Yuan Liu and co-authors improve the tensor method behind that fusion. Image values cannot be negative, yet earlier solvers either ignored that fact or enforced it by crude clipping that disturbs the optimisation.

Their algorithm folds the non-negativity into the maths itself, tying each entry to the square of a hidden parameter so the constraint holds automatically. Working through the calculus for gradients and curvature lets the solver proceed smoothly inside a least-squares framework. Experiments on the super-resolution task show the cleaner handling pays off in image quality. The authors present the method as a drop-in upgrade for coupled tensor fusion.
arxiv-2501-15297:
Mood trackers on phones promise streams of self-reports, but people skip entries exactly when their feelings matter most, so the gaps themselves carry meaning. Standard models of swinging variance assume the gaps are random, and Gehui Zhang and co-authors lift that assumption in a 2025 paper. Their method fills gaps using a representation that exploits the step-by-step memory of the variance process.

A new filtering scheme accounts for the wobble that filling introduces, completing a full sampling routine. The team demonstrates it on phone mood reports from people monitored after a suicide attempt, a setting where missing entries are anything but random. The framework opens swinging-variance models to honest gaps.
arxiv-2501-15497:
Jieli Qin, Shijie Li, Yijia Tu, Maokun Gu, Lin Guan, Weimin Xu, and Lu Zhou study a doubled quantum flow effect in a 2025 paper. The Josephson effect lets a superfluid cross a split with no push, as a steady current. Their system is a supersolid, a rare state that flows like a fluid yet holds a crystal-like pattern.

The system is made by linking cold atom clouds to a ring of light. Where the split sits turns out to change the flow in a strong way. At some spots one kind of current flows, and at others a second kind shows up. One kind grows stronger in the supersolid state while the other fades, a split the team maps in full.
arxiv-2501-15597:
Alexander Kaganovich studies how the Higgs field could have driven the early universe's fast expansion inside a two-measure theory of gravity. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. In this theory, the Higgs is the only field rolling through the young cosmos. A built-in constraint ties a key ratio to the field's value.

That tie turns fixed settings into ones that shift as the field moves. The resulting push can match what sky data say about the expansion era, with a mild link to gravity. It needs a very small self-coupling during that era. After expansion ends, the falling field flips the sign of its mass term and breaks the symmetry. The same drift then lifts the coupling to its known lab value. The model even covers strange starts where the cosmos begins in a phantom-like state.
arxiv-2501-15797:
Tianbo Yang and co-authors pair a language model with a textbook memory in a 2025 project to help it write math proofs. Models trained to mimic proof style still stumble on logic. Their system, LemmaHead, looks up relevant passages from published texts and feeds them to the model before it answers.

The task they target is automated theorem proving: given a claim, produce a proof in the Lean formal language. Retrieval gives the model near-at-hand facts and lemma shapes instead of pure recall. The project tests whether borrowed context, not just more training, can lift formal reasoning in models.
arxiv-2501-16097:
Pasquale Blasi asks what gamma rays from star clusters imply for the origin of cosmic rays. Clusters are often cast as accelerators able to push particles to peta-electronvolt energies. Telescopes have now seen very-high-energy gamma rays from the Cygnus cocoon and Westerlund 1. Blasi computes the expected glow under several models of how clusters inject cosmic rays, assuming the light comes from protons striking gas.

Under that reading, the escaping particles must have plowed through a great deal of matter inside the cluster, more than they meet crossing the whole galaxy. That burden has a price. Either clusters supply only a small share of the cosmic rays reaching Earth, or the standard picture of how cosmic rays wander the galaxy needs deep revision. A light-based origin for the gamma rays escapes the problem but caps particle energies well below the interesting range.
arxiv-2501-16597:
Fog radio access networks store popular content near users, and small helper devices with caches can relieve crowded fronthaul links when full radio heads cannot be added. The authors of a 2025 study ask where those helpers should sit so that the most users reach them. They model the chance a request hits a helper cache using outage probability and a smooth estimate of how users spread across the area, then search placements with a swarm optimization method.

Simulations confirm that the chosen spots raise the cache hit rate, which shortens delivery delays and eases fronthaul load. Careful placement, the team argues, gets more value from each helper without new heavy hardware.
arxiv-2501-16697:
Suke Li studies how peanut futures move with other farm commodities in China in a paper from 2025. Five agricultural futures supply the price history. Regression, cointegration, and causality tests map the links. Dynamic models then track how correlations shift over time. One pairing stands out: peanut and soybean oil futures show a strong, time-varying connection. Other contracts exert little influence in the vector model.

Neural networks join the toolbox for price prediction. Their accuracy hinges on the time-step setting, the author finds. The study mixes classical econometrics with machine learning on one market complex. Traders and hedgers get a map of which contracts actually move together.
arxiv-2501-16797:
Suprabha Mukhopadhyay, Yuto Bekki, Xiaojue Zhu, and Laurent Gizon test shortcuts used to model slow waves on the Sun, in a 2025 paper. These global inertial modes have only recently been observed, and they may reveal the Sun's inner spin. Modelers often simplify the gas equations to save computing time.

Using one code framework, the team computes the modes three ways: with full compressible physics and with two approximations. One shortcut, the anelastic form, matches the full result closely under both even and solar-like spin. The Boussinesq form, which drops density layering, gives clearly different modes, above all for patterns with strong radial motion. The verdict tells solar modelers which shortcut is safe and which distorts the very modes they chase.
arxiv-2501-17097:
Venu M Kalari and co-authors report newborn star candidates in a far dwarf galaxy in a 2025 paper. Using the James Webb Space Telescope, they found twelve young stars still forming in the galaxy WLM, nearly a million parsecs away. The galaxy's gas is poor in heavy elements, at about an eighth of the Sun's level.

The candidates weigh between one and five Suns and are under ten million years old, glowing extra brightly in infrared light from warm dust. They huddle in a cluster about ten parsecs wide. These are the most distant and metal-poor forming stars known, a test of how stars are born in near-pristine gas.
arxiv-2501-17197:
Morton Harris refines a classic classification of modules in the modular representation theory of finite groups, in a mathematics paper from 2025. The field studies how groups act on vector spaces when the field's characteristic divides the group size. Its basic building blocks are the indecomposable and simple modules, sorted by Green's theory.

The new classification splits the isomorphism types into disjoint, nonempty families. Modules inside one family share the same Green theory invariants, so the new sorting is strictly finer than the old. The author also proves a fresh formula counting the types of absolutely simple modules for groups in prime characteristic. The work sharpens the map of a theory that underlies much of modern algebra.
arxiv-2501-17297:
Mustafa Saeed, Diya Batool, Muhammad Muzammil, and Nomaan X probe the thermal character of gravity with spin models in a 2025 theoretical physics study. Euclidean approaches to gravity treat spacetime with imaginary time, a setting where temperature-like behavior might be built in. The authors place Ising-like models on several classic backgrounds and watch for phase transitions in the spins.

Flat space with acceleration horizons, black holes, and cosmological spaces each appear, including cases with no horizon or zero temperature for contrast. Sorting which background property, curvature, horizon, or temperature, drives the transition clarifies what hot means for gravity itself.
arxiv-2501-17597:
Sibeijn, Ahmed, Khosravi, and Keviczky design a control method for district heating networks where homes can both use and supply heat. New generation networks aim to cut supply temperatures and drop fossil fuels, using storage and building heat inertia for flexibility. Their 2025 paper, an extended version, pairs a graph based model with predictive control.

The model handles many producers, prosumers, storage buffers, and two way pipe flows in one frame built for optimization. It runs fast enough for real time control decisions. In closed loop simulations, the method cut costs by up to nine percent over rule based control. It also held system limits better than the standard approach, the authors report.
arxiv-2501-17697: Tom Banks writes a short review essay for younger physicists in a 2025 paper, the third in a series reviving old arguments. His topic is a habit of thought in string theory: treating the theory's settings as if they were the settled values of fields. Banks argues that this picture misleads. He walks through arguments first made at the start of the century, in plain terms, so a new generation can judge them. The essay is a caution about importing field-theory instincts into quantum gravity.
arxiv-2501-17997:
Chenoa Tremblay and a large team describe a search for signs of alien technology using a large radio telescope array in New Mexico, in a 2025 paper. Their system, COSMIC, runs alongside a sky survey and processes signals on the fly. The hard part is sorting real candidates from human-made interference.

The paper explains their follow-up pipeline, which flags steady interference sources and removes false alarms. By the date reported, the system had observed nearly a million pointings. A test search toward hundreds of catalog stars found no unexplained signals. The team sets upper limits on how strong such signals could be.
arxiv-2501-18097: Jung, Morales, and Tran prove a density result for shallow neural networks whose input domains are allowed to vary. Classic theorems say a shallow network can match any continuous function on a fixed compact space. Here the functions live on a compact metric space, and the domains themselves may change. The authors measure that change with the Gromov-Hausdorff distance, a standard way to compare metric spaces. Under their stated conditions, shallow networks stay dense in this wider family of functions.
arxiv-2501-18397:
Feng Wang, Zhongguo Sun, and Xiangyu Hu build in a 2025 paper a particle method for turbulent flow near walls. Wall bounded turbulence drives much of engineering, yet particle methods rarely tackle it. A mismatch between moving particles and the averaged flow model sits at the core of the trouble.

Two fix sets address the clash, one for the main stream and one near the wall. The main stream fixes curb excess dissipation and inflated turbulence energy in the flow. Near wall fixes sharpen the wall model with weighted particle tricks and a set wall distance rule. A level set offset trick keeps wall scaling steady across grid sizes for fair tests. Benchmark channels, straight and curved, check the method's convergence.
arxiv-2501-18997:
Gyuseok Lee and four co-authors bring diffusion models, the engines behind image generators, into recommender systems that suggest items to users. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Diffusion recommenders clean noisy taste signals to guess what a user wants. Adding noise, though, can wash out the personal detail that matters most.

Their model, CDiff4Rec, builds fake users from item features to enrich the signal. It then borrows taste cues from both real and fake neighbors who behave alike. That mix rebuilds fine-grained preferences more faithfully. Tests on three public data sets beat rival systems. The gains come from joining item content with shared taste signals. The work suits shops and media apps that must keep suggestions personal. It also shows generative tools can serve ranking, not just media.
arxiv-2501-19097:
Pedro Otero-Casal and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on cancer care with targeted radiation drugs. In this form of care, a drug carries radiation to the tumor over time. Doctors sum up the chance of wiping out the tumor, but that sum rests on dose rate curves rebuilt from data, and those curves carry error.

The team built varied dose rate curves from real data while holding total dose fixed. They then asked how much the tumor control chance moved as the curves changed. A simple score based on mean gaps between curves tracked the shifts best. From that score they set how much curve error can be allowed before the control chance shifts by a set small amount.
arxiv-2502-00097:
Andrea Sacchi, Kevin Paggeot, Steven Dillmann, Juan Rafael Martínez-Galarza, and Peter Kosec hunt rare X-ray sources in an archive in this 2025 paper. Their targets glow brightly at the softest X-ray energies. Such supersoft, hyperluminous sources mark extreme feeding by black holes, including stars being torn apart and other nuclear outbursts.

These events are rare, so the team wrote an algorithm to sift the Chandra catalog of chance X-ray detections for candidates. They ran it two ways: by hand, and with a new machine learning version. The search turned up promising sources for follow-up with other telescopes. Each confirmed case is a lab for studying how matter falls onto massive black holes at the edge of what is physically allowed.
arxiv-2502-00297:
Nayyer Raza and co-authors update a rapid sorting tool for gravitational wave alerts in a 2025 paper. When detectors catch a possible merger, telescope teams must decide fast whether to chase it. Some alerts are mere glitches, and some real events leave no light to see. The tool reads the sky map in each public alert and sorts the event within moments.

The new version gives clean chance scores with error ranges for four classes: glitch, two black holes, a neutron star with a black hole, or two neutron stars. Lessons from studies of the first model's reasoning shaped the rebuild. The update targets the fourth observing run of the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detectors and beyond. Sharper odds help teams spend scarce telescope time where a light show is most likely.
arxiv-2502-00397:
Rohit Girmaji and co-authors present 2025 models that predict where a viewer will look in a video, with a lean build. Guessing gaze hot spots helps in video coding, ads, and interface design. Top models can be huge and slow, which bars their use on small devices or in real time.

One model trims a known design to a 36-megabyte form with a light decoder, with no loss in scores. A larger kin adds cues from where actions take place in space and time, a shift from the class labels most past models use. An ensemble that averages the two maps tops the field on three sight-only and six audio-visual test sets. The lean model runs at over 1,000 frames per second, which beats transformer models on speed and size.
arxiv-2502-00597:
Jose Rocher-Gonzalez and co-authors work on combining two congestion tools for the fat-tree networks that link supercomputers. Their 2025 paper starts from the fat-tree shape, which offers many equal routes between any two nodes. Multi-path routing can spread traffic across those routes and lower congestion.

A second tool separates flows into queues, yet the authors' earlier work showed spreading can backfire by scattering congested flows across queues. Their proposal adds restrictions on how alternative routes are chosen, so spreading and queue separation reinforce rather than fight each other. The target is a network that handles the bursty traffic of computing centers without hot spots. The work is a design step toward pairing the two schemes in real machines.
arxiv-2502-01397:
Trifonov, Muravleva, and Oseledets show that message-passing graph neural networks cannot learn a key matrix factorization, in a 2025 paper. Sparse triangular factors serve as preconditioners that speed up linear solvers in science and engineering. Graph networks have been proposed to predict them cheaply. The catch is that good factors depend on far-apart entries, while message passing only mixes local neighborhoods.

The team back the theory with tests on synthetic matrices and real ones from the SuiteSparse collection. Across attention networks and graph transformers, predicted factors matched the true ones poorly. Even a fully global transformer failed to reach simple baselines. The authors conclude that scientific computing needs architectures built for non-local structure, not borrowed message passing.
arxiv-2502-01497:
Ulrich Bunke builds a coarse geometry theory of branched coverings and the transfer maps they support. His 2025 paper works in coarse homology, a framework that sees only large scale shape. A branched coarse covering is a map that looks like a covering at large scale but may branch. The author defines transfers, which push homology classes backward along such maps, between coarse theories.

Several forms of coarse K-homology are shown to carry this extra structure. Versions of a classic index theorem are then proved inside coarse homotopy theory. Those results feed a new argument for one step of a famous counterexample. That counterexample, due to Higson, blocks a major conjecture linking geometry and analysis. The paper is abstract, but it sharpens tools used across index theory.
arxiv-2502-01697:
Alan Zhu and co-authors make training data from almost nothing in a 2025 paper. Synthetic data now feeds many model builds, but standard recipes prompt a tuned model with tens of thousands of seed examples. Seeds that large are costly where examples are precious.

With only a few seeds, tuned models echo themselves and diversity dies. Raw base models, never instruction-tuned, wander wider but follow orders poorly. Their two-stage method, BARE, drafts with the base model, then refines with the tuned one. Three seed examples sufficed to build sets that lifted downstream scores sharply. A mid-size model fine-tuned on a thousand BARE samples matched top rivals on a coding benchmark.
arxiv-2502-01797:
Hurricane track forecasts have improved with AI weather models, but those models treat the storm as if it flew over bare air alone. A 2025 paper by Naveen Sudharsan and co-authors asks what the land adds. AI systems such as Google's operational model leave out how soil and ground feed back on a storm's path.

To test the effect, the team ran a physics-based hurricane model with varied soil moisture. The runs showed that land conditions can shift a storm's track by a real margin. No current AI system yet couples air, land, and ocean in one working forecast. The authors argue that adding land feedback would sharpen accuracy and also make the AI's choices easier to explain. They frame a fully coupled AI weather model as the next step for near real-time storm guidance.
arxiv-2502-02297:
Blot, Shadrin, and Singh give a new proof of Faber's formula for socle intersection numbers, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The numbers live in the tautological ring of the moduli space of curves. Their proof draws on Gromov-Witten theory of the elliptic curve. Recent work by Oberdieck and Pixton supplies the key relation.

A refinement of that argument yields a beautiful new tautological relation. Straightforward computation with double ramification cycles completes the proof. Those cycles enter recursion relations for KdV hierarchy Hamiltonians. The note is short but connects several deep theories. Curve counting and integrable systems meet in one formula.
arxiv-2502-02397:
Annalisa Calvi, Ursula Laa, and Dianne Cook build a visual test for whether new data still look normal in this 2025 paper. Many fields keep a reference profile of healthy conditions, from trial safety data to climate history. New samples must be checked against that profile, which is often a many-variable normal distribution.

Their method steers a guided tour through low-dimensional views of the data. A new index drives the tour toward views where the new sample differs most from the reference. The reference appears as a computed ellipse in each view, making gaps easy to see. The tools ship in a free software package for the R language.
arxiv-2502-02797:
Sunny Sanyal and co-authors offer in this 2025 paper a simple fix for a stubborn training flaw: fine-tuning makes models forget. When a pretrained model is tuned on a new task, its old skills often fade, and most cures fail when the original training data and recipe are unknown. Their scheme needs only the model's own losses on the new data.

Examples the model already finds easy get more weight; hard ones get less, which limits drift. Theory in a linear case shows the method stalls learning in one corner of the space, curbing overfit. Tests on language and vision confirm the gain: one math model kept nearly all its old skill while learning the new task.
arxiv-2502-02997:
Kiran Sharma and Parul Khurana present a 2025 study of the impact of conference papers from India in one large proceedings series. Conferences are a main channel for sharing science, yet the flood of new events has raised doubts about quality. The authors test those doubts with citation data.

They drew on the Scopus database for one Springer series. Of 570 events worldwide in the series, 177 were hosted in India alone, with 11,066 papers in total. The average paper drew about one citation, and the yearly average has been falling. The study also names the main contributors and reads what team patterns say about impact.
arxiv-2502-03097:
Kőmíves and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on sharp radio views of two faint galaxies suspected of hiding active black holes that could shine at the highest energies. Galaxies with jets aimed at Earth dominate the known sources, but a new telescope array should find fainter, off-axis ones. These two showed no nuclear activity in their light spectra.

Using two continent-scale radio networks at two frequencies, the team pinpointed each galaxy's compact radio core. They measured its spectrum, power, and heat, and compared its radio and X-ray glow. Both galaxies, despite their quiet optical look, host faint compact active nuclei with steep spectra. Such finds widen the hunting ground for high-energy sources.
arxiv-2502-03197:
Ildiko Schlotter and Katarina Cechlarova study a party nomination puzzle in elections, in a 2025 paper. Candidates are split into parties, and each party must name exactly one of them. The core question asks whether a given party can, for some set of rival nominations, see its candidate win. The pair study this for voting rules that always honor a candidate who beats every other head to head.

They run a full complexity analysis across three measures: the number of voters, the number of parties, and the largest party size. For each rule in scope, the count of voters splits the problem into hard and easy cases. For each hard case, they pin down exactly how it behaves under each parameter choice. Their map shows where the puzzle can be solved fast and where it stays out of reach, which guides anyone building tools for party strategy.
arxiv-2502-03397:
SPRI, a frame that writes fresh guiding rules for each query, is set out by Hongli Zhan and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Steering language models by fixed rule sets is cheap but blunt, since one rule set fits all inputs poorly. SPRI drafts rules on the spot for the query at hand, with little or no human work. Those rules then guide the model's reply.

Tests span three tasks. In a hard domain task, model rules matched expert rules on scores. Rule-based rubrics beat past model-judge frames. Training data made with SPRI rules also lifted truth scores a lot. Code and outputs are shared.
arxiv-2502-03597:
Byungjoon Min and Maxi San Miguel study how aging, the tendency to stick with a state the longer one has held it, changes opinion dynamics on networks that rewire as opinions spread. In the coevolving voter model, nodes copy neighbors' opinions while links also break and reform. Their 2025 paper adds aging in two ways, tied either to how long a link has lasted or to how long a node has held its opinion.

The two versions push the model's tipping point in opposite directions. Link aging shifts the absorbing phase transition one way, node aging the other. In some settings the sharp transition vanishes altogether under aging. The authors conclude that memory of durations, usually ignored, can reshape whether a network settles into consensus or stays divided.
arxiv-2502-04097:
Abe Alexander, Guillaume Lambert, and Lars Fritz sort out two ways to count losses in automatic market makers, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Such systems let people swap tokens from a shared pool priced by formula. Two loss marks dog those who stock the pool: impermanent loss, against simply holding the tokens, and loss-versus-rebalancing, against a steadily rebalanced holding. How the two marks relate was muddy.

The trio find three time regimes. At very short spans the marks are one and the same. At mid spans their shapes differ but their averages meet, linked by a classic limit law. At long spans both shape and average part ways. They then fold in fees and block times, the heartbeat of the chain, and trace the race between fee gains and loss speeds.
arxiv-2502-04397:
Xiaorui Su and co-authors present MedTok, a tokenizer that turns medical codes into rich tokens for health record models. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that patient record models need codes split into learnable units. Past tokenizers treated each code as a lone text tag.

Each code in fact carries a written meaning, a place in a medical hierarchy, and links to other codes. MedTok reads the text with a language encoder and the link web with a graph encoder. Both views are then squeezed into one shared token space. With more than six hundred thousand codes in play, this richer start should sharpen clinical reasoning by record models.
arxiv-2502-04497:
Yi Zhang, Mohamadamin Rajabinezhad, and Shan Zuo tackled a control problem in 2025 for groups of linked agents. The agents must split into two camps that mirror a leader's state in a set pattern. The system is nonlinear and runs in steps, and an attacker can jam the links at odd times, so data go missing. The team built a trigger rule that sends data only when needed and learns from the data it gets.

Their rule keeps the follower agents in step with the leader in spite of the jams. Proofs and two worked cases back the claim. The cases show the method holds up when links drop at random. The work speaks to drone fleets, power grids, and other linked systems that face attack.
arxiv-2502-05397:
William Huey and co-authors teach robots from a single demo video whose timing does not match the robot's own pace. A person may linger or rush, and a robot body moves at its own speed, so frame-by-frame copying breaks. Good learning must track the order of subgoals, not the clock.

Their reward, called ORCA, scores how well the agent covers the demo's frames in the right order at each step. Order, not raw closeness, becomes the training signal. On standard manipulation tasks, agents with this reward gained over fourfold on past best frame-matching scores. On a humanoid task the gain topped sixfold. The method held up as timing skew grew worse. One skewed video can thus still teach a clean, ordered skill.
arxiv-2502-05797:
David Pearl, James Intriligator, and Xuanjiang Liu survey wearable technology in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Wearables have moved from gadgets to daily companions in health, work, and well-being. The authors trace that history and map what comes next.

Artificial intelligence, connected sensors, and augmented reality now drive personal, adaptive devices. Good wearables, they argue, need user-centered design, ethics, and teamwork across fields. Modular builds and greener materials answer sustainability concerns. Risks such as data privacy and algorithmic bias still shadow the field. The paper offers a roadmap for wearables that enrich lives while growing in ethical and sustainable ways. Integration with daily life is the field's defining trend.
arxiv-2502-05997:
Liu, Puckett, Wu, Hariri, Zhang, and Zhang report in twenty twenty-five light-guiding chips built on full-size factory wafers with extremely low signal loss. Such chips route light for communications, sensors, and quantum tools, but making them at wafer scale without cracks is hard. The team combined tuned wafers with a new etching mask method to carve the guides.

The finished guides kept light so well that quality scores beat prior marks, with both lab-grade and factory-style patterning. Ringing the guides produced frequency combs, trains of evenly spaced colours, proving the planned light-bending trait. The authors say the route fits standard foundry lines, opening mass production of high-grade photonic chips.
arxiv-2502-06697:
Aareyan Manzoor, writing alone in 2025, proved a negative result in operator algebra, a field tied to quantum theory. The question is whether certain structures, called von Neumann algebras, can be approximated inside simple matrix models, a property known as Connes embeddability. A major quantum result had shown such algebras exist that cannot be embedded, but Manzoor reaches a new source for them.

He defines a notion of hyperlinearity for invariant random subgroups and shows some are not co-hyperlinear. As a result, there is an equivalence relation whose algebra is not Connes embeddable. The proof simplifies an earlier reduction by removing the need for subgroup tests entirely.
arxiv-2502-06897:
Turning a pencil sketch of an excavated pot into a clean inked drawing for publication can take an archaeologist hours. Lorenzo Cardarelli built PyPotteryInk, an open-source pipeline that does the inking in seconds. A one-step diffusion model, adapted from an image-to-image design, converts the sketch in a single pass while keeping fine decoration and vessel shape intact. A patch-based method with shifting overlap lets it handle drawings of any size at high resolution.

Cardarelli tested the system on Italian protohistoric pottery drawings, where it preserved both surface patterns and structural features such as rims and handles. Expert readers judged the output fit for publication. The tool can also be retrained on small samples to suit other regional styles, and its models, library, and guides are freely shared.
arxiv-2502-06997:
Behzad Hejrati and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a diffusion model that outlines regions in medical scans. Such models are famed for making sharp images, but they can be slow at sorting task work. The team's model, called cDAL, adds focus maps and a random code twist to the task.

A checker network runs at each step of the build and flags where the drawn outlines stray from real ones. Focus maps built from its reads steer the model toward the zones that matter most. A random code fed into each layer cuts the step count for both training and use. On three public scan sets, the model beat prior best scores for overlap and match.
arxiv-2502-07097:
Haque presents a 2025 physics paper testing a core belief about quantum energy teleportation. Ground states hold energy no one may simply extract. A two-step trick, though, pairs a measurement at one site with guided actions at another to pull energy out. Entanglement between sites is thought to be the fuel that always makes the trick work.

The toric code, a model quantum memory, breaks that belief. Haque measures spins there with a standard projective scheme. For the outcomes that arise, no local protocol at the far site completes the energy transfer. The result shows entanglement alone does not guarantee success; the shape of the correlation matters as much as its presence.
arxiv-2502-07197: Robert Auffarth and Sebastian Rahausen give a short 2025 note on lines that cut a Kummer variety in many points. The note works with a smooth projective curve and a special linear system on it, named in full in the text. From those data the authors build a map from the symmetric power of the curve toward that system. The fibres of the map link in a neat way to the multisecant lines of the variety. The result extends past work by the first author with two partners.
arxiv-2502-07597:
Leyun Gao, Alim Ruzi, Qite Li, Chen Zhou, and Qiang Li ask whether the spooky linked behavior of quantum particles can be tested with free-flying electron-positron pairs. Entanglement is well proven for confined electrons, but pairs traveling freely, especially at high energy, are hard to test because their spins are hard to measure.

The team studies pairs created in a fixed-target experiment, which gives a controlled source where linked events appear in known parts of the phase space. Knowing the state in advance, they show how each particle's spin pattern can be read from a second scattering off separate targets. Comparing those patterns would reveal the polarization links and allow a Bell test on the pairs.
arxiv-2502-07797:
Landslides fed by the slow warp of rock can wreck roads and towns, and a firm forecast needs maths that track the warp in three depths. Eric Ngondiep builds such a tool in a 2025 study. His method mixes a grid solve for space with a two step time march, tuned for a firm step size.

He proves the blend stays stable when the step rule holds and that its error shrinks at a set rate as the grid refines. Wide test runs back the proofs. He then turns the tool on real slides seen in the west and centre of Cameroon across the years from late 2019 to late 2024. The runs show how warp loads may grow a slide with time.
arxiv-2502-07997:
Carson Valdez and co-authors build light circuits that can cancel a signal with extreme precision in a 2025 paper. Such nulling, where two light waves erase each other, matters for sensing tasks such as imaging faint objects near bright ones. Making it work on a chip is hard because tiny build errors upset the balance.

Their design joins pairs of interferometers, devices that split and recombine light, into a mesh with built-in redundancy. A step-by-step tuning method then corrects for build flaws and stray reflections. On a silicon chip platform, the mesh reached cancellation levels above eighty decibels. The result points to compact photonic tools for astronomy and other jobs needing very high contrast.
arxiv-2502-08297:
Yu Hong and co-authors present BEAM, a pipeline that turns multi-camera footage of a moving person into a 3D video asset that can be relit, in a 2025 paper. Volumetric video lets viewers move around a captured scene, but most captures are stuck with the lighting of the day. Their pipeline rebuilds shape and surface traits using Gaussian splats, a fast rendering primitive.

Steps recover the performer's geometry over time, then add surface finish, shading, and color with the help of a diffusion model and a custom ray tracer. The finished asset drops into standard graphics pipelines for real-time or film-quality rendering. The authors aim at more flexible storytelling and shared virtual presence.
arxiv-2502-08597:
David Easley, Yoav Kolumbus, and Éva Tardos compare learning styles in asset markets in a paper from 2025. The catalog title carries a proceedings note, but the head title is clean, and the description follows the head. Bayesian learners update beliefs from a prior, while no-regret learners just minimize past mistakes. The authors link market survival ideas from economics with regret theory from computer science. A surprise emerges: very low regret does not guarantee survival.

A Bayesian rival with the true model in its prior can still drive a low-regret agent out. Yet Bayesian learning is fragile when its prior misses. Two hybrid strategies blend both styles for robustness. The work speaks to how mixed algorithms behave in real markets.
arxiv-2502-08697:
Bowen Li and co-authors teach robots to learn the very concepts they plan with, instead of receiving them from engineers. Bilevel planning lets a robot reason in abstract relational terms, then ground each step in motion. Its power depends on predicates, the learned or hand-made concepts like 'holding' or 'clear'. Hand-made ones do not scale to messy, high-dimensional worlds.

Their system, IVNTR, learns neural predicates straight from demonstrations. Symbolic learning of what each predicate does alternates with neural learning of how to recognize it, each guiding the other. A robot that invents its own planning vocabulary from watching could generalize chores to new kitchens, tools, and tasks.
arxiv-2502-08897:
Yukun He, Jiaoyang Huang, and Horng-Tzer Yau study Gaussian waves and edge eigenvectors of random regular graphs in two thousand twenty-five. Past work showed near eigenvectors of such graphs tend to Gaussian waves. The spread of those waves could sit anywhere in a set range. Their proof pins the edge case down in full.

For edge eigenvectors the variance must equal one, they show. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors also part ways in the limit. Their frame links Green's function behavior to eigenvector limits. That link may serve other problems in random matrix work. The proof is an alternate route to a known claim.
arxiv-2502-08997:
Luisa Gallée and co-authors make medical image classification explain itself in this 2025 paper. Doctors need to see why a model reached its call, above all in high-risk care. Their model, HierViT, reasons in steps a human can follow.

First it predicts visible traits that clinicians themselves use. Those trait calls then feed the final diagnosis. Each trait comes with prototype images, examples that show what the trait looks like. Attention maps mark the regions behind each trait. Together, the pieces give several views into one decision. Accuracy stays competitive, the authors report, while the reasoning stays open to audit.
arxiv-2502-09097:
Tianyi Huang and four co-authors build a fake news detector in twenty twenty-five. Their model is a transformer improved in two ways at once. A bidirectional gated recurrent unit is woven into the architecture. Bayesian optimization then tunes the combined model. The authors say this pairing is applied to fake news classification for the first time.

News text is first turned into numbers with TF-IDF features. Two experiment sets compare the designs. The recurrent-enhanced transformer alone reached very high test accuracy. Adding the Bayesian component nudged test accuracy slightly higher still. Training accuracy was perfect in both cases. Readers should note those near-ceiling scores when judging the claim. The work shows a hybrid stack squeezing the last fractions of accuracy from a benchmark.
arxiv-2502-09397:
Ardamon Sten, Paramita Dutta and Sudeep Kumar Ghosh study what dissipation does to a topological insulator Josephson junction, in work from 2025. Such junctions are a test bed where protected quantum states meet real-world loss. The team models loss as a leaky metal lead coupled to the junction, written as a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian from the Lindblad frame.

The Andreev spectrum turns lopsided: states gain finite lifetimes, one branch sinks below the gap and the famous zero-energy crossing moves off its usual phase point. Majorana states inherit the short life, losing their protection. The imbalance also drives a supercurrent at zero phase difference, an anomaly the authors flag for device design.
arxiv-2502-09497:
Zhaoyi Hou, Alejandro Ciuba, and Xiang Li improve automatic essay scoring by feeding language models linguistic features in this 2025 paper. Scoring engines split into two camps. Feature based systems score well but need heavy training for each new prompt set. Language model scorers run cheaply yet grade worse. The hybrid here hands the model the classic features, things like grammar and structure measures, beside the essay. The model then judges with evidence in view rather than from vibes.

Tests showed the hybrid beating both baselines, on prompts it trained on and on new ones. Cross prompt strength matters most in practice, since teachers will not retrain a grader for every assignment. The authors frame features as the model's missing homework: cheap, stable signals that free the language model to judge content. A scorer that travels across prompts is the deployable kind.
arxiv-2502-09597:
Siyan Zhao and co-authors test whether large language models follow a user's personal preferences in long chats. Their 2025 paper introduces PrefEval, a benchmark of three thousand curated preference and query pairs across twenty topics. Preferences appear in both plain and hidden forms, and models are judged by generation and classification tasks.

Ten open and closed models were tested in multi-session chats up to one hundred thousand tokens long. In plain settings, accuracy fell below ten percent after only ten turns for most models. Prompting tricks, repeated feedback, and retrieval help all failed to stop the slide in long contexts. The authors argue that true personalization remains an open problem for chat models.
arxiv-2502-09697:
Yanting Cheng and Shang Liu find a hidden symmetry in a stripped-down particle model in a 2025 paper. The Schwinger model, electrons chained to an electric field on a line, is a favorite testbed now that quantum simulators can build it. To fit the simulators, the field's values are cut to a short list, keeping the rules intact.

Within that cut model, flipping one sign in the rules turns a smooth phase change sharp. The border between the two behaviors is a special point ruled by supersymmetry, a deep particle-partner symmetry. A cousin model shows the same border. The finds give simulator builders new landmarks to aim their machines at.
arxiv-2502-09897:
Kehan Guo and co-authors survey in a 2025 paper how AI is changing work with spectra in chemistry. Instruments such as mass, magnetic, and light based tools pour out vast high dimension data. Expert led review can not keep pace, so smart automated study is in demand.

The survey unifies work that predicts a spectrum from a molecule and work that runs the other way. It traces the path from early pattern tools to large foundation models with strong reasoning. A map sorts net designs, from graph based to transformer based forms. Hard parts include data quality, mixing data types, and sheer scale of compute. New paths flagged include fake data, large scale pre training, and learning from few cases.
arxiv-2502-10097:
Hongye Cao and co-authors present a learning method for AI agents in a 2025 paper. Agents that learn by trial and error often waste many trials on blind exploration. The missing piece is cause and effect: which parts of a state and which actions actually drive rewards.

Their method, called CIP, maps those causal links and gives the strongest links priority. It creates extra training cases by asking what would have happened under changed key features. It also adds a goal that rewards actions with real influence on outcomes. Across 39 tasks in five test worlds, from walking to object handling, the method beat rival approaches. The gains held for both image-based tasks and tasks with sparse rewards.
arxiv-2502-10197:
Mislav Balunović and co-authors build a new test set for judging how well large language models do math. Their 2025 paper notes that many math tests use fixed answers, and models can pass them by guessing or by recall. Such tests also cover only a thin slice of real math work.

Their set, MathConstruct, holds 121 hard problems drawn from math contests. Each one asks the solver to build an object with stated traits, a form of proof used often in math. Right answers can be checked by machine, and the team can spin off changed forms of each problem to test how robust a model is. The best models solved only about six in ten problems.
arxiv-2502-10297:
Julien Siems and five co-authors present a new linear recurrent network design in a 2025 paper. Linear recurrent models rival transformers for sequence tasks while running faster, but their state transition matrices force a trade off between speed and power. Simple diagonal matrices are fast yet limited in what they can track.

Their design, called DeltaProduct, takes several small update steps per token instead of one. That yields richer transition matrices built from a product of reflection like transforms, with a knob to balance power against cost. Theory shows state tracking improves as steps increase, within finite precision limits. In tests, the model beat its predecessor on state tracking and language modeling, and handled longer sequences better.
arxiv-2502-10597:
