Huibing Dong, Wenlong Wang, Chun Liu, and David Du present a bucket-based learned index in a 2025 paper. Learned indexes use machine learning models to predict where a key sits in a sorted array, promising faster lookups than trees. Strict sorting makes insertion expensive, blocks lock-free concurrency, and punishes model inaccuracy.

Their index, BLI, is globally sorted but locally unsorted inside buckets. That relaxation eases updates and lets lookups and inserts run concurrently inside a node despite imperfect predictions. An updatable, concurrent learned index is what real database systems actually need.
arxiv-2502-10897:
Liu and colleagues found tangled filaments inside a fast hydrogen cloud in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Warm neutral gas was thought to churn too gently for filament networks. Using China's giant FAST telescope, the team mapped a cloud racing toward us at hundreds of kilometers per second. The twenty-one centimeter hydrogen line revealed its inner structure.

For the first time, such a cloud resolved into slim, velocity-coherent filaments. Curves, hubs, and webs layered through the data cube. The density pattern bore the skewed signature of shock compression. Simulations of supersonic magnetic turbulence reproduced the look. The authors propose that shocks alone can weave filaments in thin warm gas. That offers a route to structure in the young interstellar medium.
arxiv-2502-10997:
Ruihan Wu and Yu-Xiang Wang tighten the loss bound for private online choice learning, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. An open problem asked for the best case-wise rate when picks must stay differentially private. Prior bounds left a gap that grew with time rounds.

The new upper bound drops the time term and keeps only log terms in action count and privacy. A weaker fixed-loss setting is then solved exactly, with matching upper and lower bounds. That solved case guides where the main gap still sits. Readers in private learning get a sharper rate and a clean subproblem with a full answer.
arxiv-2502-11097:
The 2017 burst GRB 170817A looked odd because Earth viewed its jet from the side, seeing a narrow fast core wrapped in a slower, wider cocoon. Wang, Huang, and Liang model the burst light from electrons sped up by shear where the core and cocoon slide past each other. They ask how the viewing angle changes what an observer sees.

In their model the direct synchrotron glow peaks in the infrared and its upscattered part at hundreds of kiloelectronvolts, both fairly steady with angle. With a cocoon edge speed of 0.9 times light speed and a set viewing angle, the model matches the burst spectrum. Joint infrared and X-ray data can test it.
arxiv-2502-11197:
Tommy Mordo, Tomer Kordonsky, Haya Nachimovsky, Moshe Tennenholtz, and Oren Kurland present a 2025 paper on a simulator for ranking competitions where AI models do the competing. In search rankings, authors rewrite content to climb results, a contest older studies ran with students. Language models can now play the author role at scale.

Their simulator is highly configurable and ships with analysis tools for the contests it generates. Document authors, played by language models, react to past rankings and revise, round after round. The team generated several data sets and mined them for patterns: how content drifts, who wins, and what the ranking rewards. Code and data are public for other researchers.
arxiv-2502-11397:
Huabin Ge, Longsong Jia, and Faze Zhang work on a math question about angled pieces that fill a shape, in a paper from 2025. The shapes are triangulated forms that mimic three-dimensional spaces, called pseudo 3-manifolds. It is still not known whether every curved space of this kind admits such an angle layout.

The authors use a version of the layout that also tracks area and curve. They prove a test that tells exactly when such a layout exists. One payoff is that any compact curved space with a fully flat edge admits the layout. They also draw facts about the shape of the space itself from the mere fact that a layout exists.
arxiv-2502-11697:
Hanzhuo Huang and co-authors present MVTokenFlow, a 2025 method for turning one ordinary video into moving 3D content, called 4D. Makers want scenes that can be viewed from any angle while they move, but keeping every angle and every moment in agreement is hard. Shots drift apart in space or flicker in time.

Their method first uses a multi-view image generator to picture the scene from many angles at key moments, then rebuilds a rough 4D field from those views. Rendered flows from that field then guide a second pass that repaints all views, reusing tokens so pixels stay linked across time. The final refined field is sharper and steadier than the rough draft. In tests the method beat prior baselines on quality by a wide margin.
arxiv-2502-11797:
Sonja Kraiczy, Isaac Robinson, and Edith Elkind speed, in a 2025 paper, a fair-share vote rule for town spend picks. Towns let folk vote on which works get funds. The known rule, Equal Shares, splits the pot in a just way and runs in towns in Poland and Switzerland. Its flaw: it leaves cash on the table that could fund more works. The field fix pads the pot bit by bit till a stop mark, a slow trick that will not scale. The team works on a lean twin of the rule that keeps its good traits.

Their fix, add-opt, jumps straight to the next pot size where the result flips. They solve that jump in set time for two vote forms.
arxiv-2502-12197:
Norman Mu, Jonathan Lu, Michael Lavery, and David Wagner probe how well language models stick to their system prompts. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that system prompts set context, format, persona, and safety rules. Models often drop a guardrail or botch a clash between system and user demands. Robust holding to the prompt is thus a core safety trait.

The team built fresh test and training sets from real prompts in the GPT Store and HuggingChat. Realistic fine-tuning data lifted scores by a wide margin. Inference-time tricks, such as classifier-free guidance, helped too. New reasoning models from OpenAI and DeepSeek gained, but unevenly. The authors close that current tools fall short of sure robustness. More work is needed before system prompts can be trusted as hard rules.
arxiv-2502-12697:
Robin Vacus and Isabella Ziccardi design a leader election protocol for networks that can barely communicate, in a 2025 paper. In the beeping model, nodes can only beep or listen; in the stone-age model, they are nearly as limited. Their protocol uses just six internal states per node, needs no unique names, and assumes no knowledge of the network's size or shape. Under it, the system almost surely ends with exactly one node in the leader state.

That outcome arrives quickly with high probability, within a bound tied to the network's diameter. Knowing a rough diameter estimate speeds it further. The trade-offs are a slower finish than protocols with stronger assumptions, and nodes never learn that the election ended. The appeal is minimalism: election with almost nothing.
arxiv-2502-13097:
Olga Avsajanishvili tests in 2025 a cosmos model where neutrinos, ghostly light particles, change mass as the universe ages. In the model, the particles couple to a field whose energy drives the late expansion of space. She pits flat and curved forms of the model against the standard cosmos model.

Thirty two measures of how fast space expanded at past times set the test. Fit scores showed no firm gain for the new model over the standard one. Gaps in expansion history stayed small, within noise. One curved form did ease a known clash over today's expansion rate, thanks mostly to wide error bars.
arxiv-2502-13297:
Yunpeng Xiao, Youpeng Zhao, and Kai Shu argue that labels for personal views in text data are often wrong. Their 2025 study covers stance detection and topic-based sentiment, tasks tied to each person's outlook. Past datasets treat each text alone, which makes labels hard to judge and often flawed.

The authors set a new labeling rule that brings in other posts by the same person. They then re-labeled two datasets under that rule. Error rates in the old samples ran as high as roughly three in ten. Large language models scored well on the fixed data once personal context was added. The team urges future dataset builders to include such context from the start.
arxiv-2502-13497:
Language models often miss the norms of cultures far from their training data, and a 2025 paper by Piyawat Lertvittayakumjorn and co-authors tests two fixes. The team compared plain models with models fed facts from a custom knowledge base or from live web search.

Search-fed models scored much better on quiz-style tests of cultural facts, such as norms, objects, and institutions. The custom base helped less, held back by gaps in its coverage and weak retrieval. Yet search also raised the risk of flat, stereotyped judgments, and it did not improve how human raters judged open-ended replies. The authors draw a line between knowing cultural facts and showing real fluency in open talk.
arxiv-2502-13797:
Alessandro Caruso and five co-authors give graph neural networks a relay system for long-range messages. These networks learn from connected data, from molecules to social graphs, by passing notes between neighbors. Purely local passing chokes on big graphs: distant parts cannot hear each other, a flaw called oversquashing. Their 2025 framework, RANGE, adds special relay nodes that gather attention-weighted summaries and broadcast them back across the graph. The add-on fits existing models rather than replacing them.

Large molecules are a prime target, since weak far-apart forces shape their folds. Cheaper global talk could sharpen predictions without giant compute. The authors report strong gains over standard designs. Their relay idea treats the bottleneck as a routing problem, the same fix networks use everywhere.
arxiv-2502-13897:
Dan Zhang and co-authors present DataSciBench, a benchmark for AI agents doing data science, in a paper from 2025. Past benchmarks leaned on single tasks with easy answers and simple scores. Real data work mixes cleaning, modeling, and judgment under fuzzy ground truth.

The team curated hard, natural prompts across many task types. A semi-automated pipeline builds ground truth and checks the scoring metrics. Model self-consistency plus human review keep the answers honest. A Task-Function-Code framework grades agent work by what it computes, not just its final text. The benchmark pushes agent testing toward real analytic work. Labs can compare agents on tasks that resemble a working data scientist's week.
arxiv-2502-13997:
Ye Wang and five colleagues present SigStyle, a style transfer framework focused on an artist's signature style. Signature style means the recognizable traits of an image: geometric patterns, color palettes, and brush strokes. Earlier methods transfer style without explicitly capturing what makes a style distinctive.

SigStyle extracts that signature using the semantic priors inside a personalized text-to-image diffusion model. A hypernetwork fine-tunes the model efficiently from a single style image, and learned style tokens then reconstruct content images in that style. A time-aware attention swap preserves content during early denoising. Beyond standard transfer, the framework supports local transfer, texture transfer, style fusion, and style-guided generation, outperforming existing methods in evaluations.
arxiv-2502-14397:
Seven researchers teach a model to doodle on photos in an artist's style in a paper from 2025. The head title adds that the learning uses few-shot pairwise data, and the description follows the head. Doodles must blend with the photo, respect perspective, and keep the background intact. Earlier tools do global styling or local inpainting, not this. Training runs in two stages: a general editor first, then fine-tuning on a small set of an artist's before-and-after pairs.

A positional encoding trick keeps results consistent. The team also releases a data set with six curated styles. Experiments show strong, robust customized editing. The authors aim to widen what solo artists can produce.
arxiv-2502-14597:
Zhong-Liang Zhang and co-authors improve support vector machines for multi-class problems with lopsided data in this 2025 paper. The classic method assumes two classes of similar size. Real data often hold many classes, most of them rare. Their improved model prices errors by class to fight the imbalance. It also reshapes the separation margin inside its rules. Class pairs are then trained one against one.

An evolution-based optimizer tunes the many parameters that result. That search turns the setup into one large optimization problem. Rare classes stand a fair chance under cost-sensitive training. Fraud, faults, and rare diseases all show this data shape. The paper is a machine learning methods study. Benchmarks in the full text test the approach.
arxiv-2502-14697:
Raffaele Resta rethinks quantum geometry for moving systems in this 2025 physics paper. The ground state geometry of a material explains many still and slow changing traits, while truly dynamic behavior is usually handled with formulas that lean on excited states.

Resta shows the ground state metric and curvature tensor can be carried forward in time by a causal unitary operator, which packs the excited states' geometric effect into compact form. For materials, the widened tensor then covers the whole conductivity tensor at any frequency, in insulators and metals alike. One piece escapes: the Drude term of metals, which the paper shows is not geometric at all.
arxiv-2502-14897:
Hamid Moradi-Kamali and colleagues labeled crypto tweets by what the market did next in a 2025 study. Sentiment tools usually ask human readers whether a post sounds upbeat or downbeat, then assume price follows feelings. The authors argue that words move markets in ways readers cannot reliably guess, so past market reactions make a better teacher than opinion labels.

A finance-tuned language model trained on market-derived labels beat classic sentiment benchmarks on short-term trend calls by a clear margin. Adding market and timing context through prompt tuning pushed accuracy higher still on a curated set of major Bitcoin news events. Traders get a signal grounded in outcomes, not impressions.
arxiv-2502-15097:
Anil Ramakrishna and co-authors build LUME, a benchmark for testing whether a language model can truly forget set material without full retraining. Their 2025 paper works in machine unlearning, aimed at copyrighted, sensitive, or private text. Judging unlearning needs more than one kind of target, so the bench carries three.

The tasks ask models to drop invented short novels, invented biographies laced with private details, and a set of real public biographies. Two fine-tuned target models, at one and seven billion parameters, ship with the bench. The team ran several recent unlearning algorithms through it with tuned metrics. The results expose where each method holds and where forgotten content leaks back.
arxiv-2502-15197:
Zhaoxuan Wu and a team of co-authors present a method to speed up large language models, in two thousand twenty-five. Their method is called TETRIS, and it works when many requests are served at once. A fast draft step proposes words, and a larger model then checks them in parallel.

Older methods pick draft words for one request, or for a whole group at once. TETRIS picks the most promising draft words for each request in the batch. That choice means fewer words are rejected and less computing power is wasted. Tests and theory both showed higher acceptance rates than the older ways, which matters for providers with limited capacity.
arxiv-2502-15297:
A black hole hidden behind dust cannot be weighed by the usual tricks. Sathwik Narkedimilli and co-authors race a stable of algorithms at the problem. Their testbed holds type-2 active galaxies, whose central engines are obscured. Classical methods, from linear regression to deep networks, compete against quantum machine learning models. Scores cover error size and fit quality across many runs.

Classical algorithms won overall. A long short-term memory network took the best classical result, near ninety-nine point eight percent accuracy. Among quantum entries, an estimator-based quantum network scored best, close behind the classical champion. The comparison maps where quantum methods stand today: promising, competitive in spots, but not yet ahead. Galaxy evolution studies need black hole masses in bulk, so even small accuracy gains matter.
arxiv-2502-15397:
Holographic microscopes record interference patterns that can be turned into phase images of tiny samples, but their sharpness is limited by diffraction. The authors test whether super-resolution software, which rebuilds a detailed image from a coarse one, can help. They used a laboratory interferometer to capture patterns from a microparticle sample. Two models were compared: RCAN and Real-ESRGAN. The team judged them both on image detail and on whether the sample's shape and phase values stayed accurate.

RCAN gave the better numbers, making it the safer choice when the phase map itself must be measured precisely. Real-ESRGAN gave cleaner looking structure, which suits work where viewing matters most. The authors conclude that super-resolution can push holographic microscopy past its usual limits. They point to medical testing and materials work as fields that could gain from sharper phase images.
arxiv-2502-15497:
Kalyani Shaji and co-authors track how heat treatment changes thin films used to sense hydrogen gas, in work from 2025. The films are made of nanoparticles of two metal oxides, alone and in alternating layers. They were laid down by a magnetron based gas method and then baked in synthetic air.

Baking ran across a range of a few hundred degrees. Microscopy and several spectroscopy tools charted how the tiny structure evolved. The copper oxide films changed most, with clearer crystals and larger particles as heat rose. The other films stayed more stable. Knowing these shifts helps tune sensors that must survive heat before use.
arxiv-2502-15597:
Data science already follows the FAIR rules, which ask that data be findable, reachable, shared in common formats, and reusable. A large team of modelers argues in 2025 that computer models of living systems deserve rules of their own. They propose CURE: models should be credible, understandable, reproducible, and extensible. Each word unpacks into checks. Credibility needs verification, validation, and honest uncertainty. Understandability needs clear write-ups and labels.

Reproducibility leans on standards and open practice, while extensibility asks for open formats and code built in modules. The authors set baseline and stronger requirements for each point. Their target is trust, above all in medical models where a wrong answer can harm a patient.
arxiv-2502-15697:
Zexu Sun and co-authors build a sturdier way to pick which shoppers should get a perk, in real time. Their 2025 paper deals with uplift modeling, which forecasts who will respond to a treat such as a discount. On live platforms, the treat lands on a user viewing a specific item, so item context counts. Models that read user traits alone give biased calls, while bolting on vast context raw can skew the treat and control groups.

Their framework works with any base model through two add-ons. One groups contexts by how users respond, to shrink the context space. One models how user, context, and treat traits interact. Tests span made data and a real product set.
arxiv-2502-16097:
Haoxiang Fan and co-authors help teachers link literature to other subjects in a 2025 paper. Elementary schools now often teach stories through science, art, or other fields. Building such links asks teachers to sift huge piles of outside material and tie it to the text. Their tool, LitLinker, was shaped with 13 teachers in repeated design rounds.

A large language model powers the tool. It suggests cross-subject topics and ties them to parts of the story, such as key passages or views. In a study with 16 teachers, the tool beat a plain chat model on depth of subject blending, and it cut workload. Nine experts also rated it useful. The authors close with care points for AI help in cross-subject teaching.
arxiv-2502-16497:
Haiye Guo and Yunhua Zhou study whether a class of chaotic systems stays predictable when orderly behavior fades near an edge. The systems are hyperbolic, meaning nearby paths split apart in a steady, structured way, but only point by point on an open region of a curved space. Near the region's boundary, that clean splitting can weaken.

The authors extend two classic tools to this weaker setting. They build a version of expansiveness, which says distinct paths must separate visibly at some point, and a shadowing result, which says a rough path is always tracked by a true one. Together these give a stability result for pointwise hyperbolic systems, much like the classic theorem for fully hyperbolic ones. The work serves pure research on how motion behaves on curved spaces.
arxiv-2502-16697:
Laurin Lux and co-authors build an eye disease predictor doctors can follow. Neural networks stage diabetic eye damage from scans with high accuracy, but their reasoning is a black box. Clinicians fall back on simple measured markers, losing much of the image's detail. The team's method turns each scan into a graph whose parts mirror biology: vessel segments, the gaps between fine vessels, and the vessel-free zone at vision's center.

A graph model then stages the disease from that structure. In tests, its agreement with clinical staging matched the accuracy of image-based rivals, around eighty-four percent on the standard scale. The win is explanation: the graph points to abnormal vessels and starved patches behind a call. The authors say this detail can flag patients needing special attention. The approach works from the detail-rich scan type photo methods cannot use fully.
arxiv-2502-16797:
Erik Jones and co-authors present a method to forecast rare, risky behavior in language models before wide release. Their 2025 paper notes a blind spot in standard tests: a model can look safe in a small trial yet give harmful help once it faces billions of requests.

For each test prompt, the team measures how likely it is to draw out the target behavior. They show that the largest such values grow in a predictable way as the number of prompts rises. Their forecasts tracked the rise of harmful outputs across up to a thousand-fold growth in prompt volume. Developers could use the method to patch rare faults before launch.
arxiv-2502-16897:
Jiatong Shi and co-authors teach a text model to speak and listen in a 2025 paper. Speech language models extend text models to audio. Codec tokens, compressed audio codes, carry the sound. Balancing understanding and generation in one model is hard, since the two skills pull apart.

Continual pre-training adapts the text model to codec speech step by step. The unified model then handles speech recognition, synthesis, and speech-to-text and speech-to-speech translation. Their speech-to-speech system runs in one pass with codec tokens alone. No text detour is needed mid-task. The training step proves key for cross-modal alignment and task spread.
arxiv-2502-17197:
Asghar Ullah, Marco Cattaneo, and Özgür Müstecaplıoğlu study how a single quantum bit can serve as a thermometer when two bits share a common bath, in a 2025 paper. Each bit also leaks into its own local bath. The team asks how exact a lone probe can be when it gauges the shared bath's heat, and when it gauges a local one.

Shared effects from the common bath can sharpen the probe, above all when the second bit is tuned to match it. Local baths can hurt or, if cold enough, help. The pair can even sense a bath remotely: one bit reads the heat of the other's bath through their shared link, with no direct contact.
arxiv-2502-17297:
Zhenghao Liu and co-authors benchmark retrieval-augmented generation in multimodal settings in a 2025 paper. Big vision-language models read images and text well, but their skill at using retrieved mixed-media documents was largely unexplored.

Their benchmark, M2RAG, spans four open-domain tasks: image captioning, multimodal question answering, fact checking with mixed evidence, and image reranking. Each task forces the model to fetch relevant documents and reason over them. The team also built an instruction tuning method that trains models to use such context better. Tuned models improved response quality sharply, beating two known systems by about a third. Data and code are public, giving the field a shared yardstick for multimodal retrieval use.
arxiv-2502-17397:
Yoeri Poels and four co-authors, with two large fusion teams, present a study from twenty twenty-five on sorting plasma states in a tokamak. High energy yield needs strong confinement, which comes in distinct modes. Auto labels for these modes aid big studies and live control. Modes blur near shifts, and sensors can fail or drop out.

The team blends many data driven models, mixed by both model type and sensor group. One model type tracks change over time; the other uses boosted trees on fixed traits. A fully labeled set of just over three hundred runs will be shared in public. Scores show the blend sorts the three modes well. It also copes with lost signals and gives trust scores with its calls.
arxiv-2502-17897:
Mu Jia, Junting Chen, Ying-Chang Liang, and Pooi-Yuen Kam derive best detectors for steady-envelope signals in mobile edge gear, in work from twenty twenty-five. Steady-envelope signals suit cheap, low-power hardware and hold up well in use. Sharp detection with simple receivers stays hard, though. Tuned methods need complex sync steps that burn power and bulk. Simple envelope methods lack firm theory for their common choices.

The team builds an optimal frame around a bandpass envelope detector. At low signal strength, the classic energy detector is proved optimal for the first time. At high strength, a new amplitude detector wins with a simple rule. For unknown strength, a smart rule picks the right detector per case. Mock tests confirm each detector errs least in its own zone. The smart rule adds robust gains across the full range.
arxiv-2502-18197:
Gianluigi Silvestri and co-authors improved in 2025 the training of consistency models, the fast image generators that skip the long denoising march of diffusion models. Training them from scratch is notoriously jumpy. Their fix borrows from variational autoencoders: an encoder learns how each training image should be paired with its noise.

Learned pairings replace the fixed, arbitrary ones of the standard recipe, and the training steadies. The scheme plugs into several forward processes, including flow matching. On standard image sets the method set the best quality score among from-scratch consistency models on one benchmark. It matched the best on a larger set while sampling in just two steps. The authors release the code. Fast generators, they argue, should also be calm to train.
arxiv-2502-18297:
Zeju Li and co-authors release DeepCircuitX, a dataset built to teach language models the register-transfer level code that describes computer chips. Older datasets stop at single files or jump straight to physical layouts. This one spans whole repositories down through files, modules, and blocks. It adds step-by-step reasoning notes on function and structure at each level, plus synthesized netlists and power, performance, and area figures.

Models fine-tuned on the dataset improved at understanding, writing, and completing chip code, and at predicting those quality figures early in design. Human judges confirmed the gains. Early prediction matters because chip teams must trade power against speed before any layout exists. The authors present the dataset as core training material for machine learning in hardware design automation.
arxiv-2502-18397:
Jinyuan Fang, Zaiqiao Meng, and Craig Macdonald present a better search step for question answering in this 2025 paper. Some systems answer hard questions by searching, reading, and searching again in rounds. That loop can be thrown off by off-topic pages or by flawed lines of thought, and the search step may miss what the next round needs.

Their system, called KiRAG, breaks pages into small fact triples before the search rounds begin. It searches with those triples, which keeps the facts more sound. It also reasons during the search to spot gaps and fetch what fills them. On multi-step question tests, the system beat prior versions by clear margins.
arxiv-2502-18597:
Rikako Yamamoto, Luke Alexander Turnbull, and Marcus Schmidt lead a large team on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It gives bulk evidence for altermagnetism in MnTe, a leading hope for this new kind of magnetism.

Most past checks used thin films or surfaces, so the bulk case stayed open. The team cut a thin slice from a single crystal and shot X-rays through it, mapping magnetic domains at the nanoscale. The signal matched the marks that altermagnetic order should give, in both shape and size. Since the slice is thick, the order must run through the bulk, not just the skin. The method now stands as a tool for screening other hopes.
arxiv-2502-19297:
Teams of learning agents struggle because the world they share keeps shifting as each agent learns, and the joint choices explode in number. Nikhilesh Prabhakar and four co-authors propose a hybrid in this 2025 paper. A classical planner acts as the team's central controller, while reinforcement learning fills in what the planner cannot fix in advance.

The domains in view are relational, meaning objects and their links define the state, and expert knowledge about those links is often available but unused by standard methods. The planner uses compact state summaries, which trims the search and makes learning faster. The authors report that the blend learns from fewer tries than plain multi-agent learning. It also carries skills to new tasks more readily, a weak point of methods that learn each task from scratch.
arxiv-2502-19397:
Anna Thöni and four co-authors blend classic math models of chemical reaction nets with deep learning, in a paper from 2025. Such nets are tracked with equations for how each chemical level changes over time, but those equations rest on hand built guesses that may miss key parts.

Their method fits a neural form of those equations to data, letting the net learn what the hand model left out. Gaps between the learned form and the old form flag where the old model falls short. The authors say the blend can both test old models and guide the design of new reaction nets.
arxiv-2502-19897:
Yuxuan Yan and co-authors propose a clustering method that joins two classic views in 2025. Global clustering scores a whole split at once but can yield coarse groups. Local clustering leans on fine links between points but can lack coherence and speed. Their method, built on graphs, treats group membership as a probability.

The graph based fuzzy method merges a global goal with a local constraint. The full problem is cast as a multi constraint optimization task. A standard Lagrange approach solves it step by step. The blend aims to keep groups both tight up close and sound at the whole data scale.
arxiv-2502-20097:
Rickard Karlsson, Bram van den Akker, Felipe Moraes, Hugo Proença, and Jesse Krijthe study Qini curves when treated units interfere with each other, in a two thousand twenty-five statistics paper. Qini curves weigh a treatment policy's incremental gain against its implementation cost.

Standard estimation assumes one person's treatment never affects another's outcome. In marketing and public policy that assumption fails, and ignoring interference biases the curves. The authors formalize clustered network interference, where interfering units form independent clusters, and propose three estimation strategies suited to different conditions. A marketplace simulator mimicking an e-commerce setting lets them compare the strategies and their bias-variance trade-offs in practice.
arxiv-2502-20197:
Schoeberl presents a 2025 paper on simple RISC-V processors built for teaching and small devices. Architecture courses usually teach a five-stage pipeline from 1980s practice. Schoeberl argues that design is neither the fastest nor the easiest to learn today. The paper builds several pipeline shapes in FPGA hardware and in a real chip process.

Costs and top clock speeds were measured for each shape. Longer pipelines did not always run faster, contrary to common belief. A fat forwarding switch on the main path slowed the four and five-stage builds below the three-stage one. The author backs three stages for teaching and for embedded chips alike.
arxiv-2502-20297:
Virgile Guémard and Gilles Zémor build new families of quantum error-correcting codes. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Quantum Tanner codes pair two classical codes on graphs drawn from surfaces. Lifting a code to a covering space makes longer codes from short ones. The authors study lifts of odd index. They adapt tools from cellular homology to track the symmetries involved.

For any odd lift, the new code keeps at least the old dimension. Its distance is capped by the index times the old distance. When the dimension stays equal, the distance is at least the old one. These bounds also cover an earlier lifting method by Guémard. Several explicit families close the paper. Moderate lengths make the codes plausible for real hardware tests.
arxiv-2502-20497:
Chen and co-authors presented a 2025 paper on recommender systems, the software that picks what users see on video and shopping apps. Most such systems serve the viewer, so a few items get most views while many get almost none. Creators who get little feedback lose interest, which harms the platform over time. The team instead builds for the creator side.

Their system, called DualRec, finds the best users for each item rather than the best items for each user. Known viewer-side methods can be adapted with small changes, they show. A new module also checks whether a user is likely to be active. The system runs on the Kwai video app and improved results there.
arxiv-2502-20597: Ali Hamad wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on ultracategories, a structure from category theory built to hold limit operations of infinite size. A conjecture by Shulman held that these structures, as defined by Lurie, are a kind of loose algebra over a monad-like structure on the universe of categories. Hamad proves that claim. Under this view, the two flavours of functors between ultracategories also fall out as the natural loose and tight maps between such algebras.
arxiv-2502-20697:
Andrew Eberhardt, Elisa Ferreira, Wentao Luo, Shurui Lin, and Yin Li study a faint bending of starlight by halos of very light dark matter, in work from 2025. In this model, dark matter forms grainy, waving patterns inside halos. Stars seen through a halo should twinkle in brightness as the grains shift.

The grains shift on a set time scale tied to the particle mass. The team works out how strong the bending signal should be and how it varies in time. They count both the loose grains and the dense core that sits at the halo center. From those results, they judge how star surveys could bound the mass and share of this dark matter kind.
arxiv-2502-20797:
Rob den Teuling and five colleagues derive formulas for spin waves in the van der Waals magnet CrSBr, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. They treat both monolayers and antiferromagnetically coupled bilayers. An in-plane external magnetic field is applied throughout. The analysis spans antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, and canted phases of the material.

Closed-form expressions give the spin wave frequencies and precession amplitudes in each phase. Frequencies prove tunable by the applied field in all phases. The authors dissect what controls the magnetization dynamics. Intra- and interlayer exchange interactions both matter. So do triaxial anisotropy and intralayer dynamic dipolar fields. The results give experimentalists a map for interpreting spin wave measurements in this layered magnet.
arxiv-2502-20897:
Matthias Orlikowski and five co-authors ask whether language models can learn to judge text the way specific people do, in a 2025 study. People disagree on touchy labeling tasks, and part of that spread tracks who they are: age, background, and outlook. Models prompted with such traits label poorly, which suggests shallow social knowledge.

The team fine-tuned models on a curated set of five tasks with standardized annotator backgrounds. Prompting gains did appear after training, but the sleuthing matters: most of the gain came from the models memorizing each annotator’s habits, not from learning group patterns. The lesson tempers claims that models can stand in for demographic groups. Simulated publics may mostly be memorized individuals.
arxiv-2502-20997:
Security teams worldwide share threat reports in standard formats, but disinformation campaigns have no such shared language. Felipe Sánchez González, Javier Pastor-Galindo, and José Ruipérez-Valiente build one in 2025, adapting the machinery of cyber threat intelligence.

Their framework describes a disinformation incident with the DISARM playbook of tactics and techniques, then translates it into the STIX2 data standard that security tools already speak. A platform called DISINFOX stores the incidents and serves them to client tools. The team validated the pipeline with more than one hundred real incidents, each modeled, stored, shared, and consumed without loss. They present it as the first working bridge of its kind.
arxiv-2502-21197:
Lars Rohwedder and Leander Schnaars give a better scheduling algorithm for bundles of data flows in computer networks, in a 2025 paper. A coflow is a set of flows that must all finish before a job counts as done, as in shuffled data between servers. Schedulers want the average finishing time low. The best known plans could overshoot the ideal by a factor of four, or five when jobs arrive over time.

Their plan overshoots by a factor under three and a half, and by about four point four with release dates. In the long run of large inputs, it nears a factor of two, which is as good as possible unless a famous math guess fails. The gains come from a new edge-sharing scheme and repeated rounding of a relaxed plan. The result closes a question posed by several earlier teams.
arxiv-2503-00197:
Beatrice Moscoloni and co-authors map how male and female hearts differ in shape in this 2025 study. Heart disease shows clear sex gaps, but plain size scaling hides much of the anatomy. The team built three-dimensional shape models from scans of 456 healthy adults in a large British health archive, and tested shape against age, blood pressure, and body size.

Sex alone explained at least a quarter of all shape variation. Models could tell male from female hearts with high accuracy even after body size was factored out. The clearest gaps lay in chamber volumes, the width of the right lower chamber, and how the chambers sit next to each other. The authors argue that heart checks and risk scores should use sex-specific norms, not one shared standard.
arxiv-2503-00597:
Jayanth Mohan, Jishnu Chowdhury, Tomas Malik, and Cornelia Caragea test how well large language models can name the key topics of a document. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Such keyphrases sum up a text for search and sorting. The team used the models with no task-specific training at all.

They tried two open models and one closed commercial model. First, they varied the instructions given to the models, adding task-specific detail. Clearer instructions helped a good deal. Second, they borrowed the trick of sampling many answers and merging the best parts. That step also beat the plain baseline by a wide margin. The study shows prompt design matters as much as model size here.
arxiv-2503-00697:
Yiyang Lin and co-authors build a system that converts quick frozen-section tissue images into the richer style of standard processed slides. Their 2025 paper serves pathologists during surgery, who judge tumors from frozen sections. Those fast images suffer contamination and blurry nuclei, while the high-quality preparation takes far too long for the operating room.

Their framework transfers stain style while repairing detail. One module borrows tissue information across image resolutions to offset contamination losses. Another works in a wavelet form to guide fine detail, sharpening nuclear structure. On their data set, the method beat all competing approaches. Cleaner intraoperative images could steady the benign-versus-malignant calls that decide how much tissue a surgeon removes.
arxiv-2503-00897:
Fine-tuning image generators with reinforcement learning can steer them toward goals that resist direct scoring, yet the standard method, PPO, is touchy and costly. Shashank Gupta and co-authors study the trade-off between two classic approaches. REINFORCE is simpler and lighter but noisy and wasteful with samples, while PPO is steadier but heavy and sensitive to its settings.

Their answer is a hybrid called leave-one-out PPO, or LOOP. From REINFORCE it borrows drawing several images per prompt and correcting scores against a baseline built by leaving one sample out. From PPO it takes clipping and importance sampling, which keep updates stable and reuse data well. Across several black-box goals, LOOP improved the generators while using samples better than either parent method. The authors present it as a practical balance between efficiency and final image quality.
arxiv-2503-01297:
Anmol Biswas and co-authors present a training framework that prepares neural networks for cheap, imperfect hardware. Edge devices save power by computing in few bits and storing weights in analog memory, but those choices bring stuck bits and device-to-device variation. The framework uses regularisation during training to ready a model for all three problems at once. It handles fixed, learnable, and non-uniform quantisation schemes, and it also works for spiking networks.

On standard image sets the method matched strong results at 3 and 4 bits, including event-camera data for the spiking version. Its fine-tuning then recovered performance under damage that defeats earlier fault-aware methods: up to 20 percent of bits stuck and 40 percent variation between devices. The authors offer the framework as a general route to models that stay reliable on low-power, non-ideal chips.
arxiv-2503-01397:
Farhana Javed and Josep Mangues-Bafalluy measure how fast smart contracts settle on a live Ethereum test network, in a 2025 paper. Their application hosts agreements between telecom providers sharing 6G resources, in two phases: preliminary deals and enforcement. Four contracts split the phases. Gas fees, block size, and traffic volume were all varied and timed.

Most transactions finalized within thirty seconds, with medians from eleven to twenty-four seconds. Crowded blocks swamped fee effects when the contract logic was heavy. When logic was light, fees decided the pace. Statistical tests confirmed both patterns strongly. The authors advise matching fee strategy to contract complexity when designing such marketplaces.
arxiv-2503-01497:
Ramkrishna Acharya presents a method for drawing in the air with a finger in this 2025 paper. A camera watches the hand, and strokes appear on screen. Such input could serve sign language, sketching, and hands free writing. The method uses classic image processing rather than deep learning.

First, the system learns the background from early frames. It then subtracts that background from live frames to find the moving hand. A hand detector cuts false shapes before that step. The fingertip is taken as the top of the hand outline, and a dot is drawn there. Drawn text can be read by an optical character tool. Tests reached a delay of only 100 milliseconds, fast enough for natural use.
arxiv-2503-01597:
Fangchao Liu and co-authors design a muon beam line for a facility in China in a 2025 paper. Muons are short lived particles used in physics and materials tests. A beam that pulses about fifty thousand times a second could sharpen those tests, and the SHINE facility's electron beam offers a way to make one.

Computer runs show that an electron beam hitting a copper target could yield up to two thousand muons per pulse. With tuned parts, about sixty surface muons per bunch would reach the end of the line. That rate rivals current muon sites. The team also flags a main snag, clearing away a flood of positrons, and sketches a fix.
arxiv-2503-01697:
Da-Jian Zhang and his co-author presented Krylov shadow tomography in 2025, a way to estimate quantum Fisher information. That quantity measures how much a quantum state can reveal about a parameter, and it is central to sensing. For large systems it is very hard to compute because of its nonlinear form.

Their method joins a classic subspace tool from applied math with shadow tomography, a scheme that learns from few measurements. It yields a ladder of lower bounds on the quantity, and the top bound equals the quantity itself. Each bound can be written as an average of simple matrix values that shadow methods can reach. The result offers a practical path for lab use.
arxiv-2503-01797:
Benjamin Woods shows how a hidden valley degree of freedom can flip the sign of a key interaction for silicon spin qubits in a 2025 paper. Exchange coupling between two electrons normally cannot go negative without a magnetic field, and that restriction blocks some error-corrected gate designs. Silicon quantum dots, though, carry valley states whose phases differ from dot to dot.

Those phase differences act like a discrete gauge field in the low-energy theory, and the paper shows they can drive the exchange negative. The same field can break a classic ferromagnetic state, and its strength can be tuned by changing how electrons fill the dot array. The result offers new tools for exchange-based quantum computing and a fresh setting for quantum magnetism.
arxiv-2503-01997:
Bryce Cousins and six co-authors make the first measurement of the universe's expansion rate from the hum of merging black holes. Their 2025 paper uses the stochastic background, the combined murmur of countless distant mergers too faint to pick out one by one. That murmur depends on the expansion history, so it carries the Hubble constant within it.

Standard siren methods use single loud mergers with known distances. This team instead combine the known mergers with the telling fact that the background has not yet been detected. That silence itself sets a floor: the longer the hum stays hidden, the higher the lower bound on the expansion rate climbs. Their joint method already beats the accuracy of resolved mergers alone. It also stands apart from light-based measures in the Hubble tension debate.
arxiv-2503-02097:
Naveen Srinivasan, Nathan Naveen, and Neil Naveen present a kernel level watch tool that records what a software build truly uses, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Lists of parts that ship with software are often wrong. They miss files loaded on the fly and count files never used, which hides risks.

Their tool, Bomfather, sits in the system core and watches each file a build opens, as it happens. It stamps each file with a tamper proof hash and builds a tree of proof from the file contents. Unlike static scans, the watch catches choices made mid build, dead code, and parts loaded late. The result is a parts list and a graph of links that others can check on their own, which sharpens the hunt for flaws.
arxiv-2503-02297:
Arun Yadav, Partha Bhaduri, and Subhasis Chattopadhyay revisit how flow patterns in nuclear collisions reveal the fluid's traits, in a 2025 paper. When heavy nuclei smash at high energy, the matter flows in an oval pattern. How far that pattern falls short of a perfect fluid limit tells about the matter's thickness. The team used data from a major collider detector pair.

They rechecked the formulas used to extract key ratios from the flow data. Two models of the starting collision shape gave different answers. Even the most head-on lead collisions fell well short of the perfect fluid limit. Alternative math forms for the link were tested in depth. Extracted thickness values hinged heavily on starting shape choices. The authors stress that clearing up the initial state is essential for firm claims.
arxiv-2503-02397:
Adnan Ali, Jinglong Li, Huanhuan Chen, and AlMotasem Al Ajlouni presented in 2025 a social network dataset built for binary classification with graph machine learning. Benchmark sets for graph learning cover citations, co-occurrence, and shopping networks, with many classes, but no social network set for two-class tasks existed. Their dataset, BiSND, fills that gap.

BiSND is offered in both tabular and graph forms. The team tested it with classic classifiers such as decision trees and random forests, a deep neural network, a graph convolutional network, and three graph contrastive learning methods. Scores landed in a narrow, promising range, which suggests the set is sound for classification while leaving room for better methods.
arxiv-2503-02497:
Chat models write fair code in common tongues and stumble in quantum ones, where good samples are scarce. Abdul Basit and six co-authors stock the shelf in 2025 for one quantum tongue, PennyLane. Their set holds near thirty-three hundred code samples with tales of what each does, gleaned from books, docs, and open stores. A build frame kept the gleaning, tagging, and shaping even.

Fed to models through a fetch-first pipe, the set lifted pass rates hard. One small model leapt from under one in ten to over four in ten on quantum tasks. A big model gained less but shed false steps. The team post the set and the frame, and frame both as the fix for niche tongues beyond the quantum one.
arxiv-2503-02597:
Wei-Yao Wang and co-authors fix a one-way flaw in models that read images and text in a 2025 paper. Most such models are built on text decoders that let each token look only backward. Image tokens come first, so they can never take in the words that follow. That one-way flow can leave answers out of step with the picture.

Their design opens the flow both ways between the two kinds of tokens. Image tokens can now attend to text tokens, and text to image, in what they call modality-mutual attention. The change adds no new parameters. Across twelve tests of image and text understanding, scores rose by about six percent on average, over three model backbones. The authors offer the design as a general fix for models that mix many input kinds.
arxiv-2503-02697:
Guohui Guan, Jiaqi Hu, and Zongxia Liang study saving and investing when people value liquid wealth in this 2025 paper. Their agent holds a bond, a liquid risky asset, and an illiquid risky asset. Selling the illiquid asset costs a share of its value. The agent also gains utility from holding liquid wealth itself, not just from spending.

The team maps the decision space into buying, holding, and selling zones for the illiquid asset. All three zones are shown to be nonempty. The best policy is derived in theory and computed in numbers. Valuing liquidity makes the agent hold more liquid wealth and spend less. It can even lead to a short position in the illiquid asset. Risk aversion shapes whether liquidity raises or lowers spending.
arxiv-2503-02797:
Nathan Drenkow and Mathias Unberath align image quality metrics with network robustness causally in a 2025 paper. Image quality strongly affects vision model performance. Standard quality metrics track human perception instead. A metric predicting machine performance would serve different needs.

The authors first ask whether standard metrics predict model accuracy. Theory and experiments both say they predict weakly. Classification accuracy barely follows perceptual quality scores. A causal framework then explains the mismatch structure. New metrics built on it correlate strongly with performance. Large image collections can be scored against a target task. Dataset curation gains a model-aware quality lens. Imaging condition changes are the causal levers studied. Robustness testing benefits from knowing which degradations matter. The paper reframes quality as task-relative, not human-relative.
arxiv-2503-02897:
Hong Lu, Yali Bian, and Rahul Shah built in 2025 a grader that checks object-detection labels with a vision-language model. Good box labels are dear to make and hard to audit. Their tool, ClipGrader, adapts the CLIP model to judge both whether a box's class is right and whether the box sits tight. Tests used data sets with boxes shifted on purpose.

On COCO the grader hit ninety-one percent accuracy with few false alarms. Trained on a tenth of the data it still held eighty-seven percent. On the far larger LVIS set it reached seventy-nine percent across more than a thousand classes. It also caught real errors in COCO labels, and feeding its grades into semi-supervised training lifted detection scores.
arxiv-2503-02997:
Can Firtina's 2025 dissertation tackles a core problem in genome analysis: sequencing data are noisy, and the noise slows down fast, accurate reading of genomes. High-throughput machines now produce huge amounts of data, but unwanted variation in that data limits how well it can be scaled and trusted. The dissertation studies the types of noise first, then builds tools to reduce their effect.

Four tools anchor the work. BLEND finds matching and near-matching sequences with a single hash lookup. RawHash and RawHash2 analyze raw nanopore signals in real time, and Rawsamble overlaps raw signals directly to build assemblies without first converting them to letters. Together they open faster paths for genome work.
arxiv-2503-03697:
John Sunil, Richard Blythe, Martin Evans, and Satya Majumdar wrote a 2025 paper on the cost of a wandering search. Their model is a random walker that jumps step by step and, now and then, restarts from home. Each jump and each restart carries a cost, like time or fuel. They ask how the total cost of reaching a target is spread out.

Using a backward equation for the walk, they turn the problem into an integral equation of a classic form. They solve it exactly for broad choices of jump cost and some restart costs. For one key case, where jumps mimic run-and-tumble motion like that of bacteria, the equation shrinks to a simpler one that is easy to solve. The results show whether restarts or long jumps drive up the final bill.
arxiv-2503-03897:
Maria Parilli, Sergi Martinez, and Carlos Mastalli give a new way to hold end-point rules in a class of control methods for robots. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The base method plans a path by steps of slope, and is used in live control and fast solvers. Past ways to add end rules were rough or slow. The new way is exact and settles at a fast, squared rate. It copes with rank gaps in both end and step rules. It works for both ways of stating a robot's motion. The team shows it on a broad set of robot tasks, with code shared in a known solver.
arxiv-2503-04297:
Coline Emprin and Alex Takeda study when spheres count as coformal in a refined algebraic sense. Their 2025 paper builds a properad, a rulebook for operations with many inputs and outputs, that encodes a family of algebras tied to loop spaces of spaces with a duality property. Manifolds that satisfy Poincaré duality are the leading examples.

Coformality asks whether such a space's algebra is fully fixed by simpler data. Using sharpened versions of an obstruction tool called Kaledin classes, the authors prove every sphere is intrinsically coformal over the rational numbers. The result tidies a corner of homotopy theory where geometry is translated into algebra.
arxiv-2503-04397:
Dongdong Yang, Bin Li, and Dusit Niyato save energy in edge computing with a rotatable signal surface, in a 2025 paper. Edge computing moves work from phones to nearby servers over wireless links. A smart surface that both reflects and passes signals can widen coverage, and turning it aims the gain. The team studied such a surface helping moving users offload tasks.

The choices tangle together: surface settings, aim, server shares, power, and offload plans all interact. User movement turns the problem into a chain of decisions over time. A learning method based on soft actor-critic training handled that chain. In simulations it beat rivals on speed of learning and energy use, cutting consumption by up to about half against a fixed surface. Splitting energy across both sides worked best.
arxiv-2503-04597:
Willem Lambrichts and co-authors present in this 2025 paper a control framework that lets a hybrid microgrid leave and rejoin the main grid smoothly. Such grids mix alternating and direct current through converter units. Their method rests on a linearized load-flow model that treats both sides and the converters as one system, including converters that set the grid's rhythm.

Unlike older setups, the converters can draw on the whole DC grid rather than one battery, widening the safe range. The controller steers the grid so no limits break before, during, or after islanding, and transitions pass without jolts. Tests on a 27-bus test grid with three converters back the design.
arxiv-2503-04697:
A reasoning model that thinks longer answers better, but no one could set the think time by the ask. Pranjal Aggarwal and Sean Welleck hand the user that knob in 2025. Their training way pays the model for right answers that land inside a word budget named in the prompt itself. The trained model, L1, slides its effort smooth from terse to deep as the budget moves.

On the standard length-control test it beat the past best way. A side find surprised the pair: squeezed models kept the habits of full-length thinkers in a fraction of the words. Their small L1 matched a flagship chat model answer for answer at the same think length. Code and models are posted.
arxiv-2503-04797:
Rahul Raja and Arpita Vats review the paired text collections used to train machine translation for the languages of India. Such collections, with the same text in two languages, are the fuel of translation systems. For India's languages, which span many families, scripts, and regions, good pairs are scarce.

The review sorts the collections into plain text pairs, mixed-language pairs, and sets that add images or sound. It judges them by how well the two sides line up and how well they cover real topics. The authors also face the hard parts of building more: many scripts, little data, and much informal writing online. Their map shows where new collection work would help most.
arxiv-2503-05197:
Yu Feng and eight co-authors design StreamGrid, a framework that lets point cloud chips work in a steady stream instead of fetching data again and again. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Point clouds feed robots, cars, and scanners, but shuttling them off-chip stalls the pipeline and burns power. Classic buffers that fix this for images do not fit point clouds' odd access patterns.

Two tricks unlock streaming here. One forces the work to split along set lines, and the other ends each chunk at a fixed, known point. With those in place, data flows through once with no off-chip trips. The framework also sizes the on-chip buffers on its own. Tests cut buffer size and energy sharply for small accuracy cost. Against top accelerators it ran far faster and leaner.
arxiv-2503-05597:
Giorgia Proto presents, for the ATLAS muon community, how new particle detectors are built and certified in Munich. Her report, from twenty twenty-five, covers resistive plate chambers for the collider's phase-two upgrade. Each unit stacks three thin gas gaps in one frame. Fresh low-threshold electronics read them out.

Production began in twenty twenty-four for the high-luminosity era. Triplets are assembled at the Max Planck Institute. A cosmic ray stand then runs certification tests. Its design targets robust, efficient quality control. Performance measures decide whether each detector ships to the ATLAS cavern. Assembly steps and test protocols are laid out in full.
arxiv-2503-05697:
Julian May-Mann and co-authors show how pairing glue steers topology in odd superconductors in a 2025 paper. In valley polarized systems with Berry curvature, the sign of a topological count depends on how electrons pair. The team proves the split in a fully controlled limit.

Short range pulls, like those from lattice shake, favor states whose Chern number shares the Berry curvature sign. Overscreened pushes, as in the Kohn Luttinger route, favor the opposed sign. The rule then reads a fresh chiral superconductor in layered graphene. The sign test gives labs a way to tell pairing routes apart.
arxiv-2503-06397:
Yanyu Zhu and co-authors fix a flaw in computer-made talking faces, where lips tend to blur into an average shape. Their 2025 paper studies lip-sync models that match mouth motion to speech for film dubbing. The blur shows up most on new, real-world clips the model never saw in training. Fine lip detail fades, and the face loses its own character even when timing is right.

Their method, called UnAvgLip, pulls identity traits from a reference clip and feeds them into the making process. One part reads those traits and aligns them with the speech. A second part blends them in so the face keeps its unique look. Tests show clear gains in identity match and a smaller gain in lip timing. Training and running costs stay modest, which keeps the method practical for dubbing work.
arxiv-2503-07197:
Zebin You and co-authors unify two families of image generators into one efficient design in a 2025 paper. Masked generation models build pictures by unmasking patches step by step, while masked diffusion models arrived from a different tradition. The authors show the two are really one framework wearing different clothes, then explore its training and sampling knobs systematically.

Their tuned model, eMIGM, generates sharp images on the standard ImageNet benchmark. At matched size and sampling cost it beats a well-known rival, and when scaled up it rivals the best continuous diffusion models while using under half the sampling steps. At the largest test size it passes another strong diffusion baseline outright. Faster generation at equal quality cuts the cost of image synthesis for everyone downstream.
arxiv-2503-07397:
Kha Vo and Chin-Teng Lin present an algorithm from two thousand twenty-five for teaching large teams of agents to cooperate or compete. Multi-agent reinforcement learning struggles as teams grow, since agents affect each other constantly. Many methods lean on shared rewards or a fixed agent order, which large real systems cannot promise.

Their method, called Q-MARL, borrows a graph technique from quantum chemistry that predicts molecular traits from atom positions. Each agent sits at the center of its own neighborhood graph, and those graphs serve as training samples. A message-passing network handles interaction inside each graph, while a depth setting keeps training light. Actions blend votes from all graphs holding the agent. Tests show the method handling thousands of agents.
arxiv-2503-07997:
Shimmy Rukundo, David Wang, Front Wongnonthawitthaya, Youssouf Sidibé, Minsik Kim, Emily Su, and Jiale Zhang wrote this survey in two thousand twenty-five. It reviews the sensing tools used in shops that run with no cashier, where buyers pick goods and leave while the system tracks what they took.

The survey sorts prior work by task: tracking stock, watching the store space, tracking people, and stopping theft. It weighs the strengths and limits of cameras, RFID tags, weight sensors, vibration sensors, and LiDAR, and how they are joined. It also notes hard problems such as blocked views, scale, and speed of data handling. The authors close with paths toward systems that cost less and guard privacy better.
arxiv-2503-08297:
Apps that collect user data often scramble it on the device first, a protection called local differential privacy. When many services each scramble separately, though, users pay the privacy price again and again. Rong Du and co-authors propose in this 2025 paper a way to reuse those already-scrambled reports across services.

Their framework merges perturbed data from different collectors whatever statistic each wanted. For averages they give a plain combining method and a weighted one tuned for least noise, and for full distributions a likelihood method that treats each user's reports as a bundle. Experiments show clear accuracy gains for both tasks.
arxiv-2503-08797:
How strongly the Higgs boson couples to the charm quark is one of the Standard Model's least tested numbers. The CMS Collaboration reports the first search aimed at that coupling, looking for events where a Higgs boson appears alongside at least one charm quark and then decays into two photons. The data come from proton collisions at 13 tera-electronvolts recorded at the Large Hadron Collider.

No signal stood out. The team caps the rate of this production mode at 243 times the Standard Model prediction, and bounds the charm coupling modifier below 38.1, both at 95 percent confidence. The limits, published in 2025, leave wide room above the predicted value, showing how elusive the charm coupling remains.
arxiv-2503-09197:
Zicheng Zhang and co-authors teach one model to both score and explain image quality in a 2025 paper. Judging image quality has two halves: a number that rates the image, and words that say why it looks good or bad. The two were long handled by separate tools, although human perception links them: the explanation lists the evidence, and the score sums it up.

Their framework, Q-SiT, retrains large multimodal models on question-answer sets built from standard quality data sets, plus human-written quality notes. A balancing trick finds the best mix of scoring and explaining examples on small models first, then scales the recipe up, which cuts computing cost. The full model and a light version both scored and explained well, and the skill carried to new data.
arxiv-2503-09297:
Wojciech Broniowski and Enrique Ruiz Arriola study gravitational form factors and the mechanical properties of the nucleon, in work from 2025. Their tool is meson dominance: each spin channel of the energy-momentum tensor is built from the fewest resonances that meet short-distance limits from perturbative QCD. Lattice results at a light pion mass anchor the fits.

The fits explain the lattice data in a natural way and give a nucleon D-term near minus three. From the same frame they derive two-dimensional transverse densities, new sum rules at the origin, and the pressure and stress inside the nucleon. Threshold behaviour and a pion reaction channel shape the densities at large distance.
arxiv-2503-09397:
Sergey Simonov studies how smooth the waves are for a wire-like system on a half line. The work dates to 2025. The system starts at rest and is driven from its end point. A weight term along the line can be rough, with just a mild sum trait.

Simonov proves the wave at any set time lies in a space of smooth maps. He also shows the map from the drive signal to the wave is a two-way match in one space. When the weight term is a bit smoother, the match holds in a smoother space too. The result firms up control theory for such wave systems.
arxiv-2503-09497:
Pinpointing where things are across a scattered network, without gathering all data in one place, is the federated localization problem. Reza Mirzaeifard and co-authors propose an algorithm built for the hard parts: spread-out data, non-convex shapes, rough non-smooth terms, and outliers. Their method wraps a robust absolute-value formulation inside a federated version of the ADMM optimization scheme.

Smoothing tricks applied step by step make each round of the algorithm tame and fast. Clients can update at their own pace, several times per round, which suits real federated systems. The authors prove the method settles at a stationary point. Simulations show faster convergence and better outlier resistance than leading rivals.
arxiv-2503-09597:
Zhehao Zhang and co-authors explore, in a 2025 physics paper, what universal traits appear when a quantum-critical state is measured once and then adjusted based on the results. This single-shot feedback turns a pure ground state into a mixed state with altered long-range behavior.

Using a smoothed continuum description, the team finds the mixed state's entropy carries a constant correction term, while another entanglement measure can grow with region size at a set rate. Both constants can take universal values unlike those of any critical ground state. Two test systems are worked through: a one-dimensional topological phase boundary and a liquid of interacting spins. The results open a window on mixed-state criticality.
arxiv-2503-09697:
Antoine Dumont and a large team of co-authors present WICKED in 2025, a tool that cleans wavy flaws out of space telescope data. The James Webb telescope's infrared spectrograph undersamples its images, which stamps a rippling pattern called wiggles onto spectra.

The pipeline shipped with the telescope does not remove them. WICKED hunts the flawed pixels with a frequency transform, then models each spectrum from aperture templates and smooth curves. It works across all the instrument's medium and high settings. Cleaned spectra recovered true shapes and line strengths far better than raw ones. Velocity measures improved most of all. A test on a nearby galaxy matched earlier studies well.
arxiv-2503-09797:
Benjamin Towle, Xin Chen, and Ke Zhou offered a new way in 2025 to make a splitting model admit its doubt. In medical images, edges are truly ambiguous and annotators disagree, so a single mask hides clinically meaningful doubt. Multiple choice learning trains several forecast heads to propose other masks, but the count is frozen at design time. And its winner-takes-all training lets one head dominate while the rest drift into irrelevance.

SeqSAM generates masks one after another in an autoregressive sequence, in the spirit of a recurrent network, wrapped around the Segment Anything Model. A bipartite matching loss keeps every generated mask clinically related rather than redundant, and because generation is sequential. The system can produce as many hypotheses as a clinician wants to inspect. The authors report notable quality improvements, giving reviewers a spread of defensible segmentations instead of one overconfident outline.
arxiv-2503-10497:
Weihao Xuan and a large team built a multilingual test for language models in a 2025 paper. Most tests of these models use English only. The few tests in other tongues lack the same questions across tongues, so cross tongue reasoning is hard to compare fairly from one model to the next.

Their test, MMLU-ProX, holds close to twelve thousand matched questions in each of twenty nine languages, plus a short form for quick runs. Strong models and expert checks guarded the quality of each translation. They then ran thirty six top models through it. Scores stayed high in rich tongues but fell hard in scarce ones, with gaps near a quarter of the scale.
arxiv-2503-10997:
Aashish Anantha Ramakrishnan, Aadarsh Anantha Ramakrishnan, and Dongwon Lee wrote a 2025 paper on making image captions more varied in what they mean, not just how they are worded. Writing assistants already diversify captions with synonyms and reshuffled sentences. Human captioners do something else: they choose a message and a stance toward the scene, signaled by pragmatic cues.

Their method, RONA, steers a multimodal language model with coherence relations, the logical links between clauses like cause, contrast, and elaboration. Choosing a different relation reshapes the caption's message while staying true to the image. Across several domains, RONA's captions were more diverse overall and matched reference captions better than baseline prompting. The authors release code for the strategy.
arxiv-2503-11097:
Self-driving machines must name what their laser scans show, including things never seen in training. Wenbang Deng and co-authors built a framework that flags the unknown instead of forcing a wrong label. Their network has two decoders: one sorts known classes, the other crafts features that make unknown objects stand out. Several training goals shape both skills at once. An anomaly step then marks points whose features look strange.

Tests on two large driving datasets beat the best current methods by a clear margin. Merging the known-class map with the anomaly map gives the final open-set result. Code will be shared openly. Safer robots need this humility about the unseen.
arxiv-2503-11197:
Gang Li and co-authors test reinforcement learning as a way to train audio language models. Their 2025 report applies the GRPO algorithm to Qwen2-Audio, a model that hears sound and answers questions about it. Audio had been left out of recent gains that reinforcement learning brought to text and image models.

The trained model scored 64.5 percent on the MMAU Test-mini benchmark, a state-of-the-art result. It reached that mark with only 38,000 training samples, far fewer than rival methods used. Head-to-head, reinforcement learning clearly beat supervised fine-tuning on the same task. Step-by-step reasoning text did not help here, and the models still trail human hearing by a wide gap. The team shares its code and model openly.
arxiv-2503-11397:
Erik Burman, Alexandre Ern, and Romain Mottier design a numeric method for interface problems on meshes that do not fit the interface. In such problems, a curve or surface splits the domain, and the mesh lines need not follow it. Their hybrid high-order method pairs polynomial unknowns on mesh faces with ones inside mesh cells.

In their 2025 paper, cells cut by the interface carry doubled unknowns, which can cause ill-conditioning when the cut pieces are tiny. The fix is to use polynomial extensions when the gradient is rebuilt. The authors prove stability and consistency, leading to error bounds that decay at the best rate. Numeric tests back up the theory.
arxiv-2503-11497:
Jonas Erhardt and co-authors report a 2025 study of a special class of materials that carry electric flow along their edges. In these materials, edge flow is shielded by a deep rule of physics, so it should not bounce back off flaws. That shield holds only when the edge holds a single pair of linked paths, the authors note.

Working with a thin crystal called indenene, the team used a fine probe to watch edge flow up close. Where two path pairs shared the same energy, flow did bounce between them. Where only one pair ran, the shield held firm. The result warns that many hoped-for uses of these materials need a closer check of their edge bands.
arxiv-2503-11597:
Jennifer Yee and Scott Kenyon compare in 2025 what microlensing surveys say about the masses of stars and planets floating in the galaxy. Microlensing catches isolated objects by their gravity's brief brightening of background stars, yielding a combined mass function. The authors set two survey results beside neighborhood star counts and planet censuses.

The brown dwarf counts agree across methods. For free-floating planet candidates, the comparison suggests most heavier ones likely orbit distant stars rather than wander alone, or else some supposed planets are really the lightest stars. The data also squeeze models of planets inferred from gaps in young disks.
arxiv-2503-12397:
Woula Themistoclakis and Marc Van Barel build a family of polynomial wavelets with a free parameter. Their 2025 arXiv paper works on a compact interval. The parameter can be tuned to improve performance for a task. Wavelets arise from interpolation at Chebyshev nodes. Earlier work by the group fixed the parameter at one setting.

Scaling and wavelet functions are both interpolating polynomials here. They are not copies of one mother function shifted and stretched. The natural home is the unit interval, rescalable to any other. A non-standard multiresolution analysis supports the family. Fast transforms based on cosine methods handle breakdown and rebuild. Convergence results lay groundwork for future applications. Signal processing on bounded domains is the target use.
arxiv-2503-12597:
Zhuoqi Liu and co-authors wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about a giant glowing cloud of gas around a distant quasar called 3C 57. Gas moving between galaxies and their surroundings shapes how galaxies grow. When a quasar lights that gas, it can be seen as a large nebula.

Using the MUSE instrument, the team found the cloud is long and fairly symmetric, with gas moving toward and away in a matched pattern. Two stories could explain it: gas in slow rotation, or gas blown out in two cones. The gas is far more stirred up than gas in nearby calm galaxies. Neither story fully fits, so the authors leave the case open for more work.
arxiv-2503-12697:
Mohamed Chabab, Samir Iraoui, and Hicham Sriba wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It reads the heat phases of a charged black hole in anti-de Sitter space, under massive gravity, from the light the hole sheds.

The team first maps the hole's shadow and its emission rate. Their new recipe keys on the peak frequency of the emission spectrum. That peak, paired with the shadow's size, tracks the hole's thermodynamic state with care. The link holds for both photon modes and heavy bosonic ones. In effect the brightest tone of the hole's glow serves as a probe of its phase change points. The work ties what a far viewer sees to deep facts about the hole.
arxiv-2503-12797:
Xinyu Ma, Ziyang Ding, Zhicong Luo, and seven colleagues tackle knowledge-intensive visual grounding in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The task asks a model to locate an object named by a fine-grained, domain-specific term rather than a generic description. Multimodal large language models know many entities and ground generic phrases well, yet often fail to use that knowledge for specialized concepts. The authors call this the knowledge-grounding gap.

Their remedy first builds knowledge-guided reasoning data that pushes models to activate relevant entity knowledge while grounding. Then KARL, a reinforcement learning framework, adjusts reward signals according to how well the model has mastered each entity. The team also releases KVG-Bench, spanning ten domains with over a thousand curated test cases. Experiments showed consistent gains over baselines and stronger generalization to unseen categories.
arxiv-2503-13497:
Philipp Bomatter and Henry Gouk ask if thin subject pools cap brain wave models in a 2025 paper. Models that read EEG waves promise gains for brain science and care. Splitting each record into bits boosts sample counts, but not the count of people.

Their frame treats data as born in layers, bits in records in people. Big tests trace how scores grow with total bits versus with people count. Score growth stalls when new bits come from the same few people. Tricks like fake data and self taught pre steps are weighed in the same frame. The work guides how to spend on new records.
arxiv-2503-13697:
