Plasma simulations can cook themselves when their grid is too coarse, and a 2025 paper by Luke C Adams and co-authors measures that fake heating across the main algorithm family. The effect, grid heating, appears when the simulation cannot resolve the plasma's natural shielding length, so the plasma warms until it can.

The authors ran the first systematic sweep of heating rates for the standard momentum-conserving method, across shielding resolution and drift speed. They also built a smoother variant with a continuously bending electric field, which barely helped. Energy-conserving versions with two interpolation shapes were tested too. Every variant heated under some settings, and analysis shows no better field solver can cure it; cold-beam stability limits are derived.
arxiv-2503-13797: Jeth Arunseangroj and co-authors wrote a 2025 mathematics note on Adinkras, graphs used to picture pieces of theories with supersymmetry, a deep symmetry. The search is for complete pieces that sit inside theories formulated off shell, and the team works with sixteen-color systems. The topology of an Adinkra matches a known mathematical form, a quotient of a cube. The note revisits that match, with an eye on a named open problem: how to complete the off-shell form of a known theory of light and charge, the Maxwell theory.
arxiv-2503-13997:
Svetlana Karpova, Federico Sanchez, and Dana Douqa propose using neutrino events to map the beam that made them in a 2025 particle physics study. Long-baseline experiments shoot a neutrino beam across great distances and measure how the particles change flavor. Precision depends on knowing the beam's shape and origin, normally taken from simulations.

Events recorded off the beam axis in the near detector carry clues about where neutrinos were produced. Observables tied to the azimuthal angle of the neutrino direction can pin down the average production point from real data. The method cross-checks simulations and can reveal alignment problems in the beam line.
arxiv-2503-14097:
Weihong Chen and co-authors present SCJD, a 2025 method for finding the 3D pose of a person from video. Fast pose tools often lose accuracy, while exact ones run too slowly for live use. Teaching a small model from a big one helps, but past teaching methods ignore how joints link in space and time.

SCJD trims the frames fed to the small model while keeping the links between frames. It then teaches the small model in three ways: richer joint traits, focus on joints next to each other, and matching motion patterns over time. Tests show the method reaches top scores while staying light. The work suits uses like sports tracking and live camera apps that need speed and care at once.
arxiv-2503-14197:
Giulia Sormani, Alex Rodriguez, and Ali Hassanali weigh the traps of learn with no guide in a 2025 paper. Such learn can find the weave in a sum sea with no man's hand, but its knobs and marks can skew the tale it tells.

Their test bed is salt in water: how each salt kind warps the water at its skin. A shape mark tells how each water bit sits by its kin. A depth count steers the knob picks and reads how rich each skin is. The team then draws a free-fall map of all skins at once. Salt kinds stamp the map in plain ways. The authors warn that free learn still needs a man's eye for sense, and chart how to keep both.
arxiv-2503-14397: Timothé Alezraa and co-authors ask how the early cosmos gained more matter than antimatter, in work from 2025. They work inside grand unified models set in five dimensions, folded on a bounded shape. In such models, a process called leptogenesis can seed the excess of matter seen today. The authors search the allowed settings of the models for cases where that seeding works well. They find such cases do exist, and the extra dimension sits at a scale far above the tera-electron-volt range.
arxiv-2503-14697:
Juan Sosa and a co-author present a Bayesian way to model social networks, in a 2025 paper. Network data record who connects to whom, and some people simply form more ties than others. Sociality models capture that unevenness with a personal parameter for each actor. They avoid some identification troubles that plague models based on hidden positions. The paper builds a full Bayesian framework for fitting these models.

Two fitting methods are compared: a sampling method that is exact but slow, and a faster approximate method. Tests on real and simulated networks check fit, prediction, and clustering quality. Working in the Bayesian frame also gives honest measures of uncertainty for each estimate. The authors pitch the models as a practical, flexible tool for modern network science.
arxiv-2503-14797:
Varich Boonsanong and five colleagues build an interactive fact-checking workbench that shows its reasoning instead of stamping true or false, in a 2025 paper. Machine-generated text floods every channel, and automated verifiers usually answer with a bare score. The authors argue such verdicts, without visible evidence, cannot earn trust.

Their tool, Facts&Evidence, breaks a document into individual claims. Each claim gets a credibility view, an explanation of the model's decision, and pointers to multiple, diverse evidence sources. Users can drill into any claim and judge for themselves. The design aims to give readers agency: understand, verify, and selectively trust. The paper positions transparency as a feature, not a luxury, in verification tools. Fine-grained, sourced checking, the authors suggest, fits how careful humans actually vet a text.
arxiv-2503-14897:
Vaibhav Rathore and co-authors tackle a harder form of image grouping in a 2025 paper. The task is to sort images into known and new classes in a new setting, when only labeled images from a different setting are available for training. Shifts between settings often break existing methods, and peeking at the target setting during training is not always possible.

Their system trains in short episodes that mix real and synthetic settings, so it learns features that do not depend on one setting. A weighting scheme then adjusts the base model based on how each fine-tuned version scores. Tests on three data sets beat adapted rival methods. The approach suits cases where the target images cannot be seen until the model is used.
arxiv-2503-14997:
Benedict Burnett, Ryan McCrickerd, and Benjamin Piau present a finance paper from 2025 on pricing adjustments for derivatives. Traders often need to adjust a price for costs, risks, and funding terms. Past work gave many separate formulas for these adjustments, known as XVA, over the past twenty years.

The authors give one broad formula that covers the gap between any two pricing rules. They show how older results, from a well-known option adjustment to bank-style methods, fit inside it. They then use the formula to gauge model risk and to estimate a key credit risk case. Readers get a single frame that ties a scattered field together and supports risk checks.
arxiv-2503-15097:
Every real number can be split into parts in many ways, and number theorists ask how simple those parts can be. Wieb Bosma and Alex Brouwers study nearest integer continued fractions, a way of writing a number as a chain of whole-number steps. They ask whether any real number can be written as the sum of two numbers whose chains use only small steps, with no step larger than five, apart from the first step.

The pair adapts Cantor set methods that Hall and Hlawka used earlier for ordinary continued fractions. With these tools they prove that the answer is yes: two such numbers always suffice to reach any real target. They also prove that the bound cannot be tightened, since replacing five by four makes the claim false. The result pins down exactly how small the steps can be.
arxiv-2503-15197:
Text-to-image models can be misused to make harmful pictures, and the usual fixes blur the model's skills in hard-to-see ways. Feifei Li and co-authors propose a self-policing alternative in a 2025 paper called Detect-and-Guide. The model inspects its own work in progress and steers away from trouble spots.

First, refined attention maps, sharpened by optimizing a small set of guideline tokens, locate harmful concepts inside the half-formed image. Then guidance pushes the generation away, with strength and editing area matched to what was found. Only a small labeled dataset is needed, and the base model is never retrained, so its variety survives. In tests on erasing sexual content, the method reached state-of-the-art safety results while disturbing complex, multi-concept prompts far less than rival interventions.
arxiv-2503-15297:
Four authors forecast delay in 5G networks in this 2025 paper. For uses like remote control and human in the loop systems, what matters is not just average delay but the full spread of delays, with very high reliability.

The team feeds past network state, cut into tokens, into two deep learning models that track time patterns. The models output the shape of a delay distribution for steps ahead, not just one number. Tests used real data from a software radio 5G testbed built by the team. The attention based model gave the best scores, which supports planning links around the delays users will truly face.
arxiv-2503-15397:
Korteweg-de Vries equations describe shallow waves and other dispersive flows, and solving them accurately takes care. Seth Gerberding builds a space-time method for the generalized family of these equations. Space is handled with smooth finite elements that respect the equation's structure, while time steps mix implicit and explicit treatment for the stiff and gentle parts.

The scheme reaches high order in both space and time. Gerberding proves it stable and shows it conserves mass exactly, a property wave solvers often lose. Computer simulations round out the paper, showing the method behaving as the theory promises. The 2025 work offers wave modelers a precise, trustworthy solver.
arxiv-2503-15497:
Mingjun Ren and Wentao Xu simulate AI agents with personalities in public spaces in a 2025 study. Ten agents, each tuned to a Big Five trait profile, shared a classroom scene. Misinformation was planted for them to handle.

Both spoken replies and private thoughts were recorded. Openness showed the strongest effect on accepting new information. Curious agents accepted readily, while cautious ones stayed skeptical. Extraversion and conscientiousness also shaped the choices made. The setup used a common agent framework and a chat model. Readers see how trait settings steer machine crowds, a warning for social simulation design.
arxiv-2503-15597:
Yoshinobu Fudamoto and a large team of co-authors wrote this astronomy paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on a crowd of galaxies found deep in the reionization era. The James Webb telescope caught them at a redshift of about 8.47, roughly five hundred fifty million years after the Big Bang.

Nine galaxies share that distance, confirmed by a bright oxygen line, with a tenth likely member. The clump is six to eight times denser than the average field at that age, the richest confirmed gathering known so early. One member hosts a small active black hole, a so-called little red dot. The odds of stumbling on such a structure in so small a surveyed patch are under five percent in current simulations. The authors say dense cradles may have sped up early galaxy growth.
arxiv-2503-15697:
Panagiota Moraiti and Efstathios Karypidis report their fourth place entry to a computer vision challenge on learning that never stops, in this 2025 technical report. The challenge setting lets classes reappear across rounds, and each round covers only part of the class list. Unlabeled images arrive too, and some belong to classes the model should ignore.

Their approach fights forgetting, the classic failure where new learning erases the old. It keeps a frozen copy of past knowledge through distillation and lets the model label unlabeled images for itself where it is confident. Accuracy averaged about seventeen percent in the selection phase and twenty-one percent in the final round, more than double the baseline. The authors share their code openly for others to build on.
arxiv-2503-15897:
Junho Kim, Gwangtak Bae, Eun Sun Lee, and Young Min Kim teach machines to find analogies between three-dimensional scenes, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Understanding scene context helps machines adapt prior knowledge to new or noisy environments. Learning every possible layout from data is intractable. The authors instead target relational commonalities between spaces.

They define scene analogies as smooth maps between scene regions that align spatial relationships. Their neural contextual scene maps extract descriptor fields summarizing semantic and geometric context. Fields are aligned holistically, coarse to fine, to estimate the map. Working at region level reduces reliance on individual feature points, adding robustness to noise and shape variation. Experiments show analogies found across diverse indoor scenes. Trajectories and object placements transfer between scenes, suggesting uses in robotics and augmented reality.
arxiv-2503-15997:
Paul Schulz, Thorsten Hempel, and Ayoub Al-Hamadi automate the making of 3D data sets in two thousand twenty-five. Finding objects in 3D is key for robots, augmented reality, and image search. Training needs large, well tagged sets, but they are slow and dear to make. Few public sets exist, with a narrow range of classes.

Their pipeline uses radiance fields to build high quality 3D models of any object. Those models feed a tool that makes fake training data. The pipeline is fast, simple, and largely self run. Pose nets trained on its data scored well in standard scenes. The work eases a key block in 3D vision.
arxiv-2503-16097:
Four physicists compute higher-order corrections to a class of spin asymmetry measurements in particle collisions, in a 2025 paper. When a transversely polarized proton is struck, its fragments emerge unevenly, an effect that probes correlation functions inside the proton beyond the usual parton densities. These signals are power-suppressed and theoretically delicate. The team carries the calculation to next-to-leading order for hadron and jet production.

The work exhibits the full complexity of such an analysis, including derivatives of those functions. A key result is that the factorization framework, which separates hard scattering from proton structure, survives at one loop. They also compute the effect for electron-proton scattering and compare with HERMES data. Their results give phenomenologists a firmer base for reading spin data.
arxiv-2503-16197:
Georgios Apostolides and co-authors taught four legged robots to jump with reinforcement learning guided by an example, in a 2025 paper. Controlled jumping is hard for such robots, and harder still when the body has springy, passive parts. The team first computed a rough jumping example with a model based planner. The robot then learned by mimicking that single example, before broadening the skill.

After the first phase, the policy handled jumps of varied distance, forward and sideways. It also proved robust on uneven ground it had never seen, using only body sensing. The same method, with little reward tuning, taught a spring legged version to jump. That robot landed more precisely, used less energy, and showed lower peak joint torque than the stiff version. One demonstration, the authors show, can seed a versatile jumping skill.
arxiv-2503-16297:
Alex Viguerie and Elisa Iacomini present a mathematical modeling paper, published in 2025, on aging among people living with HIV in the United States. Effective treatment has lengthened lives, so older people now form a rising share of this population, bringing age related illnesses alongside HIV care. Planning services requires a reliable picture of how that age mix will change.

The authors feed public surveillance data into an age structured model using an ensemble Kalman method, rebuilding mortality trends by age over past decades. A new nonnegative version of dynamic mode decomposition then projects those trends forward while keeping counts physically sensible. The framework stays driven by data and needs no extra assumptions about future behavior.
arxiv-2503-16397:
Nikita Starodubcev and co-authors present a faster way to train small image and video generators in a 2025 paper. Diffusion models make strong pictures but need many steps to sample. Recent methods cut that to about four steps, yet pushing lower gets hard. The team's method, SwD, instead shrinks the work at each scale, letting the model build a picture in stages from coarse to fine.

SwD also adds a patch-level training goal based on a distance between distributions. That goal speeds up older methods and, on its own, proves a strong baseline. Applied to top text-to-image and text-to-video models, SwD nears the speed of two full-size steps. Human raters and scores both favored it at equal compute cost.
arxiv-2503-16497:
A tool that teaches people to spot propaganda works only while it is in their hands, finds a 2025 study by Nicolas Hoferer and co-authors. The work leans on inoculation theory, the idea that a weakened dose of propaganda builds resistance to the real thing.

People used a detection and context tool in a two-phase online experiment, with some getting more doses than others. Critical thinking, measured through a two-system lens, rose while the tool was in use. Once access ended, the gain vanished. A single exposure, the authors conclude, does not vaccinate the mind for long. They discuss what repeated or built-in help might do to make the defense stick.
arxiv-2503-17497:
Daniel Kuhse and co-authors reworked the YOLO object detector in 2025 so it can answer at any moment, not only at the end of its pass. Safety systems in cars and robots may need a best guess right now, even a rough one. Their family of models adds many exit points where a usable prediction can be read off.

The team first defines what counts as an anytime model, then flips the network's layout so early exits see richer features. Two algorithms choose the best order of stages and the best subset of exits for tight hardware. A new quality score weighs speed against accuracy across the whole run. The authors admit deployment still costs effort. They map the trade-offs for builders of real-time vision.
arxiv-2503-17597:
Yunhan Wang and co-authors observed a new kind of topological shift in a diamond defect in a 2025 study. Topological phases sort matter by traits that hold firm under small nudges. Richer non-Abelian shifts had been seen only in systems that keep energy whole, not in leaky ones where energy can drain.

The lab stage is a nitrogen-vacancy center, a flaw in diamond whose electron spin can be set and read with light. The team drove that spin system into the leaky regime and watched the shift happen at atomic scale. No lab had caught this class of shift before. The work opens leaky systems to richer topology hunts.
arxiv-2503-17697:
Yanan Ma and co-authors let cars teach a shared vision model as they drive in this 2025 paper. Self-driving stacks must keep learning as roads change, but cars cannot ship all their camera data to one place. Federated learning trains across the fleet instead.

Older schemes pick training cars as if their data were fixed in advance. In truth, each car gathers its data along its own route. Their framework, Sense4FL, uses crowdsensing so route-shaped data guide which cars join each round. Detection of road objects is the test task. Smarter car choice should sharpen the shared model for everyone.
arxiv-2503-18097:
Victor Blanco, Miguel Pozo, Justo Puerto, and Alberto Torrejon unify the math of ordered measures in a 2025 paper. Such measures weigh sorted values and show up across operations research and data science. The goal is to embed them inside larger optimization models so they can be computed fast and exactly.

The team covers three families: linear, nested, and quadratic ordered measures. Their methods beat standard software on speed and accuracy in the reported tests. They then solve sample problems with varied metrics, from scenario choice in linear programs to the traveling salesman task. The paper frames the measures as plug in parts for general models.
arxiv-2503-18297:
Yishen Liu and co-authors built a model that writes medical reports from scan images. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a task that needs expert skill. Big general models often miss the fine points of such reports. Medical images also look much alike, so models blur key traits and fit noise. The team aimed to sharpen how the model tells like images apart.

Their network pairs a vision part with a text part through a shared focus trick. A weight step boosts faint but key image tags. A three stage text part then polishes each line with the image parts in view. Tests on three public sets showed strong scores. Readers get a model built for the quirks of medical text.
arxiv-2503-18497:
Stefan Rass and Martin Dallinger give a way to test the data used to train an AI model for hidden flaws, such as bias or a planted poison. A model can only be as good as its data, yet the tools to guard trained models are far ahead of the tools to check the data itself.

Their method starts with rules set before the data are seen, unlike past work that builds rules from the data. Any yes-no claim can serve as the test claim, which lets the method find error patterns that other checks would miss. The aim is a ground truth that can be trusted before training starts.
arxiv-2503-18697:
Julia Le Bihan and Bartosz Kołodziejek study random perpetuities, sums that feed on themselves, in a 2025 paper. A perpetuity obeys an equation where the value equals a random multiple of itself plus a random add-on. The light-tailed case, where huge values stay rare, is their focus. They introduce a local measure of dependence and a matching transform to describe how the far right tail decays.

They then follow the running version, where each step multiplies and adds afresh. A clean scaling sequence exists so the running value, divided by it, settles between fixed bounds. Its limit is pinned down explicitly. The work sharpens the math behind insurance-style recursions and random growth.
arxiv-2503-18897:
Thomas Chabal and co-authors rebuild indoor scenes object by object while a camera is still moving. Their 2025 paper uses depth video as input and produces a model at the level of whole objects. Current neural scene models promise this but run slowly online and complete shapes poorly. Two ideas drive the fix. First, a grid interpolation scheme updates each object's neural model smoothly as new parts come into view.

Second, a library of previously mapped objects supplies shape priors. A new object starts from a similar known shape, then refines with fresh views. Synthetic past views are added so early detail is not lost. Tests ran on synthetic rooms, a public scan data set, and lab videos. The approach beat leading neural models on accuracy and completeness, the authors report.
arxiv-2503-19197:
Pierre Lazag studies how point counts fluctuate for determinantal processes spread over hyperbolic spaces. Such processes model repelling points in physics and statistics. Hyperbolic geometry stretches distances in an exponential way.

The setting covers any homogeneous space with enough symmetry. The process must stay unchanged under the space's motions. Lazag bounds the count variance from below by volume. Fluctuations thus stay large no matter the ball size. That rules out hyperuniform order for these systems. Cayley trees and classic hyperbolic spaces fit the result. Bergman kernel processes are among the covered examples. The theorem settles a basic question for the field of random point patterns.
arxiv-2503-19797:
Cynthia Richey, Joseph Cutler, Harrison Goldstein, and Benjamin Pierce speed up property-based testing by making its random case builders run faster, in a paper from 2025. Such testing feeds random inputs to code to hunt for bugs. The speed of the builders caps how much testing gets done.

Careful timing showed that top libraries in OCaml and Scala fall well short of what is possible. Two causes stood out: overhead from layered builder parts, and slow sources of randomness. Their fix, Allegro, uses multi-stage programming to strip the overhead away. A second test swapped in a faster random source. Both changes keep builder behavior the same, and together they found bugs up to 13 times faster.
arxiv-2503-19897:
Lifu Wang, Daqing Liu, Xinchen Liu, and Xiaodong He ask whether image-making models need very large text encoders. Their 2025 paper notes that encoders grew from small models to the huge T5-XXL. Large encoders read prompts well, but they also carry much skill with non-visual text that image models never use.

The team trained smaller T5 models by teaching them from the large one, using image data picked for quality and meaning. Their T5-base model made images about as good as those from T5-XXL, while being far smaller. That cut in size lowers the graphics hardware needed to run top models. The result makes high-grade image making open to more users and smaller labs.
arxiv-2503-19997:
Luyao Zhang, Fabo Feng, Yicheng Rui, Guang-Yao Xiao, and Wenting Wang turn Gaia satellite data into a catalog of star positions and speeds. The catalog uses plain three-dimensional coordinates. Such a catalog is a workhorse for studying how stars move through the galaxy. But converting sky measurements into coordinates spreads their errors in tricky ways.

The team compared three ways of carrying the errors through the conversion. A huge Monte Carlo run served as the yardstick. A second-order method proved nearly as accurate as the costly sampling method. It also ran far faster. They used it for the main values and sampling for the uncertainties. The result covers about thirty million stars with both equatorial and galactic coordinates. It is released with code for others to use.
arxiv-2503-20197:
Zike Li and co-authors present a first empirical study of the robustness of code generated by large language models. Their 2025 paper notes that most evaluations check correctness and overlook missing input validation and weak error handling.

Using the CoderEval benchmark, they tested four leading code models. About a third of outputs were less robust than human-written code. More than ninety percent of the flaws came from missing conditional checks, most of them in the first line. Curiously, the needed if token often ranked in the top three predictions anyway. They propose RobGen, a framework that improves robustness without retraining the model.
arxiv-2503-20297:
Yuhan Wang and co-authors let one image model slide between clean and pretty results in this 2025 paper. Restoring images faces a built-in clash: low error scores favor blur, while the eye favors sharp realism. Most tools pick one side and must be retrained when the goal changes.

Their tool uses a single pretrained score-based model, which knows how images grade into noise. By steering the sampling, it walks the tradeoff line without new training. Varied noise levels can also be handled by the same model. The work fits inverse problems, where a rough measurement must become a full image. Flexibility is the core gain.
arxiv-2503-20797:
Sorting news and social posts by political leaning usually takes large hand-labeled datasets that age fast. Muhammad Haroon, Magdalena Wojcieszak, and Anshuman Chhabra test a lighter route in this 2025 paper: large language models that learn from a few chosen examples shown in the prompt. They ran wide experiments on three datasets of news articles and online videos.

Picking the examples in a label-balanced way lifted the models well past both zero-shot use and classic supervised methods. Adding source and description metadata also shifted the results, in ways the authors discuss. They further show how naming a source changes how the model judges even non-political content. The work speaks to studies of bias, bubbles, and radicalization online.
arxiv-2503-20897:
Venuri Amarasinghe and co-authors tackle learning that must generalize to new domains with few labels and no domain tags, in a 2025 paper. Semi-supervised domain generalization uses a small labeled set plus unlabeled data. Most methods pseudo-label the unlabeled data and assume domain labels are known.

Domain shifts add noise, making pseudo-labels inconsistent and hurting performance. The authors propose a feature modulation strategy that boosts class-relevant features and suppresses domain-specific ones. Features shift toward averaged class representations. The method targets the harder setting where domain labels for unlabeled data are absent during training, a common real-world case.
arxiv-2503-21697:
Lorenzo Clemente asks when a formal series can be called commutative, and whether a machine can decide it. His paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. A series maps strings over an alphabet to rational values; it is commutative when the value ignores the order of symbols.

He shows the call is decidable for all classes that form an effective prevariety, a wide frame that holds the classic rational series. Three newer machine kinds, polynomial, shuffle, and infiltration automata, each form such a class, so their calls are decidable too, a new result. Uses reach past series, to solvability in sequences and power series for fenced kinds of equations.
arxiv-2503-21797:
Wenjie Qiu, Hongshu Guo, Zeyuan Ma, and Yue-Jiao Gong build a two-phase framework for solving huge optimization problems by splitting them into parts that evolve together. Splitting works well when the parts do not share variables, but real problems often overlap, which tangles the split and drags down the results.

Their framework adds a split method grounded in the math of overlapping problems, so shared variables are placed with care. A tunable test set for overlapping problems is also offered, to extend older benchmarks. In wide tests, a solver built in the framework beat current rivals by a clear margin. The runs also mapped when splitting helps and when a whole-problem solver does better.
arxiv-2503-21897:
Areen Khalaila, Gianna Everette, Suho Kim, and Ian Roy present a tactile street puzzle that helps blind and sighted children play and learn together, in work from 2025. Touch maps usually serve solo navigation. Spatial skill and teamwork, both key in childhood, get little support.

Their set uses printed tiles with raised roads and add-on pieces that children assemble into city blocks. Play tasks turn building into a game, and touch markers guide hands around the layout. The design grew through rounds of testing with users. Children can reshape the town freely, which invites stories and shared plans. The team frames touch play as a bridge across sight differences, not just a navigation aid.
arxiv-2503-22097:
Haoyan Xu and co-authors spot odd nodes in text-rich graphs with very few human labels, by pairing a language model with a small graph network. Their 2025 framework answers a cost problem: labeling nodes in such graphs is slow and dear. Language models read text well but miss graph shape.

The language model first screens a small slice of nodes, flagging likely outsiders. A light graph network trains on those noisy flags and scores the rest, blending text and structure. An informativeness rule then picks the most valuable nodes for exact human labels. The final classifier trains on that clean core. Across four real datasets, the scheme cut labeling cost and beat prior tools on both sorting and oddity spotting.
arxiv-2503-22497:
Žerjal and the Euclid Consortium hunt the smallest, coolest stars in deep space images in this 2025 paper. The targets are ultracool dwarfs, dim bodies near the line between stars and planets. The Euclid telescope's first quick data release opened fresh fields to search.

The team used colors from the images to pick out dwarf candidates in the Euclid Deep Fields. Such objects are faint and easy to miss in wide surveys. A clean search method matters for counting them and learning where they sit. The paper is one of the first science results from the new telescope's data.
arxiv-2503-22597: Vazquez-Holm and Luna set up a systematic procedure for building classical spinning Compton amplitudes in a 2025 paper. Their method exploits the factorization properties of these amplitudes. Such amplitudes describe how a spinning body scatters. The method also uses colour-kinematics duality, a deep link between gauge and gravity descriptions. They investigate how Wilson coefficients for arbitrary spinning bodies can be constrained. They also study how those constraints relate to the same duality. The work extends tools used for spinning compact body calculations.
arxiv-2503-22797:
Ayse Kotil and co-authors bring quantum computing to trade-off problems in a 2025 paper. Many real choices balance rival goals, where improving one worsens another. The best compromises form the Pareto front, the set of options no rival beats on every goal at once. Even when each single-goal problem is easy, mapping the front can be hard for classical machines.

The team used a shallow quantum algorithm, QAOA, to approximate the front for multi-objective max-cut problems. Those problems split a graph to maximize several weighted goals at once. They ran the method on an IBM quantum computer and in matrix-based simulations. Results showed the quantum approach can match or beat classical methods on these tasks. The authors present multi-objective optimization as a promising field for quantum advantage. They stress the study is an early demonstration.
arxiv-2503-22897:
Owen Medeiros and co-authors present a 2025 paper on memory built from superconducting wires. Future computers that use supercold circuits, and quantum machines that must fix their own errors, need memory that is small and uses very little energy. Older superconducting memory cells are large, which blocks scaling.

The team's cells use thin nanowires, which take far less room. They set the cells in a grid read by row and column, reaching a working density far above older designs. The grid ran at very low heat and stored states that a read pulse then cleared. Tuning the write and read pulses cut errors. Computer models of the cell explain its limits.
arxiv-2503-23997:
Thomas Meier and co-authors test whether a giant impact gave Jupiter its fuzzy core, in their 2025 arXiv paper. Spacecraft data suggest Jupiter's core is dilute, spread through much of the planet rather than compact. An ancient collision is one popular explanation. The team first simulated planetary dynamics to get realistic impact conditions, then ran impact hydrodynamics and long-term thermal evolution models.

Realistic impacts are mostly oblique; head-on hits are rare. Even a head-on collision failed to produce an extended dilute core, and post-impact heat erased what mixing occurred unless temperatures were implausibly low. The authors conclude the fuzzy core records Jupiter's formation process, not a later crash.
arxiv-2503-24297:
Carlo Vanoni, Jaeuk Kim, Paul J. Steinhardt, and Salvatore Torquato study two-phase stuff built from ultra-dense sphere packs in a 2025 arXiv paper. The packs are stealthy hyperuniform, a state where big-scale density swings vanish across a wide band. A soft push between spheres lets the packs reach record density. Hard spheres from those packs then sit in a soft host phase.

The team gauges how waves and spread move through the mix. Spread runs faster than in mixes made with no soft push. At some wave sizes the mix turns fully clear to waves. Links tie that clarity to the long-time spread, a tie with lab worth.
arxiv-2504-00097:
Gupta and co-authors release the third data set of a radio survey for cold atomic gas in our own galaxy. Their paper from 2025 uses the MeerKAT telescope array. A blind search covered 19,130 radio sources across 390 pointings, each centered on a bright source.

In all, 3,640 hydrogen absorption features were found, the largest such catalog to date. Absorption depth tracked both gas column and dust dimming up to a set dimming level, past which the two part ways. Velocity spread stayed narrow, which marks the clouds as local. Detection and non detection groups split in their gas spread, a pattern also seen in far galaxy gas systems. The data set is public.
arxiv-2504-00197:
Baptiste Gros and Jorge Ramirez Alfonsin set out, in a 2025 math paper, a frame called strong geometry for point sets in space. Two sign maps build it: the chirotope of the point set, and the wedge chirotope from the planes the set spans. The team shows how the two maps tie. A third map, the witness, lets the wedge form be writ from the plain one in a clean sum. With that in hand, a strong-form ask from Las Vergnas gets a yes: bent rope knots can be rebuilt from their sign maps.

Flat space graphs are also fixed by their strong forms, they show. The frame thus holds more of a shape than one sign map can.
arxiv-2504-00397:
Gilbert Bahati and four co-authors give a way to build safety controls for machines with a dual relative degree. Such systems have two inputs that affect the output at two distinct rates of change. Examples include wheeled robots that turn and four rotor drones. Safety functions for these systems have been hard to build in a general way.

The method joins a safety function for a simple chain of integrators with a function that proves good tracking of safe inputs. The joint design yields a safety rule that can be built step by step and used in real control. The team tests the rule in simulations and on real hardware, on a four legged robot and on a drone.
arxiv-2504-00597:
Jirui Qi, Raquel Fernández, and Arianna Bisazza tested in twenty twenty-five how consistently language models use foreign-language context in retrieval-augmented question answering. In multilingual retrieval, the passages fetched may be written in a different language than the user's question. Whether models truly use such passages, rather than being helped or hurt by language quirks, was unclear.

Across four models, three data sets, and forty-eight languages, a clear split emerged. Models are surprisingly good at extracting the needed facts from a passage in another language. They are much weaker at answering in the expected language. Distracting extra passages hurt quality whatever their language, though distractors in the question's own language pulled slightly harder. The study separates retrieval quality from context use, guiding multilingual system design.
arxiv-2504-00697:
Robots working near people are often out of sight, so their noise may be the only clue to where they are. Marlene Wessels, Jorge de Heuvel, Leon Müller, Anna Luisa Maier, Maren Bennewitz, and Johannes Kraus tested how well people can place three robots by sound alone, inside virtual reality. Hearers listened to a moving robot for three seconds, then pointed to where they thought it stopped.

Robot type changed both how close and how steady the guesses were. A wheeled service robot was hardest to place, above all without an added alert sound. Yet people rated that same sound as the most pleasant and trustworthy of the three. Skill and liking pulled in opposite directions, a tension the team flags for robot design.
arxiv-2504-00997:
The authors introduce a new bracket that tracks how measurable quantities evolve in mechanical systems that both dissipate energy and roll under constraints, in a 2025 paper. Contact geometry handles the dissipation side, describing systems like engines losing heat. Nonholonomic constraints handle the rolling side, forbidding sideways slip. Combining the two is delicate.

Working in both the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian pictures, the paper defines the contact Eden bracket. Feeding any observable into the bracket returns its rate of change, the way the classic Poisson bracket does for frictionless systems. The authors also identify a special family of observables whose motion stays unconstrained, a clean sub-behavior inside messy dynamics. The result is a tool for theorists modeling real machines, which always leak energy and rarely move freely.
arxiv-2504-01197:
Eleni Adamidi and co-authors present a virtual laboratory in 2025 for running and recording computer-based experiments. As such experiments grow in scale, keeping them repeatable gets hard, because settings and scores scatter across files and runs. Their platform, called SCHEMA lab, captures rich records of each run, from settings to performance numbers.

Researchers group single runs into experiments and manage them across their whole life cycle. The paper walks through the platform's design, core features, and build. The authors argue that tidy records of this kind can lift both repeatability and efficiency in computational research, letting other teams rerun work exactly and trust the results more.
arxiv-2504-01497:
Xudong Li, Lei Shi, and Mingqi Song use smooth flow equations to explain why some fast search methods work. Their 2025 paper studies gradient methods, which walk downhill on a cost surface to find low points. A refined equation model had shown that a correction term cuts wobble and speeds the walk.

Yet adding that term to the simpler model sometimes slows things down instead. The team builds a general perturbed equation to sort out when each term helps. They show the correction term is needed for speed, but can hurt in some cases. A second added term, based on the plain gradient, fixes the harm. Tests on sample problems match the theory, and the paper gives rules for picking settings.
arxiv-2504-01797:
Jay Lee and Hanqi Su rethink how AI should be built for factories. Their 2025 paper notes that most past work chases better algorithms while slighting the ground a system stands on. Plants need tools for smart making, upkeep forecasts, and sound choices, all tied to deep craft knowledge.

The pair propose one foundation with three parts: knowledge, data, and models. Each part feeds the others, so a system grows from plant know-how rather than raw data alone. A case on diagnosing faults in spinning machines shows the frame at work. The authors close with open paths for the field. Their aim is a shared base for plant AI that other teams can build on.
arxiv-2504-01897:
A twelve-author team asks when a fault-tolerant quantum computer could first beat the best classical codebreakers of hard puzzles. They study the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm, strengthened by amplitude amplification, on random 8-SAT problems at the edge of solvability. Their costing is end-to-end: optimized circuits, error correction with the surface code, and a classical rival charged the same energy budget as the quantum machine's decoder.

At a tuned circuit depth, the quantum method overtakes top classical heuristics at 179 variables, after about fifteen hours on a machine of some 74 million physical qubits. Friendlier assumptions about error rates shrink the machine to about nine million qubits and the run to under three hours, against a classical solver spread over a huge supercomputer. The authors read the numbers as support for the hope that large error-corrected machines will matter for optimization.
arxiv-2504-01997:
Five authors, led by Yuchen Zhang, describe a new way for cars to find their place outdoors in a 2025 paper. Their system uses a low-cost camera of the rolling-shutter type, plus a simple motion sensor set and a wheel sensor. Such cheap gear tends to blur images and drift over time, so exact location is hard to get.

The method reads road features such as lane edges, signs, and painted marks, and uses them to correct the car's position. Tests in varied city streets showed better detection of road features than rival methods. Errors stayed near one metre on average, even as light and traffic changed. The team presents the work as a low-cost path toward safe self-driving.
arxiv-2504-02097:
Surface patterns grown in a cell model are steered by Marta Chabowska and Magdalena Załuska-Kotur in a 2025 arXiv paper. The VicCa model grows crystal islands by simple cell rules. The team asks how step-edge pull shapes where islands start and how they spread. Two pattern kinds fill the study: branchy fractal forms from plain rules, and tight forms from density-led sticking.

Rule tweaks shift the patterns in big ways. Well depth at the step edge proves a strong hand on final shape. Growth recipes gain a map from rules to looks.
arxiv-2504-02297:
A team measures how fractional charge objects in gauge fields change with temperature in a 2025 paper. Models of the Yang-Mills vacuum increasingly invoke objects carrying fractions of the usual topological charge. The team built a method to assign charge to separate objects inside lattice ground state fields.

The test system was SU(3) gauge theory across the deconfinement transition. Charge structure shifted with heat in a way that ties charge to the field's holonomy, a link any finite temperature model must respect. The pattern matched the instanton dyon picture of the vacuum. The authors offer the method as a sharper probe for competing vacuum models.
arxiv-2504-02397:
Boseung Jeong and co-authors added sound to video search in 2025, where a text query should find the right clip or the reverse. Most past methods use only images and words, though sound can add a great deal of meaning. Using all sound blindly can hurt, though, when the sound carries no useful signal.

Their system uses a gate that lets helpful sound in and filters out the rest. A new training rule also handles the fuzzy line between matches and non-matches in video and text pairs. Tests on public benchmarks reached top scores across the board. The authors present sound, used with care, as a missing piece in video understanding.
arxiv-2504-02897:
A theorem about gravity in cosmology gets a clearer proof in a 2025 note by Trung V Phan. Gurzadyan's theorem names the most general force law that still fits Newton's shell result, where a hollow sphere of mass pulls like a single point at its center.

The theorem matters for cosmic models, above all for MOND, a rival idea to dark matter that has drawn fresh interest. Gurzadyan's own derivation is famously terse and hard to follow, and newer proofs use power series rather than his original perturbation approach. Phan walks through the original logic step by step, in language aimed at advanced school or early university students, while keeping the elegance of the idea.
arxiv-2504-03197:
Good math tutors point at the diagram as they explain, and Jaewoo Park and co-authors built a test for whether models can do the same, in work from twenty twenty-five. Their task asks a model to spot the visual keys in a problem, such as helper lines and marked angles, and to weave those keys into its answer.

The bench holds one thousand math problems, each marked with its visual keys and a matched explanation. Current models stumbled at spotting the keys, tests showed. Open models also strained to build answers on the keys once given. The gap marks a weak spot in how models ground math talk in what they see. The set is meant to spur work on visual teaching.
arxiv-2504-03297:
Florian Voss and Uwe Thiele model droplets that crawl, shuttle, and wander by riding their own chemical reactions, in a 2025 paper. Their droplets sit in a bath of surfactant that acts as fuel, holding the system away from equilibrium. Reactions inside the droplet change surface tension unevenly, and the resulting Marangoni flows push the droplet along, a feedback loop between chemistry and motion.

Besides steady directional crawling, the model produces shuttling droplets that reverse, and random walkers that explore the whole substrate. The authors trace each motion mode to local and global bifurcations in the system. Because the thermodynamics is generic, they expect the lessons to transfer to kindred self-organizing mixtures and biomimetic swimmers.
arxiv-2504-03497:
Alex Young and co-authors build neural networks that think partly in complex numbers in a 2025 paper. Many signals, from audio to radio, are naturally complex-valued, carrying phase as well as size. Real-valued networks can still learn such tasks, but the paper shows they reinvent complex arithmetic clumsily, wasting capacity to mimic what complex units do natively.

Their hybrid architecture mixes real and complex paths inside each block, with conversion functions passing information between the two worlds. New complex activation functions improve generalization and parameter thrift. A dedicated search procedure explores the enlarged design space. On a spoken-digit audio benchmark, the hybrid reached lower loss with fewer parameters than a purely real network in every configuration tried. The authors pitch partial complexity as a general tool for signal processing tasks.
arxiv-2504-03797:
Joaquim Barreto builds in 2025 a categorical bridge between two classic results of logic that are usually taught in different rooms. On one side stands Henkin's construction, the syntactic recipe that builds a model out of a consistent theory's own sentences to prove completeness. On the other stands Lawvere's fixed point theorem, a sweeping statement behind many diagonal arguments, including incompleteness style results.

Barreto defines two functors from theories to their models, one Henkin flavored and one built from compactness style saturation, then links them with a natural transformation. Every component of that link turns out to be an isomorphism, so the syntactic and semantic routes to models are, in this setting, the same road. The link is also rigid: any rival transformation is uniquely the same as his. The shared engine under both theorems is diagonalization. Applications are sketched for automated proving, formal verification, and type system design.
arxiv-2504-03897:
Topological data analysis finds holes in data, loops and voids that persist across scales, but noise breeds fake holes. Sixtus Dakurah and Jessi Cisewski-Kehe note that existing robust methods clean the noise at the cost of shrinking the true signal too. Their framework, MaxTDA, aims to keep the strongest real features at full size while staying robust.

It blends density estimation with level-set thresholding through rejection sampling, producing a consistent estimator of maximal persistence. They prove the estimator's stability and build rejection bands for formal inference on topological features. Simulations, including an exoplanet example, show it recovering true signals that rival methods understate. The paper appears in 2025.
arxiv-2504-03997:
Seyedeh Baharan Khatami and co-workers rebuilt offline ranking review on causal grounds in a 2025 paper. Search and pick teams judge new rankers on logged clicks before risking live tests, but logs are biased: popular, top-placed. Conforming items get clicked for reasons unrelated to quality, and the missing clicks are not missing at random. Their setup reweights the logged data to mimic random exposure, converting the bias form into a missing-at-random problem that standard metrics can handle honestly.

Black-box tuning tunes the reweighting, guided by neural estimates of information-theoretic quantities. The causal formulation is system-agnostic, applying to any ranker whose outputs can be rescored. Tests validate fairer, more generalizable offline checks.
arxiv-2504-04197:
Eleon Bach and Sophie Huiberts settle the smoothed performance of the simplex method in a 2025 paper. The simplex method solves linear programs fast in practice, yet worst-case bounds look poor. Smoothed analysis bridges the gap by adding small random noise to the input and measuring typical run time.

Earlier work cut the bound step by step over two decades. Bach and Huiberts now give a method whose smoothed step count improves on the best prior bound. They also prove a matching lower bound on the width of the feasible region after smoothing. That pairing shows their noise dependence is the best any simplex variant can reach, apart from small log factors.
arxiv-2504-04297:
Tom Ichibha, Ryo Maezono, and Kenta Hongo present a 2025 arXiv paper screening a crystal family for new superconductors. The family shares the ThCr2Si2 structure and holds many known compounds. The team ran first-principles calculations of the critical temperature, the point where resistance vanishes, across the family's stable members.

Starting from 1,883 database entries, the team dropped compounds prone to magnetism or heavy-fermion behavior, then kept 66 that vibration checks found stable. For 24 compounds with known values, the calculations matched well. The other 42 yielded fresh candidates, including one compound with a predicted critical temperature of 2.2 kelvin.
arxiv-2504-04697:
John Campbell studies a classic result in number theory, the pentagonal number theorem of Euler, and a newer twist on it. The twist cuts the long sum in the theorem at a point and asks what the first chunk equals. Two past teams found neat closed forms for such chunks. His 2025 study seeks a far more broad form that holds them all.

Campbell uses a q-series method based on a known machine proof tool. With it he builds finite sum forms for a wide class of series, set by a few whole-number choices. One choice set gives a fresh cut form of the old theorem. The work thus folds past results into one frame and adds new cases.
arxiv-2504-04897:
Tiziana Calamoneri, Federico Corò, and Giacomo Paesani study a guarding game played on networks, in a 2025 paper. Guards stand on some nodes of a graph. Each round, an attacker picks a link, and the defender slides guards along links so that every link still has a guard at one end. The question is how few guards can hold the network forever.

The team studies this eternal vertex cover problem on series-parallel graphs, a family built from simple series and parallel joins. For a smaller subfamily called melon graphs, they prove the best guard count can be computed in time that grows in a straight line with graph size. They also conjecture that the wider series-parallel family is hard in the formal sense, which would make their subfamily result a sharp border between easy and hard cases.
arxiv-2504-04997:
Yichen Kelly Chen and eight co-authors build SurvSurf, a neural survival model for events that arrive in sequence. The task is to predict, from baseline, when the first of several ordered events will hit. Standard models can break the rule that cumulative incidence must grow in order across the sequence. SurvSurf is built to never violate that monotonic pattern, while still letting predictors act in nonlinear ways.

The model also uses implicit truths about unobserved middle events during fitting, and handles both discrete and continuous time. A variant of the Integrated Brier Score tracked true prediction error well. On two simulated and two real-world datasets, SurvSurf beat modern and classic rivals.
arxiv-2504-05097:
Liu Xiao, Li Zhiyuan, and Lin Yueyu boost a fast recurrent language model at run time without retraining its weights, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The model is RWKV-7, which keeps a running state rather than a growing cache of past tokens. Their method, called state tuning, grows and tunes only that state while the model runs.

A small watcher model first learns how the state moves. A kernel trick then enlarges the state, and a decorrelated update rule tunes the larger state for the task. A small tuned model beat larger models on the target task in their tests. Readers get a cheap way to gain skill where compute is tight.
arxiv-2504-05297:
Marcell Kurbucz, Betsabe Perez Garrido, and Antal Jakovac propose a new check on the leftovers of panel data models, in work from 2025. Panel models track many units over time, and their residuals should look random if the model is sound. Classic tests each hunt one flaw, like links across units or patterns over time.

Their test reads the largest eigenvalue of a reshaped residual matrix. It leans on a law from random matrix theory that says how big that value should be under pure chance. Simulations show it catches plain flaws and also tangled, non linear links between units. One broad test can thus flag many kinds of model failure at once.
arxiv-2504-05797:
Phuc, Dang, Li, and Hung ask whether a faint nuclear resonance can sit on top of an already excited state. The pygmy dipole resonance is a small bump below the main giant resonance in neutron-rich nuclei. It probes the nuclear surface, where two kinds of vibration mix. Their test case is a neutron-rich germanium nucleus.

The team applies a phonon damping model, with and without pairing between nucleons. An exact pairing treatment predicts two gamma-ray lines with pygmy character at mild heat. Those energies match a recent experiment closely. Bookkeeping by energy levels traces the effect mainly to the first excited state of the nucleus. Surface mixing of isospin appears alongside. The hot resonance, they argue, grows from the giant mode coupling to loose particle and hole pairs.
arxiv-2504-05997: Andrii Kurkin, Kevin Shen, Susanne Pielawa, Hao Wang, and Vedran Dunjko prove universality for IQP circuits with hidden units in two thousand twenty-five. These quantum circuits form a generative model that trains on classic machines. Loss can rest on expectation values alone, which keeps training cheap. The plain model cannot make all distributions, a proven limit. Hidden units, traced out at the end, were guessed to lift that bar. Two proofs here confirm the guess. One is asymptotic, the other needs a sane count of extra qubits.
arxiv-2504-06197: Odd maths rules that crop up in the study of quantum low surfaces turn out to be old friends in a new dress. Giovanni Felder and Jens Hoppe show in 2025 that those rules are the step rules for a chain of polynomials that stand at right angles in a loose, signed sense. From that match, they write a plain form for the start values that lead to plus answers.
arxiv-2504-06297:
Shan Gao challenges a claimed solution to one of mathematics' famous open problems, in this 2025 comment paper. Hilbert's sixth problem asks for fluid equations to be derived from the laws of particle motion. A recent paper by Deng, Hani, and Ma claims exactly that, passing from particle mechanics through the Boltzmann equation to the Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations.

Gao grants the math its rigor but attacks the physics on two grounds. First, the limit used keeps the gas vanishingly dilute, so the result describes a rescaled gas rather than a dense true fluid. Second, the middle step assumes molecules move without lasting correlations, an assumption that collapses precisely in fluid like conditions. The comment concludes the sixth problem remains open and urges fresh frameworks for bridging small and large scales.
arxiv-2504-06497:
Before a classical learner can use a quantum computer's data sense, the data must be encoded into quantum states. Minati Rath and Hema Date compare three ways of doing that encoding for continuous-variable quantum systems, plus one method borrowed from qubit computing. They feed each encoding into standard learners, from logistic regression to random forests.

Across their tests, the quantum encodings made features richer and lifted accuracy and F1 scores, with the gains largest on high-dimensional, complex datasets. The benefit was not free: each method carries its own computing cost, tied to how elaborate the encoding is and which learner consumes it. The authors weigh that trade-off between expressiveness and learnability. They frame the study as practical guidance for hybrid quantum-classical pipelines that want quantum features without losing the plot.
arxiv-2504-06597:
Sayak Ray, Sudipta Ray, and Suman Chakraborty simulate two drops chasing heat through a tight channel. A lone drop in a second liquid drifts toward heat, pulled by surface tension that shifts with warmth. Real drops rarely travel alone. Their 2025 study puts a pair in a snug slot and lets them bend.

The walls of the slot warp how the pair push on each other and on the flow. Bent shapes stir the warmth field around them, which rewrites the surface pull in turn. That loop sets speeds and paths unlike the lone-drop case. Film flow between drop and wall adds its own drag. The work gives chip designers a truer picture of drop trains in heat.
arxiv-2504-06697:
Stefan Albert Horstmann and co-authors study why software developers fail to build privacy rules into their code, in work from 2025. Privacy law in Europe sets duties such as user consent, purpose limits, and data minimisation. The team ran a five-hour programming study with thirty professional developers.

Each developer solved three privacy-sensitive tasks, in one of three setups: no help, privacy prompts, or a privacy expert on call. Nearly all solutions broke the rules, with most tasks failed by most developers. Prompts and expert support helped only slightly. Developers reported deep trouble with basic duties, yet few asked the expert or searched online for help. Low confidence did not lead to help-seeking. The authors argue better tooling and training are needed.
arxiv-2504-07097:
Nikhil Nayak and ten co-authors teach old models new tasks without erasing the old lessons in a 2025 paper. Fine-tuning a language model on fresh work famously wrecks earlier skills, a failure called catastrophic forgetting. The usual patch, small low-rank updates, caps the model's power and piles up parts per task.

Their method fully fine-tunes, but steers each update into a side corridor mapped fresh for each task, keeping it clear of the directions earlier tasks live in. Nothing extra is stored per task. On standard test suites with two big model types, accuracy beat recent rivals by up to seven points, and the models kept their manners, knowledge, and safety habits.
arxiv-2504-07397:
Seyed Mojtaba Mohasel and five co-authors present a 2025 paper on automatically designing tiny neural networks for fall detection on microcontrollers. Falls endanger lower-limb amputees, and a wearable detector must run on chips with very little memory. Their tool, MicroNAS, searches network designs with the target chip's memory, a few hundred kilobytes, as a guiding constraint from the start. That differs from the usual route of designing big, then pruning down.

A pilot fall detection system for amputees built with the tool beat ensemble methods and a commercial automated machine learning platform on the standard F1 score. The team also tackles the field's chronic problem of lopsided data, with far fewer falls than normal steps. They release the code openly for biomechanics researchers. The authors frame memory-first search as the practical path to real-time wearables.
arxiv-2504-07497:
Agerskov and Splittorff give a quantum algorithm for matrix determinants in a 2025 paper. The determinant of a unitary matrix carries a phase that quantum hardware can read. Their method skips the costly step of preparing eigenstates. It reads the phase to a chosen number of binary digits with a cost that grows gently with matrix size.

For plain rotation-type matrices, the method settles the determinant's sign for sure at similar cost. The pair also discuss stretching the method to matrices that shrink vectors. Operation counts are stated in full, so readers can weigh the method against classical routes. The paper serves quantum algorithm designers.
arxiv-2504-07797:
Victor Rodrigues, Tiago Oliveira, and Miroslav Krstic design event triggered source seeking for wheeled vehicles in this 2025 paper. Source seeking steers a vehicle toward the source of a signal, such as a leak, but constant control updates waste energy and wear.

Their method updates the control only when a trigger rule fires, which can allow long gaps between updates. Math based on time scaling, Lyapunov tools, and averaging shows the average system settles near the source, and a minimum dwell time rules out endless fast switching. The authors call it the first method of its kind for this task. It matches classic performance while using the actuators far less.
arxiv-2504-07997:
Tian Xie and co-authors test whether large language models reason about causes in biased ways in a 2025 paper. Models shape public answers on social questions, and prior work shows their outputs can reflect bias. What was missing was a look at the reasoning steps behind those answers.

The team sort causal reasoning into three types: mistaken, biased, and properly grounded in context. They built nearly eighteen hundred hand-checked questions across eight sensitive traits, each probing one reasoning type, and asked four leading models to draw the causal graph behind each answer. All models showed biased reasoning on most questions designed to elicit it. Many also mixed up correlation with cause first, then reasoned in a biased way. The paper catalogs how models sometimes avoid bias.
arxiv-2504-08097:
Irina Wang and Bartolomeo Stellato wrote this 2025 paper on making robust optimization fast enough for streaming data. Distributionally robust optimization guards a decision against shifts in the data it was built on. The Wasserstein version of the method is strong but slow, and it grows as data pile up.

Their fix is online compression. Incoming data are clustered on the fly, and the robust problem is built around that small, clustered summary. The problem size then stays fixed while data keep arriving. The authors prove a dynamic regret bound against an oracle that sees the full, uncompressed stream. With the right clustering rules, the regret shrinks over time toward a gap set by the clustering error. Faster gradient updates replace full solves, and tests bear out the speed gains.
arxiv-2504-08597:
Peru d'Ornellas and co-authors show in 2025 that a split spin order once tied to neat stones can rise in glass like stuff with no neat form. In that order, twin spin kinds swap by a turn of the stone. Glass has no such turns to lean on.

Their build sets two way marks on each site of a glass grid, with rules that hold spin turns free. The order then breaks shape on its own at each atom, with a shared point form cross the whole. Bent spin flow and spin tone prints mark the phase, both fit to scan. The path spans all grids.
arxiv-2504-08697:
Zdenek Kasner and co-authors test whether large language models can label spans of text as well as people do, in a 2025 study. Span labels mark exact parts of a text, such as an error or a claim. They give clearer feedback than a single score. Until now, the work fell to human readers or to small tuned models.

The team set models and skilled humans the same three tasks. One judged text made from data, one found errors in translations, and one spotted propaganda tricks. Models agreed with humans only to a fair degree, yet they erred at a rate like that of skilled crowd workers. They also cost far less per label, and the team shares over 40,000 labels.
arxiv-2504-08797:
Federico Re and Oliver F Piattella study a gravity frame in a 2025 paper on Ehlers' Frame Theory. The frame matches Einstein's theory when a key value is not zero. When that value tends to zero, it does not give Newton's theory, as one might expect, but a linked theory with an extra field.

That extra field, called the Coriolis field, captures how spinning mass drags space at low speeds. The authors show this for a known class of space shapes. They then apply the frame to a disc of matter like a galaxy, and show how its motion could give the flat spin curves seen in real galaxies.
arxiv-2504-08897:
Jiaqi Lin and Abhronil Sengupta test how spiking neural networks trained by local rules withstand adversarial attacks in a 2025 study. Spiking networks, which communicate in brief pulses, can be fooled by inputs changed almost invisibly, like ordinary networks. Most attack studies assume training by backpropagation through time, a method with little biological realism.

Local learning rules relax those global requirements and look more brain-like, but their security was little studied. The authors examine adversarial robustness across four local training approaches. Knowing whether local learning hardens or weakens a network matters for neuromorphic hardware placed in open environments.
arxiv-2504-09297:
Huu-Phong Phan-Nguyen and co-authors train phone vision models in a 2025 paper. Phones are everywhere, but their tight hardware caps how heavy an image model can be. Accuracy and speed must be balanced with care. Their Cycle Training method runs three stages that swing between exploring and settling, tuning the model as it goes.

A semi supervised step borrows strength from large teacher models and unlabeled images. That help lets a small model learn new scenes without full labeling costs. The goal is live scene detection on the phone itself, with no server round trip. Methods of this kind decide whether smart camera features stay smooth or stutter on mid range handsets.
arxiv-2504-09497:
Aishwarya Sarath and Markus Böttcher modeled the light expected from a slowing jet blob in the X-ray binary MAXI J1348-630. During its 2019 and 2020 outburst, the system threw off a blob of plasma that later decelerated as it left an empty cavity and struck the gas between stars. An early reading of that slowdown implied more energy than the outburst could supply, but a smoother density change brought the estimate down to a realistic level.

The pair borrowed a blast-wave model from gamma-ray burst research and added energy losses and radiation drag for the fast electrons inside the blob. Their simulated radio and X-ray light curves closely match the observed ones, and the main emission peaks in X-rays.
arxiv-2504-09597:
Zhixuan Pan and co-authors explain odd traits of large language models through an old lens: compression, in a 2025 study. A model that squeezes data well must also predict well, a link rooted in classic work by Kolmogorov and Shannon. The team uses that link to frame how models store what they learn.

They propose a simple data model with two layers: common syntax patterns and rarer facts stacked on top. Under a Bayesian view, learning in that model yields the growth curves seen in real models as data and size scale up. The frame also gives clean accounts of how facts are picked up in training and why false facts slip out. Tests back the theory's main calls.
arxiv-2504-09697:
Kenan Tang, Yanhong Li, and Yao Qin present an image editing workflow called SPICE in this 2025 paper. Prompt based editors follow broad instructions well, but they stumble on detailed local edits, and image quality often drops after a single change.

SPICE needs no extra training and accepts any image size or shape. It pairs a base diffusion model with an edge guided control model, letting the strengths of each cover the other. The workflow follows free form instructions closely, keeps untouched regions intact, and can improve quality across more than one hundred editing steps. On a hard real world editing dataset it beat leading baselines on measured scores and was preferred by human judges. The code is released for common editing interfaces.
arxiv-2504-09797:
Dinh Dai Quan Tran and co-authors teach image segmentation with two teacher networks, in a 2025 paper. Labeling medical or street images pixel by pixel is costly, so the field leans on small labeled sets plus many unlabeled ones. Prior methods tend to favor either the broad scene or fine detail, not both. Their framework, IGL-DT, splits the job between two teachers.

One teacher reads global context; the other refines local regions. A discrepancy step stops the student from copying either teacher blindly. Across benchmark data sets and label budgets, the method beat current rivals. The authors argue the pairing, not a bigger network, earns the gain.
arxiv-2504-09997:
Teaching a two-legged robot to walk over real ground is hard because training worlds are usually flat or hand-made. Hanwen Wan and co-authors present GenTe, a system that generates realistic terrain for robot training. It builds a library of basic land pieces, covering both shape and physical feel, and arranges them into harder courses as the robot improves.

Vision-language models read text and images and call tools to assemble terrains that fit a described scene. The physics includes effects like soil sinking underfoot and water resistance. The team also releases a benchmark of one hundred generated terrains. Robots trained this way walked more robustly and handled new ground better than with older methods.
arxiv-2504-10097:
Five data researchers present a new model for reading sequences in a 2025 paper. Their test case is guessing what a smart device user near a car means to do. Real sensor data can be messy, with gaps and shifts over time, which makes such guesses hard.

Their model, called STaRFormer, hides parts of the input in a smart, shifting way while it learns. It also learns from both marked and unmarked data at once. Tests span 56 data sets of many types, lengths, and uses. The model beat top past methods across that wide range, which hints it can serve as a broad tool.
arxiv-2504-10197:
Gauge theories like the one behind quarks carry a winding number called topological charge, but on a computer lattice it comes out fuzzy. Pietro Butti and co-authors compare two smoothing flows that clean up simulated fields so the charge can be read, in this 2025 paper. They use gauge groups of size four, five, and six, each with one fermion in a less common slot.

The over-improved flow settles onto whole-number charges almost at once, even at short flow times. The Wilson flow gets there too as the lattice grid grows finer, splitting into clear sectors earlier. Using the sharper definition, the team finds no sign of fractional charges. Such fractions could in principle appear as lattice artifacts, so their absence matters.
arxiv-2504-10597:
A large working group of physicists, led by Chiara Arina, Benjamin Fuks, and Luca Panizzi, surveys dark matter models in a twenty twenty-five whitepaper. The models are of the t-channel kind, where dark matter talks to normal matter through a go-between particle. The report comes from the LHC Dark Matter Working Group at CERN.

The team ranges from the simplest setups, with one dark matter type and one go-between, to richer ones closer to full theories. For each class they weigh what colliders, the cosmos, and sky surveys can say. They also cover both fast-decaying and long-lived particles, and many ways dark matter could be made in the early universe.
arxiv-2504-10697:
Cuesta and co-authors tracked entropy swapping between a magnetic field and energetic particles inside a solar storm, in a 2025 paper. A coronal mass ejection swept past the Parker Solar Probe carrying solar energetic particles. Each population carries a kappa value summarizing how correlated its members are, convertible into effective degrees of freedom and entropy. The field's kappa comes from its jump statistics; the particles', from their energy spread.

Across the event, the two kappas moved in opposite directions along a straight line, trading order as the probe crossed the structure. Particle correlations answer to field fluctuations directly. Solar wind thermodynamics, long routine for bulk plasma, now extends to its fastest passengers.
arxiv-2504-10897:
Prashanti Priya Angara and co-authors frame bound pick tasks for quantum-class solvers by way of free twins. The work dates to 2025. True pick tasks oft bear hard bounds that bare solvers can't hold. Near-best picks, fast, are the work aim in the field.

Their frame turns each bound task to a free twin task. The quantum solver works the twin, then a desk step trims picks back to the bound space. Three hard tasks ground the show, from guard sets to match and cover picks. Sim runs on a known stage proved the frame works and scales. Each task ties to a live use, from stock to webs.
arxiv-2504-10997:
Haoyang Li, Robert Thomas, Pisu Jiang, and Krishna Balram build light switches for chips from a semiconductor called gallium arsenide, in a paper from 2025. These switches steer light signals in fast networks and quantum machines. Most are made in crystals that are hard to grow beside electronics. A chip-friendly material would ease building and harden the parts for harsh settings.

Their design folds the two arms of a light splitter along two crystal axes of the chip. That fold exploits a quirk in how the crystal bends light under voltage. The result is a true push-pull switch, where the arms work in opposite phase. The waveguides hang free and stretch over a centimeter scale. Yet they still confine light to a thread thinner than a hair. The work blends ideas from tiny machines into chip photonics.
arxiv-2504-11397:
Raghav Pant, Sikan Li, Xingjian Li, Hassan Iqbal, and Krishna Kumar compare two neural network types on physics problems in a 2025 paper. The rivals are classic multi-layer perceptrons and Kolmogorov-Arnold networks. The newer type has drawn buzz as a possible upgrade. Its edge on physics tasks was still unproven.

The team tested both inside two solver frames for equations. Problems ranged widely in scale and complexity. In deep networks, the new type did not win in a steady way. In shallow networks, it beat the classic type by clear margins. The authors say the new type suits shallow, efficient designs. That niche may matter for many physics uses.
arxiv-2504-11497:
Chang Liu, Emmanuel A. Olowe, and Danial Chitnis use a large language model as an agent to size parts in analog circuits, in work from twenty twenty-five. Sizing transistors by hand takes much skill and many rounds of trial. Machine learning helps, but still needs many runs and lacks design know how.

The agent links the model to circuit simulators and data tools through careful prompts. It tuned several basic circuits to meet target scores. Among the models tried, one stood out and was then used on a larger amplifier with nine score targets. In the best test group, the agent met the goals in up to sixty parts in a hundred runs. The work shows a path to faster circuit design.
arxiv-2504-11997:
Kihyuk Hong and Ambuj Tewari present a 2025 algorithm for reinforcement learning where the goal is steady average reward over an endless run. In linear Markov decision processes, a prior method improved statistics by clipping the value function, but that step needed the lowest value across the whole state space, which can be endless. Their version clips only over states the algorithm has actually visited.

The change keeps the same regret promise as the earlier work while cutting the computing cost loose from the size of the state space. The authors frame the result as the first method for this setting that is both statistically and computationally sound at scale. Very large state spaces no longer block the approach.
arxiv-2504-12097:
Theodore Kareta and co-authors track how the comet 29P/Schwassmann-Wachmann 1 changes in near-infrared light when it erupts. The comet, the first active Centaur found, is the most outburst-prone body known. Its flares can brighten it by five magnitudes or more, and what powers them is still debated. Their 2025 paper reports spectra from two telescopes across 2017 to 2022.
