The set covers one large outburst, one mid-sized flare, and two quiet spells. The quiet spectra looked alike in slope and grain size, while the outbursts differed from each other. The team suggests small grains speed up more than large ones, so timing after a flare shapes what a spectrum shows. Comet scientists get a way to read mixed outburst records.
arxiv-2504-12197:
Explaining an image classifier with a heat map says where it looked, not what it saw. Mahdi Alehdaghi and co-authors build a classifier that explains itself in parts and concepts, in a 2025 paper. Their network, PCMNet, mines part-prototypes, small meaningful image regions, without extra supervision, and bases its verdicts on them.

Rigid earlier methods cut images into fixed patches, so the examples they cited were often meaningless. PCMNet instead learns which regions deserve to be prototypes, clusters them into concept groups, and scores new images by concept activations. Across several benchmarks the system beat state-of-the-art rivals on interpretability, stability, and robustness, holding up under occlusion and hard conditions. The authors frame concept-level explanations as alignment work: decisions a human can inspect, contest, and trust.
arxiv-2504-12397:
Fine-tuning a large language model for a special job usually means swapping adapters in and out, and each swap forces the system to rebuild its memory of the conversation so far. Kristjan Greenewald and co-authors propose Activated LoRA, an adapter that only alters processing from the moment it is switched on. Earlier tokens keep the base model's cached memory, so activation is instant.

That trick enables intrinsics: small specialist models invoked mid-conversation for well-defined jobs while the base model handles the rest. The team trained a set of such intrinsics and matched standard adapter accuracy at far better inference efficiency. Their implementation joined a popular open-source fine-tuning library. The design points toward chat systems that call skills on demand without paying a recomputation toll each time.
arxiv-2504-12897:
Baptiste Cecconi and six co-authors set out a shared catalogue for astronomy, in this 2025 paper. The field is known for open science, yet its data systems still do not line up well with each other. Shared tools that fix what terms mean can bridge those gaps. The tools, called semantic artefacts, include ontologies, thesauri, vocabularies, and metadata schemas.

Such tools are now spread across many registries, in mixed formats. Few use rich web standards, and their scopes overlap. Under a European FAIR data project, the team built a trial catalogue for astronomy, heliophysics, and planetary science. The trial runs on the OntoPortal platform. It has already improved how these groups handle their shared terms. The paper reviews current practice, lists candidate tools, and gives use cases. It also charts the path to a full service, OntoPortal-Astro, for finding and reusing data across fields.
arxiv-2504-13097:
Chayan Patra and Rahul Maitra sped up a workhorse quantum lab science method in 2025. The change-based eigensolver searches for a molecule's lowest energy by tuning a quantum circuit, but noise, flat regions. Local traps in its energy landscape stall the search and waste costly hardware time. Their formalism splits the circuit's settings into a small main set and a larger auxiliary set. Based on a guessed pecking order in how fast settings matter during tuning.

Only the small set is optimized straight, under an adiabatic shortcut. The rest are rebuilt afterward without further change-based search, then folded into the energy through fixes that plunge the estimate toward better minima. Resource use and accuracy both improve in their account.
arxiv-2504-13197:
Takayuki Ishitobi wrote a physics paper in 2025 on an energy gap that was thought to belong only to one kind of magnetic order. A superzone gap usually signals antiferroic order, where neighboring units point in opposed ways. Ishitobi shows the gap can also arise from ferroic orders, where units align, in systems with sublattice structure. The test bed is a model of p-orbitals on a zigzag chain.

In that model, a familiar type of gap appears under ferroquadrupolar order or ferromagnetic order. The same gap can also be induced by an outside magnetic field. The result widens the list of orders that experiments must consider when such a gap is seen.
arxiv-2504-13597:
Jun Zeng and co-authors build a transformer net to outline polyps in colon camera views across many image modes, in a paper from 2025. Early polyp finds can stop bowel cancer, but most nets train on one mode from one center and fade in real clinics.

Their net, FocusNet, first drafts a coarse map, then sharpens shallow detail, then weighs local detail against wide context. A new multi mode, multi center test set anchors the checks. Scores topped past best nets in all five modes, with top marks in standard white light views. The code is shared in the open.
arxiv-2504-13897:
Aditya Bhattacharya, Tim Vanherwegen, and Katrien Verbert study AI explanations for lay users in a 2025 paper. What-if explanations show patients how changing habits could lower disease risk, but raw versions can confuse or suggest unworkable steps. The team built a health system that pairs such explanations with a chat agent that talks users through them.

Thirty-four people at high heart risk tried the system. Agent help made the advice clearer and more doable. Users who already knew chat AI gained more than first-timers. The authors add design rules with guards against made-up content. Readers get a template for explanations that non-experts can act on.
arxiv-2504-14397:
Shepler and Witherspoon chart how algebras bend when a symmetry group acts on them, in this 2025 paper. Their setting joins Hopf algebra actions with Koszul algebras, a tidy class of quadratic algebras. The question is which bendings, called PBW deformations, can arise, and what they look like as filtered algebras.

Maps borrowed from topology shuttle homological data between resolutions, turning abstract bracket conditions into concrete rules for the bendings. The full answer names a family the authors call Hopf-Koszul Hecke algebras. The paper frames the classification as a bridge between cohomology and explicit algebra.
arxiv-2504-14897:
Hu and three co-authors squeeze plasma sim data with a physics-first pack tool in this twenty twenty-five paper. Such sims can fill drives by the vast unit if each mote is kept in full. The speed spread of motes holds the tale of heat and beams in the gas.

Inside, bell-curve mixes stand in for the full speed spread of the mote cloud. A bin step first cuts the math load, then chip gear fits the mix live. The pack keeps the mean speed, heat, and beam birth facts that plain packs lose. Its squeeze rate ran to ten-thousand-fold in the tests the team ran. Run time sat on par with stock pack tools, or beat them in spots.
arxiv-2504-14997:
Yongwoo Choi, Hyeon-Dong Son, and Ho-Meoyng Choi compute the gravitational form factors of the pion in a light-front quark model. Their 2025 paper asks how the lightest hadron distributes momentum and pressure inside itself. Form factors encode those maps, and one of them, the D-term, probes the pion's inner mechanics.

The team apply one construction consistently to both the matrix elements and their Lorentz structures. That care removes extraction ambiguities that plague similar models. Tuned to match the pion's known decay constant and charge shape, the model yields a D-term near the value chiral theory predicts. Its mechanical radius comes out largest among the pion's radii, and its two-dimensional pressure and shear maps satisfy the required stability checks.
arxiv-2504-15097:
I N Sharykin and co-authors trace the sparks before a huge solar flare that erupted at the Sun's limb in February 2014. Big flares can disrupt satellites and power grids, so knowing how they ignite matters. The team reads the run-up through a tether-cutting lens, where tangled magnetic lines snap and rejoin low over the surface.

They blend X-ray, ultraviolet, and radio data to map where energy leaked before the blast. The early release sat in one compact spot near the line where magnetic polarity flips. A thin current sheet likely formed there. The first flare glow then lit up in that same place. Plasma fed from the sheet helped a magnetic rope grow until it burst outward. The close match backs the tether-cutting account of how this eruption began.
arxiv-2504-15197:
Luca Di Carlo, Francesca Mignacco, Christopher Lynn, and William Bialek test mean field theories on networks of real neurons in a 2025 paper. Mean field ideas promise that a system with many parts can be captured by a few collective variables. The team ask whether that promise holds for actual neural activity patterns. Simple versions of the idea, they show, fail to describe the data.

An extended theory that matches the distribution of collective variables is at least consistent with the recordings. Even so, it shows signs that these networks sit near a critical point, echoing other observations in the field. The authors present the result as a path toward analyzing data from ever larger neuron recordings. The paper is short and conceptual, aimed at theory minded readers.
arxiv-2504-15297:
Sergii Skurativskyi and co-authors analyse earthquake patterns in Azerbaijan and nearby areas, in a 2025 paper. The region sits where two vast plates collide, so quakes are strong and unevenly spread. The team study records from 2010 to 2023 and group quake sites into clusters based on how densely they pack.

Seven clusters are studied in detail. For each, they model the distance from a fixed point on the ground to quake centres, and they build formulas for how those distances spread. One case places the point at a cluster centre, and another places it outside the cluster. They apply the formulas to distances from a hydroelectric station to nearby clusters. The fits matched the real data well enough, the authors say, to help assess quake risk for key sites in the country.
arxiv-2504-15397:
Image generators often botch mirrors, placing reflections that break the rules of light. Ankit Dhiman, Manan Shah, and R Venkatesh Babu set out to fix that failure. Earlier fixes used synthetic training scenes but broke when objects moved or turned. Their pipeline randomizes where objects sit, how they rotate, and whether they rest on the ground. It also pairs objects so scenes with several items are covered.

A three-stage training plan then moves the model from synthetic scenes toward real photos. The final model, MirrorFusion 2.0, is judged in both numbers and side-by-side images. Realistic mirrors matter for design previews and virtual staging. The work shows how training data design, not just model size, drives realism.
arxiv-2504-15597:
Mirko Primc and Goran Trupčević write a short math note in 2025 on the structure of certain abstract spaces. The note extends a proof from their past work on a related family of spaces. At stake is whether a known spanning set for these spaces has no wasted parts.

The pair first proved that fact for one broad family by linking two kinds of spaces. Here they stretch the same path to the smallest case in the family, for all standard spaces of that type. The proof leans on one key term drawn from a mixing map between spaces of the linked family. Notes like this one firm up the base on which wider results stand.
arxiv-2504-15697: Ting-Wei Chang and Hung-Chun Tsui settle a uniqueness question for gamma functions in positive characteristic in a 2025 paper. The formulas they study, named for Gross, Koblitz, and Thakur, link special values in the function field world, a mirror of number theory where polynomials act as integers. They determine every continuous, non-vanishing function that satisfies the formulas, proving the fit is unique and locking down a definition later theory builds on.
arxiv-2504-15797:
Heejae Bae and co-authors explored this 2025 design question: can virtual reality hold a memorial space for the dying and the bereaved? Digital tools can cross limits of place and time that bind physical memorials. Yet personal spaces that serve both the person near death and those who remain are little studied. The team used research through design, learning by building.

The study ran in three phases: joint design with stakeholders, building the VR space, and user testing. Three lessons stood out. The VR space worked as a bonding medium between the dying and their loved ones. Involving users at every stage surfaced needs that designers alone would miss. Certain design elements deepened the memorial feel. The work lays groundwork for personal digital remembrance.
arxiv-2504-15897:
Zherui Yang, Zhengyang Xue, and Ligang Liu present a 2025 arXiv paper on faster computer solvers for partial differential equations. Neural operators learn to mimic such solvers, but their accuracy tricks carry costs: attention grows too slow on big meshes, and spectral methods demand neat grids and flat shapes. The authors rebuild attention itself to escape both traps.

They note that attention's matrix work can be read as operations on whole functions, then shrink that endless space down to a small subspace. For odd-shaped domains, the subspace is built from the domain's own vibration modes, which fit its geometry and capture smooth functions well. On several equation data sets the resulting operator, SUPRA, cut errors by up to a third while keeping top-tier speed. The work suits engineering problems on real, messy shapes.
arxiv-2504-15997:
Chengfeng Shen and co-authors present a 2025 method for solving hard optimization problems where the best answer uses randomness. Such non-convex problems are common in economics. Their answers often come as lotteries rather than fixed choices. The team works through a Lagrangian lens.

They prove the saddle point of the random problem equals the value of a plain dual problem. An algorithm descends the dual and rebuilds the random answer from plain optima along the way. For many problems it runs far faster than linear programming. A tax design case with mixed worker types shows the power. Random tax schedules there beat every fixed schedule.
arxiv-2504-16097:
Buzelin and co-authors design LGA-ECG, a model that reads heart tracings with both local and global attention. Heart disease is the top cause of death worldwide, so sharp ECG tools matter. Transformers catch rhythm patterns well but often miss fine waveform shapes.

Their fix blends convolutional bias with global self-attention in one model. Queries come from averaging embeddings across overlapping convolution windows, which spotlights local shape. Keys and values span the whole sequence, keeping rhythm context in view. Tests on the CODE-15 dataset beat prior top models. Ablation runs confirmed each part of the design earns its place.
arxiv-2504-16297:
Taylor Patti and co-authors speed up noisy quantum simulations with a new sampling technique in a 2025 paper, based on the head title. Simulating quantum systems on classical machines is costly, since noisy states need huge density matrices. Trajectory methods shrink that cost by tracking a small ensemble of noisy states, but current versions waste effort on repeat state preparation and single shot collection.

Their Pre-Trajectory Sampling method tailors error types, batches sampling without redundant work, and gathers error information along the way. On a thirty five qubit error correction code, speedups reached a million fold, and data sets of a trillion shots were produced. A tensor network test on eighty five qubits also gained.
arxiv-2504-16397:
Banruo Liu and co-authors build, in a 2025 paper, a planner for compound AI work that must hit set service marks. Such work chains many steps: meet aids, self-drive, and game worlds use it. Plans must set where each step runs, on cloud or edge, its knobs, and its share of kit. Marks span lag, truth, and cost, and crowds of asks fight for the same kit. The plan space blows up fast. Compass splits the big ask in small ones, with world grade kept. Like plans, in and cross asks, are used to slash search steps.

A profiler gauges just the plans that count, for true calls at a slice of the cost. Live plan swaps run at work time.
arxiv-2504-16497:
Hung Bui The studies a broad class of equilibrium problems in a 2025 mathematics paper. The problem asks for a point at which a pair of two-variable functions, called bifunctions, meets a balance condition for every rival point. The setting is general: the rival set carries no algebraic or topological structure at all. Earlier results usually demanded much more structure on that set.

The paper proves several theorems guaranteeing that a solution exists. Some conditions need only hold on a smaller, well-spread subset of the domain rather than everywhere. The results are then applied to variational relation problems, vector equilibrium problems, and common fixed point problems. The work widens the reach of equilibrium theory used in optimization and game-like models.
arxiv-2504-16697: Alin Bostan, Bruno Salvy, and Michael F Singer present a 2025 arXiv paper settling a stubborn question about power series. Series satisfying neat differential equations are called D-finite, and every algebraic series is one. Telling whether a given D-finite series is secretly algebraic or truly transcendental had no general decision method. The authors prove the question is decidable. They give two theoretical algorithms and distill a practical transcendence test, implemented efficiently in the Maple system.
arxiv-2504-16897:
Andrei Cordova Azevedo and co-authors measure, in a 2025 paper, how concentrated the web's trust system has become. Every secure site holds a certificate issued by a certificate authority. A small set of authorities does most of that issuing, which puts much of the web's trust in few hands. The team counted where certificates for two big political blocs actually come from: the BRICS nations and the European Union.

For both blocs, more than seventy-five percent of certificates trace back to authorities based in the United States. That is a deep dependence on a foreign system for a basic part of online life. The authors warn that such reliance cuts against digital sovereignty. They urge both blocs to build alternatives that would return some control over their own web trust.
arxiv-2504-16997:
José Barbón and co-authors model a universe inside a black hole in a 2025 paper. In brane world models, our universe sits on a thin sheet inside a curved higher space. Such a sheet inside a black hole can encode a closed cosmos in a partner field theory, a neat test bed for quantum gravity ideas.

Past models used bare sheets whose only matter came from the surrounding space. The authors add real matter fields on the sheet itself, both a smooth fluid and a field called an axion. With that matter, a flaw in the math build of these spaces in higher dimensions can be avoided. The fix widens the models that theorists can use.
arxiv-2504-17297:
Palash Dey, Ashlesha Hota, and Sudeshna Kolay study knapsack problems on graphs with relaxed rules in this 2025 paper. In the classic setup, each item has weight and profit, and a picked item counts only if its neighbors are picked too, under one of two strictness levels. The relaxed versions studied here let any set be picked. The catch: an item earns profit only if at least one neighbor, or all neighbors, join it, while every picked item still adds weight.

Both relaxed problems are strongly NP-complete even on undirected graphs. The authors then map the parameterized landscape: some variants stay hard for the knapsack size alone, while others yield when size and profit demand combine. A randomized color coding method gives a pseudo efficient algorithm for one pair of variants. They also give a near exact approximation for one relaxed version with unit weights and profits.
arxiv-2504-17497:
Radia Berreziga and co-authors mix two AI tools to screen drug candidates in a 2025 paper. Virtual screening tests many molecules on a computer before costly lab work. Graph networks read a molecule's bond map directly, while large language models hold broad chemical knowledge learned from huge data.

Their hybrid feeds the language model's molecule summaries into the graph network after every layer, not just at the end. The summaries can be stored in a library, so the big model runs only once. The mix beat a graph network alone and two classic methods on their score. The authors argue that layer by layer mixing lets local shape and global knowledge inform each other.
arxiv-2504-17897:
Nishit Patel and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a walkability index for all of Europe. Lack of activity drives obesity and chronic disease, and street design shapes how much people walk. Past indexes varied by place and used coarse data. The team built one standard, fine-grained index from matched data sets across the continent.

Seven parts define the score, from walkable street length and crossings to green space, slope, and transit access. A grid of 100-meter cells covers Europe, with distance effects modeled at scale. Scores showed a clear city-to-country gradient. Compact centers with mixed land use scored highest, and cities such as Barcelona, Berlin, and Paris led. The index is offered as a tool for planners.
arxiv-2504-18797:
Dian-Yong Chen and co-authors present a 2025 physics paper on a resonance seen when electrons and positrons collide. The state, called Y(2240), shows up in collisions that produce pairs of kaons, charged or neutral. The authors fit both production channels together in one analysis.

Their model mixes a direct production process with one that passes through the resonance, letting the two interfere. With a free isospin factor, both channels fit well, but that factor strayed from the value symmetry predicts. Fixing it to one still fit the charged channel yet failed the neutral one. That gap hints at extra states nearby, such as two named resonances. The authors call for finer measurements in two energy ranges.
arxiv-2504-19197:
Sandipan Dhar, Nanda Dulal Jana, and Swagatam Das review adversarial methods for changing a voice's identity in a 2025 survey. Voice conversion keeps the words but swaps the speaker's vocal character, enabling film dubbing, singing conversion, and aids for people whose speech is impaired. Generative adversarial networks, two models trained in opposition, became a leading engine for the swap because they produce natural sounding output.

The review sorts techniques, open challenges, and recent progress. Conversion quality still hinges on disentangling content from identity, the problem every method in the survey attacks from a different side.
arxiv-2504-19397:
Sagar Sudhakara studies how rival firms sharing trucks and warehouse space can coordinate their shipping without a boss. In a supply chain, each agent dispatches on its own information, yet all draw on the same logistics capacity, so uncoordinated choices collide. His 2025 solo paper proposes that every agent follow the same, symmetric dispatch strategy, computed once for all.

The trick is a common information approach: the problem is rewritten around what all agents share, turning a tangled multi-agent puzzle into a single dynamic program on that shared state. Solving it yields the best possible symmetric strategy. In simulations, the method cut coordination costs sharply against practical rivals, including strategies built on private beliefs and a naive always-dispatch rule. The paper argues symmetry is not a fairness garnish but a computational key to decentralized control.
arxiv-2504-20097:
Junran Guo and a large team of co-authors showed drone spotting with no camera, at city range. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a hard task: small drones far off, key for safety and watch work. Camera ways need sharp, costly shots and eat power. Their way reads one photon pixel range echoes and calls the craft by data, with no image made. Past runs of that way reach just a few hundred meters.

Their new build stretches that reach in a true field test in a city. Readers in sensing get proof that photon lean gear can name a drone across town, at low kit cost.
arxiv-2504-20197:
Aryeh Brill offers a geometric way to think about what deep neural networks learn, in a 2025 paper. A network turns raw data into internal patterns of activity, and splitting those patterns into features a human can name would make the systems safer and easier to trust. Brill treats the learned features as a coordinate grid laid over the shape of the data itself.

To study that grid, the paper models a typical data distribution as a random lattice, a mesh with random links. It borrows tools from percolation theory, the study of flow through such meshes. Features then sort into three kinds: those naming the broad context, those naming parts, and those naming the surface. The model lines up with recent findings from work that probes networks directly. Brill closes by pointing to questions the lattice picture raises for future research on how networks build their inner maps.
arxiv-2504-20297:
Imed Basdouri, Bouzid Mosbahi, and Ahmed Zahari present a 2025 paper cataloging four kinds of operators on the smallest pre-Lie algebras. Pre-Lie algebras are a non associative structure that shows up in geometry and in the math of differential equations. Operators of Rota type, named for a family of averaging and splitting rules, enrich such algebras.

Working over the complex numbers, the authors start from the known list of all two dimensional pre-Lie algebras. With computer algebra help, they describe each operator kind on each algebra in full detail. The catalog clarifies how these operators behave and what roles they can play in larger structures.
arxiv-2504-20397:
Tim Stokes studied a class of semigroups in a 2025 maths paper. These structures carry two extra operations and obey a finite set of equation laws. They include several known families used in algebra, such as restriction semigroups.

Stokes focuses on the ample conditions, a pair of laws linking the two operations with multiplication. He shows those laws hold exactly when two natural orders on the structure coincide and a set of projection elements commute. He gives examples beyond restriction semigroups, builds a partial algebra from any such structure, and proves an embedding theorem. The main result follows a known style of structure theorem for these objects.
arxiv-2504-20897:
Ekta Chaubey and Vasily Sotnikov extend a tidy recipe for particle physics integrals to the elliptic case. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Feynman integrals, which encode particle interactions, become far neater when written in a canonical form, and special integrand bases can force that form.

In the simpler genus-zero world, bases built from logarithmic forms with whole-number leading behavior do the job. Elliptic curves push the problem to genus one. The authors argue that one careful choice of algebraic forms, avoiding derivatives, is the key step. The resulting integrals obey a new special form of differential equation. Order by order, their solutions stay pure functions. The authors conjecture the recipe works in general.
arxiv-2504-20997:
Dilip Arumugam and Thomas Griffiths hand a language model a classic exploration algorithm to run in plain words, in a 2025 paper. Agents that decide step by step need data thrift: each trial costs. Exploration, knowing when to probe the unknown, is the hard part, and many language model agents botch it. Classic reinforcement learning owns elegant fixes, but their machinery resists translation into talk.

Rather than fine-tune a model to ape good play, the authors let it carry out posterior sampling, a proven method that picks each act by a sampled guess of the world. The model does the bookkeeping in natural language. On word tasks that punish rash or timid probing, the explicit runner beat designs that left exploration to the model's gut. The authors frame the lesson broadly: known algorithms, run openly, can beat hints and vibes in agent design.
arxiv-2504-21097:
Alexander Baumgartner, Temur Kutsia, Jordi Levy, and Mateu Villaret compute broadest common patterns for bound terms in a 2025 paper. Logic terms with binders, as in programming languages, need generalization tools for learning and clone hunting, but the nominal flavor lacked a guaranteed best answer.

When the allowed atoms stay finite, a least general pattern does exist and is unique up to renaming. The paper gives an algorithm that builds it, resting on a decider for when two terms match under swaps. Both parts are proven sound and complete, with cost bounds. The method suits inductive learning where binders rule.
arxiv-2504-21197:
Computers round numbers to save memory, and the rounding rule itself can poison a fourier transform. Laslo Hunhold and John Gustafson test in 2025 how the standard FFT behaves in four young number formats, from eight bits to sixty-four. Images go through round trip transforms and audio through short time ones, with accuracy and stability graded at each width.

Posits shine at low precision and their sibling takums follow closely, though posits wobble as precision grows. A tiny eight bit format fails outright, and bfloat16 trails both float16 and takum. The authors frame the choice of arithmetic as an accuracy decision, not a detail. Spectral methods, they show, notice how you count.
arxiv-2504-21297:
Wenjun Yang and Eyhab Al-Masri build a conversational system that lets citizens help design privacy-preserving AI for public decisions in a 2025 paper. Differential privacy gives hard math guarantees, yet its settings are usually chosen by experts alone.

Three parts anchor the framework. An adaptive protocol picks the privacy budget by weighing citizen preferences through multi-criteria decision analysis. An explanation layer shows live error charts and AI-written impact notes as noise is injected, so trade-offs stay visible. A compliance module adjusts budgets as regulations evolve. The authors argue this mix keeps public-sector privacy tools both mathematically sound and democratically accountable, turning an abstract parameter into a public choice.
arxiv-2504-21397:
Prakash Shukla, Phuong Bui, and Paul Parsons examine how user experience designers cope with uncertainty on real projects. Their work goes beyond the open-endedness of design problems themselves. Priorities shift, teams churn, resources run thin, and build constraints bite, all while the design is in motion. The team ran a multi-week diary study with ten designers and followed up with interviews.

Designers answered uncertainty with a kit of strategies, including reframing the problem as facts changed and negotiating with stakeholders. Judgment sat at the center of the responses. The authors name two less-studied forms of it: temporal judgment, about when to decide, and sacrificial judgment, about what to give up. They argue uncertainty in this field is not a passing glitch but a constant feature of the work. Their findings extend earlier accounts of design practice into the daily reality of UX teams.
arxiv-2505-00097:
Nishita Jadoo, Terrence Pierre Jacques, and Zachariah Etienne present superB, a tool that lets a black hole simulation code grow from one machine to a whole cluster. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Gravitational wave science needs ever sharper simulations of colliding black holes. The team's base framework writes fast code from Python, but it ran on a single node.

The new extension auto-generates a task-based, cluster-ready version of the same physics modules. It splits the grids and manages the talk between parts. On one node its results match the old code bit for bit. A head-on black hole collision run reproduces the expected ringdown tones. On sixty-four nodes it ran about forty-five times faster than the single-node code. The upgrade readies the framework for long inspirals and rapid event follow-ups.
arxiv-2505-00597:
Milo Hyde, Eric Mitchell, and Mark Spencer derive closed-form expressions for the centroid-tilt error caused by scintillation in adaptive optics. Their 2025 paper deals with how trackers and wavefront sensors measure image centroids to estimate a turbulence-degraded wavefront.

Noise, speckle, and scintillation all affect centroid accuracy. Errors from noise and speckle had been studied, but no closed form for scintillation was known. Their derivation assumes spherical-wave illumination, a path-invariant turbulence strength, and Kolmogorov turbulence. They compare the predicted values with wave-optics simulations. Agreement was quite good over a wide range of conditions, giving engineers a ready formula for this error source.
arxiv-2505-01197:
Holger Dette and Carina Graw make bootstrap methods safe for private data. Their 2025 paper tackles a clash: the bootstrap resamples data many times to gauge uncertainty. Under differential privacy, each extra look at the data costs privacy budget. Heavy reuse can wreck either privacy or accuracy.

Older fixes assume a parametric model, which fails when the model is wrong. The pair instead study an empirical bootstrap that resamples only part of the data each time. They prove it stays consistent and private under Gaussian differential privacy. Their version beats the full-size private bootstrap on several counts. The result opens honest uncertainty checks for sensitive datasets.
arxiv-2505-01397:
Skinner and Wei simulate the skies of two giant exoplanets to compare hot and warm worlds, in this 2025 paper. Both planets are locked to their stars, one face in permanent day. Though their temperatures differ sharply, the pair share similar values for the numbers that govern flow, placing them in one dynamical family.

Both skies show churning equatorial flows, swirling polar vortices, and planet-scale waves that drive banded winds off the equator. The gap between them lies in the size of those waves and eddies, set by each planet's deformation scale. The study bridges two regimes often treated apart.
arxiv-2505-01597:
Simone Servadio published an aerospace engineering paper in 2025 on particle flow filters. Such filters track uncertain systems, like spacecraft, by moving sample points. The points flow toward the most likely states instead of being reweighted. A drift term pushes them, and a diffusion term keeps them spread out.

Servadio derives new forms for both terms using high-order polynomial expansions. Older methods based on straight-line approximations become simple cases of the new one. Differential algebra carries the math directly on the polynomial forms. Two new filters result, differing in where the expansion is centered. Numerical tests showed clear gains over standard flows. The gains were largest against the exact flow comparison.
arxiv-2505-01697:
Jiangneng Li and co-authors design a database index that adapts its space-filling curve to each region of the data in this 2025 paper. Such curves flatten multi-dimensional data into one line for indexing. Classic curves use one mapping rule for the whole space. One rule rarely suits every region equally well. Their piecewise design assigns different rules to different subspaces. A tree structure grows the subspaces and their curves together.

Learning updates keep the curves matched to the data's shape. Queries then skip irrelevant regions more sharply. Multi-dimensional search powers maps, sensors, and analytics alike. The index aims to beat one-size-fits-all curves on real data. The paper is a database systems study. It reports the design and its guarantees.
arxiv-2505-02097:
Five astronomers estimate how often a class of X-ray flashes occurs across the universe, in a 2025 paper. The flashes are thought to come from newborn magnetars, fiercely magnetic neutron stars born when two neutron stars merge. A handful have been spotted in deep surveys and in follow-ups of short gamma-ray bursts. Knowing their rate would illuminate both merger physics and magnetar birth.

From population models, the team derives a local rate of about three hundred events per cubic gigaparsec each year, peaking far back in cosmic time. They also fit how the flashes spread in brightness, finding a bend at high power. Folding the two together, they predict a new Chinese X-ray mission should catch about thirty-one such flashes a year. That guess matches the mission's first year of operation, though the authors flag wide uncertainty bars.
arxiv-2505-02397:
Antoni López-Martínez wrote a 2025 math paper on operators that act on functions defined on a rooted tree. The space in question holds functions that change only slightly between nearby points, with a strict smallness rule at large distances. The operators he studies build new functions by first moving each point along a fixed rule.

He gives a full account of which increasing rules make these operators frequently hypercyclic. That term means the operator, applied again and again, comes close to every function in the space very often. His method rests on a natural match between these tree spaces and two classic sequence spaces. That match also makes many older results on such spaces simpler and stronger.
arxiv-2505-02497:
Miriam Resch and co-authors present quantum work from 2025 on cat states in multi mode systems. Cat states are large scale quantum states that resist some kinds of noise. That trait makes them a strong pick for future quantum computing. The states form on their own in driven Kerr oscillators, a type of quantum device.

Working with more than one cat at once needs a way to link them. The team shows fast switches between device settings that link the cats at once. Those switches can set the cats up as paired Bell states from the start. The method could speed up work with cat based quantum bits.
arxiv-2505-02697:
Dimitrios Ntalampekos surveys recent progress on uniformization of metric surfaces, in a 2025 review written alone. Uniformization asks when a rough surface, known only through distances, can be reshaped into a standard smooth one without tearing its geometry too far. The classic result covers smooth surfaces, but fractal-like surfaces raised harder questions.

The survey walks through a chain of landmark theorems, from a sphere result that opened the fractal study to a sphere result with weaker demands. It ends with work by Romney and the author covering general surfaces of finite area with no extra assumptions. Readers get a guided tour of how the field's main barriers fell, one by one.
arxiv-2505-03097:
Lei Wang and co-authors present in 2025 a way to improve image making with diffusion models by masking some parts of the network. Such models build a rough image first and fine detail later, yet the same layers must learn both jobs. The team studied which network weights help at each stage of cleaning noise from an image.

Turning off some weights, even large ones, could improve the result at once. Their method uses only the weights that help for a given step and sample, with two ways to tune it, one with training and one without. Tests on a large photo data set gave strong quality scores and gains on later tasks.
arxiv-2505-03397:
Chris Wise and four co-authors define a quantum feature space for a qubit coupled to a bath, in work from 2025. Qubit control usually rests on a power spectral density account of that coupling. Earlier grey-box work inferred noise operators with deep neural networks, but that structure is complex and hard to scale or run in real time.

The team shows that the same noise description has an efficient parameterization, with no costly networks needed. Distance in that feature space can classify noise processes under a given control set. A random forest fed with the space sorted stationarity and broad noise class well. Control pulse settings can also be mapped into the space.
arxiv-2505-03497:
Stijn Cambie and Michiel Provoost study edge-colouring games set by Erdős and by Bensmail and Mc Inerney. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Two players take turns to colour edges of a full graph in their own hue. Each aims to grow a graph trait in their own sub-graph, such as the largest clique or the top degree.

In the fair form, they give a first step toward a known guess, a new guess for the degree game, and spreads of both games to wider graph kinds. In the biased form, where turns colour unlike counts of edges, the degree and vertex games are settled, and one clique case is proved.
arxiv-2505-03697:
Susmita Bhattacharjee and co-authors study fairness in speech recognition for people with cleft lip and palate, in a 2025 paper. Their speech is often nasal in quality, which shifts sound patterns and lowers recognition accuracy. The head of the work frames the fix as mixing training speech by severity level.

The team defines a fairness score that balances overall error against the gap between groups. They test three recognition systems on English and Kannada datasets. Mixing typical speech with cleft speech, matched by severity, improved fairness on both datasets. Word error rates fell by more than ten points in the best cases. The authors argue severity aware mixing is a practical step toward fairer speech tools.
arxiv-2505-03897:
Miguel Coloma Puga and co-authors map glowing gas clouds around far-off radio galaxies. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses the MUSE instrument on the Very Large Telescope. Eleven galaxies at high redshift were viewed, joining nine more from past records.

Images centered on the Lyman-alpha line show each cloud shape and glow. Spectra from the core and maps of gas motion add depth. Brightness fell off with distance in a smooth curve for most clouds. Line ratios pointed to an active galactic core as the power source in most cases. Two past finds could not be confirmed, a useful caution for surveys.
arxiv-2505-03997:
Prudhviraj Naidu, Zixian Wang, Leon Bergen, and Ramamohan Paturi reported in 2025 that language models learn hidden skills before their scores improve. The catalog creator field is garbled with affiliation and email text. Training curves for algorithmic tasks showed long flat stretches, then sudden drops in loss, against standard scaling expectations.

Probing the models' inner states during the flat stretches revealed quiet features: partial computations that alone do not help the output. Removing individual features broke task performance, proving they are needed. The team argue that real learning can hide under a flat loss curve. Watching loss alone misreads training, and richer checks on inner representations are needed to see progress.
arxiv-2505-04097:
Vo and Ho train a three-dimensional neural network to spot Alzheimer's disease in brain scans. Sorting scans by eye is slow, and the disease's signs are subtle. Their network reads whole T1-weighted MRI volumes and labels each as healthy or Alzheimer's, using stacked 3D filters, normalization, and a final yes-no output.

Adding simple noise to the training scans, a cheap form of data augmentation, lifted test accuracy to about ninety-one percent. The ranking score reached about ninety-six percent, and both sensitivity and specificity cleared ninety percent. Noise injection beat plain resizing of the scans by a clear margin. The authors say even simple augmentation pays off for 3D medical imaging. They point to richer augmentation and newer architectures as the next steps.
arxiv-2505-04297: István Gaál studies whether a family of degree six number fields can be generated by a single algebraic integer, in a 2025 paper. The property, called monogenity, was settled for the family's polynomials by earlier work. Gaál turns to the fields themselves. His computation is the first real test of the method he applies, and it shows the method working efficiently on a nontrivial family.
arxiv-2505-04497:
Aditi Ramaswamy, Hana Chockler, and Melane Navaratnarajah study how to judge creative work by image tools in a 2025 paper. The head gives the work a plainer title about creative acts in image generators. Past debate on this topic had reached no firm answer, so the team takes a hands on view.

The authors build number based measures meant to help a user pick a tool for a set task. They test the measures on well known image to image models. The scores lined up with what people would expect by feel. Such checks could make tool choice less of a guess for artists and other users.
arxiv-2505-04797:
Xinyi Wang, Shaukat Ali, and Paolo Arcaini chart the road ahead for quantum AI in software engineering in a 2025 paper. Software now runs so much of life that building and testing it strains human teams, and classic AI already helps with requirements, coding, testing, and debugging. Quantum computing promises to speed some of those aids and cut their cost.

Early uses have appeared, such as smarter test case choice. The paper surveys what quantum methods could bring to each stage of the software life cycle and what blocks stand in the way, from hardware limits to skills gaps. It lays out a research agenda meant to turn scattered pilots into standard practice. Cost-effective gains, not hype, set the bar the authors propose.
arxiv-2505-05097:
Ilya Nikitin, Nikolay Masnev, and Sergey Belan model how distances inside a polymer chain change when molecular machines actively extrude loops along it, as happens with DNA in cells. Their base model is the Rouse polymer, a chain of beads joined by springs. The analysis holds when extrusion is fast and loops stay sparse.

Within a one-loop approximation, they develop a semi-analytical way to get the mean squared distance between two beads from their separation along the chain. They plot that distance and its rate of change for several settings of the chain's equilibrium behavior. Results are compared with the case of a frozen, random set of sparse loops.
arxiv-2505-05197:
Joel Leibo and five co-authors argue that aligning AI systems to one shared ethics is the wrong goal, using a quilt as their central image. Progress, in their telling, is sewing an ever-growing, many-colored patchwork, not ironing a single cloth. They blame a hidden premise, the axiom of rational convergence: the belief that ideal talk ends in one agreed morality. Real societies, they note, keep their moral diversity.

Their alternative, the appropriateness framework, designs for lasting disagreement instead of wishing it away. Four principles guide it: ground choices in context, let communities customize, keep adapting, and govern from many centers. The authors borrow support from conflict theory, cultural evolution, multi-agent systems, and institutional economics. They urge the field to swap moral unification for conflict management as its working metaphor, calling the shift both desirable and urgent.
arxiv-2505-05497:
Luca Sassoli de Bianchi and Massimiliano Sassoli de Bianchi report in 2025 a cognitive version of the famous slit experiments from quantum physics. In quantum cognition, concepts behave in some ways like quantum entities when minds test them. Sending a concept through one, two, or three choices mirrors particles passing through slits.

The data show the classic interference fringes between options, plus the embryos of secondary fringes. A Sorkin parameter that should vanish for pure quantum behavior deviated strongly from zero, signaling third-order interference with no quantum counterpart. Mind and micro-world share a conceptual flavor, the authors conclude, but the mind's version carries extra structure physics does not.
arxiv-2505-05597:
Jacek Karolczak and Jerzy Stefanowski improved this 2025 way of explaining model predictions with examples. Prototype explanations show a past case that looks like the current one. Users, though, may not see which features make the pair alike. The authors hunt the alike parts: the shared features that matter most.

They score feature importance with a model-agnostic explainer, then highlight where the case and its nearest prototype overlap on important features. The same scores feed the prototype-picking step, favoring a diverse global set. Across six benchmark data sets, users understood predictions better with the highlights. Accuracy held steady or improved. The method makes example-based explanations point at the evidence instead of just showing a look-alike.
arxiv-2505-05997:
Romain Bourneuf and co-authors give a fast approximation algorithm for finding complete graph patterns inside ordered graphs, in a paper from 2025. A minor is what remains after shrinking connected parts of a graph to single points. For ordered graphs, the allowed shrinks respect the vertex order, forming interval minors.

Deciding whether a complete graph is a minor is tractable in general, but good approximations were missing. Their algorithm runs in polynomial time and guarantees a factor that depends only on the target size, not the graph size, though that factor grows very fast. The proof rests on delayed decompositions: ordered graphs avoiding the pattern are built from three simple operations. A side result shows such graphs need only boundedly many colors.
arxiv-2505-06197:
Tronconi and Venturi ask whether the Higgs field alone, dressed by quantum corrections, could have inflated the early universe and seeded primordial black holes, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Higgs inflation needs no new inflaton particle, which makes it economical, but producing black holes requires a burst of large curvature ripples.

Their model starts from the tree-level action of gravity plus the Standard Model Higgs. A series of higher-dimension operators, standing in for quantum corrections, modifies the dynamics. Inside a minimal effective field theory framework, they present two viable versions. In both, the ripple spectrum matches cosmic microwave background observations on large scales. On small scales it grows enough to collapse into primordial black holes of asteroid-like mass. Such black holes could, in principle, make up all of the dark matter. The paper ties the universe's largest mystery to its best-known particle.
arxiv-2505-06697:
Hosseini and Karlin build flood math out of colliding particles, and fix a flaw in how it was done before. The shallow water equations govern tides, tsunamis, and flash floods. Deriving them from kinetic theory usually corrupts the friction terms. Their scheme recovers the viscous form exactly, with no error in how energy dies away.

The scheme also adds forces in a clean new way, splits pressure between two neat parts, and lets bulk viscosity be tuned on its own. Test cases confirm it is accurate and stable. Flood modelers gain a tool whose physics is right by design, not by patching.
arxiv-2505-06797:
Weiqin Sun and co-authors use low altitude spacecraft data to watch Earth's magnetic tail during the build up to a substorm, in work from 2025. During this growth phase, a thin sheet of current forms in the tail. The field near the equator weakens and its lines stretch out.

Single satellites give only local snapshots of that large change. Electron fluxes measured low down can instead sense the distant field, since strong scattering spreads the electrons evenly. Their spread varies with latitude in a way that tracks the field shape. The ELFIN mission data let the team follow how energetic electron flux evolved through the phase.
arxiv-2505-06997:
Wenhao Lu and co-authors tackle task sharing among drones, ground robots, and people in rescue work, in this 2025 paper. After a disaster, mixed teams must sense and map a site fast, with weak links and partial views. Ground robots can also recharge drones whose batteries run low.

The team frame the task as a step-by-step choice problem under doubt and build a learning method for it. The method trains with a full view but acts on local views, using memory and a mixing step that blends local and global facts. In simulations it raised task completion by about 18 percent over rival methods. A real-world case study backed its strength in changing scenes.
arxiv-2505-07097:
Shaul Zemel shows how to normalize higher Specht polynomials in a matched way so a stable version of them can be defined, in algebra tied to symmetry groups. These polynomials give bases for key representation spaces. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The author also splits a non transitive action by other scholars into its orbits. A basis of higher Specht polynomials from further work is shown to respect that split. For a set size, the orbits match subsets of the positive integers below that size. The representation for a set is then linked to two for the next size up, one the set itself and one with the top number added, a lift of the branching rule.
arxiv-2505-07197:
Yue Meng and four co-authors build a tool that reorders shopping lists for a large online store. Stores rank goods to lift clicks, sales, and total spend at once. Older methods score each item alone, which misses how items in a list sway each other and what the shopper wants right now. Reordering the whole list can fix that, but it must stay fast and keep the list varied.

Their model, called SORT-Gen, splits the task in two parts. A transformer first scores the worth of list chunks of any length across all goals. A fast search step then builds the final list from ranked queues with a spread rule built in. Live tests on a Taobao mini-app lifted clicks by about four percent and total spend by about eight percent. The gains count at platform scale.
arxiv-2505-07397:
Shilpa Sarkar and Igor Kulikov wrote a 2025 paper on flows of gas around black holes and like dense objects. Such flows must cross the speed of sound, and finding where that happens is tricky when flows lose energy. Old methods handled only some flow types.

Their new method works by steady relaxation, guided by conditions near the central object. It takes a set of flow constants as given. Viscosity, heating, and a cooling process are all built in. From those, the method can build any class of inflow or outflow, with one or many sound crossing points and shocks. They give the math and the step by step computing recipe in full.
arxiv-2505-07497:
Gerhard Schindl introduces new function transformations in a 2025 mathematics paper. The transforms extend the classic Legendre conjugate, a tool that swaps a function for a slope-based partner. Schindl defines upper and lower versions that work for pairs of functions with basic growth behavior.

He then studies how the transforms change growth indices that were defined in recent work on weight functions. A key case uses weight functions built from an underlying weight sequence. There, the transforms amount to multiplying or dividing the sequences term by term. Schindl argues this clean match shows the definitions are natural. He also points to uses in weighted function spaces in several branches of analysis.
arxiv-2505-07597:
Junfan Yi, Ke-ke Shang, and Michael Small propose a new way to locate moving objects in three dimensions in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Older methods need costly gear or fixed reference objects to measure angles. Their approach needs neither, and it leans on math plus artificial intelligence.

The model uses the time pattern of a moving object to infer its relative angles, then solves for its position with a standard matrix method. In tests, three cameras tracked a drone. An improved vision model read the drone's flat positions, and the math model turned them into three-dimensional coordinates with low error. The authors say the method suits targets that do not cooperate.
arxiv-2505-07797:
Daniel Beechey and co-authors build a theory for explaining why reinforcement learning agents act as they do. Their 2025 paper notes that such agents can beat humans at hard tasks, yet their behavior is often opaque. That opacity limits their use where safety is at stake and trust has to be earned.

The authors name three things an explanation should cover: behavior, outcomes, and predictions. Their method, called SVERL, explains all three through the influence of each feature the agent sees. The influence scores come from Shapley values, a fair-division idea from game theory that meets a set of rules for fair credit. Worked examples show the method giving clear, grounded explanations that watching the agent alone would not reveal. The paper also uses the theory to fix flaws in older explanation methods.
arxiv-2505-07897:
Stefano Rando and co-authors published a computing paper in 2025 benchmarking coding language models at million-token context lengths. Real tasks that truly need such memory are hard to find and costly to build. The team argues code comprehension and repair fit the bill, since real projects sprawl. Their benchmark draws on genuine GitHub issues, split into question answering and bug fixing tracks.

Models from mid-size open systems to flagship commercial ones were graded across difficulty tiers. Every model weakened sharply as context ballooned; one top model's score fell from twenty-nine percent to three. The dataset and code are public. The authors conclude long context remains an open weakness, not a solved spec.
arxiv-2505-08197:
Junxian Duan and three co-authors review watermarking for images in the age of diffusion generators, in a 2025 paper. Synthetic media raise copyright and misuse worries. Watermarks assert ownership and deter copying. Older detection methods passively hunt fakes and often miss skilled fakes. Diffusion models change both the threat and the defense.

Their survey sorts watermark methods tied to diffusion systems. Robustness against removal and forgery is the core test. Some methods embed marks during image generation itself. Others add marks that survive heavy editing. Strengths and open gaps are mapped across the field. The authors stress that forgery tools evolve fast. Watermarks must harden at the same pace. Better marks protect creators' rights in a synthetic media market, they conclude.
arxiv-2505-08297:
Sare Khoshdooni and two co-authors study a width measure of entanglement in non-relativistic scale-invariant theories, in a 2025 paper. The measure, called capacity, mirrors heat capacity in spirit. It reads the spread of a reduced state's eigenvalue spectrum. The theories scale with a free exponent rather than light speed. Ground states and sudden quenches are both examined.

Universal terms in the capacity depend on that exponent. After a sudden change, the measure spreads as if carried by particle pairs. In relativistic theories, a related flow function decreases steadily. Here that tidy behavior fails for both matter types. A mass quench study confirms the particle picture for dynamics. Results align with other entanglement measures, the authors note. The work maps where relativistic intuition breaks down.
arxiv-2505-08497:
Chetra Mang, Axel TahmasebiMoradi, and Mouadh Yagoubi split parameter spaces with learning tools in a 2025 paper. Simulations over wide parameter ranges strain computing budgets. Their method shrinks the data manifold by repeated principal component passes. Two ways then rebuild the map back to the full space, so results can be read in original terms.

On that shrunken map they lay out a split of the parameter domain into simpler zones. A harmonic transport problem tests the method against neural network stand ins. Zone wise models can beat one global model when behavior changes character across the range. The recipe suits design studies that must sweep many settings fast.
arxiv-2505-08597:
Laura Torchia and Massimo Capone present a 2025 theory study of a two-band superconductor that can flip into an insulator. Their model pairs an attractive pull between electrons with a repulsive exchange term tied to spin alignment. A strong sound-wave coupling in real materials can flip the base pull negative while the exchange stays put. The team solve the model at zero temperature and half filling.

Even with no exchange, two bands give the flip as the pull grows, unlike the one-band case. Exchange makes the pull act stronger and hastens the flip. The flip arrives as the particle weight fades to zero, much like the famed Mott flip. Attractive systems thus host a correlated flip of their own. The work guides hunts in real two-band materials.
arxiv-2505-08697:
Samuele Maschio and Davide Trotta give in 2025 a category theory account of a broad notion of problem solving strength. Weihrauch reducibility ranks how hard it is to turn solutions of one problem into solutions of another, which helps grade the strength of math theorems. An extended version of the ranking widens that reach.

Category tools have rarely been brought to this topic. The pair build a new tripos, an abstract logic setting, from the extended degrees, then apply a standard construction to gain a topos, a full universe for the logic. They also show a classic topos sits inside theirs as a well-behaved part.
arxiv-2505-08897:
Felipe Augusto Tasca, Paulinho Demeneghi, Víctor Marín, and Willian Goulart Gomes Velasco prove a P-theorem for inverse semigroupoids in two thousand twenty-five. Their tool is ordered partial actions and their globalizations. Every such action of an inverse semigroupoid admits a globalization, they show. That bridge links ordered actions of groupoids to McAlister style triples.

The multi-object version of those triples is the new form here. From it the P-theorem falls out in full. Each E-unitary inverse semigroupoid is a semidirect product from such an action. The action lives on a multi-object semilattice in their build.
arxiv-2505-09197:
Matthew Blackledge and eight co-authors present a Bayesian framework for judging how precisely imaging biomarkers can be measured, in a 2025 paper. Biomarkers that capture how uneven a disease is could guide precision medicine, but checking their measurement error has lagged behind. Classic repeatability methods assume simple, bell-shaped data.

Their approach uses advanced sampling to work with many distribution types, including ones for counts of categories, and returns full probability distributions for biomarker values. They demonstrate it on whole-body diffusion-weighted MRI scans of prostate cancer that has spread to bone, asking how mixed one patient's response to treatment is across lesions. The authors designed the framework to transfer across imaging types.
arxiv-2505-09497:
Sourav Pal and Abhik Basu study traffic-like shocks in single-file motion with a bottleneck in two thousand twenty-five. Particles that move one way in a narrow channel model many real flows, from cell cargo to city traffic. A shock, or domain wall, is a sharp line where density jumps.

Their model is a simple grid automaton in a closed loop with a fixed particle count and one slow spot. At high entry and exit rates with many particles, the shock shape stops depending on those rates, a new kind of universality, though edge layers still vary. At low rates the shape does depend on the rates. Extra tuning can also free the shock to wander.
arxiv-2505-09897:
Layan Badran, Kiarash Aryankia, and Rastko Selmic work out how much communication delay a swarm of agents can tolerate before agreement falls apart. Their 2025 paper models the agents as double integrators on weakly connected, leaderless networks. Delays are constant but need not match across links, which mirrors real hardware.

The analysis leans on the Lambert W function, extended here to higher dimensions. It yields an explicit upper bound on the delay that still guarantees stability and consensus. The conditions are proven, not just simulated, and they cover general undirected layouts. Numerical examples confirm the margins. The authors pitch the bound as a design rule for drone fleets, robot teams, and sensor webs that must agree while messages lag.
arxiv-2505-10097:
Meirun Chen and co-authors prove a strong graph color claim for the flip side of a known graph family. The work dates to 2025. The claim at stake grows out of the four-color claim and ranks among the hard open tasks in graph work. Its odd form adds sign marks for more strength.

The team proves the odd claim holds for flip graphs of the family in view, with a size bound on the parts. That step lifts a past result that gave the plain claim for the same family. They also show the flip graphs hold a shallow full chunk of a set kind. In one band the gap from the color count grows fast.
arxiv-2505-10297:
Chibueze Peace Obioma, Youcheng Sun, and Mustafa Mustafa defend shared learning nets against hidden backdoor attacks, in a paper from 2025. In federated learning, edge gear trains a shared model, but sly attackers can plant triggers that fire on cue while their updates look normal.

Their guard, FeRA, looks for sameness rather than odd size: planted clients must stay too steady across rounds to keep the trigger alive. It blends shape, direction, and size checks to flag such clients. Across six data sets and nine attacks, it left backdoor success very low while clean scores stayed high.
arxiv-2505-10497:
Iurii Medvedev and Nuno Gonçalves harden face recognition against a blended-photo attack in a 2025 paper. Morphing merges two faces into one image that matches both people, letting an impostor slip through border and login checks built on face matching. Defenders need networks that learn what a morph is, not networks that never see one.

Their method, MorphGuard, changes the training task itself. A dual-branch classification strategy handles the labeling riddle of morphs, which belong to two identities at once, and a morph-specific margin loss sharpens the boundary around them. Morphs join training as first-class examples, teaching the model to tell them from genuine faces. Public benchmarks confirmed stronger resistance to morphing attacks. The recipe is deliberately portable: it plugs into existing classification-based training pipelines rather than replacing them.
arxiv-2505-11297:
Gal Astrach and Yuval Pinter asked what sound facts a language model picks up on its own, in a 2025 paper. They study models trained to bend words into new forms, a task where small sound changes carry the grammar. Their test works across languages and checks where sound traits sit inside the model.

The pair ran the test on seven languages with rich word forms. Sound traits that act on nearby sounds, such as a final sound turning voiceless in Turkish, showed up well in the model's sound units. Traits that span a whole word, such as vowel harmony, sat higher up in the model instead. The results give trainers a clearer sense of which sound skills a model learns early and which ones need the full word in view.
arxiv-2505-11397:
Gregory Gabadadze and Giorgi Tukhashvili discuss an action for gravity that captures the trace anomaly while staying weakly coupled, in work from 2025. The trace anomaly is a quantum effect that breaks a symmetry of classic gravity theory. A local counter term in the action can encode that effect.

The authors argue this counter term matters most among endless options. On its own it leads to a scattering strength that blows up even at low energy. Adding a new sector, where scale symmetry breaks on its own, removes that problem. Three appendices sum up related anomaly actions in simpler theories, in both local and non local forms.
arxiv-2505-11497:
Yushi Huang and co-authors give a way to shrink video-making AI models so they run with far less cost. The work dates to 2025. Video models make sharp clips but need huge compute and memory. Shrinking tricks that work for still images fail when used on video models.

The team trains the shrunk model with extra helper parts that soak up shrink errors. Those parts help the model learn well at very low bit counts. A slow rank-cut plan then trims the helpers away, so no extra cost stays at run time. Tests on four top video models hit near full-grade quality at four bits.
arxiv-2505-11597:
Jean Somalwar and co-authors report a bright flash in the sky found sitting far from a small galaxy. Their search hunts for hot flares that sit well away from any galaxy in sky survey data. The event, named AT 2024puz, sat a clear distance from a dwarf galaxy and shone from infrared to X-ray bands.

The flare rose and fell over about twenty days, with strong X-ray output and no radio signal. Early light likely came from gas reprocessing the glare of a feeding black hole, with a possible shock in dense nearby gas. Late infrared light hinted at a wind. The team places the event between two known flare classes in strength and pace.
arxiv-2505-12097:
Ricardo Baptista and co-authors introduce a new way to measure how far apart two probability distributions lie. Their measure blends two older families, information divergences and transport distances, through an infimal convolution, a kind of best-compromise formula. It was designed to put the proximal methods used in generative modeling on firm ground.

They work out the new measure's properties: it is smooth, bounded, and computable, and it links to primal-dual formulations and adversarial learning. Its linked operator reads as a map that nudges a starting distribution toward the best generative match to a target known only through samples. A dynamic version, built like the classical flow picture of transport, becomes a mean-field game governed by two coupled equations.
arxiv-2505-12197:
Gian Marco Marin and Emeric Roulley study swirling flows on a spinning sphere in a 2025 paper. Their focus is vortex caps, broad patches of rotating fluid bounded by a sharp edge. Prior work showed that smooth, band-like profiles are stable in a certain averaged sense.

The team shows that slightly dented caps behave differently: their edges stretch and fray, a filamentation effect. By comparing flows along the smooth edge and inside the bump, they trace how the stretching starts. The result exposes an instability hiding inside a class of flows that look settled, with lessons for large-scale atmospheric and oceanic motion.
arxiv-2505-12497:
Xin An and co-authors simulate the Moon's wake in a 2025 space physics paper. The solar wind hits the Moon and leaves an empty pocket downstream, since the Moon soaks up the particles that strike it. That void slowly fills as fresh plasma streams past, forming the lunar wake.

A particle level simulation followed the refill step by step. Early on, plasma thins into the void in the smooth way classic theory predicts, with ions speeding up and cooling as they expand. Later, two fast ion beams crash head on at the wake's center. Their clash spawns tiny electric shocks and waves, which the run captures in detail.
arxiv-2505-12597:
Synthetic speech in conversation should sound like it feels what the dialogue feels. Yifan Hu, Rui Liu, Yi Ren, Xiang Yin, and Haizhou Li presented a system for that goal in 2025, called Chain-Talker. It works in three stages modeled on human thought: first reading the emotion in the dialogue history, then forming compact semantic codes, then rendering expressive speech from both.

A second tool uses a large language model to write precise emotion captions for training data, which supports the first stage. On three benchmark datasets, Chain-Talker produced more expressive and empathetic speech than existing methods. Code and demos were released with the paper for other researchers to test.
arxiv-2505-12697:
Li, Chen, Shao, Lian, and Liu wrote in twenty twenty-five about a code embedding model trained on massive synthetic data. Embedding models turn code into numbers that capture meaning for search. Retrieval tools in software work depend on such models. Good training data for code are scarce, which limits past models. The team built a huge synthetic data set under rules stressing diversity, reliability, and usability. Their model, CodeR, trains on that data with a staged learning plan.

The plan transfers knowledge across mixed data sources step by step. Tests covered sixteen varied code retrieval tasks. CodeR beat existing baselines by clear margins on those tasks. It also generalized well to domains outside its training set. The authors release code and the trained model openly. They aim to support further work on code search.
arxiv-2505-12897:
Piotr Borycki and co-authors present EPIC, a way to explain image classifiers with prototypes, in this 2025 paper. Explanation tools split into two camps. Post hoc tools work on any trained model but give coarse heat maps. Built in prototype methods explain clearly but need special training from scratch.

EPIC bridges the two camps. It runs on pretrained models with no architecture change. Yet its explanations show representative image patches, like prototype methods do. Users see concrete examples behind a prediction instead of vague hot regions. The method aims at general use across models and datasets. That breadth was the weakness of earlier prototype systems. Faithful, readable explanations support trust in deployed vision systems.
arxiv-2505-13297:
Kaitlyn Shin and co-authors report in 2025 a fast radio burst source found by the CHIME telescope that proved to be one of the most active ever seen. Fast radio bursts are brief, bright flashes from deep space. This source, named FRB 20240114A, was announced in January 2024. Its low position in the sky made even a few bursts a hint of high activity.

CHIME recorded five bursts, saving raw signal data for two. Over nearly a year the source's dispersion stayed steady, and the team measured its rotation measure and found no scattering. Its burst rate ran about forty-nine times the median for one-off sources. Active repeaters like this help test whether repeaters differ at root from single bursts.
arxiv-2505-13397:
Benoit Dherin and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on use of classic equation solvers as the engine of deep learning. Gradient descent, the workhorse of the field, is the plainest solver of the gradient flow equation: the Euler step. Far sharper solvers exist, the Runge-Kutta family chief among them. They have seen little use in deep learning so far.

The team tests high order Runge-Kutta solvers as training engines. They map where the solvers strain and craft fixes. Key tricks of modern optimizers are folded in: preconditioning, pace that adapts, and momentum. The aim is a solver that tracks the flow more true and more stable than Euler steps.
arxiv-2505-13497:
Planning agents need a model of their world's rules, but hand-writing one for every new task is hopeless. Claudius Kienle and co-authors presented in 2025 LODGE, a system that lets a language model draft the rules and then fixes its own draft by testing it.

LODGE builds the model in layers, from abstract goals down to concrete actions. Automated simulations hunt for mismatches between layers and between model and world, and flagged errors get repaired. The only inputs are a simulator and basic motor skills — no human feedback. On planning contest domains and a robot assembly task, LODGE produced more accurate models and higher success than rivals.
arxiv-2505-13597:
Yue Samuel Lu and co-authors use simulated galaxy halos to corner how cosmic rays travel, in this 2025 paper. Cosmic rays shape galaxies, but their motion through the gas halo around a galaxy is barely pinned down. The team ran the same Milky Way-mass halo under several transport models that all match the galaxy's gamma-ray glow, then compared the halos themselves.

Cosmic rays trimmed galaxy mass and star birth while propping up more cool halo gas, lifting key ion signals toward what telescopes see. Models still differed widely, and extended X-ray glow may betray the rays directly. The authors offer the contrasts as a testing frame.
arxiv-2505-13797:
B Farley and ten co-authors find a new way to gauge dust in galaxies by joining two measures that were used apart. The Balmer decrement reads how much dust dims starlight, while dust mass totals the dust present. Each alone tells only part of the story. Their 2025 paper builds two new parameters that link the pair, using light tied to star birth at ultraviolet, visible, and far-infrared wavelengths. Data come from the Galaxy And Mass Assembly survey.

The linked measures proved sensitive to thick dust that blocks short wavelengths. That helps correct star birth rates that dust would otherwise hide. The authors present the method as a sharper census of a key ingredient in galaxy growth. Dust shapes how galaxies look and how fast they make stars.
arxiv-2505-13897:
Ramon van den Akker, Bas Werker and Bo Zhou study valid inference after contextual bandit experiments, in work from 2025. Bandits sample treatments adaptively, after which researchers still want to test effects. Standard tests can fail in that setting, so the authors derive the limit experiment for multi-armed contextual bandits under weak-signal conditions.

Their limit takes a form they can express with stochastic differential equations. From it they get null distributions and local power for common test statistics. Two nuisance threats to size control are addressed, one by translation-invariant sampling and one by suitable pivots. New regularized versions of several sampling rules are proposed, and simulations support the theory.
arxiv-2505-13997:
Huaijie Wang and co-authors published a computing paper in 2025 on teaching video models new action classes over time without keeping old examples. Video adds time structure that makes forgetting worse. Their framework, StPR, splits the problem: one part guards frame-level meaning, the other routes time patterns through specialist sub-networks. No stored clips are needed at any point.

Stable meaning channels are picked by sensitivity and class value, then gently held in place. A mixture of experts chosen by motion style handles the time side, with no task label required. On three action datasets the method beat prior approaches and stayed interpretable. The authors stress privacy gains from dropping stored examples.
arxiv-2505-14297:
Jungseob Lee, Seongtae Hong, Hyeonseok Moon, and Heuiseok Lim present Cross-Lingual Optimization, a cheaper way to move an English-trained language model into a new language, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Standard fine-tuning often drags English skill down, above all when target-language data is scarce. Their method pairs public English training data with a translation model to teach across the language gap.

Across five models and six languages, the method beat plain fine-tuning on both new-language skill and English retention. In low-resource languages, about thirty-two hundred examples of their kind bested sixty-four hundred of the standard kind. The authors also map why the standard route is so touchy about data volume in smaller languages.
arxiv-2505-14997:
Jeong Rae Kim and co-authors published this materials physics paper in 2025. It reports the growth of thin films of niobium monoxide, NbO, a superconductor with an unusual crystal structure: a rock-salt lattice with a quarter of its sites empty in an ordered pattern. Making such films is tricky because the compound holds an uncommon oxidation state and needs growth temperatures above a thousand degrees.

Using molecular beam epitaxy, the team compared substrates and found sapphire worked best for clean, single-phase films. The films superconducted at temperatures up to 1.37 kelvin, on par with bulk crystals of the same material.
