The authors say the work removes key bottlenecks in growing high-temperature films of reluctant compounds. It also adds a vacancy-ordered material to the thin-film superconductor toolbox.
arxiv-2505-15197:
Pinxin Liu and co-authors taught machines to gesture with intent in a 2025 paper. When people talk, their hands add stress, point out ideas, and shape the message. Past gesture tools for speech leaned on sound rhythm or text alone, so their output matched the beat but said little.

The team's frame treats gesture making as a task of reading the speaker's aim. They built a data set that marks clips with the aim each gesture serves. The model first reasons about that aim, then forms gestures that carry it. Tests aimed to show gestures that feel meant, not just timed. Such tools could make avatars and robots seem more human.
arxiv-2505-15297:
Xintong Wang and co-authors published a paper in 2025 on cleaning up toxic Chinese text without scrubbing away its feeling. Rewriting an insult into something blandly polite betrays the speaker's intent. Chinese toxicity often hides in emojis, sound-alike characters, or context, which makes faithful rewriting harder still.

The team built the first Chinese detoxification dataset designed to preserve sentiment polarity. It holds 1,556 hand-checked triplets. Each pairs a toxic sentence with a rewrite that keeps its emotional charge, plus labels marking the toxic spans. Five everyday scenarios are covered, from plain abuse to dialogue. Seventeen large models were graded on safety, fluency, content, and feeling. Even the best stumbled where toxicity turns subtle, in emoji, puns, and back-and-forth talk.
arxiv-2505-15497:
Frederik Baymler Mathiesen and four co-authors certify how close a neural network sits to the real dynamics it imitates. Neural approximations can stand in for nonlinear systems in verification and control work. Safety-critical use, though, needs formal proof of the error size. Their method builds certified first-order models in an adaptive, parallelizable way.

The result is a formal error bound on the neural approximation of a dynamical system. That bound can be treated as a bounded disturbance on the modeled dynamics, which makes the surrogate safe to use. On standard benchmarks the method beat the state of the art and scaled well. It also handled network compression and Koopman operator training tasks.
arxiv-2505-15697:
Lennart Rohlfs and Julien Weiss wrote this 2025 paper on measuring the drag that air exerts on a surface in wind tunnels. Wall shear stress guides aircraft design, but sensors give exact values only at scattered points, while oil-film photos show the whole flow pattern without trustworthy numbers. The team fuse the two with a neural network.

Their method, SENSE, reads the oil-film image sequence and learns to correct its estimates toward the sparse sensor readings. It handles the raw sequence directly, which damps noise without averaging tricks. On a turbulent separated flow over a diffuser, just eight well-placed sensors cut the error on held-out sensors by over thirty percent. The sensor pull improves estimates even far from any sensor.
arxiv-2505-15897:
Carl Beadle and three co-authors show that dark matter detectors based on nuclear spins have wider reach than planned in a 2025 paper. One experiment uses a large polarized spin sample to sense axion dark matter through a tiny effective field. The authors note the same setup responds to real magnetic fields too.

A dark photon hiding inside the shielded chamber would generate exactly such a real field. An axion coupled to light would do the same through the lab's own magnet. The paper shows all three signals can be detected and told apart. At full sensitivity, the instrument would probe extremely weak dark photon mixing for free. A search built for one quarry may thus catch two others on the side.
arxiv-2505-16097:
Zifeng Wang and co-authors build a large data base to train language models for clinical research in 2025. Good AI for trial work needs broad, well-structured data for both training and fair testing. Their resource, called TrialPanorama, gathers 1.6 million trial records from fifteen registries worldwide.

The records link to medical term systems and to related papers. From them, the team builds about 152 thousand training and test items across eight tasks. The tasks span review work, like study search and screening, and design work, like endpoint choice and sample size. A model trained on the data beat much larger general models on all eight tasks.
arxiv-2505-16197:
Jesus Sanchez and Andres Franco Valiente generalized in 2025 a classic geometry construction to contact manifolds, spaces where motion is restricted to a set of allowed directions at each point. Splitting the space into allowed directions and a single extra field creates a non-integrable setting where singularities appear in the construction.

Taking only the finite part of the operator, they show it still has a smoothing trait called hypoellipticity. The result also holds for two-step spaces of the same family, and a tweak gives it for all such spaces. Index theory is worked out for the contact case. A link to a constrained physics model is proposed at the end.
arxiv-2505-16497:
Alex Degtyarev, Igor Dolgachev, and Shigeyuki Kondo study, in 2025, a special family of K3 surfaces threaded with lines. Each surface carries two sets of twelve skew lines, and every line from one set crosses exactly six from the other. The surfaces appear as slices of a classical cubic line complex tied to desmic quartic surfaces.

The authors describe alternative birational models of the surfaces and compute the lattice that records their curves. They also work out a group of projective symmetries and catalog the low-degree rational curves on a typical member. The study ties modern surface theory back to Humbert's classical construction.
arxiv-2505-16597:
Chuhongxu Chen and nine co-authors warned in twenty twenty-five about a trusty electrode. The silver-silver chloride type can contaminate the nanofluidic work it serves. These are prized for how stable they are in micro- and nanoscale fluidics. Yet in chloride-rich solutions the coat on one dissolves. It forms silver complexes that drift into the trial.

The team showed silver particles plating onto graphene by electrodeposition. The source was that dissolved silver and nothing else. That gives a plainer account of a recent claim of an ionic flow-induced current in graphene. The current in fact comes from silver plating. It does not come from the claimed ionic Coulomb drag effect. The team urges care with these in delicate systems. The slow loss of the coat is easy to miss. It can change how a result is read.
arxiv-2505-16697:
Larissa Schmid and co-authors review language models in software architecture in a 2025 survey. Architects have tried these models to classify design choices, spot design patterns, and draft systems from requirements, but no map of results existed. The team analyzes eighteen papers against five guiding questions.

Models are spreading across architecture tasks and often beat older baselines. Yet some jobs stay nearly untouched, like writing code from designs, cloud-native architecture, and conformance checks. Most work still uses plain prompting, though interest grows in richer techniques. The authors chart where the field stands and where the open problems lie.
arxiv-2505-16797:
Hanyue Lou, Jinxiu Liang, and colleagues turn ordinary video into training data for event cameras in a 2025 computer vision study. Event cameras report pixel changes with microsecond timing and huge dynamic range, but learning algorithms for them starve. Real event data are scarce, and existing simulators produce files too bulky to move or store. Their video-to-voxel pipeline simulates event streams efficiently enough to scale.

Compact simulated data let event vision models train at the scale their accuracy demands. Better event models serve fast robotics and low-power sensing, where ordinary cameras blur or saturate.
arxiv-2505-16897:
Ashmita Das, Anjana Krishnan, Soham Sen, and Sunandan Gangopadhyay study a 2025 radiation effect that arises when an atom falls past a horizon-like edge while sitting in a high-grade cavity. The effect is called horizon brightened acceleration radiation. It gives a way to probe how motion and gravity-like settings change the light an atom emits or absorbs.

Most past work linked the atom to the size of the field wave itself, but that choice leads to blow-ups in a key limit for light fields in low dimensions. The authors instead link the atom to the field's momentum, for both a point-like atom and one with real size. They find how the chance of a jump between energy levels changes under this choice. The new link also removes the old blow-up in a natural way.
arxiv-2505-17597:
Puthenpurakal and Reddy prove a neat identity linking two ways of measuring certain algebraic objects. Their setting is commutative algebra: a polynomial ring over a field, an ideal inside it, and the local cohomology modules that record how functions behave near the ideal's zero set.

They compare the Euler characteristic of de Rham cohomology of such a module with that of its Koszul cohomology. The theorem states the two are equal up to a sign fixed by the number of variables. Results of this kind matter because each side is computed with different tools, so an identity lets researchers transfer information between differential and algebraic methods for these graded modules.
arxiv-2505-17797:
Manuel Morante and Naveed ur Rehman present a new way to pull shared rhythms out of many signals at once. Sensors often record several channels that mix the same waves in different strengths. Older decomposition tools are slow, touchy about settings, and weak at modeling how channels link. Their 2025 method first posits latent modes: hidden waves that blend sparse coding with classic mode splitting. Each channel is then a light mix of those shared waves.

Working in the smaller latent space cuts noise and cost. A variational solver keeps the fit honest while favoring few, clean modes with steady frequencies. Tests on made-up and real data check the gains. The authors aim the tool at fields like brain recording and machine monitoring, where many channels carry one story.
arxiv-2505-17897:
Zi-Ao Ma and seven colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on judging AI-made images in a way people can follow. Text-to-image models now draw well, and someone must grade their output at scale. Human grading is slow, and using pricey closed models adds heavy cost.

Open models trained on critique sets are one fix, but good critique data is scarce. Their system, T2I-Eval-R1, uses reinforcement learning to teach an open model to reason about image quality. The grader explains its scores, not just spits out a number. Clear reasons help users trust or challenge each grade. The team aims for cheap grading that stays open to inspection.
arxiv-2505-18297:
Andersson, Gnoatto, and García Trillos solved a hard equation family with deep learning in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Backward stochastic Volterra equations model problems where today's value depends on the whole past path. Classical solvers nest time steps inside time steps, which explodes in cost. Their network learns both solution fields in a single training stage.

For the simpler decoupled case they prove an error bound with the expected time-step rate. Experiments matched that rate closely. Accuracy held steady from a few variables up to five hundred, while graphics hardware kept run times nearly flat. The same solver handled fully coupled systems too. The authors aim it at stochastic control and finance problems.
arxiv-2505-18397:
Systems made of many AI agents that talk, share information, and decide together are becoming practical, thanks to large language models that can use tools. Fangqiao Tian and co-authors take stock of this shift in this 2025 outlook paper. They set out a formal frame for judging such systems on two axes: how well they work, and how safe they are.

The authors ask when a team of agents truly beats a single agent, and when it merely repackages older tricks such as ensemble learning. They also probe how contact between agents can amplify or damp system flaws. Tests on data science automation show the promise of the approach. The paper frames multi-agent systems as a higher-level extension of classic signal processing tools.
arxiv-2505-18697:
Ziyang Cheng and co-authors ask whether large language models can stop catastrophic forgetting when a graph learner must keep absorbing new tasks. Streaming graph data forces continual learning, and past remedies all train from scratch. Pretrained models, with their broad generalization, might carry memory better.

Their 2025 study first indicts the standard benchmarks: the usual evaluation leaks task identity, flattering every method. Under cleaned, realistic conditions, small tweaks to how the language model is used already shine. The team then builds SimGCL, a simple rehearsal-free method that beats the best graph network baseline by about twenty percent. The moral is double: mind the benchmark's leaks, and do not underestimate a large model's memory.
arxiv-2505-18997:
Reggie Pantig, Ali Ovgun, and Gaetano Lambiase hunt quantum gravity traces around stars in a 2025 paper. A theory that adds non-local curvature terms changes star gravity slightly, unlike empty-space solutions. Working in weak gravity, the team computes how light and matter bend near such a corrected star.

Mercury-style orbit drift, signal delay, and redshift each gain tiny quantum corrections. Ringing modes of the star and their filtering of waves also shift, and stronger coupling steadies the spacetime. Today's instruments cannot yet see these effects. Readers get a map of where quantum gravity might one day show itself.
arxiv-2505-19097:
Xichen Ye and four co-authors work on making influence estimates more trustworthy in deep learning in this 2025 paper. Influence functions gauge how much each training example sways a model's answers. In large networks, those estimates often fail, above all with noisy training data.

The authors trace the fault not to how parameter change is estimated, but to how loss change is estimated. Sharp dips in the check-set loss make those estimates unreliable. They prove a link between estimation error, check-set risk, and the sharpness of that risk. They then design a new influence formula built for flat, broad low spots in the check loss. Tests across several tasks showed their method beat the standard approach.
arxiv-2505-19197:
Chanyeol Choi and co-authors set two chat agents to mine cash marks from firm files and field plain word asks on them, in a paper from 2025. Hand reads of such files eat hours and cap how much ground a fund team can cover. One agent pulls the marks, sets their form, and checks them by eye rules.

The twin agent turns word asks into code calls on the neat store. Marks land right at a rate that ties hand taggers. Word ask replies earn right marks from human judges in nine of ten cases. The pair holds across file kinds, the team shows. Code and marks sit in one store for fast reads.
arxiv-2505-19297:
Valerii Startsev and co-authors (2025) built a small, high-quality data set for fine-tuning text-to-image models. Pretrained models know a lot about the world but often fall short on beauty and prompt fit. Fine-tuning fixes that only when the training examples are strong. Public sets tend to cover narrow styles, and hand-picking good examples is costly. The authors instead let a pretrained generator judge which public samples would teach the most.

Their method produced Alchemist, a set of 3,350 samples. Fine-tuning five public image models on it raised their output quality. The models kept their range of styles and subjects. The team released the data set and the tuned model weights. They present the work as proof a compact, well-chosen set can beat much larger ones, and as an open resource for a field that often depends on private data.
arxiv-2505-19397:
Jiawen Zhang and co-authors test whether time series foundation models can stand up to adversarial attacks, in work from twenty twenty-five. The models forecast well with no task training and now enter high stakes systems. Their weakness under attack had barely been probed.

The team built a test frame tuned to time series limits, with scale free scores for white box and black box attacks. Across six models, small tweaks reliably bent forecasts into trend flips or false drifts. Longer context windows raised the risk, and flaws near the forecast horizon stood out. Attacks moved poorly between models, which hints at model specific flaws. Simple attack aware fine tuning gave large robustness gains at low cost.
arxiv-2505-19597:
Zheng Wang and five co-authors build a light speech-cleaning system for two-channel sound in loud noise, by a join of classic and learned parts. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Learned multi-channel cleaners do well, but they are too heavy for scant gear, most of all when noise drowns the speech. The classic part gives a rough split of speech and noise. A trimmed learned net then refines the speech. The team tests ways to use both the raw sound and the rough split to the full. The system cleans speech well with few terms and low cost. It suits small tools that must run live.
arxiv-2505-19697:
Swati Saha, Ranbir Singh, and Bedangadas Mohanty study radial flow in heavy-ion collisions with a blast-wave model. Their 2025 paper uses a new measure that tracks flow across particle momentum. Big detectors like ALICE recently recorded this measure in lead-lead collisions. The model pictures the fireball as expanding gas that emits particles as it cools.

The team let the expansion speed and freeze-out heat vary from event to event. Faster average flow sorted the measure clearly by particle mass. Swings in speed and heat boosted the signal, above all at high momentum. Fits to ALICE data for three particle types pinned down the model's settings. Freeze-out heat values from this measure ran higher than those from plain spectra fits.
arxiv-2505-19797:
Yiqun Zhang and his fourteen co-authors, publishing in 2025, ask whether teams of small open language models can beat the giant closed ones. Their recipe, called the Avengers, sorts each incoming question by topic. It looks up which small models have done best on that kind of question, and lets the top ones answer several times and vote. The system pools ten open models of modest size and needs no retraining.

Across 15 test sets covering math, coding, logic, general knowledge, and emotion tasks, the combined system beat GPT-4o and its newer siblings on average. The margin was largest in math, about 18 points over GPT-4.1, and about 7 points in coding. The team also reports the method holds up on new kinds of questions and does not depend much on which sorting or voting parts are swapped in.
arxiv-2505-19897:
Sun and a large team introduced ScienceBoard in twenty twenty-five, a testbed for AI agents doing real scientific work on computers. Language model agents can now operate software through screens and interfaces, much like a human user. Such agents could speed routine research tasks, but judging them needs realistic tests.

ScienceBoard offers two parts. One is a multi-domain environment with real professional software for fields such as biochemistry, astronomy, and geoinformatics. The other is a benchmark of one hundred sixty-nine human-made, carefully checked tasks drawn from real workflows. Leading agents, including ones based on GPT-4o and Claude, solved only about fifteen percent of tasks overall. The authors analyze the failures and draw design lessons for building more capable research agents.
arxiv-2505-20197:
Fabian Lange, Johann Usovitsch, and Zihao Wu release a faster integral reducer in a 2025 paper. Precision particle physics reduces millions of Feynman integrals to a small master set. Their program, Kira, now reaches version 3. Smarter seeding and equation selection drive the gains, with benchmarks two to three loops deep showing up to a hundredfold speedup over the previous release.

New options add numerical sampling, symbolic reductions, and user defined relations. Gravitational wave physics uses the same machinery, widening the audience. Public release matters: the whole precision frontier shares these tools. Faster reduction turns month long calculations into overnight runs.
arxiv-2505-20297:
Qinyu Zhao, Jaskirat Singh, Ming Xu, Akshay Asthana, Stephen Gould, and Liang Zheng wrote a 2025 paper on speeding up autoregressive image generation. Such models now use diffusion sampling for each token, taking fifty to a hundred steps per token. That makes image generation slow.

Their insight is that later tokens are easier than early ones. Once part of a dog exists, the rest must complete the dog, so the choices narrow. Late tokens can be guessed by a simple network, vary little, and follow straighter denoising paths. Their method, DiSA, anneals the step count down as generation proceeds, from fifty steps early to a handful late. It needs no retraining. The savings target the main cost of this model family.
arxiv-2505-20397:
Emre Can Sertöz, Joël Ouaknine, and James Worrell give an algorithm for ties among a class of periods in a 2025 paper. A 1-period is a number built by integrating an algebraic curve over an algebraic path. Two famed thinkers posed the general problem of deciding when such numbers match, still open in full. This paper settles the one variable case.

Fed any finite set of 1-periods, the method lists every linear tie among them over algebraic numbers. As a byproduct it rules on whether one such number is transcendental and whether two are equal. The engine rests on a deep result that all such ties flow from 1-motives, made concrete through divisor math on curves. The authors also sort a family of nonlinear flow equations with the same tools.
arxiv-2505-20497:
Mikhail Anokhin, a mathematician, writes fast algorithms for groups dressed with extra operations. An expanded group pairs an ordinary additive group with added operations that spread over addition. In his black-box model, members arrive as bit strings, and an oracle answers questions about them, so the algorithms must work blind.

Three tasks get probabilistic polynomial-time solutions, with error chances that shrink exponentially in the input size. The algorithms can find generators for the additive group from any generating set. They can do the same for an ideal grown from chosen members. They can also test membership in any finitely based variety of such structures with nilpotent additive part. Rings and modules fall out as special cases.
arxiv-2505-20697:
Zachary Brown and David Carlson propose, in a 2025 paper, a method for drafting causal maps of the brain that change over time. Narrowing down which brain circuits to test by intervention could cut the cost of neuroscience, but most hypothesis tools assume links stay fixed, while brain links shift with state.

Their model builds a moving graph as a weighted blend of still graphs, each able to hold curved, nonlinear links. On test data, the predicted causal patterns scored far better than baselines, sometimes by more than sixty percent. A case study on real brain recordings tied recovered links to specific behavior states.
arxiv-2505-20897:
Pingrui Zhang and nine co-authors present a 2025 paper on guiding a robot by spoken directions, using imagined descriptions instead of imagined pictures. Navigation agents must follow instructions while seeing only part of a scene. Earlier systems imagined future views as images, which costs heavy computing and adds clutter. Their Adaptive Text Dreamer instead imagines key scene features in words, built on a large language model with two cooperating branches.

One branch handles logical integration, the other imaginative prediction, echoing the brain's two hemispheres. Only a small adapter in each branch is fine-tuned, waking the model's domain knowledge cheaply. A cross-interaction step polishes the imagined text and feeds it to a navigation expert. On the standard R2R benchmark the system reached state-of-the-art results with fewer parameters. The authors release their code publicly.
arxiv-2505-21097:
Stephen Chung, Wenyu Du, and Jie Fu teach language models to think in two gears. Psychology's dual process theory splits thought into fast intuition and slow deliberation. The team reshapes question answering into four stages mirroring it. First comes a fast answer inside a tight token budget. Then the model checks that answer, rethinks it slowly, and distills the fix into clean steps.

The staged task lifted accuracy for both models tested. One model rose from twenty-five point six percent to twenty-seven point three percent. A stronger model rose from forty-five point nine percent to fifty-one percent. The fast stage alone nearly matched the pipeline for the smaller model while using under a thousand tokens. The authors read this as evidence that intuition and deliberation are separate skills that each repay direct training. Models and code are openly released.
arxiv-2505-21197:
Stefano Frixione reports a set of number identities in this short 2025 math note. The identities involve Stirling numbers, a classic pair of counting sequences, along with binomial coefficients. They turned up during his work on how parton distributions behave at small momentum fractions.

Frixione makes no claim that the results are new. He records them plainly for others who may need them. Notes like this save fellow researchers from re-deriving the same sums. The paper is brief, with the formulas as its whole content. It serves as a reference shelf item for workers in particle theory.
arxiv-2505-21297:
Teaching language models to solve hard coding problems takes large sets of problems with checked answers, and such sets are scarce. Yifei Liu and seven co-authors built one in 2025 under the name rStar-Coder. It holds 418 thousand contest level problems and 580 thousand long worked solutions, each backed by test cases.

The team made new problems from contest sets with known solutions, then built test inputs and outputs through a three step process with cross checks. Models trained on the data gained sharply: one mid sized model jumped from about seventeen percent to fifty-seven percent on a live coding bench. A smaller model even beat a much larger rival on a computing olympiad bench.
arxiv-2505-21397:
Chen and co-authors propose in 2025 DecisionFlow, a framework that guides language models to decide through structured reasoning. In health and finance, choices need clear, explainable grounds, not just right answers. Current models often give a decision first and bolt on reasons after.

Their method builds a grounded space of actions, attributes, and constraints from the prompt. A hidden utility function then weighs trade offs in the open, so reasons and choice stay tightly linked. Tests on two high stakes benchmarks gave accuracy gains up to thirty percent over strong prompting. Outcome alignment also improved, a step toward accountable decision support.
arxiv-2505-21497:
Wei Pang and four co-authors present Paper2Poster, a 2025 project on turning scientific papers into conference posters automatically. A poster must squeeze a long, mixed text-and-figure paper into one clear page. The team built the first benchmark for the task, pairing recent papers with the posters their authors designed. Their scoring suite grades visual quality, text coherence, and overall design, and adds a quiz test: can a model answer questions about the paper from the poster alone?

Their system, PosterAgent, works top-down through three agents that parse the paper, plan a layout, and paint each panel with feedback. A leading commercial model made pretty posters with noisy text and weak quiz scores. The team's open models beat rival systems on nearly all measures while using far fewer tokens, and produced an editable poster file for half a cent.
arxiv-2505-21797:
Vilasini, Lin-Qing Chen, Liuhang Ye, and Renato Renner published a paper in 2025 arguing that an event's location only makes sense relative to a laboratory. Quantum theory and general relativity define events and places in clashing ways. Quantum gravity, meanwhile, cannot fall back on a fixed spacetime stage. The authors build an operational definition from quantum information: a lab, with a chosen physical reference, is what gives an event its where.

A property they call relative measurability captures how the lab's reference correlates with the system under study. Applied to the quantum switch, a famous process with indefinite causal order, the analysis separates its classical and quantum realizations. It also settles a long interpretive dispute: rival conclusions had quietly assumed different labs.
arxiv-2505-22597:
Ngoc La and co-authors present HDDLGym, a Python tool that turns hierarchical planning problems into training grounds for reinforcement learning agents. Planning languages can state tasks as layers of subgoals, a structure that suits model based learning. Yet no tool bridged that world and the standard Gym test bed, as their 2025 paper notes.

HDDLGym reads domain and problem files in the HDDL planning language and builds Gym environments on its own. It supports many agents planning together, not just one. The paper walks through use with contest domains such as Transport, and shows how to craft new multi agent domains. A cooking game domain, Overcooked, demos the practical side.
arxiv-2505-22897:
Chahat Raj and co-authors present Vignette in 2025, a benchmark for bias in vision-language models. Bias in text models is well studied, but image-text models lag behind. Past checks leaned on portraits and gender-job links. Harmful stereotypes run far wider than that narrow frame.

The benchmark poses questions about images across four angles: factuality, perception, stereotyping, and decision making. It spans tens of millions of images in a question-answering frame. Grounded in social psychology, it tests how models tie looks to traits and roles. Results expose subtle and surprising bias patterns. The tool helps builders see how models build social meaning from pictures.
arxiv-2505-22997:
Agnideep Aich and Ashit Baran Aich build a classifier that treats dependence between features as the main event, not a nuisance. Standard generative classifiers assume features are independent given the class, which real data rarely honors. Their 2025 Deep Copula Classifier splits the job: estimate each feature's own distribution, then let a neural copula model how they move together within each class.

Theory backs the design with consistency guarantees and an explicit error rate. In a stress test with near-perfect feature correlation, the decision regions bend to match the ideal Bayes answer. On a classic diabetes dataset it outscores logistic regression, support vector machines, and naive Bayes while staying well calibrated and readable. Statisticians get a generative model that admits the world is correlated.
arxiv-2505-23297:
Daryna Dementieva, Nikolay Babakov, and Alexander Fraser built the first public test set for emotion spotting in Ukrainian text in a 2025 paper. Ukrainian language tools have grown in many areas, but sorting text by feeling had no shared yardstick. Their set fills that gap with texts marked for the emotion they carry.

The marking scheme adapts rules honed on English sets. Crowd workers marked the texts through an online platform with quality checks in place. The team then graded a range of methods on the set, from word-based baselines to data translated from English. The set gives future tools a fair way to prove their skill in Ukrainian.
arxiv-2505-23997:
Pranav Rao and four co-authors test stress support messages written with each student's own calendar in mind, in a 2025 paper. Generic wellness tips often land at the wrong moment. Calendars quietly reveal which days will hurt.

Eight university students used a working probe app for one week. Each day it drafted a short message shaped by their upcoming events. Students liked messages that named their most stressful events first. They also preferred a brief, friendly tone over formal advice. The authors draw design lessons about asking the right questions. Tone calibration, they argue, decides whether such tools earn trust.
arxiv-2505-24097:
Victor Li and co-authors tackle a calibration problem that arises when predictions change the world they predict in this 2025 paper. A loan model, for example, can alter who repays, so risk targets set on old data may fail once the model is deployed. Standard calibration assumes the data stays fixed, which performative settings break.

Their framework, Performative Risk Control, refines calibration step by step while keeping risk guarantees at every stage. They study several risk measures and tail bounds to support the math. Tests on credit default prediction show the method holding its guarantees in practice. The authors present it as a guard against strategic gaming of deployed models.
arxiv-2505-24697:
Aaron Conrardy, Alfredo Capozucca, and Jordi Cabot propose a shared user modeling language in a 2025 paper. Personal software needs full user profiles: access limits, habits, tastes, even hobbies. Past modeling tools each cover one slice, and coarsely, which caps how far interfaces can adapt.

Their language merges strands from modeling work and user-centered fields into one proposal. It sits on an open low-code platform, so profiles can be built and run, not just drawn. A proof of concept feeds such profiles into a chat agent that reshapes itself per user. The paper aims at human-centered AI that can be engineered, not hand-tuned.
arxiv-2506-00097:
Mostafizur Rahaman Laskar and Richa Goel present a quantum method for forecasting data that changes over time. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. Time series forecasts matter in fields from weather study to molecular motion. Standard tools can be heavy and slow to train. The authors aim for a leaner model that runs on real quantum hardware.

Their Quantum Time Series model writes scaled data into single-qubit rotations. Fixed patterns of entanglement then carry the time structure of the data. Training cost grows only with the log of the data size. They test the model on IBM quantum hardware. The results are set against classic methods to show where the quantum route holds up.
arxiv-2506-00197:
Shen and three co-authors probe how pet chat tools leak their fed files in this twenty twenty-five paper. Fed files lift tool replies, yet their facts may slip to sharp asks. Past work showed ask tricks lone; true leak roads may run wide.

Inside, six score ten thousand tools' files and flows fed the hunt. Five leak roads fell out, from tag lists to run-box acts. One run tool flaw let sharp asks pull whole files down near full. Near three in ten leaked files bore rights marks in the pool. The team sets fix steps for tool hosts and file feeds.
arxiv-2506-00297:
Fanglei Xue and five co-authors taught a protein design tool to favor sequences that actually fold in a 2025 paper. Design tools are usually trained to copy natural sequences, which does not promise the copy will take the wanted shape. The team changed the goal: reward designability, scored by a folding predictor.

Preference training on those scores lifted design success in computer checks. A finer version scores single residues, so good stretches stay untouched while weak spots improve. Tuned on an enzyme benchmark, their enhanced tool nearly tripled the success rate, from under seven percent to over seventeen. The authors say residue-level rewards are a general trick for sequence design tools.
arxiv-2506-00497:
Anders Westerkam and co-authors characterize the radar echo of a drone swarm in a 2025 paper. Spinning rotors stamp a flickering signature, called micro Doppler, on the return signal, and reading it can identify drones.

The swarm is made of identical drones, each with rotors of several blades. Rotor angle and speed are treated as random quantities. From that the authors derive formulas for how the echo correlates with itself over time and how its energy spreads across frequencies. Both come as series whose terms die out at a predictable point, so they can be cut short in practice. For fixed rotor speed the correlation takes a closed form. Blade length, speed, blade count, and swarm size are each traced through the formulas.
arxiv-2506-00897: Stefano Marini and Costantino Medori present in 2025 a family of manifolds that are the same at every point. These manifolds stay nondegenerate to any set order, a trait that does not depend on how one charts them. They build the family from algebras tied to a classic group. A close study follows of the Levi forms and their kernels, plus the local model equation. For each order, the work gives clear examples where this higher trait can be checked in one uniform frame.
arxiv-2506-00997:
Min Je Kim and four co-authors tackle a quiet flaw in the data sets used to train image software that finds objects in photos. Their 2025 paper focuses on MS-COCO, a standard test set whose labels contain missed objects, wrong classes, loose boxes, and repeats. Such errors teach models bad habits and blur the scores used to rank them.

The team spots suspect labels by watching loss and gradient patterns while a model learns. They then fix labels in four steps, using flipped views to redraw boxes, merging repeats, checking classes with a separate recognizer, and nudging boxes to match active image regions. The cleaned set, named MJ-COCO, trains models that beat those trained on the raw set across four test sets. No hand relabeling was needed.
arxiv-2506-01197:
Mark Muchane, Sean Richardson, Kiho Park, and Victor Veitch redesign the sparse autoencoder so its learned concepts come with a family tree, in this 2025 paper. These autoencoders translate a model's internal activity into human readable concepts, but ordinary versions treat concepts as unrelated, ignoring that some are special cases of others. The new architecture builds the hierarchy in.

Applied to the insides of large language models, the design learns the semantic ladder along with the concepts themselves. Reconstruction of the original activity improves, and so does interpretability, since broad ideas now visibly govern their refinements. The architecture also runs more efficiently than the flat version. The authors argue that structure, not just sparsity, is what makes machine concepts legible to people.
arxiv-2506-01597:
Yixian Zhang and co-authors bring a faster style of training to reinforcement learning policies written as flexible kernel functions, in a 2025 paper. Such policies can take many shapes, but training them has been stuck with slow first-order methods. Second-order methods, modeled on Newton's approach, converge faster yet seem to demand inverting an endless matrix in this setting.

The team sidesteps the inversion by training against a reshaped goal with a cubic penalty term. A classic theorem then shrinks the endless problem into a finite one sized by the amount of trial data. They prove the method settles at a local best point with fast final convergence. Tests on a toy investing task and standard benchmarks beat first-order kernel methods and other second-order rivals in speed and reward.
arxiv-2506-01697:
Shantanu Pathak and Saswata Bhattacharya study a layered perovskite whose electron spins keep a fixed pattern, in a 2025 paper. The material lacks a center of symmetry and grips spin and motion tightly together. That pairing splits energy levels by an unusually large amount and lines the spins up uniformly across momentum space, a persistent spin texture.

Uniform spin alignment promises long spin lifetimes, which spin-based electronics needs. The authors confirm the texture with first-principles calculations and a simplified model. They then show that squeezing or stretching the material tunes the splitting strength. Stress becomes a knob for dialing spin configurations up or down. The authors pitch the system as a platform for next-generation spintronic devices whose behavior can be adjusted by outside pressure.
arxiv-2506-01797:
Aguirre and co-authors studied a superconducting wedge in a 2025 paper. A superconductor can act like a diode, letting current pass more easily one way than the other. The team placed currents at the edges of a wedge and a field along one axis.

Using a standard time-based theory, they tested two setups: fixed field with varied material value, and fixed value with varied field. In both, the key currents differed by direction, proving the one-way effect. Vortex patterns also changed with current direction, in uneven ways. The authors link the diode effect to how these vortices form on each side.
arxiv-2506-01997:
Natalia Boitsova, Anna Abelit, and Daniil Stupin present open software for impedance spectra analysis in a 2025 paper. Electrical impedance spectroscopy probes everything from circuits to living tissue, yet analysis tools lag the hardware: mostly private, dated code in old languages. Their package, NELM, runs in MATLAB or its free twin Octave.

NELM fits measured spectra to equivalent circuit models through a friendly interface, accepting many data formats and model types. It brings in modern tricks like symbolic math, parallel computing, and AI assistance. Trials in semiconductor, bioimpedance, and electrochemistry work showed the package handles real problems efficiently. The authors aim it at autonomous sensing devices and implants as well as lab benches.
arxiv-2506-02097:
Pattnayak and co-authors present a hybrid chatbot design for company support desks, published in 2025, meant to stay fast and accurate over long conversations. Retrieval-based chatbots ground their answers in company documents, but real deployments strain them. Questions vary wildly, answers lag, and the bot sometimes invents facts. Fast-changing product knowledge makes upkeep worse. The design splits traffic by confidence.

Simple, well-known questions get instant canned answers. Complex or ambiguous ones are routed to the retrieval pipeline, which composes a grounded reply. A context manager tracks the conversation across turns, and feedback loops let the routing adapt. The authors built and tested the framework on enterprise-style workloads. The pitch is balance: the speed of scripts where scripts suffice, the depth of search where they do not. Hallucinations fall because risky answers are gated.
arxiv-2506-02297:
Rohan Bali and co-authors show, in a 2025 paper, hid radio talk that can be proved safe in a lab build. Hid talk sends so faint that a watch foe can not tell it runs. A square root law caps it: hid bits grow with the root of the time-band span, no more. Past that cap, the talk is caught or read wrong. Lab proof was thin: two past builds, both on light. This team built the radio form with software radios. Their first reads match the law's calls.

The build shows the math holds on air, not just on glass. It opens a path to field rigs and names the next asks for them. Safe hid talk may suit more than spies.
arxiv-2506-02497:
Jiahao Chen, Bing Su, and co-authors give a motion led frame to make long videos that hold sense and flow, in a 2025 paper. Past long makers join short clips or fill gaps by tiers, which oft loop acts or jump in odd ways. Their tier way puts motion in the lead from the start.

A big motion maker first lays key frames with wide gaps in acts. Flow fields for gaps are then made and warped frames are cleaned by a control net. Fill spans reach far past past tools with smooth acts. Tests show long clips with firm look and move match.
arxiv-2506-02797:
Paul Didier and co-authors speed up distributed sound estimation in wireless acoustic sensor networks. Their twenty twenty-five paper serves networks of mic nodes that share fused signals, not raw audio. The network shape can shift over time and need not be fully linked.

A prior method, TI-DANSE, reaches the same answer as a central solver but converges slowly. Each node saw only the total sum of fused signals in the network. The new version, TI-DANSE+, lets updating nodes use partial sums as well. That extra view cuts the wait for a stable estimate. Faster settling makes live uses, like hearing aids and smart rooms, more practical.
arxiv-2506-02997:
Speech tools that let a user steer how a voice sounds are the topic of a 2025 paper by Yongqi Wang, Chunlei Zhang, Hangting Chen, Zhou Zhao, and Dong Yu. Their system builds text-to-speech output in two stages, with a compact style code drawn from masked autoencoding sitting between the text and the final sound.

In the first stage, a transformer reads the text and control signals and picks the style tokens. The second stage then turns text plus those tokens into codec tokens that form the audio. Tests show that training the first stage on large data sets makes the speech more robust and easier to steer. By mixing set labels with speaker traits, the team could fix a speaker's tone of voice and still change traits such as emotion.
arxiv-2506-03397:
Nourozi builds fresh codes from plane curves and a learn-aided read plan. The curves rest on split forms, a set class of bends. One case uses the F3 field with a set curve form. It gives a code of length 27, width 13, and span 4. That code yields a quantum code with the same three marks. The read plan runs in two steps to fix code flaws.

Step one runs a greed search on the flaw signs first. Step two trains a Deep Q net to fix the rest. Noise tests use a mixed flip frame for the code runs. The learn step cuts fail rates by a vast span next to greed. The work thus widens both code clans drawn from such curves.
arxiv-2506-03697:
Swagat Kumar, Jan-Nico Zaech, Colin Wilmott, and Luc Van Gool automate the search for good quantum circuits in a 2025 paper. Near-term quantum computers are noisy and small, so circuit choice matters a lot. Hand design is slow, and most search tools borrow classical tricks that ignore the quantum nature of what they build.

Their method treats the search itself as a quantum mixed state that evolves smoothly, so it can be tuned by gradients rather than sampling. The mixed-state view also lets real noise models enter the search directly. On tasks such as state preparation and two standard optimization problems, the method matched or beat prior tools while needing far fewer quantum runs, and it held up better under noise.
arxiv-2506-03797:
Khalil Teber and co-authors add precise locations to the world's main disaster database. Their 2025 paper works on EM-DAT, the free global record of humanitarian disasters, which lists events without exact geography. That gap blocks researchers who want to join disaster records with weather and population maps.

The team geocoded more than nine thousand climate-related events reported between 1990 and 2023. Their method stays accurate even when the source gives only a region name, and each record carries quality flags so users can judge trust. An open framework lets others update the coding as new disasters are logged. With locations attached, the records can feed studies of hazard intensity, exposure, and vulnerability together. The authors aim the resource at anticipatory action, helping agencies act before disasters peak.
arxiv-2506-03997:
Alviano, Giordano, and Theseider Dupré set out a frame in twenty twenty-five for if-then thought in answer set programs. Such programs solve hard tasks by rules that list what must hold. Their frame adds soft rules that say what holds in the most plain or most liked cases.

The frame pairs a soft fact base with a plain program and lets users ask what follows from the pair. Its sense rests on a ranked view of worlds, with a known soft logic as a plain case. If-then claims are coded back into the same program kind. They also give a cap on how hard the task can get.
arxiv-2506-04097:
Alessandra Colla, Heinz-Peter Breuer, and Giulio Gasbarri present a 2025 quantum physics paper on systems that remember their environment. When a quantum system interacts strongly with its surroundings, the surroundings' past influence lingers, making the system's own energy hard to define. The authors build a systematic way to extract the effective Hamiltonian, the energy rule that drives the system's clean, wave-like motion.

Starting from a principle of minimal dissipation, they derive an exact expression and a step-by-step expansion in terms of the coupling and the environment's correlations. Applied to standard spin models, the method shows how environmental memory shifts energies and rotates the system's natural states. The framework should help analyze strong-coupling devices and quantum heat engines.
arxiv-2506-04197:
Roy Araiza, Marius Junge, and Peixue Wu build a noncommutative optimal transport framework for quantum channels, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Their channels act on von Neumann algebras. The central object is a Lipschitz cost measure. It prices the minimal cost of moving between quantum states through a given channel.

A companion Lipschitz contraction coefficient measures how much a channel shrinks Wasserstein-type distances. The authors establish basic properties of both quantities. These include continuity, dual formulations, and behavior under composition and tensor products. Applications recover known quantities such as expected group word length and Carnot-Carathéodory distance. When the contraction coefficient falls strictly below one, entropy contraction follows. Mixing time estimates then become available for certain non-symmetric channels.
arxiv-2506-04897:
Tianxu Wang and co-authors test whether AI models can find things in 3D scenes beyond whole objects. Their 2025 paper builds a benchmark of 2,886 text prompts paired with boxes in scanned rooms. Prompts cover four levels: activity areas, empty space, single objects, and object parts.

Top vision and language models were run on the set. Space and part prompts proved the hardest by far. Even the best models scored only about 30 percent on empty-space tasks and about 40 percent on parts. Area and object prompts fared much better. The authors say the gap shows how far models are from real spatial sense. The set is offered as a yardstick for progress in three-dimensional scene understanding over time.
arxiv-2506-04997:
Searching scanned documents by their look, not just their text, has grown powerful with models that encode each page as hundreds of patch embeddings. The cost is memory: such stores swell fast. Ma and ten co-authors study how to shrink those embeddings with the least loss of search quality. They test two trims: dropping patches, called pruning, and fusing them, called merging.

Random pruning oddly beat smarter pruning methods, yet all pruning fell short, since a page's key patches depend on the question asked. Merging worked far better. Their tuned version, Light-ColPali and Light-ColQwen2, keeps about ninety-eight percent of search quality with about twelve percent of the memory. At under three percent of the memory, it still keeps about ninety-five percent. The authors offer the result as a baseline for leaner document search.
arxiv-2506-05097: Saikat Patra and Bihalan Bhattacharya study Heisenberg-Weyl operators. These operators extend Pauli operators to higher dimensions. They also keep a key symmetry. Past work built positive maps from these operators. It also traced algebraic and spectral traits of the maps and observables. Their study carries that line forward for linear maps. The aim is to broaden the Pauli case to a wider algebra.
arxiv-2506-05397:
Vision systems need huge amounts of training footage, and rare activities like sports are hard to film at scale. Jerrin Bright and co-authors build Gen4D in a 2025 paper, a pipeline that fabricates moving human scenes automatically. Older synthetic sets lean on fixed asset libraries, which limits variety in bodies, motion, and settings.

Gen4D encodes motion from experts, grows avatars from text prompts with diffusion methods, and synthesizes backgrounds that fit the people in them. From that pipeline the team built SportPAL, a large set covering baseball, ice hockey, and soccer. No hand modeling or scene design was needed. The pair offers a scalable base for training vision tools aimed at real-world human activity.
arxiv-2506-05497:
Sima Noorani, Shayan Kiyani, George Pappas, and Hamed Hassani build sure-set calls for text models in 2025. Safe use of text models needs doubt grades, yet old sure-set tools need set score forms these models lack. Their frame works from a fixed count of asks to the black box alone.

Two rules drive the path, one for the best ask plan and one for the best set build. Both rest on the old missing mass snag in stats, read by fresh gauge tools. On three open tasks and two models, their sets tell more at like trust.
arxiv-2506-05697:
Valeria Ramirez and Christian Valqui compute the Groebner basis of a system of polynomial equations connected to the Jacobian conjecture. Their paper came out in 2025. The conjecture, a famous open problem, asks whether a polynomial map whose derivative has constant determinant must have a polynomial inverse.

A Groebner basis is a special generating set that makes a polynomial system tractable, much as row reduction tames linear systems. By computing it, the authors gain full control over the system in question. They then describe the solution set completely, listing exactly which points satisfy all the equations at once. Complete descriptions like this are rare for systems tied to open conjectures. The work gives other researchers a firm foothold for testing related cases.
arxiv-2506-05897:
Xin Zhang, Dongdong Meng, and Sheng Li sharpen a transformer segmenter for the small organs that medical scans keep fumbling. Outlining organs guides radiation therapy and surgery, but compact structures get smeared by global attention models. Their fix stays inside the Mask2Former design rather than replacing it.

An offset adjustment nudges the attention's sampling points to stay within the same organ, gathering compact foreground cleanly. A coarse feature map supplies rough organ locations, and a small auxiliary head speeds training with an overlap loss. On two public head, neck, and cancer data sets the model set the pace, with the clearest gains on mid-sized and small organs.
arxiv-2506-06197:
In a quantum guessing game, a player measures a state to guess how it was prepared, and hints can arrive before or after the measurement. Teiko Heinosaari and Hanwool Lee add a twist: metainformation, the mere knowledge that a hint of a certain kind is coming later, without knowing what it says.

Knowing a hint is on its way changes the best measurement now. In some games it lifts success all the way to the level of having the hint beforehand, a striking gain from pure expectation. In others it adds nothing. The authors map when expectation alone has operational value. The result refines how information timing matters in quantum strategy.
arxiv-2506-06397:
Arash Azizi studies a blended quantum state of light that he calls the Janus state, in a 2025 paper. A squeezed vacuum is a quantum state of light whose photons arrive in clumps, more bunched than chance. Azizi asks what happens when two squeezed vacua, squeezed in opposed ways, are laid over each other.

The blend flips the statistics: photons now avoid arriving in pairs, a sign of true quantum light. His exact solution sets a hard floor on how strong that avoidance can get, measured by a standard coherence score that cannot fall below one half. At moderate squeezing the score bottoms near 0.567, a sweet spot within reach. Making the state needs one non-standard step, but the bound gives engineers a firm target for building such light.
arxiv-2506-06897:
Mahault Albarracin and Dalton Sakthivadivel offer a theory paper from twenty twenty-five on what it means for a living or artificial system to be resilient. They work within the free energy principle, a framework that treats staying alive as keeping a workable model of oneself and the world. Earlier work used that framework to model resilience from the outside. The authors argue instead that resilience sits at the center of the framework itself, because keeping an identity requires constant adjustment.

On their view, a system holds together by reshaping its self-model as conditions change, and that reshaping takes energy. They sketch a general framework for thinking this way and give simple models to show it in action. The paper will interest readers who study adaptive systems, self-organization, and theories of life.
arxiv-2506-07197:
Jia-Jie Han and six co-authors compute rare particle decays in this two thousand twenty-five physics paper. The decays involve the Lambda b baryon, which can split into a proton plus a light meson. Of interest is CP violation, a subtle gap between how matter and antimatter behave. The team studies a list of such decays, with pions, kaons, and related mesons in the final state.

They use an approach based on perturbative quantum chromodynamics. Their sums include effects up to second order in the strong coupling. They add finer details of how quarks are shared inside the hadrons. The resulting rates and asymmetries form a clear pattern. For the best-known channels, the predicted violation is as small as current data suggest. Other channels may show larger effects worth hunting at colliders.
arxiv-2506-07297:
Lauren Levine and Amir Zeldes study how hard it is to mark bridging links in text in a steady way, in work from 2025. A bridging link joins a new entity to one named before, as the door is understood through a house named earlier. Finding such links is a matter of judgment, so annotators often part ways.

The team ran a trial marking on a known corpus test set and tried a new scheme for sorting link kinds. Overlap on the kind was fair, but overlap on which links exist at all was low. Many splits traced to how each reader pictured the entities. The authors warn that older resources likely miss many links.
arxiv-2506-07597:
Oscar Sainz and a team of co-authors studied how to teach large language models to follow instructions in Basque, in a 2025 paper. Instruction data exist for only a few languages, so low-resource languages need another route. The team assumed a realistic setup: texts in the target language, open multilingual models, and machine-made instructions from a tuned model.

They ran a wide grid of tests mixing those parts, judged by benchmarks and by 1,680 human raters. Target-language texts proved essential, and machine-made instructions still yielded strong models. The biggest lesson was that starting from an already instruction-tuned model beats starting from a raw base model. Scaled up to a large tuned backbone, their model neared far larger frontier systems for Basque, with no Basque instructions at all.
arxiv-2506-07897:
Three-dimensional Gaussian splatting rebuilds a scene from photos as a cloud of soft blobs, but the rebuild can never be sharper than the photos fed in. Shuja Khalid, Mohamed Ibrahim, and Yang Liu break that ceiling with GaussianVAE. Their 2025 method learns where a scene needs more blobs and grows them there.

A curvature-based sampling trick, guided by the Hessian, points the lightweight generative model at the spots most likely to gain from extra detail. The model then predicts and refines the added Gaussians. The whole pass takes 0.015 seconds on a single consumer graphics card, fast enough for interactive use, where GAN and diffusion rivals crawl. Tests show clear gains in both shape accuracy and picture quality, which the authors frame as resolution-free scene enhancement.
arxiv-2506-08297:
Nhat Thanh Tran, Fanghui Xue, and colleagues redesign the attention mechanism at the heart of transformers in a 2025 study. Full attention costs grow quadratically with input size, while the cheaper linear variant cannot focus sharply. The authors define attention generally enough to contain both versions, then prove a dispersion result: spread too thin, attention loses the signal as inputs lengthen.

Their design localizes tokens and averages within neighborhoods, borrowing the efficiency pattern of state-space sequence models. The goal is attention that scales to long image token streams without going blurry, a standing need in computer vision backbones.
arxiv-2506-09297:
Caio da Silva and three co-authors put Newton's method, adapted to curved spaces, through a thorough numerical trial. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Optimization on manifolds arises when answers must obey shapes, such as sets of perpendicular frames.

The team compared the curved-space method with the classic flat version patched with extra constraints. The test problem came from quantum chemistry: finding the lowest energy state of molecules. Across one hundred twenty-five molecules, the curved methods converged more often, needed fewer steps, and cared less about the starting guess. The authors also study a numerical catch when the cost lives on a quotient space. A fix that ignores the smallest curvature values proved stable.
arxiv-2506-09497:
Jaemin Seo builds a quantum version of a mixture-density network in a 2025 paper. Many real outcomes split into several modes, like forked paths in a storm track. Classic mixture networks need parameter counts that balloon as modes multiply, known or not.

The quantum model uses parameterized circuits to hold a huge number of modes in few qubits. It predicts the parts of a Gaussian mixture at fine resolution. Tests cover the quantum double-slit setup and a chaotic logistic system. Under equal parameter budgets, the quantum model beat classic rivals on mode separation and sharpness. Compact quantum circuits may thus earn a place in forecasting tools.
arxiv-2506-09897:
Tao Liu and Zhenchao Cui present a detector tuned for very small objects in images, a hard task for standard vision networks. In the usual pyramid design, the top layers hold broad meaning but often get no training examples when objects are tiny. Those layers then go untrained, while the fine layers below lack the context they need to name what they see.

Their design rescues that wasted top-level meaning and feeds it downward. One module aligns and squeezes the broad features so they blend with fine detail. Other parts balance the training between foreground and background and tune how learning signals flow. The full system aims at steadier detection of tiny objects in cluttered scenes.
arxiv-2506-10097:
Nishida, Kawaguchi and their co-authors describe the DCASE 2025 challenge task on first-shot anomalous sound detection for machine monitoring in 2025. The task asks systems to spot faulty machine sounds for new machine types with no machine-specific tuning.

The task builds on the prior year's challenge and uses a domain generalization setup, with unseen machine types held for final testing. Many teams from several countries submitted systems for scoring. Analysis showed several routes can compete well, from fine-tuning large pretrained models to training small models from scratch. Key helpers were the right cost function, score normalization and use of clean sounds.
arxiv-2506-10397:
Mir Yousuf and Shabir Sofi present a rule-based system to sort bugs in quantum software in this 2025 paper. Sorting bug reports by type and severity helps teams fix the right problems first. Quantum software adds its own bug kinds, tied to circuits and gates, that generic tools miss.

The system uses keyword rules tuned to quantum terms. To test it, the authors hand-sorted a sample of 4,984 issues from 12,910 across 36 project archives. The system reached up to 85 percent accuracy, with strong agreement on bug type and category, but weak agreement on severity. Classic bugs made up about two thirds of issues, and quantum-specific bugs about a quarter. Most issues were low severity.
arxiv-2506-11097:
Haritz Puerto and co-authors build a bench to test whether tricks meant to lift a web page in the answers of chat based search tools really work. As search shifts from lists of links to chat answers, firms have begun to tune pages for the new systems.

The bench spans two tasks and three fields each, and it can vary how many rival pages use the same tricks at once. In tests, most current tricks did little or even hurt a page's place. Older tricks that lift a page in the source list the model reads from did far better. The authors set out the bench as a shared tool for the field.
arxiv-2506-11197:
Felix Fritzsch and Pieter Claeys study in 2025 how a small quantum system forgets, using a stripped-down circuit model. The system sits in contact with a large, fully random environment. Physicists track the forgetting with layered measures called higher-order out-of-time-order correlators, which probe how information scrambles over time.

The pair prove that all such measures decay exponentially in their model, and they pin down the time scales for each order. At late times, local operations behave as if freely independent, a notion from a branch of probability theory. They show the environment's whole effect can be packed into one influence matrix of higher order. With one added helper degree of freedom, the dynamics become memoryless in form. The picture matches recent predictions from a broad theory of how isolated quantum systems settle. The authors expect the tool to travel to richer settings.
arxiv-2506-11597:
Simone Romano, Francesco Paolo Sferratore, and Giuseppe Scanniello compare students and professionals at bug fixing in a 2025 paper. Software experiments lean heavily on students, which critics say may not reflect industry skill. The authors add fresh evidence to that long dispute.

Sixty-two bachelor students and forty-two professionals from two multinationals fixed bugs in the same Java program. The professional setting was more realistic, with interruptions adding stress mid-task. Students still outperformed the professionals on the fix. That result cuts against much past evidence, the authors note. Rather than settle the debate, they urge study of what makes such tasks realistic.
arxiv-2506-11797:
Angelo Caravano releases InflationEasy, a C++ lattice code for simulating the universe's first explosive stretch. Inflation theory needs full simulations when fluctuations grow large enough to break textbook approximations — exactly the regimes that might seed primordial black holes or gravitational wave backgrounds. His 2025 code evolves a scalar field on a three-dimensional grid inside an expanding universe.

Built in the lineage of the classic LatticeEasy, it adds inflation-specific tools. A nonperturbative method reads the final curvature ripple straight off the grid. The code also follows the spacetime waves those ripples induce, both during inflation and as ripples re-enter the horizon later. Cosmologists get one instrument for the violent versions of the early universe that gentle math cannot reach.
arxiv-2506-11997:
Korbinian Pöppel and co-authors add a new member in 2025 to a family of fast neural networks that work step by step. Such networks have lately rivaled the transformer on language tasks. Their weak point is shape: most handle flat chains of data, while images, trees, and webs have a richer layout that must be forced into a chain.

Older networks built for rich layouts exist, but they run one step at a time and are slow. The new design borrows their layout skill and adds gates that let steps run in parallel, like the fast models do. It works on the line graph form of a general web of linked steps. That opens fast training to data shaped as grids, trees, and webs. The authors set out the design and how it can be trained at scale.
arxiv-2506-12097:
Suriyakumar, Sekhari, and Wilson set out UCD, a run-time way to un-teach chat tools. Un-teach aims to strip set facts from a tool but keep its skill. Facts in view may be soft or banned for the tool's use. Their way steers outs by twin small tools at run time. One small tool trained sans the strip set, one with it in. The gap twixt those two guides the big tool's outs.

That steer lifts the trade twixt strip force and kept skill. Two test sets, TOFU and MUSE, grade the way in runs. Gains show in strip grade and kept scores next to past ways. The team reads twin steer as a cheap, apt path here. It suits vast tools where re-train costs run too high.
arxiv-2506-12197:
Caio Deberaldini Netto, Zhiyang Wang, and Luana Ruiz build a learning framework for labeling points on curved data surfaces in a paper from 2025. Real data often lie on a low-dimensional manifold, a curved sheet inside a big space. Labels are scarce, so semi-supervised methods must spread them wisely.

A variational autoencoder first learns the sheet's coordinates without labels. Points then become nodes in a graph, joined by edges weighted by distance. A graph neural network spreads the few labels across the graph. Theory is the paper's core: under even sampling, the method's generalization gap is bounded. The pipeline from data to manifold to graph gets a full statistical audit.
arxiv-2506-12497:
Ali Baheri sets a team's shared plan as the mid-point of its parts' paths, weighed by a shift-cost yard stick. Team learn asks parts to play as one yet keep their own craft. His 2025 frame takes each part's state-act path weigh and finds their cost-mid, softened for sums. Each part's own aim then pays a tax by its gap from that mid.

The tax bends parts to the crew sans a forced shared brain. The work flow swaps mid sums with aim climbs in turns. Proof shows the top pair gap shrinks at a set step rate, under plain smooth terms. A team sail test beats lone-learn parts on pace and end marks.
arxiv-2506-12797:
Wenjie Zhong, Yubao Liu, and Yiqiu Ma chase a test that can tell quantum gravity from its classic rival by a moving mass. Classic self-gravity would bend a test mass path in a state-tied way that quantum frames deny. Fixed rigs of past tests missed that bend, since it hides in still states. Their plan reads the mass while it swings in a light trap, where the bend should ring.

The ring prints as extra peaks in the light that leaves the rig in their maths. Raw peak hunts would need too many runs to be worth the cost. A stats lens that wrings each run dry cuts the need to ten short runs. Mock data put false alarms below one percent at that spend.
arxiv-2506-13297:
Schmidt and co-authors show how a cloud of ultracold atoms can pretend to be a quantum field living in curved spacetime. Spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensates, where each atom carries a small internal spin, settle into several magnetic phases. Ripples on each ground state behave like relativistic fields, and the geometry those ripples feel emerges from the condensate itself.

Different phases yield different geometry counts: two overlapping metrics in two phases, three in the ferromagnetic one. In one phase a ripple mode becomes a massive vector field of the Proca type, coupled to its emergent curved spacetime. By shaping the trap and magnetic couplings over time, the setup can mimic an expanding universe of the standard cosmological kind. That opens a lab route to simulating particle creation in cosmology.
arxiv-2506-13497:
A ten-author team presents DDiT, a system that serves text-to-video models more efficiently by treating each part of the pipeline on its own terms. Video generation chains a language encoder, a diffusion transformer, and an image decoder, and older serving systems run them as one block, wasting graphics processor time. The transformer stage also gains unevenly from added parallel work at different video sizes.

DDiT picks the right degree of parallelism for each stage and watches starvation time, the cost each request pays while waiting. A split control design keeps the stages in balance, and a greedy scheduler shifts resources step by step as demand changes. In tests on the T5 encoder and OpenSora models, the system cut both average and worst-case waiting times by more than forty percent against leading alternatives.
arxiv-2506-13597:
Hikaru Tamura and co-authors watch many body coherence form in a thin, attracting Bose gas, in a 2025 paper. The head title is fuller than the catalog title, and it governs. Coherence across a whole quantum system marks collective behavior, but probing it while the system is unstable is a standing challenge.

The team flipped a cold gas from repelling to attracting and filmed density and interference in place. Coherent density waves grew, clearly unlike the soliton trains seen before, born of noise grown ripples meeting dispersive shock waves. Later the gas lost phase order beyond a set length. Flipping back to repelling surprisingly restored long range coherence on its own, through defects forming and vanishing. The results light up how order lives far from balance.
arxiv-2506-13697:
Junyoung Seo and co-authors present Vid-CamEdit, a system that re-renders a video as if the camera had flown a different path, in a 2025 paper. Moving a virtual camera through an old clip is ill-posed, and training data with many views of moving scenes is scarce. Classic reconstruction breaks under big path changes, and generative video models struggle with real footage.

The method first estimates steady 3D geometry over time, then lets a generative renderer paint detail guided by that geometry, filling gaps where the shape is unsure. Training is split so image data teaches space and video data teaches motion, avoiding the need for huge 4D sets. On wild footage it beat rivals, above all on extreme new angles.
arxiv-2506-13897:
Thomas Kreutz, Max Mühlhäuser, and Alejandro Sanchez Guinea built a joint learning model in 2025 linking four kinds of human activity data. Laser ranging sensors offer a privacy-friendly way to watch activity, but multi-way pre-training for them is little explored. Their model ties laser point clouds to skeletons, body sensors, and text.

By merging two existing data sets, the team synchronised all four data types for the same actions. Their model, DeSPITE, learns one shared space across them. New tasks became possible: matching and retrieval between skeletons, point clouds, and sensors, plus finding moments in time. The model also worked well as pre-training for activity recognition on two standard benchmarks.
arxiv-2506-13997:
Ananya Shah builds, in a 2025 paper, a topological test for gerrymandering that reads voting maps the way a geometer reads terrain. District lines are drawn by politicians, but precincts, the smallest voting units, are too small to rig one by one. So if district-level voting patterns warp away from precinct-level ones, manipulation is a prime suspect. Persistent homology, which tracks how patterns persist across scales, supplies the measuring tape.

Across North Carolina House elections from 2012 to 2024, precinct patterns stayed stable while district patterns lurched in redistricting years, a signal that classic compactness scores missed. Extended to newer maps, the method flags the Texas plan struck down as a racial gerrymander, and reads California's and Louisiana's contested maps as well. The author also turns the tool on racial vote margins directly, a first for this framework.
arxiv-2506-14297:
Victor Alves, Carla Bezerra, Ivan Machado, and three colleagues grade the quality of tests written by language models in this two thousand twenty-five study. Writing test scripts by hand is slow, costly, and error-prone, so automated generation is attractive. The team had three models, GPT-4o, Amazon Q, and Llama 3.3, generate Python test suites under two prompting styles: from text descriptions and from existing code. They catalogued errors and test smells in the output.

Most generated suites contained at least one error or smell. Assertion errors dominated, at about sixty-four percent of all errors, and lack of cohesion among test cases was the commonest smell. Detailed textual prompts produced fewer errors but more smells. GPT-4o made the fewest errors in both settings, while Amazon Q made the most. The authors also link specific errors, like assertion and indentation faults, to cohesion smells.
arxiv-2506-14697:
Aishan Liu and a team of colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on AgentSafe, a benchmark for the safety of embodied AI agents. Embodied agents are robots and virtual agents that see, plan, and act in human environments, often guided by vision-language models. When such an agent follows a hazardous instruction, the harm can be physical.

Older safety tests cover few kinds of hazard and check only the final outcome. This benchmark follows the whole chain of perception, planning, and execution, so failures can be located precisely. It systematically feeds agents dangerous instructions and scores how they respond. A fuller test helps developers find unsafe behavior before these agents are deployed around people.
arxiv-2506-14797:
Marco Nurisso and co-authors state broad laws that cap how well a mind or model can both spread a lesson and keep each input distinct, in a paper from 2025. Spread needs shared form across inputs, while ID needs sharp splits. The team shows that once the match between inputs fades past a fine grain, the two scores lock to one shared front that no shape of input space can beat.

With noise and mixed spaces the laws still hold, and a sharp fall hits when more than two inputs must be held at once. A small trained net grows its own grain line as it learns and tracks the law curves in close step. The same caps show in a photo net and in top chat models, the authors report.
arxiv-2506-14897:
Dario Mena, Maria Carmen Reguera, and Luz Roncal prove weighted bounds for square functions that arise outside the classic integral setting, in a 2025 math paper. Square functions measure how much a signal's pieces add up across scales, and weights let some regions count more than others. Sharp bounds matter because they feed many results in harmonic analysis.

The team gives weak-type estimates in the borderline case, stated in terms of two constants that describe the weight. Their proof separates the weight's role through a refined version of a known lemma. They note the method extends to other settings in the range where the square function stays controlled.
arxiv-2506-15397:
Sepehr Elahi, Paula Murmann, and Patrick Thiran wrote a 2025 paper on vaccination when the contact graph is unknown. A standard spread model tracks how a non immunizing disease moves on a graph. The best vaccine plan ties to a hard spectral problem, but past work assumed the graph was given.

Here only the infection state of each node is seen. The authors split the task: learn the graph, then vaccinate well. Their learning method rests on inclusion and exclusion counts, with a proven sample bound for graph recovery. For the vaccine step, they give an exact method that runs in polynomial time on graphs of bounded tree width, plus a greedy heuristic for any graph.
arxiv-2506-15497:
Changzeng Fu surveyed machines that sense and respond to human emotion in a 2025 book on affective computing. The book opens with the history of human-computer interaction, then builds the science base from psychology and brain research on how feelings arise and show. From there it covers the main channels machines can read: faces, voices, brain signals, and body signals.
