Chapters explain emotion theories, recognition from single and mixed channels, and ways for machines to express feeling back, including social robots. Uses in schooling, health, entertainment, and personal help get their own treatment. Open problems include merging messy data streams, guarding privacy, and handling the ethics of machines that act like companions.
arxiv-2506-15697:
Yi Liu and five co-authors built DeepRTL2 in twenty twenty-five, a language model family serving the register-transfer level where chips are designed. Language models had already helped write and explain RTL code. But the embedding-based chores of design work had been neglected. Those chores include searching code by description, checking behavioral equivalence, and predicting performance.

DeepRTL2 unifies generation and embedding tasks in one versatile model family. The authors present it as the first comprehensive model of its kind for electronic design automation. Across their evaluations it reached state-of-the-art results on every task tested, both the writing side and the retrieval-and-judgment side. A single model spanning the workflow could speed up how engineers draft, find, verify, and tune hardware descriptions.
arxiv-2506-15797:
Yaakov Malinovsky and Viktor Skorniakov settle a standing guess about the cheapest way to hunt faulty units in a batch. In group testing, pooled samples can clear many units at once, and each unit carries its own known chance of being faulty. A pairwise routine that tests units two at a time, in rising order of risk, was long suspected to be the best nested plan within a certain band of risk values.

The pair proves the guess right for that band. They also lay bare the full shape of the winning routine and give a closed formula for how many tests it needs on average. The result sharpens the theory of nested testing plans, where each round must build on the last.
arxiv-2506-16097:
Earthquakes slide along faults in pulses, where only a short patch of the fault moves at any moment. Eran Bouchbinder, writing alone in 2025, builds a single math rule for how such a pulse grows or dies. The rule tracks the pulse with just one changing value, drawn from work on rate-and-state friction laws.

Large computer runs of growing pulses matched the rule's forecasts. The rule also shows why the pulse's weakness builds so slowly. That slow build helps explain why pulses stay at work across a wide range of real faults. The work gives quake science a compact tool for a shape of rupture that drives most shallow quakes.
arxiv-2506-16397:
Amik Raj Behera, Nutan Limaye, Varun Ramanathan, and Srikanth Srinivasan bound the power of an algebraic proof system over fields of positive characteristic, in a 2025 paper. The Ideal Proof System checks polynomial identities as proofs. Its strength over fields where arithmetic wraps around, rather than the zero-characteristic case studied before, was less charted.

The team adapted a functional lower bound method to this setting. They proved exponential-size lower bounds for several fragments of the system, meaning some truths need huge proofs there. They also proved matching upper bounds: the same instances admit short, constant-depth refutations, and a whole class of symmetric instances falls efficiently too. The work matters partly because this proof system's limits connect to a famous open problem about Frege proofs. Field size conditions are stated with care, and a concurrent paper is noted.
arxiv-2506-16597:
Anupma Choudhary, Sohith Bandari, Kushvah, and Swastik turn planet-hunting light curves into pictures and let a vision transformer sort them, in a 2025 paper. Kepler's brightness records are long time series; the team redraws each as either a Gramian angular field or a recurrence plot, two image forms that expose time patterns. The transformer then judges which curves carry a planet's transit.

Recurrence plots won the comparison, with recall near 89 percent and precision near 85 percent under cross-validation. Shrinking the dataset to fight class imbalance remains a limit. The authors argue image-based reading of light curves deserves a place in exoplanet pipelines.
arxiv-2506-16997:
Software that explains itself only when asked misses the moments users silently need help. Deters and co-authors hunt for runtime signals, in behavior, system events, and feelings, that betray a need for explanation before it is voiced.

In an online study they collected self-reported signs from users. They sorted them into a catalog: 17 indicators in user behavior, 8 in system events, and 14 in emotional or physical reactions. They also mapped how each sign relates to different kinds of explanation need. The catalog can guide designers building prototypes, help teams mine telemetry from software already in use, and trigger explanations at the right moment during a session. The authors frame it as a step toward systems that notice confusion on their own.
arxiv-2506-17197:
Samuel Howard, Peter Potaptchik, and George Deligiannidis extend a generative modeling method to costs arranged on trees, in a 2025 paper. Schrödinger bridges move one probability cloud into another along the cheapest noisy path, a dynamic form of optimal transport. A popular fitting procedure solves the standard case through repeated bridge-matching steps.

Many problems, though, split cost across several linked distributions at once. When the links form a tree, the average point of the group — its Wasserstein barycentre — falls out as a special case. The team extend the fitting procedure to that tree setting. Their method keeps the elegance of the two-cloud case while covering grouped data, such as images from several related sources.
arxiv-2506-17297:
Mishra and colleagues introduced in twenty twenty-five a free Python library called SafeRL-Lite. Reinforcement learning trains agents by trial and reward, but agents can learn unsafe acts. Many toolkits lack firm safety limits or plain reasons for choices. SafeRL-Lite wraps standard training worlds and deep Q-learning agents. It adds hard limits during training and tools that explain choices after the fact.

Explanations use SHAP values and saliency maps, which highlight what drove a choice. The library also tracks how often limits were broken. Tests on a constrained pole-balancing task show both the policy logic and its safety record. The code is light, open, and can be installed with pip. It aims to make safe learning easier to build and audit.
arxiv-2506-18197:
Guowei Wayne Tu and Evgueni Filipov show in 2025 that woven baskets can act as a new class of engineered material. Weaving is an old craft, yet the mechanics of woven forms had drawn little study.

The authors find that three dimensional woven shapes match solid shapes in stiffness under small loads, because the ribbons take the load in their plane. Under large loads, the woven corners bend and buckle in a springy way and can be crushed again and again with no lasting harm. They build corner blocks that snap into larger shapes, and show uses in tough robots and surfaces whose bending can be tuned.
arxiv-2506-18897:
Chi and eleven co-authors present a robot world model in a paper from 2025 whose head title frames it as learning a dual-system model for real-time planning and risk analysis. Video generation models can predict future scenes for robots, but full frame-by-frame generation is too slow for live control. Their system, MinD, splits the work between two diffusion processes running at unlike speeds.

A slow generator sketches future scenes while a fast policy outputs actions, fed by rough one-step scene sketches instead of finished frames. A matcher module keeps the two in sync. The system succeeded often on lab and real robot tasks and flagged most likely failures in advance.
arxiv-2506-18997:
Galaxy surveys with new spectrographs will read the life stories of thousands of distant galaxies, but simulation predictions do not arrive in the same language. Ikhsanova and co-authors build the translation layer in a 2025 paper. They forge mock observations of about 750 simulated galaxies from the TNG50 simulation.

The mocks sit at three cosmic epochs and pass through radiative transfer software, then get analyzed with the same fitting code used on real spectra. The paper lays out the full methodology and releases the data. An early look follows three galaxies and their descendants across time, comparing ages, metal content, and star formation histories. The framework lets survey teams test their tools before trusting them on the sky.
arxiv-2506-19297:
Yui Tatsumi, Ziyue Zeng, and Hiroshi Watanabe present a 2025 paper on image coding that serves both human eyes and machine sight. Layered coding sends a base image, then adds detail as needed, and both people and vision models now drink from the same stream. Past learned codecs lean hard on training and leave their design opaque.

Their fix adds an explicit leftover-signal layer, in the spirit of a classic format. Two forms split the leftover at the trait level or the pixel level. Tests show clear bit savings, with a choice between coder cost and squeeze strength.
arxiv-2506-19797:
Mubaraq Yakubu, Navodini Wijethilake, Jonathan Shapey, Andrew King, and Alexander Hammers wrote this review in two thousand twenty-five, with one surname spelled in a variant way in its text. It takes stock of auto methods that cut the pituitary gland and its tumors out of MRI scans.

The team sifted dozens of studies of auto and semi-auto methods. Deep learning rules the field, with U-Net kin the most used. Scores swing wide, above all for the small gland, where auto cuts can fail hard. Tumor cuts fare better, and semi-auto cuts are steadier. Many papers skip key facts such as field strength and tumor size. Bigger, more mixed data sets are the clear need.
arxiv-2506-19997:
Geonwoo Cho and co-authors teach a virtual teacher to design better practice tasks in a 2025 paper. Reinforcement learning agents often fail in new settings unlike their training ones. One fix is unsupervised environment design, where a teacher keeps inventing tasks with high learning value while a student agent trains on them. Value is usually gauged by regret, the gap between the student's play and the best play.

Old methods estimate regret from value errors alone. The new method, TRACED, adds the agent's error in predicting how the world changes. It also adds a score for how much training on one task lifts play on others. Across benchmarks, TRACED curricula improved the agent's zero-shot play in unseen settings over strong rivals. Tests that removed parts showed the new error term drives fast growth in task difficulty. The authors argue for modeling task relations outright.
arxiv-2506-20097:
Wang Bill Zhu and four co-authors presented PSALM-V in twenty twenty-five, a system that learns the rules of actions in visual worlds by trial and error. Symbolic planners need each action's preconditions and effects written in the PDDL language; hand-writing them is the bottleneck. Language models can draft them, but earlier attempts assumed text worlds, full observability, or explicit error messages.

PSALM-V instead interacts with the environment: it proposes plans and candidate semantics, executes, and explains failures by refining a tree of beliefs about each action's rules. It even infers the problem file itself. On the ALFRED household benchmark it raised plan success from thirty-seven to seventy-four percent under partial observability. It also induced correct rules for two games and a real robot block-stacking task.
arxiv-2506-20197:
Clément Canonne, Yash Pote, and Uddalok Sarkar ask how to prove that a piece of code came from a particular AI model, in this 2025 paper. More and more code is sampled from large language models, and attribution matters for trust and accountability. Pure sample-based testing drowns in high dimensions, so the team also uses the model's own probability estimates, which providers commonly expose.

Their tool, Anubis, frames attribution as distribution testing, a branch of statistics with ready-made guarantees. Given about two thousand samples, it judges whether they plausibly came from the suspect model. On a benchmark of code, Anubis scored at least 0.9 on the standard discrimination measure when separating models such as DeepSeek-Coder, CodeGemma, and Stable-Code. The approach needs no training and no access to the suspect model's internals beyond its samples and scores. The authors release the tool openly for others to use.
arxiv-2506-20397:
Siddharth Panigrahi and three co-authors study special surfaces in this 2025 math study. The surfaces live in a three-part space used in physics, where one direction behaves like time. Each surface is built from a linked pair of functions, and the authors ask how its bending relates to where those functions hit zero.

They sort all such surfaces whose bending in one sense is zero. They also show that no non-flat surface of this kind can be maximal, and they sort the ones with fixed mean bending. Later parts trace how bending behaves far out on complete surfaces. In the last part, the authors show these surfaces can arise as solutions in certain field theories in physics.
arxiv-2506-20997:
Chao Yang and a large team take a first deep look at two faint Milky Way satellite galaxies with a new wide-field telescope, in this 2025 paper. The creator field in the catalog is cut off mid-list; the head byline names thirty-seven authors. The 2.5-meter Wide Field Survey Telescope in China is beginning survey work, and these dwarfs, Boötes III and Draco, served as pilot targets.

Combining the new images with older sky survey and Gaia data gave motions for member stars across a twelve-year baseline, precise to a couple of thousandths of an arcsecond per year. Bright and faint stars agreed, showing no motion split as the galaxies are tugged by the Milky Way. Boötes III's stretched shape and clustering in space and motion suggest it is the bound remnant of the galaxy that spawned the Styx stream. More detailed papers are promised.
arxiv-2506-21297:
Ricardo Hideki Hangai Kojo and co-authors report a case study of splitting a web shop's front end into micro frontends. Their 2025 paper asks when the style, which breaks an interface into independently built pieces, is worth its cost. The gains sought are scale, resilience, and team freedom. The costs are complexity and heavier infrastructure. The team first surveyed academic and gray literature on the style.

They then applied it at a marketplace for handmade goods that already used microservices. Its old setup tied a Java monolith tightly to a separate front end, on aging tools. The new build added gateway and back end for front end patterns, with modern frameworks. Developers answered a mixed questionnaire afterward. Adoption succeeded, yet the team judged it not strictly needed. A single front end could have met the goals, they found. Convenience in context drove the choice.
arxiv-2506-21397:
Datta and Samanta study how a supercooled phase change reshapes gravitational wave signals in twenty twenty-five. Some extensions of the Standard Model predict the early universe supercooled before changing phase. Such transitions themselves generate strong gravitational waves. The authors ask what they do to waves from other sources.

Their test source is a network of metastable cosmic strings. A supercooled phase triggers a burst of thermal inflation between the sources. That inflation suppresses the high frequency part of the string spectrum. Regions of string parameter space once ruled out by LIGO reopen. The combined signal still matches pulsar timing array hints at low frequencies. Future detectors could see the distinctive two part spectrum.
arxiv-2506-21497:
Jiashuo Wang and seven co-authors teach chat models to hold a user's interest in social talk, by learning from how the talk later unfolds. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Past work taught models to plan acts or draw on facts, but the link from such steps to true engagement is weak. The team uses the user's next move, tied to the aim of the talk, as a direct reward sign. They build a fake user to trade lines with the target model. A search method then roams through paths the talk could take. The aim is a chat partner that learns what keeps people in the talk.
arxiv-2506-21897:
Twisha Chattopadhyay and seven co-authors show how a 3D printer's secrets can leak through video in this two thousand twenty-five security paper. Factories often watch printers with cameras, since print areas can be unsafe for people. The team shows that such footage gives away the design being printed. Their system tracks the printer nozzle as it moves. It turns that path back into the machine instructions, called G-code.

The system also recovers settings such as feed rate and extrusion rate. A checker then proves the stolen instructions match the original print. The attack threatens makers in fields from health care to defense. The paper warns that camera feeds of production lines need guarding like any other trade secret.
arxiv-2506-22197:
Darius Eros and Sebastian Gieger prove a Cartan-Hadamard claim for space-times with no need for smooth form. The work came out in 2025. The old claim says a space with no more than flat bend has one path of least time span for each pair of points.

Their form is built by hand from parts, not smooth curves. It works in the young frame of Lorentz-style length spaces. There, bend is set by side-by-side checks, not slope math. It takes an old find for plain gap spaces to this new home. It broadens the smooth claim of Beem and Ehrlich. The core is a new sense of near-in bend fit for such spaces. With world-wide time form and a link term in place, time-like paths of least span exist for linked points, and each is the sole one.
arxiv-2506-22397:
Anirban Ray, Ashesh, and Florian Jug present a 2025 method, called HazeMatching in the text, for clearing haze from light microscope images. Cheap widefield microscopes cannot block out-of-focus light the way costly confocal models can, so their images look foggy. Computer dehazing promises crisp images from cheap gear, but methods tend to pick one goal: match the true data closely, or look realistic, at the cost of the other.

Their method steers a generative process with the hazy image itself, step by step, to land between the two goals. On five data sets, both synthetic and real, it held a steady balance where twelve rival methods leaned one way or the other. Its predictions were also well calibrated. The method needs no exact model of the blur, so it suits real lab images.
arxiv-2506-22797:
Kazi and three co-authors plan safe flight paths for a spacecraft that shadows another object in orbit, in a paper from 2025. The chaser must stay close to its target, which may be passive debris or a maneuvering craft, while never colliding. Thruster firings are modeled as on-off choices so fuel use enters the plan directly.

Their method writes the full nonlinear motion, split into steps with a standard solver, as a mixed-integer optimization. Scaling tricks, added valid constraints, and rounding of relaxed solutions keep the problem tractable over long horizons. A numerical case study shows the planner finding efficient, collision-free paths.
arxiv-2506-23997: Cole Durham, writing alone in a 2025 math paper, bounds a quantity tied to vibrating shapes. The quantity is the bottom of the spectrum of the Laplacian, an operator whose values set the tones a shape can ring with. His setting allows the shape's curvature to be controlled only on average, in an integral sense, rather than at every point. His proof leans on a minimal positive Green's function and its properties, and it yields an upper bound for that bottom value.
arxiv-2507-00197:
Natalia Miller and Zinovy Malkin wrote a 2025 paper on the yearly swing in Earth's polar motion. The planet's pole drifts, and one part of that drift repeats each year. How that yearly part has changed over long spans was not well charted.

They pulled the yearly signal from two long records, one modern global series and one from Pulkovo that reaches back to the eighteen forties. Math tools split the signal out and tracked its size and phase over time. Across about one hundred eighty years, the swing grew in a near steady way. Its phase also shifted by a large step over the same span. The size of the swing tracked the gap in mean warmth between the two halves of the globe in winter months.
arxiv-2507-00497:
Takami Tohyama and Hidetoshi Fukuyama published a research paper in 2025 on why swapping atoms flips the sign of a voltage that heat creates in an iron-vanadium-aluminum alloy. That voltage, the Seebeck effect, is the heart of devices that turn heat into power. A few misplaced atoms turn the voltage from positive to negative, a handy trick if it can be controlled.

Their model treats misplaced atoms as random scatterers mixing with the host bands, with electron and hole bands handled apart. The math shows the defects scatter hole carriers harder than electron carriers, tipping the balance negative. The mechanism offers a way to tune heat-to-power materials without changing their charge count.
arxiv-2507-00597:
Josh Border and co-authors model how breath and heart sync in heart failure in a 2025 paper. A nerve pacer that restores the sync has raised heart output in animal tests. Why that sync helps had long been in doubt.

Their model shows the sync cuts wasted power in the vessel network. Locked zones form where breath and heart beats align in set ratios. Output gains grew with sync strength, then leveled off at a set beat ratio. Gains were best at low heart rates, as clinics have seen. The saved power matched the rise seen in paced animals.
arxiv-2507-00697:
Huadong Gao, Yuhui Huang, and Wen Xie analyze a numerical method for a classic equation in a 2025 mathematics study. Poisson's equation links a function to its sources, but rough boundary data break standard methods. Textbook approaches need boundary values with more smoothness than many real problems provide.

The authors work with very weak solutions, which make sense of the rough case. They apply a mixed finite element method named for Raviart and Thomas directly, without first smoothing the data. Their proof shows the numerical solution converges to the very weak solution. They also establish how fast that convergence happens as the mesh is refined.
arxiv-2507-00897: Nazlı Doğan characterizes when convolution and Toeplitz operators keep two stability traits on power series spaces. The 2025 paper works in pure functional analysis. It gives needed conditions for an operator of Toeplitz type to hold the stronger of the two traits. It also works out both traits for convolution operators and their duals. Those results cover two named families of power series spaces. They then carry over to spaces of holomorphic functions on the full plane and on the unit disk.
arxiv-2507-01197:
Dhamdhawach Horsuwan tunes a common industrial controller by its spectrum in a 2025 paper. The controller is the proportional-integral type, a two-knob workhorse, and the plant is the awkward kind that integrates its input and answers late, called IPDT. The goal is one tuning that makes both following a setpoint and shrugging off disturbances decay at the same clean exponential rate.

His method minimizes the spectral abscissa, the slowest decay rate among the closed loop's poles. A semi-discrete model captures the integrator and the delay while letting the dominant poles be pulled out cheaply. Those poles are mapped back to continuous time and polished against the exact delay equation. The result is a single gain set with no hand-set trade-off weights. Simulations show faster settling and better safety margins than the classic tuning rules.
arxiv-2507-01297:
Xinxi Lyu and co-authors show in this 2025 paper that plain retrieval, done right, lifts language models on hard reasoning tests. Retrieval-augmented generation had shone on fact questions but disappointed on benchmarks like MMLU Pro, GPQA, and MATH. The team blames the store, not the idea: past stores were too small or too narrow.

Their store, CompactDS, filters the web down to a compact, high-grade subset and mixes memory search with disk search for speed. A minimal pipeline on top gained across all tests and model sizes, up to a third on MMLU Pro. No single source sufficed; variety mattered. Their store matched or beat web search engines and fancier agent systems.
arxiv-2507-01497:
Philip Rubeling and co-authors send a complex entangled light state through twenty-five kilometres of fibre, in a 2025 paper. Cluster states, groups of particles entangled so the link survives local measurement, are a key resource for quantum networks, blind computing, and repeaters. Yet sending them down ordinary fibre had not been done, because the states are fragile and hard to measure.

The team encode two photons across several time bins, creating a four-qubit cluster state directly in the generation process, which avoids a hard gate operation. To read the state out, they introduce chirped-pulse modulation and the first beam splitter that works on time bins, giving flexible measurements. The state crossed the fibre link with its entanglement certified as genuinely multipartite. They also ran basic one-way computing steps on it. The authors argue the approach lays groundwork for large quantum resource networks over long-distance fibre.
arxiv-2507-01897:
Shashi Mishra, Hitoshi Mori, and Elena Margine test in 2025 a fix to the standard theory of superconductivity in a sulfur and hydrogen compound. The standard theory works when electrons move much faster than the atoms vibrate. In this compound, that gap is small, so the theory's core shortcut may fail.

The team added the first level of corrections for how electrons and atom vibrations affect each other, using first principles math on real atomic data. For the sulfur compound, the corrections were large. When they were joined with two other effects, the forecast for the point where resistance vanishes matched lab results very well. They ran the same check on lead, a classic case. The work shows where the standard theory needs care, which matters for the hunt for better conductors.
arxiv-2507-01997: Network engineers increasingly ask AI agents to diagnose broken networks, but every lab tests its agents on homemade setups, so results cannot be compared. Zhihao Wang and co-authors propose a shared playground for the job: a standardized, open benchmarking platform where troubleshooting agents can be built and evaluated with low effort. This preliminary paper argues the case and sketches the platform's aims, reproducibility first among them.
arxiv-2507-02197:
Amogh Mannekote and co-authors test whether language model role players act in line with the beliefs they state in a 2025 paper. Such agents are used to fake human data for behavior research, so their words and deeds should match the roles they are given. The team built a framework to check that match in advance.

Using a persona bank and the Trust Game, a standard test of trust and payback, they defined a consistency score. They varied the kind of belief asked, when game details were shown, and how far ahead forecasts reached. Results show steady gaps between what the agents say and what they then do. Imposing a researcher's own beliefs also proved hard.
arxiv-2507-02797:
Suman Saha and James Jenkins study the dayside air of an ultra-hot giant planet, WASP-19b, in this 2025 paper. The planet races around its star and its dayside glows hot enough to read with the JWST telescope. Using stored telescope data across a wide band of infrared light, the team fitted models to the glow to name the gases present.

Water and carbon monoxide showed up clearly, with weaker hints of two more gases. The fits also found clouds, a first firm detection on such a planet, likely made of silica grains. The carbon-to-oxygen balance came out high, which hints that oxygen is locked away in those clouds.
arxiv-2507-02897:
Nathaniel Chen and co-authors built an AI controller for a fusion reactor that regulators could actually inspect. Fusion control systems increasingly use black-box AI, which safety rules struggle to accept. The team instead used a deliberately simple, linear, and interpretable design. It watches camera images of the DIII-D tokamak's divertor, the exhaust region where hot plasma must be cooled before it strikes the wall.

The controller doses deuterium gas to hold the exhaust plasma in a detached state, hovering off the wall without collapsing the reaction. In tests it tracked the target within about two percent, through both detachment and reattachment. Because every step of the method is transparent, the authors argue it offers a template for compliant AI control in future reactors.
arxiv-2507-02997:
Jing Bi and Chenliang Xu teach an agent to plan goal steps from first person teaching videos. Learning by watching means pulling key facts about a place from raw views. Their task asks for high level next acts in a sim world seen from the agent's eyes.

A memory of what spots afford which acts, built as a web, joins a transformer brain. That memory helps pick acts that fit the scene and flags when the agent strays off plan. Tests in a rich sim show cleaner learning and firm acts even when slips occur. Watching may thus become doing.
arxiv-2507-03197:
Jiarui Li and five co-authors open a black box in immunology in twenty twenty-five. T cells spot antigens that MHC molecules present through their receptors. Knowing how that binding works is key to grasping immunity and to building new cures. Transformer models such as TULIP predict the binding well but give no account of how they reach a call.

Older ways to explain a model cannot cope with the encoder-decoder transformers used here. The team puts forth QCAI, which puts a number on cross-attention interaction. Cross-attention is where receptor and peptide meet inside the model and weigh each other. By gauging its strength pair by pair, the method shows which contacts push the model toward its call. The gain is a read on the workings: which links the model leans on, not just its final call.
arxiv-2507-03397:
Santiago Benavides and Miguel Bustamante ask what sets the flow of energy across scales in turbulent fluids in a 2025 paper. In turbulence, energy moves from large swirls to small ones, or the reverse, and few theories can predict that flow well. The pair study simplified shell models, where the flow is split into layers of motion that pass energy to their neighbors.

They focus on the phases of the waves in each layer. By treating most neighbor effects as noise, they turn the phase motion into a solved math problem and check it against computer runs. Their results predict the energy flow from the spectrum, and they prove that models like three-dimensional turbulence always cascade energy forward, toward small scales.
arxiv-2507-03497:
Pieter Kleer and Daan Noordenbos study when to stop and take an offer, knowing only how the best offer is distributed. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A sequence of correlated offers arrives one by one. The full correlation pattern is usually unknown in practice. The authors assume just the law of the maximum value. They then guard against the worst correlation that fits it.

A simple threshold rule proves nearly optimal in that worst case. The threshold is the monopoly price of the maximum's distribution. The result needs the expected maximum to grow slower than the count of offers. A second result rounds out the picture. Decision theory gains a middle path between ignorance and full knowledge.
arxiv-2507-03597: Marchetti offers an introduction to abelian anyons, the unusual particle excitations that can arise in flat, two-dimensional systems, in a 2025 review. Written at an introductory level, it presents the theory through the lens of quantum field theory. Along the way it aims to make clear how the mathematical structure connects to both the theoretical picture and the experimental physics of these particles.
arxiv-2507-03797:
Virtual reality lets researchers study perception under controlled conditions, but the sound in most setups is plain stereo through headphones. Benjamin Kahl tests Wave Field Synthesis as a tool for cognitive research in virtual reality. The method rebuilds a sound field in space rather than mixing two channels. He built a sample experiment in which participants located still and moving sound sources, once in the synthesized field and once through a standard stereo setup.

Stereo actually gave higher raw accuracy. Yet the synthesized field felt more natural and intuitive, above all for judging direction. The system also showed limits: it could not place sounds by height and did not mimic blocking by objects. It was not tuned to each user either, which hurt most for sounds near the center. Kahl concludes that the method suits studies with rich soundscapes where direction matters most, despite its current gaps.
arxiv-2507-04097:
Plants turn sunlight into stored energy, and a 2025 paper by Trishna Kalita and co-authors asks how much of that energy could in theory be drawn back out as work. The team models the Photosystem II reaction center, the protein complex where light first splits charge, using a quantum master equation.

The measure they track is ergotropy, the most work a quantum state can give up without losing energy. Paths where charge separates between two named pigment molecules scored high, as did a route through three charge-separated states in a row. A path that skips that pigment pair scored far lower. The authors link the gaps to how populations shift between active and passive states inside the center.
arxiv-2507-04197:
Nishant Chinnasami, Rye Stahle-Smith, and Rasha Karakchi guard an encryption chip with machine learning in a 2025 paper. The AES cipher is strong math, but real chips leak through timing quirks and injected faults. Their framework deliberately injects delays and scrambled outputs during encryption to build labeled examples of trouble.

Two detectors follow: a simple timing threshold and a random forest trained on timing plus output features. Both ran in real time on a small programmable chip board. The learned detector beat the threshold method on precision and recall across block sizes and attack rates. The authors pitch the setup as cheap, fast protection for embedded devices that cannot afford heavyweight security hardware.
arxiv-2507-04597:
Vivek Kumar Tiwari examines, in a 2025 theoretical paper, how to take the chiral limit consistently in a quark meson model of strong interaction physics. The limit, where light quarks lose their mass, guides maps of how matter changes phase with temperature and density. Different ways of handling quantum vacuum effects can shift those maps.

The study uses one version of the model, with meson masses set by curvature and a quark vacuum term included. Its results are checked against chiral perturbation theory, which predicts how certain meson decay constants should scale near the limit. The paper compares phase maps across three model treatments: its own, an on shell renormalized version, and a functional renormalization group treatment. The comparison shows how first order, second order, and crossover regions move between methods. Such checks matter for trusting model predictions about dense matter.
arxiv-2507-04797:
Zuo Ye, Yubo Sun, and Gennian Ge build codes that can fix bursts of lost symbols, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Such losses can hit stored data in a tight cluster or in one small spot. A good code adds as little extra data as it can while still fixing the loss.

Their code first picks sequences whose step-by-step changes stay close to balanced. Two added checks then help pin down where the loss sits. The new codes use less extra data than the best prior ones, and the method is simpler. The authors also give a fast way to encode any input.
arxiv-2507-04997:
The link between radio units and antennas can choke a modern mobile network, and a 2025 paper by Mostafa Rahmani and co-authors studies ways to squeeze that link. Their setting is an open radio access network with many small antennas spread out and run in a decentralized way.

The team applies the open standard's own compression methods to the uplink signals that travel the fronthaul link. Link-level simulations compare their quantization plans against a case with no compression at all. The squeezed signals cut the fronthaul load a great deal while the error rates stayed close to the uncompressed case. The authors argue that smart quantization gives next-generation networks a workable balance between load and quality.
arxiv-2507-05297: Zijun Meng proves a classification theorem alone in a 2025 paper. The setting is fuzzy classification: a crowd of judges each sorts objects into types with graded confidence, and an aggregation rule must merge the crowd into one verdict. Meng shows that any such rule must be a weighted arithmetic mean. The rule must be optimal, treat judges independently, and respect unanimity at zero, with at least three objects sorted into at least two types. The paper also characterizes the borderline case where objects and types both number two.
arxiv-2507-05497:
Luka Carroll, James East, and Matthias Fresacher describe algebraic structures built from partitions in this 2025 paper. Their object, the full-domain partition monoid, surfaced in two recent studies linking diagram monoids to category theory. It packs the full transformation monoid and the lattice of equivalence relations inside one frame.

The team gives presentations, that is generator and relation lists, for the monoid itself. They do the same for its singular ideal and its planar submonoid. The planar case has its own quirks, tied to a band structure matching planar equivalences. The results round out the portrait of a newly found monoid.
arxiv-2507-05897:
Wireless receivers must pull symbols out of fading signals, and the noise itself may rise and fall with the channel. Almutasem Bellah Enad and four co-authors build a math framework in 2025 for rating simple linear detectors under such fast-fading, noise-linked conditions.

The team characterizes the effective noise left after zero-forcing filtering, a standard cleanup step. From that they derive a semi-analytical formula for the symbol error rate under Rayleigh fading with channel-dependent Gaussian noise. Simulations matched both the formula and heavier numerical benchmarks closely. Because the framework bends to other channel and noise shapes, the authors offer it as a design tool for next-generation wireless systems.
arxiv-2507-06097:
Hyojoong Kim and Nakwoo Kim glue two disc-shaped spaces into a spindle, inside a supergravity model, in a paper from 2025. Their setup pairs five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space with a disc. They then lift the solutions to eleven-dimensional supergravity, the home of M5-branes.

By computing an anomaly polynomial for the brane theory on the disc, they read off off-shell central charges for the dual four-dimensional field theory. Those charges split into parts from the disc's center and its edge, called gravitational blocks. Joining the blocks of two discs along their edges rebuilds the charge of one full spindle. The trick gives a modular way to build new solutions.
arxiv-2507-06597:
Collares, Erde, Geisler and Kang study in 2025 majority bootstrap percolation, a network infection model where a node falls once half its neighbors are infected. Earlier work on the hypercube found a sharp threshold in the starting density and universal behavior across high-dimensional graphs. Those proofs needed graph size bounded exponentially in degree. This paper relaxes the setting to a slightly narrower graph class.

The universal behavior then holds even for graphs of superexponential size, including the permutahedron. The authors also sharpen the threshold window for the hypercube and analyze an irregular example built from stars.
arxiv-2507-06697:
Magnetic monopoles would balance Maxwell's equations beautifully. Yet decades of searching have found none. Vicente Vento proposes that hunters may have been looking in the wrong sector of nature. He rebuilds electrodynamics with two kinds of light. An ordinary photon ties to the electron we know. An extraordinary photon belongs, with the monopole, to a dark sector.

A mixing between the sectors turns both the electron and the monopole into dyons. Dyons carry both electric and magnetic charge. That twist changes what experiments should expect to see, in direct searches and subtler effects alike. Vento works through those consequences. He offers a reason the monopole has stayed hidden, plus fresh signatures for anyone still determined to find it.
arxiv-2507-06797:
Antonella Barisic Kulas, Andreja Jurasovic, and Stjepan Bogdan grow drone thermal image sets with synthetic additions, in work from 2025. Heat cameras on drones serve rescue, wildlife counts, and disaster response, mostly in dim or smoky scenes. Real thermal flights are costly and rare, so training data stay thin.

Their pipeline pastes new objects into real thermal backgrounds with control of place, size, and angle. The pasted views respect the background's camera angle. Two public sets gain new classes: drones over cities in one, animals in the other. Detectors trained on the enriched sets score well on old and new classes. Thermal models beat daylight-trained ones in side-by-side checks.
arxiv-2507-06897:
Ning-An Lai and co-authors prove long-time existence for wave equations outside an obstacle in two dimensions in a 2025 paper. Waves bouncing around a star-shaped body appear in acoustics and electromagnetics. In two dimensions, decay is slow, so showing small waves survive long is delicate.

A new Morawetz-type energy estimate for the perturbed equation gives decay inside the light cone. Weighted product estimates add matching decay near the cone. Together they pin the lifespan of small-data solutions almost sharply, up to small logarithmic losses. The result extends what was known from the obstacle-free problem to real geometries with something in the way.
arxiv-2507-07197:
Trained models for vision and language hold rich knowledge, but game-playing agents usually learn from scratch. Elia Piccoli and co-authors ask how an agent in reinforcement learning can borrow from several trained models at once. In that style of learning, an agent acts, earns rewards, and slowly learns which acts pay off. Borrowing ready knowledge could speed that slow start.

The team proposes a design called Weight Sharing Attention, or WSA for short. The design blends the internal codes from different trained models into one shared picture of the world. Earlier work tended to use one large model, which is costly to run. A blend of smaller models could be cheaper and richer at once. The paper tests whether that blend gives agents a better start.
arxiv-2507-07297:
Chengfei Wu and five co-authors built a bench to test if vision models truly ground their thought in images. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with large vision-language models. Such models ace visual questions, but they may ride on surface cues and set bias, not on real sight. Their bench, MagiC, grades more than the end reply: it grades the step path and how that path lines up with image proof.

The set holds thousands of machine made questions and a core of hand built ones with marks, reasons, and boxes. Fifteen models were graded on it. Readers who build vision AI get a way to split true grounded thought from lucky pattern play.
arxiv-2507-07397:
Garv Chauhan and Patrick Huber propose a new test for a long-standing puzzle in neutrino physics, in a paper from 2025. Detectors using gallium have caught fewer of these tiny particles than expected. The gap is strong, yet most fixes clash with data from reactors and the sun. The pair suggest swapping the target metal to indium.

Indium has a low energy bar and a fair chance to catch a neutrino. Its catch rate can be tuned using the known flow of solar neutrinos at a close energy. A special detector that is opaque to light can exploit the threefold signal each catch gives off. The authors show that a hundred-ton indium target with two source runs could test the full range of the puzzle. That holds for plain and more complex fixes alike.
arxiv-2507-07597:
Giuseppe Bisicchia, Alessandro Bocci, and Antonio Brogi introduce in 2025 a software engine that runs quantum computing experiments across many kinds of machines. As quantum hardware moves from theory toward daily use, researchers need tools that are sturdy, portable, and able to grow. Today each platform tends to demand its own setup and code.

Their engine, Quantum Executor, splits experiment design from the machine that runs it. Users describe experiments in a modular, declarative way through one shared interface. The engine can run jobs in parallel and spread them across quantum and classical resources, with custom strategies for how runs proceed. Two realistic scenarios, automated benchmarking and hybrid validation, show the design at work. The paper ends with current limits and a road map for what comes next.
arxiv-2507-07697:
Qing-Min Zeng, A-Peng Liu, and Qi Guo study a small device that links light, motion, and an electric circuit. Their 2025 paper works with a mechanical oscillator joined to an optical cavity and to an LC circuit. By tuning how the cavity is driven with two tones and how the circuit is driven, they seek two quantum effects.

One effect is strong squeezing, a state where noise in one trait of a field drops below its usual floor. The other is one-way EPR steering between the light field and the moving part, an effect whose strength they can tune with drive power. The authors also test how both effects hold up as heat in the setting rises.
arxiv-2507-08297:
Reasoning models can think too long, wasting time and compute on easy questions. A large team from Kwai presents KAT-V1 in this 2025 technical report, an open model with forty billion parameters built to switch its deep thinking on and off as the task demands. Training such switching is the heart of the project.

The team built training data with two regimes, thinking and non-thinking, using a tagging pipeline and several helper agents. A special prediction trick helped pass reasoning skill from a teacher model at low cost. A cold-start step used majority votes and intent-aware prompts to seed mode choice. A final reinforcement method added guidance at each step, not just at the end. In tests, the model matched or beat leading rivals, the report says.
arxiv-2507-08397:
Bich Van Nguyen and Nguyen Cao Manh Thang worked out in 2025 the representation theory of a small matrix group and tied it to the design of symmetry-aware neural networks. The group holds upper-triangular three-by-three matrices over a three-element field. Such groups govern how features may mix in networks built to respect a symmetry.

The pair prove how equivariant feature spaces and filters split into basic blocks, and that chains of invariant subspaces survive the splitting intact. They also write every irreducible representation of the group as explicit matrices. Those formulas give builders a concrete kit for new network layers. The authors aim at symbolic visual learning as a first home for the designs. The paper is algebra with an engineering address.
arxiv-2507-08597:
Md Tanvirul Alam, Aritran Piplai, and Nidhi Rastogi present a malware detection method in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Machine learning classifiers degrade over time as malware evolves, a problem called concept drift. Keeping them current needs fresh labeled data, which is expensive to annotate. Active learning helps somewhat, but semi-supervised use of unlabeled data remains underexplored for malware.

Their algorithm, ADAPT, uses pseudo-labeling: the model confidently labels new samples itself and retrains on them. The method is model-agnostic, working with neural networks and tree-based classifiers alike. Experiments spanned five diverse datasets covering Android, Windows, and PDF malware. ADAPT consistently outperformed plain baselines and competitive benchmarks. The authors argue pseudo-labeling is a practical, cheaper route to keeping malware detectors effective as threats drift.
arxiv-2507-08697:
Waqar Muhammad Ashraf and co-authors present a 2025 paper on running a gas turbine better with machine learning. Power plants have been slow to adopt AI because models act as black boxes and ignore plant knowledge. Their framework adds a domain rule, based on Mahalanobis distance, to keep suggested settings in a sane range.

They applied it to a 395 MW gas turbine to raise thermal efficiency and cut heat rate. The method found sound best settings under varied weather, and random checks showed the answers were robust. It even matched real plant data when pushed past the design output limit. Without the domain rule, the authors warn, data-only tuning can suggest settings a plant cannot use. The work aims at safe AI in power systems.
arxiv-2507-09097:
Yunsoo Kim, Jinge Wu, and Honghan Wu present RadEyeVideo, a way to help vision-language models read chest X-rays by using radiologists' eye gaze as video. Their 2025 paper notes that gaze data can aid human-computer interaction in medical imaging.

Past work used heatmaps or text prompts, which lose the order in which a radiologist's eyes move. RadEyeVideo instead feeds eye-fixation data as a video sequence, keeping both space and time. The team tested it on report generation and disease diagnosis with three open-source models that take video input. Adding gaze videos raised report generation scores by up to about a quarter in their tests.
arxiv-2507-09197:
Romain Dujardin, Charles Favre, and Matteo Ruggiero present a 2025 math study of a family of maps acting on pairs of complex numbers. The maps strongly attract points toward the origin and keep one line fixed, stretching it by a factor of at least two. Along the line, the map has a superattracting fixed point of smaller order. The authors prove that any such map can be reshaped, by a formal change of coordinates, into a skew product of a simple form.

That form links the complex dynamics to a non-Archimedean world, where they find a compact invariant set that traps the interesting behavior. Outside it, points rush to the fixed line. Inside, the growth of curve multiplicity is governed by how the critical set returns. The team then builds an invariant current that describes the long-term picture on the complex side.
arxiv-2507-09297:
Akihiro Inoue and four co-authors work out when falling debris can bury a newborn neutron star's magnetic field, in this 2025 paper. Some young neutron stars, called central compact objects, show oddly weak fields. One idea: after the supernova, leftover material rains back and submerges the field under a fresh crust, hiding it.

The team simulated the fallback in one dimension with full relativity, magnetism, and neutrino cooling. Infalling gas squeezes the field and drives a shock outward. The shock stalls once cooling bites, then retreats, and dense gas piles above the magnetosphere, where a crust could form. Simple analytic models matched the simulated radii. Comparing the fallback time with the stall time gave a necessary condition for burial. The authors offer the result as a guide for richer multi-dimensional studies of neutron star variety.
arxiv-2507-09397:
Julian Schwingel and co-authors model a cloud of cold atoms as it spreads on a grid in a 2025 paper. The atoms shove each other hard, which makes their joint dance far richer than a lone atom's drift.

Past tools treat the cloud as one smooth wave and miss the stray atoms that fall out of step. The team's new way tracks each site's own state plus a bath that stands for the rest of the grid. Let loose in a mock light grid, the main cloud streams out at a fair clip. The stray atoms then creep out at a slow seep. A locked phase of the grid holds firm at first, then melts as the strays move. The way should serve a wide set of grid models in the strong regime.
arxiv-2507-09697:
Xi Yang, Haitao Chen, Lucas Kreiss, and five co-authors present a microscope that photographs areas at detail in this two thousand twenty-five optics paper. Large-area microscopy at submicron resolution tends to trade off field of view, resolution, and speed, and centimeter-scale samples are but rarely flat, forcing mechanical scanning to stay in focus. Their instrument, PANORAMA, takes a single shot in place of that. It re-images the sample through a telecentric photolithography lens and a large-aperture tube lens onto an array of micro-cameras.

Each camera in the array runs its focus live, so curved or uneven samples stay sharp across the whole field. The upshot is gigapixel imaging over sixteen by nineteen millimeters at under one micron resolution, with no scanning. The team stresses throughput and adaptability for biomedical and materials imaging, where large, imperfect samples are the norm, not the exception.
arxiv-2507-10097:
Yue Meng and co-authors stretched recommender memory to thousands of actions in two thousand twenty-five. Ranking models already read very long user histories. Retrieval, the first filtering stage, could not keep up. Tight speed budgets cap what retrieval may scan. It also lacked the target-aware tricks ranking uses. Their model, ULIM, closes that gap directly.

A category-aware layer learns each user's several interests. Dual-interest structure separates stable from fresh tastes. Long histories finally inform the candidate pool itself. Tests ran on real platform-scale tasks. Retrieval quality rose toward ranking-stage levels. Shoppers see candidates matching older loves, not just clicks. The design suits any sequence-heavy storefront.
arxiv-2507-10497:
The authors extend a classic statistical method to describe the changeover from matter built of hadrons to matter built of quarks. Their 2025 paper treats hadrons as bound states of quarks that fall apart at high density, when crowding blocks the quarks from pairing. The aim is one frame that works where lattice simulations cannot.

Their approach writes the gas of clusters through phase shifts that hold both bound and free states. It matches lattice results where those exist, at low chemical potential, and runs on into the high range where the lattice sign problem blocks the way. A kinetic rule then shows the freeze-out seen in heavy-ion collisions lands right where the clusters melt. Uses reach from neutron stars to the early universe.
arxiv-2507-10597:
Grégoire Pierra and Simone Mastrogiovanni wrote a 2025 chapter that introduces the use of gravitational waves to study how the universe expands. Gravitational waves are ripples from events such as merging black holes. Their signals carry a direct measure of distance, so they can act as standard sirens, much like standard candles in older astronomy.

The chapter explains two main approaches, called bright sirens and dark sirens, and what data each one needs. It covers the math used to draw cosmic measures from wave events, and how the choice of which events get detected can skew results. Worked examples show each method in action. New readers get a clear path into a fast-growing field.
arxiv-2507-10897:
Sha Wang and six co-authors use large language models to line up the tables of mismatched databases, in a 2025 paper. The catalog title carries stray grant acknowledgment text; the printed title is clean. Schema matching is the quiet grunt work of data integration.

Their framework, LLMatch, splits the job into preparation, table shortlisting, and column alignment, so each step can be judged alone. Columns are rolled up into concepts, matched, then drilled back down for fine mapping. A new benchmark, SchemaNet, supplies hard real-world cases from three industries. Matching accuracy rose sharply on complex schemas. Engineers using the tool also worked faster. Modularity keeps the system ready for better models.
arxiv-2507-10997:
Michael Hatzon, Eugene Ivanov, Aaron Quiskamp, and Michael Tobar report, in a 2025 paper, a readout trick. It lets the faintest thermal hum of a resonator stand out from the noise of the instrument itself. Measuring thermal fluctuations in microwave and mechanical resonators pushes amplifiers to their limits, because the amplifier's own noise floods the signal. Their system splits the signal into two channels and cross-correlates them.

Under the right conditions, the amplifier's intrinsic noise, shared by both channels, cancels in the cross-spectrum while the resonator's true thermal peak survives. On a room-temperature sapphire cavity at nine gigahertz, the thermal peak's contrast improved by more than sixteen decibels over a single channel. The authors note that telling broad from narrow fluctuations is exactly what dark matter searches with cold resonators need. The method is offered as a general sharpening tool for precision measurement.
arxiv-2507-11197:
Grebenkov improved a formula for how reactive a spherical target is when only a round patch of its surface can absorb particles. Such targets model cells and catalysts, and the effective reactivity depends on the patch size. A widely used approximation from 2016 worked well for small patches but, as he shows, fails when the patch covers a large share of the surface.

He proposes a simple amendment to the formula and checks it against a semi-analytical solution. The improved version stays accurate over the whole range of patch sizes, from none of the surface to all of it. It also gives the probability that a reaction happens on the patch and the capacitance of the target. The result is a short communication offering a more reliable shortcut for a long-standing problem in chemical physics.
arxiv-2507-11397:
Morteza Salehi, a solo author, studies transverse spin supercurrent at a Josephson junction with a p-wave magnet in 2025. The junction joins s-wave superconductors to the magnet, whose strength vector can be pointed in chosen directions.

The author finds that the magnet shifts electron and hole energy patterns in momentum space. The part of the strength vector that points across the junction turns bound states into modes that travel along the interfaces. Those modes carry a transverse spin supercurrent while their transverse charge current stays zero. Salehi presents this as a route to new superconducting spintronics devices that move spin without charge flow.
arxiv-2507-11497:
Schröder and co-authors measure electron emission delays across a family of iodine molecules in this 2025 paper. When light knocks an electron out of a molecule, the escape takes a tiny time, measured in attoseconds. An earlier study found that adding a chemical group to iodoethane lengthened that delay, and a simple model linked delay to group size.

The team tested iodine alkanes from iodomethane up to 2-iodobutane, at three photon energies. They measured the delay for electrons from the iodine core level. A functional group alone did not always raise the delay, they find, and no clear link between group size and delay could be established. The result complicates the earlier picture.
arxiv-2507-11797:
Diana Romero, Yasra Chandio, Fatima Anwar, and Salma Elmalaki wrote a 2025 paper on a sensing toolkit that reads group behavior inside mixed reality headsets. When teams work in immersive spaces, collaboration can break down silently. Existing analysis leans on outside observers and hand labeling, which miss moment to moment dynamics.

Their pipeline passively captures gaze, audio, and position from ordinary headsets, with no external gear. One module builds social network maps of who interacts with whom, both per session and within it. A second uses unsupervised clustering to find behavioral phases between pairs as they unfold. A trial with 48 people sorting objects together showed within session structure that session averages erase. The authors offer the toolkit for studying teamwork where it happens.
arxiv-2507-11897: Tyler Hou, Shadaj Laddad, and Joseph M. Hellerstein share early work from 2025 on speeding up programs with rewrite rules. Their topic is equality saturation, a method that tries many rewrites at once to find the best form of a program. A newer form makes rules depend on where a term sits in an expression.
arxiv-2507-12097: Shujing Pan and Bo Yang wrote a 2025 geometry paper on inverse curvature flows for cap-shaped surfaces inside a unit ball. The surfaces are strictly convex and meet the ball's edge at a set contact angle. The authors prove that a class of these flows exists and settles down over time. As a use of that result, they derive a family of Alexandrov-Fenchel inequalities for weakly convex surfaces with free boundary, which bound one size measure of a surface by others.
arxiv-2507-12297:
Yuan-Chen Shu, Zhiwei Lin, Xiaoyu Zhou, and Yongtao Wang published this paper in 2025. It helps a leading image segmentation model, the Segment Anything Model, keep learning as new domains arrive. Tools for augmented reality, remote operation, and embodied AI meet shifting scenes, from medical scans to camouflage, where the base model weakens.

Older fixes either replay old data or bolt on a fresh module per domain, both clumsy for compact systems. Their method, RegCL, merges small adapter modules into one, round by round. The merged model is tuned to agree with each specialist while carrying a compact summary of past features. Across five varied segmentation data sets, RegCL kept old skills while gaining new ones. It beat rival no-replay methods and other merging schemes.
arxiv-2507-12497:
Ogonnaya Michael Romanus and Roberto Molinari offer a 2025 method for conformal prediction that also guards privacy. Most private methods guard the data used to train a model, but they pay less mind to the calibration set that prediction methods need to set their ranges.

Their method, called P-COQS, uses a randomized binary search to find private quantiles in the calibration step. That step keeps the data in that set private and still gives sound prediction sets. Tests show the sets tend to hit the target coverage level, though small calibration sets can lead to slight under-coverage.
arxiv-2507-12597:
Cody Schimming asks what changes when a simulated material repeats on itself at the edges, in a 2025 physics paper. Computer models often wrap a flat sheet into a repeating tile to fake an endless plane. But a wrapped sheet is a different shape, topologically, from the plane itself. Materials called p-atics, whose order repeats under fractional turns, host defects where that order breaks, and defects interact strongly.

Schimming derives an exact formula for the orientation field of such defects under the repeating-tile setup. The formula predicts an odd extra pull between defects, beyond the usual charge-like attraction. Simulations of the simplest case, ordinary nematics, confirm the extra pull. It comes from smooth swirls in the field that only the wrapped shape can hold. The lesson: when defects are involved, the box's shape matters as much as its size.
arxiv-2507-12997:
Rithvik presents a modular tool in a 2025 paper that reads and draws quantum networks built by the PyTheus optimizer. Machine-designed networks can be hard to grasp, since their parts and links follow no human plan.

The tool takes networks from files or memory and sorts parts by role, such as sources, detectors, and beam splitters. It then draws both graph views and optical table views that match. Tests cover a new five-node key distribution network and known cases like W state and GHZ state setups. Checks guard against drawing errors and odd links. Quantum designers get a clear window into machine-found designs.
arxiv-2507-13097:
Adithyavairavan Murali and nine co-authors present GraspGen, a system that generates six-degree-of-freedom grasps for robot grippers. Their paper came out in 2025. Six degrees of freedom means the grasp is specified by position and orientation in space, which is what a real robot arm needs.

The system uses a diffusion model, which builds a grasp step by step from noise, paired with a scoring network that filters the samples. A new training recipe teaches the scorer using the generator's own outputs. To scale up, the team released a simulated dataset of more than fifty million grasps across many objects and grippers. GraspGen beat earlier methods in simulation, led a standard grasping benchmark, and worked on a real robot with noisy camera input.
arxiv-2507-13297:
Amy Roberts and eleven co-authors described in twenty twenty-five how a dark matter data set was opened up for wide use. Dark matter makes up most of the matter in the universe, yet no one knows what it is. Tests that hunt for it produce data locked in custom formats and one-off software, which blocks fresh analysis.

Working with the National Science Data Fabric, the team converted a calibration data set from Cryogenic Dark Matter Search detectors into an open, layered format. They built a web dashboard for viewing signals and released a Python command tool for large jobs and machine learning. The goal is to lower the bar for new collaborators and make results easier to check and reuse across fields.
arxiv-2507-13397:
Forecasting where pedestrians will walk works better when their interactions are read openly, Kaiyuan Zhai and co-authors argue in a 2025 paper. Crowd members sync steps, yield, or collide, and black-box models hide which pattern drives a forecast. Their network names interaction types while it predicts.

A transformer design tracks direction-sensitive social behavior between walkers. A training trick curbs the wild first-step errors common in sequence forecasts. On two standard crowd datasets, the model beats recent black-box rivals, above all in dense scenes. Self-driving and crowd-safety systems need forecasts they can trust and audit, not just low error scores.
arxiv-2507-13497:
Sebastián Bahamondes, Ignacio Salazar Landea, and Rodrigo Soto-Garrido wrote this 2025 physics paper on exotic matter through holography. Their model is a thin material that can switch between a semimetal and an insulator. Holography maps the hard quantum problem onto a gravity problem in a higher-dimensional space.

The authors add backreaction to the gravity side so they can measure how the material resists flow. That resistance is captured by shear viscosity, weighed against entropy density. A famous bound says that ratio can fall only so low. By breaking the symmetry between directions, they find a fresh case where the bound is broken in the critical region. The strength of the effect fades in a steady pattern as temperature falls, set by an exponent near two in the stiff direction.
arxiv-2507-13597:
Toi Tachibana, Kouichi Hagino, Kenichi Yoshida, and Qiang Zhao compute properties of spin-polarized nuclear matter in a 2025 arXiv paper. They use the relativistic Hartree-Fock method with a point-coupling model. The model simplifies the exchange terms into the same form as the direct terms.

They define a spin slope parameter for spin-symmetry energy, mirroring the known slope for isospin energy. When neutrons and protons polarize in the same direction, the two slopes move against each other. When they polarize in opposite directions, the spin slope barely depends on the other slope. The authors show both patterns follow naturally from their model.
arxiv-2507-13897:
Chemists dream of steering reactions with light, and optical cavities — tiny mirrored traps for photons — are the tool. Most theory treats a cavity with one light mode, but real planar cavities hold a ladder of evenly spaced modes. Yaling Ke and Jakob Assan run an exact quantum simulation of reactions inside few-mode cavities and find two ways the extra modes boost reactivity.

When the mode spacing rivals the coupling strength, a molecular vibration married to one mode opens side paths through its neighbours. And because molecular vibrations are not perfect ladders, different rungs resonate with different modes, letting the molecule climb by drinking photons in sequence across modes. The gains are not simply additive. The authors offer both effects as design strategies for cavity experiments aimed at catalysis.
arxiv-2507-14197:
Andriamifidisoa Ramamonjy and co-authors twin the frame of the RSA code lock, in a study from 2025. RSA guards much of the web's locked traffic with one big modulus, a hard-to-split number. A twin-lock form could stiffen it, if the speed holds.

Their form, DM-RSA, works with two moduli in mirror roles. A classic Chinese remainder trick speeds unlock, as in tuned RSA. The pair argue the twin frame stands up better to side-channel leaks, which read power or time to steal keys, and to half loss of one modulus. The build slots into stock RSA kit with ease, they add. Twin locks, in their pitch, buy calm at no speed cost worth the name.
arxiv-2507-14297:
Tomasz Szczepanski studies chains of operators that commute with each other on Banach spaces. His 2025 paper uses a shortened head title, while the catalog title adds a link to a known theorem. An operator has a given chain length if it links, step by step, to a compact operator through partners it commutes with. The work asks which operators have such chains.

The main result shows that every weighted shift on a standard sequence space has chain length three. That covers a class of operators known as non-Lomonosov, studied by others before. The author also gives a case on a Hilbert space that cannot link to a compact operator at any chain length. The paper sharpens the map of this concept.
arxiv-2507-14397:
Michael Davies and co-authors map the hard limits of language model serving in a 2025 paper. Their LIMINAL model predicts how fast a model can generate text on given hardware. It abstracts both the program's needs and the machine's traits. Against real runs, its calls landed within about eight percent on average.

The sweep ran from today's accelerator memory to future stacked designs. Five barriers proved non-negotiable, among them compute, memory size, bandwidth, and machine-to-machine talk. Passing ten thousand tokens per second, they find, will take more than better chips. Algorithmic advances must share the load. The authors offer the model as a planning lens for hardware buyers and designers. It shows which wall a proposed system hits first, before money is spent.
arxiv-2507-14497:
Weimin Lyu and co-authors present a 2025 system that answers questions about whole slide pathology images without drowning the language model in data. A single slide can reach ten thousand pixels on a side, which makes the token count enormous. Past methods read patches or classify whole slides but could not generate answers. Newer multimodal models feed in thousands of patch tokens, at heavy cost.

Their system learns a small set of compression tokens that gather the key visual and text information from the slide. Only those compressed tokens reach the language model, which then writes the answer. Input length and compute cost fall sharply as a result. On ten tumor types from a public cancer atlas, the system beat existing multimodal baselines on answer accuracy. It also used far less training resource, the authors report.
arxiv-2507-14797:
Beier Zhu and co-authors speed up, in a 2025 paper, the sampling of diffusion models, the image generators that build pictures by slow steps of denoising. Each step follows a differential equation, and cheap solvers make errors that blur quality when few steps are allowed. The authors' solver spends each step more wisely.

Their method, an ensemble parallel direction solver, gathers several slope readings at each step and blends them, which cuts the error of a plain step. Since the readings are independent, they run side by side, so the wait stays low. A small set of tuned weights, learned by distillation, keeps training cost tiny, and the solver can also plug into existing samplers. Across four image benchmarks it beat rival fast solvers by a clear margin at the same latency.
arxiv-2507-15397:
Scott Pesme, Giacomo Meanti, Michael Arbel, and Julien Mairal gave theory in 2025 for using denoiser models in image recovery tasks. Denoisers are now a common plug-in tool: a trained network cleans noise, and a loop uses it to solve a maximum a posteriori problem. The swap lacked a general proof that it leads where theory says it should.

The authors show that a simple method, close to ones used in practice, does converge to the right operator when the prior has a log-concavity trait. The method can be read as gradient descent on smoothed versions of the target problem. Readers get firm ground under a popular practice. The rates and conditions in the proof tell users when the plug-in approach can be trusted and when it may drift.
arxiv-2507-15697:
Vaibhav Tiwari, writing alone, tests whether the mass distribution of merging black hole pairs has a real gap. The 2025 paper uses the chirp mass, a combination of the two masses that gravitational wave detectors measure best. The inferred distribution shows peaks, with a sparse stretch between two of them.

Comparing models with and without a suppressed rate in that stretch, the data strongly favor suppression, at very high confidence by one test. A second, more cautious test still supports a feature at good confidence. A similar gap in single-object masses had drawn doubt. The author traces the difference to a correlation between the heavier and lighter partners, which clusters chirp masses at set values. Formation theories for black hole pairs gain a sharper target.
arxiv-2507-15797:
John Burke and Ciaran McGoldrick present a quantum search that always lands on its target. Their 2025 paper offers an alternative to Grover-style search, which finds the marked item only with high chance, not certainty. Other certain methods lean on arbitrary phase tweaks that are awkward to build. Their scheme instead grows the oracle step by step.

Each expansion marks every state sharing the target's first two bits, exactly a quarter of the space, then narrows the superposition round by round until measurement must give the target. The query cost sits between Grover's and the classical plod. Two-qubit neighbor gates suffice, keeping the design close to real hardware.
arxiv-2507-15897:
Yoo, Kim, and Hong made discrete generators take fewer steps in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Discrete flow models produce high-quality text-like or image data, but they decode step by step. That slowness traces to a factorization shortcut the models need for large data. The authors measure the shortcut's error with a quantity called conditional total correlation.

Their method, ReDi, repeatedly re-pairs starting noise with target data to shrink that error. Each round provably lowers the error measure, so the process converges. Fewer decoding steps then suffice for good output. The repaired pairings also trained strong one-step image generators. The authors pitch the idea as a principled route to fast discrete synthesis.
arxiv-2507-15997:
Onyinye Dibia, Mengyi Lu, Prianka Bhattacharjee, Joseph Near, and Yuanyuan Feng interview in a 2025 paper experts toward a standard privacy label for differential privacy. Public deployments of the method often hide the numbers that set its strength. Vague claims breed wrong reads of how safe a release really is.

Twelve experts sat for semi structured talks on what a label must show. The group converged on a core set of parameters that drive the guarantee. Reasons for each item, and how to phrase it plainly, were drawn out in the talks. The aim mirrors food labels, a fixed panel users can trust at a glance. Trust in the method itself rides on such openness, the authors argue.
arxiv-2507-16297:
Dietmar Ferger derived in 2025 conditions for a kind of convergence used in statistics and optimization. The objects are normal integrands, functions that mix randomness with a variable to be chosen. His approach works through a topology designed for how functions approach a limit from above.

As a main tool, he gives a new characterization of when random closed sets converge in distribution. The results show that when such functions converge in his sense, their sets of near-best solutions also converge in distribution. Under extra conditions on boundedness and uniqueness, the convergence holds in a stronger topology. Measurable choices from those sets also converge in a weak sense, he shows.
arxiv-2507-16697:
Junqi Yin and co-authors train an AI model that reads turbulence down to its finest swirls, in a 2025 paper. Turbulence spans huge whirls and tiny eddies, and full data can reach trillions of grid points. Even giant computers strain under that load, and standard vision models choke on the sequence length.

Their layered Transformer shrinks the sequence from billions to a few million steps. A ring method splits long sequences across many chips in parallel. Runs on the Frontier supercomputer hit 94 percent scaling efficiency across 32,768 graphics chips. The model is billed as the first to catch eddies down to the range where motion dies out. Flow forecasts for jets, fusion, and burning fuels stand to gain.
arxiv-2507-16897:
Markus Amano, Minoru Eto, Muneto Nitta, and Shin Sasaki study a lattice of twists in dense quark matter under a strong magnetic field. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses holographic QCD, which maps the strong force to a gravity dual. The pattern in play is the chiral soliton lattice, a ranked stack of twists. Set edge terms on the gauge field and quark mass let it form.

The team shows this lattice is the ground state when a magnetic field and baryon density are present. In the dual view, the twists act as spread-out branes. Each twist matches a vortex type in the five-dimensional bulk. Two sources of baryon count merge into one bulk charge. The pion decay constant shifts with field strength. For massless pions they give a closed form that fits lattice results well at strong fields.
arxiv-2507-16997:
Maria Titova and co-authors study how governments hide repression and how that hiding corrupts measurement, in this 2025 paper. Counts of visible crackdowns can fall even as total repression rises, because regimes conceal acts and because fear deters protest. Naive statistics then reward the very policies meant to curb abuse.

Their model has a regime choosing concealment while activists choose whether to challenge it. From the balance of that game they build indices that use only observable data. Two distortions, one from hiding and one from deterrence, are handled separately. As a test, they estimate monthly repression indices for Russia across 2020 to 2025.
arxiv-2507-17097:
Dey, Kimura, Liu, and Otake study local rings, a core object in algebra, and ask when they can be sorted into a small set of types. Their 2025 paper centers on rings where building blocks called syzygies come in only finitely many forms. The work also looks at what happens when a ring is completed, a standard way to fill in its gaps.

The authors pin down when the completed ring has an isolated singularity, which sharpens an older known result. They also track how finite type passes between a ring and its completion. One outcome settles a standing conjecture in the field in full. Other results deal with rings of Cohen-Macaulay type and with dominant local rings.
