arxiv-2507-17197:
Hyunjin In and co-authors study a math model of tropical climate spread over a flat plane. The model splits air flow into a broad barotropic part and a layered baroclinic part, with heat-driven spread in one and plain drag in the other. They ask whether small starting states settle down for all time.

For two cases, with and without drag on the broad flow, they prove that smooth solutions exist for all time when the start is small. They also prove sharp rates at which the solutions decay. The rates hold across a wide range of smoothness measures for the flow fields.
arxiv-2507-17497:
Yuxiao Chen and three co-authors propose new states of matter in layered quasicrystals, in a 2025 physics paper. Quasicrystals have ordered patterns that never repeat in the usual way. Stacking eight sided tiles into layers, with magnetic order added, may create surface states that twist as they wrap around the material.

The team builds a simple model based on a known eight sided tiling. One magnetic layout gives a phase guarded by a combined symmetry. Tilting the magnetism with an in plane field breaks that guard but keeps a glide symmetry, producing the twisted surface states. Other magnetic layouts give hinge states that can be switched by rotating the field. The authors offer the system as a test bed for such phases.
arxiv-2507-17597:
Sue Min Cho and three co-authors test explainable artificial intelligence for checking image alignment in surgery, in a 2025 paper. Aligning a flat scan with a three dimensional model must be exact, since small errors can mislead an operation. Pictures alone do not let staff spot those errors reliably.

Their model judges alignment quality and explains its verdicts in readable form. The study compared four setups: the model alone, humans alone, humans with the model, and humans with the explained model. The model alone was most accurate overall. Teams of humans plus the model caught more true errors and made fewer false calls than humans alone. Workload fell in the team setups, and explanations raised understanding of the model's thinking. Trust did not shift between the two team setups.
arxiv-2507-17697:
Keck studies how variational Laplace acts in the long run, in a 2025 paper. The method is a widely used way to approximate in Bayesian modeling. It is also much used in cognitive neuroscience, yet its properties in theory had never been studied in a systematic way. Keck takes up the tools of frequentist asymptotic statistics, which judge estimates by how they act as data grow without bound.

In two worked cases, the estimates prove both consistent and efficient, the two classic marks of a good estimator. The paper then gives broad conditions under which those traits hold. It also studies how the whole approximate distribution moves toward the truth. Simulations back the theory.
arxiv-2507-17797:
Shubham Toshniwal and co-authors present GenSelect, a way to pick the best answer from many model outputs, in this 2025 paper. Language models can sample many candidate solutions in parallel. Scoring each one alone wastes the model strength at comparing options. Pairwise comparison, in contrast, grows costly as the pool grows.

GenSelect has the model reason at length over the whole pool and choose the best one. That uses comparison strength while scaling well with pool size. Tests focused on math reasoning. Strong reasoning models did well at the task with simple prompts. They beat existing scoring methods. The approach offers a practical route to better test time scaling for hard problems.
arxiv-2507-17897:
Semih Eren and co-authors entered the Algonauts 2025 challenge with a model that predicts brain responses to movies, described in a 2025 paper. Four viewers watched nearly eighty hours of films while fMRI ran. The model must turn film sight, sound, and meaning into brain signals. Pretrained video, audio, and language features feed their system.

Separate recurrent networks read each stream over time. A second layer fuses them, and small per-person heads finish the job. Training mixed error and correlation goals with a staged curriculum. Averaging one hundred model variants steadied the output. The system placed third on the leaderboard.
arxiv-2507-17997:
Yayan Zhao and Matthew Berger test how well people can spot linked patterns in field maps, in this 2025 study. The maps show values spread over a flat area, like heat or pressure, drawn with color. Judging whether two regions rise and fall together matters in fields from weather to medicine. That judgment, though, depends on how the maps are shown.

Their study asked viewers to judge sets of fields, not just one map at a time. They compared moving displays, where fields play in sequence, with side-by-side still views. They also varied the color scales used to paint the values. The level of true pattern linkage in the data was set by the team, so errors could be scored against ground truth.
arxiv-2507-18297:
Sergei Shumilin and four co-authors shrink computer grids for physics simulations while keeping the answers sound, in a 2025 paper. Fine grids make flow and wave problems slow to solve. Coarser grids run fast but can distort results.

Their method learns where grid points can merge. It clusters points, then tunes the coarse grid with tools borrowed from machine learning. Tests covered fluid flow through porous rock and a wave problem. The grids shrank to a tenth of their points. The values that mattered still tracked the fine grid closely. The trick works for any system ruled by changing equations over time.
arxiv-2507-18497:
A team of physicists tests selenium light detectors at very low temperatures in a paper from 2025. The catalog names a single author, but the text head lists ten authors, and the team framing here follows the head. The detectors target faint light, including ultraviolet, for future particle physics instruments. They use a flat layout of amorphous selenium run near avalanche conditions, where one signal multiplies.

At liquid argon temperature, the devices reliably detected small photon bursts. Detection quality stayed high even after accounting for inactive areas. A tellurium-doped variant also reached avalanche behavior at low temperature. The authors report the first such results for this layout. They propose the detectors for next-generation argon chambers.
arxiv-2507-18697:
Shraddha Mohnani and a large team model the afterglow of a gamma-ray burst in a 2025 arXiv paper. The burst, GRB 230812B, was among the brightest seen by the Fermi monitor. Its afterglow spans many wavelengths and carries clues about relativistic shocks.

The team studies the spectrum and timing from X-rays to very-high-energy gamma rays. Two emission parts overlap in this range, and telling them apart needs data near the turnover. A single 72 GeV photon was among the key finds. The modeling tests what the data imply for spotting such bursts with Cherenkov telescopes. Microphysics of the shock and the burst's surroundings are the wider stakes.
arxiv-2507-18897:
Rongkun Xue and co-authors introduce HH-Codec, a speech codec that squeezes spoken audio into very few tokens without losing fidelity, in a 2025 paper. Speech language models work on discrete tokens, much like text models. Older codecs either stream many parallel token layers or cost too much to run. Both traits strain large speech-to-speech systems.

HH-Codec uses a single quantizer and an extreme compression rate. Its vector quantization space was designed for spoken language modeling from the start. An asymmetric design encodes audio to a mel view and back. Dual supervision and stepwise training protect sound quality. Voice assistants gain a cheaper, cleaner token stream. The work targets real-time spoken dialogue at scale.
arxiv-2507-18997:
Real 3D scans are messy: points go missing behind other objects and sensor noise freckles the rest. Zixiang Ai and co-authors refuse to fix the cloud before using it, and instead teach the analysis model to prompt itself clean, in a 2025 paper called UPP.

A Rectification Prompter first predicts a small correction vector for each suspect point, filtering noise while keeping fine geometry. A Completion Prompter then grows auxiliary points on the cleaned cloud to stand in for what occlusion stole. A Shape-Aware Unit finally fuses the features for whatever task follows, sorting, part labeling, or detection. By folding denoising and completion into the model as prompts, the method stays parameter-light and travels across domains where separate cleanup pipelines, trained apart from the task, fall out of step.
arxiv-2507-19097:
Jouko Vaananen, a solo author, gives an overview of interpolation in model theory in a 2025 paper. Interpolation is a property that links what can be said in one part of a logic to what can be said in another. He asks what role it plays when first-order logic is extended.

The extensions he covers include logics with infinite steps, added quantifiers, and higher-order logic. His abstract approach shows how different forms of interpolation relate to each other when studied on their own. It also shows how they relate to other traits of a logic, such as compactness. The paper maps those links for other logicians.
arxiv-2507-19197:
Youngmin Seo and eight co-authors built WACA-UNet in twenty twenty-five to predict voltage droop, called IR drop, across chip layouts. IR drop threatens chip reliability, but full simulation is slow. Recasting the prediction as pixel-wise regression on physical layout maps is faster, yet prior models treated all input channels — metal, via, current maps — as equals, though their importance varies.

Their Weakness-Aware Channel Attention recursively boosts weak feature channels and reins in dominant ones, in two gating stages, inside an attention U-Net. On the public ICCAD-2023 benchmark it cut mean absolute error by about sixty-one percent versus the contest winner and raised F1 score by about seventy-one percent. The lesson: channel imbalance is a real signal in physical design data.
arxiv-2507-19397:
Andrei Aralov and five co-authors give a recipe for building any desired multi-photon light state exactly, in this 2025 arXiv paper. States with many photons across many channels power photonic quantum computing and sensing, but cooking them up reliably has been hard. Their method uses only standard optical parts: multiport interferometers, photon counters, and small photon additions and shifts.

The key move links the optical task to an algebra problem, splitting a symmetric tensor into simple pieces. Known geometry results then guarantee a build with a predictable number of steps. Along the way, photons are added and later caught again, a catalytic trick that creates entanglement beyond what gentle optical operations allow. Computer checks confirmed perfect fidelity on several state families.
arxiv-2507-19497:
Alex Leitch and Celia Chen argue that AI art research asks the wrong questions about style, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Detection, authenticity, and automation dominate the field, they say. Yet human style grows from creative struggle, as artists wrestle with influences and technical limits to find a way of seeing.

Modern generators flatten those choices into copyable patterns and drop their origins. The authors propose tools that record where a style came from and how it changed inside generated images. That shift would steer the field toward lineage and choice, not just polished output. Historical cases back the argument.
arxiv-2507-19697:
Alrubyli and five colleagues predict which places people visit in pairs, using business type codes in twenty twenty-five. Knowing that a coffee shop visit leads to a gym visit helps city and retail planning. Past models leaned on distance alone, which misses why unlike businesses draw unlike crowds. Their network learns a code for each industry type as it trains.

The data held near ninety-five million paired visits across most United States states. Their model more than doubled the fit of the best past methods. Rank quality of the top guesses rose by about a third. Splitting the huge task by state made it run at scale. Business meaning, they show, is a strong signal.
arxiv-2507-19997:
Lallement and colleagues describe in twenty twenty-five upgrades to TAPAS, an online service that predicts how Earth's atmosphere dims starlight for any site, date, and direction. Astronomers must subtract this telluric veil from their spectra, and modern air models plus molecule databases make sharp predictions possible. The service blends global weather profiles with extra climate data and runs a line-by-line radiation code at resolutions that keep every absorption line's shape.

Upgrades stretch coverage into the near-ultraviolet and deeper into the infrared, refresh the molecule data, and add nitrogen dioxide to the species list. Users can also force the water column to match their observatory's own reading. Checks against telescope spectra of a hot star showed close agreement, and the models even calibrate instrument blur.
arxiv-2507-20097:
Mahboob Ul Haq models charge noise in superconducting qubits with a new stochastic process in a 2025 physics study. Charge noise is a main source of decoherence, the loss of quantum behavior that limits these devices. Standard noise models often assume steady statistics, while real noise drifts and remembers its past.

A memory multi-fractional Brownian motion framework lets noise statistics change over time while keeping long-range memory. The author reports that the model reproduces key experimental features of decoherence. Matching real noise more closely can sharpen predictions for qubit lifetimes. That in turn guides shielding, materials, and control choices for quantum hardware.
arxiv-2507-20197:
Fabrizio Nunnari and co-authors test in this 2025 paper how well machines read feelings on the faces of sign language users. Their data set's odd color cast could skew results, so the pipeline first evens out color by histogram equalization, then fine-tunes the recognizer. The team also graded half-faces, upper or lower, to compare how emotion shows in deaf and hearing people.

Full faces scored about eighty-four percent sensitivity with even results across classes. The lower half beat the upper, echoing human judges, and the upper-half score topped human level. The authors offer the recipe for fairer expression tools in sign language research. Signers' own faces set the test, not actors.
arxiv-2507-20297: Shenghao Hua studies the size of special values tied to one fixed elliptic curve, in a 2025 paper whose abstract is brief. For each imaginary quadratic field where the curve has rank one, a derivative of its L-function can be formed. Hua proves a one-sided central limit theorem for the logarithms of these derivatives as the field varies, mirroring a known result for a related family. He also shows that many of these derivatives are not small, so the values do not all huddle near zero.
arxiv-2507-20397:
Levente Tempfli and co-authors label 3D street scenes for self-driving cars with barely any human help. Cars gather LiDAR point clouds far faster than people can annotate them, and LiDAR alone sees sparse, half-hidden shapes with no names. Their pipeline, VESPA, fuses LiDAR's exact geometry with the rich labels camera images carry.

Vision-language models supply open-vocabulary names for objects, and their judgments are refined right inside the point cloud. The system can surface categories no one listed in advance and needs no ground-truth labels or high-definition maps. On the nuScenes data set it found objects at about 53 percent average precision. Multi-class detection reached about 47 percent. The authors pitch it as a scalable path to scene understanding.
arxiv-2507-20997:
Deployed AI models keep changing: new skills are added, old ones merged in, and sometimes a piece must be removed for legal reasons. Khan and co-authors propose Modular Delta Merging with Orthogonal Constraints, a framework for composing fine-tuned models cleanly. Each task's changes are stored as a delta from a shared base model. Before merging, every delta is projected into its own orthogonal subspace, so tasks cannot collide.

The projected pieces are then fused by optimization into one model that keeps each task's skill. The design supports adding new models over time and unmerging a piece on demand, for example to meet data rules. Extra stabilizers guard old knowledge during updates. On vision and language benchmarks, the method beat earlier baselines in accuracy, knowledge retention, and unmerge fidelity, while staying light on memory.
arxiv-2507-21097:
Abraham Itzhak Weinberg presents a cipher that hides data in both math and pictures, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The scheme borrows from topology, the study of shapes that bend without tearing. Its muse is the Klein bottle, a shape with no inside or outside, stitched from two twisted strips. Twist functions mimic travel over that odd surface to scramble a message.

The scrambled bits are then tucked into visual paradox images, such as the missing square trick, which fool the eye. The double layer aims at both code-breaking strength and hiding that a secret exists at all. The paper lays out the steps, tests the design's safety traits, and weighs it against classic, quantum-safe, and hiding methods. Uses named include secret talk and watermarking.
arxiv-2507-21397:
Hairi and eight co-authors present a learning algorithm for tasks with several competing goals, in a 2025 paper. Reinforcement learning agents often must balance rewards that pull in opposite directions, and good compromises form a set of Pareto-stationary points. Exploring that set in a systematic way, with proof of how much data it takes, was an open gap. The authors build an actor-critic method around a weighted-Chebyshev way of blending the goals.

Their algorithm, called MOCHA, is shown to reach good compromise points within a bounded number of samples. The bound reveals a notable dependence on the smallest weight given to any goal. The work gives multi-objective learning a firmer theory base, which matters for real systems that juggle cost, safety, and quality at once.
arxiv-2507-21597:
Adrien Bourgoin, Pascale Defraigne, and Frederic Meynadier review how to set a standard clock time for the Moon. Future Moon missions need a shared time frame that fits relativity, the physics of gravity and motion. Rules for building such a frame exist, but the choice of a lunar time scale is still open. Their 2025 paper sizes up the effects at play.

Clocks on the Moon tick at a different rate than clocks on Earth, due to gravity and motion gaps. The authors weigh options for a lunar scale, each with gains and drawbacks. What is picked for the Moon will likely be reused for Mars and beyond. They close with ways to realize the scale in practice and link it to Earth's coordinated time.
arxiv-2507-21897:
Naratip Nunchot and Youichi Yanase wrote a paper from 2025 on a superconductor that lets more current pass one way than the other. Such a one-way effect could serve in future circuits. The pair studied a dirty, flat superconductor with two added traits: a twist that links electron spin to motion, and a magnetic field lying in the plane. Dirt and weak trapping of electrons make the theory hard to get right.

They built a full theory that counts the push between electrons and the weak trapping effect at a first level of detail. Heat and field limits for the super state both shrank once those forces were counted. The one-way effect, though, held firm in the hot range they studied. They also worked out how the material carries current once the super state breaks. There, the trapping effect showed up clearly as the current slowed and stuck.
arxiv-2507-22097:
Ghaffar, Aleksejevs, and Barkanova compute fine corrections to a classic scattering test in a 2025 physics paper. When a lepton grazes a proton, tiny asymmetries can betray new physics. Reading them right demands that known effects be subtracted with great care, down to two loops of quantum corrections.

Using a covariant method, the team worked the corrections to second order, counting both squared and stepwise two-loop terms. They give numbers at the energies of current and planned programs in the United States and Europe. The corrections prove large enough that searches for new physics cannot skip them.
arxiv-2507-22697:
Analía Herrero and a large team described in two thousand twenty-five how to make high-grade blazed gratings with electron-beam writing. These grooved parts are vital for light science across ultraviolet and X-ray ranges. Supply is tight because they are hard to make and few shops can make them well.

The team studied which settings shape the optical quality of gratings made this way. They built a sturdy process that uses a fine plastic resist and ion beam etching to cut the grooves. Their work offers a fresh supply route for parts that photon science labs depend on for sharp, bright beams.
arxiv-2507-23197:
Proving that a neural network can never misbehave on some inputs is slow when every switch-like unit must be branched on. Yuke Liao and co-authors revisit a divide-and-conquer tactic: run many small partial optimisation problems instead of a few huge ones. The trick is picking the few units that truly deserve expensive exact treatment. Their solution-aware scoring grades units by how they behave in actual candidate solutions, not just by static bounds.

The new scoring needs about six times fewer exact variables than earlier attempts at the same accuracy. Paired with a fast approximate checker that clears easy cases first, the system cut undecided cases to roughly eight to fifteen percent. Average runtimes stayed between tens of seconds and a few minutes, even on networks with two million parameters.
arxiv-2507-23497:
David Kelly and Hana Chockler give a causal account of image classifier answers in a 2025 paper. Many tools that explain such answers lack formal rigor, while logic based tools rest on claims that fail for image models. The pair show causal accounts keep the rigor yet work as black box tests.

Their method splits an image into parts that suffice for the answer and parts that are needed for it. A new form adds a trust threshold, marking when an account earns the same trust as the full image. Tests on a standard model took about six seconds per image. Distinct models showed distinct patterns of what parts matter.
arxiv-2507-23597:
Zijian Dong and four co-authors rebuild animatable 3D avatars from a single photo, in a 2025 paper. One view hides most of a person's shape and look. Two-dimensional generators can invent missing views, but their guesses clash across angles. The team instead starts from a learned 3D avatar generator. Sampling it yields varied avatars built from 3D blobs.

The input photo is projected into that generator's latent space. Extra constraints keep appearance and shape faithful in 3D. Synthetic views from image generators then refine the fit. The prior supplies a strong starting point and pose help. Results beat prior methods and transfer to real photos. Avatars come out ready to animate. Fewer 3D artifacts and less blur are the visible gains. The approach suits games and virtual presence tools.
arxiv-2507-23697:
Thomas Eiter and Ana Leonor Silvestre study periodic fluid flow past a moving rigid body and how to approximate it in a cut-off domain, in a paper from 2025. The full problem lives on an unbounded region outside the body. Computers need a finite box, but cutting the flow can distort it.

First they prove existence and uniqueness of strong solutions outside the body, with pointwise bounds on speed and pressure built from a periodic fundamental solution. Then they set matching problems inside large balls with crafted boundary rules and prove weak solutions exist. Error shrinks as the ball grows, in a precise norm.
arxiv-2508-00497:
Jinghui Zhang and five co-authors present SocialAlign, a system that forecasts public response to events at two scales at once. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes past tools made two misses. They gave generic replies with no personal flavor, and they tracked single sentiments while missing the crowd's spread. Crisis teams and policy makers need both views.

At the micro level, a tuned language model crafts personal comments with matching sentiment. Expert modules split the work by topic and user profile. At the macro level, the system models group sentiment spread and aligns it with real trends. A new data set, SentiWeibo, gathers true exchanges from the Weibo platform. Tests on it and a second benchmark beat strong baselines. Gains showed in accuracy, clarity, and spread to new cases.
arxiv-2508-00797:
Frieder Lindel, Carlos Sánchez Martínez, Johannes Feist, and Francisco García-Vidal introduce crystal polaritons, hybrids born when orderly arrays of quantum emitters lock onto orderly patterns of light, in a 2025 paper. Most light-matter platforms treat one side or the other as periodic. Here both are: emitter arrays meet metasurfaces whose Bloch modes resonate at the same rhythm. The authors build the theory in momentum space, mapping the surface's resonances onto a cavity-style Hamiltonian at each momentum.

Two kinds of surface resonance, plasmonic lattice modes and bound states in the continuum, both reach strong coupling with one emitter per unit cell. The hybrids inherit the emitters' nonlinearity, which makes them efficient generators of quantum light, far beyond ordinary nonlinear metasurfaces. The platform is offered as a new playground where light's crystal and matter's crystal are designed together.
arxiv-2508-00997:
Anton Ilderton and Karthik Rajeev compare two famous quantum tunneling effects in a 2025 paper. Black holes emit Hawking radiation, and strong electric fields pull particle pairs from empty space in the Schwinger effect. Both can be read as tunneling through a horizon-like barrier. The team builds the tunneling amplitudes with a worldline method, which follows particle paths through curved backgrounds.

For the electric case, the key paths are complex curves in spacetime. For the black hole case, the paths stay real but look complex when stretched past a coordinate edge. Matching the two pictures sharpens both. The work gives a shared language for particle creation in gravity and in electromagnetism.
arxiv-2508-01297:
Shiro Sakai and co-authors offer a unified account of cuprate superconductors in a 2025 physics paper. These copper based materials conduct without resistance at high temperatures, but their electron structure has long resisted a single story. Two kinds of spectroscopy give rich data that have seemed, in places, to conflict.

The team combined both data sets in one analysis. A simple model with two kinds of fermion, standing for an electron split into parts, matched both data sets across energy and momentum. One measured pattern matched the model in a way that a single part model cannot, which supports the split electron idea. The authors predict a further pattern at high energy as a test.
arxiv-2508-01397:
Kosei Hatakeyama, Daisuke Miki, and Kazuhiro Yamamoto ask whether specially prepared light can help prove that gravity itself can entangle two objects. If massive objects in a lab become entangled through their mutual gravitational pull, that would show gravity behaves quantum mechanically, but the signal is vanishingly faint.

Their setup hangs the test masses in an optical system where squeezed light, whose noise is hushed in one direction, flows in. The squeezing calms the optical noise in the masses' prepared state and strengthens the expected entanglement. Counting both steady and random errors over a finite run, they estimate the observing time needed for a first detection. Squeezed light cuts that wait by a useful margin, which they argue makes the experiment more realistic.
arxiv-2508-01497:
Sebastián Bahamondes uses holography to model a quantum material that hovers between conductor and insulator in a 2025 thesis. The approach builds a strongly interacting field theory in two space dimensions from a curved gravity theory one dimension higher, with a gauge field and a scalar. Fermion probes in the bulk then reveal the material's band structure.

Two phases appear: a Dirac semimetal and a band insulator, separated by a critical phase at finite temperature and a critical point at zero temperature where bands touch with semi-Dirac anisotropy. The critical geometry is of Lifshitz type with a dynamical exponent near two. The anisotropy also makes the viscosity-to-entropy ratio scale oddly as temperature falls. The thesis maps thermal and quantum transitions of the holographic semimetal in detail.
arxiv-2508-01697:
Shiqi Huang and co-authors present PromptReg, a training-free way to align medical images by searching for matching prompts, in a 2025 paper. Image registration usually means segmenting regions in each scan and then matching them. Instead, their method asks which prompt in a second image makes a foundation segmentation model outline the same region as a given prompt in the first.

An inverse-prompt step generates candidate prompts in the target image, and the algorithm gathers multiple matched region pairs from them. Tests covered prostate and abdomen MRI, lung CT, tissue slides, and aerial photos. The approach beat both classic iterative registration and learned deformation networks, rivaling methods that need fully labeled training data.
arxiv-2508-01797: Meshach Ndlovu and Jean Baptiste Gatsinzi settle the rational homotopy type of a bundle space in a 2025 math note. The space is built from the tangent bundle of complex projective space by projectivizing each fiber, a standard move in geometry. Rational homotopy type captures a space's shape as seen by rational algebraic tools, ignoring torsion detail. Their result names the type exactly: it matches a quotient of a unitary group by a product of three smaller unitary groups.
arxiv-2508-02397:
Lida Zhao and twelve co-authors build in 2025 JC-Finder, a tool that detects cloned third-party libraries inside Java projects. Copying library code directly into a project is common in Java, yet it hides what code a product contains and can misuse copyrighted sources. Existing composition scanners were not made for this clone style of reuse.

JC-Finder reads features at the class level, keeps the links between functions, and strips trivial or repeated elements before matching. It was checked against nearly ten thousand popular Maven libraries. Accurate clone detection helps teams patch known flaws in copied code and respect licenses. The tool fills a gap in software supply-chain auditing for the Java ecosystem.
arxiv-2508-02497:
The authors studied whether large language models can translate open-source project documents, in this 2025 paper. Most project guides, such as readme and contributor files, appear only in English, which shuts out many would-be helpers. Translation work in projects is often led by the community itself.

Two leading models were tested as translators and as judges of translations. Both gave accurate sense in most cases, but they often broke the layout, code, links, and format marks that technical documents rely on. Translation activity was most common in larger projects. The authors see promise for model help with wider access, paired with checks that guard structure and technical content.
arxiv-2508-02597:
Saikat Sur and co-authors surveyed in 2025 how molecular processes might serve as quantum information resources. The piece, written for a festschrift honoring Abraham Nitzan, gathers years of theory pointing one way. Under the right control, splitting a two-atom molecule can produce entangled motion between the fragments. The reverse process, colliding atom pairs, works in the same spirit.

That motion-level entanglement is strong enough, in theory, to support teleportation of molecular wavepackets. When splitting involves excited electronic states, the light emitted afterward can witness the entanglement. The authors also describe odd thermodynamic behavior, such as a cavity field gaining temperature from entangled fragments. The survey argues chemistry itself holds unused quantum hardware. Experimentalists are invited to test how far the effects can be pushed.
arxiv-2508-02897:
Jesus Hernandez Hernandez, Christopher Leininger, and Ferran Valdez construct fibrations of handlebodies over the circle. A fibration maps a three dimensional body onto a circle so that each layer above a point is a surface. The authors focus on the open handlebody of genus two, a basic infinite type test case.

They show that this handlebody admits uncountably many such fibrations whose fiber is the Cantor tree surface. The return maps of these fibrations are not conjugate in the mapping class group, so the fibrations are truly distinct. The construction extends to other tame manifolds with infinite type fibers, including the blooming Cantor tree and many further surface types.
arxiv-2508-02997:
Sri Durga Sai Sowmya Kadali and Evangelos Papalexakis present CoCoTen in 2025, a detector for adversarial prompts aimed at language models. Jailbreak prompts trick models into harmful answers, and their variety makes them hard to catch with keyword rules. Strong detection is now basic safety infrastructure for model deployment.

Their method builds tensors of how words co-occur in context, then reads hidden features from those tensors. Attack prompts disturb normal co-occurrence patterns in ways a tensor model can spot, even when the wording is novel. Tests pit the detector against known jailbreak families. The work adds a statistical tripwire that complements model-side training, catching attacks before they reach the model at all.
arxiv-2508-03197:
Tao Chen and co-authors build a network that outlines abnormal blood vessels in eye scans, in this 2025 paper. The vessels mark wet age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of blindness. Eye scans show the growths faintly, tangled with artifacts and blurred edges, and no public training set existed.

The team first assembled CNVSeg, a public data set for this task. Their network then reasons over graphs that link region and vessel views of the same scan. Two modules pass messages between the views, enforcing shape and meaning agreements. The multi-task design separates lesion area, surface, and vessel features before recombining them. The authors target clinical grading of the disease.
arxiv-2508-03597:
Meng Cao and Kun Zhou construct error-correcting codes for quantum data in this 2025 paper. The codes are locally repairable: a lost piece can be rebuilt from a small set of others, which limits the cost of repair. The authors ask when codes built as matrix products reach the best possible repair profile.

They prove a condition that decides exactly when a matrix-product code counts as an optimal locally repairable code. From that condition they characterize the optimal quantum versions whose building blocks nest inside each other, and they treat the non-nested case as well. Using building blocks that contain their own dual codes, they produce five endless families of optimal quantum codes with flexible parameters. The families widen the menu of codes available for fault-tolerant quantum storage.
arxiv-2508-03797:
Soobeom Chung and Jeff Dror propose hunting the universe's axion background with arrays of tuned microwave cavities. Their 2025 paper targets the cosmic axion background, a sea of fast-moving axions possibly left from the early universe. Axions are a favored candidate for extending known particle physics, but a broadband background is hard to hear over noise.

A good cavity acts as a narrow filter that rings at one frequency. The team's insight is spatial: the axion-driven field should correlate across separate cavities in a set pattern. They compute that correlation for several array shapes and find stacked, wide designs could sharpen the signal. Applied to planned upgrades of a leading axion experiment, current layouts gain little, but better geometry could win an order-one improvement. The paper is a design study for a search not yet run.
arxiv-2508-03897:
Kristen Hendricks proves a localization result in real Heegaard Floer homology, a recent tool for studying three-dimensional spaces with a symmetry. The theory, built by Guth and Manolescu, adapts Floer homology to manifolds carrying an involution, a flip of the space onto itself. Localization spectral sequences are prized because they let global data be computed from the fixed parts.

Hendricks constructs such a sequence for the hat variant of the theory. Applications follow to branched double covers and to strongly invertible knots, knots unchanged by a flip of space. The method extends to real Lagrangian Floer homology in exact symplectic settings, giving symplectic geometers a tool of their own.
arxiv-2508-04397:
Oorna Mitra, Mallika Roy, and Enric Ventura solved a twist matching puzzle in a class of solvable groups, in a mathematics paper published in 2025. The groups, BS(n,1), mix a loop with a stretching rule. The puzzle asks: given two members and a self-map, can a third member twist one onto the other by the set rule? Earlier work left this class open.

Their method settles it with a step-by-step test that always ends. They also prove a related fact: the self-map group of these groups can tell whether two words name members that some self-map can swap. Both facts aid the wider craft of group tests. The paper speaks to those who build such tests.
arxiv-2508-04497:
Sutirtha Sengupta and co-authors modeled the shells massive stars shed before they blow in a 2025 study. Red supergiants, the swollen last stage of heavy stars, shake with pulses that drive strong winds. Late burning stages can also fling off shells in bursts, so the star dies inside a dense shroud it made itself.

With a star growth code, the team set time-based loss rates for stars of twelve to twenty sun masses. Pulsation winds and shock ejections both fed the shroud. They then built the density maps of that gas for the blast to hit. The maps explain why some blasts shine so brightly at first touch.
arxiv-2508-04797:
Mohab Kishawy, Ali Hussein, and Jun Chen present a method to restore very high resolution images in this 2025 paper. Such images suffer from rain, blur, haze, and low light, and older fixes either shrink the image, losing detail, or work only in the frequency domain, losing local flaws.

Their method, called RetinexDual, splits the job in two. One sub-network fixes the reflectance part with a coarse to fine pass, while the other fixes color and light in the frequency domain. Tests on four tasks, from deraining to low light enhancement, beat recent methods. The dual design is the core idea: handle local damage and global light at the same time.
arxiv-2508-04997:
Fubao Xi, Yafei Zhai, and Chao Zhu wrote a 2025 math paper on systems that switch between states while they evolve. In their systems, the switch rates depend on the past path of the moving part, not just its present state. The set of states is countable, with no fixed top count. Such past dependence fits biology, ecology, and finance, but it makes the math much harder.

The hard part is joining two copies of the system so they meet and stay together. With past dependent switching, a first meeting is not enough, since the pair can split apart again. The authors build a joining where the pair stay the same for a long stretch after meeting. Under stated conditions, they prove strong stability for the system and show it in a mean field model with many bodies.
arxiv-2508-05697:
Lammers, Holik, and Fernandez study how quantum software must handle scarce hardware. Today's quantum machines sit in the NISQ era, with few qubits and high error rates. Their coherence times are also short, so long tasks fail. The authors argue that resource care shapes both design and use of quantum code. They review how current NISQ work treats physical and logical resources.

The paper ties those limits to software engineering practice. It backs the field of quantum resource estimation, which gauges cost before code runs. Good estimates help teams pick hardware and plan for scale. The goal is quantum software that stays reliable as machines grow.
arxiv-2508-05797:
Sreeharsha Udayashankar, Abdelrahman Baba, and Samer Al-Kiswany present a 2025 paper on faster data storage. Deduplication systems save space by storing each chunk of data once. Content-defined chunking picks the chunk borders by scanning each file in full. That scan is slow and often the main bottleneck. Hashless chunking methods rely on two scan patterns: hunting extreme bytes and scanning ranges.

Their method, called VectorCDC, speeds both patterns with vector CPU commands. Those commands work on many bytes at once. Three top hashless methods were sped up with the approach. Gains ran from about eight to twenty-six times base speed across Intel, AMD, ARM, and IBM chips. Storage teams get chunking that keeps its space savings without eating the compute budget. Faster scans lift the whole backup and archive pipeline.
arxiv-2508-05897:
The authors set out in 2025 a framework for quantum clocks that respects the symmetries of spacetime from the start. A quantum clock is a small quantum system whose inner motion tracks the passage of its own proper time. Such clocks may reveal quantum gravity effects at scales far larger than expected, if superposed paths stay coherent.

Their formalism handles clocks that move freely and clocks that are pushed, by coupling them to outside fields. It works in first quantization, where the clock's position is itself a quantum variable. A framework that stays covariant avoids mixing frames mid calculation. That care matters when the clock's time and the lab's time are compared. The work readies theory for lab tests of time itself.
arxiv-2508-06097:
Simon Buhrer and co-authors extend logic-gate networks to tasks that unfold in sequence, in this 2025 paper. Such networks compute with soft versions of logic gates and can run fast on chips. Until now they had been used only on fixed inputs, not on streams like language.

The team added a memory loop so the gates can handle step-by-step input. They tested the model on English-to-German translation from a standard set. Scores during training came close to a standard gated memory model. When the soft gates were hardened for final use, scores fell only modestly. The authors say the result opens logic-based sequence models and chip speed-ups to study.
arxiv-2508-06197:
Xu Du, Karl Johansson, and Apostolos Rikos design a split optimization method for linked nodes with thin links in 2025. Nodes must agree on one best answer while each holds its own goal curve, and messages can carry only rough, quantized values. Their method joins a cut-down consensus scheme with a fast quantized pact step.

Proofs show straight-line approach to a zone near the best answer, with zone size set by the rough grade of messages. The same pace holds for plain convex goals. Tests beat current rivals while using far less link space.
arxiv-2508-06397:
Spin glasses, magnets whose atoms freeze into disagreement, are a proving ground for probability theory, and Hong-Bin Chen and co-authors tidy up their central formula. For multi-species spin glasses with convex covariance, the Parisi formula already gives the limiting free energy as a best-case search over monotone probability measures. The team shows the same formula can be rewritten as a search over all probability measures of a concave functional, a friendlier landscape.

That rewrite proves the best measure is unique, settling which configuration the formula picks out. A second rewrite, through convex duality, expresses the energy as a worst-case search over martingales in a Wiener space. The authors offer both forms as tools for the next round of questions.
arxiv-2508-06797:
Alexander Hammerl and four co-authors design evacuation control for large cities in a 2025 paper. Their framework plans releases of cars into a road network when demand is uncertain. A bathtub-style model tracks how trips complete over time across the whole network. Control takes the form of staged departure orders or ramp metering at entry points.

They prove that under a common condition on trip distances, the best release pattern falls steadily over time. With an entry cap it becomes a single switch from full release to throttling. A flood case study on a low, dense island in Copenhagen tested the policy on thousands of random demand cases. Controlled release cut expected queue buildup clearly.
arxiv-2508-06997:
Helbert Paat and Guohao Shen study how to pick the right human experts to pair with an AI's prediction sets, in a paper from 2025. Decision support tools hand experts a shortlist of likely labels, and teams beat either side alone. Most research assumes one expert, but real panels have many.

Only some experts suit each case, so choosing a subset per case is the problem. Their greedy algorithm uses the prediction sets themselves to select whose judgments to combine. Simulations on two datasets with real human predictions reached near-optimal subsets. The method improved final accuracy over simple selection rules.
arxiv-2508-07197:
Ian Martiny and co-authors measure internet censorship of the newer IPv6 network across the world, in a paper from 2025. Most past measurement work used the older IPv4 network. As IPv6 spreads, it was unclear whether censors block it as well as they block IPv4.

The team found resolvers that serve both network versions and sent them more than twenty million name requests. Blocking was measured at resolver, network, and country levels, and the traits of blocked domains were studied. Nearly all censors did block on IPv6, but their rules were uneven and often weaker than on IPv4. The authors argue that censors must spend more to reach parity. For now, the gap offers new routes for circumvention research.
arxiv-2508-07297:
Hongbo Zhu and Angelo Cangelosi take stock of influence scores, a tool that traces the calls of a model back to its training rows. To ask what one row did, the tool nudges the weight of that row and reads the shift, with no costly retraining. Their 2025 review lays out the base math, then the speed tricks that make the core sum cheap for deep networks.

Uses span credit for a call, hunts for wrong labels, and plain sense of why a model acts as it does. The pair grade how well the tool does at each use in the tests to date. Gaps stay: scale, shaky math on big networks, and thin checks in the wild. They close with paths they judge most ripe, from faster core sums to firmer trust in the scores.
arxiv-2508-07397:
Jun Li recast neural networks as spin glasses in a 2025 physics paper. A spin glass is a magnet-like system with a rugged energy landscape, full of traps and splits. Li builds such a model out of any given feedforward network, then reads the network through the glass lens.

He runs paired copies of the glass and measures how alike their states are. That overlap score serves as a compact sketch of the network's inner form. Tests showed the sketch tracks key traits such as how well the network fits data, how much it can hold, and how it holds up under noise. The method gives one score per network, not just group trends.
arxiv-2508-08197:
Tommy Martinov presents three recent Belle II measurements of beauty meson decays in this 2025 paper, on behalf of the Belle II collaboration. B mesons are particles that contain a bottom quark, and their decays test the Standard Model of particle physics. All results use the full Run 1 data set, in which electron and positron collisions produced pairs of B mesons. The data total 365 inverse femtobarns.

One result measures the rate of a rare leptonic decay, where a charged B meson turns into a tau lepton and a neutrino. The team found those events with a hadronic tagging method. Two further results use semileptonic decays, where a lepton and neutrino appear beside other particles. One pins down a key mixing value, written |Vcb|, with an inclusive tagging method. The other tests lepton flavour universality by comparing decay rates across lepton types.
arxiv-2508-08497:
Xiang Lv, writing alone in 2025, proves a general test for steady behaviour in random systems. Random dynamical systems mix fixed rules with noise, and a stationary solution is a random state that the rules keep in place. Knowing such a state exists, and that all paths settle toward it, anchors much of the theory.

Lv's test is short and easy to check, the paper claims. Applied to noisy equations with either added or multiplied noise, it shows all paths end in sets built from true random steady states. The proof takes a route unlike the classic scheme for such systems. In the cases studied, the stated conditions turn out to be not just enough, but sharp.
arxiv-2508-08597:
To learn what state a photon is in, researchers must measure it in many ways and rebuild its full description, a task called quantum tomography. Flat optical surfaces called metasurfaces could shrink this equipment, but so far they handle only a few states at a time. Yuming Niu and Kai Wang ask whether a metasurface with random nanostructures could handle richer spatial states, called qudits. They test the idea in large computer simulations rather than in the lab.

The team simulates over 16,000 random metasurfaces, each more than 200 wavelengths wide. With enough detectors to add redundancy, the random designs perform reasonably well for spatial qudits with up to about ten states, encoded in Hermite-Gaussian beams. The authors also discuss what changes when several photons are involved. They present random metasurfaces as a path to small, error-tolerant quantum measurement devices that are cheap to design.
arxiv-2508-08897:
John Parker and Manvendra Somvanshi study closed billiard paths inside polygons drawn on a hyperbolic surface, where space curves away like a saddle, in a 2025 paper. A billiard path bounces off the sides at equal angles and returns to its start. For any set of such loops, the authors define the average loop length and ask which polygon shape makes it smallest.

They take two families of shapes. The first is even-sided polygons with all right angles, whose loops come in cyclic families. The second is a four-sided Lambert shape with one sharp corner, whose loops come in mirrored families. In the first family, the regular polygon, the most even shape, wins. In the second, the winner is the shape with a mirror symmetry along its long axis. The proofs draw on the theory of surface deformations.
arxiv-2508-08997:
Sizhe Yuen and co-authors present a framework that gives each agent in a multi-agent language model system its own structured memory. Such teams promise strong collaborative problem solving, but fixed context windows erode memory consistency, role adherence, and procedure following. Their method keeps role-aligned memories that grow out of each agent's own outputs. The memory stays focused on task-relevant content and keeps each specialist's viewpoint.

A generic memory template applies to new problems without hand-crafted prompts. Benchmarks on three datasets, covering planning, fact checking, and a household task world, show performance at or above leading rivals, with the highest consistency. On a complex data pipeline design task, the approach scores better on five quality measures, from scalability to documentation. The authors argue intrinsic memory is a practical fix for a core weakness of agent teams.
arxiv-2508-09097:
Handed molecules trip up graph neural networks, and Rylie Weaver and Massamiliano Lupo Pasini build a test kit for that skill in a 2025 paper. Their library generates synthetic molecular graphs with set shape traits and shuffled atoms, so stray clues cannot leak the answer. Each graph holds exactly one handed center, marked left or right.

Networks must flag that center as a sorting task. Clean benchmarks showed where top architectures fail, which guided the design of two new ones. Chirality decides drug safety, so a fair yardstick for machine chemists matters before models screen real compounds.
arxiv-2508-09997:
Johannes Schneider and co-authors sort, in a 2025 study, how school students actually use generative AI in class. Their data are real classroom chats, gathered over months across schools and subjects, with names stripped out. More than seventeen thousand messages from students, teachers, and ChatGPT were sorted two ways: by topic, such as nature or people, and by task, such as writing or explaining.

Older sorting methods worked poorly on this much text, so the team used top language models with careful setup to build layered topic trees. The sort turned up uses of classroom AI that earlier studies had missed. The authors share example prompts at each level, giving teachers a concrete map of real use. They also flag worries and open questions for schools.
arxiv-2508-10097:
Michael Shull and co-authors measure, in a 2025 paper, the harshest light given off by two very bright quasars. A space telescope's spectrograph caught both far- and near-ultraviolet light from the pair. That full span let the team pin down each quasar's true spectrum and correct for gas clouds that block part of the light. Both quasars shine at mid-range distances and rank among the most luminous known.

In the extreme ultraviolet, their light fell off more gently than the average quasar's. A stack of one hundred fifty-nine bright quasars gave a steeper norm, which makes this pair outliers. Their extreme glow, huge black holes, and inner disk winds may explain the odd shape. The readings matter because quasar light of this kind ionizes gas across the young universe.
arxiv-2508-10897:
Mengyuan Liu and co-authors present a 2025 computer vision paper on one model for all kinds of 3D human motion data. Pose and mesh data come from many tasks and datasets, and earlier unified models needed special parts per domain plus staged training. The authors propose training a single model in one pass, taught by examples in context.

Their earlier pose-only system generalized across tasks but stumbled over mixed data types. The new system, Human-in-Context, unites pose and mesh inputs, widens task coverage, and trains on larger data. A max-min sampling rule picks instructive context examples, and a two-branch design injects that context more carefully. Across domains it beat its predecessor on flexibility and scores.
arxiv-2508-11097:
Yossef Nissim Kindi and co-authors simulate plasma shocks between two regimes in this 2025 paper. Some shocks form through frequent particle collisions, while others form through collective plasma effects alone. Real systems can sit between those extremes.

The team ran particle-in-cell simulations with a collision module added. They varied how collisional the plasma was and tracked shock width. The width changed smoothly across the middle range, near a key ion parameter value of one. Results matched classic formulas at both ends of the range. The findings matter for space settings where shock breakout sparks particle acceleration.
arxiv-2508-11397:
Marko Orozović and co-authors show, in twenty twenty-five, that adding holes can raise the magnetic ordering temperature of an atom-thin magnet. Two-dimensional magnets offer atomic-scale control of magnetism. The team studied monolayer chromium triiodide, a prototype layered ferromagnet, with a multi-scale theory: density functional calculations, spin models, and orbital analysis. Charge doping, done by gating or charge transfer, tunes the exchange forces between spins and the spin-orbit effects that set direction. Hole doping proved remarkably efficient at strengthening both.

In the undoped sheet, symmetric exchange governs ordering. When hole-doped, directional terms grow to rival it. At high hole levels, the Curie temperature, where magnetism fades, can pass two hundred kelvin. The work shows how anisotropy engineering can stabilize warm magnetic order.
arxiv-2508-11497:
Feiyue Zhao and Zhichao Zhang add graph reasoning to image recognition in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Standard vision networks read images on a fixed grid, which limits how they capture links between distant parts. Their framework builds graphs at two levels inside the network.

One level models links within small windows of the image, and the other links summary nodes across windows for a global view. A further module balances low and high frequency signals, keeping edges and texture while avoiding over-smoothing. The module is light and can plug into standard networks. Tests on classification, detection, and segmentation data sets showed broad gains.
arxiv-2508-11797:
Calkin Garg and five co-authors propose a 2025 system for sharing medical records with researchers without exposing patients. Privacy laws guard health data, yet research needs real records to move forward. Their frame, AegisBlock, puts the patient in charge of each release.

Records sit behind patient consent on a blockchain ledger, with miners checking that shared data is sound. A researcher asks for records from a set time range, and the patient can approve or refuse. Tests showed the system scales with more patients and hospitals, and it stays sound even when half the miners act badly.
arxiv-2508-12197:
Maria Vasilyeva and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on flow in wet, elastic ground with mixed traits. The coupled set of sums for this flow is not linear, which makes it slow to solve. They use a grid method in space and a two grid solver for the coupled sums. The solver pairs a sharp coarse grid with smooth passes on fine patches.

Building that solver each step would cost too much. So they split the sums into a fixed linear part, solved in a hidden way, and a rest part handled in the open. The split keeps the scheme stable, which they prove. Tests on a two dimensional case show the solver is robust and the time steps stay true.
arxiv-2508-12497:
Rupak Chatterjee used modular operator theory in twenty twenty-five to study how entanglement can be harvested from a quantum field. He also studied how it bends under change. In harvesting, two detectors start apart. Each one couples to the field. They come out entangled. They draw on the links that are in the field itself.

Chatterjee works in the Tomita-Takesaki framework. He builds the modular conjugation operator for detector qubits of Unruh-DeWitt type. The harvested entanglement then equals a simple expectation value. That value uses the same operator. He extends the work to open, noisy qubit dynamics. He defines a curvature of entanglement as a second derivative. It gauges how sensitive the result is. At special self-dual points, this curvature matches quantum Fisher information. The results tie two settings together through one algebraic structure.
arxiv-2508-12597:
Drones can be identified by the radio accent of their own hardware, and a 2025 paper by Haolin Zheng and co-authors teaches a small model to hear it. In low-altitude networks that mix sensing and communication, telling one drone from another is a security staple.

The team built a fingerprint reader on a trimmed-down language model architecture, GPT-2 reshaped for signal data. Because that model is heavy, a dynamic distillation scheme squeezes its knowledge into a lightweight network, with reinforcement learning adjusting the teaching temperature on the fly. Their own data set recorded twenty commercial drones. The squeezed model reached about 98.4 percent identification accuracy while staying tiny, a practicality aimed at real deployments.
arxiv-2508-12697:
Merging neutron stars and black holes spiral inward, and their orbits may keep a hint of ovalness from birth. Hemantakumar Phurailatpam and co-authors built a waveform model in 2025 to read that hint from gravitational-wave signals. Their formula describes the inspiral of non-spinning pairs in eccentric orbits, with careful treatment of the orbit's slow turning.

They applied the model to two famous events, GW170817 and GW190425. In both, the starting ovalness at low frequency was tiny, with no strong evidence favoring oval over round orbits. Adding the orbit's turning made no clear difference at such small values. The authors also argue that future models must carry the effect to higher accuracy, or risk bias in tighter future measurements.
arxiv-2508-12797:
Michele Campisi's 2025 paper joins two lines of work on ergotropy, the most energy that can be drawn from a sealed system. The hosted text carries the title Unified Theory of Classical and Quantum Ergotropy, and that is the work described here. Physicists had long solved the question for classical fluids, while the quantum version grew up apart.

Campisi gives a general formula for the classical case that holds for any system size and any kind of interaction between parts. He shows it is exactly the classical limit of the quantum formula for systems that behave in an ergodic way. The split of quantum ergotropy into coherent and incoherent parts survives in the classical world too, and the theory settles an open extraction problem.
arxiv-2508-13097:
Sara Karimi and Nikolaos Vlassis present a 2025 method for designing inflatable structures that take a wanted shape when pumped up. Soft robots, deployable space hardware, and medical devices all use pressure-driven bending. The hard part runs backward: given the final inflated shape, find the starting shape and material layout that will produce it under pressure.

Their framework treats that backward problem as conditional generation. A denoising diffusion model, the family behind modern image generators, receives descriptors of the target shape and outputs a picture-like map of the uninflated design. A fixed pipeline turns those maps into simulations and back. Tests with simple and richer descriptors produced many candidate designs quickly, each inflating into the target form. The authors highlight parallel exploration of designs under complex constraints.
arxiv-2508-13497:
Chayan Purkait and co-authors study a pack of quantum batteries that charge as a group. Each cell is a qubit, all tied to one driven charger qubit in a star shape. Noise that scrambles phase is dosed on the charger. Their 2025 study asks if the pack can reach a neat state where all stored charge can be drawn back as work.

That full-draw state does come, the team shows, as a steady rest state of the pack. The share of charge that can be drawn climbs with pack size and nears the cap in a set shrink law. Ground-state crowding in a big pack drives the trait, though the pack state stays mixed. Charge time growth with size is also mapped. The work hints noise need not bar top-grade quantum stores.
arxiv-2508-13597:
Tang and a team including Wang and Rong found in twenty twenty-five the first firm sign that galaxy groups spin as a whole. Spin of such groups may tell how they formed and grew. They use two large lists of groups built from a sky survey, with thousands of groups in each.

They split each group by a trial line and read the speed gap of its parts. True groups show a gap far from the shuffled fake groups. Stacked pics show red and blue sides split by the spin line in a clean way. Spin speed grows with group mass and with range from the core.
arxiv-2508-13897:
González-Santander presents a 2025 mathematics paper on hypergeometric formulas. Hypergeometric series are sums built from ratio patterns, common across physics and combinatorics. Reduction formulas collapse special cases into simple closed forms. The author starts from one new general identity. That identity is then worked systematically to yield new summation formulas. Special cases get second proofs as a consistency check.

New finite sums involving the psi function fall out along the way. A recursive formula for Bateman's G function also appears as a byproduct. Every result is checked numerically with MATHEMATICA. Analysts gain fresh closed forms for sums that resist standard tables. Computer-checked proofs suit a field where sign errors hide easily. The single-identity engine is the elegant part: many formulas from one source.
arxiv-2508-14197:
Tinghan Yang, Md Ashiqur Rahman, and Raymond Yeh detect image symmetries with CLIPSym, asking a vision-language model to lend its semantic eyes to a geometric task. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that symmetry detection has resisted decades of hand-crafted cues. CLIP's pretraining on captioned images may hide symmetry hints in language itself. A rotation-equivariant decoder, part transformer and part group convolution, reads the CLIP features.

A prompting scheme groups frequent object-based prompts so the language encoder's cues land where they help. Three standard datasets fall to the new state of the art. Ablations credit each ingredient: the pretraining, the equivariant decoder, and the prompt grouping. Geometry tasks gain a semantic ally.
arxiv-2508-14597:
Nitish Kumar Mahala, Muzammil Khan, and Pushpendra Kumar build a smoke detection system in a 2025 paper that aims to be both sharp and honest about its doubt. Early smoke warnings can save lives, but smoke shifts shape and light in ways that fool older detectors.

Their system first encodes motion in single camera video through an optical flow step that guards motion edges. Motion maps are fused with appearance cues to mark smoke regions and build a data set. A transformer model then reads those fused inputs. It is trained in two phases: first for accuracy, then to gauge how plausible each call is, counting both data noise and model doubt. Tests used many measures of success.
arxiv-2508-14697: Jacob Thompson and Elizabeth Winstanley study quantum effects on a curved space-time in twenty twenty-five. The setting is three-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, a standard model space in gravity research. They look at static solitons, stable lumps with a regular center, that solve a linearized quantum-corrected form of Einstein's equations. The correction comes from a quantum scalar field in a thermal state. They compute the soliton mass two ways, by quantum field theory and by relativistic kinetic theory, and compare the answers.
arxiv-2508-15597:
Ahmed Mimouni and Ludovic Patey published this logic paper in 2025. It studies Ramsey-like theorems, statements saying that however the pairs of natural numbers are colored in two colors, some infinite set of numbers has pairs that avoid a given pattern. Such theorems sit inside a larger program that ranks math statements by the computing power they hide. The authors ask whether any of these statements are computably trivial.

Their answer is no. They build a single computable two-coloring such that any infinite set avoiding any pattern can be used to compute a function that no simple diagonal method can produce. They also sort the theorems by whether they preserve various forms of immunity, a notion of sets that resist computable intrusion. The sorting depends on the shape of the pattern being avoided. The work feeds into the reverse mathematics of Ramsey theory.
arxiv-2508-15797:
Nouar AlDahoul and Yasir Zaki test how well today's large language models handle medicine in Arabic. Most model testing happens in English, leaving Arabic clinical skill largely unmeasured. Using the AraHealthQA dataset from a 2025 shared task, the authors put several leading models through multiple-choice questions, fill-in-the-blank items, and open questions graded against expert answers.

Accuracy on the choice questions varied widely between models, while the open answers stayed semantically close to the experts' across the board. The best result came from teamwork: a majority vote among three models reached 77 percent on the multiple-choice task, taking first place in that track. For open answers, top models scored as high as 86.44 percent on a semantic similarity measure. The authors see real promise, bounded by the uneven choice-question results.
arxiv-2508-15997: Mark Allen and Gilles Bokolo-Tamba study the moving front in an unstable heat problem in this 2025 math paper. The model comes from combustion, where a heat front advances into fresh material and the front itself is part of what must be solved for. The authors consider the physical case in which the heat advances. They prove the free boundary is a smooth hypersurface, with regularity of class C one alpha over two, giving the combustion model a firm footing.
arxiv-2508-16097:
Ayyüce Begüm Bektaş and Mithat Gönen argue that medical AI must be built for trust from the start, in a 2025 paper. Models that predict survival or risk can be very accurate yet hide how they reach a call. In a clinic, hidden logic blocks trust, review, and legal sign-off. The authors set four design bars: models should be readable, shareable, repeatable, and answerable for their calls.

They point to model styles that show their work, such as sparse kernel methods and case-based learners. Such styles can match black-box scores while letting doctors inspect each call. The paper also urges hard tests for fairness and honest doubt ranges on each output. New tools for shared training and fake-data making can spread work across hospitals without moving patient data. Built this way, the authors say, medical AI can earn a place in real care.
arxiv-2508-16197:
Niels Sorgenfrei and six co-authors identify a mystery radiation defect in silicon, in a paper from 2025. The defect appears after irradiation as a shoulder in current measurements and had resisted firm naming for years. Pinning its charge state matters for predicting how detectors age.

They combined current scans, transient spectroscopy, and simulations of field-boosted charge release, then compared all traits to a known candidate. Activation energy, capture size, trap type, and release process all matched a singly charged double vacancy. Field tests confirmed one tunneling mechanism over another. Naming the defect as neutral in the key region resolves past contradictions about doping effects.
arxiv-2508-16497:
Jacob Calvert and Dana Randall study when a simple formula describes a system's steady state, in a 2025 paper. Many systems, at rest or in motion, settle into patterns that roughly follow a Boltzmann-like law, where a local score plays the role of energy. How well that law fits depends on a correlation between the score and the log of exit rates. The pair give the first exact estimates of that correlation in two test cases.

One case is a simple line of moving particles; the other is random motion in a classic spin glass model. In both, they find a sharp threshold. Above it the fit is strong; below it the fit collapses. They trace the threshold to a flip in how the local and global parts of the score relate. The result explains a pattern seen across many fields, from physics to computing.
arxiv-2508-16797:
William DiCarlo and Lorenzo Sadun explore, in a 2025 paper, the typical shape of random networks under two constraints at once: how many links they contain and how many triangles. In one puzzling region, theory expected the typical network to split into two blocks, but simulations hinted at three. The authors map that region of link and triangle densities numerically to find where the three-block, or tripodal, pattern actually holds.

They show the tripodal region ends at a sharp boundary, where the typical graph jumps suddenly to the two-block form rather than shading into it. They also find at least one more sudden jump inside the tripodal region itself, where the numbers describing typical graphs change abruptly. The work clarifies a corner of random graph theory where smooth expectations failed, and shows phase changes hiding where none were predicted.
arxiv-2508-17197:
Jingquan Luo and Lvzhou Li study in this 2025 paper how small a quantum circuit can be while building a special class of states. The states, called fixed-Hamming-weight states, spread evenly over all bit strings with exactly k ones. Such states serve in many quantum algorithms, yet the cheapest way to build them was unsettled, above all when spare qubits are scarce.

The authors give a construction that builds any such state with circuit size at the theoretical floor. It needs at most n minus three spare qubits, and none at all for small cases. They note the tricks may carry to other state-building methods that rest on decision diagrams, trimming spare qubit needs elsewhere.
arxiv-2508-17297:
Parviz Ahmadov and Masoud Mansoury open the black box of shop picks in a 2025 paper. Pick engines push a few hit goods hard and leave the long tail in shade. That skew cuts worth for users and fair show for goods, yet fixes run as sealed boxes.

Their fix reads a trained pick model through a sparse twin that mimics it cell by cell. Fake users with clear love for hits or for shade goods then light up which cells drive the skew. Once named, those cells can be tuned down in plain view. Shops gain a cure they can audit, not just trust.
arxiv-2508-17497:
Yang Qiao and co-authors teach image-text models to shape their outputs around a stated relation, in a 2025 paper. Tools like CLIP give each item one fixed embedding, a point in a shared space. That single point must serve every task. Yet real links between items hinge on the relation at play: two photos may match by place but not by mood.

Their frame, RCML, takes a plain-language relation as an input beside the item. The same item then earns a new embedding for each relation. Training pairs carry relation tags, and one contrastive goal handles both cross-modal matching and the links relations create. Tests on retrieval and sorting tasks beat strong rivals in zero-shot, tuned, and out-of-domain runs. The authors say relation-aware outputs fit real use far better.
arxiv-2508-17597:
Lee and co-authors present a prototype that lets deaf and hard-of-hearing users design their own sound-reactive visuals in augmented reality. Existing AR tools caption speech or picture sounds, but users cannot shape those pictures to their taste. Their 2025 system, SonoCraftAR, takes typed plain-language requests and builds animated overlays through a team of AI agents working with a vector graphics library.

The system listens in real time, finds the main pitch of a sound, and maps it to visual traits such as size and color. The overlays then move and shift as sounds change. The authors call the work an early proof of concept. They discuss how personal, AI-assisted authoring could widen sound access beyond fixed designs.
arxiv-2508-18297:
Dhananjay Ashok and co-authors report a controlled study in 2025 on a gap in vision language models. The models recall facts far worse when an entity is shown as a picture than when it is named in text. A model may know a great deal about a famous person or place. Shown a photo instead of a name, it often fails to bring that knowledge to bear.

Forcing the models to rely on the image cut their fact recall by about half. The failures line up with distinct patterns in the models' inner states. Simple probes on those states flagged unreliable answers with over 92 percent accuracy. A built in doubt flag of that kind could warn users when a visual answer should not be trusted. The paper names a clear weak point in how these models join sight and knowledge.
arxiv-2508-20097:
Andrew Blair-Stanek, Nils Holzenberger and Benjamin Van Durme ask whether large language models can spot tax abuse in United States law. They test the best models on real tax plans meant to cut tax for wealthy clients. The task is hard even for expert humans.

Models were asked to check a plan, fill gaps in a partial plan, and build a full plan from scratch. Tax law spans hundreds of thousands of pages of statutes, cases and guidance, and it changes often. One model-based search found a wholly new tax strategy. The authors say such tools could change how tax agencies fight abuse.
arxiv-2508-20397:
Wu-zhong Guo builds a broader tool for quantum theory in a 2025 paper on the spacetime density matrix. The standard density matrix sums up a quantum system at one slice of time. The new version also captures links between different slices, so change over time sits inside one object.

Guo gives the general build for quantum systems and a path-integral form used in field theory. He places the matrix inside a wider operator frame, which suggests further extensions. He also shows it obeys an equation of motion much like the standard one. For parts of a system, a reduced form can be defined by tracing out the rest. The paper lays groundwork for studying time-linked quantum effects.
arxiv-2508-20697:
Feng and co-authors defend language models against being re-tuned for harm with reinforcement learning, in a 2025 safety paper. Most misuse research assumes attackers fine-tune with labeled examples. The team show that reinforcement learning, under equal compute, strips safety training more effectively and unlocks stronger harmful help. Their defense, TokenBuncher, attacks the fuel such learning needs: varied model responses.

By holding down response entropy, the method starves the reward signal that reinforcement learning exploits. Two mechanisms do the work, an entropy-based reward scheme and a token noiser. Across several models and learning algorithms, the defense blocked harmful re-tuning while benign performance and normal fine-tuning survived. The authors frame response diversity as a safety surface worth guarding.
arxiv-2508-20797:
Peter Forrester and Fei Wei characterize a family of random matrix integrals with differential equations, in a 2025 mathematics paper. The integrals average a power of a determinant times an exponential over the unitary group. Such averages show up in counting long rising runs in random shuffles and in deep questions about the Riemann zeta function. The team describes them with two kinds of linear equations.

A first-order matrix equation tracks a vector whose size grows with the matrix size. A single scalar equation of matching degree then follows from it. The matrix form gives an efficient way to expand the integrals as power series. The authors compare this route with a known nonlinear equation approach. A natural generalization to other symmetry classes keeps the same equation types.
arxiv-2508-20997:
High-frequency wireless links send data in narrow beams, and a beam aimed the wrong way wastes the link. Siyao Li and co-authors study how well such a system can sense its own beam angle in this 2025 paper. The setting fits 5G and 6G tools that use millimeter waves and higher bands. The true angle stays fixed within each block of time slots, then changes for the next block.

The sender gets feedback after each slot, from radar or from the receiver, and must guess the angle at the end of each block. The authors ask how much can be learned in the best case, a limit they call sensing capacity. They give an upper bound for that limit using a step-by-step planning method. Earlier work by the group covered the data side of the same channel.
arxiv-2508-21397:
Andreas Leibetseder and Klaus Schoeffmann present their lifelog search system as entered in the 2020 Lifelog Search Challenge, in a paper cataloged in 2025. Lifelogs are vast personal archives of photos and video from wearable cameras. The annual challenge races teams on finding a described moment inside such an archive, fast.
