Their system, lifeXplore, mixes map-style browsing of visual features, concept search, filtering, and hand-drawn sketch queries. For this edition they added a deep object detector, text reading from images, and uniform sampling as an alternative to shot-based splitting. The paper reports the upgraded system’s design and challenge run. Tools like this point toward personal archives that answer questions instead of merely storing the past.
arxiv-2509-00197:
Ruojing Jiang and Franco Vargas Pallete study minimal surface entropy on hyperbolic three-manifolds in 2025 and how Ricci flow helps bound it. Minimal surface entropy counts how fast the number of minimal surfaces grows with area, in an exponential sense. Minimal surfaces are surfaces that locally minimize area, like soap films.

For metrics close to hyperbolic in shape, with sectional curvature at most minus one, entropy reaches its minimum only for the hyperbolic metric itself. Conversely, among metrics with scalar curvature bounded below and non-positive curvature on the cusps, entropy is maximized at the hyperbolic metric, given infinitesimal rigidity. Ricci flow convergence rates drive the second result. The work ties a counting invariant tightly to the most symmetric shape.
arxiv-2509-00397:
Murayyiam Parvez, Annus Zulfiqar, Roman Beltiukov, Shir Landau Feibish, Walter Willinger, Arpit Gupta, and Muhammad Shahbaz present SpliDT in 2025, a system for running decision trees inside programmable network switches. In-network machine learning enables real-time traffic analysis and security checks at line rate. Decision trees suit data planes, since they map to match-action tables, but prior builds must compute all input features upfront.

That upfront rule forces a small, fixed feature set per flow, which caps accuracy and scale. SpliDT partitions inference over sliding windows of packets, assigning distinct, variable feature sets to parts of the tree. Stateful inference thus grows richer without breaking hardware limits. The design targets scalable monitoring inside the network itself.
arxiv-2509-00597: Thibault Damour, writing alone, remembers Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat. He describes the impact of some of her key results on gravitational physics. Her work helped put Einstein's theory of gravity on firm math ground. Damour also traces how his own contact with her changed over the years. The piece is both a personal tribute and a guide. It shows why her work on the equations of general relativity still matters. Readers in physics and math both have reason to care.
arxiv-2509-00697:
Chandradew Sharma, writing alone, analyzes thirty-four years of Nifty 50 index data, from 1990 to 2024, to map how Indian equity returns behave across horizons from days to decades. The study asks whether the price-to-earnings ratio, a common valuation measure, can predict the shape of return distributions.

Sharma finds return profiles are strongly asymmetric: one-year returns gain with a stated high probability, while worst cases stay negative for up to ten years. Low valuations historically show no losses at any horizon, while high valuations bring unstable returns and long breakeven periods. Tools from complexity science, including entropy and Hurst exponents, reveal weak persistence, long memory, and low-dimensional chaos, with valuation directionally influencing future returns.
arxiv-2509-00797:
Jakob De Moor, with two co-authors, Hans Weytjens and Johannes De Smedt, introduces ProCause for evaluating prescriptive process monitoring methods, which recommend real-time interventions in business processes from event log data. Evaluation is hard because ground-truth outcomes for every possible intervention are missing.

A prior generative method, RealCause, estimates outcomes but overlooks temporal dependencies and relies on a single causal model, TARNet. ProCause supports sequential models such as LSTMs and several causal architectures, including S-Learner, T-Learner, TARNet, and an ensemble. In a simulator with known ground truths, TARNet is not always best; ensembles are more reliable, and sequential models help when time matters. Real-world analysis validates practical effectiveness.
arxiv-2509-00897:
Neda Amirirad and Hiroki Sayama use network methods to find underexplored hub genes in rheumatoid arthritis. The disease is an autoimmune condition that inflames joints. Modular structure and central elements of gene networks can reveal disease mechanisms. The pair builds weighted gene co-expression networks from RNA data. The data come from synovial tissue of patients.

Community detection with Louvain and Leiden algorithms reveals robust modules. Node-strength ranking then identifies the top fifty hub genes. Novelty scoring compares genes against association studies and the PubMed literature. Five central genes show little prior link to the disease. Enrichment checks confirm their roles in immune processes. They correlate strongly with T- and B-cell markers. They correlate negatively with NK-cell markers instead.
arxiv-2509-01297:
Meta-learning teaches a model to adapt quickly to new tasks, but many methods mix all task factors into one tangled representation. Seonsoo Kim, Jun-Gill Kang, Taehong Kim, and Seongil Hong propose a framework that gives each task factor its own context vector. Separating the factors should make the model's behavior easier to read and its skills easier to share.

On a sine wave fitting task, their model beat baselines on unseen tasks and handled new functions by reusing vectors tied to shared traits, such as amplitude or phase shift. On a four-legged robot task, the method split robot traits from terrain traits inside the dynamics model. Passing the split vectors to new settings aided transfer. The work argues that clean factor separation is a route to robust, general task learning.
arxiv-2509-01397:
Modern machine learning has upended the old rule that bigger models must generalize worse once they can fit training data exactly. Matthias Vigl and Lukas Heinrich demonstrate that double descent behavior, where test error falls again after an early rise, in particle physics data for the first time. Overparameterized models, with far more parameters than data points, are the setting for this effect.

The pair explores when and where double descent appears in their physics tasks, and under what circumstances extra parameters actually help. Classical bias-variance thinking predicts steady harm past the interpolation threshold, the point where a model can fit every training point. Their results show the newer pattern instead. The study gives particle physicists a concrete case for judging when very large models are worth their cost in analysis pipelines.
arxiv-2509-01597:
Protecting business data is harder than protecting personal data, because a few huge firms dominate totals and their records matter most to the answers. Kaitlyn Webb, with five co-authors, proposes a confidentiality framework for establishment data that policy makers can actually interpret. Legacy methods and standard differential privacy, built against membership inference, give poor trade-offs on such skewed data.

Earlier personalized approaches let privacy guarantees weaken for outlying large firms, which the authors call problematic as policy, since some entities would be protected strictly less than others. Their framework instead guards against attribute disclosure, the risk that a value itself is exposed, which they argue fits business data better. The method is applied to a major employment statistics program. Webb and the team aim for protection that stays statistics-friendly, keeping published figures useful.
arxiv-2509-01897:
Raunak Kunwar and Aera Kim LeBoulluec predict top car safety ratings from vehicle traits and driver aid features. The national NCAP program grades crash safety, now counting active aids alongside passive gear. Their data hold thousands of vehicle variants across fifteen model years from program reports. Features span collision warnings, lane warnings, auto braking, and blind spot alerts, plus weight, year, type, and drive layout.

Four learning models are compared with repeated cross checks, and the top two are tuned further. Weight and model year dominate the prediction strength in the best model. Driver aids still add real predictive value on top of basic traits. The tuned forest model scores high accuracy and ranking quality on held out data.
arxiv-2509-02397:
Yang Xu, Siyuan Yang, Yunong Zhou, and Liang Luo wrote a 2025 technical note revisiting a key derivation in Persson's theory of contact, which models how rough surfaces touch. The theory grew from work on tyre-road interaction and now covers many friction and wear questions.

At its heart sits a diffusion equation describing how contact pressure changes as surface detail is magnified. Persson's original derivation, in an appendix, is hard for non-physicists to follow. The authors walk through each step with added explanation and background. Their aim is clarity rather than new results. By making the foundation readable, the note hopes to widen use of the theory across tribology, the study of interacting surfaces.
arxiv-2509-02497:
Vsevolod I. Ivanov wrote a 2025 solo math paper. It gives new characterisations of pseudolinear functions. Such functions act like linear ones in key ways, yet they may curve. A full characterisation tells researchers exactly which functions share those traits.

Ivanov proves several new results. Two use first-order data. One needs no derivatives at all. All are stated with the Clarke-Rockafellar subdifferential. That tool handles functions that are not smooth. A further result covers semi-strictly quasilinear functions in a like style. The paper also gives conditions for such a function to become pseudolinear. These tests help researchers check function classes that support strong claims about solution quality.
arxiv-2509-02697:
Sam B. Ponnada wrote a 2025 solo astrophysics paper on cosmic ray pressure in galaxy halos when the cosmic ray sources vary with time. Star formation comes in bursts, and black hole feeding is episodic, so steady-state models may misjudge the pressure that pushes on halo gas.

Ponnada develops semi-analytic approximations plus numerical solutions for how cosmic ray pressure around a galaxy evolves. The formulas allow fast scans across the wide range of transport settings that observations still permit. Bursty injection changes pressure profiles substantially, especially beyond the virial radius in halos of massive galaxies. Benchmarks against a full cosmological simulation that models scattering directly support the approach. The author urges care with time-dependent softening effects in the simplified feedback recipes used by large simulations.
arxiv-2509-02797:
Sagnik Bhattacharya, Abhiram Rao Gorle, and John M. Cioffi wrote a 2025 wireless paper. It allocates power and spectrum in multi-user interference channels. Users cannot cooperate there. Each receiver decodes amid others' signals. Future cell-free 6G networks make that allocation problem central.

Their minPIC framework chooses power, subcarriers, and decoding order jointly. It drops the fixed order heuristics used by current access schemes. A dual-variable sorting rule finds the globally best successive cancellation order. Convex optimisation with auxiliary constraints, solved by binary search, finishes the task. The authors call minPIC the first algorithm to trace the full Pareto boundary of achievable rates for Gaussian interference channels. They target demanding uses such as immersive extended reality.
arxiv-2509-02897:
R. W. Stevens and 3 co-authors studied clouds of carbon dioxide ice high in the Martian polar air in a 2025 paper. Such clouds affect how the poles gain and lose energy and how carbon dioxide moves around the planet. Yet their grain sizes and light-scattering traits have stayed uncertain.

The team read brightness data from an instrument aboard a Mars orbiter. Grains in the south proved large and strikingly uniform in size, with northern grains only slightly smaller. A simple cooling model helps explain that uniformity: the air itself is mostly carbon dioxide, so grains grow fast. Mars's thin air also lets big grains fall out quickly, narrowing the range that can linger.
arxiv-2509-03297:
Lin Lu and 4 co-authors studied online multiple testing with feedback in 2025. In streaming settings, hypotheses arrive one by one and each decision is made before later data exists. Unusually, the true answer here is revealed after each decision, instantly or with delay, fully or only as win-or-lose feedback.

Their framework, generalized alpha-investing with feedback, adjusts decision thresholds dynamically using revealed outcomes. Adaptive variants keep false discovery control, meaning only a bounded share of positive calls are wrong, in finite samples. They extend the idea to conformal testing, a distribution-free style of inference, with valid p-values and feedback-driven rules. A feedback-based criterion also picks which candidate score function should drive the tests. Simulations and real-data applications support the approach.
arxiv-2509-03697:
A 2025 mathematics paper by Adrien Rezzouk covers the critical behaviour of the one-dimensional abelian sandpile model with dissipation. The sandpile model drops grains onto a line of sites; overloaded sites topple and spread grains to neighbours. Certain sites act as traps where grains can leave the system entirely, and those traps can sit at arbitrary positions.

The question of criticality becomes whether a trapped random walk on the integers has a finite expected stopping time. Rezzouk gives a precise description of the phase transition, splitting behaviour into three distinct regimes. The analysis follows the long-run behaviour of an explicit recursive sequence. A counterintuitive phenomenon appears along the way: traps can sit farther apart, yet the expected stopping time becomes shorter. The result sharpens understanding of when one-dimensional sandpiles with losses settle down and when they run on indefinitely.
arxiv-2509-03897:
In a 2025 research paper, Xiaofu Chen and two co-authors examine SPECS, a metric for judging long, detailed image captions without needing reference captions. Older n-gram metrics are cheap but miss semantic correctness. Similarity metrics built on embeddings correlate poorly with human judgments in practice. Large language model judges correlate well but cost too much for repeated use during model development.

SPECS modifies the CLIP model with a new training objective built around specificity. Correct details earn reward, and incorrect details earn penalty, instead of treating all content alike. The metric is reference-free: a caption is scored against its image alone. In their tests, SPECS matches open-source language-model metrics in correlation with human judgments, far more efficiently, since no large model runs for every score. The authors position it as a practical tool for checkpoint evaluation during model development, with code released.
arxiv-2509-04097:
Víctor Duarte Melo and one co-author, William J Buchanan, design a new elliptic curve for public-key cryptography in a 2025 research paper. Elliptic curves are mathematical shapes used to exchange keys and sign messages safely. Widely used curves offer a solid security level, yet users increasingly want stronger options whose numbers nobody chose in secret. Their curve, ECCFROG522PP, aims at roughly double that protection class.

Every setting derives openly from one fixed public seed through a published hashing method, so anyone can rebuild the curve exactly. Tests cover its twisted partner curve, resistance to known shortcut attacks, and other safety checks. Speed is not the goal, the authors stress. Trust, repeatability, and long-term auditing come first.
arxiv-2509-04197:
Alessandro Porcarelli and three co-authors examine flickering hydrogen flames under strain in a 2025 engineering paper. Lean premixed flames burn fuel mixed with extra air beforehand, and hydrogen flames can destabilize because heat and fuel spread at unequal rates. Their setup faces two such flames against each other in a flat counterflow, while detailed chemistry simulations track the reaction. Strain rate, how hard the flow stretches the flame, is the dial under study.

Below a strain threshold, the flame front never settles and wobbles in growing waves. Stronger strain calms every tested disturbance after a brief transient. Wave growth first stretches disturbances sideways, with strain setting the amplification. Cleaner hydrogen burners could use these limits to stay steady.
arxiv-2509-04297:
Hritam Chakraborty and eleven co-authors track a changing shadow pattern as a planet crosses its star in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The planet, TOI-3884 b, is smaller than Saturn and orbits a cool red dwarf star. Its crossing shape looks lopsided and color-dependent because it passes over a persistent starspot, a dark magnetic patch, near the star's pole. The star's tilted rotation axis explains the effect. Three years of observations with a Swiss telescope in Chile watched the spot pattern evolve.

No two crossings matched exactly across the campaign. Careful fitting blames a slight offset between the spot's center and the pole, not changes in spot size or temperature. Precise tilt angles for the planet's orbit also came out of the data.
arxiv-2509-04497:
Syed Ahmad Chan Bukhari and two co-authors mine clinical notes for early signs of clinician burnout in a 2025 research paper. Burnout threatens patient safety, above all in intensive care units, yet surveys catch it late and record metadata misses the story inside notes. The team read ten thousand ICU discharge summaries from the public MIMIC-IV database. Their hybrid pipeline mixes BioBERT sentiment embeddings tuned for clinical text, a custom stress-word lexicon, topic modeling across five themes, and workload proxies.

A provider-level classifier reached strong precision and recall on held-out data, beating metadata-only rivals by a wide margin. Radiology, psychiatry, and neurology staff showed elevated risk in the specialty breakdown. Story-rich records could power early well-being monitoring.
arxiv-2509-04597:
Jin Ma and six co-authors disarm adversarial patches stuck onto real objects with a regeneration strategy in a 2025 research paper. Printed patches can fool object detectors into hiding real items or hallucinating fake ones, threatening surveillance and security systems. Earlier defenses tried to detect and remove patches. Their framework, DisPatch, instead regenerates the whole image with a diffusion model, so the picture aligns with benign data, then swaps the adversarial regions for their regenerated counterparts.

No knowledge of the attack is required beforehand. Across several detectors, DisPatch beat the best prior defenses on both hiding and creating attacks, keeping detection accuracy high while slashing attack success. Robustness held against adaptive attackers who know the defense.
arxiv-2509-04697:
Vacuum packed particle dampers use a granular core whose damping can be tuned by applying vacuum. Pawel Chodkiewicz, lead author with two co-authors, model a whole such damper in a 2025 engineering paper. They present the devices as a more sustainable alternative to magnetorheological fluid dampers.

Their model uses the discrete element method, which tracks many interacting particles. A new discrete model of the flexible foil transmits the vacuum pressure consistently, implemented in the open-source Yade framework. A tested prototype allows calibration and validation. The calibrated model then supports a parametric study of material, geometry, and process effects.
arxiv-2509-04997:
Depth, a measure of ramification, should be preserved when the local Langlands correspondence matches representations with parameters. In short, the match should not change the depth. Manish Mishra revises that notion for tori in a solo 2025 mathematics paper. The new definition restores that preservation under the match over a non-archimedean local field.

Mishra uses it to transfer broad harmonic analysis results from characteristic zero to characteristic p. For fields of large enough characteristic, he proves block-by-block equivalences with a nearby field of characteristic zero. A match in characteristic zero then yields a canonical one in characteristic p. Results on close fields, Hecke algebras, and regular supercuspidal cases support the build.
arxiv-2509-05097:
Sequences with constant amplitude and zero autocorrelation are prized for synchronisation in communications and radar. Karine Amis, lead author with two co-authors, present a method to generate such sequences of any length in a 2025 paper. Known analytic families cover only a shrinking fraction of possible alphabets as length grows.

Their algorithm projects iteratively onto the unit circle, turning any random seed into a near-perfect sequence. For length eight, they classify the outputs and give analytic representatives for each class. They also embed the method in simulated annealing to shape sequences whose autocorrelation lobes suit radar use.
arxiv-2509-05197:
Websites can pass code tests yet still frustrate real users. Naimeng Ye, lead author with four co-authors, present an agent-based testing framework in a 2025 paper. Traditional automated testing focuses on coverage and load. It misses complex user behaviour and usability problems.

Given a web address, their prototype agent explores the site on its own, simulating real interactions. It identifies bugs and usability issues and writes a human-readable report. In a case study of academic personal websites, it uncovered dozens of usability issues. Many had been missed by traditional tools. The authors outline directions for user-centred testing frameworks.
arxiv-2509-05697:
Neural networks built from shape operations rather than sums are trained by a new procedure from Iara Cunha and Marcos Eduardo Valle in a 2025 machine learning paper. A morphological perceptron uses elementary operations from mathematical morphology, and adding a winner-take-all layer makes it classify into several classes.

Those shape operations have no useful derivatives, so gradient training does not apply. The authors recast training as a difference of convex functions and solve it with the convex-concave procedure, an iterative method that turns the problem into a sequence of linear programs. Experiments on classification tasks show the training method works well. The approach gives these unusual networks a principled optimiser.
arxiv-2509-05797:
Trust between separate mobile network domains is the focus of a 2025 paper by Hai Dinh-Tuan and two co-authors. As 5G networks split into many software functions run by different operators, those functions must talk across domains without weakening security. The authors propose building that trust on Decentralized Identifiers, web-standard identities that need no central registry.

They add a communication agent that plugs into standard 5G network functions and carries messages over a DID-based protocol meant to protect secrecy, tamper-evidence, and proof of sender. Two versions of the protocol are compared, with the newer one fitting existing functions better. Overhead tests against classic TCP/TLS show better security at some speed cost, and the authors point to where tuning is still needed.
arxiv-2509-05897:
John M. Campbell constructs new q-analogues of famous series for the reciprocal of pi in a 2025 paper. A q-analogue rewrites a classic formula with a parameter q so the original returns as q approaches one. Ramanujan's 17 formulas for one over pi are landmarks of this area, and Guillera added series for one over pi squared.

Campbell's tool is a method he calls EKHAD-normalization, built from q-polynomial coefficients inside difference equations produced by a q-version of Zeilberger's algorithm. With it he proves four new q-analogues covering three of Ramanujan's formulas, plus q-analogues of Guillera's first two series. A survey of earlier q-analogues supports his claim that the method is truly new, and he shows how it can extend Guillera's pairs further through hypergeometric expansions. The proofs are short to state but rest on deep facts about series.
arxiv-2509-06097:
Spots of light that hold themselves together inside a driven optical cavity are reviewed in a 2025 paper by Gian-Luca Oppo and William J. Firth. These cavity solitons, bright or dark, sit on a uniformly lit background while diffraction or dispersion tries to spread them and the nonlinear medium pulls back. Cavity losses are balanced by the energy fed in, keeping the spots stable.

The review covers their history, properties, and physical interpretation, then their uses. Across the beam, cavity solitons serve optical information processing. Along the beam, they generate high-quality frequency combs, with applications in communications, frequency standards, optical clocks, navigation, astronomy, and quantum technologies. The authors present one phenomenon spanning both a computing medium and a precision light source.
arxiv-2509-06197:
Abel-Jacobi mappings on Fano threefolds get a Lagrangian reading in a 2025 paper by Rodolfo Aguilar and two co-authors. These mappings send algebraic cycles on a variety to points of its intermediate Jacobian, a torus that measures cycle information. The authors work inside the Donagi-Markman and Markushevich framework, where certain Lagrangian submanifolds carry the geometry.

They derive an expression for the differential of the mapping built from data normal to those submanifolds. The formula is not an end in itself: it can be applied to give new proofs of several classical results about Fano threefolds. The paper ties an integrable-systems viewpoint to concrete cycle theory.
arxiv-2509-06297:
Shrinking a large language model by quantization should track the whole model's output, not just each layer's, argue Li Lin and Xiaojun Wan in a 2025 paper. Most layer-wise post-training quantization approximates weights locally, and the local objective drifts from the real goal. Their method, LoaQ, adds output-matching factors when quantizing each linear layer, with a simple closed-form solution.

LoaQ slots into existing pipelines rather than replacing them, and works for weight-only and weight-activation quantization. Experiments on the LLaMA and Qwen families show consistent gains, and pairing LoaQ with other strategies improves quality further. The authors present output approximation, taken seriously, as a frontier for post-training compression.
arxiv-2509-06897:
A magnetic field that switches values over time reshapes a lattice model's energy bands, in a 2025 condensed matter paper by Ian Emmanuel Powell and one co-author. The system is the square-lattice Harper-Hofstadter model, electrons in a magnetic field, with the flux per cell jumping periodically among chosen rational values.

Switching folds the Floquet quasienergy spectrum into a number of bands set by the least common multiple of the flux denominators. For the case switching between negative and positive one half, the authors solve the spectrum and Chern numbers in closed form, and compute the Rudner-Lindner-Berg-Levin winding invariants numerically for general driving periods. A topological phase diagram follows. Generic switching drives produce interlaced Hofstadter butterfly spectra, and each gap is labeled by a Diophantine equation tying it to the fluxes and their windings.
arxiv-2509-07097:
Adam E. Lanman and 18 co-authors use fast radio bursts to weigh the gas in galaxy groups and clusters, in a 2025 paper. A burst that has been pinpointed to its home galaxy is a strong probe of ordinary matter spread through the universe. The delay of a burst, its dispersion measure, grows in direct proportion to electron density. It does not depend on how hot the gas is.

Three bursts in the first CHIME/FRB Outrigger sample sit in, or behind, clusters and groups. For each halo in the way, the team worked out how much of the burst's delay that halo should add. They tried several shapes for the halo's density profile. For the heavier halos, the predicted cluster shares match the delay measured beyond our own galaxy.
arxiv-2509-07497:
Smart factories need computing that can move work between factory floors, edge sites, and clouds as demand shifts. Hai Dinh-Tuan, Tien Hung Nguyen, and Sanjeet Raj Pandey present DREAMS in a 2025 research paper. DREAMS places software microservices across the compute continuum without a central controller. Centralized placement scales poorly, adds delay, and creates single points of failure.

Each domain runs its own agent, and the agents coordinate through a consensus algorithm and cost-benefit voting. That design keeps decisions responsive, private, and fault tolerant. Evaluations show key operations, like registering a domain manager or voting on migration, scale well as domains multiply. The framework targets modern manufacturing, where several stakeholders share infrastructure. It aims for globally good placements while no single failure can halt the system.
arxiv-2509-07697:
Abolfazl Ahmadirahmat and 3 co-authors derive a mode-coupling theory of the glass transition for a liquid in a periodic potential in a 2025 paper. Mode-coupling theory is the standard microscopic account of how liquids freeze into glasses. The freezing happens with no crystal order. A one-dimensional periodic potential acts like a washboard. It breaks translational symmetry, so the liquid's density itself becomes modulated.

The authors use techniques familiar from solid-state theory. They define generalized intermediate scattering functions from density fluctuations in wave-vector space. Exact equations of motion follow from the Mori-Zwanzig projection formalism. Currents are split into parts parallel and perpendicular to the modulation, for lack of rotational symmetry. A mode-coupling closure approximates the force kernel. The theory keeps the usual traits of correlation functions. It reduces to the standard theory when the modulation vanishes.
arxiv-2509-07797:
Isabel Donoso-Leiva and 3 co-authors analyze convergence of elementary cellular automata under sequential updates in a 2025 paper. A cellular automaton is a row of cells that update by simple local rules; elementary ones are the simplest family. Under synchronous updating, all cells change at once, but under sequential modes the cells take turns in some order, which can change the outcome entirely.

The theoretical analysis covers rules that have at least one fixed point, a configuration that never changes. The authors classify rules by whether every starting configuration reaches a fixed point under all, some, one, or no sequential update modes, in relation to their fixed points under synchronous updating. Such classification tells modelers when update order is a harmless implementation detail and when it silently changes the science.
arxiv-2509-08097:
Internet delays between cities become curved surfaces you can inspect, in a 2025 networking paper by Stephen Jasina and 6 co-authors. Their system, Matisse, infers manifolds, smooth geometric spaces, from real latency measurements and projects them onto a flat geographic map. The representation exposes topological features like curvature that raw tables of ping times hide.

A chain of graphs captures the critical structure inside the measurements before the manifold is drawn. Anomalies in the data show up as visible distortions of the surface. Network operators diagnosing strange routes or creeping congestion could spot trouble geographically at a glance. Turning measurements into shapes trades precision for insight, which suits exploratory debugging of a network as tangled as the public internet.
arxiv-2509-08197:
Robots mapping a moving world need updates in real time, and Jesse Morris and 2 co-authors bring incremental optimisation to dynamic SLAM in a 2025 robotics paper. SLAM builds a map while locating the robot inside it; dynamic versions also track moving objects, but existing accurate methods are too slow for online use.

A new factor-graph formulation and system architecture reuse incremental smoothing techniques, which update only what changed instead of resolving everything. On multiple datasets, camera pose and object motion accuracy match or beat the state of the art while running online. Delivery robots and self-driving cars cannot pause to recompute their world model at every doorway, so incremental speed is enabling, not cosmetic.
arxiv-2509-08397:
A new species of submodule is defined and dissected by Hani Khashan and Ece Yetkin Celikel in a 2025 algebra paper. Semi n-submodules extend two earlier notions, semi n-ideals and n-submodules, from rings to modules over commutative rings. The defining test involves squares: if a squared ring element times a module element lands inside, under side conditions on annihilators and nilpotents, the unsquared product must land inside too.

Properties and characterisations are developed with supporting examples throughout. Semi n-submodules of amalgamated modules, a gluing construction, receive special investigation. Classification work of this kind grows the vocabulary of module theory carefully, checking each new concept against the old ones it claims to generalise.
arxiv-2509-08697:
Backpropagation trains neural networks brilliantly, but brains clearly do not do it, and its backward pass locks layers in sequence. James Gong and 6 co-authors reshape an alternative, the Forward-Forward algorithm, in a 2025 research paper. Forward-Forward replaces the backward pass with a second forward pass. It has trailed backpropagation in accuracy and needs several passes at inference time.

The team merges Forward-Forward with similarity learning, calling the result FAUST. The similarity-based objective removes the need for multiple forward passes when the network is used. On three standard image datasets, FAUST substantially improved Forward-Forward's accuracy. On the hardest set, it came close to the backpropagation benchmark using the same simple network. Brain-inspired training still lags the standard, but gaps like this show the deficit is engineering, not destiny.
arxiv-2509-09097:
Honghui Xu and 4 co-authors propose DP-FedLoRA for private federated fine-tuning of on-device language models in a 2025 paper. Federated tuning trains across many devices without centralizing data, but user data are still sensitive. LoRA adapts a model by training small low rank matrices.

Each client clips and adds Gaussian noise to its LoRA matrices to meet differential privacy guarantees. Theory shows updates stay unbiased and bounds the extra variance from noise, guiding privacy budget choices. Benchmark tests deliver competitive performance with strong privacy. The authors present the method as a scalable path for private on-device deployment.
arxiv-2509-09197:
Chin Yuen Kwok and 2 co-authors improve synthetic data training for contextual biasing models in a 2025 paper. Contextual biasing helps speech recognition favor rare words. Training the biasing module on synthetic rare word data works, but synthetic artifacts can cause overfitting.

A keyword aware cost function adds focus on biased words during training. One term masks cross entropy to biased word prediction, and another detects biased word positions. Together they support decoding of rare words at test time. Adapting Whisper with ten hours of synthetic data cuts word error rate sharply on a test set. The method builds on the TCPGen biasing approach.
arxiv-2509-09397:
Medical vision-language models stumble when a new hospital's scanners and report styles differ from their training data. Umaima Rahman and 3 co-authors present DRiFt, a framework for steadier adaptation, in a 2025 research paper. These models often latch onto task-agnostic correlations planted by imaging protocols and free-text habits. Such shortcuts fail dangerously under distribution shift.

DRiFt separates clinical signals from task-agnostic noise by construction. It tunes the model efficiently with low-rank adapters and learnable prompt tokens. The team also curated high-quality image-text pairs grounded in clinical practice, to tighten cross-modal alignment. In-distribution accuracy rose clearly over earlier prompt-based methods. Performance held up on unseen datasets as well. For clinical deployment, where the next hospital is never identical to the last, that kind of boring reliability is the whole game.
arxiv-2509-09597:
Maysam Behmanesh and 2 co-authors propose a new way to line up two graphs node by node in a 2025 machine learning paper. Matching graphs matters in many fields, yet unsupervised methods must compare embeddings built without any known pairs. Two faults spoil those embeddings: smoothing in graph neural networks washes out what makes each node distinct, and separate training leaves the two latent spaces rotated away from each other.

Their encoder runs twice to inject sharp, high-frequency detail back into node features. A geometry-aware functional map then learns a reversible, distance-keeping alignment between the spaces while smoothing the matches themselves. Across standard benchmarks the method beat existing unsupervised baselines and held up better under structural damage.
arxiv-2509-09697:
F. Minotti and 1 co-author question a basic recipe of electrodynamics in a 2025 paper on how scalar fields couple to light. The standard local gauge recipe works beautifully for Dirac spinors, but for scalar fields it produces a coupling current that does not match the conserved Noether current of the global symmetry. The authors ask what follows if the scalar field is instead coupled exactly through its conserved current, as spinors are.

That choice, they show, forces local gauge symmetry to be given up. The electromagnetic field must then be described by a theory that tolerates the loss, such as the extended electrodynamics linked to Aharonov and Bohm. Fermion systems under strict charge conservation show no difference, so the fork matters mainly beyond the familiar case.
arxiv-2509-09897:
Florian Lindenbauer's 2025 paper computes how gluons split inside a quark-gluon plasma that is not the same in every direction. Splitting rates are a core ingredient of the AMY framework for tracking energetic particles through such a plasma, but a direction-dependent collision kernel makes the maths far heavier. Lindenbauer splits the extra angular information into Fourier modes, turning the problem into a much larger coupled system that a computer can grind through.

Tests on a simple anisotropic kernel show the payoff clearly. Rates from a plain angular average track the full answer surprisingly well, even far from equilibrium. A popular shortcut kernel built on an infrared temperature scale, by contrast, misses the true rates badly, especially for slower partons.
arxiv-2509-09997:
Richard Jozsa and 2 co-authors study private network traffic classification in this 2025 paper. Federated learning lets many sites train one shared model without pooling raw data, which suits sensitive traffic records. In practice, daily rises and falls in traffic make each site's data come and go, and that uneven timing can destabilize training — a problem earlier work largely overlooked.

Using a real-world QUIC traffic data set split across fourteen clients, the team first shows how unstable standard federated training becomes. They then add a simple client-side data buffer that steadies local training against live traffic swings. The buffered system converged well and scored close to a centralized, non-private model, which the authors offer as a blueprint for stable federated network tools.
arxiv-2509-10097:
Ahmed Al-Tahmeesschi and 6 co-authors tackle the power bill of 5G networks in this 2025 paper. Radio access networks use much of a mobile system's energy, and Open RAN designs, which split the network into parts from different vendors, make power harder to manage. The team built a hybrid control app that mixes simple rules with unsupervised learning to switch radio units into sleep modes.

A digital twin of the network, fed by a scenario generator, let them test the app on a large, realistic setup before touching live equipment. The controller saved about 13 percent of energy while keeping user quality intact. The authors argue the mix of heuristics, learning, and a twin makes the savings safe to deploy.
arxiv-2509-10697:
Pengcheng Jiang and five co-authors survey Retrieval and Structuring Augmented Generation in this 2025 paper. Plain language models hallucinate. They grow stale. They lack specialist depth. The surveyed approach fights all three flaws. It fetches outside information at answer time. It organizes that information into structured knowledge before the model writes.

The survey walks the pipeline in three parts. First comes retrieval, from sparse keyword search to dense and hybrid methods. Second comes structuring. Taxonomies, hierarchical classification, and information extraction turn raw text into organized form. Third comes the meeting point. Prompts, reasoning frameworks, and knowledge embeddings connect structures to the model. Open problems close the survey. Retrieval speed, structure quality, and integration all need work. Multimodal and cross-lingual systems offer fresh chances. For practitioners, the survey is a map of a fast-moving technique.
arxiv-2509-10997:
Adam J. C. Singor and 3 co-authors extend a link between light absorption and timing in atomic physics in this 2025 paper. When light knocks an electron out of an atom, the electron leaves with a tiny time delay, measured in attoseconds. Near a Cooper minimum, a dip in the ionization rate, that delay connects directly to the cross section, as an earlier study showed for noble gases.

The team demonstrates the same relation for the outer shells of alkali and alkaline-earth metal atoms, from sodium to cesium and magnesium to barium. Their fully relativistic treatment splits two ionization channels whose phases swing in opposite ways near their minima. After a universal correction, the remaining delay is specific to each atom and open to measurement.
arxiv-2509-11097:
Nhut Le and 2 co-authors release the first three-dimensional benchmark for judging disaster damage from drones in this 2025 paper. After a hurricane, crews need fast, accurate maps of structural harm. Most earlier work reads flat images, which hide depth, block views, and lose spatial context. Three-dimensional data describe a scene far more fully, but no benchmark targeted disaster zones.

The team flew low-cost drones over hurricane-damaged areas and rebuilt the scenes as dense point clouds from overlapping photos. Human labels painted on the images were projected into three dimensions. Leading 3D segmentation models were then run on the data to show where they stand. The authors offer the set to push robust 3D vision for emergency response.
arxiv-2509-11197:
Yunheng Wang and eight co-authors present DreamNav in this 2025 robotics paper. It concerns vision-and-language navigation. A robot must follow spoken or written instructions through real space. It uses only its own camera view.

Earlier zero-shot systems lean on heavy perception. They choose between single points. That makes them costly and short-sighted. It also matches instruction wording poorly. Instructions describe whole routes, not points. DreamNav corrects the camera view first. It plans entire trajectories instead of single steps. An imagination module pictures what lies ahead before moving. Tests covered standard benchmarks and real-world trials. DreamNav set new zero-shot records. It beat the strongest comparable baseline on success and path efficiency.
arxiv-2509-11297:
Carl Bettosi and three co-authors explore robot-led physiotherapy in this 2025 robotics paper. A friendly social robot could guide patients through exercise sessions alone. It must adapt instructions to each person's effort and progress. Real patient data for training are scarce.

The team recruited thirty-three expert healthcare practitioners. They acted as stand-in patients. Their interactions with the robot fed a patient behavior model. The model generates exercise performance measures. It also generates self-reported exertion scores. A reinforcement learning policy trained in simulation against this model. It learned to adjust instructions to each person's tolerance. It handled changing performance too. It also handled patients at different recovery stages. Their exercise plans differed as well.
arxiv-2509-11397:
Rafi Beinhorn and 5 co-authors stabilize a hard class of inverse problems with generative priors in this 2025 paper. Many recovery tasks boil down to solving polynomial equations built from low-order moments of a signal, and those systems are notoriously ill-conditioned: tiny noise swings the answer wildly.

Their framework pairs moment-based estimators with score-based diffusion priors, using the learned prior as a regularizer. That gives generative models a new job, steadying polynomial recovery rather than producing samples. The test case is multi-target detection in heavy noise. Diffusion priors clearly improved recovery from third-order moments and made a super-resolution version of the problem, otherwise unsolvable, feasible. Experiments on handwritten digit data confirmed the gains across noise levels.
arxiv-2509-11797:
A modified version of the rational six vertex model on a rectangular lattice gets a new partition function formula in 2025, from Matthieu Cornillault and one co-author. The work continues a 2024 study by Belliard, Pimenta, and Slavnov on the same statistical mechanics model.

The new expression writes the partition function for the inhomogeneous model as a single determinant that blends a modified Izergin determinant with a Vandermonde one. That compact form pays off twice over. It lets the authors take the homogeneous limit on the rectangular lattice cleanly. From there they push into the thermodynamic limit. There they extract the first-order term of the free energy, boundary effects included, a result they report as new.
arxiv-2509-12297:
Divisor counts at the integers can be lifted into entire functions. Such functions stay smooth across the whole complex plane. A solo 2025 paper by Sebastian Fuchs builds that lift. The Fejér kernel sits at its core. For well-behaved weights, the lifted function gives back the divisor-summed values at every integer. It also carries a clean factorization in its Dirichlet series.

Two applications headline the work. One builds an entire function that vanishes at every prime. It stays positive at composites. A sharp variant pins down its real zeros near odd primes, past an explicit threshold. A second lift recovers the von Mangoldt function. It also exposes a classic zeta ratio.
arxiv-2509-12397:
Sachin Sharma and 6 co-authors report an experiment in which a shock wave bends around an empty region in dusty plasma in a 2025 paper. Dusty plasma is a gas of charged particles mixed with tiny dust grains. The void is a dust-free bubble larger than the wavelength of the incoming wave.

When the flat shock front reached the void, its center was blocked while the edges kept moving, so the front bent inward. The bent wave later collapsed and briefly trapped dust particles inside the void. Those particles then burst outward in a Coulomb explosion, creating a bow shock. Experiments in a glow discharge plasma matched molecular dynamics simulations, giving a clear picture of the interaction.
arxiv-2509-12497:
Alessandro Crimi and Andrea Brovelli test a time-series foundation model on brain signals in a 2025 paper. Predicting brain activity and finding causal links between neural populations could illuminate cognition and disease. Foundation models, trained broadly and applied to new tasks, raise the question of whether they can work without task-specific training.

The authors evaluated the model in zero-shot and fine-tuned settings for forecasting functional magnetic resonance imaging signals, which track brain activity in people. They also assessed causality by comparing model-based estimates with standard Granger causality, a method that tests whether one signal helps predict another. Validation used synthetic time series from known causal models. The study asks how such general models compare with traditional neuroscience methods.
arxiv-2509-12797:
A. Rebesh, B. Lev and A. Zagorodny derive in 2025 a heat rule for systems where crowd density shifts from place to place. Standard heat rules assume an even spread, so they miss cases where clumps and thin zones shape how a system acts.

They blend a known non-even state method with a field trick to get a rule that depends on place. A peak method then pulls out the main terms for systems that pull together, push apart, or pull by gravity. They argue the peak forms share one cause at all heat levels and spreads. The work gives a shared frame for uneven matter.
arxiv-2509-12897:
Jianfei Zhao, Feng Zhang and three co-authors add Cross-Layer Vision Smoothing in 2025 to help large vision-language models keep focus on key objects. Such models can find the right object, but their focus fades fast in deeper layers.

Their fix keeps a vision memory that smooths focus across layers. It starts from an even first-layer focus, then each layer blends past memory with new focus while the memory updates. A doubt signal stops the smoothing once seeing is done, since most seeing happens early. Tests on four benchmarks across three models show top overall scores and strong caption results.
arxiv-2509-13297:
Sabyasachi Dhar and Santosh Nadimpalli prove in 2025 that Tate cohomology of finite-length forms stays finite length under a prime-order twist. The group is reductive over a local field. Twist order is a prime distinct from residue characteristic.

Forms live over the mod-prime field and extend by the twist group. Tate groups for each degree are shown finite length as forms of the fixed subgroup. A use for genericity of those Tate spaces follows. Finiteness unlocks dimension counts that later genericity work needs. The result is a clean finiteness anchor.
arxiv-2509-13497:
The PHENIX Collaboration measures in 2025 the forward eta meson transverse single-spin asymmetry in polarized proton hits at RHIC. Data from 2012 at high collision energy form the base. Asymmetry is tracked versus Feynman-x and transverse momentum in set bands.

Large asymmetries at positive x appear, matching prior pion and eta marks, with reach to higher x and momentum than before. Mean asymmetry sits near a tenth in the forward band. Twist-three initial-state accounts fall short of the data. Fragmentation impact looks significant in the gap. Spin-momentum links alone cannot carry the signal.
arxiv-2509-13997:
Yu Zhu and six co-authors redesign object storage for AI clusters in a 2025 systems paper. Training and inference jobs hammer storage with sustained, fine-grained reads and writes. The usual host-mediated TCP paths waste the expensive machines waiting on data. Kernel-bypass networking suggests a leaner route.

Their system, ROS2, is RDMA-first. It offloads the storage client onto an NVIDIA BlueField-3 SmartNIC, a network card with its own processors. The server-side engine stays unchanged. A light control plane handles namespaces and permissions. The data plane streams over RDMA or TCP. Tests showed RDMA beating TCP on the host for both large and small transfers. The offloaded client matched host performance. That frees the host and enables services like encryption at the card.
arxiv-2509-14097:
Yaru Chen and six co-authors improve audio-visual video parsing in a 2025 paper. Parsing means labeling which events in a video are heard, seen, or both, moment by moment. In the weakly supervised setting, training data carries only whole-video labels. A model must guess where each event sits in time. Earlier methods leaned on global predictions that wobble at segment level.

Two strategies stabilize the guesses. An exponential moving average teacher generates pseudo-labels for segments. The labels are chosen by adaptive thresholds or top picks, giving steady temporal supervision. A class-aware agreement loss then pulls audio and visual embeddings together. It acts only at segment-class pairs judged reliable. On the LLP and UnAV-100 datasets, the method reached the best reported results across several metrics.
arxiv-2509-14397:
Ruiqi Huang, Anton Leykin and Michela Mancini give a new method in 2025 for initial orbit determination from angles only. Given sight lines to a moving body, the task is to find its orbit with no prior guess. Geometrically, a conic with a known focus must meet those lines.

Their algebraic version confirms five sight lines are the minimum for finitely many solutions in general position. The complex solution count is in the dozens. A subdivision search then hunts the orbit plane direction as a point on the real projective plane. Searching that plane avoids wasting time on non physical roots. The algorithm returns only the handful of real, meaningful orbits, and runs fast enough for practical tracking use.
arxiv-2509-14497:
Sebastián Alí Sacasa-Céspedes, writing alone in 2025, puts forward a way to predict material traits from topological marks, the traits that stay fixed when a shape is bent smoothly. Standard tools lean on fitted models that miss that quantum side. The plan rebuilds forecasts on string and graph ideas.

Molecular and dense matter systems become graphs. Branes form the nodes and open strings form the edges, holding twistor data. High energy blow ups are treated as topological blocks, smoothed through Calabi-Yau maps that keep symmetries in place. A graph Laplacian spectrum then sets stability, excited states and phase shifts. A nematic liquid crystal case shows the method at work. The plan is bold and early stage.
arxiv-2509-14597:
Seungjun Yi and ten co-authors argue in 2025 for clearer standards when language models help analyse unstructured clinical transcripts. Thematic analysis finds patterns in patient and provider stories, but skilled coding takes heavy time. Language models promise relief, yet practice is fragmented.

A systematic review of recent studies, plus an interview with a practising clinician, maps the fragmentation. Studies differ in analysis type, data sets, prompting and models, and most sharply in evaluation. Expert review and automatic similarity scores are used inconsistently, blocking progress comparisons. The position paper calls for shared evaluation and reporting norms. Clinical insight tools need audit standards before hospitals can trust themes a model claims to find.
arxiv-2509-14797:
Alba María Mármol-Romero, Flor Miriam Plaza-del-Arco, and Arturo Montejo-Ráez report on their SINAI team entry to the eRisk lab at CLEF 2023, in a 2025 write-up. The task was early detection of signs of pathological gambling in online text. Catching such signs early matters because help can reach people sooner.

Their system combines pre-trained Transformer models with careful preprocessing and data balancing. A long short-term memory network is integrated with Transformer auto-models to read sequences of posts over time. Out of forty-nine submissions, the team placed seventh overall. Their scores were strongest on recall and on measures that reward genuinely early detection, which is the point of the shared task.
arxiv-2509-14997:
Richard Stiskalek, Harry Desmond, and Guilhem Lavaux test claims that the local Universe expands at different rates in different directions, in a 2025 cosmology paper. Such anisotropy in the Hubble constant has been claimed from galaxy and supernova distances nearby. If real, it would challenge the standard picture of a uniform cosmos.

The authors revisit the claim with several Tully-Fisher galaxy catalogs and the Pantheon+ supernova compilation, all within low redshift. Their forward model calibrates the distance relations, handles distance uncertainty, and corrects for galaxy motions using a reconstruction of the local flow. One dataset does show a dipole signal at higher significance than before. Even so, Bayesian model comparison decides the overall verdict: no convincing evidence for local Hubble anisotropy once all samples are weighed.
arxiv-2509-15197:
Anamitra Chaudhuri, Yang Ni, and Anirban Bhattacharya develop a Bayesian method that provably recovers true causal structure in a 2025 statistics paper. Their setting is a linear structural equation model whose graph is acyclic and whose error terms, not necessarily Gaussian, share equal variances. Under those conditions the true causal graph is known to be identifiable in principle.

A key observation drives the design: total prediction error across variables is minimized exactly when the fitted graph contains the true graph. Their Bayesian selection method assumes Gaussian errors with equal variances and places independent g-priors on each equation's coefficients. Building on the key property, they prove the method consistently selects the true graph as data grow. Equal error variances, often treated as a nuisance assumption, become the lever that makes causal discovery reliable.
arxiv-2509-15297:
Richard H. Benavides and three co-authors hunt for heavy Higgs-like particles and massive neutrinos inside a 3-3-1 model in a 2025 particle physics paper. The model extends the Standard Model's gauge structure, and mild experimental deviations in two-photon processes hint at new scalar resonances at a few hundred gigaelectronvolts. The authors test whether those anomalies fit the model's scalar sector.

Focusing on the most relevant parameter regions, they extract preferred scalar mass ranges as probability distributions. Their benchmark version adds right-handed neutrinos and is implemented in the SARAH model-building package. The scalar sector uses the most general potential allowed by the symmetries, built from three Higgs triplets and one sextet. The neutrino sector is analyzed alongside, tying two beyond-Standard-Model puzzles into one framework.
arxiv-2509-15397:
Simantika Bhattacharjee Dristi and Matthew Dwyer study how code written by models is graded. Grading code by tests is costly, so many tools score new code by how much it looks like a known good answer. Past work showed those scores track real correctness weakly. The causes were guessed at, and fixes were scarce. The pair set out to test the cause directly.

They check four leading tools and find a strong bias toward surface traits over real function. Code that looks alike but acts unlike can fool them, and the reverse can fail them. They build a test set of over three thousand code pairs aimed at those weak spots. The set gives tool makers a hard, fair test.
arxiv-2509-15497:
Kealan Dunnett leads a team that defends neural networks against hidden backdoors. A backdoor makes a model act wrong only when a secret trigger appears. Cutting parts of the model can remove backdoors, but past cutting often missed the parts at fault. The team wanted a sharper cut that keeps normal skill intact.

Their method learns which parts matter for both the main task and the backdoor task. A mask that can be flipped then does two jobs: its normal form removes the backdoor, while its flipped form keeps it. Training runs at two levels, making fake triggers from clean data and refining the mask. Broad tests back the plan.
arxiv-2509-15597:
Yi Dong leads a team that helps unlike robots settle at a shared balance point. In an aggregative game, each robot's cost depends on its own act and on the group's average act. A Nash equilibrium is a state where no robot gains by moving alone. The team's robots differ in how they move, so one control law cannot fit all.

Their method runs in a spread out way, using only facts shared with nearby robots. A spread optimizer finds the balance point as a target for each robot. Output control laws then steer each unlike robot to its target. They prove the method converges and yields good outcomes. Tests on mock and real robots back the claim.
arxiv-2509-16497:
A superoptimizer that rewrites code for speed must prove each rewrite safe, and that proof step eats most of its time. Ange-Thierry Ishimwe and four co-authors add a learning-based pruner that guesses which candidate rewrites are doomed, so the costly solver never sees them. The pruner reads features from the code and drops unlikely candidates early.

Paired with a leading dataflow filter, compile time fell by about half against the plain baseline. Users can tune the pruner to trade speed against missed chances. Mixing a learned filter with exact checks gives the best of both.
arxiv-2509-16597:
Luyan Zhang proposes a new way to run large multimodal models in a 2025 solo paper. Big models can be slow and costly on hard tasks. Their inner steps can also be hard to follow. Zhang splits model work into three parts: reasoning, generation, and retrieval. A control layer then routes each task to the right mix.

The design borrows ideas from control theory, a field that steers systems toward goals. Learned routing picks paths as a task unfolds. The paper claims this is the first full link of control theory with dynamic model reasoning. The goal is lower cost with clearer steps. Tests are offered to back the design.
arxiv-2509-16697:
Sonali Vasant Kawale, Yogesh M Joshi, and Ranjini Bandyopadhyay study memory in dense gel glasses in a 2025 physics paper. Glassy matter can recall past heat or strain long after the fact. Past work framed that recall with a classic model of slow recovery. The team heat and cool dense microgel mixes and watch how stiffness returns.

They find that lost energy plays a key role. Tiny rearrangements in the gel drain away odd, path-based gaps in stiffness. Ramp speed and how tightly particles pack both tune the effect. Free space in the mix sets how much can shift. The findings help explain why some glasses forget their past faster.
arxiv-2509-16997:
Ali Nassar, working alone, finds number theory inside random matrix models in a 2025 paper. A Hermitian matrix model in a two-cut phase yields a spectral curve of genus one. Such a curve is an elliptic curve. Nassar works out a closed form for its key invariant. The form depends on a coupling in a quartic potential.

At specific coupling values, the curve gains extra symmetry, called complex multiplication. That trait means its endomorphism ring is larger than the integers. The result ties number-theoretic structure directly to spectral data of random matrices. Bridges like this often enrich both sides, giving each field new questions and tools.
arxiv-2509-17697:
D. Zakharova, G. De Lucia, B. Vulcani, F. Fontanot, and L. Xie trace the past environments of galaxies that now live in filaments. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from a known link: galaxy traits track a galaxy's place in the cosmic web. But a galaxy's address today says nothing about where it has lived, and past processing leaves marks on its stars.

Using the GAEA semi-analytic model and the IllustrisTNG simulation, the team rebuilt the histories of filament galaxies across most of cosmic time. Today's filament dwellers turn out to be a mixed crowd with distinct pasts. Most have passed through groups, and only a small share stayed central galaxies all their lives. For mid-mass galaxies, group processing does the heavy lifting: satellites stop growing and quench more often. Galaxies that stayed central look much like field galaxies, so the filament itself is not the main actor.
arxiv-2509-18197:
Abdelmalek Boumali studies a spinning particle oscillator in a space-time with a twisting cosmic string. His 2025 paper deals with the Dirac oscillator for spin-half particles. The string adds both a bend, which cuts a wedge from space, and a screw twist along its length.

He writes the Dirac equation in round coordinates with a local frame, and solves it in exact form. Three cases are worked through: twist split in time, twist in time alone, and twist in space alone. Each gives energy levels shifted by the bend, the twists, and the motion along the string. Flat space comes back when both twists vanish.
arxiv-2509-18497:
Computer graphics scenes need light bounced correctly to look real and to be relit later. Kaiwen Jiang and five co-authors present a fast, tunable light transport framework in this 2025 paper. It builds on Gaussian surfels, small flat discs that stand in for surfaces. Classic radiance field methods skip true material and light modeling, which blurs geometry and blocks relighting.

The team adapts an old idea, radiosity, to discs that can be partly see-through. All math runs in a compact harmonic coefficient space, covering both matte and glossy materials. New solvers plus a hand-derived gradient step make tuning far cheaper than automatic methods. At run time, light effects need no recompute when the view changes, so speeds reach hundreds of frames per second. Across tests, the method beat prior systems on geometry, view quality, and relighting.
arxiv-2509-18597:
Language models can write robot control code, but very long tasks expose their limits: vague wording, noisy output, and short memory. Yuan Meng and six co-authors present LYRA, a framework that learns skills for life with human help. Their 2025 paper distills human feedback into modular, reusable skills. Those skills grow step by step across sessions.

An external memory stores learned skills and past examples. Retrieval picks relevant knowledge for each new task, and user hints fill the gaps when retrieval falls short. Old behavior is guarded, so new corrections do not cause forgetting. Across five test suites, from simulated benches to real tasks, LYRA reached a 0.93 success rate. That beat baselines by up to 27 percent, and fixes took less effort over time. It even solved a build-a-house task spanning over twenty steps.
arxiv-2509-18697:
Identifying plants from photos works well for common species, but tropical floras lack field photos for training. Hervé Goëau, Pierre Bonnet, and Alexis Joly overview the PlantCLEF 2021 challenge in this paper. The challenge asked whether herbarium sheets, pressed specimens kept for centuries, could teach models to name plants in field photos. The focus was the Guiana Shield, a region of extreme plant diversity.

The data set held about a thousand species. Training mixed hundreds of thousands of herbarium sheets with a few thousand field photos, plus trait data for each species. The test set was field photos only, so systems had to cross from pressed sheets to living plants. The article gathers the resources, scoring, and the approaches of the competing teams. It then analyzes the main results. The challenge probes how far old collections can stretch modern identification.
arxiv-2509-19597:
Safety filters guard self-driving systems by nudging control only when danger nears. Sander Tonkens and five co-authors tackle a flaw in filters built from learned value functions: they assume all disturbances are known in advance. Real drones meet shifting winds and payload effects that vary from place to place. Their method, SPACE2TIME, rewrites place-based variation as time-based variation.

That rewrite lets a filter trained offline adapt on the fly to unknown local conditions. The filter keeps its light touch, changing the nominal plan only as much as safety needs. The authors target uses such as urban air mobility, where conditions vary street by street. Adapting without fresh training could widen where learned safety tools can be trusted. Tests and theory in the paper support the recasting idea.
arxiv-2509-20197:
Harrison Agrusa and Camille Chatenet wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on asteroid dynamics. In 2022, the DART spacecraft struck Dimorphos, the small moon of the asteroid Didymos. The impact cut the moon's orbital period by about thirty minutes at once. Over the next months, the period seemed to shrink by about thirty more seconds.

One proposed cause was binary hardening: the moon scattering loose debris away and losing angular momentum. The authors tested that idea with N-body simulations of the pair plus a cloud of massive test particles. Scattering turned out too weak to explain the extra drop under any conditions they tried. Dimorphos moves fast in its orbit but has low escape speed, so it scatters poorly. Slow debris would more likely fall back and lengthen the period. Some other mechanism must have driven the observed decrease.
arxiv-2509-20497:
Prompts rot like code, and Ahmed Aljohani and Hyunsook Do measure that rot in a 2025 arXiv study of technical debt in language model projects. Developers often admit debt in comments, a practice called self-admitted technical debt. The authors mined more than ninety-three thousand Python files across major model APIs. Theirs is the first large study of debt specific to these integrations.

Over half of the debt instances traced to one provider's integrations, with a framework for chaining models in second place. Prompt design was the largest single source of model-specific debt, ahead of tuning and framework issues. Instruction-based prompts attracted the most debt, followed by few-shot prompts, since both depend on fragile clarity and example quality. The team released its dataset and practical guidance for managing this new kind of debt.
arxiv-2509-20697:
Decoding a classical error-correcting code is believed to be hard, but the quantum case stayed open for years. Andrey Boris Khesin and four co-authors close that gap in a 2025 paper on quantum stabilizer decoding. Their paper runs to seventy-seven pages.

The authors prove that decoding a random stabilizer code, even one holding just one logical qubit, is no easier than decoding a random classical code at constant rate. That classical regime is the hardest known. In other words, the simplest random quantum decoding task matches the toughest random classical one in hardness. The result shapes expectations for quantum error correction and for cryptography built on decoding hardness.
arxiv-2509-20897:
Finding the root of an equation by repeated refinement is a basic task in applied mathematics. Wei Guo Foo and Chik How Tan propose a higher-order root-finding algorithm in a 2025 paper set to appear in the International Journal of Computer Mathematics. Their method uses only Taylor expansions of the function.

Classic higher-order methods, such as Householder's, need higher derivatives of a reciprocal function. Computing those symbolically is slow, and numerical differentiation piles up errors. The new method avoids both problems and carries an explicit convergence factor, sharper than earlier rough estimates. It can also implement Householder's method numerically. The authors apply it to computing quantities such as option-related values, showing the scheme at work.
arxiv-2509-21097:
Graph models are usually tested on the very graph they trained on, which says little about new graphs. Louis Van Langendonck and three co-authors build GraphUniverse in a 2025 paper accepted for ICLR 2026. The tool makes whole families of synthetic graphs to test inductive generalization.

Each family keeps the same semantic communities from graph to graph, so the concepts stay fixed. At the same time, traits such as degree spread and homophily can be set by hand. That control allows robustness tests that single-graph benchmarks cannot run. A team can ask whether a model learned the concept or just memorized one network. The authors aim to make inductive generalization, the real-world case, measurable at scale for graph learning.
arxiv-2509-21197:
The h-principle in complex analysis, better known as Oka theory, gets a broad survey treatment here. Credit goes to Franc Forstnerič. The h-principle says that some hard problems can be solved if a loose, formal solution exists. In complex work, this idea grew into Oka theory. It is named for work by Oka and Grauert, and for later work by Gromov.

The paper first gives a brief history of the principle in smooth geometry. It then sets out the key notions of Oka manifolds and Oka maps. It reviews new and ongoing work, open problems, and uses of the theory. It also surveys new h-principles for minimal surfaces. The piece was invited for a major maths congress and aims at a wide maths audience.
arxiv-2509-21797:
Robots must turn camera views and spoken orders into exact actions, and world models help them plan by predicting how a scene will change. Models that rebuild every pixel waste effort on detail that does not matter. Compact models save effort but miss fine detail that precise hand work needs. Yangcheng Yu and six co-authors present MoWM in this 2025 paper to get both strengths at once.

MoWM mixes motion-aware features from a compact latent world model with detail from a pixel-space model. The blend helps the robot pick out the visual details that matter for choosing an action. On the CALVIN benchmark and on real robot tasks, MoWM reached top success rates. It also handled new settings better than rivals, and the paper compares the strengths of each feature type for future work.
arxiv-2509-22097:
AI coding agents now write real software, but the code they produce can carry security holes. Junkai Chen and twelve co-authors present SecureVibeBench in this 2025 paper, a benchmark for secure code generation, accepted at ACL 2026. Earlier benchmarks miss how flaws actually enter code: they do not recreate the situations in which human developers introduced real vulnerabilities, so agents and humans cannot be compared fairly.

The benchmark holds just over one hundred secure coding tasks in C and C++, drawn from dozens of projects in a large fuzzing program. Each task demands edits across several files in a big repository. Scoring combines working-code tests with security checks, both static and dynamic. Five popular agents, backed by five large models, were evaluated. Even the best produced correct and secure solutions in under a quarter of the tasks, which the authors read as a warning about current coding agents.
arxiv-2509-22197:
Duc Thien Nguyen, Konstantinos Slavakis, Eleftherios Kofidis, and Dimitris Pados present a method for filling in missing entries of multi-way data. Their 2025 framework, called KReTTaH, treats the filling-in task as regression inside kernel spaces, a nonparametric approach that makes few assumptions about the data's shape. The data are stored as tensors compressed into tensor trains, a chain format that keeps the parameter count low. A further trick, called Hadamard overparametrization, nudges the model toward sparsity inside that format.

Learning takes place on the curved space of fixed-rank tensor trains. The showcase application is dynamic graph flow: estimating how much traffic moves along each edge of a network over time, when many readings are missing. On real graph data sets, KReTTaH beat leading alternatives, including a neural network method and another tensor method, at imputing the missing time-varying flows.
arxiv-2509-22297:
Sander Beckers, writing alone, examines how to ask what a language model would have said if the prompt had been different. Such counterfactual questions matter for explaining and improving model behavior. Recent work produced the first methods for generating them, by treating the model as a deterministic causal system with a modified sampling step. His 2025 paper, accepted at a knowledge representation conference, argues that this reading is ambiguous: it is neither the model taken literally nor the model as intended.

Beckers proposes a simpler method founded on the intended reading. The model is represented as a nondeterministic causal model, which matches how its outputs are actually meant to be understood. The method applies to any black-box model without modification, since it ignores implementation details. The older method keeps an advantage for one specific, useful kind of counterfactual.
arxiv-2509-22697:
Abhiroop Chatterjee and Susmita Ghosh align hyperspectral images with text while training almost no parameters. Each pixel in such an image carries hundreds of spectral channels, forming a heavy three-dimensional data cube. Vision-language models shine on normal images, but the hyperspectral case is little explored. Their framework uses CLIP-style contrastive training. Voxel embeddings from a vision backbone are mapped into the space of a frozen large embedding model.

A trainable probe aligns vision features with text tokens. Training uses a curated mix of hard negatives, random distractors, and positive pairs. Descriptive prompts that encode class meaning anchor the image embeddings. Updating a tiny fraction of parameters still beat prior methods on two standard scenes.
arxiv-2509-23197:
K-pop hits that chart worldwide mix Korean and English lines as a matter of strategy. Aditya Narayan Sankaran, Reza Farahbakhsh, and Noel Crespi measured that mix. Their data set covers Billboard Hot 100 and Global 200 songs from 2017 to 2025. Fourteen groups and eight solo artists appear. English share, switch frequency, and style traits were all coded.

English dominates the lyrics of globally charting K-pop. Code switching runs high for male and female performers alike. Tests found no significant gender gap, though female solo acts lean English more steadily. A gender classifier on lyrics reached solid scores. Higher English share may matter more for the US chart.
arxiv-2509-23497:
Trust in an AI helper can swing too far either way, and both extremes hurt decisions. Bruno M. Henrique and Eugene Santos propose a live way to calibrate that trust. Their measure is standardized, so it can travel across settings. It also splits two steps that older work blurred: forming an opinion and then acting on it. A contextual bandit, an algorithm that learns from context, drives the indicator.

The bandit judges, case by case, when AI input deserves trust. Across three varied data sets, good calibration raised reward scores by ten to thirty-eight percent. The authors point to high-stakes uses such as disease diagnosis and criminal justice.
arxiv-2509-23997:
Splitting a quantum gate into fractional steps lets a quantum heat engine pace its work strokes. Elliot John Fox and 3 co-authors apply Nth-root gates inside thermodynamic protocols for two- and three-qubit circuits. They compare the circuits on maximum work production and efficiency across regions of starting parameters. For most regions and all circuits considered, adding quantum coherence to one qubit strongly raised the maximum work.

Work came out at efficiencies between eighty-four and one hundred percent in their results. They also uncover a strong linear correlation between work production and the many-body correlations the gates generate in the working medium. Coherence, imprinted at the start, does the heavy lifting.
arxiv-2509-24297:
Good multimodal science benchmarks are costly to build by hand. Junying Wang and 10 co-authors ask whether text-only question pairs can be turned into multimodal ones of high quality. They set out a conversion framework and a multi-part quality rubric to judge the results. Two benchmarks then test leading models at both making such items and grading them.

Top models could generate multimodal items, but gaps remained, so reliable grading matters. The best understanding models graded quality close to human judgment.
