SCOPE slightly beat a leading language model based agent on success rate. The dramatic gain was speed: inference time fell from well over two minutes per episode to a few seconds. One round of teacher guidance carries much of the benefit of constant supervision.
arxiv-2512-09997:
Basabendu Barman and colleagues use gamma ray data to constrain dark matter that was created by gravity itself in the early universe. Such gravitationally produced dark matter barely interacts, making it hard to test. The team uses diffuse high energy gamma rays from our galaxy, measured by the LHAASO observatory and the Fermi-LAT satellite. Four candidate particles are tested: a dark photon, a heavy right handed neutrino, a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson, and a non-minimally coupled scalar.

For the first three candidates, the combined data force the interaction strength down to extremely small values for particles heavier than about a teraelectronvolt scale. The scalar is bounded less tightly but still strongly. Photon to dark photon oscillation adds further limits, closing a region of parameter space for heavier dark photons that earlier work had left open. The results narrow where gravitational dark matter can hide.
arxiv-2512-10097:
Mira Littmann and colleagues check whether a future muon collider could catch long lived particles that other searches miss. A ten teraelectronvolt muon collider would probe the energy frontier, but decaying muons flood its detector with background. Timing cuts tame that background with little loss for ordinary particles. The authors ask what those cuts do to metastable charged particles, using a supersymmetry benchmark where the stau partner of the tau lepton lives long and appears as a heavy, slow track. Nominal timing selections prove too restrictive for such particles.

Loosening the time acceptance recovers sensitivity, even to particles nearly as heavy as half the collision energy allows. The team draws concrete recommendations for tracker design and reconstruction. The stakes are general: long lived particles are a generic prediction of theories beyond the Standard Model, and a detector optimized only for prompt particles could be blind to them.
arxiv-2512-10597:
R Bailhache and H Appelshäuser review dileptons, pairs of a lepton and its antiparticle, as messengers from the quark-gluon plasma. Colliders smash heavy ions to recreate the deconfined soup of quarks and gluons that filled the early universe. Dileptons are emitted at every stage and then escape untouched, unlike hadrons, which only report on the final moments.

The pair's mass separates radiation from the hot partonic stage from later hadronic emission, opening measurements no hadron can give: how fast the plasma settles into equilibrium, its average temperature. And signs of chiral symmetry returning in the hot medium through vector meson decays. The price is a heavy background from ordinary hadron decays. The review, published in the Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science, gathers what colliders have learned so far and the push for more sensitive future experiments.
arxiv-2512-10897:
Thomas Borsoni and Virginie Ehrlacher prove that a quantum system in a crystal can be watched without disturbing the result. An observability inequality bounds how well measurements on part of a system reveal the whole state. And for the von Neumann equation, the law of motion for density matrices, a bound was known in free space but not in the periodic setting of a crystal.

Their proof follows the strategy of Golse and Paul: a stability argument between the quantum dynamics and its classical Liouville counterpart, with the gap measured by an optimal-transport-style pseudo-distance. The work lies in rebuilding every tool for the periodic case, using the Bloch decomposition, periodic Schrödinger coherent states, periodic Töplitz operators, and periodic Husimi densities. The resulting bound holds uniformly as the reduced Planck constant shrinks, exactly the regime where quantum and classical descriptions meet.
arxiv-2512-10997:
Anija R. and co-authors introduce a new measure of uncertainty for lifetime data, built from the Mathai Haubold entropy applied to remaining life. Entropy measures help describe how spread out or unpredictable a distribution is. The authors also define a dynamic version that changes with time and show it can pin down the underlying distribution uniquely.

Practical use needs ways to estimate the new measures from data, so they build non-parametric estimators based on smooth estimates of the survival curve. A large Monte Carlo simulation study checks how well those estimators perform. Real examples use failure times for aircraft windshields and for mechanical switches, showing how the dynamic measure can be applied to reliability questions in engineering.
arxiv-2512-11597:
François Le Gall, Yupan Liu, and Qisheng Wang sharpen a bound in quantum proof theory. The class QSZK covers problems with quantum proofs that leak almost no extra facts to the checker. The best known home for it was the class QIP(2) and its mirror image, based on two message quantum proofs.

The team shows the same home works even when the honest prover has little memory. The prover needs space that grows only in line with the proof length. The same gain holds for the no message form, NIQSZK. Their tools are working versions of two classic quantum steps, the Holevo-Helstrom measure and the Uhlmann transform.
arxiv-2512-11797:
Junjie Ye and co-authors present AnchorDream, a system that grows robot training data from a handful of real demonstrations. Robots that learn by copying need many varied examples, but filming real ones is slow and costly, and simulators look fake and behave unlike the real world.

AnchorDream reuses pretrained video diffusion models, guiding them with renderings of the robot own motion. The robot body stays fixed and physically sound, while the system paints in matching objects and scenes around it. Policies trained on the synthetic data gained 36.4 percent in simulation tests and nearly doubled their scores in real world trials. The trick, the team argues, is grounding made up video in true robot motion.
arxiv-2512-11897:
Yihan Cui studies when maps between Carnot groups can be lifted through a central extension, a way of adding one central direction. Carnot groups are layered spaces where motion is allowed only along certain directions at each step, a model for constrained geometry. Lifting asks whether a map downstairs comes from a smoother map upstairs.

Cui proves contact lifts exist for Lipschitz and Sobolev maps, two broad classes with weak derivatives. A rigidity result follows for quasiconformal maps: if such a map lifts in the contact sense, it must in fact be bi-Lipschitz, fully tame both ways. A needed rule for Hölder lifts is also given when the exponent passes one half.
arxiv-2512-12197:
Minghao Mou and Junjie Qin extend a classic traffic puzzle to power grids in a 2025 paper. Braess's paradox says adding road capacity can make travel worse for all. As cars go electric, road and power networks link through charging points, and the same trap may span both systems.

The authors model both networks as graphs joined at chargers. Power runs by cheapest dispatch, while drivers pick routes and charging spots. In simple cases, added capacity in either system can hurt both. They give exact conditions for when the paradox occurs in general networks. They also design charging prices that can reduce the harm.
arxiv-2512-12297:
Radu-Gabriel Chivereanu and Tiberiu Boros extend the F5-TTS speech system to Romanian in a 2025 paper. F5-TTS clones voices and speaks English and Chinese. Adding a new language often means retraining the whole model, which risks losing what it already does well.

Their adapter keeps all old weights frozen and adds a small network at the input. It acts as a soft letter to sound layer, turning Romanian text into a form the model can speak. Twenty human listeners judged likeness, pronunciation, naturalness, and mixed Romanian English speech. Voice cloning still worked, and mixed speech worked to some extent, though a faint English accent remained.
arxiv-2512-12397:
The BESIII Collaboration reports a first amplitude analysis of a charm meson decay in a 2025 paper. The decay sends a D+ meson into a positive pion and two neutral pions. Data came from electron positron collisions at 3.773 GeV with the BESIII detector, totaling 20.3 inverse femtobarns of integrated luminosity.

Amplitude analysis splits the decay into intermediate steps and measures each share. The path through a rho(770)+ and a neutral pion dominates, with branching fraction 3.08 times 10 to the minus 3. The full decay's branching fraction is 4.84 times 10 to the minus 3. The team also measures CP asymmetries for parts and for the whole.
arxiv-2512-12497:
Ioannis Anagnostides, Zachary W Sollie, Arman Kilic, and Tuomas Sandholm optimize heart transplant allocation in a 2025 paper. Transplant saves patients with advanced heart failure, but donor hearts are scarce. The allocation policy revised in 2018 still weighs pre and post transplant mortality poorly, the authors argue, leaving gains on the table.

They build a simulator from historical UNOS data to test policies head to head. A myopic policy that gives each heart to the patient gaining the most years already beats the status quo by a wide margin. Adding potentials, a measure of a patient's value in future rounds, improves results further, as does batching a handful of donors. The simulator also tests geography and offer rejection effects.
arxiv-2512-12597:
Miriam Horovicz introduces AgentSHAP, a tool for explaining which tools a language model agent actually used, in a 2025 paper. Agents call external tools to solve hard tasks, but no explainability method showed each tool's share in a given answer. AgentSHAP treats the agent as a black box, so it works with any model, from GPT to Llama, without weights or gradients.

Using Monte Carlo Shapley values from game theory, it runs the agent with varied tool subsets and assigns fair importance scores. Sampling cuts the cost from exponential to practical levels. On the API-Bank benchmark, scores stayed consistent across runs, and the method separated relevant tools from irrelevant ones correctly.
arxiv-2512-12797:
Mohammad H Taufik and Tariq Alkhalifah make Bayesian full waveform inversion practical at field scale in a 2025 paper. Full waveform inversion builds subsurface images from seismic data, and its Bayesian form adds uncertainty estimates. But sampling the posterior on real shot records usually needs many wave equation solves per sample, making it too costly for large surveys.

Their sampler couples diffusion based sampling with simultaneous source data, cutting forward and adjoint solves roughly in proportion to the supergather size. A learned prior trained on velocity patches suppresses source related artefacts, and a Langevin refinement step works under the wave equation likelihood. On synthetic and field data sets, it beat a particle based baseline on model error and data fit at far lower cost.
arxiv-2512-12997:
Wenjing Lu and co-authors address a reliability gap in CLIP, a model that sorts images into classes without task specific training. Attackers can nudge an image so CLIP misreads it. Worse, the model often stays overconfident on such attacks, hiding the danger.

The team reframes CLIP outputs as the settings of a Dirichlet distribution, capturing both what the model favors and how sure it is. Their fine-tuning goal aligns the whole distribution between clean and attacked images, not just the top answer. Across zero-shot test sets, the method improved uncertainty calibration. It also kept clean accuracy while reaching competitive robustness against attacks.
arxiv-2512-13397:
Malte Silbernagel and co-authors present rNCA, a method that repairs broken segmentation masks with neural cellular automata. General segmentation models often output fragmented masks with wrong topology, and fixing them usually needs hand-crafted rules or specialized designs. Their automaton applies local, repeated updates guided by the image.

Trained on flawed masks paired with true ones, the automaton learns the target shape's structure from local information alone. Applied to vessel masks from retinal images, it raised Dice scores by 2 to 3 percent and cut Betti errors sharply. On heart muscle masks, it repaired 61.5 percent of broken cases with no retraining for that task.
arxiv-2512-13697:
Vivan Doshi and Mengyuan Li map how human creative writing is changing alongside large language models. Their paper asks what happens to human agency when people write in a close, symbiotic way with creative machines. A common fear is that AI pushes all writing toward one flat style.

Using a large corpus from before and after the LLM era, they find a dual-track pattern. Themes converge around AI-related topics, while styles split in structured ways. Some authors grow closer to AI style, some move away, and some stay stable while taking up AI themes. Their Creative Archetype Map frames these paths. The work bears on collaboration with AI, detection of AI text, and keeping creative diversity alive.
arxiv-2512-13797:
Shyam Balaji, Damon Cleaver, and Pedro De la Torre Luque propose excited dark matter to explain two excesses at the center of our galaxy. New COMPTEL analysis shows a continuum excess near 2 MeV whose shape matches the long-known 511 keV line seen by INTEGRAL/SPI. Both point to low-energy positrons that known sources struggle to explain.

In their minimal model, a dark matter particle is scattered into an excited state, which then decays back and emits an electron-positron pair. With a particle mass near 1.5 TeV and a mass split near 4 MeV, the fit is excellent. The same positrons add a flat contribution to the ionization rate in the Central Molecular Zone, linking three observables in one testable story.
arxiv-2512-13997:
Aaron Wei, Milad Jalali, and Danica J. Sutherland extend Maximum Mean Discrepancy two-sample testing to unequal sample sizes. MMD compares two distributions through a kernel, but standard theory often assumes equal sample sizes. In practice, that premise can force users to discard valuable data and lose test power.

By extending generalized U-statistics theory, they characterize the asymptotic distributions of the MMD estimator for unequal sizes, well beyond the proportional regimes past partial results needed. The theory also gives a new criterion for optimizing the power of an MMD test with unequal samples. They give cleaner variance formulas for MMD estimators, and show a degenerate estimator can occur with nonzero MMD in special constructions, though not in common situations.
arxiv-2512-14297:
Agrippina Mwangi and five coauthors build a self healing system for software defined industrial networks in a 2025 paper. Random disruptions, from benign traffic bursts to switch heating, can break quality rules for control traffic in wind power plants and risk turbine downtime.

Their agent uses a threshold triggered Deep Q Network, a reinforcement learning method, to detect, analyze, and fix disruptions on its own. It adapts routing and resource use in real time and starts external rack cooling when switches overheat. Trained on an emulated three cluster switch network, it improved disruption recovery by 53.84 percent over a baseline routing method. It also beat two state of the art methods by 13.1 and 21.5 percent.
arxiv-2512-14597:
The semiconductor germanium telluride, in its ferroelectric alpha phase, has drawn a decade of attention for its unusual electronic behavior. Most studies have mapped its occupied electron bands, the states electrons fill, while its unoccupied states, especially those near the conduction band minimum, stayed largely unexplored.

Six researchers report the detection of image potential states in this material, states in which an electron is held outside a surface by its own induced charge. Finding them above the vacuum level in GeTe fills a gap in the picture of its electronic structure. The work is relevant to surface science and to devices that would use this ferroelectric semiconductor.
arxiv-2512-14697:
Yue Zhao and five co-authors revisit non-parametric quantization, a way of compressing neural network activations into a codebook without learned lookup tables. The approach is prized for parameter efficiency and for scaling to very large codebooks. It now underpins visual tokenization and generation.

The team gives a unified formulation of existing methods through lattice coding. The geometry of lattice codes explains why some variants, such as BSQ, need auxiliary loss terms when auto-encoders are trained. Their spherical Leech quantization builds on that view. A clearer theory of quantization helps builders of image and video generators choose compression schemes on principle rather than habit.
arxiv-2512-14897:
María Benito and nine coauthors use a simulated galaxy to ask why disk galaxies show two chemical families of stars. Stars split into high and low groups in alpha elements compared with iron, a split seen in the Milky Way. The puzzle is what creates the two tracks over a galaxy's life.

Their test galaxy, from the FIRE-2 simulation suite, had no major mergers and little shuffling of stars, yet it still grew both families. A thick high alpha disk formed early, in a chaotic phase of clustered star birth. Then a minor merger diluted the hot gas halo and stalled the rise of iron, opening a gap. Later, gas from small mergers fed a low alpha sequence in the outer disk, which flowed inward. The study shows merger history and gas flows together shape a disk's chemistry.
arxiv-2512-15097:
J. G. Li and four coauthors test whether the proton rich nucleus silicon-22 is doubly magic. Magic nuclei, with full shells of protons or neutrons, are extra stable and prized as benchmarks. New magic numbers have turned up on the neutron rich side, but the proton rich side is less explored, and silicon-22's mirror, oxygen-22, is doubly magic.

Using an ab initio method, the valence space in medium similarity renormalization group, the team computes silicon-22, oxygen-22, and their neighbors. The method describes oxygen-22's double magicity well and tracks shell evolution across the region. Silicon-22's first excited state energy comes out 800 keV below its mirror's, so its proton shell closure is weaker. Mirror energy differences for silicon 24 and 26 pairs match measured data well. The authors conclude silicon-22 is doubly magic, like its mirror, but less strongly.
arxiv-2512-15297:
Yue-Hong Wu and a coauthor study how a qubit loses its quantum phase when coupled to a bath that breaks the usual rules. The setting is the pure dephasing spin boson model, where the qubit keeps its energy but its phase information leaks away. The bath can be Hermitian, the standard kind, or non Hermitian, an exotic kind with gain and loss.

The authors first prove a suspected link between the non equilibrium and equilibrium correlation functions of the model. Looking at short and long times, they find the decay depends in a singular way on the coupling strength and the bath exponent exactly at integer values. The headline result: a non Hermitian bath tends to suppress decoherence for all values of those parameters. That runs against an earlier claim by Dey and coauthors, and it suggests engineering odd baths to protect qubits.
arxiv-2512-15397:
Lev Kharlashkin and three coauthors build ORACLE, a platform that turns daily news into foresight for a Finnish university of applied sciences. Leaders need week over week, decision ready views of the world, sorted by the PESTEL lenses of politics, economy, society, technology, environment, and law. Raw news volume makes that impossible by hand.

ORACLE crawls and versions news, filters it for the university's relevance, embeds and classifies each item into PESTEL dimensions. It then builds a time dependent recursive summary graph: two layers of clusters, each summarized by a language model, rebuilt weekly. A change detector flags what is new, removed, or altered, and groups the differences into themes. The paper details the pipeline and the design choices that keep it stable in production, and it presents a curriculum intelligence use case with an evaluation plan.
arxiv-2512-15497:
Martin Ochmann and co authors report the first reverberation mapping of a Bowen fluorescence line in a 2025 astronomy paper. Reverberation mapping times how long light from a black hole region takes to make gas at a known distance respond. Until now it had only been done for recombination lines, not for lines lit by Bowen fluorescence.

Using a 2016 Hubble campaign on the galaxy NGC 4593, the team finds the oxygen line OI 8446 varying on day timescales, with a delay of about 2.5 days relative to Lyman alpha. Line ratios show Lyman beta pumping drives the emission. The result suggests future campaigns can use two drivers at once to map larger black hole regions.
arxiv-2512-16197:
Sean Doan and a large team report a light source for quantum technology in their arXiv paper from 2025. Tiny defects in hexagonal boron nitride, a layered crystal, can emit one photon at a time, which quantum networks need. The team used a simple oxygen plasma treatment to create such emitters reliably across the material.

The emitters shine in the near-infrared, from 700 to 971 nanometers, without blinking. They reach single-photon purity up to 99.9 percent and very narrow spectral lines, down to 2.7 gigahertz when cold. They resist fading and hold their color steady over long periods. Chemical mapping and first-principles calculations point to oxygen-based defects as the cause. The results make this crystal a strong platform for free-space quantum links and future photonic chips.
arxiv-2512-16297:
Taozhao Chen and three co-authors make AI forget more carefully in a 2025 arXiv paper. Deployed models may retain sensitive or banned knowledge, and machine unlearning tries to remove it. Real data rarely separates cleanly into forget and keep piles, though, and clumsy unlearning either wrecks general skill or leaves the target knowledge in place.

Their method, SRMU, edits internal activations instead of weights. A structured misdirection vector, guided by a map of which activations matter, suppresses harmful representations while sparing useful ones. On the WMDP benchmark, across low and high entanglement settings, SRMU reached state-of-the-art unlearning with minimal utility loss. It stayed effective even with 20 to 30 percent overlap between forget and keep data, where rival methods collapsed. A replication package is available.
arxiv-2512-16397:
Haodi He, Jihun Yu, and Ronald Fedkiw rebuild faces in 3D in a paper uploaded to arXiv in 2025, submitted to CVPR 2026. Their goal is one consistent model of a face from a handful of uncalibrated photos. They use Gaussian splatting, a representation of many soft 3D blobs, because it accepts constraints more readily than neural radiance fields.

Face segmentation labels align the semantic regions, so a neutral pose emerges from just 11 images instead of a long video. The blobs are softly tied to a triangle mesh, and each improves the other in turn. The finished mesh drops into standard graphics pipelines, and the splats convert into a view-dependent neural texture usable on any scene asset. A relightable model separates texture from lighting, yielding a clean high-resolution albedo map. The team shows the assets feeding a text-driven creation pipeline.
arxiv-2512-16597:
Sajad Salami and Arman Shamsi Zargar answer open questions in number theory in a paper posted to arXiv in 2025. A congruent number is the area of a right triangle with rational sides. That is a classical problem. Theta-congruent numbers generalize it. Here n counts when a rational triangle has area n and a set angle theta, whose cosine is rational.

Das and Saikia had set criteria over certain real number fields. They closed with four open questions about properly theta-congruent numbers. The authors answer all four in full. They remove a side condition from the case of fields whose degree is coprime to 6. They settle real cubic fields with no congruence limits. They extend the work to fields of degree 6. They also check the small cases n equals 1, 2, 3, and 6.
arxiv-2512-16997:
Felipe Espinoza-Arancibia, Bogumił Pilecki, and Matylda Łukaszewicz pin down the instability strip for classical Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud, the band of heat and brightness where these stars pulsate. Exact edges test stellar models and sharpen Cepheids as distance markers.

Using OGLE-IV data, the cleaned sample holds 2,388 fundamental-mode and 1,560 first-overtone Cepheids. Edges were traced in two photometric bands and in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, with breaks at periods of 1.4 to 3 days. The blue edge matches theory well, the red edge does not. The Cloud strip is wider than that of the Large Magellanic Cloud, and period counts match counts for periods over one day only.
arxiv-2512-17297: Ulrich Abel, Ana Maria Acu, Margareta Heilmann, and Ioan Rasa give a formula for the kernel of two Bernstein-Durrmeyer operators applied one after the other. These operators smooth and approximate functions defined on a simplex, the higher-dimensional cousin of a triangle. A compact formula for the combined kernel helps analysts compute what repeated smoothing does to a function and how fast it settles toward the original.
arxiv-2512-17497:
Ingo Rehberg and Peter Blümler build magnetic spheres from off-the-shelf cube magnets and find one shape wins by a wide margin. A Halbach array arranges permanent magnets so their fields add up inside and cancel outside, making a smooth, strong field for scanners and sensors. True spherical versions are elegant but hard to build and hard to reach inside.

The pair instead set cube magnets at the corners of regular solids and test each shape in math, simulation, and the lab. Icosahedral layouts, with twenty-fold symmetry, gave the best mix of strength, smoothness, and open access. Their even zone runs up to 260 times larger than classic disk or cylinder arrays, holding within 1 percent over several cubic centimeters. Portable magnetic resonance is one target use.
arxiv-2512-17597:
Tosan Omabegho rebuilds the logic of a molecular motor out of plain mechanical linkages. Real ATPases burn the cell's fuel, ATP, to do work, and they coordinate two binding sites through allostery, a poke at one site reshaping the other. That inner signaling is still murky, so a tabletop-style model that shows the logic plainly has real value.

The linkage machine has two sites and two ways to flex. Its geometry forces a trade: when one site grips fully, the other cannot. A tight-binding fuel copy kicks the regulator copy out; splitting the fuel copy loosens the frame so the regulator returns and pushes the spent products out. Run in sequence, the parts cycle like the enzyme. The work sketches design rules for synthetic molecular machines.
arxiv-2512-17697:
Alatz Alvarez-Ahedo, Mikel Garcia de Andoin, and Mikel Sanz extend a hybrid style of quantum computing to atoms and ions with more than two usable levels. Digital-analog computing mixes a always-on natural interaction with crisp single-unit gates, avoiding long gate chains. Its theory, though, was built for qubits, the two-level case.

Qudits, units with d levels, store more per particle but needed their own recipe. The team gives one: wrap the natural interaction block in single-qudit gates from the Weyl-Heisenberg set, and any two-body spin model can be simulated. The cost grows as a stated formula in d and the number of units. A worked example simulates many-body qudit spins with quadrupolar terms, physics qubits cannot hold natively.
arxiv-2512-17797:
Andrei Rasputnyi and four co-authors bend a bright beam of quantum light out of its tidy Gaussian shape, on purpose and at full brightness. Non-Gaussian light is a prized fuel for quantum computing, but it usually comes faint and filtered, throwing most photons away. Their starting material is bright squeezed vacuum, a macroscopic glow with quantum correlations already built in.

Passing it through a Kerr medium, where light's speed depends on its own intensity, twists the glow's statistics into an S shape, the signature they record with a single-shot interferometer. One quantum marker, Wigner negativity, stays hidden because losses muddy the state. Yet the team shows components inside the mixture do carry that marker robustly. Bright quantum light could power sensors and processors that faint light cannot.
arxiv-2512-17897:
Tomer Borreda and four coauthors built RadarGen, a tool that invents car radar data from camera views. Radar helps self driving cars see in rain and fog, yet real radar records are scarce for training. Their system paints a top down radar map, tagged with strength and speed clues, then turns it into a point cloud.

Hints about depth, object type, and motion, drawn from ready made vision models, steer the results toward scenes that could be real. On large driving data sets the fake radar matched the spread of real radar well. Tests also showed a smaller gap for sensing models trained on the fake data versus real data.
arxiv-2512-17997:
Matteo Cantiello leads an eight author team asking whether some Little Red Dots are really quasi-stars: black hole seeds wrapped in huge envelopes of gas. One lensed dot, RX1, brightens and dims over about a century, a hint that its surface pulses like a star. The team tests that idea with star building and ringing codes.

Their models show a clear edge. Envelopes hotter than about 5,000 to 5,200 K stay calm, while cooler ones pulse with periods of 20 to 180 years, matching the pace seen in RX1. The pulses likely shed mass in strong winds, which would shape how long the quasi-star phase lasts and how big the seed grows.
arxiv-2512-18097:
Mohammad Taghi Dabiri leads a six author team hardening quantum key sharing over open air links. The method swaps faint light signals whose quantum traits expose any listener. Real links suffer wobble from air turbulence and shaky aim, and stray light leaking at wide angles can hand a listener extra clues.

Their guard is an angular filter that accepts light only from a safe cone around the true beam. A full channel model in their study counts turbulence, aim error, and the filter's effect on secrecy. The safe zone cut leakage sharply, though beam width, angle limit, and lens size all needed care. Long links, they find, demand aim finer than 100 microradians.
arxiv-2512-18297: José M. Zapata sharpens the math for the largest value in a batch of random draws from a standard normal spread. He proves tight large deviation estimates for that maximum across all Borel subsets of the positive real line, giving tail estimates more accurate than the classic Gumbel limit law.
arxiv-2512-18497:
Cédric Bernardin and three co-authors trace how a chain of tiny oscillators gives rise to a famous noisy equation. The chain vibrates under a Hamiltonian rule with an exponential potential, shaken by a symmetric noise. Earlier work showed its fluctuations settle into the stochastic Burgers equation. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, adds a moving heat bath coupled to the chain.

The bath's strength, set by an exponent delta, decides the outcome with a sharp threshold. At delta of one or below, the fluctuations converge to the stochastic Burgers equation with a Dirichlet boundary condition at zero, and the authors characterize those boundary solutions two ways. Above one, the bath fades away and the boundary vanishes, recovering the full-line result. The study shows how a microscopic nudge can, or cannot, create a macroscopic wall.
arxiv-2512-18697:
Giuseppe Cosma Brusca analyzes energies that are both nonlocal and finely patterned. The functionals he studies, posted in an arXiv paper in December 2025, mix two small scales. One is epsilon, the reach of nonlocal interactions. The other is delta, the period of a fine repeating structure in the material. As both shrink, the energy's limiting behavior decides what macroscopic model engineers should use.

He proves the two scales separate cleanly, and the outcome hinges on lambda, the limit of their ratio. For each value of lambda he computes the Gamma-limit of the functionals in the strong Lp topology and finds three distinct regimes. The interesting one is the critical case, lambda between zero and infinity, where localization and homogenization truly interact. The results guide multiscale modeling of composites and other patterned media.
arxiv-2512-18797:
Lisan Al Amin and Vandana P. Janeja test quantum kernels for catching fake voices. Deepfake speech detectors trained as giant neural networks overfit when labeled data are scarce and recording conditions shift. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and accepted at an ICDM 2025 workshop, keeps a plain support vector machine and changes only the kernel, swapping in a quantum feature map.

Across four corpora, including ASVspoof sets and in-the-wild recordings, the quantum-kernel SVM posts lower equal error rates everywhere: 0.183 against 0.299 on ASVspoof 5, and 0.081 against 0.188 on ADD23, for instance. False positives drop by up to 56.9 percent at the balance point. Nothing else changes, no extra trainable parameters, and the quantum kernel is computed on an ordinary computer. Expressive similarity, it turns out, can substitute for model size.
arxiv-2512-19097:
Danny Dongyeop Han, Yonghyeon Gwon, Ahhyun Lucy Lee, and Taeyang Lee built DIVER-1, a foundation model for brain signals recorded from inside the skull. Such intracranial recordings differ wildly between patients, since electrode layouts and coverage change each time. That variety has blocked reusable pretrained models.

DIVER-1 handles any electrode layout through attention over channels and time, resampling, and embeddings that adapt to the input. It was pretrained, without labels, on more than five thousand hours of recordings. On held-out tests it beat earlier models at decoding natural activity, and stayed competitive on seizure detection, even though it never trained on the benchmark's own corpus.
arxiv-2512-19197:
Mohamad Maassarani compares two families of local rings built from polynomials over a field. Take an irreducible polynomial and form the ring of polynomials modulo a power of it. Different starting polynomials can give look-alike rings, and Maassarani asks exactly when the rings are truly the same.

For separable irreducible polynomials, he proves the power rings are isomorphic exactly when their residue fields are isomorphic. Partial results cover the harder non-separable case. He also proves a clean structural identity: the power ring matches a polynomial ring over the residue field, again modulo the same power. The work is pure commutative algebra.
arxiv-2512-19297:
Linzhi Chen, Yang Sun, Hongru Wei, and Yuqi Chen expose a stealthy backdoor risk in shared LoRA adapters. Small adapter files fine-tune big language models cheaply, and they pass hand to hand on open platforms with little review. A poisoned adapter can hide a trigger that flips the model's behavior on cue.

Their attack, CBA, needs no access to the original training data, which earlier attacks often assumed. A coverage-guided generator synthesizes fitting inputs by probing behavior, and causal guidance keeps false triggers rare. The result is a case study in how easily open adapter sharing can be abused, and why platforms need checks.
arxiv-2512-19697:
Parsa Hatami, Ahmadreza Majlesara, Ali Majlesi, and Babak Hossein Khalaj test whether a language model can stand watch over a 5G core network. Modern telecom systems carry mission-critical traffic, and faults must be caught fast, yet traditional diagnosis tools strain under the scale and data volume involved. Their approach fine-tunes a compact commercial model on records from a deliberately broken test network.

The testbed, built on Kubernetes, had faults injected on purpose: pod failures and kills, network delay and loss, and disk input-output failures. Logs, events, round-trip tests, and pod status fed the training data. Fine-tuning GPT-4.1 nano through its API improved fault detection and classification markedly over the base model. The authors present the result as a step toward closed-loop, operator-free fault management.
arxiv-2512-20297:
Jin-Yu Ni, Xia-Ming Zheng, Peng-Tao Wei, Da-Yong Liu, and Liang-Jian Zou map the topological phases of magnons in two-dimensional kagome ferromagnets. Kagome lattices naturally host Dirac points and flat bands, fertile ground for topology. Real materials, though, mix several anisotropic interactions, which complicates efforts to control magnon topology.

The authors compare the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction and pseudodipolar anisotropic exchange, alone and combined. Each produces its own phase diagram, and together they generate multiple phases with high Chern numbers and rich transitions. Certain phases even show thermal Hall and Nernst conductivities flipping sign with temperature, an effect tied to gaps and Berry curvature near the magnetic transition. The results point to kagome magnets as tunable platforms for magnonic devices.
arxiv-2512-20697:
Hao Chen, Titus Neupert, and Juraj Hasik simulate a fermionic topological phase with a tensor network built for bosons' cousins. Infinite projected entangled-pair states handle two-dimensional quantum matter well, including bosonic order of that kind. Extending them to fermion order requires symmetric fermion ansätze, which the authors optimize for a fractional Chern insulator.

A critical bond dimension emerges: above it, the ansatz faithfully represents the phase; below it, it does not. The state is described by single-particle Green's functions, pair correlations, and the momentum-resolved edge entanglement spectrum. A new squeezing scheme makes the spectrum reachable for large unit cells, and its low-lying part settles at small cutoffs. These insulators could host exotic particle-like ripples, so faithful simulation tools matter.
arxiv-2512-21397:
Evolutionary biologists search the space of family trees by small edits: swapping neighboring branches, or pruning a subtree and regrafting it elsewhere. Distances based on those moves are usually too hard to compute, so the field leans on the Robinson-Foulds distance, which is fast. Lena Collienne and Frederick Matsen IV ask how that cheap yardstick behaves along editing paths.

Between any two trees, a path exists whose Robinson-Foulds distance to the target never increases under neighbor interchanges, and strictly decreases under prune-and-regraft moves. A strictly decreasing interchange path, however, does not always exist. The results reassure search heuristics that hill-climbing by the cheap metric will not strand them, with one named exception.
arxiv-2512-21697:
Johanne Elise Vembe, Hicham Agueny, and their co-authors present GaDE, a GPU solver for the time-dependent Dirac equation in three dimensions. The Dirac equation governs relativistic electrons, and solving it is how physicists simulate atoms blasted by intense laser fields. Such simulations are communication-heavy and demand the largest supercomputers.

GaDE combines message passing across machines with CUDA and HIP, so it runs on both NVIDIA and AMD processors, keeping most computation on the accelerators. The team evaluated it on LUMI, a supercomputer with AMD processors and a fast interconnect. Single-processor results were comparable between the AMD and NVIDIA cards tested, with the newest NVIDIA chip ahead. Scaling tests stood out: weak scaling kept about eighty-five percent efficiency across two thousand forty-eight processors. Strong scaling gave a sixteen-fold speedup on thirty-two processors. The solver targets exascale machines and laser-matter simulations.
arxiv-2512-21897:
Carolina Aparício, Qiwei Han, and their co-authors predict whether clinical trials will succeed, using a framework that fuses the very different kinds of data a trial generates. A trial's outcome depends on the drug's molecular structure, the protocol design and entry text, and the disease's place in ontologies. Combining such mixed signals is the hard part.

Their system, MMCTOP, first converts the structured inputs into controlled natural language, a step called schema-guided textualization, and checks the conversion kept the input faithfully. Encoders then produce embeddings for each modality. A transformer backbone with a sparse mixture-of-experts, conditioned on the drug and disease, fuses them, turning on only a few experts per input. On benchmarks the system improved precision, F1 score, and ranking over unimodal and multimodal baselines. Ablations credit both the textualization and the selective routing. Temperature scaling calibrates the probabilities.
arxiv-2512-22097:
Wei-Ming Chen, Yu-tin Huang, Zi-Xun Huang, and Yohan Liu work out the wavefunction coefficients for fermion processes in de Sitter space, the expanding geometry used to model the early universe. They use a bootstrap approach: fixing how the total-energy pole is structured, then imposing conformal Ward identities and cutting rules until the coefficients are pinned down. The cutting rules for fermionic exchange are derived here for the first time.

The identities fix the leading pole residue to the flat-space amplitude and the next residues to curvature corrections. As an application, the authors derive a four-point coefficient for massless spin one-half particles exchanged through a graviton. They also show that de Sitter and Euclidean anti-de Sitter spaces give genuinely different three-point coefficients for spin three-halves operators.
arxiv-2512-22597:
Guikun Xu, Xiaohan Yi, Ziqiao Meng, Peilin Zhao, and Yatao Bian introduce EnFlow, a generative system that hunts for molecules' lowest-energy shapes. Finding ground-state conformations is central to computational chemistry, but mapping the energy landscape with physics-based pipelines is expensive. Generative models produce variety without reliable energy sense, while deterministic predictors return one structure and miss the ensemble. EnFlow couples the two approaches.

Flow-based generation is guided by an explicitly learned energy model, steering sampling toward low-energy regions and enabling energy-based ranking of what it generates. On the GEOM-QM9 and GEOM-Drugs benchmarks, the system performed strongly while needing only one or two sampling steps. Independent quantum-chemistry spot checks confirmed its learned energy scores rank conformations in a physically meaningful order.
arxiv-2512-22697:
Isaac Meza and Rahul Singh study instrumental variable regression when the data are rich but noisy, with many measured covariates and many instruments that only imperfectly reflect a few hidden factors. Their key assumption is repetition: the true covariates and true instruments each mirror a small set of underlying factors, though the two factor sets may not line up. Estimation has to recover signal through two layers of noise.

Their method runs two-stage least squares with spectral regularization, meaning the first stage learns canonical correlations between covariates and instruments and the second stage regresses on those learned combinations. The authors prove matching upper and lower bounds on the estimation error, so the method is optimal for this noisy setting. Practical guidance explains which form of spectral regularization to choose in different regimes.
arxiv-2512-22997:
Pawel Caputa, Abhigyan Saha, and Piotr Sułkowski generalize entanglement entropy so the measure survives rescaling of the state. Standard singular value decomposition underlies the usual von Neumann entropy. Its values shift when a non-Hermitian or rectangular operator is rescaled. That is a nuisance in settings like biorthogonal quantum mechanics, where scale changes are meaningless. The authors build on unit-invariant versions of the decomposition, in left, right, and two-sided forms.

Each variant yields an entropy that stays fixed under its matching class of diagonal transformations. The definitions work when input and output spaces differ in dimension or carry different metric weights. The paper applies these entropies within biorthogonal quantum mechanics, where their scale stability is the point. It also tests them on bipartite states, random matrices tied to quantum chaos and holography, and Chern-Simons theory. Across these cases the spectra stay stable and interpretable.
arxiv-2512-23097:
Yingru Li, Ziniu Li, and Jiacai Liu write a note unifying two standard ways of fine-tuning large language models. One is imitation learning, which copies demonstrated behavior. The other is reinforcement learning, which chases task rewards. Rather than treating the two as separate pipelines, they write one composite objective that combines a trajectory-level divergence penalty against demonstrations with the reward signal, then examine its gradient.

The gradient splits naturally into two pieces. One is a dense gradient for token-level imitation, which turns out to have a closed-form expression at the level of output logits, so it can be implemented efficiently on graphics hardware. The other is a sparse gradient for long-horizon reward optimization, which must be estimated by Monte Carlo sampling. This decomposition gives designers one framework where the supervised part is computed exactly while the exploratory part is sampled.
arxiv-2512-23297:
Khaled Elbassioni gives a deterministic approximation algorithm for the art gallery problem: how few guards can watch an entire polygon. Exact solutions are hard, so the algorithm settles for a provable near miss on two criteria at once. It uses somewhat more guard points than the optimum, while guaranteeing coverage of almost all of the polygon's area. The user picks how much area may be missed through a small parameter.

The guarantees cover polygons with holes and rational vertices of bounded description length. The guard set grows like the optimum times logarithmic factors in the hole count. Running time is polynomial in the polygon's description and in the log of the inverse missed-area parameter, so near-total coverage stays affordable. Determinism matters: earlier bicriteria guarantees often relied on randomization. Removing the dice makes the promise hold on every run.
arxiv-2512-23497:
Giuseppe De Palma, Saverio Giallorenzo, Ivan Lanese, and Gianluigi Zavattaro implement the Adaptable TeaStore, a reference model for microservice systems that must change configuration while running. Their tool is AIOCJ, a choreographic language in which the communication plan of a whole multiparty system is written from a global viewpoint, rather than service by service.

Because the choreography is written globally, correct communication, including freedom from deadlocks, is guaranteed by construction before, during, and after adaptation. Adaptation itself is dynamic: the scenarios for switching configurations can be fixed only at runtime, when conditions are known. Modeling TeaStore this way shows off the strengths of the approach and its current limits, and the authors suggest refinements to bring choreographic programming closer to real cloud practice.
arxiv-2512-23697:
Joon-Hwi Kim writes a technical note on how spinning particles move in the gravitational field of a Kerr black hole, the rotating black hole solution. The equations of motion for a spinning probe in Kerr are famously intricate. Finding their exact form is a long-standing problem with direct bearing on gravitational-wave physics, where spinning bodies inspiral and merge.

Kim implements a probe version of the Newman-Janis algorithm, a complex rotation trick long used to generate Kerr from simpler solutions. Applying it, he Wick rotates the all-orders geodesic deviation equation into part of the exact spinning-particle equations of motion. As a consequence, the point-particle effective theory of Kerr turns out to be fully constrained in its self-dual sector by a hidden symmetry. This implies that same-helicity gravitational Compton amplitudes exponentiate in spin to all orders.
arxiv-2512-24097:
Wenzheng Zeng, Difei Gao, Mike Zheng Shou, and Hwee Tou Ng tackle temporal grounding in video. A model watching a clip should point to supporting moments. Fluent text alone is not enough. The two tasks form a hierarchy, the authors note. Reliable answers rest on well-grounded evidence. Most systems still train the tasks tangled together.

Their framework separates the jobs but keeps the dependency. The model first grounds event-level evidence. Special evidence tokens mark that evidence. The model then answers by referring to it. A training algorithm teaches both skills at once. Grounding is treated probabilistically inside that algorithm. A synthetic dataset fills a gap in existing data. Across several tasks, the approach beat coupled baselines clearly. The team released its code in public.
arxiv-2512-24197:
David Fuentes-Jimenez and five colleagues build a reader for ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs. Their source material is famous. The Pyramid Texts and Coffin Texts survive in editions by James Allen and Adriaan de Buck. The system photographs signs from these texts. It then transcribes each sign into Gardiner's standard codes. A web tool organizes results by spell and witness.

Two recognition methods were compared. A MobileNet network learned a hundred forty hieroglyph classes. Its accuracy reached about ninety-four percent. Rare classes troubled it, though. A newer approach uses deep metric learning instead. It adapts better to signs with little training data. Its accuracy rose to near ninety-eight percent. It also recognizes more hieroglyphs overall. The final system therefore adopts metric learning as its default classifier.
arxiv-2512-24597:
Hiroki Kajiura and Makoto Matsumoto settle a seventy-year-old problem in combinatorics. A difference set is a subset of a finite group with perfectly even difference counts. The parameters (120, 35, 10) mark one stubborn case. Bruck introduced nonabelian difference sets long ago. Whether such a set exists stayed open ever since.

The answer is no, and the proof is categorical. The authors generalize finite groups to association schemes, and difference sets to equi-distributed functions. Pushouts along quotients preserve the key property. The problem then reduces to linear programming over a nonnegative integer lattice with quadratic constraints. That finite check closes the case. The method matters beyond one parameter set. Category-level tools now attack existence questions across design theory.
arxiv-2601-00197:
Shaswat Mohanty, writing alone, reports that a plain old network beats fancy new ones at forecasting stock prices. StockBot 2.0 grows out of his earlier recurrent system. It tests attention, convolution, and recurrent models side by side. All models share one fair experimental setup. Default settings keep the contest honest and simple.

Extensive tests give a clear verdict. A carefully built vanilla LSTM wins on accuracy. Its buy and sell calls also stay more stable. Transformer style models offer more flexibility on paper. That freedom does not pay off here. Data are cut into single day steps, so samples stay scarce. In that regime, recurrent bias fits the task better. Mohanty stresses a wider lesson for finance. Architecture fit can matter more than novelty. Data efficiency is a real edge in noisy markets.
arxiv-2601-00297:
Liang Zhang and coauthor Kang Zhou study how scattering amplitudes with extra derivative terms split apart. Yang Mills and gravity amplitudes are their main targets. Special higher derivative vertices are inserted into each. A known split property holds for the basic theories. The question is whether the dressed versions still split cleanly.

They expand the amplitudes into sums of simpler theory pieces. Yang Mills pairs with a scalar theory in one split. Gravity pairs with Yang Mills, or with both at once. Basic split rules then carry over piece by piece. A surprise shapes the final answer. These amplitudes do not factor into one product of currents. Their split always appears as a sum of several terms. A new hidden zero effect sits nearby in the story. The universal sum form gives amplitude builders a firm rule.
arxiv-2601-00497:
Lev Sorokin and three co-authors present STELLAR in 2026, a tool that hunts for bad inputs to AI chat systems. Such systems can give wrong, made-up, or harmful replies. Their input space is huge, so hand tests miss many weak spots. STELLAR treats the hunt as a search task. It splits inputs by style, topic, and small tweaks. It then breeds new tests from the ones that worked best.

The team tried STELLAR on three chat systems that answer questions. One test set was about safety, with both open and closed AI models. The other two helped drivers find places to go. STELLAR found far more failures than the older test methods. At best it found more than four times as many. On average it found about two and a half times as many. The tool gives app builders a sharper way to find flaws before launch.
arxiv-2601-00597:
Davide Franco improves the physics model behind a leading search for dark matter particles called WIMPs. The DarkSide-50 detector, filled with liquid argon, set strong limits on very light WIMPs using only ionization signals, despite its modest size. Turning those signals into particle limits depends on knowing exactly how much ionization a recoiling nucleus produces at low energies.

Franco combines recoil measurements from four experiments into one global fit within a standard theoretical framework. A Bayesian comparison of screening models firmly favors one of them, the Lenz-Jensen form. The refined model sharpens DarkSide-50's sensitivity to the lightest WIMPs and improves the projected reach of its successor, DarkSide-20k, guiding the next round of the hunt.
arxiv-2601-00697:
Claudio Buzzi, Daniel Panazzolo, and Paulo da Silva study piecewise smooth dynamical systems, where different rules of motion apply in different regions and the rules switch at boundaries. Smoothing such a system, called regularization, is usually done by convolution, but hard cases arise when the switching boundary has crossings, like several surfaces meeting.

The authors give a general regularization procedure for discontinuity sets shaped like normal crossings. They show a finite sequence of blowings-up, a geometric surgery, turns the problem into studying a smooth vector field on a manifold with corners. Examples in two and three dimensions illustrate the method, and even for piecewise constant fields they find unexpected dynamical phenomena emerging from the smoothing process.
arxiv-2601-00897:
Sai Teja Erukude, Jane Mascarenhas, and Lior Shamir automate the grading of individual corn kernels, a job still done mostly by eye. Seed certification, directional planting, and breeding all depend on judging kernels accurately. Their framework, CornViT, mimics the staged reasoning of a human analyst with three convolutional vision transformers in sequence.

The first stage separates pure kernels from impure ones. The second classifies pure kernels as flat or round, and the third reads embryo orientation, up or down, for the pure flat kernels. Starting from a public seed image collection, the team relabeled and filtered images into three stage-specific benchmark datasets, which they release. High-resolution color images feed each classifier in the chain.
arxiv-2601-01097:
Xuan Son Nguyen, Shuo Yang, and Aymeric Histace build neural networks that live on curved spaces known as symmetric spaces of noncompact type. This family includes hyperbolic spaces and spaces of certain matrices, which suit data with tree-like or covariance structure. The core building block of a network layer is a score based on the distance from a point to a flat cut, called a hyperplane.

The authors give one unified formula for that distance and show that earlier versions for special spaces fall out of it as cases. They also derive a closed form for harder, higher-rank spaces. With the distance in hand, they design full layers and an attention method for these spaces. Tests on image sorting, brain signal sorting, image creation, and language inference tasks support the approach. The result is a single toolbox for deep learning on a broad class of curved spaces.
arxiv-2601-01397:
Rajat Shinde, Julia Djuvsland, Davide Dapaoli, and Jim Hinton refine predictions for a glow that dark matter might cast at the center of our galaxy. Heavy dark matter particles, called WIMPs, can annihilate and produce electrons, which then bounce starlight up to gamma-ray energies. Earlier work by the team showed this secondary glow matters; now they model the galactic center more faithfully.

Their update spans a broader mass range and lets the environment vary across space. Dark matter density, radiation and magnetic fields, and electron drift all change from place to place. They test how each factor shapes the glow's brightness map and energy spectrum. The secondary signal proves robust, and including it improves the odds of spotting heavy WIMPs in inner-galaxy observations. The team releases its data products so other groups can use them in their own searches.
arxiv-2601-01497:
Tabachová and 3 co-authors examine a tool for tracing which part of a complex system drives another. Transfer entropy tracks directed flow of information, and its Renyi form adds a dial that favors rare or common events. In practice, short or messy data sets make the tool hard to estimate and even harder to read.

The authors test a nearest-neighbor estimator on made-up data with known cause and effect, varying sample size, dimension, memory, and the dial setting. They set three reliability checks and give tuning advice to handle odd negative values. When checks pass, the estimator tracked the true direction of flow across linear and nonlinear cases.
arxiv-2601-01597:
Yang and 5 co-authors simulate how gas around a young star cluster changes the fate of paired stars. Gas can drag on stars, slowing them, but outflows from stars can also push back in a less familiar effect that speeds spreading. Using a direct simulation code, they evolve a cluster of ten thousand stars inside gas of varied density.

The push-back effect widened the cluster faster and sent more stars to its edge. Pairs made of a neutron star and a normal star broke up sooner under that effect. Surviving pairs tended to keep wider orbits and rounder paths than under drag alone, showing gas shapes cluster families.
arxiv-2601-01797:
Tamim Aziz and Sanjoy Ghosal merge two generalizations of convergence. One is ideal convergence. There, a filter-like family decides which index sets are negligible. The other is convergence in probability for random variables. Those are measured with the Ky Fan metric. Their combined notion, rough ideal convergence in probability, also allows a roughness margin around the limit.

The authors show the rough ideal limit set is closed and bounded in the Ky Fan metric, and for a certain class of ideals it has a specific descriptive form. They introduce strong and weak cluster points for this convergence. The strong cluster set is always closed. The weak one is only conditionally closed. They also characterize maximal admissible ideals through these sets. The work unifies several strands of generalized convergence theory.
arxiv-2601-01997:
Beyond accuracy, recommendations should be diverse, novel, and free of runaway popularity bias. Dario Di Palma, Giovanni Maria Biancofiore, Vito Walter Anelli, Fedelucio Narducci, and Tommaso Di Noia test ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 as recommenders on three datasets, in both standard top-N and cold-start settings.

ChatGPT-4 matched or beat traditional recommenders while balancing novelty and diversity rather than parroting hits. In the cold-start scenario, where a new user has no history, both ChatGPT versions led on accuracy and novelty together, suggesting large language models are especially helpful for newcomers. The study maps strengths and limits of conversational models as recommenders when the criteria go beyond getting the rating right.
arxiv-2601-02097:
Pulsars are usually found by their flashing in time-series data, but they also twinkle: interstellar scintillation gives them a signature visible in interferometric images. Jitendra Salal, Shriharsh Tendulkar, and Visweshwar Ram Marthi simulate pulsar populations. Their aim is to map the reach of a scintillation technique. They developed it in earlier work.

Half of the pulsars detectable only by scintillation have unusually wide duty cycles, a population time-domain searches disfavor. The simulations pick out an optimal observing setup near fourteen hundred twenty megahertz with narrow channels. Applied to a future instrument like DSA-2000, the technique could add many pulsars. The gain is fifty-six percent of normal pulsars and eighty-four percent of millisecond pulsars, beyond time-domain yields. Those finds cannot be confirmed by the usual searches, though.
arxiv-2601-02397:
Alireza Rezaee computes Nash equilibria in dynamic games, the settings where several players choose strategies over time and each outcome depends on all choices together. Games like these model multi agent decisions in control and economics. Classical solvers lean on strong structural assumptions and break down for nonlinear dynamics, many players, or long time horizons, where several local equilibria can exist.

Rezaee shows by example that classical methods can miss the true global equilibrium even in small games. He then proposes two population based evolutionary methods that search the joint strategy space directly, a co evolutionary genetic algorithm and a hybrid that mixes a genetic algorithm with particle swarm optimization. Neither needs the restrictive assumptions, and both are less likely to get trapped at a merely local equilibrium.
arxiv-2601-02597:
K. Amini and six co authors demonstrate an electron source for ultrafast electron diffraction that resolves the usual trade offs of the field. Short pulses want little charge per pulse, weak samples want high flux, and high repetition rates help averaging but most systems run at about one thousand pulses per second or less. Their source combines a direct current and radio frequency design at ninety kilovolts and runs at forty thousand pulses per second with direct electron detection.

Terahertz streaking measurements retrieve compressed pulse lengths near one hundred femtoseconds at low charge, and still close to that at higher charge. Long term timing drift sits among the lowest reported for radio frequency systems. At the lowest charges an intrinsic duration near fifty six femtoseconds is inferred, among the shortest for this energy range. The source pushes throughput and brightness together instead of trading one for the other.
arxiv-2601-02897:
Jian Huang, Muyang Chen, and Xian-Hui Zhong compute how single quarks inside charmonium respond to electromagnetic probes. Charmonium particles are bound states of a charm quark and its antiquark, and their form factors describe how charge and magnetism are spread inside them. The study covers a broad set of twelve such states, from the well-known J/psi to less studied excited states with spin up to two.

The calculations use a relativized quark model, with the frame dependence of the results taken as an error estimate. Most values agree with results from lattice simulations and other approaches where those exist. The authors also give first predictions for six states whose single-quark form factors had no direct comparisons available.
arxiv-2601-03097:
Omayra Yago Nieto and three co-authors design a learning controller that steers autonomous vehicles and robots along a planned path while keeping safety guarantees. The controller works in the dual quaternion framework, a compact way to describe rigid-body motion, and commands angular and linear velocities directly. Gaussian process regression learns the unknown disturbances and modeling errors online, compensating for them inside a geometric feedback law.

Because the learning sits inside the feedback structure, the method needs no explicit parametric model of the unwanted effects, which can come from sensors, actuation couplings, or the environment. A Lyapunov-based analysis shows the tracking error stays probabilistically bounded under bounded model uncertainty. Simulations show accurate, smooth tracking even with realistic, localized disturbances acting on the vehicle.
arxiv-2601-03297:
Eduardo Santana builds a dictionary between a broad family of dynamical maps and the thermodynamic formalism of statistical mechanics. The maps work by splitting a space into two pieces and applying different rules on each, a family that includes the Syracuse maps behind the famous Collatz problem. Santana's treatment is set-theoretic, topological, and ergodic, built around a key topology and its Borel structure.

Within that frame, he argues that recurrence implies periodicity, that the topological entropy is zero, and that invariant measures decompose into ergodic parts. Cycles of the map correspond to equilibrium states of continuous potentials. Applied to Syracuse maps, the dictionary is claimed to prove that their cycles are finite in number and that no orbit diverges, which would amount to the weak Collatz conjecture. These are the author's claimed results on a long-open problem.
arxiv-2601-03397:
Hei Shing Cheung, Qicheng Long, and Zhiyue Lin present PIVONet, a learned simulator for fluids governed by advection and diffusion. The model keeps the physics inside it. It unifies neural ordinary differential equations with continuous normalizing flows. A physics-based model, parameterized through the flow, is trained offline. It becomes a fast stand-in for one specific fluid system. Later runs no longer need to integrate the full dynamics step by step.

A second part of the model captures the hidden randomness in observed fluid paths. The network output is treated as a variational distribution, and a pathwise evidence lower bound is optimized. That allows stochastic integration of the equations. The randomness lets the stand-in reproduce turbulence and random fluctuations, not only the average flow. It stays cheap enough for visualization and repeated runs.
arxiv-2601-03797:
Sayan Goswami, writing alone, studies difference sets of dense subsets of the integer lattice, a problem in additive combinatorics. For a set with positive upper Banach density, meaning it occupies a real share of the plane's grid in the long run, its difference set collects all gaps between its points. Fish asked in twenty eighteen whether some scaled copy of the integers must appear among products of coordinates of those differences.

That question remains open. Goswami proves a weaker form: for any finite sequence of natural numbers, infinitely many scaling factors work with a Milliken-Taylor configuration, a structured pattern built from the sequences, inside the product set. Partial progress on density problems like this often supplies the tools that later settle the full conjecture, so weaker structured results are genuine steps.
arxiv-2601-03897:
Ziad Ismaili Alaoui and Detlef Plump implement binary search trees inside GP 2, a rule-based graph programming language. Binary search trees are a textbook data structure, and showing they can be built idiomatically with graph transformation rules tests the language's practical reach. Their implementation uses GP 2's rooted graph transformation rules for speed and supports insertion, deletion, and query operations.

The authors argue each operation takes worst-case linear time in the number of nodes, matching naive expectations for unbalanced trees. On average, they expect logarithmic time, the classic balanced behavior target. That would put the graph-based implementation on par with imperative versions in complexity terms. Extended abstracts like this one stake out feasibility early, inviting the community to scrutinize both the construction and its runtime claims.
arxiv-2601-03997:
José Pedro Evans and six co-authors introduce a new extraction task drawn from Portuguese town meeting minutes. Minutes record local votes, but they tell the story in free, varied prose that differs by town. That variety makes automatic reading hard, unlike the fixed formats of national parliaments.

The team defines voting information extraction and builds the first benchmark for it from the CitiLink corpus. A fine-tuned encoder model with a CRF layer reaches a macro F1 score in the low ninety percent range in-domain. On unseen towns its score falls sharply, while few-shot large models drop less but cost far more to run. The group releases its benchmark, models, and scoring code for others to use.
arxiv-2601-04097:
J. Sourd, B. Vignolle, E. Gaudin, S. Burdin, and S. Tencé map how a hydride family changes its ground state as cerium replaces lanthanum. The material mixes iron-based and cerium-based electron behaviour in one crystal. Cerium share acts as a single tuning knob from zero to full replacement.

At low cerium share, superconductivity from iron electrons appears and then fades as cerium grows. A middle range shows the single-ion Kondo effect, which briefly coexists with superconductivity at the low end. Beyond half replacement, Kondo coherence and a heavy Fermi liquid emerge. At the highest shares, magnetic order sets in at low temperature. The five authors combine these scales into a phase diagram of temperature against cerium share.
arxiv-2601-04597:
A team at KBTG Labs with seven named co-authors shows that capable language models can be assembled by merging instead of trained from scratch, in a 2026 arXiv technical report. Thai organizations want models that handle Thai well and also know finance, but privacy and regulation push toward on-premise systems, and training one model with every skill is prohibitively expensive. Model merging — averaging the weights of specialists — is their economical alternative.

Two experiments carry the argument. Merging a general Qwen model with the Thai-specialized ThaiLLM improved Thai school examination performance over the general model alone. Merging in a third specialist, a finance model trained toward chartered analyst material, lifted both the Thai examinations and financial benchmarks, in English and Thai, at once. The report presents merging as a practical route to multi-capability models for industry, with the ThaiLLM initiative's open models as the base.
arxiv-2601-04797:
Victor Armegioiu studies the semigeostrophic system, a simplified model of large-scale atmospheric and ocean flow, in a 2026 mathematics paper. He works in two dimensions on a flat torus and in the small-amplitude regime, where motions stay gentle. His aim is to show how this system approaches the better-known Euler equations as the amplitude shrinks.

Armegioiu rewrites the dynamics as a flow driven by a renormalized optimal-transport energy, then expands that energy. The leading term gives the Euler model. Past it sits a correction term, a cubic Monge-Ampère expression he writes out in full. From this he derives estimates, a lifespan for strong solutions, and a measured rate for velocity convergence, making the limit precise rather than assumed.
arxiv-2601-04997:
Patrícia Gonçalves, Adriana Neumann, and Maria Chiara Ricciuti study how a driven chain of sites shakes around its steady state in a 2026 math paper. Their chain holds grains that hop from site to site, and tanks at both ends feed grains in and take grains out. The feed rates scale with the size of the chain in a set way. In the long run the chain rests in a state that is still fed and drained, yet no longer drifts.

They prove that, when the view is scaled the right way, the shakes settle to a known wave rule. The rule's shape is set by how dense the grains sit in the steady state. Edge rules of three known types show up as the tank strength shifts. Such proofs link the small-scale rules of grains to the smooth laws that physics uses at large scale.
arxiv-2601-05297:
Rohan Vitthal Thorat and Rajdip Nayek call the acts of real frames when the frame's model is off in a 2026 paper. A frame here is a built thing: a bridge, a wing, a pump. Its screen twin must stay true through the thing's whole life of use. Yet screen models use fixed, named values and skip true traits, by plain cuts in shape, stuff, drag, or edge rules. Those skips make form faults. The faults eat at how well the twin can call what is next.

Their frame grades those faults and puts them right in big screen models of frames. It casts the miss as a force no one named, learned from data in a smooth, loose way. It trims the model down by its main modes, so the work stays light. A twin kept true in this way could spot wear and risk ere a real frame fails.
arxiv-2601-05397:
Faeq Abed and 3 co-authors propose, in a 2026 paper, ways to spot much smaller dark matter signals in liquid argon detectors. These detectors watch for rare collisions that leave tiny flashes of light and charge. The team combines better light collection with a correction that strengthens the expected response at very low energies.

A second design uses quantum bits on two chips to sense single phonons, which are tiny packets of heat and vibration. Simulations suggest such a device could catch energy deposits far below normal thresholds with high efficiency. If built, the approach could widen searches for light dark matter particles, axions, and dark photons.
arxiv-2601-05597:
Silvia Casacuberta and Moritz Hardt show, in a 2026 paper, that good treatment allocations do not require precise estimates of who benefits most. Targeting usually ranks groups by estimated treatment effect and spends the budget down that list. Estimating every effect accurately demands many samples, and that cost is unavoidable for estimation itself.

Allocation is different, the authors argue. Coarse estimates can still produce nearly the same total benefit, cutting the needed samples sharply for natural effect distributions. Allowing some budget flexibility reduces the requirement further. Tests on real randomized-trial datasets found near-optimal allocations with surprisingly few samples. The result separates two goals often conflated: measuring effects precisely versus spending a treatment budget well.
arxiv-2601-05697:
The DUNE Collaboration reports, in a 2026 paper, how well its horizontal-drift far detector module can reconstruct atmospheric neutrino interactions. DUNE is a large underground neutrino test using liquid argon time projection chambers, which image particle tracks in fine detail. These neutrinos arrive from all directions and span wide energies.

The workflow adapts tools built for long-baseline analysis, retraining some machine-learning models and adding heading reconstruction for these events. Three heading methods were compared: lepton-only information, all reconstructed particles, and hit correlations. Including more than the lepton clearly raised both heading and energy resolution. Efficiencies and flavor identification showed no strong dependence on particle direction, an encouraging step toward a first oscillation analysis. In short, using the whole event, not just the lepton, gives a much sharper picture of each incoming particle.
arxiv-2601-05897:
Jakob Piribauer and Vinzent Zschuppe build in 2026 a modal logic for reasoning about abstraction refinement in system verification. Abstraction shrinks a huge or infinite state space into something checkable, and refinement restores detail step by step. Traits stated in computation tree logic can change truth value as refinement proceeds, and engineers need to know which changes are possible.

Their operators read naturally: one says a claim holds in some refinement, the other that it holds in all refinements. Upper and lower bounds for the resulting logics are given under three scenarios, covering finite abstractions, all abstractions, and all transition systems. New control-statement techniques supply the upper bounds, contributing tools to modal logic beyond this application. The bounds say, in plain terms, how strong such a logic can and cannot be in each of the three settings.
arxiv-2601-06397:
Two classic studies disagreed on how much rotation slows gas falling into a black hole. Dongho Han and 1 co-author revisit that dispute in a 2026 astrophysics paper on generalized Bondi accretion, the spherical inflow model extended to rotating gas. Angular momentum should resist inflow, but by how much was unclear.

Exploring a much wider parameter space with a slim disk model and a flexible viscosity description, the authors find the answer depends on the Bondi radius. For small Bondi radii, the accretion rate falls steeply as rotation grows; for large ones, it falls gradually, reconciling the two earlier claims. Adding outflows through a standard model, stronger winds slightly raise inflow at the outer edge, yet the mass actually swallowed drops by orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2601-06597:
Can a tool be taught so that its own drills push it toward a prized kind of fix? Nicola Aladrah and 5 co-authors say yes, if the bias is built into how its weights are named and tied in a 2026 paper. With no fine or ban in the loss, the drill can still lean. The lean comes from ties in the name scheme and the chance in the drill.

Their frame builds new name schemes and the ties that go with them. Clean math forms make the build and the sums plain to read. One scheme leans weights to the two poles, plus one and minus one. Drills in code matched the math calls. The same lean showed up as with a fined tool, yet no fine was paid. The work turns a side effect of drills into a design dial.
arxiv-2601-06897:
Viktoriia Borovik and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with elimination ideals of plücker ideals and algebras with straightening laws. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. It is well known that the Plücker ideal defining the Grassmannian is generated by quadratic Plücker relations.

These relations form a reverse lexicographic Gröbner basis and endow the Plücker algebra with the structure of an algebra with straightening laws (ASL). Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07297:
Bo-Lun Huang and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers WISE/CatWISE constraints on dysonian Waste-Heat technosignatures in nearby galaxies facilities. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. We search for galaxy-scale ( Dysonian ) waste heat in the mid-infrared using WISE .

Starting from the 2MASS Redshift Survey , we cross-match to CatWISE2020 and AllWISE , apply standard MIR AGN/starburst vetoes (Stern. Assef R90, Jarrett), and treat W1 and W2 as stellar baselines and W3 and W4 as constraining bands. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07497:
Sergio Conti and coauthors treat sharp edges in solids with smooth fields, in a 2026 analysis preprint. Their phase-field approach targets energies set on splits of a solid, built to model grain edges in polycrystals. Grains are small crystals with different orientations inside a metal or ceramic.
