The paper also separates de Broglie's two distinct pilot-wave theories, and credits Bohm's later rediscovery of the second with reviving an ontological wave function. It then traces Schrödinger's and Bohm's influence on Everett's many-worlds interpretation.
arxiv-2602-09897:
Surfaces can be studied through the curves drawn on them, and mathematicians collect those curves into a shape of their own called a complex. The fine curve complex uses every essential simple closed curve as a corner point, joining curves that never meet into higher groupings. A 2026 paper by Ryan Dickmann, Zachary Himes, Alexander Nolte, and Roberta Shapiro asks what kind of shape this fine version is, and how it compares with the older curve complex.

The authors prove the fine curve complex has the same homotopy type as the curve complex, meaning the two can be deformed into each other without tearing. They also prove the fine arc complex is contractible, so it can be shrunk to a single point. Together, these results tie a finer, more detailed construction back to known objects, giving topologists firmer ground for working with curves and arcs on surfaces.
arxiv-2602-09997:
Creative markets run on feedback, and crowd favor is its loudest signal. A 2026 paper led by Lucas Gautheron, with seven co-authors, tests what crowd scores do to collective creativity in a large online experiment. Just over a thousand participants again and again picked images from changing markets and produced their own edits.

Showing crowd scores reduced cultural diversity and slowed innovation, delaying beauty gains. During selection, popular images drew a snowball edge as participants built on them. During creation, participants made tamer changes and grew patterns already in play. That feedback thus steers not only what gets chosen, but the form and direction of new work itself.
arxiv-2602-10097:
Training-data influence scores usually collapse a whole recurrent computation into one number, hiding when an example mattered. A 2026 paper led by Georgios Kaissis, with four co-authors, studies looped transformers, where one shared block repeats for many iterations to enable latent reasoning. The team introduces Step-Decomposed Influence, which unrolls the recurrent graph and attributes influence to specific loop iterations.

A TensorSketch implementation makes the method practical at transformer scale without ever materializing per-example gradients. Tests on looped GPT-style models and algorithmic puzzles show the method scales well. It matches full-gradient baselines closely and supports varied attribution and interpretability tasks with per-step insight into latent reasoning.
arxiv-2602-10297:
Mean-field systems keep joint effects alive as degrees of freedom grow, raising questions about integrability and chaos in large finite systems. A 2026 paper led by Matheus Rolim Sales, with two co-authors, investigates a quartic mean-field Hamiltonian model, focusing on how the thermodynamic limit relates to finite-size chaotic dynamics. The thermodynamic limit is studied in the Vlasov no-collision framework, yielding a self-matching single-particle account.

Conditions are found under which mean-field dynamics becomes effectively self-ruled, and swings of intensive quantities fade algebraically with system size, backing integrability's emergence as size grows infinite. Finite-size dynamics via the largest Lyapunov exponent over a wide range of sizes shows that exponent fading algebraically, matching chaos suppression in the thermodynamic limit. Non-extensive methods further track the entropic index over time.
arxiv-2602-10497:
Khai-Hoan Nguyen-Dang proves a trait of the zeros of a special extremal function in a 2026 paper. The Hormander-Bernhardsson function has real zeros whose squares form a sequence of interest to spectral theory. The question is whether that sequence is admissible in the sense of Quine, Heydari, and Song.

Using a recent analytic description of the zero set, the author shows the heat trace admits a full small-time expansion. That expansion runs in pure powers of the square root of time. The proof rests on an analytic normal form for the squared zeros, a uniform Taylor expansion, and a Mellin-Hurwitz zeta analysis of weighted Gaussian sums. Uses include meromorphic continuation and special values for the associated spectral zeta function.
arxiv-2602-10797:
Felix Naunheimer and six co-authors explain puzzling spin-wave steering in etched magnet films in a 2026 paper. Spin waves carry information for analog and wave-based work, and focused ion beam work tailors their spread in yttrium iron garnet. But wave size responds unevenly to rising ion dose, blocking forward design.

The team presents a system checked in tests linking noted strain-induced bias to its magnet-elastic origin. Beam-induced lattice flaws drive elastic and plastic bending growing toward partial mess, each stage shaping spread clearly. Joint etching and atomic force scope images measure thickness changes, grounding the model. The system turns a puzzling dose response into a planned bounce landscape.
arxiv-2602-10897:
Lea Reuter and three co-authors extend multi-track reconstruction at Belle II to multiple detectors in a 2026 paper. High backgrounds and sensor ageing degrade track finding in the central drift chamber, reducing purity and speed. New recipes must mitigate that degradation as the test runs.

Building on an earlier end-to-end multi-track recipe, the team incorporates inputs from both the drift chamber and the silicon vertex sensor. Those inputs feed a multi-modal network. Graph neural networks handle the irregular sensor structure, while object condensation addresses the unknown, varying particle count per event. The approach at once identifies all tracks in an event and determines their settings, demonstrating improved reconstruction under Belle II settings.
arxiv-2602-11197:
Wave spread in high-contrast media defeats many neural tools. Advait Balaji and five co-authors propose a hybrid that splits the spread tool in two: smooth background propagation and a high-contrast correction. A Fourier neural tool learns the background, producing globally coupled trait tokens.

Those tokens pass to a vision model, where focus models the strong, spatial spread correction. On high-rate Helmholtz problems with sharp contrasts, the hybrid beats standalone Fourier tools and models on phase and amplitude scores, with favourable scores-per-setting scaling. The work suits seismic imaging and inversion, where salt bodies and sharp interfaces dominate.
arxiv-2602-11297:
Splitting the Ricci scalar into bulk and edge parts opens a new route to stellar models. Sudan Hansraj and two co-authors study stellar structure in f(G,B) gravity, where the edge term does not affect motion. That keeps structure equations at second order, avoiding ghost instabilities.

For the pure quadratic case, they derive equations for thermodynamic factors and shape, since the straight case reduces to general relativity. Vacuum shape yields two possible metrics, and the isotropy equation proves autonomous, a rarity in stellar building. Dynamical systems analysis, via a chosen gauge and phase portraits, shows invariant submanifolds are mostly stable, with nearby paths approaching them.
arxiv-2602-11597:
Detecting slow neutrons cleanly matters for security and science, and glass scintillators offer a transparent alternative to classic detectors. Yuhang Liu and seven co-authors characterize SG101, a thermal-neutron-sensitive glass, against the established EJ426 scintillator under neutron irradiation. Paired with organic scintillators, SG101 reaches strong separation scores for thermal neutrons versus gamma rays, and one pairing resolves three populations at once: gamma rays, fast neutrons, and thermal neutrons.

Coincidence counts also tell a story: fast-thermal pairs and gamma-fast-thermal triples both far exceed accidental background within a 100-microsecond window, confirming real physical correlations rather than chance overlaps. The authors conclude SG101 is a promising candidate where high-efficiency thermal neutron detection and precise event tagging are both required.
arxiv-2602-11697:
Linked microring resonators create band-like optical states with nonlinear behavior no single resonator can match. Luca Trinchão and eight co-authors study hybridized optical parametric oscillation in three coupled silicon nitride microrings, where four-wave mixing links bands across spatial and spectral modes. In a symmetric layout they observe varied phase-matching pathways set by the dispersive band structure.

An analytical model captures the gain of these interband processes and yields closed-form expressions for the main gain peaks, extending readily to larger coupled networks. An asymmetric design then co-engineers mode overlap and dispersion to run on a compact 7-gigahertz spacing without mode competition. The work sets design rules for nonlinear dynamics in coupled-resonator platforms, with uses in photonic computing and quantum information.
arxiv-2602-11997:
A decade of work has transformed calculations of heavy-hadron decays, driven by striking puzzles and a stubborn puzzle. Aoife Bharucha reviews progress in decays of B and D mesons and baryons holding a heavy bottom or charm quark. Measurements of branching ratios, angular observables, and lepton universality ratios in bottom-to-strange and bottom-to-charm transitions rank among the only signs of physics beyond the Standard Model.

A second driver is the two-way split in pinning down the CKM elements Vub and Vcb. The review first covers recent work for bottom-to-strange and charm-to-up decays that could shed light on neutral-current anomalies. It then summarizes progress on Vub and Vcb, and finally discusses the theory status and lab prospects for the lepton ratios in decays with leptons.
arxiv-2602-12197:
Entanglement entropy offers a bridge between quantum information and gravity, but most versions assume spacetime has no torsion, or twist. Dušan Đorđević led this work with one co-author, Dragoljub Gočanin, extending holographic entanglement entropy to five-dimensional Chern-Simons gravity with torsion. The classic Ryu-Takayanagi idea already reaches beyond Einstein gravity, yet torsion had been left out.

Their proposal adds a universal divergent term tied to the logarithm of the ultraviolet cutoff, and they argue that torsion alone creates that term. The result matters for theories where geometry twists as well as curves, and it gives a clean marker to test whether torsion leaves a trace in boundary entanglement.
arxiv-2602-13197:
Robots can learn manipulation by watching human videos, but videos teach post-grasp motion better than grasping itself, especially for non-human-like hands. Albert Zhai and five co-authors present Perceive-Simulate-Imitate, a framework for modular manipulation policy learning from human video motion data filtered in simulation. A dedicated grasp generator proposes stable grasps, but arbitrary stable grasps often fail downstream tasks, so paired grasp-trajectory filtering in simulation adds grasp suitability labels.

Those labels enable supervised learning of task-oriented grasping alongside motion imitation. Real-world experiments show precise manipulation skills learned efficiently without any robot data, significantly more robust than naive grasp-generator use. The framework shows that simulation filtering can turn abundant human video into robot skills, bridging the embodiment gap between human hands and robot grippers.
arxiv-2602-13397:
Cepheid stars anchor the cosmic distance ladder through period-luminosity relations, but Milky Way calibrations have carried hidden errors. This paper revisits multi-wavelength period-luminosity-color relations for Cepheids in the Magellanic Clouds and the Milky Way. The relation is grounded in stellar physics: luminosity follows radius and surface temperature, with period and color as proxies. In the Clouds, the relation recovers known disk geometries and tilts, validating its power.

For Milky Way Cepheids, residuals proved achromatic across all filters. That points to parallax errors as the main scatter source rather than dust or physics. Band-averaged corrections sharpened parallaxes roughly twofold, yielding a final relation with 0.04 magnitude scatter, about 2 percent distance precision per star. Barry F. Madore leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13497:
Empty space in quantum field theory behaves like a nonlinear optical medium, giving effects such as vacuum birefringence. ModMax is a notable model: a conformally invariant nonlinear extension of Maxwell theory that keeps classical symmetries while predicting new optical effects. This paper studies ModMax optics under uniform external fields, revisiting index solutions for constant magnetic and electric backgrounds.

From those solutions come wave modes and phase shifts for plane waves in a pure magnetic background, plus a Goos-Hanchen analysis at an interface between a simple dielectric and a ModMax medium. A general reflection analysis then yields complex Kerr rotation for both background field orderings, with the gamma parameter and field ratios playing central roles in rotation and shape. M. J. Neves leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-14297:
Andreas L. Teigen and two co-authors test a 2026 arXiv hybrid for camera motion estimation. Two-frame relative pose optimization usually relies on photometric error or re-projection error, each tied to a feature paradigm with its own accuracy and robustness tradeoffs. The paper investigates a third route that merges both strengths.

Densely sampled geometric feature descriptors replace photometric error with a descriptor residual, bringing sub-pixel accuracy to differential photometric methods while keeping descriptor expressiveness. Experiments show accurate tracking from the hybrid, yet it ultimately does not beat re-projection-based pose optimization despite using more information. The authors analyze why the extra information fails to translate into gains.
arxiv-2602-14497:
Tobias Schmidt and one co-author prove a 2026 arXiv set of bounds for self-pushing random walks. The class holds the two-dimensional simple random walk, re-weighted by a self-pushing Gibbsian pair potential. Lower bounds on the diffusion constant are proved for short-range pushes, while far-reaching pushes yield super-spreading acts.

In the super-spreading regime, faster time fade can be offset by stronger space push, and vice versa. The trick joins GKS-based link bounds on path space with recursive multi-scale gauges. The results sharpen lore of how self-push reshapes spread, from plain spreading to faster-than-spread motion under long-range push.
arxiv-2602-14597:
Symmetry in spaces that mix ordinary and odd directions needs a wider form of group theory. Alexandr Zubkov works in that wider setting, with quasi-reductive supergroups. He sorts the cases where the largest ordinary part is small, matching one of three classic groups.

The three types are the general linear group in two dimensions and its special and projective forms. Zubkov gives a full list of the supergroups in each case. He then uses the list to describe centralizers of certain tori. That step links the classification to concrete structure inside these groups.
arxiv-2602-14697:
Lunjun Zhang and colleagues propose Evolutionary System Prompt Learning, a way for language models to improve both their weights and their prompts at once. In each round of reinforcement learning, the method samples trajectories under several system prompts in parallel. It then updates model weights by learning and evolves prompts by mutation and crossover, driven by the model's own reflection.

Selection rests on relative performance ratings, so stronger prompts survive and weaker ones fade. The joint approach treats context and weights as partners rather than rivals, aiming at agents that improve from experience on their own. Zhang's paper frames prompt evolution as a practical route to self-improving systems.
arxiv-2602-14797:
Ken-Ichi Yoshikawa tracks a twist measure, analytic torsion, as curved shapes with a group of symmetries sink toward a bad edge. A kind, semi-positive bundle with the same symmetries twists the core bundle, and the log of the twist measure for smooth fibres gains a clean edge form.

The lead term blows up like a log, the next like a log of a log. Without the group, the lead size comes from an integral of shape classes, as the paper shows. Sinking shapes thus gain a precise edge law for their twist.
arxiv-2602-14997:
Mangliers and colleagues bring spectral convolution to orbifolds for geometric deep learning. Geometric deep learning handles data beyond flat Euclidean form, such as graphs and manifolds, and new application data keeps demanding fresh structures that learning methods can use. Spectral convolution already serves as a building block for network-like designs on non-Euclidean data. This paper extends that tool to orbifold-structured data.

The extension gives practitioners a block for learning on orbifolds within geometric deep learning. Theory is the focus, and the authors illustrate it with an example from music theory. The result widens the class of structured domains that can be made accessible to machine learning methods.
arxiv-2602-15297:
Polson and colleagues develop a setup for fit checks through Bayes risk. Old methods are tuned either at fixed strictness, the CLT scale, or through fast powers, the LDP scale. They show Bayes-risk best tuning works on the middle-shift scale, giving square-root-of-log-n growth of refusal limits and fading Type I error.

First, they state the Rubin-Sethuraman plan for KS-type stats as a risk-tuning theorem with rules on beliefs and tools. Second, they develop the link between Bayes-risk series and Sanov info limits, showing how log-n-order cuts arise when risk, not powers, is the rule. Third, they provide uses for place checks under Laplace groups, shape checks via Bayes parts, and Fisher info. The rule is that data size enters Bayes-optimal limits through the middle-shift scale, joining KS and Sanov views under one rule.
arxiv-2602-15397:
Dong and colleagues tackle coding in Vision-Language-Action models, which use the built-in self-feeding model of Vision-Language Models and show better task chasing. Key to this model is coding, yet its plan has aimed on rebuild truth, missing its effect on tuning. The puzzle of what makes good action coders stays open.

The team closes this gap by setting rules for VLA tuning. They name habits based on info ideas: maxed time token sharing, cut words overlap, multi-mode shared info, and token freedom. Led by these rules, they offer ActionCodec, a high-speed coder that lifts training speed and VLA speed across sim and real-world tests. On LIBERO, a SmolVLM2 2B fine-tuned with ActionCodec hits about 95 and a half percent wins without robotics pre-training. With design boosts, this hits about 97 percent, a new SOTA for VLA models without robotics pre-training.
arxiv-2602-15497:
Skresanov works alone on a classic hard task: deciding whether two finite groups, given by their full multiplication tables, are the same group in disguise. For groups in general, the best known test runs in quasi-polynomial time, but some families admit much faster tests. This paper gives a polynomial-time test for extensions of abelian groups by groups with a bounded number of generators.

Two gains follow. Abelian-by-cyclic extensions get a fast test that extends a 2009 result of Le Gall for coprime cases. Abelian-by-simple extensions get a fast test that extends a 2017 result of Grochow and Qiao for central cases. The key new tool is a fast method to compute the unit group of a finite ring, which may prove useful on its own.
arxiv-2602-15697:
Almudevar and Almudevar revisit a famous 2015 claim: that a large share of published results in psychological science failed to reproduce. The Open Science Collaboration study behind that claim was highly influential, and this article reviews it from several angles. First comes an extended analysis of the study methods.

The authors show that the OSC methodology induces a bias strong enough on its own to explain the gap between OSC reproducibility estimates and more optimistic estimates from similar studies. A broader literature review and discussion of reproducibility in experimental science follow. For scientific and ethical reasons, they argue that a considered balance of false positive and false negative rates beats a single-minded focus on false positives alone.
arxiv-2602-16097:
Claudia Zendejas-Morales leads a team of three researchers fighting a fade-out problem in quantum kernels. Fidelity-based quantum kernels link quantum feature maps to classical kernel methods, but as systems grow or circuits grow more expressive, the similarity matrix drifts toward the identity and informative structure washes out. This exponential concentration threatens the practical use of such kernels.

The team tests two fixes built in Qiskit: local kernels that aggregate similarities patch by patch, and multi-scale kernels that mix local and global similarity across patch sizes. Benchmarks on several tabular data sets, under matched preprocessing and SVM protocols, show both fixes ease concentration and enrich kernel spectra versus the global baseline. Effects on classification accuracy vary with data set and feature dimension, so mitigation helps structure even when accuracy gains depend on context.
arxiv-2602-16197:
Multi-channel systems can lose input channels at deployment, partly or fully, which undermines reliability in real settings. Rong Fu and coauthors present ModalImmune, a training design that enforces channel immunity by intentionally and controllably collapsing chosen channel information during training. The model then learns joint codes robust to destructive channel influence. Four parts drive the design: a spectrum-adaptive collapse regularizer, an information-gain guided controller, curvature-aware gradient masking, and a certified Neumann-truncated hyper-gradient step for automatic meta-parameter tuning.

Tests on standard multi-channel benchmarks show improved resilience to channel removal and corruption, while retaining convergence stability and rebuild capacity. The approach treats channel loss not as an edge case but as a condition to train for directly. By cutting chosen channels on purpose during training, it prepares models for the degraded inputs they will actually face.
arxiv-2602-16897:
Seongsu Kim and co-authors benchmark machine learning Hamiltonians as direct energy-force predictors. Such models have gained traction as fast approximations of electronic structures such as orbitals and electron densities, also enabling direct evaluation of energies and forces from predictions. Yet existing models were judged mainly by reconstruction scores, leaving their energy-force skill unclear.

The new benchmark computes energies and forces directly from predicted Hamiltonians. Within it, the authors propose QHFlow2, with an SO(2)-equivariant backbone and a two-stage edge update. It cuts Hamiltonian error by forty percent against the prior best model with fewer parameters. On MD17 and rMD17, it is the first Hamiltonian model to reach NequIP-level force accuracy, and on QH9 it cuts energy error by up to a fifth against MACE. Hamiltonian accuracy gains translate into better energy and force scores.
arxiv-2602-17197:
Wei Dai led a three-author paper in algebra on which finite-dimensional algebras arise as endomorphism algebras of silting complexes over hereditary abelian categories. Call that class E. The paper proves E is closed under three operations: taking idempotent quotients, idempotent subalgebras, and tau-reduction.

The same closure holds for the smaller class of shod algebras, the authors show. Several classic families, including laura, glued, and weakly shod algebras, are also proved closed under idempotent quotients. That result extends a known theorem once proved only for special idempotents, giving algebraists a broader stability picture for these classes.
arxiv-2602-17397:
Panagiotis Koletsis led a six-author survey of optical remote sensing at a high level. Advances in computer vision have propelled remote sensing forward, while drone use expands across organizations. Most drones carry RGB cameras by default, robust sensors that are among the easiest to use and interpret. The literature on optical remote sensing is vast, spanning diverse tasks, capabilities, and methodologies, each of which could merit its own survey.

This work provides a comprehensive overview of the field's capabilities, presenting key information such as datasets and insights. It aims to guide researchers entering the field, offering high-level insights and helping them focus on areas most relevant to their interests. To the authors' knowledge, no existing survey addresses this holistic perspective, making the work a rare one-stop entry point for optical remote sensing.
arxiv-2602-17497:
Wen-Tse Chen led a seven-author team on retrospective in-context learning for temporal credit assignment with large language models. Agents learning from their own samples and thin environmental feedback face a core hurdle. Temporal credit assignment eases it by turning thin feedback into dense training signals. Older routes use task-specific value functions, which learn slowly and transfer poorly. The team instead taps pretrained language model knowledge to turn sparse rewards into dense signals, namely the advantage function, via retrospective in-context learning.

They add RICOL, an online frame refining policy step by step from RICL credit results. Tests show RICL gauges the advantage function well from few samples and picks out key states. In four BabyAI settings, RICOL matches standard online reinforcement learning on final performance while using samples far more thriftily. The work points to language models as a route to thriftier, more portable reinforcement learning.
arxiv-2602-17697:
Nada Zine and team treat large language models as tunable systems to tame run-time costs. Run time dominates total compute, so its tuning matters for energy and lasting use, yet the setup space of inference servers defies full testing. Variability models from software building offer an orderly alternative.

The team models output settings and their constraints with a feature-based variability model, using the Hugging Face library. They sample typical setups and measure energy use, latency and scores, then learn forecast models from the data. Results show variability models manage run-time tangle well, revealing setting effects, links and trade-offs. They also predict run-time conduct from limited measures, opening a bridge between software building and machine learning for green setup choices.
arxiv-2602-17997:
Zehao Jin and colleagues build a neural controller for a simulated fruit fly directly from the wiring of the adult fruit fly brain. The whole-brain connectome becomes a graph-structured model that steers whole-body movement, trained with deep reinforcement learning. Connectomes map brain-wide neural connections, but their use as controllers for embodied agents had barely been explored.

The resulting Fly-connectomic Graph Model held stable performance across varied locomotion tasks and learned more efficiently than both graph and non-graph baselines. The authors present the approach as a biologically informed route to control policy design, turning whole-brain wiring principles into architectural priors that guide learning. Dynamic information flow through the model also aids interpretability. The work offers a computational platform for studying how brains convert sensation into movement, and a step toward intelligent systems aligned more closely with nature.
arxiv-2602-18097:
Aarati Andrea Noronha and Jean Oh present a framework for self-driving cars meeting cyclists, weighing safety and speed. The approach mixes Hamilton-Jacobi reachability analysis with deep Q-learning, jointly handling safety pledges and fast travel. A value function, found as the answer to a time-based Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman inequality, gives a numeric safety measure for each system state.

That safety metric enters reward learning as a shaped reward signal. The method also models the cyclist's latent response to the vehicle, letting noise inputs reflect human comfort and habit shifts. It is tested through trials and checks against human driving habits and a current state-of-the-art method.
arxiv-2602-18297:
Usman Anwar and four co-authors study when chain-of-thought monitors can be trusted. Their 2026 paper treats monitors as language-model systems that read reasoning traces to flag traits like test-hacking in code generation. Using information theory, the team shows shared information between reasoning trace and output is necessary but not sufficient for monitorability.

Two error sources can sink monitors: the information gap, how much of the trace's information the monitor actually extracts, and elicitation error, how closely the monitor nears the ideal monitoring function. Worryingly, trace obfuscation can appear even without pressure against monitoring. A practical label-free training objective based on trace-output mutual information keeps traces readable even under training against a monitor, and eases reward hacking when task rewards are imperfect. The work gives monitor builders both a diagnosis and a fix.
arxiv-2602-18397:
Wenqi Jiang and three co-authors map the inference performance of vision-language-action models for robots. Their 2026 paper asks a practical question: how should future VLA models and systems be designed for real-time inference? Real robots demand strict timing, yet the performance landscape stays murky across the huge space of model and system combinations.

The team introduces VLA-Perf, an analytical performance model covering arbitrary pairings of VLA models and inference systems, then runs the first systematic study of that landscape. Model-side factors include scaling, architecture, long-context video, asynchronous inference, and dual-system pipelines. Deployment-side factors include on-device, edge, and cloud execution, plus how hardware power and network speed jointly set end-to-end latency. Fifteen distilled takeaways offer practical guidance for future VLA design.
arxiv-2602-18497:
Suraj Ranganath builds a pipeline for enterprise question benchmarks over knowledge graphs. His 2026 paper notes firms rely on RDF knowledge graphs and SPARQL for exposing operational data via natural language interfaces, yet public benchmarks miss proprietary schemas, prefixes, and query patterns.

Ranganath presents PIPE-RDF, a three-phase pipeline building schema-specific natural-language-to-SPARQL benchmarks with reverse querying, balanced templates, retrieval prompting, deduplication, and validation with repair based on execution. He tests it on a fixed-schema company slice of five thousand companies from public data. It generates a balanced benchmark of four hundred fifty question-SPARQL pairs across nine categories. After repair, the pipeline reaches one hundred percent parse and execution validity, with pre-repair validity above ninety-six point five percent. Entity diversity metrics, template coverage, and cost breakdowns support deployment planning, and structured artifacts and operational metrics are released for evaluation and planning.
arxiv-2602-18597:
Philipp Bartmann and one co-author study heat flow. Their 2026 paper examines the heat equation for the Hodge Laplacian operator. Using new techniques, the team proves Davies-Gaffney-Grigoryan bounds for the heat semigroup kernel on square-summable sequences.

Those bounds extend the semigroup to p-summable sequences for every p from one to infinity. The team further establishes p-independence of the Hodge spectrum under bounded curvature and uniform subexponential growth. While the main focus is the Hodge Laplacian, the results are proven for general positive magnetic operators on graphs.
arxiv-2602-18997:
SMD is a widely used tuning method. How it acts with matrix params is less clear. Danil Akhtiamov, with three co-authors, investigates that case in 2026. Vector-valued predictions are used. The setting matters for multi-class classification and matrix completion.

Focus falls on the overparameterised regime. There, parameters outnumber training samples. SMD with matrix mirror functions converges exponentially to a global interpolator. The work also generalises classical implicit bias results for vector SMD. Matrix SMD reaches the unique solution with least Bregman divergence from initialisation. It must interpolate the data. Mirror maps thus dictate inductive bias in high-dimensional, multi-output problems.
arxiv-2602-19397:
Quantum state discrimination means telling quantum states apart, a task that matters for sensing and communication. Min Namkung and Hyang-Tag Lim study it under a fixed failure chance, a unified setting where both errors and failures can occur. Earlier methods show contextuality enhancement, beating classical bounds, in both minimum-error and unambiguous discrimination.

The authors show in theory that enhancement persists at fixed failure chance, but vanishes in a certain middle range of failure chances. That gap has no counterpart in standard methods, where both standard approaches beat the noncontextual bound for equal priors. How the gap appears depends on how confusable the states are, linking the effect to state geometry.
arxiv-2602-19497:
Unified models that handle many modes can reason over several related images, yet benchmarks rarely test multi-image context creation. Mingrui Wu and four co-authors introduce MICON-Bench, a benchmark with six tasks testing cross-image composition, contextual reasoning, and keeping identities intact. Most current tests focus on text-to-image creation or single-image editing, leaving multi-image skills unmeasured.

The paper also proposes an evaluation-by-checkpoint system in which a multi-mode large language model checks semantic and visual consistency. A training-free tool, Dynamic Attention Rebalancing, shifts attention during inference to improve clarity and reduce made-up details. Broad tests show the benchmark and tool pushing forward multi-image creation in unified models.
arxiv-2602-19797:
Polynomial identity algebras carry a cocharacter sequence that records which partitions appear, and how often, in their identities. A 2026 arXiv paper by Elitza Hristova, working alone, studies that sequence for several classes of algebras over a field where the characteristic is zero.

Berele's eventual arm width measures how many very large parts a partition in the sequence can have, and he showed it equals one for Lie nilpotent algebras. Hristova proves the converse for unital algebras: arm width one holds exactly when the algebra is Lie nilpotent, via the finite size of the proper polynomial algebra. She also bounds the counts when the identity ideal is a product of long-commutator ideals, with applications to noncommutative invariant theory.
arxiv-2602-19897:
NGC 4051 is a nearby active galaxy known for rapid X-ray flickering and a complex wind, and new high-resolution spectra now sharpen the picture of that wind. A 2026 arXiv paper by James Reeves and nine co-authors presents a first high-resolution XRISM Resolve spectrum for this galaxy, taken while it was historically bright.

The spectrum resolves two blue-shifted iron absorption troughs from two outflow components moving at different speeds. Time-resolved analysis shows the absorption varies within a day, with velocity rising across the observation. That rise fits either two separate passing absorbers or one accelerating outflow. In the latter case the acceleration looks too large for radiation pressure, favouring magnetic driving, and the wind's kinetic power sits below the Eddington level, unlike recent powerful quasar winds.
arxiv-2602-20297:
Haochen Zhang and two co-authors sharpen regret theory for reinforcement learning with linear function approximation. Earlier gap-dependent guarantees did not cover algorithms that reach nearly minimax-optimal worst-case regret. This 2026 paper closes that gap for the optimism-based algorithm LSVI-UCB++. It gives the first gap-dependent regret bound for it, improving the dependence on feature dimension and horizon over prior results.

To explain the cost of optimism, they also prove a lower bound for algorithms built on persistent ellipsoidal optimism. For LSVI-UCB++, it shows the leading terms of their upper bound are tight up to logarithmic factors. A further lower bound for arbitrary algorithms shows the logarithmic dependence on episode count and the cubic dependence on horizon are intrinsic to gap-dependent regret in linear settings. The bounds narrow the gap between upper and lower limits and clarify optimism-based exploration.
arxiv-2602-20397:
Erik B. Monson and nineteen co-authors study star formation and hot interstellar gas in NGC 4254, also known as M99, on sub-galactic scales. Star formation rates come from modeling ultraviolet-to-infrared data with flexible histories, and X-ray maps come from Chandra data with point sources removed. Spectra from five regions, chosen by star formation density, yield gas luminosities and plasma temperatures.

The team tests how gas temperature and luminosity scale with star formation density against feedback models. Hot gas emission matches thermalization of forty to fifty percent of supernova energy, with mass-loading falling as density rises. Fitted relations show temperature and efficiency rising with density to a power near one third. Diffuse X-rays run two hundred times fainter than hydrogen-alpha emission, and the hot gas looks over-pressurized for equilibrium pressure, consistent with expansion into surrounding gas.
arxiv-2602-20497:
Diffusion transformers generate striking images and video, but their compute demands block practical use. Peiliang Cai and five co-authors propose LESA, a learnable stage-aware predictor method trained in two stages. A Kolmogorov-Arnold network learns temporal feature mappings from data. A multi-stage, multi-expert design assigns specialized predictors to different noise-level stages. This gives more precise and robust feature forecasting than simple reuse or training-free prediction.

Experiments show significant acceleration with high-fidelity generation intact. Speed is five times faster on FLUX.1-dev with a one percent quality drop. It is over six times faster on Qwen-Image with about twenty percent quality improvement over TaylorSeer. It is five times faster on HunyuanVideo with about twenty-five percent PSNR improvement over TaylorSeer. State-of-the-art results on text-to-image and text-to-video synthesis validate the training-based method across models.
arxiv-2602-20597:
Parsing hands and active objects in first-person video matters for next-generation embodied agents, yet current methods stumble. Yuejiao Su and four co-authors note three flaws. Query starts lean on semantic cues or learned settings and adapt poorly when the active object changes. Pixel-level features can smuggle interaction-irrelevant content into masks. Models can suffer interaction illusion, predicting physically inconsistent scenes. Their end-to-end method, InterFormer, tackles all three flaws.

InterFormer grounds query starts in the spatial dynamics of hand-object contact through a Dynamic Query Generator. A Dual-context Feature Selector fuses coarse interactive cues with semantic features, cutting irrelevant noise and stressing interactive links. A Conditional Co-occurrence loss adds hand-object relationship rules to enforce physical consistency. The model leads methods on the EgoHOS set and the hard out-of-distribution mini-HOI4D set, showing generalization. Code and models are public.
arxiv-2602-20797:
Nayanthara and one co-author work on the inverse eigenvalue problem: which lists of numbers can appear as the eigenvalues of a non-negative matrix? They narrow the classic question to persymmetric matrices and ask which spectra those matrices can realize.

The authors settle an open problem posed in earlier work. They prove that the persymmetric and general problems agree for trace-zero spectra of five complex numbers. They also give new sufficient conditions for other classes of spectra. Their method is constructive, built on structural features of persymmetric matrices and their characteristic polynomials, with perturbation results for imaginary parts included.
arxiv-2602-20897:
A single post can spark a wave of reactions, but how individual activity drives collective response is still an open question. Samuel Martin-Gutierrez, Juan Losada, and Rosa Benito measure that link in this 2026 arXiv paper. They define efficiency as reactions per action and study its distribution across systems.

The efficiency distribution shows the same universal shape in three very different systems: Twitter, Wikipedia, and the scientific citation network. To explain it, the authors build three minimal statistical models with different levels of dependence between activity and response. The models reproduce the data and can serve as null models for richer, domain-specific theories.
arxiv-2602-20997:
Checking a quantum network means pinning down the causal order of its channels, ideally with no trust in the devices. Masahito Hayashi, Longyang Cao, Baichu Yu, and Yuan-Yuan Zhao offer such a test in this 2026 arXiv paper. Two lone players infer the fixed-order plan of an unknown setting from input-output stats alone, testing Markovian rules proved needed and enough for each plan class.

Under a stated generic-sampling rule, a randomly picked binary measure-and-prepare setup keeps exact identifying power with chance one. An optical trial with a low-randomness build still sorts every tested process right for causal order and memory presence. The authors hint the random-draw premises may be eased. Readers get a working setup for causal reading in quantum nets.
arxiv-2602-21097:
Turbulent fluids usually spread passive tracers like Brownian motion, but heavy-tailed jumps may break that rule. Paolo Cifani, Franco Flandoli, and Lorenzo Marino test the question numerically in this 2026 arXiv paper, modeling a tracer advected by divergence-free fields weighted by heavy-tailed jump processes. The outcome hinges on the tail behavior of the driving noise.

With standard stable processes, very large jumps survive interaction with spatial complexity and produce anomalous super-diffusive transport. When the noise is truncated or exponentially tempered, suppressing extreme jumps, transport returns to a classical diffusive regime. The dichotomy shows small-scale spatial structure alone does not guarantee Brownian dispersion.
arxiv-2602-21297:
Rank boards grade language models by head-to-head match-ups forced into a single order, breaking basic social-choice rules. Hadi Khalaf, Serena Wang, Daniel Halpern, Itai Shapira, Flavio du Pin Calmon, and Ariel Procaccia offer a many-sided other path in this 2026 arXiv paper: robust draws. Standard maximal draws pool tastes with no forced structure, but they prove highly touchy to taste mix.

They can favor models that fail badly on own tasks or user groups. Robust draws instead tune worst-case scores under plausible taste shifts. On large taste data sets they give more steady win-rate promises across raters and recover a stable set of top models. Moving from rankings to sets of winners backs a world of matching systems serving varied tastes.
arxiv-2602-21397:
Sajjad Ghiasvand and three co-authors propose MMLoP, multi-modal low-rank prompting for adapting vision-language models like CLIP. Pretrained weights stay untouched. Deep prompting of both vision and text encoders boosts scores but normally needs millions of trainable parameters. That gives up the efficiency that makes prompt tuning attractive.

MMLoP factorizes prompts at each transformer layer into a low-rank form. It needs only 11,500 trainable parameters, close to early text-only methods like CoOp. Three added parts close the accuracy gap. A consistency loss anchors prompted features to frozen zero-shot CLIP. A drift correction removes global embedding shift. A shared up-projection ties vision and text prompts together. Across 11 datasets it reaches a harmonic mean of 79.70 percent on base-to-novel generalization.
arxiv-2602-21697:
AI code-editing tools score well on benchmarks, yet studies find developers finish tasks 19 percent slower with AI help, and most recommendations break their train of thought. The mismatch comes from static commit snapshots that lack timing, pushing models to aim at final results rather than the stepwise edits developers actually make. Chenyan Liu and seven co-authors present EditFlow, which rebuilds developer editing flows to benchmark and tune recommendation systems against that real process.

EditFlow tackles three hard problems: collecting edit-order data without costly hand labeling, and simulating a developer's ongoing flow with a digital twin. One tuning strategy works across systems of very different size and design. The goal is recommendations that respect a developer's mental flow instead of disrupting it.
arxiv-2602-22097:
A moving conductive fluid stirs up magnetic fields, and reading those fields backward could reveal the flow itself. Yacine Mokhtari and three co-authors study that inverse problem: rebuild an incompressible velocity field from observations of the magnetic field it induces, under a strong steady background field. They work both on the whole space and on a periodic box modeling a uniform medium.

The analysis splits into two parts: showing the forward map is injective, and solving a divergence-free transport sub-problem. On the whole space, that sub-problem is well behaved when data are set on a suitable surface across the background field. On the periodic box, uniqueness turns on a sharp number-theoretic condition about field-to-size ratios.
arxiv-2602-22197:
Generative AI has pushed artists and platforms to shield images with invisible perturbations meant to block style copying and deepfakes. Xavier Pleimling and six co-authors show those shields are far weaker than believed. Where earlier attacks needed custom-built methods, the team repurposes ordinary off-the-shelf image-to-image models as generic denoisers, guided by a simple text prompt.

Across eight case studies spanning six protection schemes, the generic attack not only breaks the defenses but beats existing specialized attacks, while keeping the image useful to the attacker. The finding exposes a widespread vulnerability: many schemes offer a false sense of security. For creators, the message is stark: current protections cannot be trusted to hold.
arxiv-2602-22497:
How deep does an X-ray probe reach into diamond when it generates second harmonics? Daniel Schacher and three co-authors study the surface reach and probe depth of diamond second harmonic generation, both with math and with computer models. They use velocity-gauge real-time time-dependent density functional theory with a full multipole expansion. Two routes, varying which layers generate harmonics and exploiting crystal symmetry, yield a similar pattern.

By a thousand electron volts, well above the carbon K-edge energy, diamond's response is dominated by the bulk quadrupole response, matching analytic calculations. The bulk response keeps growing as energy rises. Near the K-edge the measurement is quite surface sensitive, but that surface bias fades with energy until the response is largely bulk sensitive. Crystal orientation also matters: differently cut surfaces differ a lot in surface sensitivity.
arxiv-2602-22697:
Ning Gao and eight co-authors balance kindness and cost in real-world service agents. Language-model agents now handle full tasks, but marrying empathetic talk with budget-aware choices is still open. Existing methods miss the strategic trade-off between pleasing users and controlling spend.

InteractCS-RL reframes task dialogue as multi-granularity reinforcement learning. A user-centred interaction framework provides a high-fidelity training gym where agents explore strategies against persona-driven users. Cost-aware multi-turn policy optimization then steers learning with hybrid advantage estimates, generative process credits, and a PID-Lagrangian cost controller toward the Pareto edge between reward and cost. Tests on real business scenarios and tool-agent-user benchmarks beat baselines on all three evaluation fronts.
arxiv-2602-23197:
Chungpa Lee and two co-authors analyze a tension in how large language models are tuned. Such models can adapt to new tasks from a few examples, a skill called in-context learning. Fine-tuning often improves zero-shot answers and cuts inference cost, but it can damage that few-shot skill on tasks the model never saw in tuning.

Using linear attention models, the authors show how tuning goals reshape attention parameters and when the damage appears. Updating every attention parameter can harm in-context learning. Restricting updates to the value matrix lifts zero-shot performance while preserving few-shot skill. Adding an auxiliary few-shot loss helps the target task but costs few-shot skill elsewhere, a pattern confirmed on synthetic and real-world data.
arxiv-2602-23297:
Yiqing Wang and seven co-authors present PRIMA, a pre-training design that aligns medical images with clinical metadata for diagnosis, then aggregates signals with a language model. Diagnosis needs visual signs plus patient context, but older methods treat data fields as isolated tags and miss the semantic knowledge inside case notes.

PRIMA first curates a corpus of risk-disease links via retrieval-augmented generation to refine Clinical ModernBERT, embedding diagnostic priors in the text encoder. A dual-encoder design pairs DINOv3 with the refined text encoder under four complementary losses, capturing multi-granular alignment and handling ambiguous correlations with soft labels. Qwen3 then fuses the aligned signals for disease classification. Across PAD-UFES-20 and AQUA, average F1 scores reach 72.04 and 85.22 percent, beating image-only, metadata-fusion, and medical vision-language baselines without massive data collection or exhaustive compute.
arxiv-2602-23797:
Saicharan Ritwik Chinni and Anupama Sharma model how smoking and awareness of its harms spread together through social contacts. The 2026 paper treats quitting and starting as linked contagions, shaped both by peer influence and by knowledge of health risks.

The team first builds a deterministic model with differential equations, which yields smoke-free and smoke-persistent steady states and shows when awareness can shrink or end persistence. They then extend the model to networks, where contacts are local rather than fully mixed. Simulations on real social networks show that uneven contact patterns and local awareness spread change how well interventions work. The findings stress that population structure matters when planning cessation campaigns.
arxiv-2602-23997:
Florent Delgrange outlines a vision for foundation world models that let agents learn, verify, and adapt reliably beyond fixed environments. The 2026 solo paper argues that standard approaches assume static tasks with little novelty, which limits world models that must evolve policies as conditions change in open worlds.

The agenda rests on four components. One component is learnable reward models drawn from specifications. A second is adaptive formal verification woven through learning. A third is online abstraction calibration that quantifies prediction reliability. A fourth is test-time synthesis of programs and world models guided by verifiers. Together those pieces let agents synthesize verifiable programs, derive new policies from few interactions, and maintain correctness while adapting to novelty. Foundation world models, the author argues, should serve as a substrate for learning, reasoning, and adaptation, and as a basis for agents that can explain and justify their behavior.
arxiv-2602-24097:
Yue Xie and three co-authors present a bi-level reinforcement learning and heuristic optimization framework for real-world winter road maintenance. The 2026 paper addresses large-scale gritting and snow routes on UK strategic roads, where existing methods struggle with scale and lean heavily on human planning.

At the upper level, a reinforcement learning agent partitions the road network into manageable clusters, allocating resources from multiple depots. Within each cluster, the lower level solves a multi-objective vehicle routing problem. It minimizes the longest vehicle travel time and total carbon emissions. It respects vehicle constraints, depot capacities, and segment requirements. Results on real operational data show balanced workloads, longest travel times below a two-hour target, lower emissions, and substantial cost savings. Those results demonstrate how AI-driven bi-level optimization can improve operational decisions for highway operators.
arxiv-2603-00097: Jackson, Gertz and Hesser build a knowledge-graph framework that merges drug-target data, trial literature, trial metadata and post-market safety reports into one evidence-weighted network of drugs and conditions. Applied to 400 protein kinase inhibitors, it enables side-by-side comparison of efficacy, target similarity and adverse-event prediction through target-to-event links. A lung-cancer case study spotlights known and candidate drugs, target groups and tolerability gaps. The tool is meant to complement current models, aid hypothesis generation and sharpen drug-safety watch.
arxiv-2603-00197: Sen Sarma, Akkamahadevi and Hitzler test whether a Concept Induction framework for labelling hidden neurons transfers from ADE20K to the SUN2012 scene benchmark. Using the same workflow, they tag neurons with interpretable semantic labels, checking them against web-sourced images and statistical tests. Their findings confirm the method transfers to SUN2012, showing broader applicability.
arxiv-2603-01197: Kar and Mukhopadhyay tune entanglement routing in quantum networks for maximum utility, dropping the usual rule of fixed routes for rival demands. They write single-path utility routing as a mixed-integer convex program, exact when negativity gauges it or output rates run high, and over 99.99 percent true else on real cases. Random rounding and min-jam rules with upper bounds make the problem tractable, with the min-jam variant faster and often stronger, carrying flow-based routing ideas to quantum networks.
arxiv-2603-01297: Sahoo and three colleagues show safety classifiers trained on frozen embeddings collapse under tiny embedding drift, challenging the idea that safety transfers across model versions. Normalized perturbations of magnitude 0.02, about one degree of angular drift, cut classifier performance from 85 percent to 50 percent ROC-AUC. Mean confidence falls only 14 percent, so 72 percent of misclassifications happen with high confidence, a silent failure that defeats standard monitoring. Instruction-tuned models also separate classes 20 percent worse than base models, making aligned systems oddly harder to safeguard.
arxiv-2603-01697:
Gokdeniz Gulmez loosens two rigid habits in mixture-of-experts networks in this 2026 work. Such networks split work among expert sub-models, yet most designs wake a fixed count of experts per token. They also spread expert capacity evenly across all layers, as if each layer needed the same help.

His frame, DynaMoE, lets the active expert count vary with how hard each token is. Capacity per layer follows one of six schedules, such as descending, ascending, pyramid, or wave shapes. Theory work backs gains in expressive power and gives bounds on compute cost. Tests span image tasks and language modeling at several model sizes. The best schedule depends on task and scale, with early-heavy layouts winning on image tasks in the tests.
arxiv-2603-01897:
Maximilian Kogler, Nicolas Neel, and Jorg Kroger control light emission from a pair of molecules by flipping one molecule state. Their 2026 lab work uses tin-phthalocyanine molecules on a thin salt film over gold. A scanning tunneling microscope drives a current that makes the molecules glow, a process called electrofluorescence.

A single molecule shows how glow yield grows with current, which pins the glow to a one-electron excitation step. Its spectrum carries vibrational structure and hot luminescence, signs of excited molecular states. In a pair, fine spectral structure comes from coupling between the two optical dipoles. Flipping one molecule between its two stable states changes the pair yield a lot. One state amplifies light past the single-molecule level, while the other dims it below that level.
arxiv-2603-01997:
Hari Prasanth S. M, Pejman Habibiroudkenar, Eerik Alamikkotervo, and colleagues forecast drone paths from event camera data alone. Their 2026 work uses sensors that report pixel changes with extreme time resolution, ideal for fast aerial targets. No normal video frames and no training data enter the pipeline at all.

Propeller spin speed is read straight from the raw event stream as a motion cue. That spin signal feeds an RPM-aware Kalman filter, a classic tracker upgraded with the spin data. On a public drone data set, the method beats learning-based rivals and a plain Kalman filter. Gains show in both average and final distance error at short and medium forecast horizons. Robust, training-free tracking suits airspace monitoring and anti-drone work where targets may not cooperate.
arxiv-2603-02097:
Xiang Zheng, Han Li, Wenjie Luo, and colleagues benchmark Chinese medical language models on open-ended clinical cases. Their 2026 benchmark, ClinConsensus, was curated and quality-controlled by clinical experts. Static, task-isolated tests miss the openness and safety stakes of real clinical workflows, the team argues.

Cases span prevention, intervention, and long-term follow-up across dozens of specialties and task types. Difficulty rises progressively, which exposes where models break as care grows complex. A rubric-based grading protocol scores responses, with a new consistency metric that rewards clinically usable answers. A dual-judge setup pairs a top model judge with a distilled local judge for scalable scoring. Fifteen leading models show wide variation, and actionable treatment planning stands out as the key bottleneck.
arxiv-2603-02297:
Nancy Lau, Louis Sloot, Jyoutir Raj, and colleagues benchmark AI agents on fresh security flaws in this 2026 paper. Coding agents now write and patch software in real projects. A key hoped-for gain is finding and fixing security holes on their own. Their benchmark, ZeroDayBench, uses twenty-two severe flaws that models have never seen.

Agents must both find each flaw and patch it in open-source code. Three leading agentic models were tested on the full set. None could yet solve the tasks on their own, the team reports. Still, their behavior showed clear patterns in how they searched and failed. Those patterns point to concrete ways future agents could improve. The work frames a hard, honest test for proactive cyber defense.
arxiv-2603-02497:
Vittorio Palladino, Tsai Idden, and Ahmet Enis Cetin build a hybrid quantum-classical vision network in this 2026 paper. Convolutional networks filter images with linear operations that transform domains can speed up. Some structured transforms also run on shallow quantum circuits. Earlier hybrid designs used the Hadamard transform for that quantum step.

Their network swaps in the Haar wavelet transform instead. Haar gives localized, multi-resolution views that suit vision tasks better. They show Haar decomposes into unitary steps fit for quantum circuits. On two image benchmarks, the network cut parameters sharply while keeping competitive accuracy. It beat both a standard ResNet and Hadamard-based baselines on the harder set. Runs on real IBM quantum hardware confirm near-term feasibility.
arxiv-2603-02597:
Venu Gopal Kadamba and Kanishkha Jaisankar move text tokenization onto the GPU in this 2026 paper. Tokenizers split text into pieces before a language model can read it. With million-token contexts, CPU tokenizers become a serious bottleneck while GPUs idle. Their byte-level BPE tokenizer follows the merge rules of GPT-2.

A basic GPU kernel is joined by an optimized version using modern CUDA libraries. On long WikiText sequences, the optimized tokenizer produces identical tokens to CPU versions. For the longest inputs it beats two leading CPU tokenizers by clear margins. Profiling shows memory allocation eats most of the API time. Pooling memory should give the next big speedup, they note. Generation quality stayed within a point of the CPU tools.
arxiv-2603-03097:
Muyukani Kizito and Elizabeth Nyambere present Odin, a system that explores knowledge graphs on its own. Search tools answer preset questions, but Odin hunts for patterns nobody asked for. The authors describe it as the first such engine at work in tightly ruled fields like health care and insurance.

A blended score steers the search. It mixes how central a node is, how plausible a link sounds, how fresh the facts are, and how well a step bridges groups. That last signal fights echo chambers, where search gets trapped inside one dense cluster. A beam search guided by the score stays cheap while finding most of what a full scan finds. Each find keeps its full trail of proof.
arxiv-2603-03197:
Samuele Angheben, Davide Berasi, Alessandro Conti, and colleagues push image classifiers to name the exact species, not just the family. Open-world fine-grained classification has no fixed label list, and reasoning multimodal models often answer too generically despite knowing better. Their 2026 framework, SpeciaRL, trains for correctness and specificity together.

A dynamic reward, anchored to the best answers the model itself produces during online rollouts, rewards finer labels only when they stay within the model's verified reach. That design discourages wild guesses while rewarding precision. On out-of-domain fine-grained benchmarks, the method delivered the best balance of correctness and specificity among rivals. The code and model are public. The work shows latent knowledge can be surfaced by the right training signal.
arxiv-2603-03297:
Haoyang He and five colleagues propose a way for a language model to keep improving while it is being tested. Test-time training adapts a model using only the test questions, but hard questions make self-made answer keys unreliable. Their 2026 framework, TTSR, also targets a second problem: generic practice ignores the model's own specific weaknesses.

One pretrained model plays two roles in turn. As Student it attempts problems; as Teacher it studies the failed attempts, names the recurring weaknesses, and writes targeted variant questions at the right difficulty. The Student then learns from those variants, and the loop repeats. On hard mathematics reasoning benchmarks, TTSR improved scores steadily and worked across several model backbones and general reasoning tasks.
arxiv-2603-03497:
Yejin Moon, Gábor Orosz, and Hosam K Fathy design safety controls that fail gracefully instead of all at once. Their 2026 paper defines grace as layered assurance: a primary safety layer worth defending, backed by a secondary failsafe layer. A graceful controller may lose the primary layer under pressure, but the failsafe must never be breached. The challenge is proving that property for real nonlinear systems.

The construction merges two barrier function styles in one constraint, zeroing style for the primary set and reciprocal style for the failsafe. The blend behaves like a stiffening spring, which lets the authors build energy-based proofs of the graceful guarantee. Versions cover systems of relative degree one and two, the latter suiting mechanical systems. A wall collision avoidance demonstration shows the method beating traditional benchmarks from the literature.
arxiv-2603-03597:
Hadi Mohaghegh Dolatabadi and nine colleagues, of Pluralis Research, make a popular new optimizer produce models that compress better on purpose. Compression pipelines exploit low-rank structure in trained weights, structure usually credited to the Adam optimizer. The newer Muon optimizer updates in full rank, so its weights should resist compression. Their 2026 paper reports the surprise: Muon-trained weights are strongly low-rank anyway, and compress readily under standard pipelines.

Building on that, NuMuon adds a nuclear-norm constraint to Muon's update direction, steering weights further toward low-rank form during training. On billion-parameter models, NuMuon raises compressibility and improves the quality that survives state-of-the-art compression, while keeping Muon's favorable convergence behavior. The result reframes optimizer choice as a compression decision made before training even starts.
arxiv-2603-03797:
Jong-In Park and four colleagues count galaxies by mass in nine of the heaviest nearby clusters. The stellar mass function, how many galaxies exist at each mass, tests how environment sculpts galaxy growth. Their 2026 measurements use deep, complete spectroscopy from the MACH survey, reaching far down the mass range inside clusters and comparing against field galaxies over the same cosmic epoch.

The average cluster function mirrors the field's shape but sits higher at modest masses, with a clear excess at the top end where brightest cluster galaxies live. Dead, quiescent members peak at intermediate mass; star-forming members thin out steadily toward high mass. Against the IllustrisTNG simulation the shapes agree well overall, except the real clusters hold roughly twice as many mid-mass galaxies as the simulation grows. Complete spectroscopy, the authors show, can put real pressure on galaxy formation models.
arxiv-2603-03997: Alexander Lehner studies bandwidth choice for spatial heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation steady standard errors. Spatial autocorrelation biases standard errors downward and distorts inference. The widely used Conley correction depends on kernel bandwidth, the distance within which residuals may correlate, yet formal guidance is lacking. Lehner documents an inverse-U relationship between bandwidth and error magnitude, so both narrow and wide bandwidths underestimate standard errors.
arxiv-2603-04097: Teguia Kouam and others use selective vibronic excitation for coherent energy transport. Matching excitation to underdamped resonances of the Fenna-Matthews-Olson complex yields dressed states with reduced coupling, giving biexponential decay and a wide window. The gain beats static disorder and extends to agrivoltaics, where organic photovoltaics act as spectral filters co-optimizing transport and crop needs.
arxiv-2603-04397: Kadir and colleagues test gas around galaxies with Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effects in simulations. Thermal, kinematic, and relativistic signals probe density, temperature, pressure, feedback, and velocity. Kinematic data hint gas extends farther than expected, suggesting strong feedback and lensing corrections. With DESI-like galaxies in IllustrisTNG and Abacus, projected profiles bias gas fraction values. The 2-halo term matters even at small radii, satellite uncertainty spreads into halo terms, and masking massive objects cuts levels sharply. These checks thus sharpen claims about gas and lensing.
arxiv-2603-04697: Contant and colleagues build a multi-fidelity tensor emulator for outputs. Earth system models cost much and depend on uncertain inputs. Statistical emulation offers a practical alternative. The driving case is MPAS-Seaice, the Arctic sea-ice part of the Energy Exascale Model. The emulator combines tensor split, Gaussian priors, and an added gap model. It scales to complex space-time fields with good guesses and well calibrated uncertainty. In MPAS-Seaice tests it attains the lowest prediction error, especially in summer melt season, and best matches space-time links.
arxiv-2603-04897: Arina Kostina and colleagues test whether large language models can capture expert uncertainty when reading interviews for the values they express, using the Schwartz Theory of Basic Values. Against expert annotations, models approach the human ceiling on set-based measures but fall short on value rankings. Value distributions mostly match human analysts, yet uncertainty patterns across values diverge, and Qwen comes closest to expert agreement. Ensemble methods improve results consistently, though overemphasis on Security hints at model-induced bias needing further study.
arxiv-2603-04997: Lucas D. Konrad and team present a unified Bayesian method that detects shape breaks in longitudinal data when their timing is unknown and their chain arbitrary. The design builds on indicator-saturated regression with a spike-and-slab prior for indicator picking. They set up that using a non-local prior as the slab is necessary for model picking sameness in this model class. Runs show the method beating comparable frequentist ways, where shape breaks are highly probable, and the authors show it on climate policies in European road transport.
arxiv-2603-05697: Xu and team present MultiHaystack, the first benchmark testing search and thinking jointly at large cross-modal scale. Existing benchmarks limit search to small, single-mode sets, puffing up trust. MultiHaystack holds over 46,000 multi-mode items across texts, images, and videos, plus 747 checkable questions, each grounded in a checked proof item. Models perform well with the matching proof, but scores drop sharply when they must retrieve it from the corpus. Even the strongest finder, E5-V, reaches only 40.8% Recall@1, showing mixed-pool search remains a primary choke point.
arxiv-2603-05897: Zamolodtchikov looks at non-param fitting under co-vary shift, watching samples from both a target spread and another source spread. The paper gives a transfer function, showing that traits of its domain set minimax rates. Those rates exhibit varied zones, including old rates where the better of the two single-spread rates governs, plus zones with times sample-size mixing beating the best-of-two benchmark. A design-smart guess tool hits these rates up to log factors. Against old theory, results cover co-vary inputs with endless support.
arxiv-2603-06097: Tao Huang and colleagues present X-ray intraday variability and power spectrum analysis of OJ 287, a binary black hole blazar candidate. Eight pointed observations by the EPIC-pn camera aboard XMM-Newton span November 2005 to November 2022, with good intervals reaching 24.1 hours. Low amplitude variations appear across 4 soft-band, 5 hard-band, and 6 total-band light curves, while only two observations vary in all bands. The soft-hard correlation peaks at zero lag, suggesting cospatial emission from one lepton population, while red noise dominates light curves' power spectra.
arxiv-2603-06397: Jiang and colleagues propose R4T, using reinforcement learning once as an objective transducer. Many retrieval problems are set valued: a broad intent demands a collection optimizing diversity and coverage grounded in a fixed database. R4T trains a fan out language model with set level rewards, synthesizing objective consistent training pairs. It then trains a diffusion retriever for set valued outputs. Across fashion and music benchmarks, R4T improves retrieval quality over strong baselines and cuts query time fan out latency tenfold.
arxiv-2603-06797: Hsu and colleagues frame a dilemma in alignment at inference time: optimistic Best-of-N selection invites reward hacking, while pessimistic guarded methods stifle search for high-quality responses. Through a regret lens they show the best choice turns on reward tail shape. When tails are light, optimism wins by surfacing high-quality outliers. When tails are heavy, pessimism guards against miscalibrated rewards in extremes. Their Best-of-Tails framework uses Tsallis divergence as a regularizer, blending between extremes in steps, and sizes up tails with the Hill estimator.
arxiv-2603-06997: Dicks proves quadratic congruences for half-whole cusp forms with the eta multiplier, taking earlier work further, to any character type. For a prime of at least five and an odd integer, recent work by Ahlgren, Andersen, and Dicks showed such matches for many forms. Their factor mixes a real Dirichlet character with Dedekind eta powers, going far past matches Atkin found for partitions. Here Dicks shows the congruences hold when the character is any type, using modular Galois maps tied to whole-number eigenforms with any Nebentypus.
arxiv-2603-07197: Wang and colleagues teach language models to abandon bad reasoning paths and restart, with Re-squared, reinforcement learning with re-solving. Even after extensive reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, models still produce needless, low-quality chain-of-thought steps, and a poor start often dooms the answer despite many extra tokens. Re-squared uses pure reinforcement learning, with no preliminary supervised fine-tuning, to amplify the rare redo behavior in vanilla models. Models learn to drop unproductive paths and re-solve when needed, improving efficiency and answer quality.
arxiv-2603-07297: Lewis and Constante-Amores hunt for exact coherent states inside chaotic falling-film flow, a two-phase setting where the moving interface drives the dynamics. They rebuild the classic long-wave interface equation and map regimes across domain size and dispersion, from travelling waves to full chaos. On the chaotic side they chart a low-dimensional manifold and use it to locate waves, periodic orbits and equilibria embedded in the attractor. Chaotic paths keep revisiting those states, which the authors present as the first such identification for falling films.
arxiv-2603-07397: Espigule and Juher construct explicit semialgebraic interior layers inside root closures of bounded-height integer polynomials. Outside the unit disk these closures match Mandelbrot sets for affine iterated systems with collinear digits. The layers earn certification when finite inverse orbits land inside canonical self-covering parallelograms, which exist exactly in the non-real lens. Within that lens each capture level closes within two more steps, and the layers expose gaps that no finite level can fill.
arxiv-2603-07597: Zhao and colleagues test how sensitive anisotropic flow in lead-lead collisions is to the neutron skin of the lead-208 nucleus. Varying neutron surface spread in a transport model, they trace skin cases from initial density profiles and shapes to final particle production and flow stats. Geometric effects survive the full run, yet matching model to data rejects only the most compact and most diffuse profiles. Standard and moderate skins describe data alike, a tie from dominant collision shape.
arxiv-2603-07797: Mehrdad and colleagues test whether one unified cost function explains and predicts human reaching, against narrow rules. Using Minimal Observation Inverse Reinforcement Learning with seven cost terms, they gauge changing weights for planar reaching. MO-IRL converges far faster than bilevel formulations on a fraction of data. Three breadth levels are tested, from fully narrow to fully general. Changing weights improve path rebuild, cutting RMSE by 27 percent on average. Found costs highlight joint-speedup control as top, with torque-change smoothness backing one unified rule.
arxiv-2603-07897: Ma and colleagues tackle Databricks job scheduling, where cheap compute must still meet latency and dependency limits. Older pipelines lean on hand-built features that miss runtime effects like partition pruning, data skew, and shuffle growth. Their LeJOT-AutoML framework puts language-model agents across the learning cycle. It pairs retrieval over a knowledge base with a toolchain of log parsers, metadata queries, and a read-only SQL sandbox. It creates over 200 features, shrinks the loop from weeks to under an hour, and cut costs by about 19 percent.
arxiv-2603-07997: Li and colleagues give vision-and-language navigation agents a memory. Current language-model agents cannot recall experience for long-horizon or unfamiliar tasks. Their CMMR-VLN framework builds a multimodal memory indexed by panoramic images and salient landmarks. It pulls relevant runs during navigation through a generation pipeline that mimics how experienced humans use prior knowledge. A reflection-based update stores complete successful paths plus the key first mistake from failures. Tests show average success-rate gains over NavGPT, MapGPT, and DiscussNav in sim and real settings.
arxiv-2603-08097: Halpern and colleagues offer PathBench, a shared yardstick for scoring pathological speech. Until now, comparison was hard because work was split across private data sets with uneven rules. PathBench instead draws on public data and tests methods that need no reference, a reference text, or reference audio, under three setups: Matched Content, Extended, and Full. The setups mirror a linguist using controlled prompts versus a machine learning specialist using as much data as possible. Baselines span six data sets, with DArtP topping reference-free methods on average correlation.
arxiv-2603-08197: Martin-Higueras and colleagues use E0 transition strengths to pin down nuclear structure models, tested on even-even Xe isotopes. E0 rates are hard to get right in any such model, yet those observables tightly bound its parameters. They survey rho-squared E0 values and ratios across the interacting boson model's full parameter space, plotting Casten triangle contours. Superimposing the Xe results shows which regions survive and which fine tuning of Hamiltonian parameters can never reach, confirming that certain ratios in particular fence the parameter space in.
arxiv-2603-08297: Cârstea and colleagues study inverse boundary value problems for doubly nonlinear parabolic and elliptic problems. Their first main result shows that when m exceeds p minus 1, the lateral Cauchy data determine both coefficients. The proof reduces the parabolic case to an elliptic one. A second main result proves uniqueness for a coefficient pair from the nonlinear Dirichlet-to-Neumann map, finding one from asymptotic series and the other by linearization.
arxiv-2603-08597: Marion Campisi and colleagues build a graph that maps when knots can turn into each other by crossing changes. A knot counts as n-adjacent to another when flips at any nonempty bunch of its crossing circles land on that other knot. Their new graph, Gamma n, turns those links into edges, and the paper proves several facts about how the graph behaves.
arxiv-2603-09397: Xiao-Xu Fang and colleagues generate four-photon entanglement on a chip, in the telecom band, inside a thin-film lithium niobate waveguide that is periodically poled. Wavelength-multiplexed networks could send quantum correlations down many channels at once, yet broadband sources of entanglement beyond photon pairs are rare. Type-0 down-conversion gives phase matching over more than 200 nm, so the entangled photons spread across separable spectral channels. The photons carry time-bin encoding for fiber use, with a coherent interface swapping between time-bin and polarization forms.
