These give Betti, de Rham, and Dolbeault versions of cohomology, the algebraic way of counting holes and shapes.

Dang develops derived categories on superstacks, proving base change and recollement results that let categories be glued and compared. With that machinery he gives new proofs of Penkov's theorem on D-modules. He also proves that de Rham cohomology matches its super counterpart, a key consistency check. The paper argues that derived and super geometry face parallel problems, so methods from one setting transfer naturally to the other.
arxiv-2606-10297:
Han and Xiao develop a method for sorting how individual firms reacted to a crisis from noisy market data, in a 2026 arXiv paper on financial econometrics. Their multi-method approach combines difference-in-differences causal estimation with cluster-robust inference, unsupervised trajectory clustering and hidden Markov models, and logistic regression for resilience prediction. They show it on two hundred forty-six Chinese A-share IT firms during the January 2020 COVID-19 shock, using non-IT index firms as controls.

The return decline proved market-wide rather than limited to IT, while the IT effect was elevated volatility, robust after a multiple-testing fix. Clustering produced three trajectory groups: fast recovery firms that gained strongly, a resilient moderate group, and a persistent drag group that lost ground, the largest of the three. The framework offers a template for splitting partial market signals in other crises.
arxiv-2606-10697:
Zhang and colleagues rethink how fashion search sees clothing in this 2026 arXiv paper on information retrieval. Attribute-specific fashion retrieval answers queries about one feature, a neckline or a sleeve. But vision transformers chop images into square patches that cut across the regions attributes live in, letting background noise leak in. Their framework, Super Fashion, uses attribute-guided attention to crop meaningful regions. It then segments those regions into superpixels, clusters of similar pixels following real boundaries, and feeds superpixel tokens, not patch tokens, to its transformer.

Separate codes let attribute and superpixel tokens interact and fuse, sharpening where the feature sits. On 3 benchmarks it improves mean average precision over the prior best by 1.84 percent on FashionAI, 9.27 percent on DARN, and 9.35 percent on DeepFashion. The authors argue that coherent tokenisation, respecting shapes in the image instead of a rigid grid, is the key ingredient for fine-grained search.
arxiv-2606-10797:
Waman and colleagues compute how strong magnetic fields reshape baryon magnetism in this 2026 arXiv paper on nuclear theory. The eight lightest baryons, the octet containing the proton and neutron, sit in matter that can be hot, dense, strange, and strongly magnetised, in collisions and magnetars alike. The team combines a chiral SU(3) quark mean-field model of the medium with a constituent quark model of the baryons, including the Dirac sea, the polarised vacuum.

With the sea included comes magnetic catalysis: condensates grow with field strength, and the baryons' masses rise with the magnetic field. At 100 megaelectronvolts, the field's effects are strongest at low density and moderated as density grows. Strangeness shifts weight between light and strange quark sectors, separating the Lambda, Sigma, and Xi baryons from the nucleons. Decomposing the moments shows valence quarks carry most of the medium dependence, with sea and orbital parts as corrections.
arxiv-2606-10897:
Moser characterizes critical points of a worst-case energy for maps in this 2026 arXiv paper. For maps between Riemannian manifolds, the infinity-harmonic functional measures the largest stretch anywhere, rather than an average. That max-type energy is not differentiable, so such points are defined through a subdifferential, covering cases like energy minimizers within a fixed homotopy class.

Moser derives a geometric condition exactly equivalent to criticality, stated through a vector-valued 1-current on the domain that packages its key properties. The current itself turns out to be a critical point of a generalized mass measure. The result gives these non-smooth variational problems a concrete handle.
arxiv-2606-11597:
Dong-Xu Yu and Zhe Wang model how supercooled liquids flow in this 2026 arXiv paper on soft matter physics. A supercooled liquid is cooled below its freezing point without turning solid, so it flows extremely slowly. Rheology, the study of how materials flow, shows odd behaviour in such liquids, including thinning under steady push and a stress overshoot when flow starts.

Their model pictures the liquid as a shifting mixture of solid-like and liquid-like regions. Two ingredients do the work: a correlation length describing medium-range order, and a local elastic interaction limiting how stress spreads inside solid-like patches. Every parameter is fixed from the still, equilibrium state, with no fitting to flow data. Even so, the model quantitatively matches measured flow across a wide range of shear rates. It also tracks how molecular motion becomes uneven, or heterogeneous, linking the large-scale flow to microscopic behaviour.
arxiv-2606-11697:
Priyank Vasu and three colleagues decompose special surfaces into simpler pieces in this 2026 arXiv paper on geometry. The surfaces have zero mean curvature, meaning they are perfectly balanced between bending in and out at every point, like soap films. The work spans three spaces with different distance rules: ordinary Euclidean space, Lorentz-Minkowski space from relativity, and isotropic space.

The authors derive new Euler-Ramanujan identities, formulas splitting one quantity into an endless sum of parts. These split the conjugate of Scherk's first minimal surface into stretched catenoids, soap-film shapes formed between two rings. Factorisation and power series methods then split broad families of such graphs into helicoids, spiral ramps, and Enneper surfaces. Finite versions are proved too, including tower-like splits. The theory is aimed partly at lamellar structures, layered materials built from such surfaces.
arxiv-2606-11997:
Shay Nadel, Amir Sivan and Aviv Karnieli propose a way to see invisible quantum states in this 2026 arXiv paper. Arrays of emitters coupled to a waveguide can host dark states: collective modes whose radiation cancels by interference, giving them very long lifetimes. That same decoupling makes them unmeasurable by standard techniques. The trade-off is fundamental for quantum technologies, which need states both protected and accessible.

The authors' solution probes the array with weakly squeezed light from a nonlinear waveguide, light whose quantum noise is redistributed. They show the resulting fluorescence spectrum reveals transitions between the dressed dark states of the array. Numerical studies of four- and six-emitter arrays confirm the spectrum maps onto the dark-state transition frequencies. The readout also survives realistic flaws such as free-space decay. Beyond measurement, the squeezing strength offers a knob for controlling the dark-state manifold itself.
arxiv-2606-12197:
Kothari and Tudose prove a conjecture about the vibrations of networks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A graph is a network of vertices joined by edges. Its Laplacian, a matrix built from vertex degrees and connections, has eigenvalues that act like vibration frequencies. Brouwer's conjecture bounds the sum of the largest few: it may not exceed the edge count plus a small triangular correction. Partial results covered special families for decades.

The authors prove the bound for every graph and every cutoff. Their route uses the Grone-Merris-Bai theorem, a known result comparing Laplacian eigenvalues with the degree pattern of split graphs, a family whose vertices divide into a clique and an independent set. Surprisingly, they also prove the reverse direction. Brouwer's conjecture and the Grone-Merris-Bai theorem therefore imply each other exactly. Two problems treated as separate turn out to be one statement in disguise.
arxiv-2606-12297:
Lionas and co-authors propose that the universe's speeding expansion is a quantum bookkeeping effect, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cosmic acceleration is usually blamed on a cosmological constant or dark energy. Quantum theory allows post-selection: conditioning results on a final state as well as an initial one. With coarse-graining, ignoring fine detail, post-selection can bend effective classical dynamics. The authors build a cosmological model on that idea.

Their model needs no cosmological constant, dark energy, or modified gravity. The expansion history depends on at most two parameters beyond standard evolution. Fits to supernova and cosmic chronometer data rival the standard model. The coincidence problem, why acceleration starts now, dissolves naturally. Early radiation and matter eras come out standard. One sharp difference: the model predicts a present-day jerk parameter, the expansion's third derivative, far from the standard value. Future data can kill or confirm the idea.
arxiv-2606-12497:
Cherepanov and co-authors ask what memory alone buys a robot, stripping away every other gadget, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language-action models predict action chunks from the view, which fails when a needed cue has left the screen. Existing memory-augmented models change many things at once, so recurrence's contribution stays unclear. Their muVLA adds memory tokens, carried across timesteps and updated by self-attention, to an OpenVLA backbone. Training uses truncated backpropagation, with no auxiliary losses.

On MIKASA-Robo, success across five training tasks jumps from 0.42 at baseline to 0.84 at the strongest setting, while held-out tasks climb from 0.07 without memory to 0.23 with it. Cue-recall tasks drive the gain: remembering a color goes from near zero to above nine in ten. Tasks needing different memory stay near baseline. On LIBERO, success hits about ninety-six percent; nothing is lost when the world is fully visible.
arxiv-2606-12597:
Diaz-Uriarte and co-authors teach cancer progression models to answer what-if questions correctly, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Evolutionary accumulation models infer the order in which tumors gain mutations, from snapshots across patients. Clinicians hope such models can nominate drug targets. But the obvious trick, conditioning on a mutation's absence, predicts intervention effects wrongly. The authors formalize intervention, using Pearl's do-operator, for every model family.

For most models, intervening becomes a tweak to parameters. They flag which implementations are equivalent and test the modularity assumption. Drawing causal diagrams at the individual level, with fitness explicit, splits interventions models conflate. Killing cells that carry a mutation is not inactivating the mutation itself. Since the goal is choosing targets, they recast evaluation as ranking, defining intervention objectives and a protocol for scoring model rankings. The framework travels beyond cancer to any model read as a structural causal model.
arxiv-2606-12997:
Greenbury and colleagues compare, head-to-head, the reliability of 2 leading methods for probabilistic emulation of physical systems, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The 2 options are generative models, such as diffusion or flow matching, and ensembles of fixed-rule models with added randomness trained with the continuous ranked probability score loss. Both predict well, but how reliable their uncertainty is had not been checked under matched terms.

Across 2-dimensional spatiotemporal physical systems, with matched model size and computing budget, the authors check coverage of forecast ranges with accuracy and speed. Continuous-ranked-probability-score-trained ensembles usually achieve more reliable error bars in both single-step prediction and autoregressive rollouts, with better coverage than generative models trained in a latent space, and they run faster. Generative models trained in ambient space match the ensembles' coverage but with larger latency. Score-trained ensembles keep coverage when trained in latent space.
arxiv-2606-13097:
Chun and colleagues present FCGraft, a functional cache grafting framework for synthesising code policies for embodied agents, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Code-writing language models generate executable control programs from natural-language goals. But in open-domain environments this suffers 2 limitations: delayed decoding from prefill computation over long prompts, and limited robustness. Generative decoding produces application-interface mismatches, missing safety guards, and unstable control logic.

FCGraft maintains a library of function-level checked code skeletons with their linked prompt-level key-value caches from the Transformer. For a new task, it retrieves relevant functions and grafts their caches. It builds policies by stitching, which composes cached function segments into a composite policy. It also patches: adapting the necessary code regions to task-specific parameters and constraints with less decoding. Against the prompt-level caching method RAGCache, FCGraft achieves an 18.31 percent higher task success rate and 2.3 times faster policy synthesis.
arxiv-2606-13397:
Das and colleagues present Mod-Guide in this 2026 arXiv paper, a moderation feedback system aimed at insensitive speech toward Indigenous ethnic and religious minority communities. Online language can sideline minority groups, yet moderation now relies on large language models whose judgements may miss local cultural context. Rather than simply deleting flagged content, Mod-Guide gives feedback intended to address the insensitivity itself. The work is situated in social computing research, with attention to how affected groups experience harmful speech.

The system uses a language model to analyse flagged text and respond with guidance, helping users understand why their words may wound minority readers. The authors frame moderation as a learning opportunity rather than only enforcement. Their study examines how such feedback can be designed for groups whose languages and norms are poorly served by mainstream moderation tools. The paper contributes to research on computing for societies.
arxiv-2606-13497:
Blank and colleagues present SPARC in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework that labels robot demonstration data automatically and honestly. Structured annotations, such as object bounding boxes, trajectories, and phase labels, are valuable for training robot policies and planning systems. Automated pipelines can generate them at scale, but they offer no trustworthy quality signal. A detector's confidence turns out to be poorly calibrated for whether an annotation is actually correct. Users are forced to accept noisy labels wholesale or discard useful data.

SPARC exploits the spatio-temporal structure built into robot tasks to derive a reliability score for each annotation. Consistency across time and space exposes labels that a single-frame detector would pass silently. The framework is risk-aware: downstream users can keep high-reliability annotations and treat the rest with caution, instead of guessing. The authors argue that calibrated reliability, not just volume, is what demonstration datasets need.
arxiv-2606-13697:
Deng, Gao, and Wang improve a classic investing method that must cope with faulty forecasts. Mean-variance portfolio choice balances expected return against risk, but suffers when estimates of returns and their spread are wrong. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies the multiperiod version, where holdings are adjusted over time. They add reference regulation, a penalty that keeps the chosen portfolio from straying too far from a trusted reference policy.

The authors derive how the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio, a reward-per-risk score, behaves when assets are many relative to the data. They show how penalty strength and investment horizon jointly shape performance. A new effect appears: reference weights can correct errors in risk estimates, while the risk matrix corrects errors in return estimates. Simulations and real market data confirm the approach. Portfolios grow more stable, and Sharpe ratios improve markedly.
arxiv-2606-13897:
El Haskouki and Gernandt ask when energy-based models of physical systems stay well behaved after delays are added. Port-Hamiltonian systems describe machines and networks by stored energy, losses, and connection ports. Transport delays are natural here, but they can destroy passivity, the property that a system never creates energy at its ports. Their 2026 arXiv paper derives passivity conditions for linear versions with several constant delays.

The conditions use a chosen storage function with Wirtinger-based inequalities, ending as linear matrix inequalities a computer can check. Passivity also survives negative feedback interconnection, a key structural benefit. The authors recall stability conditions under both delay-dependent and delay-independent assumptions. Two applications ground the theory: district heating networks and an oscillator with delayed damping.
arxiv-2606-13997:
Aranda's team defines polarization as resistance to consensus, measured as the cheapest way to end disagreement. Existing measures compute a number from an opinion spread but never say where agreement could be reached. Their 2026 arXiv paper defines Minimum Effort to Consensus: the least cost of transforming a spread into a consensus one, minimized over all consensus points. The measure outputs the optimal consensus point itself, the cheapest meeting place.

In the basic case it equals the one-Wasserstein distance to the nearest consensus distribution. Special cases recover mean absolute deviation about the median, and variance-like dispersion. Two parameters weight masses and movement costs: group identification and the cost of revising beliefs. The optimal point anchors a Minority Principle and a closed-form Tipping Point method, which finds the critical mass where moving opinions away stops reducing it and starts increasing it. It is not monotone in extremism.
arxiv-2606-14097:
Czygrinow and Parvatikar sharpen the color threshold forcing a rainbow four-cycle in triangle-free graphs. A rainbow cycle uses a different color per edge; color-degree counts distinct colors at a vertex. Ding and others had forced such a cycle once the minimum color-degree passed n over five plus three root n. Their 2026 arXiv paper cuts the additive term to a constant.

The theorem: for large n, if every vertex of a triangle-free edge-colored graph on n vertices sees at least n plus seven over five distinct colors, a rainbow four-cycle must exist. The bound is provably best possible. A second result gives rainbow cycles of length four k under a weaker condition, color-degree above n over five plus three. Regularity and stability methods drive the proof. The threshold had fallen from n over three toward n over five; this pins it.
arxiv-2606-14597:
de Villeroché and co-authors test whether neural PDE solvers can scale to bigger domains in a 2026 arXiv paper. Neural operators learn to map inputs to full PDE solutions. Transformer versions excel on complex geometries. But they silently assume the domain size seen in training. So they fail on larger regions.

The authors argue this zero-shot task needs two traits. It needs spatial locality. It also needs translation equivariance, where shifting the input shifts the output equally. They build locality through a bias added to attention scores. The bias stays decomposable, so fast attention kernels still work. They pair it with rotary positional embeddings. Across two PDE benchmarks and a 3D industrial flow case, the approach helped a lot. Zero-shot generalization to much larger domains improved sharply. The transformer design itself stayed unchanged.
arxiv-2606-14797:
Watanabe models self-copying chemistry in a 2026 arXiv paper. The system has three layers. Raw molecules feed catalytic proteins. Large RNA-like chains act as genes. The chains fold, and their folded shapes set how active each protein is. A small noise term keeps the system out of balance, as real living chemistry is.

The model was searched for settings where the chemistry sustains itself. Two trends appeared together, as theory predicts. Disorder in the surroundings rose while the gene layer grew more ordered. The cost was steep: about five hundred eighty-nine nats of outside disorder per nat of gene order. Standard bounds on speed and precision sat far below the model's values. A stripped one-cycle version behaved far better. Its precision product fell to about five, near what ribosomes show.
arxiv-2606-14997:
Kwon and coauthors hunt for memory traces inside neural networks, modeled on brain engrams, in a 2026 study. Neuroscience defines an engram by four tests: specificity, reactivation, sufficiency, and necessity. Whether trained networks hold such identifiable units has been unclear, since parameters serve many behaviors at once. The team turns the four tests into a constrained inverse problem.

Solving that problem gives a closed-form estimator that isolates one memory trace from entangled weights. The solution also matches a natural gradient step on the parameter manifold, tying biology to information geometry. With a trace in hand, memories can be composed or erased by plain linear arithmetic, with no retraining loop. Experiments range from small multilayer perceptrons to billion-parameter language models. Traces show a condensed localization pattern even in large models. The authors frame the method as a structural route to machine unlearning, replacing slow gradient search with direct identification.
arxiv-2606-15497:
Yamada and colleagues present The AI Scientist in 2026, the strongest demonstration yet of end-to-end automation of machine learning research. The system creates research ideas, writes code, runs experiments, plots and analyses data, writes the full manuscript, and even performs peer review. Earlier tools automated single steps of science; none covered the whole cycle from conception to publication.

The team tests the system in two modes: a focused mode seeded with human code templates, and an open-ended, template-free mode that searches more widely. Both modes produce diverse ideas and test, report, and evaluate them automatically. One AI-generated manuscript passed the first round of peer review at a workshop of a major machine learning conference, where about seventy percent of submissions are accepted. The authors flag risks, including strain on review systems and noise in the literature, but argue such systems could greatly speed discovery.
arxiv-2606-15697:
Matsuzaki and colleagues apply equation-of-motion coupled-cluster theory to a tungsten antifluorite in 2026, to pin down how electrons and lattice vibrations entangle in Cs2WCl6. Its tungsten sites have degenerate spin-orbit states coupling to Jahn-Teller active vibrations, which should distort the lattice. Yet experiments see no symmetry lowering in the low-temperature ordered phases, a standing puzzle.

The team derives model Hamiltonians for the embedded tungsten sites, then computes the X-ray scattering spectra and effective magnetic moment. Vibronic coupling makes several spectral peaks asymmetric, and the calculated moment tracks the measured temperature dependence closely. The verdict: the Jahn-Teller effect here sits in the weak regime, too feeble to deform the lattice. Its dynamic form still reshapes the spectra and shifts the moment, which reconciles theory with the missing distortion. The study also showcases coupled-cluster methods for metal sites inside correlated insulators.
arxiv-2606-15897:
Wyrwal, Ceylan, and Tong introduce topological flow matching in 2026, a generative modelling framework for signals that live on structured spaces rather than flat Euclidean ones. Standard flow matching treats data such as brain activity on a brain graph as plain vectors, discarding the domain's topology. The authors reinterpret flow matching as solving a degenerate Schrödinger bridge problem, which opens a principled place to inject structure: the reference process.

They augment that process with a drift derived from the domain's Laplacian, a prior that smooths signal components which do not correspond to topological features. The modification provably keeps flow matching's attractions: a stable, simulation-free training objective and deterministic sample paths, so the method drops into existing pipelines. Across brain fMRI, ocean currents, seismic events, and traffic flows, it improves over standard flow matching and over topological Schrödinger bridge matching, with the largest advantage on the most complex structures.
arxiv-2606-16297:
Krolewski and the DESI Collaboration map where gamma rays come from in 2026 by cross-matching the gamma-ray sky with galaxy surveys. The Fermi-LAT satellite sees extragalactic gamma-ray emission, but much of it stays unresolved, its sources unknown. Cross-correlating that sky with maps of large-scale structure reveals the redshift distribution of the sources, layer by layer. The galaxy maps come from the DESI DR2 release and the unWISE catalog.

First, known gamma-ray point sources cross-correlate clearly with structure, with a clustering bias near 2, like the massive galaxies that host bright active galactic nuclei. The unresolved gamma-ray background then shows a cross-correlation detected at about 10 sigma in total, strongly in both surveys. Its redshift pattern fits a mix of known source classes. The fits also flag some Galactic contamination at low energies, which softens earlier claims about the background's energy spectrum.
arxiv-2606-16997:
McLean bounds the size of curve-counting invariants in a 2026 algebraic geometry paper. Gromov-Witten invariants count curves on a geometric space with marked points, anchoring much of enumerative geometry and mirror symmetry. Knowing they exist is one thing; bounding their growth is another.

For any smooth projective variety, McLean bounds each primary genus-zero invariant using only concrete data. The inputs are the maximum degree of the defining polynomials, the norms of the inserted forms, the number of marked points, and the curve degree. The bounds grow factorially in the marked points. One consequence is analytic: the Borel transform of the generating function converges absolutely on part of the ample cone. The proof starts from Siebert's formula, expressing the invariants through Segre and Chern classes, and routes through an intermediate curve count in projective space. Explicit growth control turns a formal series into a function with a genuine domain.
arxiv-2606-17497:
Nasser and Adcroft present a 2026 arXiv paper on design rules for data-driven numerical schemes that solve the linear advection equation, a basic transport law in fluid simulation. Neural schemes can drift unstable or fail on new data when built without numerical analysis principles. Working with finite-volume methods in one dimension, the authors vary normalisation, training data, and architecture to see which choices govern stability, accuracy, and shape preservation in the learned schemes they train.

Reconstruction from cell averages alone makes the learning problem multi-valued, which explains poor generalisation across curvature regimes. Enforcing a semilinear form through local stencil-scale normalisation restores stability and good generalisation in their tests. A new data-driven flux limiter beats a classical scheme at preserving shapes by adding mild antidiffusion in near-linear regions. Training on polynomial profiles also yields stable, high-order schemes, with degree setting the accuracy order.
arxiv-2606-17597:
Čap and Gover present a 2026 arXiv paper in differential geometry on how spaces that open out to infinity can be described near their boundary, with general relativity as the motivating case. Scattering theory and relativity both use metrics with specific asymptotic shapes near infinity, and projective compactness captures some of them. The authors weaken that notion to projective pre-compactness, defined for torsion-free connections and, through the Levi-Civita link, for the metrics physicists use near infinity.

Under mild conditions on Ricci curvature, such a structure appears on the boundary itself. Slightly stronger conditions make the standard tractor bundle and its connection arise there naturally, through a smooth extension in Melrose's b-calculus. The boundary then splits into curved orbits matching space-like, time-like, and light-like infinities. A new normal form for such metrics ties the theory back to relativity's usage.
arxiv-2606-17997:
Qiumu and colleagues simulate the radioactive glow of matter blasted off a magnetar, in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Magnetars are neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields, and their rare giant flares may eject neutron-rich material where the rapid neutron-capture process can forge heavy elements. Late gamma-ray emission seen from the flare of SGR 1806-20 hints that this really happens.

Running nuclear reaction networks, the team finds the synthesized nuclei cluster near the first and second r-process abundance peaks. Because of that mix, the ejecta block kiloelectronvolt gamma rays about a thousand times more strongly than megaelectronvolt ones. The escaping nuclear light is thus dominated by MeV photons in the first thousand seconds, giving future telescopes concrete line signatures to search for after the next nearby giant flare.
arxiv-2606-18797:
Lu and the team study whether language models can judge how much errors in radiology reports matter, in a 2026 medical AI paper. Report scoring matters, because an omitted critical finding can change patient care. Yet existing metrics collapse quality into a baseless score. Smart language models blur the line between errors that matter and harmless rephrasings.

Using the ReEvalMed benchmark, the authors score evaluators on discrimination, catching clinical errors, and robustness to small, harmless variation, across eight of them in one-pass and two-pass settings. They find a common discrimination bias. Models detect errors well, but over-punish benign variation. Building four thousand report pairs, they trained lightweight metrics on open models that sharpened the boundary. Those beat larger medical models and rivaled closed ones. The costlier two-pass setting did not help throughout, mainly trading discrimination for robustness. So the paper advises one-pass trained metrics for use.
arxiv-2606-18897:
Xia and the team build a recommender system whose user intents are discovered from text by sparse autoencoders, rather than imposed, in a 2026 information systems paper. Intent-based recommenders model what drives clicks and purchases, to improve accuracy and interpretability. But most derive intents by clustering behavior. That makes them sensitive to sequence quality, forces a preset intent count, and leaves the intents without meaning.

SAERec applies a sparse autoencoder to large language model embeddings of a textual corpus. It pulls human-interpretable intents out of noise. For each user, it retrieves two kinds of intent priors. Personal intents match interests. Public intents capture item patterns shared across users, such as quality or price sensitivity. SAERec injects them into sequence modeling, through a multi-branch attention mechanism with fusion. Experiments on public datasets showed gains over leading baselines. SAERec also produced human-understandable explanations of its recommendations.
arxiv-2606-18997:
Galeano and colleagues introduce DIPHINE in 2026, a neural estimator for breaking down how information flows in complex systems over time. The framework behind it splits information into sixteen distinct atoms. These atoms capture what parts store alone, what they share, and what they create only together. Past tools could compute this split only for Gaussian or discrete systems, which blocked use on many real continuous systems.

DIPHINE uses score-based diffusion models to gauge all the mutual information terms the split needs, from a single trained network. A Möbius inversion step then recovers the sixteen atoms. The authors study how errors spread through that inversion. They show the key mapping has whole-number entries, and that the synergy-to-synergy atom is provably the hardest to gauge. On synthetic tests, the method recovers atoms well and beats older tools on continuous non-Gaussian dynamics.
arxiv-2606-19197:
Haak and colleagues study ABox abduction under repair semantics in 2026, asking whether hypotheses can satisfy several desirable properties at once. Abduction explains a missing entailment by proposing facts that, if added, would make it true. Under repair semantics, recent work has mapped properties like signature limits and small size. Hypotheses meeting more than one property would be even better for applications, but they had not been studied.

This problem is considered for a lightweight logic under brave and AR semantics. Hypotheses must combine properties, or pair a property with a best-score rule. The main observation is encouraging. Requiring extra properties often does not raise cost at all. Combined requirements can thus be imposed in many cases for free. That finding widens the design space for explanation systems.
arxiv-2606-19297:
Kachaev and colleagues ask in 2026 whether vision-language-action models retain basic commonsense and world knowledge after robotics fine-tuning. Such models start from powerful pretrained vision-language models, then adapt to robot data. Failures on knowledge tasks are ambiguous, since missing knowledge and poor low-level control look alike. The team introduces Act2Answer, a protocol that adapts knowledge benchmarks so agents must answer through action, not text.

Each question becomes a short tabletop episode. The agent makes one object-placement action to pick among candidate answers, yielding an action-grounded success rate with reduced control confounds. A curated suite spans diverse commonsense and world-knowledge categories. Layerwise intent probing further localizes where answer-relevant information lives across the backbone and action head. The large-scale study measures how much knowledge survives embodied adaptation, and where it fades. That map helps builders protect knowledge during fine-tuning.
arxiv-2606-19497:
Hamed Talebian and five colleagues tackle blocked radio paths in Bluetooth indoor positioning in 2026. Bluetooth Low Energy direction finding can locate gear inside factories, but walls and machines reflect the signal. Those reflections create non-line-of-sight paths that bend angle estimates and spoil the fix.

The team built a controlled test setup that records labelled clear and blocked signals in two distinct indoor settings. Signal features pass through robust scaling, then checks with principal component analysis and density estimates confirm the two classes separate. A Nyström kernel map feeds a light support vector classifier, lifting accuracy by about 7 to 14 percent over raw features. A neural network scores slightly higher, but the kernel route costs less memory and power. Tuned thresholds then let small devices flag bad paths in real time.
arxiv-2606-19697:
Yanhong Li, Anej Svete, Ashish Sabharwal, and William Merrill show in 2026 that chain-of-thought transformers can run standard algorithms efficiently. Reasoning models emit thought tokens before answering, and theory says they can simulate Turing machines. Turing machines, though, are a clumsy yardstick for how algorithms are really designed.

Algorithms live in the Word RAM model, with random-access memory and unit-cost word operations. The team ask whether chain-of-thought can simulate Word RAM at matching speed. Sorting and shortest-path routines set the test cases. The answer is yes, up to small poly-logarithmic overhead. Three settings support the result: finite-precision models, continuous vector-valued thought, and a hybrid with a recurrent base layer. Flat instruction sets shrink the overhead further, to log-square or even a single log factor. Older Turing machine simulations needed quadratic overhead, making the new bound far sharper.
arxiv-2606-20097:
Zhentao Tan and six colleagues redesign hybrid attention for language models around one observation: attention heads inside a layer do different jobs, even though they read the same input. Their 2026 paper, HydraHead, mixes full attention, accurate but costly as context grows, with linear attention, cheap but weaker, along the head axis rather than layer by layer. Earlier hybrids assigned whole layers to one type, ignoring the specialization that interpretability studies reveal among heads.

HydraHead keeps full attention only for heads proven critical to retrieval, picked by an interpretability-driven selection, and fuses both output types through a scale-normalized module. A three-stage pipeline reuses parameters and distills knowledge, so training stays light. At a seven-to-one ratio of linear to full heads, it matched a three-to-one layer-wise hybrid on long-context tasks. Training on only fifteen billion tokens still beat rival hybrids by wide margins.
arxiv-2606-20497:
Antonio Varagnolo and four colleagues bring readable meta-learning models to chemical search with several goals at once. Their 2026 paper tackles the vast space of molecules that can actually be made, where stand-in models must juggle competing aims. Deep learning struggles here under the cost limits of quantum-level chemistry.

A modular pipeline pairs linear meta-learning models, whose rules chemists can read, with uncertainty scores that adapt their confidence, inside an Efficient Global Optimization loop. Training across chemical aims and cheap side properties lets the linear models borrow strength between tasks. Meta-learning of this kind is used in a multi-goal chemical search for the first time. Chemists get stand-in models they can actually read, which matters when a model steers costly synthesis choices.
arxiv-2606-20597:
Nia George and Simeon Sayer chart six decades of U.S. juvenile justice with topic modeling and LLM-assisted analysis. Their 2026 paper applies the methods to 60,470 appellate opinions from 1970 to 2025. Juvenile courts handle both delinquency cases and child welfare cases, and both streams have changed dramatically.

The analysis identifies 182 legal topics organized into 10 themes across juvenile justice litigation. Child welfare litigation tripled its share of the corpus, and sex offender registration cases more than doubled. The shifts trace the system's move from punishment toward protection, the arc the title names. Computational tracking shows legal change at a scale no manual review could cover.
arxiv-2606-20797:
M Abumusabh and the Belle II Collaboration report in 2026 the first measurement of mixing-induced CP violation in a rare B meson decay to two neutral pions. CP violation is a difference between matter and antimatter behavior. Such tests probe the standard theory and search for new particles or interactions. The data come from 190 million events collected with Belle II at the SuperKEKB collider in Japan.

A new method uses quantum entanglement of the produced B meson pair. It enables a time-dependent analysis without reconstructing the decay position of the signal meson. The mixing-induced coefficient is measured with large uncertainty, centered at 0.61. Precision matches what a conventional analysis would need twenty times more data to reach. A direct CP coefficient is also measured. Rare decay channels like this one can expose effects that common channels hide.
arxiv-2606-20897:
Zeyuan Chen and four colleagues propose PeerCheck in 2026 to raise the quality of language model academic reviews toward human level. Submissions keep growing, and peer review struggles to keep pace. Models are increasingly used to assist. PeerCheck first compares model reviews with human reviews. It finds different emphases: models prioritize theory, while humans stress methods and experiments.

Two improvement routes are then tested. Prompt methods such as chain-of-thought reasoning are applied. Retrieval-augmented generation, which fetches source text, is also tried. Chain-of-thought improves review quality clearly. Retrieval gives mixed results, an effect called the RAG paradox. For some models it even lowers quality. Knowing which aid helps and which hurts matters as journals consider model help. A fluent review that misses methods may look strong while failing the core job of peer review.
arxiv-2606-21197:
Sergio Lanza, Jae Lee, and Stefan Wermter propose a framework in 2026 to extract multimodal concepts from vision-language models through sparse autoencoders. Such models caption images and answer visual questions well. Their internal processes remain poorly understood. Sparse autoencoders can surface interpretable concepts inside a model. Most earlier work treats text and visual concepts separately, missing concepts that join both.

For each neuron, a candidate human-interpretable concept is proposed. Alignment between the concept and dataset samples is scored by cosine similarity. Visual, textual, and multimodal concepts are all analyzed in one frame. Earlier visual methods often gave vague or incomplete descriptions, limiting their use. Joint concepts matter because a vision-language model may encode ideas like a pictured word's meaning that belong to neither modality alone, and interpretability tools must catch them to explain model behavior.
arxiv-2606-21397:
Sebastian Neef and four colleagues benchmark language models as web security auditors in 2026, testing whether they can find real flaws in WordPress plugin code. The flaws targeted are classic web vulnerabilities: SQL injection, stored cross-site scripting, path traversal, and remote code execution. Six frontier and open-weight models were run under five prompt designs of varying structure and scope, across three repeated rounds.

Every model found genuine issues, but rates ranged widely, from 63 percent for Claude Opus 4.6 down to 35 percent for a self-hosted Qwen model. Prompts that narrowed the vulnerability scope beat open-ended ones, while prompt complexity mattered little. No model reported consistently across rounds, with some near fifty percent, and one baseline flaw escaped every model, a sober limit for automated auditing.
arxiv-2606-21497:
Neeraj Mohan Sushma and six colleagues propose Hierarchical Block-Local Learning in 2026, a training method that breaks the sequential bottleneck of backpropagation. Backprop forces errors to travel through every layer before any update, locking layers together and demanding symmetric forward and backward paths. Their framework splits a deep network into hierarchically linked blocks, each trained on local objectives drawn from variational principles, so no full backward pass is needed.

The authors claim this is the first method able to train deep networks in logarithmic parallel time in the number of layers. The hierarchy also defines a family of subnetworks along different paths, letting inference use varying effective depths. Tests on vision and language tasks reach competitive accuracy, and an extension covers recurrent sequence models that normally rely on backpropagation through time.
arxiv-2606-21797:
O'Keeffe studies swarmalators in 2026, models of moving oscillators whose positions and internal phases influence each other. His one-dimensional ring model adds van Hemmen pair disorder, meaning the coupling strength between each pair is randomly signed rather than uniform. Disorder of this kind is known from spin-glass physics, and the paper asks how it reshapes the ring's collective states.

Disorder first splits the static states into four branches: sync, split, splay, and phase wave. New order parameters that track glass-like order organize them. Because the oscillators move, two active states appear that the immobile version lacks: a bursty asynchronous state and, for balanced sign patterns, a glassy phase wave with rotating glass order. O'Keeffe derives a six-field reduced model, the exact sync boundary at any population size, and an exact antiphase phase-wave branch. A nonlinear theory covering both active branches remains open.
arxiv-2606-21997:
Galloway and colleagues examine, in 2026, a technical step inside the proofs of the Lorentzian splitting theorems. Those theorems describe when a spacetime must split into a time line times a fixed space. Distance functions to points along a complete timelike line are known to be locally equi-Lipschitz, meaning the whole family shares one local slope bound. That fact is essential to the classical proofs, and the paper asks whether it survives a natural generalization.

The generalization replaces points with the level sets of a Cauchy temporal function, a time function whose slices cut across the whole spacetime. The authors show the equi-Lipschitz property fails in general for these families of Lorentz distances. They then formulate conjectures about when temporal functions with the good property exist in such spacetimes. Those conjectures turn out to be equivalent to Bartnik's cosmological splitting conjecture.
arxiv-2606-22197:
Wang and colleagues introduce Multi4D in 2026, a framework for dynamic Gaussian splatting that aims to keep both motion consistency and visual fidelity. Dynamic splatting renders moving 3D scenes from Gaussian primitives. Deformation-based methods preserve object identity but oversmooth fast detail, while 4D methods capture detail at heavy storage cost and break identity over time.

Multi4D instead spreads modelling capacity over three levels: static structure, dynamic geometry that persists, and short-lived appearance primitives. Through shared rendering and residual-driven optimization, the levels compete to explain image error and specialize without any pre-assigned split. The split preserves long-term motion consistency while still capturing fine dynamic detail. The authors report top rendering quality in real time, with significantly fewer dynamic primitives. Because compact persistent Gaussians are tracked over time, the system also reaches top 4D segmentation accuracy, with a tenfold speedup.
arxiv-2606-22397:
Chengnan Shentu and four colleagues, including Jessica Burgner-Kahrs, work on soft robotics in this 2026 paper. Their robots are tendon-driven continuum robots, flexible arms steered by pulling cables. Learning to manipulate objects with the whole body is hard because good simulators for soft robots lag behind those for rigid ones.

The team derives a discretization informed by continuum mechanics, a way of splitting the flexible body into pieces for computation. It places the soft robot natively inside MuJoCo, a physics simulator, uniting tendon forces, body contact, and motion in one pipeline. They validate the simulator against a Cosserat rod reference model and against real robot hardware. Policies trained by imitation learning from teleoperated demonstrations then transferred, with no further training, to a physical three-segment robot mounted on a Franka arm. The authors report success on two contact-rich manipulation tasks, a first for continuum robots.
arxiv-2606-22497:
Tianqi Wei, Xin Yu, Zhi Chen, Scott Chapman, and Zi Huang present a benchmark for vision-language models in this 2026 paper. Such models answer questions about images, but existing tests focus on ordinary photographs. Microscopic plant images, which reveal cells and pathogens, remain largely untested even though plant biologists rely on them.

Their benchmark, PlantMicro, gathers more than five thousand images from diverse hosts, biological domains, and imaging methods. Over nine thousand visual question-answering pairs probe different aspects of understanding these images. When leading models were evaluated, they struggled with fine-grained recognition and biologically grounded reasoning. On pathogen classification, the strongest example given scored about thirty-five percent accuracy. That is only modestly above the random guessing baseline of about twenty-five percent. The authors offer PlantMicro as a standard foundation for improving microscopy-level plant understanding in future models.
arxiv-2606-22597:
Srinivas Venkatanarayanan and Clement Pakkam Isaac test whether vision-language models can make verifiable decisions from street maps in this 2026 paper. Models increasingly read maps to support logistics, delivery, and accessible navigation, where the result is an action that must respect the road network. Most benchmarks grade free text, which cannot be checked against the underlying street graph.

Their benchmark, MapReason-OSM, renders maps of ten US downtowns at two zoom scales, each panel paired with a hidden street graph and oracles. Six thousand instances span twelve tasks covering routing, facility location, and visual disambiguation. Model decisions are snapped back to the graph and scored for validity, legality, optimality, and consistency across zooms. Across seven models, the systems read maps and routed simply, but failed at graph-cost reasoning. Placing a single facility pin was near chance even for frontier reasoning models, and answers often changed with scale.
arxiv-2606-22797:
Tianjia Dong, Nadav Kunievsky, and James A. Evans ask whether a language model's behavior travels, in this 2026 paper. Two decision settings can share identical payoffs yet differ in surface presentation. A model that behaves one way in the first may act differently in the second, which makes suite-based evaluation fragile.

The authors define behavior portability formally. They fit an interpretable behavioral model on data pooled from several source environments, then test it on a held-out target environment. Performance is compared against an oracle trained directly on target data, and their measure gives worst-case bounds for the target setting. Across seven classic economic decision problems, they found substantial, systematic portability losses. Behavioral profiles measured in one setting, they conclude, cannot be assumed to transfer to an equivalent setting with different wording or framing. That warning applies to any benchmark that treats one phrasing as the model's true character.
arxiv-2606-22997:
Dakai Guo and colleagues settle a number theory conjecture about binomial coefficients in a 2026 paper. Binomial coefficients count how many ways items can be chosen from a set. The conjecture, recorded in a public sequence database, concerns the greatest common divisor of a certain family of these numbers. It predicts exactly when that shared divisor equals one. The condition involves the largest prime power piece of a related whole number.

Guo and colleagues prove the criterion holds in full. The proof is also formalized in Lean, a computer proof assistant that checks each logical step. The formal version was accepted into the Formal Conjectures project, a shared library of checked statements. The text states that an AI agent system built by the authors generated both the plain-language proof and the Lean version.
arxiv-2606-23197:
Sophie Corallo and colleagues present the EVerest dataset for secure software engineering in a 2026 paper. Checking security end to end means tracing a system from written requirements through architecture down to code. No existing dataset spans all three levels with fine-grained security labels. EVerest fills that gap using a real open-source stack of software for charging electric vehicles, built with industry partners. The dataset holds eighty-four hand-elicited security requirements, each tagged with its security objectives.

Corallo and colleagues add over fourteen hundred fine-grained security elements, covering components, data, data flows, and states. Acceptance windows, cross-references, and trace links connect the requirements to the architecture model. Source code and documentation in natural language complete the package. The resource lets researchers test verification tools on one consistent, realistic system instead of toy examples.
arxiv-2606-23397:
Murtazo Nazarov builds a high-order finite element method that respects physical bounds in a 2026 paper. The method solves nonlinear scalar conservation laws, equations where a quantity is transported without being created or destroyed. A good scheme must keep the solution inside its invariant domain, never overshooting into impossible values. Nazarov combines a high-order scheme with a low-order bound-preserving scheme built on a fine submesh. The split avoids restrictions from lumped masses and wide stencils.

Nazarov links the two updates through a graph-Poisson flux reconstruction. Their difference becomes a set of conservative antisymmetric fluxes on a graph. Convex limiting coefficients then trim those fluxes, and a redistribution step restores exact conservation where room allows. Tests show high-order accuracy, convergence to the entropy solution, and robustness near discontinuities.
arxiv-2606-23497:
Talamini proves that solutions of certain wave-like systems have well-defined boundary values, in a 2026 paper on partial differential equations. The systems are two-by-two conservation laws, equations that track two quantities whose totals are preserved as they flow. Bounded entropy solutions can develop sharp features, so asking what value a solution takes exactly on a curve is delicate. For single scalar equations, strong traces have been known for years. For systems, the theory largely stalled.

Talamini shows that bounded entropy solutions of genuinely nonlinear, strictly hyperbolic systems do admit strong traces on Lipschitz curves, curves without sharp corners. The proof hinges on a new half-space theorem of Liouville type, for isentropic solutions whose normal trace stays constant. That theorem unlocks the first extension of scalar strong trace results to general genuinely nonlinear systems. Strong traces support boundary value problems and recent uniqueness arguments for rough solutions.
arxiv-2606-24697:
The Euclid Collaboration, with F. Passalacqua among the lead authors, tests how well the Euclid space telescope will measure galaxy redshifts. The test uses simulated data for NISP, the mission's near infrared spectrometer and photometer. Euclid relies on slitless spectroscopy, where spectra of nearby sources overlap on the detector. That overlap, cross contamination, is a main risk to redshift accuracy. The study runs pixel level simulations and pushes them through the Euclid spectroscopic pipeline.

First, an idealised case with no overlaps sets a baseline for accuracy against emission line flux and galaxy size. Realistic contamination is then added in stages. Adding ever fainter contaminants shows no clear harm from sources fainter than magnitude 20. The team therefore limits its main analysis to galaxies brighter than magnitude 24, to be safe. One early estimate says same redshift contaminants cause about 4 percent of the total degradation blamed on cross contamination.
arxiv-2606-24997:
Livia Betti and four colleagues open up location embeddings to ask what geographic knowledge they contain. Geographic neural models map any coordinate on Earth to a vector, absorbing geospatial data into their weights. Such embeddings are used off the shelf as general purpose features, yet users lacked a principled audit. The authors decompose the embeddings three ways. Sparse autoencoders yield latent concepts. Sparse linear concept embeddings over a geospatial dictionary recover natural language concepts. Saliency maps give visual features.

The decompositions keep high reconstruction ability while exposing readable structure. Forests, deserts, and urban features appear as distinct components. Sparse versions also reveal clear differences between encoders: some emphasise urban structures, others broader biome and climate signals. Saliency maps from the pretraining space highlight other features such as roads and landmarks. Betti and colleagues offer the analysis as an audit toolkit: check what the vectors encode before trusting them blind.
arxiv-2606-25097:
Speculative decoding speeds up language model inference: a small draft model proposes tokens and the target model checks them. Sahil Kadadekar asks whether draft side behaviour can leak into safety scored outputs when decoding runs at temperature zero. He builds a screen, the Typical Acceptance Invariance Screen, that runs target only and speculative decoding side by side on the same safety battery. The screen demands byte identity evidence, statistical equivalence within a tight margin, and effect sizes below a calibrated cutoff.

Across a confirmatory core and a large matched expansion, the tested stacks show no detectable safety divergence. The largest effect size on refusal behaviour is an order of magnitude below the trivial effect floor. An adversarially tuned draft produces byte identical output to the standard draft across thousands of samples. A change of numerical precision rewrites a large share of output bytes, yet no safety rate moves outside equivalence.
arxiv-2606-25197:
Choosing what to measure next is the core problem in adaptive data collection, from lab experiments to tuning models. Daolang Huang and colleagues present Polar in 2026, a method that separates learning a summary of past data from learning what to do next. The summary comes from a pretrained foundation model for tables, whose internal features act as a belief state, meaning a compact picture of what the data so far imply. A small policy head then learns choices on top of that summary.

Across Bayesian experimental design, Bayesian optimisation, and active learning tasks, Polar beat the leading purpose-built methods the team compared it with. It also needed far fewer training examples to reach that level. Because only the goal function changes between tasks, one simple framework covers all three settings instead of a separate design for each.
arxiv-2606-25697:
No polynomial surface can be exactly a sphere, so geometric designers approximate it with smooth patches. Ema Češek and Aleš Vavpetič construct such an approximation in 2026 from quadratic spline patches with geometric continuity, meaning the surface looks smooth across seams even where its parametrisation bends. Their building block covers a regular spherical polygon split into three times as many triangles as it has sides. Stacking those blocks over the faces of any uniform polyhedron, the Platonic and Archimedean solids included, tiles the whole sphere.

Only quadratic triangular patches are used, the lowest degree that can bend convincingly. Control points come out as explicit formulas depending on the polyhedron's geometry plus a single free parameter, which tunes the fit. The pair analyse how close the approximation sits to the true sphere and how its curvature behaves, a practical recipe for modelling pipelines that prefer polynomials over rational surfaces.
arxiv-2606-25797:
A Markov decision process mixes choice with chance, and checking its behaviour statistically usually assumes you may peek, sample, and peek again. Konstantin Kueffner, Tobias Meggendorfer, Maximilian Weininger, and Patrick Wienhöft supply the right statistics for that online rhythm in 2026. Classical workflows sample in rounds and widen bounds with blunt union bound corrections. Worse, existing implementations are often subtly incorrect, or wasteful, or both. The team's confidence sequences are built for continuous monitoring: valid at every moment, not just at preplanned checkpoints.

All variants are implemented in one efficient tool and tested for practical use. They beat the classical union bound style approaches head to head. Against the previous state of the art, the implementation needed fifty times fewer samples on average to reach its guarantees. For engineers verifying systems with unknown probabilities, that is the difference between a check that runs and one that merely exists.
arxiv-2606-26097:
Lukáš Gráf, Jenni Kotila, and Oliver Scholer study rare double-beta processes that emit positrons or capture electrons. The usual double-beta decay gets most attention as a probe of new physics. These sibling modes could complement it, especially for the proposed NuDoubt-plus-plus experiment. Three candidate isotopes are analysed: krypton-78, cadmium-106, and xenon-124. Matrix elements and phase-space factors are computed for both versions.

Standard Model channels split by reachability. The two-neutrino modes with electron capture look most accessible to experiment. The double positron mode stays strongly suppressed by phase space. For the neutrinoless channel, a projected half-life sensitivity is translated into new-physics reach. Lepton-number-violating scales from about one to one hundred tera-electronvolts come into view. Measurements across several isotopes can untangle competing operator effects. The modes thus earn a place beside conventional searches.
arxiv-2606-26297:
Ali Rajabi, Milad Hasanzadeh, and Amin Kargarian release a simulator that spreads quantum optimization across many processors. The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm tackles QUBO problems, the yes-no optimization form behind much engineering design. Their distributed simulator runs inside the Qiskit ecosystem. One workflow handles everything: the problem is standardized, mapped to a cost Hamiltonian, split across quantum processors, and turned into circuits.

Single-processor and multi-processor modes share the tool. Processor counts and capacities are user settings, so problem size studies are easy to run. Reused parameterized circuits and batched evaluations trim repeated overhead. Parallel multi-start runs speed the search further. A browser interface built on Streamlit lets users upload problems and watch solution quality without touching code. General, reusable QUBO simulation was the gap; this package fills it openly.
arxiv-2606-26597:
Yiwei Bao, Jie-Shuang Wang, and Hao Zhou build a cleaner calculation tool for cosmic-ray electrons and positrons from pulsars. Pulsars, spinning neutron stars, can accelerate these particles. Their travel to Earth is modelled as diffusion through two zones. Diffusion is slow near the source and normal in interstellar space. Direct calculations in this setup suffer from cancelling oscillations and blurred cooling boundaries.

Their two-zone kernel solves the propagation in series form. Energy losses from magnetic fields and starlight are included along the way. The method keeps the sharp cooling boundary seen in detailed numerical checks. Applied to local fluxes, it shows distant pulsars matter collectively at moderate energies. Sources beyond a thousand light-years-scale distances can supply a large share of the mid-energy flux. Geminga-style slow-diffusion halos remain compatible with current positron and anisotropy data.
arxiv-2606-26797:
Hongyi Henry Jin and four colleagues show that the quality of reasoning training data reveals itself in its first few tokens. Fine-tuning on a small set of strong reasoning traces teaches language models to reason well. Curating that set usually needs expensive checks by stronger models. The first tokens of a trace, the authors find, already carry the signal.

Hard problems show up in the loss of the first hundred reasoning tokens at a slightly perturbed model checkpoint. Loss measures how surprised the model is. Examples with similar early loss patterns provoke similar learning gradients, a claim the authors prove. Fine-tuning two open models on medical and mathematics reasoning data followed. Their method beat existing curation baselines slightly while using far fewer tokens. The curation cost falls sharply as a result.
arxiv-2606-27097:
Podzolkova and Melnik model how the Milky Way's central bar stirs star orbits near a key resonance. Stars near the outer Lindblad resonance can fall into libration, a trapped swaying motion around a steady path. Their analytic bar model reproduces those radial velocity profiles seen in Gaia DR3 data. In their 2026 study, extra models that differ only in bar growth time let the team ask when the trapping begins.

Velocity curves from models with different growth times keep the same shape but slide sideways in time. The slide that best aligns them grows in direct proportion to the growth time, with a factor just over one half. Librations therefore start before the bar is fully grown. They begin once the bar reaches a little over half of its final strength. That timing gives a new handle on how quickly the galactic bar assembled.
arxiv-2606-27197:
Biswal and Polo build new pieces inside a doubled representation of a Kac-Moody algebra. These algebras generalise the symmetry algebras behind much of modern representation theory. The module named L of rho is the basic irreducible integrable module, built from the special weight rho. Tensoring it with itself splits it into components that are hard to enumerate directly. In the 2026 paper, rooted trees enter through a subgraph of the Dynkin diagram.

For each subset of that subgraph, the authors form a combined root sum and a candidate crystal element. Crystal elements are combinatorial shadows of module pieces, easier to track than the pieces themselves. Choices of a root vertex in each connected part fix the construction. Each candidate is proved rho-dominant, the key property certifying a genuine component. Whole new families of tensor product components thereby appear, tied explicitly to tree-shaped choices.
arxiv-2606-27397:
Feng, Chen, and He build a bargaining arena where language model agents trade, produce, and invest against each other. Static benchmarks miss the open-ended, mixed-motive character of real economic life. SidConArena formalises a multiplayer economy as a finite-horizon, partially observable stochastic game with three coupled phases. Agents negotiate in natural language with binding trades, run deterministic converter-based production, and bid in sealed auctions for long-term assets. Structured observations and a neural-symbolic action interface keep free-form play rule-grounded in this benchmark paper from 2026.

Tournaments pit identical and mixed model lineups against each other. Stronger frontier models earn higher economic outcomes, as expected. Yet agents still misvalue resources, bargain passively, and plan poorly over long investment horizons. The arena exposes economic weaknesses that question-answering scores never touch. Negotiation skill, not just reasoning, becomes measurable.
arxiv-2606-27597:
Ocean internal gravity waves carry energy through layered water. The Garrett–Munk spectrum has long been the standard model of this wave field. It rests on hydrostatic assumptions and idealised layering, though. Those limits bite where dynamics turn non-hydrostatic or layering grows uneven. Leticia Fabre-Lima, Jeffrey Early, and Miles Sundermeyer build a broader framework in 2026.

Their version uses non-hydrostatic vertical modes. The modes live in horizontal wavenumber and mode space, not frequency space. That choice keeps wave modes energetically separate. Each mode has a deformation radius. The radius flags whether a mode behaves hydrostatically or not. Modes come from a numerical Sturm–Liouville problem, so any layering profile works. Worked examples show departures from the older theory near boundaries. Vertical variance and high-frequency vertical energy are represented better. Familiar features of measured wavenumber spectra are still reproduced.
arxiv-2606-27897:
Shopping catalogues let users filter watches by metadata. They poorly support open-ended browsing by look and feel, though. Kai Lawonn, Tobias Günther, and Monique Meuschke present a visual analysis system in 2026 for large wristwatch collections. Each watch is represented through separate attribute graphs. Dial colour and dial design get their own graphs. Watch type serves as an explicit semantic organiser.

The pipeline segments dials with a U-Net and predicts types with a vision transformer. Colours map to a shared perceptual palette, and dial structure is captured by a gradient-based descriptor. The authors extend the UMAP embedding method, merging attribute graphs under one objective. A class-aware layout term keeps global type structure apart, while local visual neighbourhoods stay intact. An interactive interface offers spatial navigation, filtering, detail inspection, and search by example. A pilot study with experts and novices suggests the system supports discovery and comparison.
arxiv-2606-27997:
Benchmarks with many datasets make model evaluation expensive. Selecting a small representative subset is the usual fix, but heuristics rarely check whether rankings survive. Rostislav Gusev and Alexey Zaytsev introduce a framework in 2026 for dataset selection judged by rank preservation. Bootstrap aggregation supplies valid confidence intervals, so methods can be compared on principle. Clustering, design criteria, random baselines, and greedy farthest-first selection are all tested.

Three domains supply the evidence, with 112 time series datasets, 57 language tasks, and 30 recommender datasets. In time series, the best strategy reaches a Spearman correlation of zero point nine five with full-benchmark rankings using only five datasets. Several methods beat random subsets there and in the language benchmark. In recommender systems, gains over random are small and usually insignificant. How well a method works depends on representation quality and benchmark size.
arxiv-2606-28197:
Yusuke Tsukamoto, writing alone, tackles a numerical headache in smoothed particle magnetohydrodynamics, a method that simulates magnetized fluids as moving particles. Simulations must keep the magnetic field free of divergence, a quantity that physics requires to be exactly zero but that computer errors keep making nonzero.

Tsukamoto corrects the field after each update by solving a projection problem built from the very operator that measures the error. Choosing the adjoint gradient, matched to a volume-weighted measure, makes the correction shrink magnetic energy rather than add to it, and yields a system solvable by a standard iterative method. In collapse calculations the projection pushed the normalized error far below a rival cleaning method, while costing only a small share of the update time.
arxiv-2606-28397:
Shaoxuan Li, Xiangyu Dong, Xiaoguang Ma, Junfeng Chen, Haoran Zhao, and Yaoming Zhou make aerial navigation agents check their own work. Drones following spoken instructions usually act in open loop. A big model proposes actions and the drone executes them unverified, so small early errors snowball into losing the target entirely.

Li's team built CLOSER-VLN around a closed loop of reasoning, verification, targeted retrieval, and correction before any action flies. A hierarchical reasoner drafts candidate actions, a multidimensional verifier grades their reliability, and only failed checks trigger a search of a memory bank for helpful examples. On the CityNav benchmark's unseen split, the system reached a success rate of about thirty-two percent, with path efficiency to match, supporting the value of self-verification in the air.
arxiv-2606-28497:
Taras Panamarev, Xiang Zou, and Bence Kocsis ask whether a hidden black hole tore apart the young stars at our galaxy's center. Those stars show several orbital planes and a spread of eccentricities, odd if they were born together in one flat, spinning gas disc. An intermediate-mass black hole orbiting the central supermassive one could have done the damage.

The authors first derive a criterion for where the intruder's torque beats the disc's own self-torque, then test it with direct N-body simulations. Orbit and mass decide everything. A prograde intruder quickly aligns with the disc and does little harm. A massive retrograde one anti-aligns and fragments the disc into three angular-momentum components, an inner disc, a misaligned overlap, and an untouched outer disc, while pumping eccentricities up. At two thousand solar masses the wreckage forms within the population's known age.
arxiv-2606-28597:
Davide Benussi, Ioannis Kosmidis, Alessandra Salvan, and Nicola Sartori make a statistical fix practical in daily use. Median bias reduction improves maximum likelihood estimates a lot, but the general methods are implicit. They require solving nonlinear systems, demand a fully spelled-out nuisance parameterization, and turn into algebra slogs whenever the target is a transformation of the fitted ones.

Their focused version is direct. For a smooth scalar transformation of a reference fit, they solve an equation built from the Cornish-Fisher expansion of the estimator. It needs only the original estimate, the change's gradient and Hessian, and values that the literature or Monte Carlo can supply. The result is third-order median unbiased and matches one-step versions of the indirect methods. Examples span post-selection inference, distances, and quantiles across regression, circular, and layered models.
arxiv-2606-28897:
Zhang settles a conjecture about special metrics, ways of measuring distance, on complete geometric spaces of five to nine dimensions. The metrics in question are critical points of a functional that integrates the square of scalar curvature, a summary of how space bends at each point. Earlier work by Catino, Mastrolia and Monticelli proved that in dimensions ten and above, every complete noncompact critical metric with finite energy must be scalar-flat, meaning its scalar curvature vanishes everywhere.

Those authors conjectured the same from five upward, but their methods left the lower range open. Zhang closes the gap. He verifies scalar-flatness for the remaining dimensions, five through nine. Together with the earlier result, the theorem now covers every dimension from five onward. Critical metrics of this functional there are forced to be scalar-flat.
arxiv-2606-29097:
Tu, Niu and Zhang present TrafficAlign, a framework that teaches language models to generate realistic traffic scenarios for testing self-driving systems. Pretrained models often produce scenarios that do not match real-world traffic distributions, limiting their value for finding dangerous cases. TrafficAlign instead synthesises scenarios from real driving videos, validates the data, and aligns the model with the validated scenarios.

The results cut both ways in a useful direction. Scenarios from TrafficAlign revealed up to about eleven percent more collisions, on average across three self-driving models, than rival methods produced. The scenarios are thus better at exposing weaknesses. Fine-tuning the driving models on them then cut collision rates by about thirty-six percent. A qualitative study across six diverse regions showed the scenarios matched local traffic well.
arxiv-2606-29697:
Liu, Plotegher, Roura, and He present MF-UAVPose6D, a framework that estimates the full pose of a fixed-wing drone from a single camera image. Six-degree-of-freedom pose supports airspace awareness, tracking, and counter-drone work. Non-cooperative targets usually lack CAD models and keypoint priors, the reference information that model-based or keypoint-matching methods rely on.

The method is model-free and monocular: at inference it needs only one RGB image and the camera intrinsics. A heatmap-guided step first finds a stable target anchor. A Perspective-Aware Module models observation-ray priors, while Dynamic Topological Sampling draws out weak structural cues from wings, fuselage, and tail. A decoupled translation-rotation decoder then estimates the pose. The team also builds a synthetic dataset. Experiments show accurate estimation without CAD models.
arxiv-2606-29897:
Tushar, Miao, and Tong study voice anonymization for children. Anonymization hides who is speaking while keeping the words usable, but most systems are built on adult speech and work worse on children's voices.

The team adapts a pipeline based on self-supervised learning, where a model learns speech structure from unlabelled audio, using child speech from the MyST corpus. They test single speakers and mixtures of two speakers. Child-domain adaptation improves how intelligible and natural the anonymized speech sounds while keeping privacy protection strong. For two-speaker recordings, first extracting the target speaker and then anonymizing protects privacy while keeping the conversational structure of the exchange.
arxiv-2606-30297:
Mahan Vaz Silva and Daniel Skurt build neighborhood semantics for modal logics with a deliberately weak negation. The base logic, CLoN, is a sublogic of the four-valued system FDE. Its negation lacks the usual axioms, making it both gappy and glutty. Modal extensions let the logic speak about necessity and possibility. Two neighborhood functions serve each modal operator here.

Careful definition of rejection sets does the heavy lifting. With them, non-trivial axioms involving weak negation become valid. The framework builds on earlier work on FDE-based non-normal modal logics. Its philosophical aim concerns deontic logic, the logic of obligation. A good deontic system must hold ordinary principles and admit moral dilemmas. It must do both without collapsing into triviality. This semantics is offered as groundwork for such systems. Weak negation, handled rightly, need not mean weak results.
arxiv-2606-30597:
Taixi Chen and Nancy Guo tackle a practical weakness of large multimodal models: they expect every input channel, such as image and text, to be present. In real use, channels often go missing, and performance drops sharply. Earlier fixes generated prompts from each input's own features. Those features grow unreliable as more data goes missing, so the prompts wobble too.

Chen and Guo flip the approach. Their learnable latent prompts are fixed anchors, trained once and independent of any single input. The prompts carry stable knowledge about each modality, meaning each kind of input, and can compensate when one kind is absent. Even with ninety percent of a modality missing, the method kept working. Across three benchmark datasets it reached state-of-the-art results over a wide range of missing-data settings.
arxiv-2606-30697:
Yogeswar Reddy Thota introduces LUMOS, a semantic layer that lets AI agents operate computers through meaning rather than screenshots. Today's operating systems are built for human eyes: pixels, icons and windows. Agents forced to read screenshots and guess coordinates pay high token costs and suffer ambiguity and delay. Yet systems already hold the needed facts in accessibility metadata, structured descriptions meant for assistive technology.

LUMOS converts that metadata, plus browser interface structures, into machine-readable blueprints. Each element gets a stable identifier, role, name, value, bounds and allowed actions. It can also ground a live pointer by asking the system which element sits under the cursor. The agent then works in an observe-act loop using only visible-interface primitives, not app-specific scripts. Thota stresses that LUMOS complements visual agents rather than replacing them, and points toward AI-native operating systems.
arxiv-2606-30897:
Antonella Fruscione, Kenny Glotfelty, William Joye and Jonathan McDowell describe SAOImageDS9, the image display and analysis tool built at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory.
