Willems and co-authors traced how a drug-resistant gut bacterium, Enterococcus faecium, spread through hospitals worldwide. They compared 411 isolates, both resistant and susceptible to vancomycin, gathered from people, animals, hospitals, and the community on five continents.

One family of the bacterium, known as clonal complex-17, had gone global and kept turning up in hospital outbreaks. It also shrugged off ampicillin and carried an extra island of genes tied to disease. The authors warn that spotting this lineage early matters, because its resistance gene has already jumped into more dangerous germs, and stopping its spread is critical.
europmc-pmc3383997:
Whittle and a large team described in 2012 how a protein called BMP8B turns up heat production in brown fat. Brown fat burns energy as heat and helps balance body weight. Signals called BMPs were known for shaping fat, but not for running its furnace.

Food and cold switched BMP8B on in mature brown fat, sharpening its response to nerve signals and fat-burning enzymes. Mice missing the gene burned less energy, gained weight, and still ate less than normal. The protein also acts in the brain's appetite center, where giving it centrally fired up brown fat through nerve pathways. That two-way action makes it a tempting obesity target.
europmc-pmc3405197:
Varrin-Doyer and co-workers characterized in 2012 the T cells that attack a water channel in neuromyelitis optica, a disabling disease of the optic nerve and spinal cord. Patients make antibodies against the channel, called aquaporin 4, and such antibodies need T cell help. The team compared blood T cells from patients and healthy controls.

Patient T cells multiplied more strongly in response to the channel, especially to one standout stretch of it. That stretch closely resembles part of a transport protein from a common gut bacterium, and patient cells answered the bacterial piece too, a case of mistaken identity. The responding cells leaned toward the inflammatory Th17 style. The findings open fresh routes into how this disease begins.
europmc-pmc3429397:
Ahuja led a collaborative group that pooled individual records for more than nine thousand patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis in 2012. Such tuberculosis shrugs off the two best first-line drugs, leaving longer, harsher, weaker regimens. No randomized trials existed to say which drug mixes and durations work best, so the group combined patient-level data from many centers.

Overall results were poor: only slightly more than half of patients were treated successfully. Success rose with particular treatment durations, with more likely-effective drugs in both phases, and with certain later-generation quinolone antibiotics and related drugs. The analysis, built for the World Health Organization's guideline panel, gives regimen design a firmer evidence base than study-level pooling could.
europmc-pmc3512497:
Big health surveys miss people, and Arnulf Langhammer and four colleagues test how much that skews Norway's HUNT study in 2012. The third HUNT round drew 50,807 people, 54 percent of those invited. The team checks those who took part against those who did not, using forms, GP records, registers, and drug data.

Taking part varies with age, sex, income, symptoms, and disease. Those who stayed away carry more heart disease, diabetes, and mental illness, a pattern GP records confirm. Yet adding data from 6,922 non-participants shifts the overall disease rates only a little. Under age 80, daily aches like muscle pain and headache are in fact reported more by those who took part. Taking part also links to how long people live.
europmc-pmc3526497:
Many valuable proteins need disulfide bonds to fold, and Julie Lobstein and five colleagues engineer a bacterium that forms them in the wrong compartment on purpose in 2012. Escherichia coli normally keeps its cytoplasm reducing, so bond-needing proteins are shipped outside or misfold; yields suffer.

Their SHuffle strain starts from a mutant with weakened reducing pathways, letting bonds form inside. The key addition is a chromosomal copy of the folding helper DsbC, stripped of its export signal so it stays in the cytoplasm. Built in both K-12 and B strain backgrounds, SHuffle produces correctly bonded, active proteins at high yield. The paper details the strain's redox behavior and bench-scale production settings.
europmc-pmc3532497:
Insulin resistance may forecast heart disease before diabetes appears, and Karin B. Gast and five colleagues compare three measures head to head in 2012. Their meta-analysis pools cohort studies of adults without diabetes, asking how strongly fasting glucose, fasting insulin, and the HOMA-IR index each associate with new cardiovascular events.

All three markers predict events. On a standardized scale, one standard deviation more HOMA-IR raises coronary heart disease risk by 46 percent. Fasting glucose manages 21 percent, and fasting insulin only 4 percent. The composite index, built from both glucose and insulin, carries the signal best. It is presented as the first direct comparison of the three.
europmc-pmc3591697:
Premysl Jiruska and colleagues rethought synchrony in epilepsy in the Journal of Physiology in 2013. Epilepsy was long pictured as too much synchrony: vast neuron crowds firing in lockstep in a seizure. New recordings complicate that picture. Seizures grow from shifting networks where firing is uneven, and synchrony rises and falls as an event unfolds, so the old story cannot be the whole truth.

Loss of synchrony often shows just before a seizure or in its early phase, the review notes, while strong synchrony near the end may help the seizure stop. Work at cell level points to specific excitatory and inhibitory cell types steering these swings. What distant electrodes register can also diverge from the firing right beneath them, and many neurons sit silent yet involved. The authors argue for a stricter, more dynamic account of how seizures organize and end.
europmc-pmc3614697:
Lien Ai Pham-Huy, Hua He, and Chuong Pham-Huy wrote a mini-review of free radicals and antioxidants in the International Journal of Biomedical Science in 2008. Free radicals are unstable molecules spun off by normal cell chemistry, and also delivered by pollution, smoke, radiation, and some medicines. In small doses they do useful work, including cell signaling and defense. When production outruns the body's ability to clear them, the pile-up is called oxidative stress.

That stress is tied in the review to cancer, autoimmune disease, aging, cataracts, rheumatoid arthritis, heart disease, and nerve disorders. Defense comes from antioxidants the body makes itself and from those eaten in food or taken as supplements. The authors sort the radical families, explain how they form and are dismantled, weigh the helpful against the harmful effects, and discuss whether supplements genuinely protect health or merely promise to.
europmc-pmc3667097:
A risk model earns trust only when tested on fresh patients, Royston and Altman argue in a 2013 BMC Medical Research Methodology article. Their subject is the Cox model, a standard method that foretells survival over time. Outside checks for such models were thin in print. A sound check must test two things: how well the model sorts patients by risk, and how close its foretold chances run to what happens.

How much can be checked depends on what the first study printed. The authors give methods for three levels of detail, from the risk score alone up to the full survival curve. The hardest task, judging accuracy of foretold chances, gets a way to rebuild the missing base curve. They run the methods on two breast cancer data sets, one to build and one to test.
europmc-pmc3701697:
Li and colleagues present tools that predict network activity from mass spectrometry data on small molecules, without first naming each molecule. Naming the chemicals in a sample is slow and often impossible, which stalls the reading of these experiments.

Their approach leans on pathway knowledge instead. Spectral features are mapped together onto metabolic networks, and activity is inferred from the whole pattern. The team tested the tools on the switching-on of innate immune cells, a setting where the expected pathway changes are known. They offer the method as a shortcut from raw spectra to useful answers.
europmc-pmc3705297:
Koskella and Meaden review how specific bacteriophages are for the bacteria they infect, and why that specificity matters in wild microbial communities. Phages shape bacterial diversity and community dynamics, but most knowledge comes from laboratory pairings rather than nature.

The review covers experimental evolution studies, then introduces new data on phages collected from the leaves of horse chestnut trees. A recurring theme is that bacterial sensitivity to a phage is rarely all-or-nothing; it varies by degree. The authors caution that evidence is still too thin for broad claims about host range in nature, and argue for combining field sampling with experiments and genomics.
europmc-pmc3759197:
Manuel Arruebo and six co-authors wrote a review in Cancers in 2011 tracing the evolution of cancer treatment. Cancer therapy has swung between hope and disappointment through its history, with real cures in some cases and harsh failure in others. The review starts with the classic trio of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation.

From mustard gas observations in wartime came the first chemotherapy drugs in the 1940s, followed by a growing arsenal of antitumor drugs. Immunotherapy then rose to become the first choice in many cases. The review moves on to the newest fronts: gene therapy and nanomedicine. In nanomedicine, tiny structures can deliver drugs in a controlled way, combine imaging with treatment, apply heat, and carry targeting add-ons such as antibodies. Each approach is traced from its arrival in the clinic to its promises and challenges.
europmc-pmc3829197:
A descriptive study in The Lancet Infectious Diseases, dated 2011 in the record, comes from Laura García-Álvarez and a large team of co-authors. A milk sample held Staphylococcus aureus that resisted the drug meticillin yet tested negative for the known resistance gene. The team hunt for the cause and check how far such strains spread.

Genome reading found a variant of the resistance gene, quite unlike the known forms, sitting in a new gene cassette. The variant turned up in both cattle and human samples from the United Kingdom and Denmark. Standard gene tests would miss it, since they look for the old gene shape. The find warns that animal herds can seed new resistant strains in people, and that labs need tests that catch this hidden form.
europmc-pmc3839397:
Päivi Peltomäki and Hans Vasen update a mutation database in Disease Markers in 2004. The database tracks gene faults in families with Lynch syndrome, a heritable state that raises colon cancer risk. Faults sit in DNA repair genes, which fix copying errors as cells divide.

An international group set up the database in 1994 and first summed it in 1997. By this update, after a merger with a sister group, it held hundreds of distinct faults across three repair genes, found in families worldwide. Two genes, MLH1 and MSH2, account for most cases. The shared list helps labs judge a new family's fault and guides testing. The paper records the state of the list at that time.
europmc-pmc3893097:
Barriers to blood pressure care are reviewed in PLoS One, with the record dated 2014, by Rasha Khatib and co-authors. High blood pressure is well understood and treatable, yet most patients worldwide stay uncontrolled. The path from proof to practice leaks at many points, and no one had mapped the leaks in a shared way.

The team pooled dozens of interview and survey studies of patients and care providers. They sorted barriers by a behavior change frame: will to change, skills to change, and system blocks. Health system barriers came up most in interview studies, for both patients and providers. Survey studies added clashes over targets and follow-up habits. The map shows that fixing knowledge alone will not control blood pressure; systems must change too.
europmc-pmc3906697:
Paul James Barr, Rachel Thompson, Thom Walsh, Stuart W. Grande, Elissa M. Ozanne, and Glyn Elwyn test a decision measure in the Journal of Medical Internet Research, with the record dated 2014. Shared decision making, where doctor and patient choose care together, is a policy goal. Measuring it in patients' own reports has lacked a tool that is short, sound, and fit for scale.

Their measure, CollaboRATE, asks just three items, built with patients. Adults online watched staged doctor-patient videos in which explanation, preference asking, and preference use were varied by design. Scores on the short measure tracked those shifts and lined up with two longer measures. The team report the scale as fast and frugal, a candidate for routine use in clinics and surveys alike.
europmc-pmc3969297:
Emily J. H. Jones, Teodora Gliga, Rachael Bedford, Tony Charman, and Mark H. Johnson review studies that follow babies at high risk of autism from birth, in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews in 2014. These prospective studies enroll infants with an older autistic sibling and watch development unfold, instead of looking back after diagnosis. The aim is to trace the pathway from early brain and behavior differences to the full condition.

Social and communication difficulties become clear in the second year of life. Earlier markers are subtler: unusual brain responses to another person's gaze, and slow shifting of attention away from a stimulus. Because autism emerges gradually through these steps, the authors argue, mapping the pathway matters for spotting risk sooner and designing interventions that start before symptoms consolidate.
europmc-pmc4054597:
Franck Rapaport and eight colleagues run a head-to-head trial of methods that find changed genes in RNA sequencing data, in Genome Biology in 2013. Software for this job has multiplied, and labs choose largely by habit. A fair benchmark was overdue.

Using a standard reference data set plus deeply sequenced cell data, the team compared the common pipelines. They scored normalisation, detection accuracy, and the hard case where a gene is silent in one group. Methods differed clearly, but not along the expected line: tools adapted from microarray analysis performed as well as those built for sequencing. The clearest practical finding concerns design. Adding replicate samples bought far more detection power than sequencing the same samples deeper. The authors publish the full comparison so groups can pick a method by evidence and spend their budgets where the power actually is.
europmc-pmc4058297:
Darcy A. Krueger and Hope Northrup presented updated care guidance for tuberous sclerosis complex on behalf of an international consensus group. The recommendations appeared in Pediatric Neurology in 2013. The genetic disorder can affect every organ, yet its signs vary widely from person to person and can become life threatening.

A consensus group of seventy-nine specialists from fourteen countries, split into twelve subcommittees, reviewed the evidence for each disease area. They set standard advice for watching and managing the condition across the body and across age groups. Earlier guidance dated from 1998, so the update brings in newer science and current best practice. The aim was a shared, evidence-based standard to replace care that varied greatly by region.
europmc-pmc406397:
Adam Amsterdam and colleagues screened zebrafish lines carrying lethal mutations for hidden signs of cancer. Their study appeared in PLoS Biology in 2004. Because many tumour suppressor genes are lethal when fully lost, fish carrying one faulty copy might reveal new cancer genes through early deaths or visible tumours.

Twelve lines showed raised cancer rates, mostly malignant tumours of the nerve sheath, sometimes with other tumour types. Surprisingly, eleven of the twelve carried a fault in a different ribosomal protein gene, the genes that build the cell's protein factories. The twelfth matched a known tumour suppressor. The authors propose that many ribosomal protein genes can act as tumour suppressors, a role that may also exist in humans.
europmc-pmc4100097:
Hitoshi Suzuki and Toshifumi Tsukahara reviewed what hard-to-digest RNAs reveal about splicing, the process that stitches gene exons into messenger RNA. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2014. An enzyme called RNase R chews up straight RNA strands but leaves circles intact.

Splicing by-products include lariat RNAs, loops pinched off during cutting, and fully circular RNAs. Both resist RNase R, so treating a sample with the enzyme isolates them from ordinary RNA. Studying these survivors exposed repeating events such as re-splicing of finished messages and splicing nested inside splicing. Circular RNAs are widespread and may soak up small regulatory RNAs like sponges. The authors present RNase R as a fresh tool for probing non-linear RNA.
europmc-pmc4120697:
Ohad Gal-Mor, Erin C. Boyle, and Guntram A. Grassl reviewed why two branches of the same Salmonella species cause very different human diseases. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2014. Salmonella enterica holds more than twenty-six hundred serovars, split into typhoidal types causing enteric fever and non-typhoidal types causing gut illness.

Despite close genetic kinship, the groups differ in spread, symptoms, and the immune response they provoke. Comparing the genomes of many serovars has begun to reveal the basis for these contrasts. New mouse models of both fever and gastroenteritis now let researchers probe bacterial and host mechanisms side by side. Understanding the difference, the authors say, sharpens knowledge of Salmonella disease, host immunity, and host specificity.
europmc-pmc4150797:
Daniel Jost, Pascal Carrivain, Giacomo Cavalli, and Cédric Vaillant used polymer physics to model how the epigenome, the pattern of chemical marks along DNA, folds in three dimensions. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. Chromosome regions with distinct marks fold into topologically associated domains, separate neighbourhoods inside the nucleus.

Their block copolymer model builds a chain whose blocks carry the epigenetic pattern measured in fruit flies. The simulated folding matched chromosome contact experiments very well. The model also shows why the same stretch of genome can settle into several stable folds, a multistability at sub-chromosome scale. That gives a physical basis for how marks and folding reinforce each other to lock in gene programmes.
europmc-pmc4217497:
Anna Carolina Carvalho da Fonseca, Flavia Regina Souza Lima, and five co-authors reviewed microglia and the blood-brain barrier in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2014. The barrier is a sealed layer of vessel cells that guards the brain's chemistry. Microglia, the brain's own immune cells, sit close by as part of the same working unit.

When microglia switch on during disease, they change the proteins that seal the barrier, and leaks follow. The vessel cells in turn can calm or rouse the microglia, so the two hold a two-way conversation. The review follows that exchange in infections, epilepsy, stroke, and degenerative diseases. Understanding the crosstalk may point to treatments that protect the barrier by settling microglia, rather than only patching the vessel wall.
europmc-pmc4252997:
Gilberto E. Flores, Noah Fierer, and ten co-authors tracked personal microbiomes over time in Genome Biology in 2014. A single stool or skin sample is often treated as a person's microbial portrait, but communities drift. How much they drift, and whether drift itself is a personal trait, had not been measured in many people at once.

The team sampled forehead, palm, tongue, and gut microbes from 85 adults every week for three months. Skin sites changed most in which species were present, while gut and tongue changed more in species proportions. People differed widely in stability, and the best predictor was diversity itself: richer gut and tongue communities held steadier over time. Studies tying microbes to health, the authors warn, must reckon with this personal tempo of change.
europmc-pmc4309497:
J A Bell, M Kivimaki, and M Hamer pooled long term studies to ask whether obese adults who look healthy on metabolic tests still face a raised risk of type 2 diabetes. Their meta-analysis appeared in Obesity Reviews in 2014. Some obese people show normal blood pressure, blood fats, and insulin response, and whether that spares them future diabetes was unsettled.

Seven published studies plus new data from an English aging study gave close to eighteen hundred healthy obese participants. Diabetes still arrived more often in this group than in healthy normal weight adults, though less often than in metabolically unhealthy obesity. The verdict: healthy obesity lowers risk compared with unhealthy obesity but does not erase it.
europmc-pmc4376797:
Leandro Martínez presented a method to find stiff and flexible parts of molecules in computer simulations, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Molecular dynamics simulations track how biomolecules move, and standard measures compare each frame to a reference shape. That alignment breaks down when one small part moves a lot: the whole molecule then looks mobile, and real local motion gets hidden. His approach aligns only the least mobile fraction of the structure, again and again, until the still core is found.

The method, named LOVO, picks out rigid substructures on its own and gives a cleaner picture of where motion truly sits. Worked examples show how the view improves over standard alignment. The software, MDLovoFit, is free for other labs to use. Clearer motion maps help link a molecule's flexibility to its biological job.
europmc-pmc4379497:
Sonal Nagarkar-Jaiswal and a large team built a library of gene-tagging inserts in fruit flies, in eLife in 2015. Antibodies to tag most proteins do not exist, and making them is slow and costly. Their collection holds about 7,434 inserts of a cassette called MiMIC, placed inside genes, of which 2,854 sit in coding sections. From these they built strains with 400 genes tagged by a glowing green marker, letting the proteins be seen and manipulated in living tissue.

About 72 percent of the tagged proteins still worked normally, and over 90 percent could be imaged in fresh tissue. The tagged proteins could be knocked down with two matched tools, giving effects like full gene loss. Knockdown could be reversed and limited in place and time, in larvae and adults. The set gives fly genetics a flexible new toolkit.
europmc-pmc4383097:
Steven Lin, Brett Staahl, Ravi Alla, and Jennifer Doudna improved precise genome editing by timing the delivery, in eLife in 2014. CRISPR/Cas9 cuts DNA at a chosen site, and cells can repair the cut by copying a template, inserting new information exactly. That precise route, homology-directed repair, competes with a sloppier repair route and often loses. The team delivered ready-made Cas9-guide complexes at timed points in the cell cycle, when the precise route is most active.

Timed delivery raised precise editing sharply in three human cell types, including primary fibroblasts and embryonic stem cells, reaching rates up to 38 percent in one standard line. Checks of the target and likely off-target sites showed high fidelity, and cell death stayed low. The trick needs no drugs or genetic tricks, just scheduling, which makes it easy for other labs to adopt.
europmc-pmc4451897:
J W M van der Linden and a large international team tracked azole resistance in the fungus Aspergillus fumigatus in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2015. Azole drugs are a main treatment for aspergillosis, the diseases this common mold causes. Resistance, thought to be selected partly by azole fungicides used outside medicine, can make those drugs fail, so its true spread needed measuring.

Centers in many countries screened thousands of clinical Aspergillus isolates in a planned, forward-looking survey. Resistant A. fumigatus turned up more often than earlier reports suggested, at a few cases in every hundred isolates. Resistant strains caused both invasive and milder disease and badly weakened the clinical value of azole drugs where they appeared. The authors present the survey as a baseline and warn that resistance crosses borders with ease.
europmc-pmc4455997:
Mohammad Ali, Allyson Nelson, Anna Lena Lopez, David Sack, and Justin Remais updated world estimates of cholera in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2015. Cholera's true toll is largely unknown because most cases are never reported. Weak surveillance and lab capacity hide cases, and countries may also gain politically or economically by staying silent, so reported figures understate the disease.

An earlier estimate had counted cases in countries classed as endemic by their own reports, a circular approach. Here the team used a spatial model to classify countries as endemic, non-endemic, or cholera-free based on predicted incidence over several years. They combined that with the share of each population lacking sound sanitation and with incidence from field studies. The update gives health agencies a less biased map of where cholera help, vaccines, and clean water work are needed most.
europmc-pmc4506997:
Agnese Irkle leads a broad author team in a 2015 Nature Communications paper on spotting risky calcium in artery walls. Hard deposits in plaques can steady them, but tiny early deposits mark plaques more likely to cause harm. A PET scan tracer called 18F-sodium fluoride might flag that early stage, yet how it binds in plaque was not settled.

The team combined electron microscopy, film-based radiation mapping, tissue staining, and PET/CT scans in animals and patients. The tracer stuck to calcified deposits with high affinity and good selectivity. Scans could tell small active deposits apart from large settled ones. The group presents the scan as the only clinical tool that can now find this early micro-scale calcium without cutting tissue.
europmc-pmc4509697:
Markus Loeffler leads a long author list describing a big German health study in BMC Public Health. The LIFE-Adult-Study signed up 10,000 adults picked at random from Leipzig, a city of 550,000 people in eastern Germany. Its aim is to track how common diseases of modern life begin, covering heart and metabolic disease, thinking and brain health, mood, sleep, eye nerve damage, and allergies.

Baseline checks ran from August 2011 to November 2014. Each person, mostly aged 40 to 79, went through five to six hours of interviews, forms, body measures, and sample collection. People over 60 came back for two extra deep-check visits. The paper sets out the design so later findings from the cohort can be read in context.
europmc-pmc4526997:
Sohrab Saeb leads a ten-author team testing whether phone sensors can flag depression, in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2015. Depression is common and often missed. Phones are carried everywhere and packed with sensors, so their data might reveal daily patterns that track mood. The team set out to explore that link.

Forty adults carried a phone running a data-gathering app for two weeks; 28 gave enough data to analyze. Each person also filled in a standard depression survey at the start. Location patterns, such as how regular a person's daily movement rhythm was, lined up with symptom severity, as did some phone-use measures. The authors frame the work as an early step toward passive mood screening.
europmc-pmc4548997:
Gavin J. D. Smith and Ruben O. Donis report updated names for bird flu virus branches, in Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses in 2015. The H5 viruses behind highly pathogenic avian influenza keep evolving since their Guangdong ancestor emerged. Names for their family branches, called clades, must be revised when new branches drift beyond set bounds, or tracking breaks down.

Working for the WHO/OIE/FAO H5 evolution group, the authors analyzed hemagglutinin gene sequences posted in public databases through the end of 2014. Three branches had split enough to earn new designations, covering viruses from Indonesia, Egypt, and a widespread Asian-European-North American group. That group includes new subtypes H5N2, H5N3, H5N5, H5N6, and H5N8. Fast sequence sharing, they stress, keeps naming current.
europmc-pmc4574297:
Uri Manor leads a ten-author team finding a new anchor protein that helps mitochondria divide, in eLife in 2015. Mitochondria must split to survive, and the squeeze comes where the endoplasmic reticulum wraps around them. An ER protein, INF2, builds actin cables there to supply force, but what switches it on at the right spot was unknown.

The missing trigger is a mitochondria-bound form of the protein Spire, named Spire1C. It latches onto mitochondria, grips INF2, and sparks actin assembly on the mitochondrial surface. Breaking either its actin or its partner grip reduced constriction and division in cells. Computer simulations confirmed that growing actin filaments can supply the needed squeeze. Spire1C sits as a hub linking three cell systems.
europmc-pmc4580597:
Yin Paradies leads a ten-author team pooling three decades of studies on racism and health, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Evidence that experiencing racism damages health had grown study by study, but no one had synthesized it in one meta-analysis with racism itself as the exposure. The team gathered 293 studies reported in 333 articles published between 1983 and 2013, mostly from the United States.

Reported racism went with clearly worse mental health, including depression, anxiety, and stress, in pooled results across 227 studies of negative mental health. Links with general and physical health were smaller but still negative. Effects shifted with study and exposure features. The authors frame racism as a measurable determinant of health, not background noise.
europmc-pmc4639797:
Marjolein J. Peters and a very large consortium published a 2015 study of how gene activity in blood changes with age. Disease risk climbs with age, yet the molecular side of aging is poorly mapped. The team combined blood gene expression data from 14,983 people of European ancestry. The work appeared in Nature Communications.

They found 1,497 genes whose activity shifts steadily with chronological age. From those patterns they built a transcriptomic age score for each person. People whose score ran ahead of their real age tended to show higher blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, and body mass. Age-linked genes were rich in regulatory DNA marks that track both age and gene activity. The score gives aging researchers a blood-based tool that complements DNA methylation clocks.
europmc-pmc4728597:
Paula S. Azevedo, Bertha F. Polegato, Marcos F. Minicucci, Sergio A. R. Paiva, and Leonardo A. M. Zornoff reviewed cardiac remodeling in the Arquivos Brasileiros de Cardiologia in 2016. Remodeling names the cluster of changes, in molecules, cells, and tissue, by which an injured heart changes size, mass, shape, and function. It predicts poor outcomes, feeding heart failure and dangerous rhythms. The review traces how the term's meaning grew from scar replacement after heart attack to the broad modern definition.

Mechanisms get systematic treatment: cell death, energy failure, oxidative stress, inflammation, scar collagen, calcium handling, and hormone-driven signals. Drug treatment is sorted into three tiers, proven strategies, promising ones, and possible future ones. The authors aim the piece at clinicians who must recognize remodeling early, since its changes, once advanced, are hard to reverse. It stands as a compact teaching review.
europmc-pmc4810097:
Frank Christian and three co-authors review a fine control on the immune system's master switch in Cells in 2016. The switch, NF-κB, is a family of gene activators that run inflammation, immune growth, and cell survival and death. Blocking the whole switch harms healthy tissue, which has stalled drug efforts against diseases where it runs wild.

The review focuses on phosphorylation, the phosphate tags placed on the switch's parts. Those tags tune which genes a given switch pairing turns on, rather than flipping the whole system at once. That gene-by-gene control is the opening drug makers need: in principle, one can mute the harmful gene sets and spare the rest. The authors map the known tag sites and enzymes and weigh the proof for each.
europmc-pmc4820297:
Ludmylla Cunha, Ana Grenha, and Paola Laurienzo review seaweed sugars as drug carriers in Marine Drugs in 2016. Seaweed cell walls are rich in sulfated polysaccharides, chains of sugars carrying sulfur groups. Three stand out: carrageenan from red algae, ulvan from green, and fucoidan from brown. Each has shown biological activity of its own, and all three form gels and beads that suit them to carrying drugs.

The review gives each material's structure, extraction, and physical traits, then tours delivery uses: particles, gels, and beads that release a drug in a controlled way. A closing section treats targeting, above all designs that home on macrophage cells, which matters for infections that hide inside them. The authors present the seaweed polymers as renewable, body-friendly carrier stock.
europmc-pmc4844197:
Eilis Hannon, Katie Lunnon, Leonard Schalkwyk, and Jonathan Mill measured DNA methylation across blood and brain in 122 people, in work from 2015. Methylation is a chemical mark that helps set gene activity, and it differs by tissue. Brain tissue is hard to sample in life, so studies of brain disorders often use blood and hope it mirrors the brain.

For most sites, a person's blood pattern did not predict that person's brain pattern well. Links were stronger for cortex regions than for the cerebellum. A small set of sites did track across tissues. The authors warn that blood-based scans will miss much of the brain signal in studies of nerve and mental disorders, so tissue choice matters.
europmc-pmc4878797:
Matthew J. Page and co-authors took a cross-section of systematic reviews in biomedical research in 2016 and graded their reporting. Reviews guide care choices, but a flawed or half-told review misleads. The team pulled reviews indexed in February 2014 and studied a random sample of 300 in depth, comparing Cochrane and other reviews and change since 2004.

Reporting stayed patchy: many reviews skipped key methods, and abstracts often hid the limits of the underlying proof. Cochrane reviews reported more fully on the whole. Users who read only an abstract risk taking shaky verdicts as firm. The study presses journals and authors to report reviews in full, plain view.
europmc-pmc4931497:
Hemma Mistry and ten co-authors make copper catalysts that turn carbon dioxide into ethylene with record selectivity. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Using renewable power to convert waste carbon dioxide into fuels could cut emissions. Copper can drive that reaction, but it makes many products at once and wastes energy. The team treated copper with plasma, a hot ionized gas, to form oxidized catalysts whose settings can be tuned.

The treated catalysts needed less extra voltage and sent 60 percent of the product to ethylene, a key industrial gas. Careful imaging and X-ray tests during the reaction showed copper oxide resisted being reduced back to plain metal. Positive copper ions stayed on the surface while the reaction ran. The authors argue those ions, more than surface roughness, explain the low onset voltage and the sharp product choice.
europmc-pmc4932097:
Miriam Ries and Magdalena Sastre review how glial cells clear amyloid-beta from the brain in Alzheimer's disease. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience in 2016. Glial cells support neurons and defend the brain. Two types, microglia and astrocytes, help control levels of amyloid-beta, the sticky protein that builds up in the disease. How they break it down and ship it out is the focus here.

The review covers enzymes glia release that cut amyloid-beta at set points, including neprilysin and insulin degrading enzyme. It also covers helper proteins that carry the fragments toward the blood for removal. The authors weigh a tension in the field. Activated glia can release harmful inflammatory signals, yet the same cells do much of the cleanup. They argue that boosting the cleanup side, without the harm, is a promising treatment aim.
europmc-pmc5062097:
Anil K. Seth and Karl J. Friston review interoceptive inference in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2016. Interoception is the sensing of the body's inner state: heartbeat, breath, gut, and blood chemistry. The authors recast it inside predictive processing, the view that the brain constantly predicts its inputs and corrects the errors.

On this account, the brain does not passively wait for body signals. It sends predictions down to the reflexes that control the body, and those reflexes act to make the predictions come true, holding inner conditions steady or shifting them ahead of demand. How much trust each signal gets, its precision, may be set by neuromodulators. The frame reshapes thinking about the emotional brain and the sense of being an embodied self. It also reshapes thinking on disorders from autism to depression, all of which the authors survey as test cases for the theory.
europmc-pmc5075697:
Torbjørn Rognes and five co-authors introduce VSEARCH in PeerJ in 2016, a free program for working with DNA sequence data. Metagenomics studies whole communities from their DNA, and the field's standard tool, USEARCH, is closed source, partly undocumented, and free only in a memory-limited 32-bit form. VSEARCH was built as an open alternative covering the same ground.

It searches and clusters sequences, flags chimeras, removes duplicates, aligns pairs, and handles the FASTQ files that sequencers produce, plus a few commands of its own. In the team's tests it proved more accurate than USEARCH at searching, clustering, chimera detection, and subsampling, and matched it at merging paired reads. It runs slower at clustering and chimera detection but faster elsewhere, and its 64-bit design handles datasets bounded only by memory. The authors pledge continued work on speed and accuracy, and the open code lets anyone inspect or extend it.
europmc-pmc5123897:
Biola M. Javierre and a large team, including the BLUEPRINT Consortium, mapped long-range gene control in blood cells in Cell in 2016. Enhancers, DNA switches far from genes, must physically loop to the gene starts they control, and most such contacts were uncharted. The team charted contacts for 31,253 gene promoters in 17 human blood cell types.

Contacts proved highly specific to each cell type and linked active gene starts with marked enhancers. The contact maps mirrored the blood family tree, reshaping as cells matured. Regions touching a promoter were rich in variants that change that gene's activity. The team used the maps to tie thousands of disease-linked variants outside genes to the genes they likely control, naming candidate genes and pathways for follow-up.
europmc-pmc5133697:
Cynthia M. Kallenbach, Serita D. Frey, and A. Stuart Grandy gave direct proof that microbes build soil organic matter, reporting in Nature Communications in 2016. Soil carbon drives nutrient cycles and climate feedbacks, and models long credited preserved plant material for stable soil carbon, though evidence pointed to microbial remains instead.

In controlled soil systems, they showed microbes produce chemically varied, stable organic matter that accumulates in soil. Which microbe community was present mattered more than the clay type, and soils with more fungi and with microbes that grow efficiently built up the most microbial carbon. The findings shift the model of soil formation from plant leftovers toward microbial production, with consequences for how soils store carbon.
europmc-pmc5147797:
John J. Wiens surveyed climate-driven local extinctions in PLoS Biology in 2016. Species are shifting their ranges as the climate warms, moving uphill and toward the poles, but the local losses at the warm edges of those ranges had not been tallied. Wiens mined published range-shift studies for exactly those losses.

Across 976 species, 47 percent had already suffered local extinctions tied to recent climate change. The pattern was broad across zones and habitats. It ran heavier in tropical species than temperate ones, and in animals than plants. Freshwater species, at 74 percent, suffered more than land or sea species. Wiens warns that warming so far is modest next to what is projected, so such losses should grow much more common in coming decades.
europmc-pmc5304397:
Thomas C. Mathers and a large team of co-authors published an aphid study in Genome Biology in 2017. The subject is the green peach aphid, a pest that feeds on plants from about forty plant families. Most plant-feeding insects use only a few hosts. One aphid clone can move among far apart hosts, and the team asked how.

The group read the aphid genome and tracked gene use after a host switch. Same-clone aphids turned whole clusters of copied genes up or down within two days. Many of these genes came from gene families that had grown large in aphids. Blocking one family, cathepsin B, hurt aphid health only on the host that had switched those genes on.
europmc-pmc5316197:
Ana María López-Colomé, Irene Lee-Rivera, Regina Benavides-Hidalgo, and Edith López reviewed a cell protein called paxillin in the Journal of Hematology & Oncology in 2017. Paxillin sits at focal adhesions, the spots where a cell grips the surface around it. There it acts as a scaffold, pulling in the parts that let a cell crawl. Its grip work is switched by tags added at set sites.

The review maps the tag sites and the signal chains they start. Some tags build adhesions up; others, added by the ERK path, tear them down so the cell can move on. Paxillin also times the action of small switch proteins that shape the cell. The same system drives growth of the embryo, immune response, and wound repair. When it goes wrong, it feeds swelling, leaky vessel walls, and cancer spread.
europmc-pmc5321797:
Janet Lau and co-authors asked where a cancer shield protein must sit to block immune attack, in Nature Communications in 2017. The protein, PD-L1, fits a brake on T cells and helps tumors hide. Drugs that block this pair have given long gains for some patients. Response is most likely when tumor or immune cells carry PD-L1 first. Which source counts was a hot open question.

The team used mice with the gene cut from set cell types. PD-L1 from tumor cells, from immune cells of the myeloid line, and from other host cells each dulled killer T cell work in the tumor. The sources did not simply back each other up. Loss from either the tumor or the host lifted immune pressure. Both sources, they conclude, shape response to drugs that target this brake, and both may help predict who gains.
europmc-pmc5374697:
Kok Pin Ng and co-authors checked a tau scan tracer in human brains in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy in 2017. The tracer, THK5351, sticks to tau tangles, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, and lights them on PET scans. But it also glows in zones that should hold few tangles, which clouds the read. Kin chemicals are known to bind an enzyme called MAO-B, a prime suspect for the stray glow.

Eight patients with memory loss or kin diseases had base scans, then a repeat scan an hour after a dose of selegiline, a drug that blocks MAO-B. The glow fell after the blocker in the suspect zones. Dish tests on post-mortem brain slices backed the same clash. The team concludes that MAO-B is an off-target site for the tracer, and that standard reads of its scans bake in that flaw.
europmc-pmc5478797:
Fitzpatrick, Darcy, and Vierhile report a randomized trial in JMIR Mental Health. They test Woebot, a fully automated chat agent that delivers cognitive behavior therapy content. Web therapy apps often suffer from poor adherence. A chat format might hold users better, the team reasoned. Their subjects were young adults with depression and anxiety symptoms.

Seventy people aged 18 to 28 took part for two weeks. One group used Woebot, and the other read an information ebook. The Woebot group used the agent about 12 times on average. Their depression scores fell, while the control group's did not, the authors report. Users praised the chat process itself.
europmc-pmc5490197:
Purcell and co-authors report a large sleep study in Nature Communications. They characterize sleep spindles, brief bursts of brain activity in stage 2 sleep. Spindles may aid memory and mark risk for mental illness. Past samples were far too small for gene studies. The team pools records from the National Sleep Research Resource.

The dataset holds 11,630 people aged 4 to 97 years. Spindle traits proved stable within each person, they report. Their paths across life differed by trait, though. Body mass index skewed measures through heart signals in the EEG. After such checks, genes clearly shaped spindle traits. The work sets up future genetic studies of sleep.
europmc-pmc5492997:
Leyns and Holtzman present a review in Molecular Neurodegeneration on glial cells in tauopathies. Tauopathies are dementias marked by clumps of the tau protein. Alzheimer's disease is the best-known case. Activated glia and inflammation also appear in the affected brain regions. The authors ask how that inflammation shapes the disease course.

Microglia may help spread tau from cell to cell, they report. Inflammatory signals such as interleukin-1 beta and tumor necrosis factor can worsen tau faults. Those signals also disturb the support work of astrocytes. Cell and animal studies plus human brain data are all weighed. The authors propose a tangled, self-feeding loop of damage.
europmc-pmc5506197:
Guo and co-authors present a systematic review and meta-analysis in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. It covers dengue outbreaks worldwide over 25 years. Dengue infects 50 to 100 million people each year. Aedes mosquitoes spread the virus between people. The team pooled 243 studies describing 262 outbreaks.

Most outbreak cases clustered in the Western Pacific, above all after 2010. The average patient was about 30 years old. Roughly a quarter developed the severe hemorrhagic form. Deaths ran at 1.3 percent of cases. Open water containers near homes raised infection risk, they report. Virus type 2 outbreaks carried the highest death rate.
europmc-pmc5508697:
Denissen, Winne, and Du Prez present a mini-review in Chemical Science on vitrimers. Thermoset plastics are strong and stable, but their fixed links bar reshaping or recycling. Vitrimers keep permanent cross-links yet can still flow when heated. Their bonds swap partners without ever breaking the network. The name echoes glass, which softens the same gradual way.

The review surveys vitrimer chemistries reported from 2011 to 2015. Early systems used a catalyst to swap ester bonds in epoxy networks. Later variants drew on other exchange reactions. Each is grouped by the chemistry behind its swapping. The authors hope the survey sparks fresh work in this young field.
europmc-pmc5529997:
Skwarczynski and Toth present a review in Chemical Science on peptide-based synthetic vaccines. Classic vaccines use whole germs, live or killed. They protect well but carry real risks: allergic shocks, reversion to virulence, and cold-chain storage needs. Subunit vaccines trim the formula to germ fragments. Peptide vaccines go further, using only the smallest trigger pieces.

Such minimal pieces promise precise, safer immune training, they argue. No live pathogen enters production at all. Designers can aim at the exact response they want. Weak immune punch is the known drawback to solve. The review surveys delivery tricks and adjuvant partners under study.
europmc-pmc5572397:
Sánchez and co-authors upgrade a yeast metabolic model in Molecular Systems Biology. Genome-scale models predict cell behavior from reaction networks. Most cap growth only by carbon uptake. Real fluxes also obey enzyme limits, which the models ignored.

Their method, GECKO, puts enzymes inside the reactions. Each flux is capped by enzyme amount times turnover rate. Applied to baker's yeast, the model gained new reach. It matched growth on varied carbon sources in excess. Stress responses and pathway overexpression also fit better. Feeding in proteomics data shrank flux uncertainty sharply. Over 60 percent of reactions tightened. The model also maps how enzyme effort spreads across pathways. Readers get a practical upgrade for model-based strain design.
europmc-pmc5602797:
Yamana and co-authors check the accuracy of Japanese hospital billing data in the Journal of Epidemiology. Big claims databases fuel much health research. Their value rests on the codes being right. The team tested two systems against patients' actual charts.

Charts for 315 patients in four hospitals served as the truth. The DPC data named the main diagnosis well, at about 79 percent sensitivity. Its codes rarely claimed a disease that was absent. Comorbidity codes missed many real cases, though. Procedure records were strong for most common items. The newer SS-MIX lab data agreed with charts over 95 percent on all 13 tests. The authors back both systems for future studies. Readers learn where the data can be trusted.
europmc-pmc5606297:
Carhart-Harris and Nutt propose a two-part theory of serotonin in the Journal of Psychopharmacology. Past attempts at one unified account never won agreement. Their model splits the job between two receptors. Each handles a different response to hard times.

The 5-HT1A receptor supports passive coping. It helps a person tolerate stress and wait it out. The 5-HT2A receptor supports active coping instead. It opens a window of mental flexibility for change. The authors cast 1A coping as the brain's default mode. As adversity peaks, the change-oriented path matters more. Two drug families map onto the split. Standard antidepressants boost the 1A path. Psychedelic drugs boost the 2A path. Readers get a frame that makes both drug classes look complementary, not opposed.
europmc-pmc5622197:
Burnstock reviews drug progress in purinergic signalling for Frontiers in Pharmacology. The idea that nucleotides signal between cells dates to 1972. It gained ground once receptor subtypes were cloned. Nineteen subtypes now span the P1, P2X, and P2Y families.

Several purinergic drugs already serve patients. Clopidogrel blocks the P2Y12 receptor to prevent clots and stroke. Diquafosol treats dry eye through P2Y2. Adenosine drugs steady fast heart rhythms. A2A blockers look promising for Parkinson's disease. Newer candidates target other receptors. P2X3 blockers are in trials for chronic cough and bladder problems. P2X7 blockers are studied for inflammation and brain disease. Work also spans bone loss, diabetes, epilepsy, and cancer. Readers get a field survey from the scientist who named it, focused on what may reach the clinic.
europmc-pmc5715197:
Malhotra and co-authors review the outsized harm of strokes from blocked large vessels. Their review covers acute ischemic strokes caused by large-vessel occlusions. These strokes cause severe deficits at onset. The authors asked how much of all stroke disability and death they explain.

Their search screened 197 articles, and two studies met the entry rules. Together those studies enrolled 1,467 patients. Dependence or death followed 64 percent of large-vessel strokes, versus 24 percent of others. Such strokes made up about 39 percent of acute cases. Yet they caused about 62 percent of dependence or death and 96 percent of deaths. Clot removal treatment thus offers outsized gains at the population level.
europmc-pmc5725597:
Shi and co-authors report a mouse study of bone growth in Nature Communications. The work asks which early cells give rise to osteoblasts, the cells that build bone. No single marker was known for all such progenitors. The team used the gene Gli1 as a marker to follow these cells.

Using lineage tracing in fetal and young mice, they find Gli1 cells produce osteoblasts at all skeletal sites. Cells just below the growth plate prove key for spongy bone growth. Those cells also yield marrow fat and stromal cells. Blocking Hedgehog signals harms their growth and bone making. After fractures, Gli1 cells help form both cartilage and bone.
europmc-pmc5727697:
Mangano and co-authors review intraoral scanners, devices that take optical impressions inside the mouth. The review asks how these scanners compare with older plaster methods. It also asks which scanners are on sale and where they can be used. The search covered work in English from 2007 to mid 2017.

The review includes 132 studies, from trials and case reports to lab tests. The authors find that optical impressions cut patient discomfort and save time. The scans are accurate enough for crowns, inlays, and many other fixed work. Deep margins, bleeding, cost, and a learning curve remain limits. Long span work lacks support so far.
europmc-pmc5753397:
Carson and co-authors review links between physical activity and health in children aged 0 to 4 years. Fast growth in the early years makes this window important. The team searched for studies with measured or reported activity in healthy young children. Health signs ranged from body fat to motor and cognitive growth.

They kept 96 studies with 71,291 children from 36 countries. Activity programs improved motor and cognitive growth in most tests. In daily life data, activity linked to better fitness and bone health. Moderate to vigorous activity showed the most steady gains. Types such as active play and dance also helped.
europmc-pmc5792697:
Marcolino and co-authors review systematic reviews on mobile health tools. Phones now reach nearly everyone, and health programs ride on them. Proof of their value stays mixed, though. The team searched five databases and rated each review's quality with a standard checklist.

They kept 23 reviews covering 371 studies and near eighty thousand patients. Text messaging was the most common tool, used for reminders, alerts, and coaching. Gains showed in chronic disease care, from asthma and lung disease to diabetes and blood pressure. Review quality varied widely, from low to high, they note.
europmc-pmc5796597:
Arango-Argoty and co-authors present DeepARG, a deep learning tool that predicts antibiotic resistance genes in DNA samples. Watching resistance spread needs broad monitoring of water, waste, and food. Standard searches match reads to known genes by best hit. That method misses many true genes.

Two models serve short reads and full length genes. They learn from a matrix of gaps between all known resistance classes. In tests across 30 classes, the models kept precision and recall both high. False negatives fell below the best hit method. A hand checked database ships with the tool.
europmc-pmc5812897:
Kaya and co-authors introduce SCCmecFinder, a web tool for MRSA typing. MRSA is a drug-resistant staph germ that burdens hospitals. Its resistance rides on a DNA cassette called SCCmec. Naming the cassette type guides infection control.

Lab typing by PCR struggles with the cassette's variety. Genome sequencing helps, but good reading tools were lacking. SCCmecFinder spots all accepted cassette types from genome data. It also flags odd elements that may be new. The tool is free online and will be updated as types emerge. Readers get a practical aid for tracking resistant staph strains.
europmc-pmc5869197:
Ivanenko and Gurfinkel review human postural control. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience. Standing upright needs constant work against gravity. The authors split control into two linked levels. One level sets the tonic muscle activity called posture. The other corrects for pushes and disturbances, called equilibrium. Each level seems to rest on distinct muscle mechanisms.

The review traces ideas from ancient Greece to modern models. It covers the inverted pendulum view of quiet standing. It also weighs muscle tone, reflexes, and sensory input. The special build of skeletal muscle matters for control, they argue. Disturbed tone can in turn spoil movement. Readers get the neuromechanics behind everyday balance.
europmc-pmc5872097:
Bodratti and Alexandridis review how poloxamers are built into drug delivery systems. Their review appeared in the Journal of Functional Biomaterials. Poloxamers, also sold as Pluronics, are block copolymers. One part loves water and the other part avoids it. That split gives them strong self-assembly traits. They also show low toxicity, the authors note.

The review first explains how poloxamers gather into micelles, gels, and liquid crystals. It then shows how those forms can carry drugs that dissolve poorly in water. Methods covered include direct solubilization, solvent displacement, and emulsification. Kinetically frozen nanoparticles are also discussed. Careful design can improve drug uptake and patient compliance, the authors argue. Readers get a map from basic behaviour to real product forms.
europmc-pmc5895597:
Wang and co-authors study how Staphylococcus aureus releases tiny parcels called extracellular vesicles. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. The parcels carry proteins from cell to cell without contact. Parcels from the drug-resistant strain held many protein types. Toxins called cytolysins rode inside them. The team traced what drives parcel release. Surface agents called phenol-soluble modulins break the cell membrane open. Wall cross-linking and autolysin activity tune release by changing how leaky the wall is.

The team then built a strain whose toxins were made safe. Its parcels raised strong immune responses in mice. Antibodies from those mice disarmed the toxins. Treated mice survived a lethal sepsis challenge. The work supports these parcels as a vaccine base.
europmc-pmc5897397:
Romera-Castillo and co-authors show that plastics leach carbon that feeds ocean microbes. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. About 5.25 trillion plastic pieces float at the sea surface. Effects on the smallest food web levels were unknown. The team found that plastics release dissolved organic carbon. Microbes consume much of that carbon within days. Global leaching may reach 23,600 metric tons per year.

Sunlight made the leached carbon less usable to microbes. The authors warn that plastic inflow keeps rising fast. More plastic carbon could shift the base of ocean food webs. Composition and activity of microbial communities may change. Such effects have gone uncounted until now, they say.
europmc-pmc5899097:
Xue and co-authors anchor single nickel and iron atoms on graphdiyne for hydrogen making. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. Atomic catalysts use each metal atom, in theory. Keeping lone atoms from clumping is the hard part. Graphdiyne is a thin carbon sheet with even pores. Its triple bonds bind metals strongly.

The team measured very narrow atom sizes for both metals. That showed the atoms stayed single and apart. The catalysts drove hydrogen evolution with high activity, they report. They also stayed stable in use. The method may extend to other transition metals. Readers get a general route to single-atom catalysts.
europmc-pmc5926497:
Gelders and co-authors link neuroinflammation to degeneration in Parkinson's disease. Their review appeared in the Journal of Immunology Research. Parkinson's brings misfolded alpha-synuclein deposits and neuron loss. Dopamine neurons in one brain region die off over time. Why those neurons die is still not settled. Inflammation has been proposed as a key driver.

Many study types show immune activity in the disease, they report. Brain scans, post-mortem work, and animal studies all point that way. Immune responses to outside-cell synuclein may speed progression. Whether inflammation starts the disease or follows injury is debated. Current drugs treat symptoms only, with fading effect. Readers get the case for immune targets.
europmc-pmc5984097:
Cole and co-authors show that brain-predicted age from brain scans predicts mortality. Their study appeared in Molecular Psychiatry. Ageing hits people at very different rates. A marker of biological age could flag those at risk early. The team trained machine learning on scans from 2,001 healthy people. They then tested the marker in the Lothian Birth Cohort 1936. That cohort held 669 participants.

An older-appearing brain tracked with weaker grip strength, they report. It also tracked with poorer lung function and slower walking. Fluid intelligence was lower and death risk was higher. Pairing brain age with DNA-methylation age sharpened prediction. The two measures give complementary views of ageing.
europmc-pmc5995197:
Eshaghi and a large team of co-authors chart how regional grey matter atrophy progresses in multiple sclerosis. Their study appeared in Brain. Grey matter shrinks faster in these patients than in healthy people. Some regions waste earlier and faster than others. The team built a data-driven model of that sequence. It predicts the order in which regions atrophy. Patients can then be staged by their place in the order.

Atrophy starts in deep grey matter nuclei, they report. Posterior cortical regions follow early as well. It then spreads to other cortical areas. The staging links this spread to disability build-up.
europmc-pmc6017297:
Bernatoniene and Kopustinskiene review catechins in this article for Molecules. Catechins are plant flavanols found in green tea, wine, and cocoa. The authors explain how these compounds act inside cells. They focus on oxidative stress, which harms cells over time. Such stress is linked to aging and many chronic diseases.

Catechins can scavenge reactive oxygen species directly. They can also chelate metal ions that drive radical formation. The review describes indirect effects as well. Catechins can raise antioxidant enzyme activity. They can also block enzymes that promote oxidation. Readers get the chemistry of the main catechin forms. They also get a clear account of possible health benefits and pro-oxidant risks.
europmc-pmc6096297:
Johnson and co-authors review whether gamification truly helps health and wellbeing. Their systematic review appeared in Internet Interventions. Gamification adds game elements to non-game programs. Health apps use it to push behavior change. Solid proof of benefit lagged behind the hype.

The team found 19 papers with real outcome data. Fifty-nine percent reported positive effects. The rest reported mixed ones. Evidence was clearest for health behaviors. Results for thinking outcomes were mixed. Most studies carried moderate or weak methods. Few compared against a non-game version. Readers get a careful verdict: promising, but far from proven.
europmc-pmc6159997:
Burton and co-authors present a research article in Journal of Clinical Investigation on faulty antiviral B cells in hepatitis B. B cells help control hepatitis B virus over time. Antibodies against the viral surface antigen mark recovery from acute infection. Making those antibodies is also a goal of cure research.

The team studied B cells taken directly from the blood and liver of patients with chronic hepatitis B. To their surprise, virus-specific B cells persisted in many patients. Those cells carried T-bet, a sign of antiviral potential. Yet in lab tests they failed to work properly. Blocking the PD-1 pathway improved their responses. The findings point to a fixable defect in chronic infection.
europmc-pmc6194997:
Menon and Dhamija wrote a mini-review in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology on Beclin 1, a protein at the center of autophagy control. Autophagy lets stressed cells package damaged proteins and organelles into vesicles for breakdown. The recycled materials feed new building work. One early step uses a complex built around Beclin 1.

That complex switches on the membrane machinery that forms autophagosomes. Chemical tags on Beclin 1, chiefly phosphorylation and ubiquitination, fine-tune its activity. Different tag sites answer different stimuli. The balance struck decides between life-saving autophagy and cell death pathways. The mini-review maps the tag sites and the enzymes that place or remove them.
europmc-pmc6292797:
Carreira and co-authors review mental health outcomes in breast cancer survivors. Their systematic review appeared in JNCI, the Journal of the National Cancer Institute. It compared women at least a year past breast cancer with women who never had cancer. The team searched four databases and tracked citations. Two reviewers picked studies, pulled data, and judged bias.

Sixty studies met the bar for inclusion. Most work on depression found higher rates in survivors. The same pattern held for anxiety in most studies. Survivors also showed more sleep problems and sexual problems. Memory and thinking problems were more common too. The authors see strong proof of added risk. They call for care plans that prevent and treat these harms.
europmc-pmc6302597:
Delamater and co-authors explain why the basic reproduction number is easy to misuse. Their article appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases. The number, called R0, gauges how contagious a germ is. Above one, an outbreak is expected to grow. Below one, it should fade out.

The authors stress that R0 is not a fixed trait of a germ. Biology, behavior, and surroundings all move its value. Models estimate it, and each model rests on choices. Those choices change the number a lot. Reported values can also go stale as conditions shift. The article urges care in estimating, reporting, and using R0. It warns against treating one figure as simple fact.
europmc-pmc6303397:
Ovadya and co-authors test how immune surveillance limits senescent cells in aging. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Senescent cells have stopped dividing after damage. They build up in old tissues and can drive decline. The team used mice with weak cell-killing power. These mice lacked the perforin gene.

The mutant mice carried more senescent cells in their tissues. They also showed chronic inflammation and more age-related disorders. Their survival was shorter than normal. A drug that clears senescent cells eased this early aging. The same drug extended life in fast-aging progeroid mice. Results tie immune strength to healthy aging.
europmc-pmc6376797:
Stangl and co-authors present a framework article in BMC Medicine. They propose the Health Stigma and Discrimination Framework, a single model for health-related stigma across all conditions. Past frameworks treated one disease at a time and focused on individual psychology, which kept research in silos.

The new framework spans drivers, facilitators, manifestations, and health outcomes at several levels. The authors apply it to leprosy, epilepsy, mental illness, cancer, HIV, and obesity. They also show how race, gender, class, and other stigmas intersect with health stigma. A shared framework, they argue, lets researchers compare conditions and design stronger interventions and policies.
europmc-pmc6520497:
Dennis and co-authors compare diabetes subgroups with simple clinical models. Their analysis appeared in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology. A past cluster study proposed five subgroups of type 2 diabetes. The subgroups seemed to differ in progression and risk.

The team rebuilt the five clusters in the ADOPT trial, with 4,351 patients. Clusters did differ in blood sugar progression. But age at diagnosis alone explained a like amount of variation. Baseline kidney function beat clusters at predicting kidney disease. Therapy checks used the RECORD trial, with 4,447 patients. Simple features again beat clusters for picking treatment. The authors favour outcome-specific measures over fixed subgroups.
europmc-pmc6551897:
Kaneko and co-authors survey interleukin-1, a master signal of inflammation, writing for Inflammation and Regeneration. The review starts from the classic signs of inflammation and the sensors that detect damage and germs. IL-1 sits downstream of those sensors, which gives it a hand in far more than fever and swelling.

The family now counts eleven members, including IL-18 and IL-33, several of them matured by the inflammasome machinery. The authors trace IL-1 into metabolic inflammation, where low-grade signals smolder for years, and into cancer, where it can draw in cells that shield tumors. A closing section reviews drugs that block IL-1, from anakinra to canakinumab, and what their results teach about the diseases involved.
europmc-pmc6624997:
Meers, Tenenbaum, and Henikoff introduce a peak caller for CUT&RUN data. Their article appears in Epigenetics & Chromatin. CUT&RUN maps where proteins bind across the genome. It yields high signal with very low background. That spareness trips up callers built for ChIP-seq data.

Their method, SEACR, sets thresholds from the global background spread. It needs no statistical model or hand-picked parameters. On gold-standard data sets it split true from false peaks with near-perfect specificity. It found enriched regions for several protein targets with ease. A free web server runs the tool for users of any skill level. The authors present SEACR as the natural choice for CUT&RUN analysis.
europmc-pmc6689897:
Kessler and co-authors report drugging a supposedly undruggable pocket on KRAS. Their study appears in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. KRAS is the most frequently mutated oncogene. No approved drug targeted it directly. A shallow polar pocket sits between switch regions. The field had written it off as undruggable. The team started from weakly binding fragments. Structure-based design optimised them stepwise. The result, BI-2852, binds with nanomolar affinity. It grips both active and inactive KRAS forms.

The compound blocks SOS1 interactions with KRAS. Effector binding to CRAF and PI3Kα also falls. Phospho-ERK and phospho-AKT levels drop in cells. KRAS-mutant cells stop proliferating in response. The probe proves the pocket druggable.
europmc-pmc6702897:
Franke and Gaser review ten years of BrainAGE as a brain ageing marker from scans. Their review appears in Frontiers in Neurology. BrainAGE estimates a person's brain age from structural MRI. It was the first such method published. It remains the most widely applied concept. The gap between predicted and actual age carries meaning. Genes, environment, and life burden all shape it. Diseases speed apparent brain ageing measurably. The review sums up a decade of studies. Uses span degenerative and psychiatric risk checks. Single-person predictions are the method's hallmark.

Future approaches may add functional markers. Tailored brain-protecting treatments are the aspiration. Risk checks could shift earlier in life. The authors close with that outlook.
europmc-pmc6717897:
Tejera and co-authors tested how body-wide inflammation affects the brain in Alzheimer's disease. Inflammation elsewhere in the body raises the risk of cognitive decline. The team used live brain imaging in mice to watch microglia, the brain's immune cells, after a peripheral immune challenge. They checked the mice 2 and 10 days later.

Microglia pulled in their branches and covered less area at 2 days, then recovered by day 10. The challenge also cut microglial clearing of amyloid-beta, a protein that builds up in Alzheimer's. Removing the NLRP3 inflammasome blocked many of these changes. Blocking NLRP3 may protect the brain from outside inflammation.
europmc-pmc6844097:
Oleribe and co-authors identify the main problems facing African healthcare, in the International Journal of General Medicine. Health systems across Africa suffer neglect and chronic underfunding. Weakness shows in all six pillars the World Health Organization uses to judge care delivery. The authors set out to rank the challenges and match them with fixes.

The study ran as a structured group exercise at an African epidemiology meeting in Maputo, Mozambique. Participants came from 11 African countries plus Cuba, Portugal, and the United Kingdom. Ten groups brainstormed and scored problems and solutions. Training and capacity building topped the solution list. Health insurance, more funding, and stronger leadership also ranked high.
europmc-pmc6925497:
Li and co-authors measure the worldwide burden of breast cancer over nearly three decades. Their study appeared in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. Sound numbers on cases, deaths, and lost healthy years guide health policy. The team drew on the Global Burden of Disease Study 2017.

They tracked breast cancer in 195 countries and territories from 1990 to 2017. New cases worldwide reached 1,960,681 in 2017. Death rates fell in richer countries, yet the overall burden kept growing in poorer ones. Alcohol use stood out as the leading linked risk factor in most regions. High body mass index and high blood sugar also contributed. Cutting such risks, they argue, matters most where resources are thin.
europmc-pmc6959997:
Parker and co-authors apply direct RNA sequencing to read plant messages in full. Their study appeared in eLife. How RNA is started, spliced, ended, and chemically marked shapes what genes can do. Standard sequencing copies RNA into DNA first, losing some of that detail.

Using nanopore sequencing, the team read full-length RNA molecules from the model plant Arabidopsis. They mapped a chemical mark called m6A across whole messages at once. The reads revealed combined variety in start sites, splicing choices, end sites, and tail lengths. A mutant that cannot add m6A showed weaker message levels and faulty end formation. Its body clock also ran long, a real-world cost of losing the mark. The approach, the authors say, can refine genome maps and extend to less-studied species.
europmc-pmc7005297:
Yang and co-authors review how to attack cancer stem cells through their control pathways. Their review appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Cancer stem cells, first found in leukaemia in 1994, can renew themselves and spawn varied tumour cells. They are blamed for relapse, spread, drug resistance, and radiation resistance.

A handful of master switches, including OCT4, Sox2, Nanog, KLF4, and MYC, keep these cells in their stem-like state. Signal pathways such as Wnt, Notch, Hedgehog, and PI3K/AKT/mTOR steer them too, as do sheltered niches, low oxygen, and helper cells around the tumour. The authors explain how stem cells are identified, map the factors that govern them, and survey drugs, vaccines, antibodies, and engineered T cells built to hit them. Some agents are already in clinical trials. The goal is therapy that kills the roots, not just the bulk.
europmc-pmc7025897:
Li and co-authors map structural change across human cancers in Nature. Structural variants are rearrangements that delete, copy, or reorder stretches of DNA, from small bits to whole chromosomes. The team built ways to group and sort these changes, then used them on whole-genome data from a large pan-cancer project.

The data cover 2,658 cancers across 38 tumour types. Sixteen patterns of structural change stood out. Deletions were spread unevenly across tumour types and favoured parts of the genome copied late. Tandem copies favoured parts copied early. One striking form strings together 2 to 7 copied pieces from far apart regions, and in liver cancer it often switches on the telomerase gene TERT. The work shows how many ways a genome can be reshaped in cancer.
europmc-pmc7026697:
The GBD 2017 Colorectal Cancer Collaborators measure the world burden of colorectal cancer in The Lancet Gastroenterology and Hepatology. Policy makers need country-level figures on cases, deaths, and disability to plan screening and treatment. The collaborators assembled the picture for 195 countries and territories over the years 1990 to 2017.

They built estimates from vital registration, verbal autopsy, and cancer registry data, and also scored disability-adjusted life-years linked to proven risk factors. In 2017 the world saw 1.8 million new cases of colorectal cancer. The age-standardised incidence rate reached 23.2 per 100,000 person-years, up 9.5 percent since 1990. Deaths in 2017 numbered 896,000. Burden rose with development level in many regions, a pattern the report ties to diet and lifestyle change.
europmc-pmc7059597:
Myers, Chanock, and Machiela introduce a software package in Frontiers in Genetics. Linkage disequilibrium, the tendency of nearby gene variants to travel together, underpins population genetics and disease mapping. The web tool LDlink already calculates population-specific values from the 1000 Genomes Project, but running long variant lists through a browser, one request at a time, is slow.

LDlinkR moves that work into the R programming environment. Its functions query the LDlink server programmatically and download pairwise disequilibrium estimates for large variant lists in bulk. Researchers can then fold the statistics straight into analysis pipelines instead of copying tables by hand. The package is free, installable from the CRAN archive or from GitHub. The authors present it as an efficiency upgrade for integrative genomics, where studies routinely juggle thousands of variants across diverse populations.
europmc-pmc7074197:
Linton and co-authors estimate the incubation period of the new coronavirus in the Journal of Clinical Medicine. As infections spread from Wuhan, publicly reported case dates offered a chance to study the virus's natural history. Incubation time, from infection to symptoms, governs quarantine policy, yet early estimates were rough. The team analysed event-date data with methods that correct for right truncation, the bias from recent cases still mid-course.

The incubation period fell within 2 to 14 days with 95 percent confidence, averaging around 5 days under the best-fit distribution. Time from symptom onset to hospital admission ran 3 to 4 days unadjusted, and 5 to 9 days with truncation handled. The median delay from onset to death was 13 days. On that upper estimate, the authors recommend at least 14 days of quarantine. Their figures, comparable to SARS and MERS, became reference points for control policy.
europmc-pmc7156397:
Boo and Kim review how chemical modifications to RNA control how long messenger RNAs survive, in Experimental and Molecular Medicine. An mRNA's lifespan helps set how much protein a gene makes. Hundreds of RNA modifications exist; about 170 were catalogued at the time of writing, and new sequencing methods keep revealing their roles.

Six modifications are examined closely, including m6A, the most studied, and pseudouridine. Each can stabilise or destabilise the messages it marks, acting through writer, reader, and eraser proteins. These effects ripple into many cell and body processes. The review maps the known mechanisms for mammalian cells and frames RNA editing as a control layer rivalling DNA-level regulation.
europmc-pmc7156897:
Xu, Zhou, and Xu propose mechanisms for the low platelet counts seen in some COVID-19 patients, in the Annals of Hematology. Platelets are the blood fragments that form clots.
