Amico took the side of Moses Provencal in that fight. His rulings were couched in mild terms. He urged both sides to act with care.

A second case dealt with the law of levirate wedlock. That case came up in the year 1573. Amico held that the levirate duty comes first. Release by the rite of halizah comes after, he held. No date or place marks his rulings. Where he lived can not be fixed with sureness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-andrada-salvado: Salvador d'Andrada was one of the earliest Jewish settlers in New York. His name first appears in 1655. He seems to have been richer than most of his fellows and active in trade. He led efforts to secure Jewish civil and political rights under Dutch rule. He claimed rights to own land, to equal tax treatment, and to trade across Dutch lands. His surname also appears among Maranos in Brazil, Mexico, and the West Indies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antipas-herod-a:
Herod Antipas was the youngest son of Herod the Great by his Samaritan wife Malthace at the time of his father's death. Born before 20 B.C., he died in exile about the year 39. Like most of his family, he was schooled at Rome and kept close to the imperial court.

Greek inscriptions from Kos and Delos show that he traveled widely. The entry then follows his rise: Herod first named him heir to the whole kingdom after a poisoning plot came to light, then changed the plan. Antipas became tetrarch instead. The entry traces his rule, his marriage scandal, and his dealings with John the Baptist and Jesus from the sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aquin-philippe-:
Philippe d'Aquin was a Hebraist born at Carpentras about 1578 who died at Paris in 1650. Early in life he left his home town for Aquino, where he converted to Christianity. There he changed his name from Mordecai to Philippe d'Aquin.

In 1610 he went to Paris, and Louis XIII made him professor of Hebrew. He appears among the accusers in the 1617 trial for the crime of Judaism against the Marquis d'Ancre and his wife, in whose household he had served. His works listed here run from Hebrew roots and rabbinic sayings in 1620 to a study of the Tabernacle and a Hebrew dictionary in 1629. The entry gives his long list of books in full.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arakin-estimati:
Arakin, or Estimations, is a treatise of the Mishnah, the Tosefta, and the Babylonian Talmud, in the order Kodashim. Its Mishnah has nine chapters and fifty paragraphs in all. Its chief task is to fix exact rules for the vows in Leviticus, chapter 27, verses 2 to 29.

Those verses set fixed rates for buying back persons or things vowed to the sanctuary. The entry explains that a vow over a person means a pledge to pay that person's rated value. Chapter one asks who may vow and whose value must be paid. Chapter two sets the most and the least a dedicator must give, scaled to his means. That topic opens side paths into the highest and lowest measures for many other duties.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arnold-1797:
Arnold, cardinal-bishop of Cologne, who died on April 3, 1151, was one of the few church leaders who shielded Jews during the Crusades. In the Second Crusade, preaching by the French monk Rodolphe stirred crowds across the Rhine provinces to attack Jews. Jews who refused baptism were tortured and killed. Arnold was persuaded, by a gift of money, to act.

He set aside the castle of Wolkenburg in Lorraine, near Konigswinter, as a refuge. Jews who fled there on September 23 and 24, 1146, could defend themselves with arms. Their left-behind property went to the bishop. When two Jews, Abraham and Samuel, were murdered on the road to the castle, a second gift moved him to have the murderer cruelly put to death. The account rests on Ephraim ben Jacob, who was himself shut up in Wolkenburg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ascher-simon-18: Simon Ascher, born in Holland in 1789, served as hazan, reader and cantor, of London's Great Synagogue for thirty-seven years. He died at London in December 1872. Working with Mombach, the well-known composer, he helped systematize English synagogue music. English Jews kept his voice as a living tradition long afterward. The entry recalls his clear tenor and his florid recitative, full of roulades, as the sounds that defined his long tenure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashmun-or-eshmu:
Ashmun, or Eshmun, was a Phenician god worshiped at Sidon and Carthage, and in Cyprus and Sardinia. A three-language inscription from Sardinia matches him to Aesculapius, the Greek god of healing. Near Sidon, King Eshmunazer built him a temple on a mountain and consecrated a spring and a grove to him. Strabo calls that place the Aesculapius grove.

His worship spread wide. Many personal names in the inscriptions of Cyprus carry his name. At Carthage he shared a temple with Tanith and Baal. In many names he is called Adonis, from Adon, Lord. That link leads the entry to a closing guess: Ashmun may be a local name for Tammuz, whom the Greeks called Adonis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-attestation-of-:
Attestation is the signing of a paper by witnesses. Jewish law starts from a strict rule: a fact stands only on the word of two witnesses. In time, a written paper signed by two witnesses gained the same force as spoken testimony. But the entry draws a sharp line with modern practice. Modern witnesses vouch for a signature. Jewish witnesses vouch for the event itself.

That is why the rules are strict. Witnesses have to go through the paper word for word before signing. They must know both parties by name, or have them pointed out. The entry gives the approved wording of an attestation, built around the rite of symbolic possession. It then treats deeds of debt. A duly signed deed becomes like a public record, and the debt follows the debtor's land even into a buyer's hands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bacharach-2297:
Bacharach is a name borne by many German Jews. It appears from the twelfth century, or at any rate the fifteenth, in many spellings. They do not form one family. The name only shows that a line came from the city of Bacharach on the Rhine, or once lived there.

The first notice of the name is doubtful. A Samuel Bacharach is cited in 1175, but the reading may mean Samuel in the city of Bacharach. A firmer case comes in the fifteenth century, with Ephraim Gumprecht Bacharach of Frankfort. From the late sixteenth century the name grows common in western Germany. The entry traces a Frankfort line through Mendel and Moses down to Naphtali Herz Gans Bacharach, who died in 1709. That Naphtali praised the responsa of Jair Ḥayyim Bacharach yet never claimed kinship, proof that same name did not mean same blood.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-balak-2397:
Balak was king of Moab when Israel came out of the wilderness toward the land east of the Jordan, as Numbers xxii.-xxiv. tells it. Alarmed by Israel's numbers and victories, he called Balaam from the Euphrates to curse them. Like most ancients, Balak trusted a curse to work real harm. He offered rich sacrifices to bind the Deity to his wish. Instead, Balaam blessed Israel and foretold its victories.

A rabbinic section fills out the man. In that telling, Balaam had foretold that Balak, son of a minor prince, would one day be king. Balak had served Sihon and succeeded him. The rabbis call him a skilled sorcerer who knew a calamity was coming for Israel but not his own part in it. They fault his lavish promises and small deeds. A critical note closes the entry, tracing the tale to the old sources J and E.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baraita-on-salv:
Baraita on Salvation is a haggadic Baraita first printed by Schönblum at Lemberg in 1877. It lists twenty-four sins that delay the Messianic salvation and put off "the end," the destined redemption. For each sin a Bible verse is quoted to show its gravity. In most cases haggadic tales from the Talmud and Lamentations Rabbah are added to the same end.

No clue fixes the work's age, the entry says. Its heavy use of the Yerushalmi and Lamentations Rabbah, and its lack of quotes from the Babylonian Talmud, point to an early Palestinian origin. It must predate the start of the eleventh century, since Alfasi's list of twenty-four hindrances to repentance matches it closely. The two are likely two versions of one Baraita. Maimonides later reduced Alfasi's list to a system. A Solomon judgment tale at the end is called a later addition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barzilai-giusep:
Giuseppe Barzilai was an Italian lawyer and Biblical commentator born at Gradisca, near Triest, in 1828. He studied at Casalmaggiore and took his law degree at the University of Padua. He then practiced law at Triest and won note in several hard criminal cases there.

Barzilai was also a strong Hebraist and archeologist. His works include a translation of Lamentations with notes in 1867 and a metrical version of the Song of Songs. He wrote studies on the Behemoth, the Leviathan, and Semitic ideography. He served for years as secretary of the Jewish congregation in Triest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bebai-biblical-:
Bebai, without any added name, appears often in both Talmuds and in Palestinian Midrash as a teacher of the third century. Writers on chronology long treated all of those sayings as one man's. The entry argues that they come from two men who share a name and an age.

One Bebai taught in Palestine and sat under Johanan and Assi. The other taught in Babylonia and gave rulings of his own on oaths and daily conduct. The entry supports the split by noting that almost no topic appears under the name in both Talmuds at once. Tales and sharp exchanges fill out each man's portrait.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belais-abraham-:
Abraham ben Shalom Belais was a rabbi and poet born in Tunis in 1773. He died in London in 1853. First rabbi in Tunis and treasurer to the Bey, he fled his creditors for Jerusalem. From 1817 he toured Europe gathering alms and rich gifts.

A king at Turin gave Belais a thousand francs at one meeting. He served as rabbi at Nice, then joined a London academy from 1840. His many Hebrew books treat morals and Bible comment. One, on Ecclesiastes, appeared in Hebrew and English in 1850. Occasional poems by Belais mark public events, among them a French capture of a city in Algeria.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benaiah-hebrew-:
Benaiah, in rabbinical teaching, was president of the Sanhedrin under David and a leader of Jewish scholars. The rabbis read II Samuel xxiii. 20 as praise of his zeal for the Torah. They said he stayed alive, in a sense, even after death.

Under Solomon he held a high post as chancellor and close friend. Solomon sent him, famed for beauty like the morning star, to meet the queen of Sheba. The entry adds tales of Solomon's return from wandering and notes that cabalistic writing counts Benaiah among the thirty pious ones in each generation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-ha-zad: Benjamin ha-Zaddik, the Pious, was a giver of alms in the tannaitic period who managed funds for the poor. A Baraita tells that a woman once begged help when the treasury stood empty. She cried that she and her seven children would starve without aid. Benjamin then fed the family from his own means. Later he fell sick unto death, and legend says the angels pleaded his case above. The decree was lifted, and twenty-two years were added to his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berlin-samuel-3: Samuel Berlin, a German jurist, was born at Bamberg on Oct. 11, 1807. He died at Fürth on Dec. 21, 1896. A son of Löb Berlin of Bamberg, he took his law degree at Munich in 1834. He was the first Jewish lawyer in that kingdom. From 1848 he practiced law at Gerolzhofen and formed a close friendship with a fellow young lawyer who later rose to high office. Berlin himself gained a court title and led a town council body at Ansbach from 1860 to 1869.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beth-aram-josh-: Beth-Aram was a city east of the Jordan. Numbers calls it Beth-Haran. The Talmud knew it as Bethramta. Josephus called it Betharamatha. Herod the Great built a palace there. That palace was destroyed after his death. Herod Antipater later rebuilt the city. He renamed it Julias for the wife of Augustus. Since her first name was Livia, some called it Livias. The entry places the site at Tell-er-Rameh. That hill stands in a fertile part of the Jordan valley.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-ballagi-m:
Moritz Bloch, later Ballagi, was a Hungarian theologian and lexicographer. He was born on March 18, 1815, at Inócz. He died at Budapest on September 1, 1891. His father taught him Bible and Talmud. As a Jew he could not earn a diploma. In 1840 he published a pamphlet on the Jews. His Hungarian Pentateuch translation followed.

In 1843 he was baptized at Notzingen. He then served Protestant colleges and ministries. In 1851 he became professor of theology in Budapest. He founded a leading liberal Protestant journal in 1858. His Hungarian grammars and dictionaries long shaped the culture. They aided the Magyarizing of Hungary greatly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boston-3597:
Boston is the capital and chief city of Massachusetts in the United States. Nothing definite is known of Jews there before 1842. In that year the first congregation was established, with William Goldsmith as founder and first president.

A Jewish cemetery in East Boston followed in 1843. A second congregation, now Temple Adath Israel, formed in 1853. Godfrey Morse won a school committee seat in 1875, the first such office for a Boston Jew. Judah Touro gave 10,000 dollars toward the Bunker Hill Monument. In a population of 500,000, the entry counts about 40,000 Jews, mostly Russian and newly arrived in the prior ten years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-breuer-joseph-3:
Joseph Breuer was an Austrian physician born on Jan. 15, 1842, at Vienna. He took his medical degree at Vienna in 1863. He served at the Vienna General Hospital and then assisted Oppolzer.

Breuer became a lecturer at the University of Vienna, then gave up teaching in 1890. He turned to practice and to writing on medicine full time. His special field was the physiology and pathology of the nervous system. In 1873 he set out a full theory of balance seated in the ear's semicircular canals. With Sigmund Freud he published Studies on Hysteria at Leipsic and Vienna in 1895. That joint book closes the entry's list of his works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-budek-3797: Budek was a Polish Catholic priest, canon of Wislica at the start of the fifteenth century. The entry is very short and treats him only as an attacker of Jews. It calls him one of the most vigorous Jew baiters of his time. It credits him with stirring up the attack on the Jews of Cracow on March 27, 1407, the third day of Easter. He charged the Jews with murdering a Christian boy and with attacking a priest who carried the sacrament. No other facts about his life are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cahen-albert-38: Albert Cahen was a French composer born at Paris on Jan. 8, 1846. He studied composition with Caesar Franck and piano with Madame Szarvady. The entry lists seven stage and vocal works by him. They begin with a Biblical poem in 1874 and a comic opera in 1880. A mythological poem followed in 1883 and a fairy operetta in 1886. His four act opera came in 1890, a ballet in 1891, and a three act lyric drama in 1896. No judgments on the music are offered.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-casimir-ii-the-: Casimir II, called the Just, was a king of Poland born in 1138. He took the throne in 1177, after his brother Mieczyslaw III was deposed, and died in 1194. The entry praises him as a peace-loving ruler and friend of the people. He shielded Jews from oppression and extortion by the nobles. His laws at the Diet of Leczyc in 1180 paved the way for the noted Jewish privileges granted in Poland in 1264 by Duke Boleslaw of Kaliscz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chabris-4197: Chabris, a son of Gothoniel, was one of the three governors of Bethulia. That city was besieged by Holofernes, and the siege brought great suffering on the Israelites. Near its end, Chabris and his fellow governors agreed to hold out five days more in hope of rescue. If no help came by then, they would yield. Judith rebuked them for that promise. She pledged her own help instead, and kept the pledge by killing Holofernes, as the Book of Judith tells the story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chenaanah-4297: Chenaanah is a name borne by two men in the Bible lists. One was a son of Bilham, of the tribe of Benjamin, and a leading warrior in David's time, as I Chronicles vii. 10 reports. The other was the father of the false prophet Zedekiah. Zedekiah urged Ahab on against Micaiah, as I Kings xxii reports. Fürst linked such names among the Benjamites to marriages with earlier peoples of the land. War losses, he argued, may have forced Benjamin into alliances with Phenician neighbors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-citron-samuel-l:
Samuel Lob Citron, a Hebrew writer of fiction and literary critic, was born at Minsk, Russia, on May 24, 1862. He studied at the rabbinical school at Wolozhin. At fourteen he first appeared as a Hebrew author in the periodical Ha-Maggid. In 1884 he rendered Leon Pinsker's Autoemancipation into Hebrew.

His fiction list runs to four works, from a set of translated short stories in 1885 to Yonah Fotah in 1888. The entry then names five major essays. They judge the writers Mapu and Smolensky, trace Hebrew letters in Russia across the nineteenth century, and profile Levanda. A study of the poet in life and death, from 1900, closes the list.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-michel-44:
Michel Cohen, a Dutch soldier, was born on Nov. 27, 1877, at Goes in Zeeland, Holland. After common school he joined the Second Regiment of Hussars in April, 1894. Two years later he quit and signed on with the Dutch-Indian army for six years, sailing for the East Indies in June, 1896.

In Sumatra he rode with a cavalry regiment and won notice under fire at Batoe Menek on Sept. 8, 1897. Promoted corporal, he earned the Military William Order in 1900 for bravery at Tjot Kala on Nov. 14, 1899. Under heavy fire he lifted a wounded sergeant-major onto his own horse and ran beside it, bringing the man back safe to the division.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-conflict-of-law:
Conflict of Laws covers the clash when the laws of two states both claim a private case. Mosaic law knows no split between native and foreigner, the entry opens, citing one law for both in Exodus and Numbers. For ritual matters the Talmudic rule is local custom: settle where a stricter holiday custom rules, and you follow it.

Criminal law is surrendered to the law of the land. The Sanhedrin left Jerusalem forty years before the Temple fell, and Jewish courts lost capital power from then. Civil rules follow in detail. A long later thread treats marriage and divorce, ending with the Paris Assembly of Notables in 1806 and the Sanhedrin of 1807. Their rulings held mixed marriages binding in civil terms, with no religious ban.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coster-abraham-: Abraham Coster was a Dutch preacher who wrote against the Jews. He lived at Amsterdam in the seventeenth century. His book, Histoire der Joden, came out at Amsterdam in 1658. It told the history of the Jews from their dispersion to his own time, describing their manners, customs, and fables. His aim was plain: to sway the authorities against the Jews of Amsterdam. He hoped to stop them from building a new synagogue. The brief entry gives no dates for his birth or death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dapiera-de-pier: Astruc Dapiera was a martyr who lived in Barcelona. He was probably kin to Isaac de Piera of the same city. Isaac was baptized in 1391 under a Christian name. Astruc faced a darker charge. In 1370 the grand inquisitor of Aragon, Nicolas Eymeric, jailed him for witchcraft. His sentence was harsh but stopped short of death. He had to show repentance in public, in the cathedral. Then he was to spend the rest of his life in prison. Two old histories supply the facts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-davin-solomon-b: Solomon ben David Davin of Rodez was an astronomer who lived in the second half of the fourteenth century. He studied under Immanuel of Tarascon. His main work was a Hebrew translation of an Arabic book on astronomy and astrology by Abu al-Ḥasan Ali ibn Abi Rijal, titled "Sefer Mishpeṭe ha-Kokabim." That book had already passed through Spanish and Latin versions. He also translated the astronomical tables of Paris and added notes. Both works survive only in manuscript, at Paris and at Munich.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dillmann-august:
August Dillmann was a German theologian and Orientalist born at Illingen, Württemberg, on April 25, 1823. When Hengstenberg died in 1869, Dillmann was called to Berlin as his successor. He catalogued Ethiopic manuscripts for the British Museum and the Bodleian Library in 1847-48. He also edited the Ethiopic Old Testament in part and translated the Book of Enoch in 1853.

Dillmann is chiefly known to Old Testament students for his commentaries in a standard handbook series. He prepared editions on Job, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Isaiah, and other books between 1869 and 1892. The entry praises him for carrying Ewald's historical criticism forward without its wildness. He rejected the Graf hypothesis yet opposed the traditional handling of Scripture. He died at Berlin on July 4, 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dowry-aramaic-n:
A dowry is the property a wife brings her husband at marriage. In earliest times Israel knew no dowry. Instead the groom paid a price, the mohar, to the bride's father. Gifts could also go straight to the bride, as Eliezer's gifts to Rebekah show.

Over time the bride's portion replaced the groom's payment. By Talmudic days the dowry, nedunya, was a settled custom. The rabbis set a floor of fifty zuzim, scaled to a father's means. A poor girl's share came from community charity funds. The entry then tracks how the dowry was recorded, claimed, and used during the marriage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ejectment-5497:
Ejectment is a suit to recover land from one who wrongfully holds it. Jewish law starts from a fixed rule. Real property is presumed to belong to its owner, not its holder. Mere holding counts for little with land. Only three years of unbroken possession gives a holder standing.

A claimant against a known owner had to prove his title well. Every doubt was settled for the owner. No writ was needed to restore the owner. If strong enough, he could throw the holder out himself. Even land passed through many hands stayed recoverable. A tenant whose term had run out could be put out at once. A monthly tenant first had to get thirty days' notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-god-is-:
Eliezer was the servant of Abraham in the Book of Genesis. The name means God is help. Genesis names him in one hard verse as steward of Abraham's house. Most readers link him to the unnamed servant of a later chapter. That servant went to find a wife for Isaac. The entry weighs how scholars read the hard verse. Some hold the text sound as it stands.

A long rabbinic section fills out the man's figure. Tales show him outwitting the cruel customs of Sodom. One tale has him talk his way to a free wedding meal. The rabbis credit him with all the virtues of his master. They even say his face looked like Abraham's own face. That likeness once led Laban to mistake him for his kin. The entry gathers notes from Josephus and other old writers too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-b-moses-: Elijah ben Moses de Vidas was a cabalist at Safed. He lived in the sixteenth century. He learned under Moses Cordovero in that holy town. He went to Poland for a time, then came back. He died at Hebron in the end. His book Reshit Hokmah treats the moral life. It falls into five parts, on fear, love, repentance, holiness, and humility. In it he gathers moral sayings from many old books. Venice printed it in 1578, and towns across Europe reprinted it. He later cut the book down himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ellinger-elling: Nathan Ellinger was a German rabbi of long service. He was born in 1772 and died on July 4, 1839. Town records make him a rabbi of Mayence in 1808. From 1809 to 1821 he ran the Talmud school at Hamburg. From 1821 he served as rabbi at Bingen till his death. His Talmud notes in handwriting rest at Oxford today. The Bingen memorial book calls him holy and pure. That praise is most often kept for martyrs alone. His brother Lob was rabbi of Mayence as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephraim-b-isaac:
Ephraim ben Isaac of Regensburg was a German tosafist. Men called him Ephraim the Great in his own age. He died at Regensburg about the year 1175. He was one of the oldest pupils of Rabbi Tam. On his return from France he settled in Regensburg. With two peers he set up a rabbinical college there. His son Moses was a noted scholar of the town.

Ephraim stood out for his free and bold mind. He would own no post-Talmudic voice as binding on him. That stand set him at odds with teachers and peers. He sought to soften the strict rules of Passover. He let pictures of lions and snakes stand in a synagogue. Old custom had barred such images from the house of prayer. Where a custom had no ground, he struck it down. The entry shows that streak in case after case.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-etting-5897:
Etting is the name of an American family tied to Maryland and Pennsylvania, chiefly Baltimore and Philadelphia. The entry first lists members of whom little is known. Benjamin Etting fled New York when the British took it and died at Norwalk in 1778. Reuben Etting joined the Revolutionary army at nineteen and was captured at Charlestown.

Fuller lives follow. Charles Edward Etting fought at Sharpsburg, Fredericksburg, Chancellorsville, and Gettysburg, rising to adjutant. Henry Etting spent fifty-three years in the navy, retiring as a commodore in 1871. Reuben Etting of Baltimore became United States marshal for Maryland under Jefferson in 1801. Solomon Etting, born at York in 1764, closes the part of the entry read most closely here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-falkson-ferdina:
Ferdinand Falkson was a German physician and political writer born at Konigsberg on August 20, 1820. He died there on August 31, 1900. He took his medical degree in 1843 and practiced in his home city. From 1844 until his death he served as doctor to the poor of the Jewish community.

In 1845 he became engaged to a Christian, but Prussian law barred the marriage. The couple wed in England in 1846, and he was charged on his return. The case ran three years before he won in 1849. He wrote books on his marriage trial and on mixed marriage, plus memoirs and travel pieces. At his death he was senior of Konigsberg's aldermen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-florentin-samue: Samuel ben David Florentin was rabbi of Salonica in the eighteenth century. He was a nephew of Ḥayyim Samuel Florentin. The brief entry names two books by him and little else. The first is a gathering of the ritual laws of daily life. It has an index and notes on a great law code. It was printed at Salonica in 1758. The second book holds responsa, homilies, and comments on the Bible. It was printed at Salonica in 1776.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankel-seckel-:
Seckel Isaac Fränkel was a German banker born at Parchim on January 14, 1765. He died at Hamburg on June 4, 1835. By private study he gained a high degree of general culture. He also mastered nine languages, ancient and modern, while supporting himself by teaching. At Hamburg he became a bookkeeper in a large banking house. He soon founded a bank of his own and built a large fortune.

Fränkel was not ill-disposed toward Reform, the entry says. Yet he opposed one German hymn-book as too radical a break with the Jewish past. With a Reform leader he issued a rival prayer-book at Hamburg in 1819. In it Hebrew prayers were mixed with the new German hymns. He turned the apocryphal books from Greek into Hebrew, printed at Leipsic in 1830. He also wrote a Hebrew poem on the stay of the French in Hamburg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gamaliel-iv-649: Gamaliel IV was son and successor of the patriarch Judah II and father of Judah III. His dates cannot be fixed with care. Gratz places him in the last third of the third century. Halevy makes him a fellow worker of Hoshaiah. One tale says Hoshaiah blocked his plan to extend a fruit tithe rule into Syria. In a law reply to Abbahu, Gamaliel calls himself a small man of little learning beside the questioner.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gerasi-daniel-b: Daniel ben Elijah Gerasi, a Turkish Talmudist and preacher of the seventeenth century, lived at Salonica and died there about 1705. He wrote Odeh Adonai, a book of sermons printed at Venice in 1681-82. Hayyim Benveniste cites some Talmud sayings of his in several works. The entry gives no birth date and no other book for Gerasi. His standing rests on that sermon book and on the note later scholars took of his sayings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-glaphyra-6697: Glaphyra was a daughter of the Cappadocian king Archelaus. Her first husband was Alexander, son of Herod I and Mariamne; after his execution in 7 B.C., she married King Juba of Mauretania. That marriage failed, and she went back to her father. She then met Archelaus, a son of Herod the Great, who cast off his own wife to marry her. Because she had children by her first husband, Archelaus's stepbrother, the match drew strong censure as unlawful. It lasted briefly, for she died soon after reaching Judea.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gompertz-isaac-: Isaac Gompertz was an English poet. He was the brother of Benjamin and Lewis Gompertz. He was born in 1774 and died in 1856. Three poems carry his name in the entry. The first is "June, or Light and Shade" in six parts, London, 1815. The second is "The Modern Antique, or the Muse in the Costume of Queen Anne," London, 1813. The third is "Devon, a Poem," Teignmouth, 1825. Dr. Jamieson praised him highly. In his "Grammar of Rhetoric" he groups Gompertz with Dryden, Pope, Addison, and Gray.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-groves-and-sacr:
Groves and sacred trees were holy places for many peoples, the entry begins. Oaks, terebinths, tamarisks, and palms marked spots where gods dwelt. Old belief held trees to be alive, or home to spirits. Trees also spoke of birth, life, and death in winter. Hebrews shared some of this world. God showed Himself at an oak in Genesis xii.

Hebrew words for oak and tamarisk recur at scenes of revelation and judgment. Treaties, sacrifices, and verdicts all took place under such trees. Later prophets attacked the green-tree cults of Israel's neighbors. The entry then reads the Asherah of the Bible. Modern scholars, it says, take it for wooden pillars set by altars, not groves at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hachuel-sol-699:
Sol Hachuel was a Moorish Jewish martyr who was beheaded at Fez in 1834. Troubles at home drove her to flee to Muslim friends. Two women there swore she had agreed to accept the Muslim faith. She denied it and was thrown into prison.

On appeal she came before the sultan. Struck by her beauty, he offered her a place in his harem if she would give up her faith. She refused, and she was beheaded outside Fez. Her beauty and firmness drew wide notice. Her fate became a play, "La Heroina Hebrea," by Antonio Calle in 1852, and a prose account came out at Gibraltar in 1839.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halfan-uri-sher: Uri Sheraga Phoebus ben Eliezer Halfan, surnamed Manneles, was rabbi of Ungarisch-Brod, Moravia, in the first half of the eighteenth century. He wrote one work, "Dat Esh." It holds responsa and a commentary on the laws of Kilayim in Maimonides' code, and it came out at Berlin in 1743. The entry notes a neat point about the title: the second word holds the initials of his name, Uri Sheraga. No birth or death dates are given here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-harvest-7297:
Harvest describes how grain was gathered in ancient Palestine. Barley cutting began in April, with wheat and spelt about two weeks later. Lowland fields ripened first, and mountain fields could lag by weeks. The whole grain harvest ran about seven weeks. Reapers used a sickle, and binders tied the cut ears into sheaves.

The article ties the work to Bible law and feasts. Reapers had to leave field corners and dropped sheaves for the poor and the stranger. Workers ate parched grain in the field. Grape gathering led into the Feast of Tabernacles. Yield figures are given too, with thirtyfold called a common return.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-ben-tobi: Hayyim ben Tobiah was a Russian rabbi of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. He studied under Elijah of Wilna. Later he settled in Safed, in the Holy Land. A letter he wrote from Safed in 1810 survives in the sources. In it he urges the Jews of Russia to give money for students in the Holy Land. He also names a study house there set up by pupils of Elijah of Wilna. The entry is short and gives no birth or death dates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heilprin-joel-b: Joel ben Isaac Heilprin was a Polish Hasidic rabbi who lived at Ostrog in the middle of the seventeenth century. He was known as Baal Shem the First. His Talmudic and cabalistic learning won him a great name. Contemporaries called him a man of God. A cabalistic book records a wonder from 1648. It says he saved Jews who had fled pursuers by taking refuge in a ship. Some of his writings were printed in a cabalistic work at Zolkiev in 1724.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hermon-7597:
Hermon is a mountain on the northeastern border of Palestine. It is the high point of the Anti-Lebanon range, at the springs of the Jordan. The entry gives name meanings such as prominent peak and sacred mountain. Sidonians called it Sirion, and Amorites called it Shenir.

Hermon marked the northern limit of Israelite land in several Bible passages. It held a shrine suggested by the name Baal-hermon, and temples stood there in Roman times. In Enoch its summit is where fallen angels landed. The entry praises its dews and cypresses. Its modern name is given as Jabal al-Shaikh.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hoshaiah-rabbah:
Hoshaiah Rabbah was a Palestinian teacher of the first generation of amoraim, about 200. He compiled early traditions that explain the Mishnah and Tosefta. His school sat for years at Sepphoris, where crowds of pupils gathered. His pupil Johanan said even colleagues could not always follow his arguments.

Men called him father of the Mishnah for the skill of his explanations. He overruled both the house of Shammai and the house of Hillel on one offering rule. He resisted a bid to extend a tithe doubt rule into Syria. His sayings fill Midrash Rabbah. In one, the Torah is God's architect tool at creation. In another, he answers a philosopher on circumcision.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-husain-abu-: Daud ibn Husain, called Abu Sulaiman, was a Karaite liturgical poet of the first half of the tenth century. He compiled a Karaite prayer book, Tefillat Bene Mikra. Into it he wove his own poems and prayers, mixed with sermons, Bible notes, and arguments for Karaite doctrine. He attacked Rabbinite practice there, above all the claim that the Eighteen Benedictions must be said morning and evening. He was a bitter foe of Saadia Gaon and struck at him in writings now lost. His prayer book is lost too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-janah-abu-a:
Abu al-Walid Merwan ibn Janah is counted the greatest Hebrew philologist of the Middle Ages. He was born at Cordova between 985 and 990 and died at Saragossa in the first half of the eleventh century. He studied at Lucena and practiced medicine with skill. Turmoil drove him from Cordova in 1012, and he settled at Saragossa.

There he wrote all his works amid attacks from local Talmudists and a bitter feud with Samuel ha-Nagid. His chief work, the Book of Minute Research, was the first full account of Hebrew words and grammar. One part treats grammar, the other the lexicon. He read Scripture eight times to build his first book, a supplement to Hayyuj. His writings sank from view after Kimhi and rose again in the nineteenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isserles-moses-:
Moses Isserles, the ReMA, was a Polish rabbi, code annotator, and philosopher born at Cracow about 1520, who died there on May 1, 1572. His father was a rich Talmudist and head of the community. Isserles studied at Lublin under Shalom Shekna, whose son-in-law he became. A fellow pupil was his relative Solomon Luria. About 1550 he came home and founded a large yeshibah, supporting his pupils at his own cost.

By 1550, still young, he was already an authority: an aged relative at Padua asked his help in a printing dispute, and Joseph Caro answered his letters with care. In 1556 plague drove him to Szydlowiec, where he wrote "Mehir Yayin." The entry dwells on his friendship and friction with Luria. Both sought truth in rulings and prized custom. But Luria fought philosophy while Isserles defended it, holding that man's aim is to search out the cause of things.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-cadique-z: Jacob Cadique, or Zaddik, was a Spanish physician and writer born at Ucles in the second third of the fourteenth century. He became body-physician to Lorenzo Suarez de Figueroa, the Maestre de Santiago. That lord commissioned him to translate a work of moral philosophy from the Limousinian dialect into Castilian. The book gathers proverbs and sayings from the Old and New Testaments and from Aristotle, Seneca, and Cicero. Jacob finished it at Velez on July 8, 1402. It survives in manuscript at the Escurial.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jaffa-hebr-yafo:
Jaffa, called Yafo in Hebrew and Joppa in older English versions, is a city of Palestine and a Mediterranean port 35 miles northwest of Jerusalem. In ancient times it was the land's only link with the Mediterranean. Cedar wood for Solomon's Temple landed there, and the prophet Jonah sailed from there for Tarshish.

Later history in the entry runs from Maccabean princes who took the port from the Syrians to Roman attacks that burned and razed it. Jewish settlement stayed thin for centuries, then grew again in the 1800s. The entry ends with town counts: 2,970 Jews among 17,713 residents, in three named Jewish districts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jericho-and-onc:
Jericho was a walled city in the Jordan valley, west of Gilgal and facing Nebo. Strong gates shut at dusk, a king ruled it, and its wealth in cattle, gold, and silver drew notice. Since it guarded the entry into Palestine, Joshua sent two spies there while Israel still camped east of the Jordan. The spies lodged with Rahab, who let them down by a rope from her house in the wall.

After the crossing, Joshua's army marched around the city once a day for six days and seven times on the seventh. At the trumpet blast and shout the walls fell. All inside were destroyed except Rahab and her house, and Joshua cursed any man who rebuilt the town, a curse later filled on Hiel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joceus-joce-of-: Joceus, or Joce of York, was an English Jew of the time before the expulsion and the leader of the York community at the massacre of 1190. He is named in an English deed of 1176. He went to the crowning of Richard the First as York's spokesman and escaped the killing there. Back home, a mob attacked his great house, and he fled with his wife and children into Clifford's Tower. When the trapped Jews chose death by their own hands, Joceus acted first.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jose-of-mallaha: Jose of Mallahaya was a Palestinian amora of the fourth generation. Reading a verse from Psalms, he taught that the troubles of the Jews came from their habit of slander. He said this failing was common even in the days of David. Only two legal rulings from him survive in the entry. One deals with the transfer of land. The other sets rules for purifying dishes that had been used by Gentiles. The entry gives no dates or life story beyond these teachings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-justinian-9097:
Justinian was emperor of the Eastern, or Byzantine, empire from 527 to 565. In that long reign he issued many decrees touching the Jews. His rule, the entry says, was guided by care for the Orthodox Church, not by statecraft. The Samaritans fared worst of all under him, and their sad story fills much of the entry.

His laws barred Jews, Samaritans, and heretics from escaping civic office on grounds of faith, while denying them its honors. A decree of 545 kept heretics from gaining church land. Jews might build no new synagogues under a later rule. Other laws shielded church property at the cost of Jews and pagans alike. The entry closes with a list of his law books and their editors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kantor-judah-lo:
Judah Löb b. Joseph Kantor was a Russian journalist born at Wilna in 1849. He served as government rabbi of Libau, in Courland. He studied at rabbinical schools in Wilna and Jitomir. He then took a medical degree at Berlin, though he never worked as a doctor. Writing drew him early, in both Russian and Hebrew.

At St. Petersburg Kantor taught in a gymnasium and wrote for the press. He edited the Russian "Russki Yevrei" in 1883-84. In Feb. 1886 he launched "Ha-Yom," the first Hebrew daily paper in that city. He ran it until it closed in 1887. He also edited a Hebrew monthly, "Ben 'Ammi." About 1892 he became rabbi of Libau, a post he still held in 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-knefler-frederi: Frederick Knefler was an American soldier. He was born in Hungary in 1833 and emigrated to America. When the Civil War broke out he enlisted as a private. He became successively captain, major, colonel, and brigadier-general. For meritorious service at Chickamauga he was promoted to brevet major-general. He also marched with Sherman to the sea. The entry states that no other Jew attained so high a rank. After the war he was made United States pension agent at Indianapolis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lebensohn-abrah:
Abraham Dob Bär Lebensohn, a Russian Hebraist and poet born at Wilna about 1789, died there on Nov. 19, 1878. Talmud study came first; grammar caught him at eleven. Eight years with his wife's kin at Michailishok gave him his surname and his pen name Adam. Teaching and a spell as broker filled his Wilna years.

His verse book of 1842 opened a new epoch for Hebrew letters in Russia, and young Maskilim learned it by heart. From 1848 he taught nearly twenty years at Wilna's rabbinical school. A Bible edition with German rendering ran from 1848 to 1853. His drama of 1867 weds science and religion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lemmlein-lammli:
Asher Lemmlein, called Lammlin, was a self-styled forerunner of the Messiah. He appeared in Istria, near Venice, in 1502. He announced that the Messiah would come that very year, if the Jews showed repentance and gave to charity.

Lemmlein won many followers in Italy, then traveled through Austria and Germany to sympathy and belief. The entry says even some Christians trusted his prophecy. Fasting, prayer, and almsgiving spread wherever he passed, and that year was named the year of penitence. One man, the chronicler Ganz reports, broke his Passover oven, sure he would spend the feast in Palestine. Then Lemmlein vanished, and the stir ended.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leventritt-davi:
David Leventritt, an American lawyer and judge, was born at Winnsboro, South Carolina, on Jan. 31, 1845. He took his first degree in 1864 at the Free Academy, now the College of the City of New York. He earned his law degree in 1871.

Leventritt practiced law in New York. He served as special counsel for the city in big land-taking cases. Since Jan. 1, 1899, he has been a justice of the Supreme Court of New York state. For years he was vice-president of the Aguilar Free Library. He is also tied to many Jewish charities in New York city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-louis-edwa:
Louis Edward Levy, an American photochemist, was born at Stenowitz, Bohemia, on Oct. 12, 1846. He came to America young and studied at Detroit and at Michigan University. Work in tiny-scale photography led him to a new way of photo engraving. His Levytype was patented in 1875.

In 1877 Levy invented the Levy line-screen, which his brother Max perfected. In 1896 he invented the Levy acid blast for etching. Both inventions won medals at the Franklin Institute. He also ran Philadelphia newspapers for a time, and he wrote on Cuba, on business and credit, and on Russian Jewish refugees in America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lindo-mark-prag:
Mark Prager Lindo was a Dutch writer born in London on Sept. 18, 1819, and he died at The Hague on March 9, 1879. He went to Holland in 1838 to teach English. He later studied Dutch literature at Utrecht and served as inspector of schools in South Holland from 1865 until his death.

Lindo linked Dutch and English writing for Dutch readers. He translated Dickens, Thackeray, Fielding, Sterne, and Scott. Under a pen name he wrote novels, and his best known work was Afdrukken van Indrukken from 1854. He also wrote a history of England in Dutch and helped publish a weekly paper.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lomza-lomzha-10:
Lomza, capital of its government in Russian Poland, stands on the left bank of the River Narev. In 1897 it had a total population of 26,075, and 9,822 of its people were Jews. Clear records of an organized Jewish community there begin in the early nineteenth century. Its first known rabbi, a cabalist named Solomon Zalman Hasid, served for thirty years and died about 1840.

Later rabbis included members of the Diskin family. A destructive fire in 1884 left eighty families homeless. A large school founded in 1885 fed and clothed hundreds of boys who studied there. The entry also counts the town's Jewish schools and charities in detail. It lists a hospital, a poor-house, and a free-loan group. It ends by noting 1,327 Jewish artisans in the town in 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lutsk-lutzk-101:
Lutsk, a district city in Russian Volhynia, receives a long historical entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The city stands on the right bank of the Styr river. Between 1224 and 1227 about three hundred Karaite families moved there from Wilna. Rabbinite Jews arrived around the same time.

The article follows the community through charters, wealth, and expulsion. Lutsk Jews appear in Witold's 1388 charter of privileges for Lithuanian Jews. By the late fifteenth century the community was rich, with members farming the taxes. In 1495 the Jews were expelled from Lithuania and their estates were handed to nobles. They returned in 1503 and formed two communities, one Rabbinite and one Karaite, each with its own synagogue. The entry preserves a detailed record of a mixed Jewish town under Polish and Russian rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maier-joseph-vo:
Joseph von Maier, a German rabbi honored with nobility, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in 1797, he presided over the first rabbinical conference, held at Brunswick in 1844. He also sat on the Jewish Consistory of Wurttemberg. He died at Stuttgart on August 19, 1873.

The article is brief but points to a singular honor. The King of Wurttemberg ennobled Maier for his charity and his part in the religious movements of the day. That grant made him the first German rabbi to belong to the nobility. The entry cites the Allgemeine Zeitung des Judenthums of 1873 for the fact. For readers, the short notice marks a milestone in the standing of rabbis within German society. It also places Maier among the organizers of modern rabbinic conferences, where reform questions were first debated openly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marcus-lewi-lew:
Lewi Marcus, called Lewin, a German lawyer, receives a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Rhena, Mecklenburg, on October 15, 1809, he worked tirelessly for his fellow Jews. That labor earned him the nickname the Gabriel Riesser of Mecklenburg. He died at Manchester, England, in 1881.

The article lists the civic heights he reached. Marcus was the first Jewish deputy of the Mecklenburg Diet. He rose to become its vice-president. The city of Schwerin made him an honorary citizen. For seventeen years he served as acting president of its municipal council. He also presided over Schwerin's Jewish community. The brief notice preserves a lawyer whose public career marked how far Jewish emancipation had come in one small German state.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maurice-charles:
Charles Maurice, who built Hamburg's Thalia Theater into a famous house, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels. Born at Agen, in France, on May 29, 1805, he knew not a word of German until he followed his father to Hamburg at twenty-two. In 1831 he took charge of a minor Hamburg playhouse. When the great fire of 1842 destroyed it, help poured in, and he rebuilt it as the Thalia. He died at Hamburg on January 27, 1896.

Maurice managed the city theater as well for a time, then gave his whole strength to the Thalia until 1885. His son's death forced him back to work in 1893, in his late eighties. The entry praises his eye for acting talent: he developed Bogumil Dawison and Friederike Gossmann and encouraged several other stars before their fame was made.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mekize-nirdamim:
Mekize Nirdamim, the “Awakeners of Those Who Slumber,” was a society for publishing old Hebrew books and manuscripts. Richard Gottheil and A. S. Waldstein describe it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was founded at Lyck in 1864 under patrons including Nathan Adler, Sir Moses Montefiore, and S. D. Luzzatto. It was refounded at Berlin in 1885. Its committee spanned Rome, Paris, St. Petersburg, Philadelphia, and Budapest, a map of Jewish scholarship.

The entry is mostly the publication record of the society, a rescue list. On it stand the Diwan of Judah ha-Levi, 120 responsa of the Geonim, and the Mahzor Vitry. On it stand the Halakot Gedolot, the commentary of Maimonides on Tohorot, and the responsa of Meir of Rothenburg. And dozens more join them, works that existed only in manuscripts or rare printings. For anyone tracing how editions of medieval Hebrew literature came to be, the entry is a checklist.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meridian-date-1:
Meridian, the date-line where the calendar day changes, poses a peculiar problem for Jewish law. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein work it through in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. On which side of the line is it Sabbath? Civil Jewry can follow the international line at 180 degrees. But religious law cannot rest on so recent a convention, the entry argues. The convention is unsettled too. The Talmud never mentions the matter.

The trail begins with Judah ha-Levi's "Cuzari" in the twelfth century. It sets Jerusalem as the world's navel and puts the Jewish date-line ninety degrees east of it. That reckoning leaves China in the far east, divides Korea, and gives Australia the American date. The article continues to the polar question raised in the "Sefer ha-Berit." Where day and night last six months, count twenty-four hours. Then let the sun go.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-micrococcus-pro:
Micrococcus prodigiosus, the microbe of miracles, is a blood-red bacterium whose spots on food were once read as signs from heaven. Joseph Jacobs and L. Errera wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on it in 1906. An Italian doctor, Vincenzo Sette, first described it in 1819, growing on polenta, and later scientists renamed it three more times.

The article describes a tiny, motile bacterium that spreads by simple division, forms no spores, and stains its colonies red, pink, or brown. It thrives on potatoes, bread, milk, meat, and even communion wafers, carried by germs in ordinary dust. Those accidental blood-spots, the writers explain, were long taken as Heaven's wrath and fed the old belief in bleeding miracles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mnemonics-hebre:
Mnemonics, in Hebrew simanim, signs, are the catchwords and catch-sentences of rabbinic tradition. They helped memory hold long chains of law. Crawford Howell Toy and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach treat them in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The Talmud is full of them. They appear wherever a sequence of rulings might blur together and need a hook.

The first class the article describes is built from a Bible verse, a proverb, or a saying from daily life. It is introduced by the formula, and let thy sign be. The Babylonian teacher Naḥman bar Isaac invented them by the dozen. A verse like Thou hast set me behind and before could pin down the order of a discussion. It kept similar cases from being confused.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-jo:
Mordecai ben Joseph of Avignon was the most prominent Jew of thirteenth-century Provence. Solomon Schechter and A. Peiginsky profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 as the man who fought the badge. His adversary was the Dominican Pablo Christiani. Pablo persuaded the pope to order southern France's Jews to wear humiliating badges on their clothing. Until then they had been exempt.

Mordecai and a fellow Jew named Israel resisted. They were imprisoned by the inquisitors and bought their freedom for a large sum. Then Mordecai went over their heads. As delegate to the royal court with Solomon of Tarascon, he won a decree from Charles I against the inquisitors. The decree is dated March 26, 1276. It was unopposed, since Pablo was dead. Ibn Verga tells the story in Shebeṭ Yehudah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mudawwar-elias-:
Elias ibn al-Mudawwar was an Arabic poet and physician who lived at Ronda, probably in the early twelfth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry is credited to its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn. The Arab historians knew him chiefly as a poet. The entry tells one sharp anecdote about him.

At Ronda, Elias quarreled with another Jewish physician, as rivals in one trade often do. One day he learned a secret that could ruin the man. Instead of spreading it, he sent his rival a two-line poem in Arabic. It said that no friendship can exist between two of one profession, as when sun and moon collide, no light comes of it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahum-ben-simai:
Nahum ben Simai was a Palestinian amora of the third century, the son of the tanna Simai. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He is sometimes cited under the name Menahem. The sages called him the most holy man and the son of the saints.

The reason given is striking: all his life he never looked at the portrait stamped on a coin. At his funeral every statue was covered, so that even in death he would not see a human likeness. Only a few of his halakic sayings survive. He is also said to have preached at Tarsus on a verse from Exodus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nazir-isaac-113: Isaac Nazir stands near the start of the Cabala. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his brief entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. One account calls him the real founder of cabalistic science. It says Elijah showed him its secrets in a vision. The entry warns that this account is not fully trustworthy. Isaac passed the secrets to Jacob Nazir. Jacob taught Abraham b. David in turn. Abraham entrusted them to his son, Isaac the Blind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-norzi-11597:
Norzi is an Italian family of scholars and rabbis. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name likely comes from the town Norcia. Mantua held two distinct branches of it, Mortara says. Many of its members won note across centuries.

Benjamin wrote on the calendar in 1477. Eliezer glossed figures in Ibn Ezra's Sefer ha-Shem. Isaac of Ferrara ruled on a slaughter dispute in print. Raphael wrote ethics at Ferrara and Mantua. One name towers over the rest of the line. Jedidiah Solomon gave his life to the Bible's text. His Masoretic commentary collated manuscripts far and wide. He traveled abroad hunting one rare work for it. Finished in 1626, it became a standard aid. Print spread it later as Minḥat Shai.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-omar-i-ibn-al-k:
Omar the First was the second calif, or chief, of Islam. Joseph Jacobs and Mary W. Montgomery wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took the post after Abu Bakr in 634. He was killed by a foe in the year 644. Men call him the great shaper of Islam.

Under Omar, Syria, Persia, and Egypt fell to Arab rule. He set up the divan, a state office for funds. It kept lists of Arabs who shared the spoils of war. It kept strict counts of tax and tithe as well. He set the count of years from the Hegira flight. His name is tied to a harsh decree for Jews. It set Jews and Christians apart by dress and tax.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ostrogorski-moi:
Moisei Yakovlevich Ostrogorski was a Russian writer on rule and wealth. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in the year 1854. His father was a Jewish teacher at Grodno. He read law at the University of St. Petersburg.

For a time Moisei held a small post in the courts. His first books were time lines of the Russian past. One such book came out in the year 1872. It was oft reprinted and used in schools for years. In 1876 he began a yearly book on the law. His famed works came later in his life's work. One treats the rights of women in public law. One treats how parties are formed in the United States. That work grew into a three part study of parties.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pappus-11897:
Pappus was a chief of a revolt under Emperor Hadrian. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Hadrian ruled the Roman realm from 117 to 138. Pappus is named at all times with Luliani by his side. Luliani was most likely the brother of Pappus in blood.

The two men came at first from Alexandria, in Egypt. They lived in Palestine in the days of the revolt. Men called them the pride of Judaism in that age. They were seized at Laodicea, for a cause not now known. Their judge died all at once, and they went free. The day of that escape is kept as a feast day. When the Temple was to be built, they set up funds. They set coin stands on the road from Acre to Antioch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pelican-ka-at-1:
The pelican is named in the Bible as an unclean bird. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It appears in the food laws of Leviticus and Deuteronomy. The prophets picture it alone among ruins.

Two kinds of pelican live on the Syrian coast. The white pelican is the common one there. The bird stores food in the pouch under its bill. It presses the pouch to its breast to feed its young. That habit bred a famous false tale. People said the pelican fed its young with its own blood.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pizzighettone-d: David Pizzighettone was an Italian Talmudist and physician. The Executive Committee and A. Peiginsky wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked in the first half of the 1500s. He practiced medicine at Cremona, in Italy. At Venice he edited books for the Bomberg press. He wrote the introduction to its Maimonides edition. One old claim makes him rabbi of Ferrara. The entry flatly calls that claim wrong.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-portsmouth-1229:
Portsmouth is an English seaport on the coast of Hampshire. Joseph Jacobs and Isidore Harris wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jewish congregation dates from 1747. It is one of the oldest in the English provinces. It had a rabbi of its own from the start.

In the wars with France the town grew rich and busy. Many Jews came for trade in those years. For a time the town had two synagogues. Peace in 1815 shrank the Jewish group again. The newer building fell out of use at last. It was sold off to a dealer in dry goods. The older building serves the congregation to this day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-portugal-ancien:
Portugal is a kingdom in the southwest of Europe, called Lusitania in old times. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote its long article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived there as long as they lived in Spain. Their lot was much like that of Spanish Jews. Church law pressed on them later here, and less hard.

Until the expulsion, Portugal saw no open attacks on its Jews. The first king, Affonso Henriques, found Jews settled in his land. They lived at Santarem, Lisbon, and Beja. The article traces their life under king after king. It shows a long calm that Spain did not match. That calm ended with the forced choice of exile or baptism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbiner-mordec:
Mordecai ben Abraham Rabbiner was a Russian rabbi of Courland. Herman Rosenthal wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Sloboda, a suburb of Bauske, in 1758. He died at Bauske in 1830. Through his mother he came from Mordecai Jaffe. That man made the famed law books called Lebushim.

Rabbiner held the rabbinate of Bauske for thirty years. He held it from 1800 until his death. He wrote a book of rulings called Gedullat Mordekai. He wrote a book of sermons as well. His grandson printed both books after his death. The grandson added rulings of his own house to the set.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rausuk-samson-1:
Samson Rausuk was a Hebrew poet born in Lithuania in 1793. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Wilkowiski and first worked as a merchant. He died in London on September 11, 1877.

The article says he helped welcome Sir Moses Montefiore to Russia in 1846. In 1848 he went to London for good. There he served as librarian of the bet ha-midrash. He held that post for nearly a quarter century. London Jews saw him as their poet laureate for years. His Hebrew poems often marked events of the day. The entry honors a learned poet far from his birthplace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-resurrection-12:
Resurrection is the belief that the dead will rise again. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board, George A. Barton, and Kaufmann Kohler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Early Hebrews pictured the dead in Sheol. Life there was colorless and dim, they believed.

The article traces how hope for rising grew slowly. Job first longs for resurrection in his suffering. Jeremiah and Ezekiel made the person the moral unit. That shift made individual hope possible, the writers argue. Some psalm writers instead sent righteous souls straight to God. Later, messianic hope brought resurrection back. Isaiah promises the dead will live again. Daniel expects many sleepers in dust to awake. The entry follows a doctrine across centuries of texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-of-escal:
A. Peiginsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel of Escaleta, also called Samuel Sulami. He was a French Talmudist, poet, and giver to charity in the fourteenth century. Jacob of Provence ranked him among the first poets of Provence. He lived first at Narbonne, then at Perpignan.

Samuel took a side in the religious disputes of 1303 to 1306. He backed the liberal party. He sheltered the hunted Levi of Villefranche in his own house. He held firm despite warnings from Ben Adret. Then his daughter died, and grief shook his resolve. He read his losses as punishment for sin. He withdrew his help from Levi and joined Ben Adret. In the end he backed the ban on young students studying the sciences.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sarasohn-kasrie:
Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Kasriel H. Sarasohn. He was an American journalist. Sarasohn was born in Paiser, in Russian Poland, in 1835. He died in New York City on January 12, 1905. He trained for the rabbinate at home. In 1866 he gave up that plan and emigrated to America.

In New York, Sarasohn founded the Jewish Weekly and the Jewish Gazette in 1874. In 1886 he added the Jewish Daily News. No Hebrew Jewish paper then existed in the United States. He struggled even to obtain the needed type. In 1882 he founded the Hebrew Sheltering House. It later became a home for the aged. He also chaired the relief committee for the Kishinef sufferers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schomberg-meyer:
Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Meyer Löw Schomberg. He was an English physician. Schomberg was born at Fetzburg, in Germany, in 1690. He died in London on March 4, 1761. His family's original name was Löw, which he changed to Schomberg. He took his medical degree at Giessen in 1710.

Schomberg practiced at Schweinburg, Blankenstein, and Metz in turn. About 1720 he came to England. The Royal College of Physicians licensed him in 1722. He was then so poor that the college took his bond for the fees. Through London's Jewish merchants he built a glittering practice. His income reached 4,000 guineas a year. He joined the Royal Society in 1726. He backed his son Isaac in the son's long fight with the college.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shamir-13497:
Shamir names a substance harder than any stone in Bible and legend. Wilhelm Bacher and Ludwig Blau wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. In three Bible verses it means adamant, fit for a cutting point. Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Zechariah all use the word that way.

Later Jewish and Christian tales gave the shamir wondrous power. It could split the hardest material without effort. Tradition counts it among ten marvels made at twilight on creation's first Friday. It was no bigger than a grain of barley. Nothing hard enough to resist it could be found. The entry follows one small word from stone tool into legend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shklovski-isaac:
Isaac Vladimirovich Shklovski was a Russian journalist born at Yelisavetgrad in 1865. Isidore Singer and Max Rosenthal wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was schooled at his home town's gymnasium. At sixteen he began placing poems and prose in South-Russian papers.

In 1886 officials charged Shklovski with revolutionary activity. He was banished to Sredne Kolymsk in Yakutsk province. He stayed in Siberian exile until 1892, studying Yakut life. He learned native languages and wrote sketches of the region. His book on northeastern Siberia appeared in 1895. A French version followed the next year. From 1896 he reported from London for a Moscow liberal daily. Exile had turned a young writer into an expert on Siberia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ben-jose:
Simeon ben Joseph of Lunel was a Talmudist of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Wilhelm Bacher and Isaac Broydé wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His Provençal name was En Duran of Perpignan. He lived at Montpellier, Lunel, and, after 1306, Aix.

The expulsion of Jews in 1306 drove him to Aix. Simeon is known chiefly for the Abba Mari controversy. He backed Abba Mari as his active partisan and lieutenant. Almost no writings of his survive beyond three letters. One letter, Hoshen ha-Mishpat, answers Meiri of Perpignan sharply. Meiri had refused to sign a ban on philosophy students. Simeon set out the orthodox grievances against those students. Another letter asks Solomon ben Adret to uphold the ban. The entry recalls a fighter in the culture war over philosophy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-slander-13797:
Slander is false and harmful defamation of a person's good name. Wilhelm Bacher and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Spreading evil reports to injure a name brought a fine. It also brought an award of damages. The article sets slander apart from evil speech about true faults. True but harmful speech was banned, but not fined in the same way.

One case deals with a husband who questions his new wife. If his charge about her virginity proves baseless, he is whipped. He must also pay one hundred silver shekels to her father. He loses the right of divorce as well. Rabbinic rules against slander stayed very strict in later law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-vabian-:
Vabian L Solomon was premier of South Australia, born about 1849. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was the son of Judah Moss Solomon. Early in life he went to the Northern Territory. There he engaged in business and became mayor of the chief town.

He also became linked with the Northern Territory Times newspaper. Returning to Adelaide, he entered the House of Assembly. He won recognition as an authority on finance in Parliament. In December 1899 he became premier for a short time. He also sat on the Federal Council for Australian federation. That council brought about the union of the colonies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steblicki-sebli:
Joseph Abraham Steblicki was a German convert to Judaism of note. Gotthard Deutsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was the son of a Catholic butcher at Nikolai. He was born there about 1726 and died in 1807. He was well educated in Jesuit colleges in his youth.

He became a teacher, city treasurer, and council member at Nikolai. Retiring in 1780, he turned to religious studies in earnest. He began to observe the Sabbath and the dietary laws. On the Day of Atonement in 1785 he attended synagogue services. The law then in force prescribed death for his conversion. Frederick II suspended the case, and officials left him unmolested.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tagin-aramaic-h:
Tagin are the small crowns drawn atop certain Hebrew letters. Crawford Howell Toy and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Each crown holds three strokes shaped like tiny zayin letters. The New Testament calls such a mark a tittle. Only scrolls of the Law carry these ornaments.

Seven letters bear the crowns on their upper bars. Printed Pentateuchs leave the flourishes out entirely. The tagin belong to the Masorah tradition. A manual called Sefer ha-Tagin tracked their forms. Tradition traced it to stones Joshua set in the Jordan. The book passed from high priest Eli to Samuel. Later hands hid it under the Temple threshold. Ezekiel carried it to Babylon in exile, legend says. The entry mixes scribal fact with a chain of legend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-teller-leopold-:
Leopold Teller was a Hungarian actor born at Budapest in 1844. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on April 3 of that year. He studied medicine briefly at Vienna's university. In 1862 he quit for a Laibach theater company.

For ten years Teller played small theaters across the region. Iglau, Klagenfurt, Troppau, and Leipsic fill that list. From 1874 he belonged to the famed Meininger troupe. His roles included Shylock, Iago, and Franz Moor. He also played Gessler and Marinelli on stage. Hamburg's city theater engaged him in 1890. He retired from acting in 1899 at Hamburg. There he taught elocution in his later years. His own play met with considerable success. The entry follows a doctor turned villain specialist.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tiktiner-rebecc:
Rebecca bat Meir Tiktiner was an Austrian authoress who lived at Prague. Schulim Ochser wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. She died there, apparently, in 1550. Few women of her century published in Hebrew. Her name survived through two printed works.

Her main book, Meneket Ribkah, appeared at Prague in 1609. Cracow reprinted it in 1618. Seven gates, or sections, treat a housewife's duties. Talmudic and Midrashic anecdotes fill its pages. She also wrote a poem for Simhat Torah. That festival marks the yearly end of Torah reading. The entry preserves one of the earliest known Hebrew women writers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trent-german-tr:
Trent, oldest city of the Tyrol, was a bishop's seat from 1027 to 1803. Joseph Jacobs and Aaron Tänzer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A few Jews, likely from Italy, settled there in the 1300s. Bishops favored them as useful businessmen. Jews owned houses, estates, and their own school.

Good relations ended with the Simon of Trent case. A priest's preaching stirred the ritual-murder charge of 1475. Rich Jews were killed and their property seized. Survivors were expelled, and the community dissolved. Pope Sixtus IV sanctioned the proceedings in 1478. For centuries no Jews dwelt in Trent again. Even in 1638 the old case barred Jewish settlement.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ur-14597: Ur of the Chaldees, Abram's original home, is identified with a Babylonian ruin mound. Emil G. Hirsch wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. The Bible mentions Ur four times in all. Genesis twice, and Nehemiah once, name the place. Modern scholars place it at Al-Mukair, south in Babylonia. The mound stands on the Euphrates' right bank. Ur was an ancient seat of moon worship. It ruled as a political center by 3000 B.C. Some scholars link its moon god Sin to Sinai.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolfler-bernard:
Bernard Wolfler (born 1816) was an Austrian doctor who ran the Jewish hospital of Vienna. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Bohemia, he read thought at Prague first. He then took up medicine at Vienna from 1836 to 1842.

He worked two years at the town hospital of Vienna. He then practiced on his own at Prague for four years. In 1849 he took charge of the Jewish hospital of Vienna. A rich gift from Baron Rothschild gave the hospital a new home. Wolfler ran the new house with great care and zeal. He toured the hospitals of the West to learn their ways. In 1872 he set up free care for the sick poor. His homes took in lung cases each summer at no cost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-ben-hako: Yizhak ben Hakola was a scholar of Palestine in the third century. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at the same time as Joshua ben Levi. He passed on rules in the names of four older men. One tale of his lives on in a midrash. It treats the clash of the herd men of two kings. Those kings were Abimelech and Abraham of the old tale. It tells how that clash was brought to a calm end.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zebulun-15197:
Zebulun was the sixth son of Leah in the Book of Genesis. Emil G. Hirsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. From him came the tribe that bears his name. That tribe is named in the Books of Numbers and Psalms.

In the split of the land the tribe got a set tract. It lay north of Issachar in the hills of the north. It lay west and south of Naphtali at the same time. It lay east of the tribe of Asher in the west. Yet two old songs hint at land by the sea as well. Those songs stand in Genesis and in Deuteronomy. The bounds in Joshua are hard to make sense of now. The tribe's lands were rich and crossed by great roads. Those roads ran from the Jordan to the sea in the west.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zunser-eliakim-:
Eliakim Zunser was a Russian badhan, a wedding entertainer, and a poet in verse and song. Joseph Jacobs and G. Selikovitch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Wilna in 1845, he had a local name as a poet by sixteen. He set his rhymes to music and sang them at weddings and other feasts.

Zunser's method was more refined than the old wedding fooling, and hosts paid him well. After his Shirim Hadashim appeared in 1861, he composed over six hundred songs. Most sing of the Jewish nation; others praise railroads, light, Columbus, and the golden land of America. In 1889 he toured America and settled in New York as a printer and publisher.
kent-repertory-homoeopathic-materia-medi:
James Tyler Kent changed how homeopaths find remedies when his Repertory appeared in 1897. A repertory works backward from the usual books: start with the patient's symptom, then find which remedies match. Kent arranged symptoms under rubrics, headings for each kind of sign, and graded the drugs under each one.

Grades show at a glance which remedies fit a sign most strongly, a Kent hallmark. His school, the Kentian line, made this the finding tool of daily practice. Later repertories copied its plan, which is why the 1897 first edition counts as the most influential book of its kind in the field.
kingsley-travels-in-west-africa-1897:
Mary Henrietta Kingsley paddled, traded, and collected her way through West Africa in 1893 to 1895, and Travels in West Africa of 1897 made her famous. Her route ran through French Congo, Corisco, and the Cameroons, often where no European woman had gone. Religion, law, and daily life pass under her sharp, funny gaze.

Kingsley wrote with a trader's respect for African systems and a naturalist's eye for fish and forest. Her vivid first-hand observation corrected armchair ideas of the coast at a stroke. The book remains one of the great travel works of its century, bold and alive on every page.
lang-book-of-dreams-and-ghosts-1897:
Andrew Lang was a Scots scribe of tales, myths, and verse. His Book of Dreams and Ghosts came out in 1897. Lang had a foot in both camps: folk lore and the new mind hunt. The book gathers tales he found strong and strange.

Houses with ghosts, wraiths of kin at the point of death, and dreams that come true fill the text. Lang tells each tale well, then asks what it may mean. He will not force a creed on the reader at the close. The book is a chief text of the ghost hunt in its prime years.
lang-modern-mythology-1897:
Lang returned to the fight over myth in this 1897 book, answering Max Muller and the school that explained myths as a disease of language. Muller had read the gods as faded metaphors for sun and storm; Lang thought that reading ignored the evidence of living peoples.

Drawing on folklore and anthropology, Lang argued that myth grows from early beliefs and rites, not from wordplay. He defends the savage origin of tales that classical writers polished into literature. The argument is sharp, learned, and often funny. The book marks a turning point, when the study of myth passed from philology to anthropology.
libavius-alchemia-1597:
Andreas Libavius was a German schoolmaster and doctor whose Alchemia, published in 1597, is the first full textbook of chemistry. He gathered the scattered recipes of the art into one ordered course. He wrote to defend honest work at the furnace against quacks and scoffers alike.

The book treats workshops, furnaces, vessels, and the making of salts, metals, and medicines in clear order. Libavius insists that each claim be tested and written down so that another worker can repeat the trial. Students of the science see in his book the bridge from old recipe lore to chemistry as a taught and tested craft.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
Volume Eleven carries Motley's story from 1619 to 1623. Chapter Twenty-One describes Barneveld's execution at The Hague. Motley details the Advocate's conduct on the scaffold. The printed sentence went out to all the provinces.

He judges the proceedings irregular and deeply inequitable. The scene centers on the Inner Court beside the old castle. Brown brick buildings and a beechen grove framed the execution ground. The volume closes the Barneveld tragedy with its author's verdict attached. The Inner Court's beechen grove overshadowed its eastern side, he notes. Three-storied brown brick ranges surrounded the spacious paved quadrangle.
loma-a-citizen-of-venus-1897:
