plaw-105-46-1997: Stopgap funding for a new fiscal year is set by Public Law 105-46, a joint resolution approved September 30, 1997. It makes continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1998 for departments, agencies, corporations, and other government units. Amounts needed may be spent under the authority and conditions of the fiscal year 1997 appropriations acts, for projects run in 1997 that the coming 1998 acts would fund. The sample lists the agriculture act and the commerce, justice, and state act among those carried forward.
plaw-105-47-1997: Earthquake research money is authorized for two years by Public Law 105-47, approved October 1, 1997. It amends section 12 of the Earthquake Hazards Reduction Act of 1977 for fiscal years 1998 and 1999. Stated sums are added for each year in two subsections, with an equal set-aside in both years for the Global Seismic Network. At least a stated floor amount each year must support a competitive, peer-reviewed program run by the Director, coordinated with related work of other agencies named in the text.
plaw-105-48-1997: Au pair programs become permanent under Public Law 105-48, approved October 1, 1997. The law gives permanent authority to administer au pair programs, ending a string of temporary extensions. It amends a 1995 act titled An Act to extend au pair programs, Public Law 104-72. In section 1(b) of that act, the closing phrase through fiscal year 1997 is struck. Removing those four words removes the program's expiration date. The Senate passed the bill September 25 and the House September 29.
plaw-105-49-1997: Unused farm land in California becomes a school under Public Law 105-49, approved October 6, 1997. The Secretary of Agriculture must convey about twenty-two acres at 18296 Elgin Avenue in Dos Palos to the Dos Palos Ag Boosters, for a farm school teaching students and beginning farmers. The boosters pay fair market value, set by the Secretary, with size fixed by survey. At the boosters' request, the land may go instead to the Dos Palos School District. The conveyance is final, with no future liability for the Secretary.
plaw-105-5-1997:
A trade appointment bar is waived for one named official in Public Law 105-5, a joint resolution approved March 17, 1997. It waives part of the Trade Act of 1974 on appointing the United States Trade Representative. The limit in section 141(b)(3) took effect January 1, 1996, and does not reach anyone who held the trade post on that date and kept serving.

Charlene Barshefsky became Deputy United States Trade Representative on May 28, 1993, with Senate consent, and she was serving on January 1, 1996. The limit therefore never applied to her as deputy. Congress calls it fitting to keep waiving the same paragraph for her appointment as United States Trade Representative itself. The resolution then waives the provision for that appointment notwithstanding the paragraph's text.
plaw-105-50-1997:
Surplus federal goods reach poor families more easily under Public Law 105-50, approved October 6, 1997. It amends the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949 in two directions. Personal property and real property are treated in separate sections, both aimed at States and nonprofit groups.

For personal property, states may receive surplus items for donation to providers of help to families and individuals whose yearly incomes fall below the poverty line. That phrase is added right after homeless individuals in the existing list. For real property, the Administrator may assign surplus land to the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development for disposal. States, their subdivisions, and nonprofit groups may then use it to provide housing or housing help for low-income people.
plaw-105-51-1997:
A religious leader receives Congress's gold medal in Public Law 105-51, approved October 6, 1997. The President may present the medal, for Congress, to Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew. The honor recognizes his outstanding and lasting work for religious understanding and peace.

Congress found that Bartholomew leads nearly three hundred million Orthodox Christians worldwide, including millions in America. He is known at home and abroad for seeking world peace, respect for the Earth's environment, and deeper understanding between faiths. His efforts bring people of all faiths closer, and his courageous leadership for peace in the Balkans, Eastern Europe, the Middle East, and the Eastern Mediterranean inspires others. Many governments and universities had already honored him before Congress acted.
plaw-105-52-1997: Five fallen agents are memorialized in a building name by Public Law 105-52, approved October 6, 1997. The federal building at 601 Fourth Street, Northwest, in the District of Columbia becomes the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Washington Field Office Memorial Building. The act says its purpose is to honor William H Christian Jr, Martha Dixon Martinez, Michael J Miller, Anthony Palmisano, and Edwin R Woodriffe, who were slain in the line of duty. Later references to the building must use the memorial name.
plaw-105-53-1997: Court arbitration funding becomes open-ended under Public Law 105-53, approved October 6, 1997. In the Judicial Improvements and Access to Justice Act, one phrase changes. For each of the fiscal years 1994 through 1997 becomes for each fiscal year. That authorizes money for arbitration in district courts every year. Other sections improve judicial information sharing under the Civil Justice Reform Act of 1990, making one set of requirements permanent. Temporary judgeships are extended: the first vacancy ten years out ends them, except for western Michigan and eastern Pennsylvania districts.
plaw-105-54-1997: Religious workers from abroad gain three more years under Public Law 105-54, approved October 6, 1997. The special immigrant religious worker program is extended in the cited Immigration and Nationality Act clause. The year 1997 becomes 2000 wherever it appears, effective at enactment. The act's title adds two items. One is a later deadline for paperwork changes in the employer sanctions program under the 1996 immigration law. The other is a duty for the Secretary of State to waive or reduce nonimmigrant visa fees for people coming for charitable purposes.
plaw-105-55-1997:
Congress funds its own operations for fiscal year 1998. It does so in the Legislative Branch Appropriations Act, 1998, Public Law 105-55, approved October 7, 1997. Title I is the Congressional Operations Appropriations Act, 1998. Money comes from the Treasury for the year ending September 30, 1998, starting with the Senate.

Senate expense allowances match the familiar pattern: ten thousand dollars each for the Vice President, the President pro tempore, and both leaders. Each whip gets five thousand dollars, and each conference chairman three thousand. The total is fifty-six thousand dollars. Leaders also receive fifteen thousand dollars each for representation. Compensation for Senate officers and employees totals more than seventy-seven million dollars. That total includes one million six hundred twelve thousand dollars for the Vice President's office.
plaw-105-56-1997:
Military pay and operations for fiscal year 1998 are funded by the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 1998, Public Law 105-56, approved October 8, 1997. Title I is military personnel, for the year ending September 30, 1998. Each service receives its own personnel account in turn.

Army personnel funding is set at more than twenty billion dollars in the sample's long figure. It pays active duty soldiers, cadets, and aviation cadets their pay, allowances, clothing, food, and interest on deposits. Gratuities, permanent change of station travel, and temporary duty travel between stations are covered too. Payments owed under a 1982 benefits law, the Social Security Act, and the Department of Defense Military Retirement Fund are charged to the same account. Navy personnel funding follows next.
plaw-105-57-1997:
Wildlife refuges receive a clearer mission in the National Wildlife Refuge System Improvement Act of 1997, Public Law 105-57, approved October 9, 1997. It amends the National Wildlife Refuge System Administration Act of 1966 to improve management of the system. Amendments in the act are read as changes to that 1966 law.

Congress found the system held more than ninety-two million acres in 509 units, spread across all fifty states and United States territories. The system was created to conserve fish, wildlife, plants, and their habitats. That mission was helped by letting Americans take part in compatible wildlife recreation, including fishing and hunting, on refuge lands. Such chances also taught the value of conserving fish and wildlife, and the system played a pivotal role in that wider conservation work.
plaw-105-58-1997:
A bombing that shook the nation is memorialized by the Oklahoma City National Memorial Act of 1997, Public Law 105-58, approved October 9, 1997. The law establishes the Oklahoma City National Memorial as a unit of the National Park System and designates the Oklahoma City Memorial Trust.

Congress found that few events in a quarter century had rocked Americans' view of themselves and their institutions so hard. The April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P Murrah Federal Building in downtown Oklahoma City did so with great intensity. One hundred sixty-eight people died, some of them children, and thousands of family members were left with lasting scars. Survivors, including children, faced their own physical and emotional injuries. The response of Oklahoma's public servants and citizens, Congress adds, is part of the story the memorial must tell.
plaw-105-59-1997: A federal claim on Michigan land is released by Public Law 105-59, approved October 10, 1997. The Secretary of Agriculture must release the United States reversionary interest in a parcel in Iosco County, Michigan. That interest was kept when the land was conveyed to the county in 1960, under a deed recorded at Liber 144, page 58. The parcel is one and ninety-two hundredths acres in Baldwin Township, in section 11, described by survey lines from the section center. The Secretary may add terms to the release.
plaw-105-6-1997:
Crime victims may watch the whole trial under the Victim Rights Clarification Act of 1997, Public Law 105-6, approved March 19, 1997. It amends title 18 to protect a victim's right to attend and observe the trial of the person accused of the crime. A new section 3510 is added to chapter 223.

In non-capital cases, a district court may not exclude a victim merely because that victim may speak or present information at the sentencing hearing. Capital cases receive a parallel rule. A victim may not be shut out for planning to testify about the offense's effect on the victim and family. Nor may the victim be shut out over any factor needing notice under section 3593(a). Victim is defined by a cross-reference to section 503(e)(2) of the Victims' Rights and Restitution Act language in the sample.
plaw-105-60-1997:
Private inholdings inside an Alaska monument are traded to the government in the Hood Bay Land Exchange Act of 1997, Public Law 105-60, approved October 10, 1997. The exchange concerns lands within Admiralty Island National Monument. Congress sets out its findings before authorizing the swap.

The monument, created by the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act, is run by the Secretary of Agriculture through the Forest Service. Forest Service policy favored buying private inholdings from willing sellers, a policy Congress backed in the Greens Creek Land Exchange Act of 1996. Alaska Pulp Corporation owned about fifty-four acres at Hood Bay on Admiralty Island, inside the Kootznoowoo Wilderness, and those acres were available for federal ownership. The United States also held reversionary interests in about one hundred forty-four acres nearby.
plaw-105-61-1997:
Treasury, the Postal Service, and the White House are funded by the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 1998, Public Law 105-61, approved October 10, 1997. It also covers certain independent agencies for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1998. Title I is the Department of the Treasury, styled the Treasury Department Appropriations Act, 1998.

Departmental Offices receive more than one hundred fourteen million dollars for salaries and expenses, including running the Treasury Building and Annex. Caps ride on the sum. One cap is two million nine hundred thousand dollars for official travel. A second cap is one hundred fifty thousand dollars for reception and representation. A third cap is two hundred fifty-eight thousand dollars for confidential emergencies. Emergency spending is directed by the Secretary and accounted for on the Secretary's certificate alone. Overseas leased property costs are also covered.
plaw-105-62-1997:
Water projects and energy work for fiscal year 1998 are paid for in the Energy and Water Development Appropriations Act, 1998, Public Law 105-62, approved October 13, 1997. Title I covers the civil works of the Department of the Army. The Corps of Engineers spends the money under the Secretary of the Army and the Chief of Engineers, for rivers, harbors, flood control, and beach erosion work.

General investigations receive more than one hundred fifty-six million dollars, to stay available until spent. That account pays for collecting and studying basic information on river, harbor, flood control, and shore protection projects, restudying old projects, and preparing surveys, studies, and plans before construction. Named project amounts follow, including sums for the Delaware Bay coastline in Delaware and New Jersey, Tampa Harbor in Florida, and Laulaulei in Hawaii.
plaw-105-63-1997: A Kansas courthouse honors a senator under Public Law 105-63, approved October 22, 1997. The United States courthouse at 500 State Avenue in Kansas City, Kansas, must be known and designated as the Robert J Dole United States Courthouse. Any reference in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record to that courthouse counts as a reference to the Robert J Dole United States Courthouse. The Senate passed the bill in July 1997 and the House in September.
plaw-105-64-1997: Fifteen more days of stopgap funding are granted by Public Law 105-64, a joint resolution approved October 23, 1997. It makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1998 by editing Public Law 105-46, the first stopgap that fall. In section 106(3), October 23, 1997 is struck and November 7, 1997 is inserted. The same swap applies inside sections 118, 122, and 123 of the earlier law, so every deadline tied to that date moves together.
plaw-105-65-1997:
Veterans, housing, and other agencies share a spending law in Public Law 105-65, approved October 27, 1997. Its long title names the Departments of Veterans Affairs and Housing and Urban Development, plus sundry independent agencies and offices. Funding runs for the fiscal year ending September 30, 1998.

Title I is the veterans department. Its benefits office pays compensation to veterans. It also funds a pilot program for disability exams. The same account covers pensions and burial payments. It pays emergency and other officers' retirement pay and adjusted-service credits. It also pays premiums on life policies backed under the Soldiers' and Sailors' Civil Relief Act of 1940. Later titles cover housing and the other agencies.
plaw-105-66-1997:
Transportation for fiscal year 1998 is funded by the Department of Transportation and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1998, Public Law 105-66, approved October 27, 1997. Title I is the Department of Transportation itself. The first account is the Office of the Secretary, for salaries and expenses.

That office receives sixty-one million dollars. No more than forty thousand dollars of it may be used, as the Secretary decides, for official reception and representation inside the department. Up to one million dollars in user fees may be credited back to the account. One proviso bars using the money to keep custody of airline tariffs that the public and the department can already reach at no cost. The Office of Civil Rights follows, with more than five and a half million dollars.
plaw-105-67-1997:
An entertainer becomes an honorary veteran in Public Law 105-67, a joint resolution approved October 30, 1997. It confers status as an honorary veteran of the United States Armed Forces on Leslie Townes (Bob) Hope. Congress stresses that the honor had never been given before and should stay extraordinary.

Hope himself was not a veteran. He tried to enlist in World War II and was told his best service was entertaining the troops as a civilian. Across that war, Korea, Vietnam, the Persian Gulf War, and the Cold War, he traveled to ships and combat zones to perform for millions of servicemembers. His honors already included the Congressional Gold Medal, the Presidential Medal of Freedom, a Distinguished Service Medal from each service branch, and more than one hundred other citations.
plaw-105-68-1997: Two days are added to a funding deadline by Public Law 105-68, a joint resolution approved November 7, 1997. It edits section 106(3) of Public Law 105-46, the fiscal year 1998 stopgap, striking November 7, 1997 and inserting November 9, 1997. Provisions changed by sections 122 and 123 of that law are applied as if November 9 replaced October 23, 1997. Both chambers passed the measure on November 7 itself.
plaw-105-69-1997: Public Law 105-69, a joint resolution approved November 9, 1997, adds a single day to the same stopgap deadline. Section 106(3) of Public Law 105-46 is changed again, from November 9, 1997 to November 10, 1997. Sections 122 and 123 of that law are applied as if November 10 replaced October 23, 1997. The House and Senate both passed this one-day extension on November 9, the day the prior deadline would have run out.
plaw-105-7-1997: Residency rules for District investigators may be waived under Public Law 105-7, approved March 25, 1997. Its name is the District of Columbia Inspector General Improvement Act of 1997. It amends section 906 of the District's merit personnel act of 1978. At the Inspector General's request, the Director of Personnel may waive the residency rules for staff of that office. The waiver power sits in a new part, (d). Part (a) is amended to point to it, so the exception shows in the main rule.
plaw-105-70-1997: A Rhode Island post office is renamed by Public Law 105-70, approved November 10, 1997. The Postal Service facility at 551 Kingstown Road in South Kingstown, Rhode Island, must be known as the David B Champagne Post Office Building. Any reference in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record to that post office building counts as a reference to the David B Champagne Post Office Building. The House passed the bill in October and the Senate followed days later.
plaw-105-71-1997: Four days, not one, are granted by Public Law 105-71, a joint resolution approved November 10, 1997. It makes the fourth change to section 106(3) of the fiscal year 1998 stopgap, Public Law 105-46, moving the date from November 10, 1997 to November 14, 1997. Sections 122 and 123 are applied as if November 14 replaced October 23, 1997. The House acted November 9 and the Senate November 10, keeping the government funded into mid-November.
plaw-105-72-1997: Pension investment managers registered with a state are clarified by Public Law 105-72, approved November 10, 1997. It amends title I of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, section 3(38)(B). A fiduciary counts as an investment manager when registered under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. The count also holds when federal registration is barred by section 203A(a)(1). In that case the fiduciary must be state registered where its main office sits. That state filer must file a copy of its state registration form with the Secretary.
plaw-105-73-1997: Adopted children from abroad are excused from a vaccine rule at entry by Public Law 105-73, approved November 12, 1997. It amends the Immigration and Nationality Act's immunization requirement. The rule does not apply to a child ten years old or younger, described in section 101(b)(1)(F), seeking a visa as an immediate relative. Before admission, the adoptive or prospective adoptive parent must sign an affidavit promising the child will receive the listed vaccinations within thirty days of admission, or at the earliest medically fitting time.
plaw-105-74-1997: Colorado ranch land and federal land swap under Public Law 105-74, from 1997, in the Larson and Friends Creek Exchange. Lake City Ranches, Ltd., a Texas limited partnership, receives five hundred sixty acres in Hinsdale County. A June 1996 map shows the land. The price is equal-value land near the Handies Peak or Red Cloud Peak study areas, or the Alpine Loop. The exchange requires a permanent conservation easement on the four hundred forty-acre Larson Creek part. The easement limits use to farming, wildlife, recreation, or open space.
plaw-105-75-1997: A Colorado wilderness grows if a parcel is bought in time, under Public Law 105-75, approved November 12, 1997. If the United States acquires the Slate Creek parcel before December 31, 2000, it joins the Eagles Nest Wilderness. That wilderness lies in the Arapaho and White River national forests. The boundary adjusts at once. The parcel is about one hundred sixty acres in Summit County next to the wilderness, shown on a February 1997 map. Eagles Nest was designated by Public Law 94-352.
plaw-105-76-1997: Bad surveys that put homes inside a wilderness are corrected by Public Law 105-76, approved November 12, 1997. Landowners in Gunnison County, Colorado, had occupied and improved land beside the Raggeds Wilderness in the White River National Forest, trusting surveys that later proved wrong. A 1993 Forest Service resurvey fixed the true line and showed a small part of the wilderness was occupied. The act removes that property from the wilderness boundary so the Secretary may convey it to those owners under the Small Tracts Act.
plaw-105-77-1997: A ranger district changes forests in Colorado under Public Law 105-77, approved November 12, 1997. All National Forest System lands in Summit County forming the Dillon Ranger District leave the Arapaho National Forest and join the White River National Forest, whose boundary expands while Arapaho's shrinks. Any reference to the Dillon Ranger District, Arapaho National Forest, in a statute, rule, manual, or other document now means the White River district. Valid existing rights, permits, and contracts are not affected, and a forest receipts rule is addressed.
plaw-105-78-1997:
Jobs, health, and schools are funded together in the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1998, Public Law 105-78, approved November 13, 1997. Title I is the Department of Labor, for the year ending September 30, 1998.

The Employment and Training Administration training and employment services account receives nearly five billion dollars, plus reimbursements. Most of it, more than three point seven billion dollars, is available from July 1, 1998 through June 30, 1999. A further sum runs through June 30, 2001. The account carries out the Job Training Partnership Act and the Stewart B McKinney Homeless Assistance Act. It also carries out the Women in Apprenticeship and Nontraditional Occupations Act, the National Skill Standards Act of 1994, and the School-to-Work Opportunities Act.
plaw-105-79-1997: Forest land in California becomes tribal trust land under the Hoopa Valley Reservation South Boundary Adjustment Act, Public Law 105-79, approved November 13, 1997. The land lies in the Six Rivers National Forest. It is described by township and range in the Humboldt Meridian. The Interior Secretary will run it, held in trust by the United States for the Hoopa Valley Tribe. It becomes part of the Hoopa Valley Reservation. Roads 8N03 and 7N51, and the Trinity River access spur, become Indian reservation roads once the land is included.
plaw-105-8-1997: Ninety extra days before a securities law takes effect are granted by Public Law 105-8, approved March 31, 1997. It extends the effective date of the Investment Advisers Supervision Coordination Act. In section 308(a) of that act, the number 180 is struck and 270 is inserted. That one-number change is the entire law, moving the deadline from one hundred eighty days to two hundred seventy days. The Senate passed the bill March 12 and the House March 18.
plaw-105-80-1997: Satellite royalty rates are corrected by Public Law 105-80, approved November 13, 1997. It makes technical amendments to title 17, starting with the Satellite Home Viewer Act of 1994. A rate of twelve cents becomes seventeen and a half cents for some superstations. Those are the ones carrying programs covered by cable syndicated exclusivity rules. The rate is fourteen cents for syndex-proof superstations. Other fixes strike a December 31, 1992 phrase, drop a cross-reference, and move a deadline to December 31, 1999 or a contract date, whichever is later.
plaw-105-81-1997:
Ranch open space beside Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming is studied under Public Law 105-81, approved November 13, 1997. The Secretary of the Interior must study grazing use and open space in and near the park, and certain grazing privileges are extended for a time. Congress frames the problem as vanishing land.

Open space near the park keeps declining as Teton County grows, hurting wildlife migration routes and visitors. A few ranches form the remaining open space, and they depend on summer grazing inside the park. The act that created Grand Teton let some permittees graze for the life of a named family heir, and the last heirs are dying. Without a fix, the land will likely be split and built on, so the Park Service must find workable, fiscally responsible solutions.
plaw-105-82-1997:
The woman who taught America what the Everglades are is honored by Public Law 105-82, approved November 13, 1997. The Marjory Stoneman Douglas Wilderness and Ernest F Coe Visitor Center Designation Act names a wilderness for Douglas and a visitor center for Coe. Its findings explain the Douglas honor at length.

Her 1947 book The Everglades: River of Grass defined the Everglades for the United States and the world. It first built wide understanding of the ecosystem and woke a public wish to restore it. In her one hundred seventh year, Douglas was the sole survivor of the group that spent decades creating Everglades National Park. When drainage and development threatened the water and ecology, she spent the rest of her life defending the Everglades and inspiring others to act.
plaw-105-83-1997:
Public lands and parks for fiscal year 1998 are funded by the Department of the Interior and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1998, Public Law 105-83, approved November 14, 1997. Title I is the Department of the Interior. The first account is the Bureau of Land Management, for management of lands and resources.

That account receives more than five hundred eighty-three million dollars, available until spent. The money pays for protection, use, improvement, development, and disposal of public lands, plus surveying and buying easements. Of the total, about two million dollars assesses mineral potential of public lands in Alaska under a 1980 law. Three million dollars comes from a special receipt account created by the Land and Water Conservation Act of 1965. A further one and a half million dollars is set for a fiscal year purpose the sample cuts off naming.
plaw-105-84-1997: Twelve more days close the stopgap series for 1997 in Public Law 105-84, a joint resolution approved November 14, 1997. Section 106(3) of Public Law 105-46 is changed from November 14, 1997 to November 26, 1997. Sections 122 and 123 are applied as if November 26 replaced October 23, 1997. Earlier extensions that fall had bought as little as one day at a time; this longer jump carried funding past Thanksgiving week. Both chambers passed it November 13.
plaw-105-85-1997:
Defense work for fiscal year 1998 is authorized by the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1998, Public Law 105-85, approved November 18, 1997. It authorizes appropriations for military activities of the Department of Defense, military construction, and defense activities of the Department of Energy. It also prescribes personnel strengths for the armed forces for that year.

The act is organized into three divisions. Division A is Department of Defense Authorizations, Division B is Military Construction Authorizations, and Division C is Department of Energy National Security Authorizations and Other Authorizations. Division A opens with procurement, split by service: Army first, then Navy and Marine Corps, then Air Force, then defense-wide activities. Congressional defense committees are defined early, before the money titles begin.
plaw-105-86-1997:
Farm and food programs for fiscal year 1998 are paid for in Public Law 105-86, approved November 18, 1997. It is the Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1998. Title I is agricultural programs, starting with production, processing, and marketing through the Office of the Secretary.

The Secretary's office receives two million eight hundred thirty-six thousand dollars for necessary expenses. No more than seventy-five thousand dollars of it may fund outside employment under a cited civil service section. No more than eleven thousand dollars of it, joined with leftover Foreign Agricultural Service representation funds, may pay official reception and representation costs. Two provisos then bar using the act's money for named section 793 duties of a 1996 farm law, a policy fight written straight into the spending text.
plaw-105-87-1997: A New York post office building is renamed by Public Law 105-87, approved November 19, 1997. The United States Post Office building at 153 East 110th Street in New York, New York, must be known as the Oscar Garcia Rivera Post Office Building. Any reference in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record to that building counts as a reference to the Oscar Garcia Rivera Post Office Building. The House passed the bill October 21 and the Senate November 9.
plaw-105-88-1997: A California post office building takes a congressman's name under Public Law 105-88, approved November 19, 1997. The United States Post Office building at 313 East Broadway in Glendale, California, must be known as the Carlos J Moorhead Post Office Building. Any reference in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record to that building counts as a reference to the Carlos J Moorhead Post Office Building. The House acted October 21 and the Senate November 9, the same pattern as a companion naming bill that fall.
plaw-105-89-1997:
Foster children move faster toward permanent homes under the Adoption and Safe Families Act of 1997, Public Law 105-89, approved November 19, 1997. The act's stated aim is to promote adoption of children in foster care. Title I sets reasonable efforts and safety requirements for foster care and adoption placements.

Title I clarifies when states must try to preserve families. It adds safety to case plans and case reviews. It requires states to start or join proceedings to end parental rights for certain children in foster care. It also covers notice of hearings, use of the Federal Parent Locator Service, and criminal records checks for prospective foster and adoptive parents. Title II pays adoption incentive money, supports adoptions across state and county lines, and grades how well states protect children.
plaw-105-9-1997: A Washington irrigation deal is settled in Public Law 105-9, from April 14, 1997. Its name is the Oroville-Tonasket Claim Settlement and Conveyance Act. It approves a deal between the Bureau of Reclamation and the Oroville-Tonasket Irrigation District. The Secretary of the Interior may carry out the deal. That includes passing the project works that lack national importance to the district. The district is run under Washington law. It runs the Oroville-Tonasket unit of the Chief Joseph Dam Project, built under a 1976 act.
plaw-105-90-1997: Public Law 105-90, approved on November 19, 1997, gives the building that houses the Indianapolis Main Post Office in Indianapolis, Indiana, a new name: the Andrew Jacobs, Jr. Post Office Building. The short act has only two sections. One makes the designation. The other says any reference to the building in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record counts as a reference under the new name.
plaw-105-91-1997: Terre Haute, Indiana, gained a named post office building under Public Law 105-91, passed by the 105th Congress and approved on November 19, 1997. The law names the Postal Service facility then under construction at 150 West Margaret Drive as the John T. Myers Post Office Building. From then on, federal laws, maps, regulations, and records referring to that facility were to use the new name.
plaw-105-92-1997:
The Savings Are Vital to Everyone's Retirement Act of 1997 became Public Law 105-92 in the 105th Congress. Congress wrote it after finding that the coming retirement of the baby boom generation would strain the entitlement system. Fewer than a third of Americans, the findings say, had even tried to figure out how much money they would need in retirement.

The act amends title I of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 to push harder on saving. Its stated aims are to teach the public why retirement savings matter. It also provides for a regular bipartisan national retirement savings summit with the White House. And it starts a broad public education program. That program would help workers commit to a personal savings plan of their own.
plaw-105-93-1997: Miami's federal building and courthouse at 300 Northeast First Avenue took the name David W. Dyer Federal Building and United States Courthouse under Public Law 105-93. Congress passed the naming act in the 105th Congress, and it was approved on November 19, 1997. A second section makes the new name the one used whenever federal laws, maps, or records mention the building.
plaw-105-94-1997: Public Law 105-94 changed the name of a Georgia courthouse in 1997. The courthouse at 100 Franklin Street in Dublin, until then called the Dublin Federal Courthouse, became the J. Roy Rowland United States Courthouse. The act, approved on November 19, 1997, also directs that references to the courthouse in federal records be read as references to it by its Rowland name.
plaw-105-95-1997:
Congress turned to parking at Washington's performing arts center in the John F. Kennedy Center Parking Improvement Act of 1997, Public Law 105-95. The act amends the John F. Kennedy Center Act, the law that governs the center. Its subject is narrow: bigger parking facilities and changes to the grounds around the building.

Following a site master plan dated April 29, 1997, the center's board may design and build garage additions. One addition would sit at the north end of the center, the other at the south end. The board may also carry out site improvements and modifications. The plan itself must stay on file at the center, open for the public to inspect.
plaw-105-96-1997:
Asian elephants were losing ground across their home range when Congress passed the Asian Elephant Conservation Act of 1997, Public Law 105-96. The findings say wild populations had fallen so far that the species' long-term survival was in serious danger. The elephant already stood listed as endangered under United States law and under the international wildlife trade treaty.

Congress blamed the decline above all on lost habitat, alongside fragmented herds, conflict with people, poaching for ivory and other body parts, and capture. Because elephants also shelter many other forest species, the act backs conservation with money. It supports programs run by the Asian nations where elephants live and projects led by people with proven skill in protecting them.
plaw-105-97-1997: Steubenville, Ohio, is the setting for Public Law 105-97, a short naming act from the 105th Congress. It designates the United States Post Office at 150 North 3rd Street as the Douglas Applegate Post Office. Approved on November 19, 1997, the act also provides that federal laws, maps, regulations, and other records referring to that post office use the Applegate name.
plaw-105-98-1997:
Veterans with disabilities from their service received a cost-of-living raise under the Veterans' Compensation Rate Amendments of 1997, Public Law 105-98. The act amends title 38 of the United States Code. It covers disability compensation for veterans hurt in service and dependency and indemnity compensation for their survivors.

Rather than set a percentage, the law rewrites the rate table dollar by dollar. The lowest monthly rate in its opening section climbs from eighty-seven dollars to ninety-five dollars. Higher disability ratings rise in step. One listed rate moves from five hundred fifteen dollars to five hundred sixty-nine dollars. Each new figure replaces the old one in the statute.
plaw-105-99-1997: Public Law 105-99 names a Pennsylvania postal building for Peter J. McCloskey. The United States Post Office at 450 North Centre Street in Pottsville became the Peter J. McCloskey Postal Facility under the act, which the 105th Congress passed and which was approved on November 19, 1997. Any later reference to the building in a federal law, map, or record is treated as a reference to the McCloskey facility.
plaw-1997: Private Law 105-4, approved on November 21, 1997, is a private law for the relief of John Andre Chalot. The law fixes the date from which his citizenship counts. For the purpose of a 1995 pact with Germany on final benefits for United States nationals who faced Nazi persecution, Chalot counts as a naturalized citizen as of September 3, 1943. No other naturalization rule is changed by the law.
plos-pbio-0020097:
Mark Jung-Beeman, Edward M. Bowden, Jason Haberman, and co-workers scanned brains during sudden insight for PLOS Biology in 2004. People solved word problems either by steady work or by a flash of insight, the classic aha moment. Brain imaging let the team compare the two routes.

The insight route lit up a distinct pattern, including an area tied to loose word links, just before the answer came. A burst of activity marked the moment the solution broke through. The study gives hard data on a mental event that feels instant and mysterious. It suggests insight is not magic but a real brain process that can be measured, timed, and perhaps trained.
plos-pbio-0020197:
Marcel Cardillo, Andy Purvis, Wes Sechrest, and a broad team assessed risk in the world's carnivores in PLOS Biology in 2004. They asked whether crowded human areas raise the extinction risk of meat-eating mammals like lions, wolves, and bears. Data covered species across the globe.

The team found that where people live densely, carnivores face higher risk, even after accounting for other traits like body size and range. Big predators need space, and dense human settlement eats that space. The result gives conservation a clear, testable driver to watch. It suggests that saving carnivores will depend as much on managing human spread as on guarding the animals themselves.
plos-pone-0000097:
Reijo Laaksonen, Mikko Katajamaa, Hannu Päivä, and a large team used systems biology to hunt drug side-effect markers in PLOS ONE in 2006. Some widely used drugs harm a small share of patients, and doctors cannot yet tell in advance who is at risk. The team studied a statin known to cause muscle problems in rare cases.

By reading genes, proteins, and blood chemistry together, they found pathways tied to the toxic response and candidate markers in plasma. A blood test that flags risk before harm starts would change how such drugs are prescribed. The strategy, reading the whole system at once, is the paper's lasting point, beyond the one drug studied.
plos-pone-0000197:
Jonas Binladen, M. Thomas P. Gilbert, Jonathan P. Bollback, and colleagues published this sequencing methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The team used coded PCR primers, molecular barcodes attached during copying, so many samples could be sequenced at once by 454 parallel sequencing. That let them run high-throughput sequencing of multiple related gene copies in one batch.

Barcoding samples cut the cost of sequencing many specimens at once, a bottleneck in genetics at the time. The authors show the coded primer approach works on real amplification products. The trick became standard practice in the sequencing era that followed, from ancient DNA to microbiome studies.
plos-pone-0000297:
Barry Nicholls and Paul A. Racey published this bat study in PLOS ONE in 2007, posing a practical question in the title. Bats avoid radar installations, the authors report. That raises the idea that electromagnetic fields could deter bats from colliding with wind turbines, a growing cause of bat deaths.

Wind farms kill many bats, and a cheap deterrent would help both wildlife and operators. The authors document bats steering clear of radar and ask whether the effect can be borrowed. The paper links an odd behavioral observation to a real conservation technology problem.
plos-pone-0000397:
Naotaka Fujii, Sayaka Hihara, and Atsushi Iriki watched the monkey brain adapt during social interaction, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Neurons in the parietal cortex respond to movement, both one's own and others'. The team asked whether those motion-related neurons change their behavior as social situations unfold, a process they call dynamic social adaptation.

Reading others' movements is basic to social life: it underlies imitation, joint tasks, and judging intent. If single neurons adjust on the fly during interaction, the brain's social machinery is more flexible than a fixed wiring diagram suggests. The work helps connect brain cell activity to the give-and-take of real social behavior.
plos-pone-0000497:
Claudia Rodríguez-Almazán and colleagues found that unrelated proteins can help a folding protein succeed, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Proteins must fold from loose chains into exact shapes, and many fail and clump. The team showed that interactions with unrelated proteins increase the stability and formation of native proteins from unfolded monomers.

The result is counterintuitive: bystanders are usually expected to interfere, not assist. It suggests the crowded cell interior may actively support folding through weak, nonspecific contacts. That idea reframes how chemists think about making proteins in test tubes, where adding inert partner proteins might rescue yields of hard-to-fold products.
plos-pone-0000597:
Patric Hagmann and colleagues mapped the human brain's wiring as a network, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. They used diffusion MRI, which tracks water movement along nerve fibers. With it, they mapped human whole-brain structural networks. Those networks are the web of connections between brain regions in living people.

A structural network map is the scaffolding on which all brain activity runs. Network analysis reveals hubs and communities in that scaffolding, giving neuroscience a common map for comparing healthy and diseased brains. This paper was an early statement of the connectome idea, that the brain's connection pattern is itself a key to how it works.
plos-pone-0000697:
Heng Tao, Anthony J. Berno, David R. Cox and co-authors linked skin cell movement in a dish to gene variants, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Wound healing after injury to the epidermis remains hard to promote, partly because its factors are poorly understood. One essential step is re-epithelialization, where keratinocytes, the skin's main cells, migrate to cover the wound.

The title reports that migration rates in vitro are associated with SNPs in the KRT1 interval, a genome region named for a keratin gene. If inherited variants predict how fast skin cells crawl, healing speed may be partly written in DNA. That link could guide treatments for slow-healing wounds.
plos-pone-0000797:
Dev Churamani, Michael J. Boulware, Timothy J. Geach and colleagues characterized a new enzyme that makes calcium-releasing messengers, in PLOS ONE in 2007. ADP-ribosyl cyclases are remarkable enzymes able to catalyze several reactions. Among their products are cyclic ADP-ribose and NAADP, potent messengers that mobilize calcium inside cells. Not all cyclases, however, had been characterized at the molecular level.

Their subject is a novel intracellular cyclase, working inside the cell rather than on its surface. Characterizing it at molecular level means its sequence, its products, and how it is regulated. Calcium signals control everything from fertilization to secretion, so a new source enzyme redraws parts of that map.
plos-pone-0000897:
Thomas Webb and Robert Freckleton tested a classic size rule in animals where females are the larger sex, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In most species the sexes differ in size, and females are often bigger. Rensch's rule describes how that gap tends to change as species get larger overall.

Webb and Freckleton asked whether the rule holds when females lead in size. Their answer, flagged in the title, is that such species break the rule about half the time. A half kept rule is still useful, but it needs a better explanation. The study pushes biologists to ask what drives size gaps, not just describe them.
plos-pone-0000997:
Cheng Ding, Yan Liu, Yin Wang and colleagues found a brake on a special class of B cells, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. B1 B cells follow their own development path and do jobs distinct from standard B cells. What sets the size of that lineage was largely obscure.

Using mice that lack the Siglecg gene, marked with a glowing protein, the team show Siglecg limits the B1a branch. It does so by down regulating NFkappaB activation, a master switch for immune cell growth. A defined brake explains why this lineage stays a minority. It also gives immunology a handle for raising or lowering that population on purpose.
plos-pone-0001097:
Jason Slot and David Hibbett traced a nitrate eating gene cluster that jumped between fungi, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Some fungi carry a cluster of high affinity nitrate assimilation genes that switch on together. The cluster holds a transporter, a reductase and a related enzyme, a full kit for feeding on nitrate.

Using phylogenetic analysis, the pair present evidence the cluster moved by horizontal transfer between fungal lineages. A whole feeding kit moving at once can shift a species' ecology in one step. Their study ties that transfer to ecological transitions in fungi, changes in where and how species live. Gene clusters make such leaps visible.
plos-pone-0001197:
Age-related macular degeneration is the leading cause of blindness in the Western world, mainly affecting people over fifty. Peter Francis and colleagues studied variation in the complement factor H gene in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. That gene had repeatedly been shown to be a major factor in susceptibility to the advanced disease.

The authors examined haplotypes, the inherited blocks of variants in the gene. They checked their associations with drusen, the deposits that mark early disease, and with advanced macular degeneration. Sorting out which variant patterns raise risk sharpens genetic counseling and points at the complement system as a treatment target.
plos-pone-0001297:
DNA helicases are enzymes that unwind the double helix, a step required for repair, recombination, and replication. Sudha Sharma and Robert Brosh studied one human helicase, RECQ1, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Humans have five helicases of this family, several tied to diseases of premature aging and cancer risk.

The authors report that human RECQ1 responds to DNA damage. It is also required for resistance to genotoxic stress and for suppression of sister chromatid exchanges, a sign of faulty repair. Their work assigns concrete duties to the least-studied member of the family. It matters for understanding how cells guard their genomes.
plos-pone-0001397:
Yunfeng Li and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two proteins that uncouple energy use in cells. One protein, when raised, had been tied to weak insulin release. The other tends to drop in the muscle of people with type 2 diabetes. The team asked whether sugar drives these two proteins in unlike ways.

Working with insulin making cells of the pancreas, they tested how sugar levels shift each protein. The two did not move in step, which fit their hunch of opposed effects. The result helps clarify how fuel use is tuned in these cells. It may bear on why insulin release fails as diabetes takes hold.
plos-pone-0001497:
Jan Brascamp and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how past views shape what we see now. When an image can be read two ways, sight flips between the reads. Shown at gaps, the image tends to return in the same read as before. The team asked how long that memory of a past read lasts.

They found the pull of past views works on more than one time scale at once. Both brief and longer spans shape the next read. That layered memory helps the brain settle vague input fast. It also shows past sight aids, rather than biases, clear seeing in many cases.
plos-pone-0001597:
Kristine Briedis, Ayelet Starr, and Philip Bourne published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the human kinome, the full set of kinase enzymes. Kinases are prime drug targets, but some stay hidden when gene codes stray too far from known ones. Shape based searches can catch what code searches miss. The team ran such a search across the human set.

Their search found two kinases that code based hunts had missed. New kinases widen the list of druggable targets. They also show the known kinome was not yet closed. Each such find can seed a new drug line for cancer and other ills.
plos-pone-0001697:
Robert G. Wallace and Walter M. Fitch studied how bird flu crosses borders in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The strain is highly pathogenic influenza A H5N1. Its geographic spread is a necessary step toward the virus evolving human-to-human spread. As it travels, it diversifies in response to local farming and social conditions.

The authors report that H5N1 immigration is filtered out at some international borders, meaning the virus fails to establish in certain countries it reaches. The full text gives the family-tree analysis of virus samples and the border patterns they found. Knowing which borders hold, and why, could help target surveillance where the virus is most likely to break through.
plos-pone-0001797:
Blerina Kola and co-authors studied how the hunger hormone ghrelin acts in the brain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Ghrelin and cannabinoids both stimulate appetite, possibly through the hypothalamic enzyme AMPK, a key regulator of appetite and metabolism. Rimonabant, a blocker of the cannabinoid CB1 receptor, can block ghrelin's hunger effect.

The team reports that ghrelin's hunger effect is mediated through central activation of the endogenous cannabinoid system. The full text gives the feeding experiments and the blocker tests. Two appetite systems acting as one pathway helps explain why CB1 blockers cut hunger so strongly, and why their side effects were so broad.
plos-pone-0001897:
Antoine Lutz and colleagues scanned the brains of meditators in a 2008 PLOS ONE study on compassion. Past scans had shown that two brain areas, the insula and the front cingulate, react when a person feels another's pain. What no one knew was whether training the mind to feel compassion on purpose would change that response.

The team used brain scans while skilled and new meditators heard sounds of people in distress. They compared how each group reacted as they held a kind, caring state of mind. The study tests whether long practice reshapes the brain's response to suffering. That bears on how mental training might aid care work and health.
plos-pone-0001997:
Alfredo Rodriguez and co-authors built a program that finds and sorts tiny knobs on nerve cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The knobs, dendritic spines, are where most excitatory synapses sit, and their shape is tied to learning and memory. Gauging their three-dimensional forms by hand was slow and imprecise, which blocked firm statistics.

Their software detects spines in fluorescence microscope images in three dimensions and classifies their shapes on its own. Fast, precise counts let labs compare spine types across health and disease. Such tools turn a craft task into data that large studies can trust.
plos-pone-0002097:
Karthik Jayapal and co-authors compared gene messages to proteins over time in a soil bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Streptomyces coelicolor is a model for the bacteria that make most of our antibiotics. Many biological processes are dynamic, with deep shifts at both the molecular and body level. Systems analyses profile either gene messages or proteins to watch them.

The team looked for genes where the two do not move together, divergent mRNA-protein dynamics. Where message and protein part ways, control must sit after the message is made. Such genes warn against reading gene activity as protein truth.
plos-pone-0002197:
Sophie Colomb and co-authors traced how two genes guide nerve growth in the fruit fly embryo, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A hard problem in brain science is finding the cues that tell growing nerve fibers where to go. Those cues build the neat, repeated wiring of a nervous system.

In the fly, the genes Engrailed and Gooseberry-Neuro work together in a nerve cell called neuroblast 6-4. The team shows their joint action triggers the growth of the rear commissure bundles, bridges of fibers that cross the embryo. Small switches like these lay down the roads that whole brains are built from.
plos-pone-0002297:
Tomonori Takeuchi and co-authors studied a protein found only at one kind of synapse in the cerebellum, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The cerebellum tunes movement. In its Purkinje cells, a protein called delphilin sits exactly at parallel fiber synapses. There it binds a glutamate receptor, GluR delta2, essential for long-term depression and motor learning.

Mice lacking delphilin let the team test its role head-on. They found both long-term depression, a lasting weakening of synapses, and the optokinetic response, a learned eye movement, were enhanced. An unusual result like this refines the model of how this region learns.
plos-pone-0002397:
Agudelo-Romero, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Patricia Agudelo-Romero, Pablo Carbonell, Miguel A. Perez-Amador, among others. Its subject is virus Adaptation by Manipulation of Host's Gene Expression. Viruses adapt to their hosts by evading defense mechanisms and taking over cellular metabolism for their own benefit.

Alterations in cell metabolism as well as side-effects of antiviral responses contribute to symptoms development and virulence. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002497:
Dettenhofer and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Markus Dettenhofer, Fen Zhou, Philip Leder, among others. Its subject is formin 1-Isoform IV Deficient Cells Exhibit Defects in Cell Spreading and Focal Adhesion Formation. Regulation of the cytoskeleton is a central feature of cell migration.

The formin family of proteins controls the rate of actin nucleation at its barbed end. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002597:
Krach and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Sören Krach, Frank Hegel, Britta Wrede, among others. Its subject is can Machines Think? Interaction and Perspective Taking with Robots Investigated via fMRI. When our PC goes on strike again we tend to curse it as if it were a human being.

Why and under which circumstances do we attribute human-like properties to machines? The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002697:
In 2008, Miao Hao and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was Structure-Activity relationship and Substrate-Dependent phenomena in effects of ginsenosides on activities of Drug-Metabolizing P450 enzymes. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Miao Hao, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Ginseng, a traditional herbal medicine, may interact with several co-administered drugs in clinical settings, and ginsenosides, the major active components of ginseng. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002797:
In 2008, Jianqiao Ge and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about distinct neurocognitive strategies for comprehensions of human and artificial intelligence. The catalog record names Jianqiao Ge first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Although humans have inevitably interacted with both human and artificial intelligence in real life situations. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002897:
Darby Harris and Seth DeBolt measured how orderly plant cell walls are in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The wall is the main load-bearing frame of a plant and shapes growth, form, and defense against stress. Yet how its parts are built and adjusted was still not well understood at the level of mechanism.

Their topic was relative crystallinity, meaning how much of the wall material sits in neat crystal form. They studied how that trait is assembled and how plants adapt or adjust it. Growers and materials scientists both care, since wall structure affects crop strength and plant-based materials.
plos-pone-0002997:
Xiaomin Yu, Qing Zhou, Sung-Chou Li and co-authors catalogued silkworm microRNAs across development in 2008. MicroRNAs are tiny regulators that tune gene activity after genes are read, affecting development and metabolism. The silkworm Bombyx mori is both an industry animal and a model insect, and its genome had been sequenced.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team describes the silkworm's microRNAs and how their expression changes across multiple developmental stages. Stage patterns hint at which growth steps each microRNA governs. The catalog supports silk biology and wider insect development research. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003097:
Qian-Jin Zhang, Xiao-Lin Li, David Wang and co-authors studied dendritic cells taking up tumor material by trogocytosis in 2008. Two parts of the antigen presentation pathway, TAP and MHC class I, are often deficient in tumor cells. Restoring them was shown to restore presentation, but tumors find other escapes.

Trogocytosis is nibbling membrane from another cell. The team reports it moves MHC-I peptide complexes from tumors and infected cells to dendritic cells, enhancing cross-priming and adaptive T cell responses. Published in PLOS ONE, that transfer could help vaccines work around tumor hiding. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003197:
Jonathan Livny, Hidayat Teonadi, Miron Livny and colleagues present a large-scale method to find bacterial small RNAs in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Diverse bacterial genomes encode many small non-coding RNAs, called sRNAs, that regulate a wide range of biological processes. Computer algorithms had proven effective at finding sRNA-encoding sites, but tools and infrastructure to run those computations at scale were lacking.

The team offer high-throughput, kingdom-wide prediction and annotation of bacterial non-coding RNAs. Readers get a pipeline meant to work across many species, not just one model bacterium. Broad coverage can reveal regulators that single-genome studies would never see.
plos-pone-0003297:
Yaron Ideses, Yifat Brill-Karniely, Lior Haviv and colleagues rebuild actin structures in the lab in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. During cellular migration, regulated actin assembly takes place at the cell leading edge, with steady breakup deeper in the cell interior. Actin polymerization at the plasma membrane pushes out cell protrusions such as lamellipodia and filopodia.

The title reports that the Arp2/3 branched actin network drives filopodia-like bundle formation in vitro. Readers see one network produce structures usually credited to another system. Rebuilding cell edges from parts helps settle how protrusions really form.
plos-pone-0003397:
Jennifer M. Tsuruda, Gro V. Amdam, and Robert E. Page studied honey bee behavior in this 2008 paper. Some bee colonies store far more pollen than others. That hoarding habit comes with a set of linked body and behavior traits. The authors tested whether the habit shares roots with female traits linked to reproduction.

They compared bee strains bred for high and low pollen storage. The bees' senses responded to sugar and other cues in line with their strain. Those responses tied social behavior to the reproductive side of the colony. The link hints that one gene network shapes both sets of traits.
plos-pone-0003497:
Yasuhiro Watanabe, Eri Morita, and Yasuyo Fukada studied a faulty enzyme in ALS for this 2008 paper. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis kills the nerve cells that move muscles. Some inherited cases trace to mutations in an enzyme called SOD1. How that mutation causes such wide cell damage stayed elusive.

The team focused on single misfolded units of mutant SOD1. Those units stuck to cell surfaces in an adherent form. Such sticky misfolded protein may seed damage in motor neurons. The work offers a concrete form to target in therapy design. ALS moves fast once it starts, and no cure exists for it yet.
plos-pone-0003597:
Liliana D. Kojic and co-authors eyed a tumor entry route in this 2008 paper. A protein called AMF/PGI acts outside cells as a motility signal. Its receptor, gp78/AMFR, is overexpressed in many human cancers. Earlier work showed raft-based uptake of the signal is high in metastatic cells.

That uptake did not rise the same way in non-metastatic cells. Raft-dependent endocytosis thus marks aggressive tumor behavior. Hijacking the route could smuggle drugs straight into tumor cells. The study maps a doorway worth targeting. Few such routes are known, which makes each mapped one worth study.
plos-pone-0003697:
Uri Yerushalmi and Mina Teicher published this modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Synaptic plasticity, the change in strength between neurons, is a leading candidate for how brains learn and remember. How such plasticity itself arose is a separate question. The authors built a model of evolving cellular development.

Within their model, networks grew whose synapses could change with experience. Watching plasticity evolve in the simulation offers clues to how real brains came to rewire themselves. The work links two fields that rarely meet: the evolution of development and the study of learning.
plos-pone-0003797:
Stefan Kulick, Claudia Moccia, Xavier Didelot, and colleagues published this bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Helicobacter pylori lives in the stomachs of half of humanity and can cause gastritis, ulcers, and cancer. It naturally takes up DNA from its surroundings, and mixed infections let strains swap genes.

The team examined what that imported DNA looks like after transformation. They found mosaic imports, with pieces of the recipient's own sequence sprinkled inside the new DNA. The interspersed pattern reveals in fine detail how this ulcer bacterium shuffles its genes with neighbors.
plos-pone-0003897:
Camille Macé, Damien Seyer, Chanez Chemani, and co-authors hunted for biofilm genes in a hospital germ in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a germ that often infects patients in hospitals. It forms biofilms, slimy layers that protect it from drugs and defenses. An earlier protein study had flagged one unknown protein made more in biofilms.

The authors traced that protein to a gene cluster they named bac. They report the cluster helps the germ build biofilms and cause disease. Naming such a cluster gives drug hunters a fresh target. Weakening biofilms could make stubborn infections easier to treat.
plos-pone-0003997:
Sergey Kuznetsov and Andrei V. Khokhlatchev reported a new way tumor suppressors get destroyed in 2008. NORE1A and RASSF1A are proteins that restrain cell growth. Both are switched off in many kinds of cancer. Silencing of their promoters was the best-known route to losing them.

Their PLOS ONE article describes cutting of both proteins by calpain enzymes. That cutting, called proteolysis, offers another route to losing their restraint. Cancer cells may exploit more than one route at once. Blocking the cutting could help keep tumor suppressors in place. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004097:
Hua Shen, Bethany M. Tesar, Wei Du, and co-authors studied aging and transplant responses in 2009. More older people now wait for solid organ transplants. How aging changes immune responses to a graft was not well understood. Both donor cells and recipient immunity prime the response.

Their PLOS ONE article tested whether aging impairs those priming steps. They found aging weakens recipient T cell factors, both intrinsic and extrinsic. Weaker priming could mean older recipients reject grafts differently. The results may guide gentler drug regimens for older patients. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004197:
Edith Roussel and colleagues published this insect study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Social insects owe part of their success to a division of labour. The standard explanation is a response threshold model. Workers differ in how strong a task signal must be before they respond. So different workers pick up different jobs.

Roussel's team reappraised that picture using aversive responsiveness and learning, asking how bees respond to unpleasant stimuli and what they learn from them. Their angle tests whether the same thresholds that assign work also shift with experience. The study refines a core idea about how insect societies organise themselves.
plos-pone-0004297:
Terence Murphy and colleagues published this plant genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Arabidopsis thaliana, the standard lab plant, has three genes resembling the abasic endonuclease genes of bacteria, yeast, and animals. In those organisms, such enzymes perform base excision repair, fixing DNA bases damaged by oxidation and other insults.

The team tested whether the plant versions are required for seed development. Their analysis of mutants shows the roles these repair genes play as seeds form. Seeds must guard their DNA through dormancy, since a seed's genome is the whole future plant.
plos-pone-0004397:
The earliest dinosaurs come from Late Triassic rocks in South America. Ricardo Martinez and Oscar Alcober described one from the Ischigualasto Formation in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper names it a basal sauropodomorph. That group later gave rise to the giant long-necked sauropods. The fossil dates to the Carnian age, near the group's dawn.

By the Carnian, the main dinosaur branches were already split. A very early sauropodomorph called Saturnalia was already known. A second basal form helps show how the line began. The authors use it to trace early sauropodomorph evolution. Finds like this anchor the family tree of the largest land animals ever.
plos-pone-0004497:
Breathing, not just wings, may have made giant flying reptiles possible, argue Leon Claessens, Patrick O'Connor, and David Unwin in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pterosaurs were extinct reptiles of the Mesozoic era and the first backboned animals to fly by flapping. Evidence shows their wings were efficient and their flight control strong.

Far less was known about the lungs that powered that flight. The authors reconstruct how the pterosaur breathing system evolved. They argue that advances in respiration came first and made true flight, and later aerial gigantism, possible. Some pterosaurs grew to the size of small planes. Tying their size to their breathing gives a fuller account of how the largest flying animals ever lived actually worked.
plos-pone-0004597:
A faulty PINK1 gene tangles several cell systems at once in Parkinson's models, report Wencheng Liu, Cristofol Vives-Bauza, Rebeca Acin-Perez, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. PINK1 is a mitochondrial kinase, an enzyme inside the cell's power plants. Mutations in it cause an autosomal recessive, early form of Parkinson's disease, known as PARK6.

The team reports that PINK1 normally exists as a dimer, a paired unit, in mitochondrial protein complexes that travel with the respiratory chain. When PINK1 is defective, mitochondria malfunction. The proteasome, the cell's protein shredder, also falls short, and alpha-synuclein, the protein that clumps in Parkinson's brains, aggregates. One broken gene linking energy, cleanup, and clumping explains much of the disease picture.
plos-pone-0004697:
William Stork and colleagues studied how plants handle a defense hormone after bug attack, for PLOS ONE in 2009. When insects chew a leaf, the plant makes a fast burst of jasmonic acid. That burst turns on many defenses that slow further feeding and help heal the wound.

Far less was known about how the burst fades or spreads. The team tracked how the hormone is changed after repeat attacks and how it moves through the leaf. Their work frames the burst as a kind of plant memory. It may help crops resist pests with less spray. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be.
plos-pone-0004797:
Anne Farina and colleagues studied post transcriptional regulation of cadherin-11 in prostate and breast cancer cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cadherin-11 is a cell adhesion molecule important in embryo growth, bone formation, cancer invasion, and homing of cancer cells to bone. It also plays roles in rheumatoid arthritis, yet very little was known about how its expression is regulated.

The team found control after transcription by GSK-3 and beta catenin pathways. That layer of control affects how much protein cells make. It may influence spread to bone, a major clinical problem. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area.
plos-pone-0004897:
Jennifer Shen and colleagues deciphered von Hippel Lindau linked pancreatic manifestations by inactivating Vhl in pancreatic cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The syndrome is a pleomorphic familial disease marked by highly vascularized tumors including hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytomas, renal carcinomas, cysts, and neuroendocrine tumors of pancreas. Cell specific inactivation in mice separates which pancreatic lineages generate which lesion types during growth and adult life.

Different cells of origin produce cysts versus tumors. Mouse models mirror human pancreatic spectrum. Lineage knowledge guides surveillance imaging. Rare disease steps illuminate angiogenesis. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004997:
In southern Africa, HIV hits the general population hard. Men who have sex with men were largely excluded from surveys. Epidemiologic data for them were among the sparsest anywhere. Stefan Baral and colleagues filled part of that gap in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied Malawi, Namibia and Botswana. They measured HIV prevalence, risk and human rights.

The data reveal a hidden, high-risk group. Its members face stigma and legal threats alongside the virus. Excluding them leaves a blind spot in epidemic control. The findings argue for including them in surveillance and care. They also document rights abuses that shape risk. Public health cannot succeed while ignoring this population.
plos-pone-0005097:
Muscle cells prune themselves as they mature. That pruning is apoptosis, controlled cell death. Runaway pruning destroys muscle in disease. Michelle Smith, Yolanda Huang and Mohanish Deshmukh studied how pruning is restrained. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They focused on myotubes, the young fibers of skeletal muscle.

As muscle cells differentiate, they switch on a brake called XIAP. XIAP restricts the apoptotic pathway. The cells evoke their own protector at the right moment. That self-brake keeps pruning in check. The finding points to a built-in defense for muscle. Boosting it might fight muscle loss in neuromuscular disease. The study shows development builds in its own safeguards.
plos-pone-0005197:
A family of proteins called SREBPs acts as a master switch for fat and cholesterol in mammals. These switches control genes for taking up and making cholesterol, fatty acids, and triglycerides. Chatterjee and colleagues hunted for new controls on that switch in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team identified novel genes and pathways that regulate how strongly SREBPs work. Each new regulator is a possible handle for drugs aimed at high cholesterol or fatty liver. The work widens the map of fat control beyond the few switches that were already well known.
plos-pone-0005297:
Chloroplast genomes in grasses evolve faster than those of most other flowering plants. Why that speedup happened, and when, stayed obscure for years. Zhong and colleagues traced the pattern in ancestral grasses in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study estimated how the pace of chloroplast evolution changed over time. Change came in episodes, with bursts of adaptation rather than a steady fast rate. Episodic evolution helps explain the grass family's success and gives plant scientists a timeline for genome change in a vital crop family. Grasses feed much of the world, from wheat to corn to rice. So the pace of change in their green cells is a clue to how these crops may cope with a hot, dry world.
plos-pone-0005397:
TRAIL is a protein that can order infected or abnormal cells to die, and it takes part in HIV disease by depleting CD4 T cells. Huang and colleagues studied what controls TRAIL in HIV-infected macrophages in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Type I interferons, the early antiviral signals, regulate TRAIL in those macrophages. Interferon regulatory factors carry out part of that control. The pathway links the innate alarm system to a death ligand that harms the very cells HIV patients can least afford to lose. Drugs that curb this virus must save CD4 cells, not just block the germ. So a path that links the alarm to the loss of those cells is a fresh place to aim a cure or a shield.
plos-pone-0005497:
Oren Parnas and colleagues studied a yeast gene tied to genome stability in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. When the gene ELG1 is faulty, yeast suffer extra DNA swaps, lost chromosomes, and gross breaks in their genome. The gene's protein resembles part of the tool that loads clamps onto DNA during copying.

The team found that the Elg1 complex also helps hold sister copies of DNA together after copying. That holding step, called cohesion, keeps chromosomes paired until the cell divides. A fault there can scramble the genome, which links this small yeast gene to big questions about cancer.
plos-pone-0005597:
Gal Markel and co-authors tested a way to boost natural killer cells against tumours in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Natural killer cells are immune cells that can kill cancer cells without prior training. They are used in cell therapies, above all around stem cell transplants.

The team matched a receptor on the killer cells with its partner on target cells to pick stronger pairings. Choosing donors whose cells match in the right way could make the therapy hit tumours harder. That would be welcome in cancers that resist other treatments. Stronger killer cells could also help patients whose own immune systems are weakened by transplant drugs.
plos-pone-0005697:
Alana Conti and colleagues studied in 2009 how alcohol changes a key learning site in the mouse brain. Mice lacking two enzymes, AC1 and AC8, react to alcohol in unusual ways. Those enzymes help nerve cells adjust the strength of their links, a base of memory.

The team found that the two enzymes start a self-correcting response at the synapse when alcohol arrives. This presynaptic response acts like a brake, steadying the circuit. Knowing which molecules set that brake helps explain why alcohol's effects differ between people. It also marks paths for drugs aimed at problem drinking.
plos-pone-0005797:
Iain Anderson and co-authors read the genomes of a little-studied order of methane-making microbes in 2009. Methanomicrobiales make methane in swamps, guts, and sediments. By ribosomal genes they sit near one class of methanogens, yet their metabolism looks like another's.

Full genomes let the team sort them into three classes with distinct toolkits. That order sharpens how scientists model methane output from nature, a greenhouse concern. It also shows how genome reads can settle mismatches between a family tree and a lifestyle. These microbes punch far above their size in climate terms.
plos-pone-0005897:
Mareike Selcho and co-authors tested in 2009 what role dopamine plays when fly larvae learn to link a smell with a taste reward or punishment. Even fly larvae form and recall such odor associations. Their simple brains make them a clean model for the basics of learning.

The team probed dopamine signaling during classical conditioning in the larvae. Dopamine is a universal teaching signal in animal brains, but its exact classroom duties vary. Pinning them down in a minimal brain informs models of learning everywhere. The study adds larval data to a story mostly built on adult flies and bees.
plos-pone-0005997:
African horse sickness can kill more than nine in ten horses it strikes. Rachael Chiam, Emma Sharp, Sushila Maan and colleagues worked on a safer vaccine in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper gives ponies a vaccine built on MVA, a weakened virus used as a carrier, loaded with parts of the horse sickness virus.

Current vaccines carry worries of their own, so a carrier-based shot is an appealing swap. The team measured the antibody response the ponies raised after the shot. Antibodies are the first sign a vaccine has taught the body its lesson. The study supports the carrier route as a path to guard horses against a dreaded disease.
plos-pone-0006097:
A family of fertility genes runs through the animal kingdom, from flies to people. Hongyan Xu, Zhendong Li, Mingyou Li and colleagues added fish to that family's map in 2009.
