The other wavelength, 950 nanometers, produced no real recovery at any dose, apart from a hint of benefit at one middle dose. Energy molecule levels rose under some treatments but did not line up neatly with recovery, suggesting several processes are at play. The authors say wavelength choice matters as much as dose.
plos-pone-0354897:
Karar Zunaid Ahsan and four colleagues published this 2026 study of fairness in mothers' health care in Bangladesh. They linked national surveys of mothers and health facilities across 2001, 2010, and 2016. They asked whether gaps between poor and non-poor women in pregnancy care, facility births, and complication treatment closed faster where clinics were better prepared.

Overall use rose, yet poor and non-poor gaps persisted and sometimes widened, especially for giving birth in facilities. Ahsan concludes that upgrading clinics alone does not deliver fairness, and policy must target the women still left behind.
plos-pone-0354997:
Subina Bajracharya, Sadikshya Neupane, and Parita Shrestha published this 2026 community study of a simpler way to spot overweight children in Bharatpur, Nepal. Body mass index needs proper scales, height boards, and trained staff, which large school screenings often lack. The team measured three hundred children aged six to eleven, comparing neck size with standard body measures.

Neck circumference tracked the established measures closely and identified overweight children with useful accuracy, and the authors derived cutoff values for local use. Bajracharya presents the tape-around-the-neck check as cheap, quick screening for schools with few resources.
plos-pone-0355197:
Satoshi Kondo and colleagues surveyed 630 Japanese citizens about a proposed answer to doctor shortages: letting hospital paramedics take on more medical tasks. Their 2026 study measured the public's general trust in hospital paramedics and their acceptance of specific procedures, then repeated the questions after a short educational briefing about the paramedics' role.

Trust and acceptance started high and stayed high. The briefing nudged acceptance of paramedic procedures up slightly but did not move general trust, which the authors suspect already rests on confidence in ordinary ambulance paramedics. For policymakers, the results suggest the public is not the obstacle to task shifting; building credible certification and training systems is the work that remains.
plos-pone-0355297:
Pingping Xie, Jinfa Gu, and Jie Huang pool in 2026 trials of neuromuscular training for young male tennis players, covering power, speed, and skill drills. Earlier reviews mixed groups and lumped outcomes together, blurring what helps. Their search kept controlled trials of healthy male players and split outcomes such as stroke speed, serve accuracy, sprint, jump, and agility.

Training favoured stroke speed, short sprint, jump height, agility, and serve accuracy in pooled results, but not placement accuracy. Certainty was low or very low for every outcome. No single drill type is proven, the authors warn, and better trials with longer follow up are needed.
plos-pone-0355397:
Isaac Faustino and co-authors checked whether children in state protective custody face more forceful interventions in emergency departments. They studied thousands of behavioural health visits by children between 2021 and 2023. Their 2026 analysis compared children in protective custody, children with a new report filed, and children with no involvement.

Children in custody received sedating injections and physical restraints more often than the other groups. By three days into the visit window, about one in six had received an injection, well above the other groups. Adjusted models confirmed a higher risk rate for custody children. Faustino and colleagues argue the gap demands scrutiny of how departments care for the most vulnerable children in crisis.
plos-pone-0355497:
Mirinae Kim and Young-Hoon Park ask in 2026 whether bleeding inside the eye in advanced diabetic eye disease follows the seasons. They reviewed several thousand affected eyes seen at a Seoul hospital over three years and compared monthly bleeding rates with weather records. Pressure inside the eye before and at bleeding was also checked.

Bleeding peaked in late spring and early summer. Temperature, humidity, and rain did not explain the pattern in their models. Eye pressure at bleeding differed from pressure at the prior cold season visit, hinting that pressure shifts or seasonal blood sugar changes may play a part. More study is needed, the authors say.
plos-pone-0355597:
Baoguo Luo and co-authors built a machine learning shortcut for judging whether bridges can safely carry permitted overweight vehicles amid normal traffic. Such vehicles need official authorisation, and full engineering simulation of every crossing is far too slow. Their 2026 framework learns from a detailed grillage model of bridge behaviour under mixed traffic.

The model predicts how much the heavy vehicle amplifies load effects compared with ordinary traffic alone. Training data came from systematic runs of the high-fidelity simulation, which captures how loads spread across the deck. The learned surrogate then answers in a fraction of the time. Luo and colleagues aim the tool at permit offices facing rising volumes of exceptional loads.
plos-pone-0355697:
Tomoki Sakaguchi and three colleagues compare the spores of four fission yeast species under the microscope, in this 2026 study. Fission yeasts are workhorse organisms for cell biology, and the best-known species makes spores with a distinctive bumpy coat tied to toughness. Whether its relatives share that design was unknown. The team imaged spores from all four species with light and electron microscopy, then stress-tested them.

Surface structures differed sharply between species. The fibrous coat and the dense outer layer seen in the famous species were largely missing from the other three. Its spores also survived heat and alcohol best. The authors conclude that each fission yeast evolved its own spore architecture, possibly tuned to its habitat, a reminder that even close relatives solve the survival problem differently.
plos-pone-0355997:
Shinhyun Kim and colleagues ran a computer-based hunt for new drug candidates that mimic risperidone, a medicine that blocks dopamine D2 receptors, but stay out of the brain. Their 2026 study starts from a quirk of such drugs: raising the hormone prolactin outside the brain may protect nerve cells, while brain exposure causes sedation and movement side effects.

Starting from four hundred look-alike molecules, the team filtered for ones predicted not to cross into the brain, then docked the survivors against the receptor in simulation. Eight beat risperidone's docking score, four kept the key contacts inside the receptor, and one stayed most stable in motion simulations. The shortlist now awaits real lab testing, which the authors stress has not yet happened.
plos-pone-0356197:
Yan Zhao and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE grading how well hospitals across China's thirty-one provinces turned resources into care between 2019 and 2023. They combined a three-stage efficiency model that strips out outside influences, a dynamic index tracking change over time, and a spatial statistic that tests whether efficient provinces cluster together.

Average efficiency sat below the ideal frontier, leaving real room for improvement, though the trend rose over the five years. Stripping out those advantages lowered scores, showing that good conditions had propped some provinces up, and the regional ranking reshuffled: the center briefly passed the east, while the west trailed throughout. Technical progress, not better management alone, was the main brake on output growth. Efficient provinces clustered stably below the Yangtze River, while low-efficiency clusters mostly dissolved by 2023, suggesting catch-up. The map is offered as guidance for national hospital reform.
plos-pone-0356497:
Kinza Shahid and colleagues produced the largest protein catalogue yet for Fasciola gigantica, a liver fluke of buffalo and cattle that also infects people. They worked from adult worms taken from naturally infected buffaloes in Punjab, Pakistan. Their 2026 proteomics study separated the fluke's proteins. It verified them by antibody blotting and identified them by mass spectrometry. The focus was the proteins the parasite secretes into its host.

Nearly five thousand proteins were catalogued, including a large set of predicted secreted ones. The functional profile leaned heavily on enzymes that cut, dissolve, and oxidize. That is the toolkit of a parasite that burrows through tissue and feeds on its host. A further slice tied to immune manipulation. Each such protein is a candidate target for drugs or vaccines against a costly livestock disease.
plos-pone-0356597:
Eric Pelzl and four colleagues study a well-known Mandarin sound change inside real conversation, in this 2026 experiment. When two low tones follow each other, the first traditionally rises, becoming indistinguishable from a genuine rising tone, a puzzle called third tone sandhi. Ten pairs of native speakers played a phrase-matching game. One read a phrase aloud and the other picked it from a screen, under conditions that did or did not trigger the change.

The setup produced real confusion exactly where the sound change predicted it. Pairs coped mainly by keeping the first low tone lower toward its end, effectively avoiding the full change and preserving the contrast. The authors say even a tightly structured game can reveal how speakers steer around ambiguity, a first step toward understanding how this rule behaves in everyday talk.
plos-pone-0356697:
Xingyue Pu and Zhigang Zhong track whether China's cancer hospital beds are shared fairly, using fifteen years of national statistics in this 2026 study. Oncology beds grew steadily from 2008 to 2022, though growth slowed. The authors measured fairness two ways, against population and against land area, using standard inequality tools that also separate disparities within regions from those between them.

Judged by population, bed allocation was quite equal and improved over the period. Judged by geography, it was severely unequal throughout, with no improvement, meaning patients in sparse regions face long journeys regardless of headcounts. Most inequality in both views came from within regions rather than between them. The authors argue policy should now chase geographic accessibility and local balance, to ease the notorious difficulty cancer patients face getting admitted.
plos-pone-0356797:
Chaoqun He and Racidon P Bernarte surveyed six hundred Chinese livestream shoppers. Half were young digital natives, and half were older adults. The survey asked what makes them buy again from a live commerce host. Their 2026 study modeled three facets of service quality. They were the host's professionalism, the interactive experience, and after-sales support. Trust served as the middleman. Generation was the dial that turns each effect.

All three facets built trust, and trust fed intentions to return. But the generations weighted them differently. Older shoppers leaned hardest on professionalism and after-sales care. The young prized interactivity. The authors advise platforms to segment their playbook. They suggest certifying hosts for older audiences. For the young, they suggest investing in interactive features, even augmented reality try-ons.
plos-pone-0356997:
Kathleen O'Connor and coauthors published a 2026 genomics study in PLOS ONE on a quiet kind of variation in Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium behind many skin and hospital infections. Genes can spell the same protein with different codons, and bacteria prefer some spellings, affecting how much protein gets made. The team measured codon bias across thousands of genes in a reference strain and compared it with all public complete genomes of the species, sorted by disease, institution, and site.

Bias varied gene by gene and isolate by isolate. Ribosome machinery genes showed the strongest, most consistent bias everywhere, suggesting heavy pressure to keep them highly expressed. One hospital's genomes, from Nairobi, stood out as most different. In a well-known strain, higher bias scores did tend to mean more protein in culture. Silent spelling choices, they say, are a real layer of this pathogen's diversity that evolution studies have largely skipped.
plos-pone-0357497:
M. Arunadevi and colleagues published a 2026 engineering paper in PLOS ONE on a common manufacturing defect: layers splitting apart when glass-fiber composite panels are drilled. Delamination weakens the finished part, and it depends in tangled ways on drill shape, size, speed, and feed. The team ran a full grid of drilling trials on glass-fiber laminates, photographed the damage, and trained a neural network that also had the physics of cracking built into its learning rules.

The physics-informed network predicted the damage measure very accurately on held-out trials. Feed rate mattered most, followed by laminate thickness and drill diameter, while faster spindle speeds actually reduced damage by cutting more cleanly and pushing less. Interactions mattered too, especially between feed and speed. Adding the physics constraints made predictions sturdier and better at generalizing. The authors offer the model as a planning aid for shops that drill composite parts.
plos-pone-0357597:
Shuang An, Dan-ni Gu, He-jun Huang, Jun-qiang Luo, and Rong-rong Liu wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about tourism in Tianshui, China. It models tourist loyalty, the choice to return or recommend a place. Three forces are built into the model: how crowded the place feels, what social value visitors think the trip gives them, and how good they judge the service to be.

The method is structural equation modeling, which tests how several influences act on each other at once. Crowding can sour a trip even when service is good, and the model weighs that tension. Destination managers in Tianshui and other growing Chinese tourist cities can use the results to balance visitor numbers against experience.
plos-pone-0357797:
Veronika Frybortova and coauthors published a 2026 mouse study in PLOS ONE on whether a ketogenic diet changes how the body handles ozanimod, a drug used in multiple sclerosis. High-fat, very-low-carbohydrate diets are being explored alongside MS therapy, but diets can retune the liver enzymes clearing drugs. Female mice ate a normal or ketogenic diet for four weeks; the team then measured metabolism, gut microbes, liver enzymes, and the drug's path through the body.

The diet produced the expected ketosis, raised blood cholesterol, and reshaped gut microbial communities, while most other measures moved only modestly. Liver enzyme activity shifted both ways: one family sped up, another slowed, and a third trended down. Drug exposure in ketogenic mice ran somewhat higher, though the difference was not statistically firm. The signal is small, they say, but real enough that diet-drug interactions deserve attention as the therapy spreads.
plos-pone-0358597:
Yueyi Tan leads a team of six using machine learning to map how two kinds of shops compete for space in Shenzhen, China, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Convenience stores run light, cheap, and everywhere; supermarkets and malls are capital heavy and choosy. The team fed geospatial data and measures of how people perceive streets into a stack of interpretive models that can reveal bends and interactions, not just straight line effects.

The two formats followed distinct locational logics. Convenience stores spread widely and reacted strongly to nearby competition, to the proximity of everyday services, and to how a place feels to pedestrians. The big formats clustered where returns justify their cost. Untangling which urban features pull each format helps planners zone commercial districts deliberately, and helps chains pick sites with their eyes open about which game they are playing.
plos-pone-0358797:
Sarah Alexandra Marshall leads a team of six asking what a health program for low income Black men with chronic illness would need to succeed, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The group studied is underserved in the southern United States, and one proposal on the table uses a universal basic income to open access to care. Before any launch, the researchers interviewed thirty-one interest holders, including men from the target population, about conditions such an intervention must respect.

Five themes emerged. The men typically delay seeking care. Relationships are strained by incarceration and poverty. Prison health services and ordinary healthcare are not built to help them. Community level barriers pile up. Racism and poverty are intertwined and entrenched. The authors argue any fair intervention, income based or not, must work at individual, family, community, and institutional levels at once, or it will fail the very people it names.
plos-pone-0359197:
Kateřina Abrhámová, Alexandra Gredová, Karolína Navrátilová, Mohamed Boumaiza, and Petr Folk wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on yeast genetics. It studies the intronic RNA of RPL22 paralogs, copies of a ribosomal protein gene, and reports that this RNA acts as an allosteric switch, a molecule whose binding changes a protein's behavior.

Introns were long treated as waste cut out of genes, so finding a working switch among them changes how yeast gene control is pictured. Paralogs are near-duplicate genes, and cross-talk between them can fine-tune protein production. Molecular biologists studying gene regulation are the readers for this small RNA with an outsized job.
pmc-10654397:
Dorn and co-authors peer in a 2023 study at the tin inside toothpaste with a boosted magnetic resonance method. Tin fluoride fights germs and supplies fluoride, but only its lower oxidation state does the germ work, and no one could tell how much of each state sits in a tube.

A sensitivity boost called dynamic nuclear polarization made the faint tin signal readable. Reference powders tied each signal shape to an oxidation state. Three of four shop brands held at least eighty percent of the active state; one brand held far more of the spent state. Shelved tubes can now be audited for what their labels promise.
pmc-10654497:
Shun Gao and co-authors build a gene-based grouping of lung cancer patients tied to an iron-driven form of cell death, aiming to forecast outcomes and drug response. That death process, ferroptosis, interacts with a huge family of transporter proteins that move substances across cell membranes. Members of that family can feed or block the process.

Starting from gene activity data, the team clustered lung adenocarcinoma patients by transporter genes linked to ferroptosis. The resulting groups differed in survival outlook and in the immune makeup of their tumors. A model built on the grouping predicts prognosis and likely benefit from immunotherapy. Such sorting could steer treatment choices for the most common lung cancer.
pmc-10655397:
Made Rai Dwitya Wiradiputra and four co-authors compared two drug-proof bacterial strains gene by gene in a 2023 paper. The bacterium, Acinetobacter baumannii, haunts hospitals and resists many drugs, including carbapenems, a last-line class. The team examined two clinical strains from different lineages.

One strain carried more resistance genes than the other, matching how each behaved in drug tests. A mobile DNA element sat in front of a key resistance gene in a way known to switch it on strongly. Only one strain held a class A resistance enzyme, while the other leaned on different drug-blocking tools. The study shows how two strains of one species build resistance by different genetic routes.
pmc-10655997:
Nkechinyere Uche and co-authors ask what sways glaucoma patients to join gene studies in a 2023 paper. Genomic work needs willing subjects, and views in southeast Nigeria were unmapped. The team polled 228 glaucoma patients at two Enugu tertiary centers.

Nearly all said they would join a glaucoma genetic study. That share crashed when no results would come back to them, a drop the stats marked as sharp. No one would give eye tissue, and almost none would allow samples after death. Wanting to learn more about glaucoma was the top lure. Feedback of results is the hinge for trust.
pmc-10656797:
Tamer Mohamed Elsherbiny reports a diagnostic trap in this two thousand twenty-three case report. A premenopausal woman had years of osteoporosis with normal blood calcium and low vitamin D. She was first diagnosed with secondary hyperparathyroidism, where the parathyroid glands overwork in response to vitamin D deficiency. That diagnosis fit the standard picture. The author treated her vitamin D deficiency with parenteral loading doses to restore normal levels.

Once vitamin D normalized, the picture flipped: persistent mild to moderate high calcium appeared, with parathyroid hormone still elevated, the signature of primary hyperparathyroidism. She also had excess calcium in her urine and calcium deposits in her kidneys. Imaging found a left upper parathyroid adenoma, and surgery restored normal calcium for years of follow-up. The lesson is that vitamin D deficiency can mask the high calcium of primary disease, delaying diagnosis; such patients deserve re-evaluation after repletion.
pmc-10656897:
Mohamed Mostafa Kotb and two co-authors free wrist nerves with a wide-awake, no-band cut that uses full-strength bleed-stop shots. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. Two hundred folks, most women and half with both wrists hit, had three hundred eight day-case cuts from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-one by one hand. The shot mix held a bleed-stop dose two and a half times the first-form mix.

Mean cut time was near ten minutes. No one need more numb shots, full sleep, or a night stay. Most were back to plain day acts in near five weeks. No finger blood harms hit, and one wound ill cleared with plain care.
pmc-10657597:
Zhao and co-authors studied a family of immune genes in acute myeloid leukemia, in a paper published in 2023. The genes switch on when the body senses viral-style signals, and they play roles in several cancers. Their value in this blood cancer was unclear. The team pulled gene and clinical data for 173 patients from a public cancer atlas. They used several public analysis tools to map the genes' levels, their links to survival, and their partners inside the cell.

All four family members ran higher in leukemia samples than in healthy ones. Their levels separated patients from controls sharply. Levels also tracked with how long patients lived, which makes the genes candidate warning markers. Lab-style analysis pointed to the roles these genes play in the cancer's growth. The authors propose the family as both a diagnostic aid and a lead for treatment research.
pmc-10669097:
Su-Jeong Lee and co-authors feed olive flounder two bacteria taken from flounder guts, and the fish grow better on them. Their 2023 feeding trial isolates two host-associated strains, characterizes them as candidate probiotics, and mixes them into feed for eight weeks. Control fish ate the same diet without the supplement.

The supplemented fish grew faster and used feed more efficiently. Of four immune measures, one enzyme activity rose; blood chemistry stayed unchanged. Gut microbial diversity by some measures held steady while its composition shifted, with community richness in one index enriched. The authors argue host-derived probiotics, evolved for this exact gut, may outperform generic strains borrowed from other species. Korean flounder farming is a serious industry, and growth margins of this kind compound across a production cycle. The study supplies strain-level evidence rather than the usual probiotic hand-waving.
pmc-10670697:
Emily F Santos, Ramona T Daltro, and a large team of co-authors checked whether lab made Chagas disease test antigens misfire on a look alike parasite. Their 2023 study addresses a diagnostic headache: the Chagas parasite shares features with kin, so tests can cross react and mislead. Four engineered antigens were built to sharpen accuracy.

The antigens stayed clean against leishmaniasis in earlier work. This study tested them on samples from seven patients carrying Crithidia sp. LVH-60A, a parasite tied to leishmaniasis like illness in Brazil, plus three patients with Leishmania infantum. Cross reaction readings show whether the antigens hold their specificity against close cousins. Clean results would strengthen confidence in the new Chagas tests where several of these parasites circulate together.
pmc-10671397:
Sivagangi Reddy Nagella and co-authors built tiny gel carriers, made from a shrimp-shell material called chitosan, to release a numbing drug slowly after surgery. Steady local release can ease pain for longer and cut the need for repeated doses. The carriers blend chitosan with plastic-like partners in several recipes.

The team measured how much drug each recipe could hold, with loading ranging widely across versions. They checked the carriers with heat, light, and microscope methods, and used computer models to see how the drug binds inside. Release tests at body-like acidity showed slow, steady output. Such gels could one day be placed in a wound to keep pain down for days.
pmc-10672197:
Mauro Riccardi and co-authors review a blood marker called sST2 in heart failure care in this 2023 paper. When heart muscle is hurt or strained, the marker is released. Too much of it may block a helpful signal and add to scarring and shape changes in the heart. The team asks what this marker adds beyond the standard markers now in use.

Unlike those standard markers, sST2 levels shift little with age, sex, weight, or kidney health. Its power to predict outcomes is well shown. Still, guides in Europe and America back only the standard markers. The authors argue that using both taps two distinct body systems and may guide care better.
pmc-10674497:
Alexander Sukhorukov opens a special issue on plant invasion ecology with an overview of the field's main fronts. Naturalized and invasive plants have spread fast across the world in recent decades. Invaders can swamp meadows, steppes, and forests, forming single-species stands that rank among the top threats to native wildlife.

In his 2023 editorial, the collected work sorts into four strands. One weighs the genetic and body traits that make a species invasive. A second builds methods, often across fields, for studying invasions. A third tracks how natives and newcomers interact and how community diversity shifts. A fourth follows garden and farm plants that escape into the wild. Prediction of spread, he notes, stays hard.
pmc-10674597:
Jiahui Hua leads a team that compares silk gels made four ways. Their study from twenty twenty-three deals with silk fibroin hydrogels. Silk gels draw much use in medical materials work.

Gels were made by sound, by chem links, by light, and by enzymes. Light made gels were the strongest under squeeze in tests. Chem and enzyme gels were the toughest of the set. Sound made gels were brittle due to more stiff crystals. All gels let vein cells grow in lab tests. Gels sans chem agents kept cells most alive.
pmc-10688197:
Umar Nishan and co-authors wrote a 2023 paper on a simple sensor for vitamin C in blood. Vitamin C levels matter for many body processes, and abnormal levels signal illness. The team built the sensor from silver nanoparticles made with the help of paracetamol, the common pain drug, then coated them with an ionic liquid.

Standard tools confirmed the particles' size and makeup. The coated particles change color in the presence of vitamin C, letting a simple reading stand in for a lab assay. The team tuned the recipe, from the color dye dose upward, for the sharpest response. Cheap color tests like this suit clinics without advanced instruments.
pmc-10689697:
Lixuan Huang and co-authors compare two ways to place dental implants in 2023. Placing an implant at the planned spot is key to a good fit and bite. One method uses a positional guide, while the other relies on the free hand of the dentist. The team ran a forward looking clinical study with patients who had lost a single tooth.

Dozens of implants were placed by each method in turn. The team measured the gap between planned and actual spots in four ways. Guided implants landed closer to plan on every measure. The authors call the guide a practical, low cost tool for implant surgery.
pmc-10691697:
Han Chen and co-authors found two small molecules that jam a herpesvirus's exit door from the cell nucleus, in a 2023 study. Human cytomegalovirus troubles patients with weak immunity, and fresh drugs are scarce. Like its cousins, the virus escapes the nucleus through a two-part complex whose parts must clasp. The team built a fluorescence test for the clasp and screened over two hundred thousand compound wells.

Two hits, GK1 and GK2, blocked the clasp, cut virus growth more than they harmed cells, and ignored a related herpesvirus. A single amino acid change in one part of the complex made the virus resistant, proving the target. Structure work suggests the drug wedges into a pocket and blocks the partner's grip. The authors call the pair a proof of concept and a seed for new antivirals.
pmc-10693597:
Qiang Shan and co-authors traced why novelty seeking fades with age, in a 2023 mouse study. Curiosity drives animals to explore and learn, and it supports human well-being. Its decline with age even tracks later cognitive decline. The brain change behind that fade was unknown.

Aged mice sought both social and object novelty less than young mice. The team then measured dopamine neurons in two midbrain areas. Those cells fired less often in old animals. Dopamine fuels drive and reward, so quieter cells fit weaker seeking. The finding names a target for keeping curiosity alive in old age. It may also inform care for aging brain disease.
pmc-10693697:
Telila Mesfin and co-authors report a rare body layout case from 2023 in a fifteen-year-old boy in Ethiopia. His heart sat in the left chest as usual, but his liver and spleen were swapped side to side. This pattern is called situs inversus with levocardia. He came to a referral hospital with belly pain that had lasted four months.

Scans confirmed the swapped organs with the heart's tip on the left. He had been admitted three times before for the same pain. Treatment with antibiotics sent him home improved. The authors stress that imaging confirms what a physical exam may hint at. The pattern often pairs with heart defects, which darken the outlook.
pmc-10694897:
Six authors present a study from two thousand twenty-three on early warning signs of pancreatic cancer. The cancer kills many of its patients, in part because it is hard to spot early. The team looked for markers in blood that can be checked without invasive tests.

They drew on a large Korean health study, matching one hundred twenty-eight people who later got the cancer with two hundred fifty-six who did not. Blood samples taken at the start were scanned for small molecules. A learning method picked out eleven that separated the groups. Gene scans then found DNA variants tied to those molecules, adding clues about how risk builds.
pmc-10695497:
Long Huang and co-authors review what computation can reveal about a classic herbal pair used against hepatitis, in a paper published in 2023. The pair joins Radix Bupleuri with Radix Paeoniae Alba, two roots long combined in Chinese medicine. Their chemistry is complex, so the review uses network pharmacology and molecular docking to map ingredients onto disease targets.

Pooling ingredient data and hepatitis genes from several databases yielded 176 overlapping genes, narrowed to fourteen core targets. The main active compounds included quercetin, kaempferol, isorhamnetin, and beta-sitosterol, and docking checks confirmed they fit the hub targets in shape and energy. Thousands of biological processes and 174 pathways were explored. The pair's effect likely runs through several of these routes at once.
pmc-10696397:
Monica Danilevicz and co-authors adapt, in a 2023 study, a language model built for DNA to find long non-coding RNAs in plant genomes. These long RNA strands do not make proteins but steer gene activity, and spotting them from raw genome sequence would free researchers from needing expression data first.

The model, based on DNABERT, was trained on seven model and crop species, from maize to rice. Accuracy peaked at about eighty-three percent in maize and fell near fifty-eight percent in one cabbage relative, a spread the authors tie to genome assembly quality. The model also explains its calls, showing which sequence parts drove each decision, which builds trust in its picks.
pmc-10696697:
Thomas Keggin and co-authors simulated how diversity at the population level becomes diversity at the species level in reef fish, in this 2023 study. Diversity exists at many levels, from genes to communities, but patterns across levels often disagree. Their spatial model grows populations and lets them split into species.

Links between population and species diversity were real but shifted with the measure and map scale used. The key driver was the divergence threshold at which a population splits. The authors propose that splitting breaks smooth continuity across levels. They frame the mechanism as universal, rooted in the genetic clash that isolates groups.
pmc-10696797:
Chayanis Kositamongkol and a large team weigh the costs and savings of letting Thai women collect their own samples for cervical cancer screening, in a study from 2023. Cervical cancer is the third most common cancer in Thai women, yet screening rates lag. Self-collection for HPV DNA testing could clear barriers like clinic access and embarrassment.

The team modeled lifetime costs and health gains for women aged 25 to 65 under four policies, from no screening to the status quo Pap-style testing. Every screening policy saved money versus none. Adding self-collection was compared against clinician-collected testing for both cost per healthy year and the ten-year budget hit for payers. Sensitivity checks probed how firm the numbers were.
pmc-10697997:
Hyowon Jang and nine co-authors build a one step test for antibiotic resistant bacteria that skips the usual lab prep, in a 2023 paper. The target is a Klebsiella strain that defeats carbapenem antibiotics. Current tests need DNA extraction and copying steps that slow diagnosis.

Their method, ANCA, uses an Argonaute protein in a self feeding reaction circuit. It detects the germ's DNA at constant temperature, with no amplification. The test found the target in urine and blood samples directly. It also worked on surface swabs paired with a nanostructured chip. In patient rectal swabs it scored perfect sensitivity and specificity. Faster answers could curb hospital spread.
pmc-10698697:
Ashley Allen and co-authors published this case report in 2023. It presents a seventy-one-year-old Black woman who came to an emergency department with a widespread itchy rash. The rash had not responded to an over-the-counter allergy drug. Three weeks earlier she had been diagnosed with gout and started three medicines for it, including allopurinol. Her history included diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol.

Examination found a flat, bumpy rash that did not blanch, covering her whole body including palms and soles, with slight peeling. Blood tests showed raised eosinophils, a type of white cell linked to drug reactions. Inflammatory markers were high, liver enzymes were raised, and her old kidney disease had worsened. The report documents the presentation and lab picture. Cases like this matter because rashes and drug reactions can look different, and be missed more easily, on brown skin.
pmc-10698897:
Wei Wang and co-authors fed a fungus culture to weaning piglets to test its effect on growth and gut life, in a 2023 study. The fungus is already used in dairy feed to spur growth and curb disease. Its effect on the gut microbes of young pigs was little known. Sixty piglets got the culture in their feed for twenty days, and sixty matched piglets ate the plain diet.

Fed piglets gained weight faster and used feed better than controls. Blood levels of growth hormones and immune proteins all ran higher in the fed group. Gut microbe mixes shifted in clear ways: several groups fell, while others, including a known anti-swelling species, rose. That species helps guard the gut wall and makes a useful acid. The authors conclude the culture can lift piglet health at weaning, a fragile stage in pig farming.
pmc-10700497:
Rui-Meng Yang and a large team study how the thyroid gland builds its working units, in this 2023 paper. The gland is made of tiny balls called follicles, and faults in their making cause thyroid dysgenesis, a cause of low thyroid function from birth. How thyroid cells move out and form new follicles was not well understood.

Using single-cell and spatial gene maps in mice, the team found a group of thyroid cells at the gland's center with an active NF-κB switch and a partly loose, mobile character. Traced in zebrafish, these cells pushed out and seeded new follicles. Blocking the switch stalled their movement and mimicked the disease. Immune cells of the myeloid type helped by touching the cells and releasing a signal, TNF-α. Fish lacking myeloid cells showed the same movement fault.
pmc-10700597:
Moritz Sexauer and co-authors identify a signal that lets a plant's shoot direct how its roots branch. Their 2023 paper starts from a puzzle: roots adjust their growth to soil nitrogen, but the shoot seems to give the orders. The team shows that a tiny RNA called miR2111 travels from shoot to root. There it acts on a target gene known as TML, which reins in new root branches.

The same pair already had a known role in hosting nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the legume Lotus japonicus. Strikingly, the system also works in Arabidopsis, a plant with no such partnerships. That conservation marks the pair as a core, shared tool for shoot control of root shape across dicots.
pmc-10702097:
Sharma and a large team ask in twenty twenty-three whether the male hormone testosterone explains the link between poor sleep and frailty in older men. Past studies tied disturbed sleep to frailty, but the mechanism was unknown. Data came from a European study of men aged forty to seventy-nine across eight centres, with sleep surveys, hormone measures, and a broad frailty index.

Men with the worst sleep quality had much higher frailty than the best sleepers. Both short and long sleep also linked to higher frailty. Hormone levels did fall as sleep quality worsened. Yet adjusting for testosterone left the sleep-frailty link unchanged in strength. The authors conclude the link runs through other paths, not this hormone.
pmc-10702397:
Jessica Jakubowicz and co-authors report a rare liver defect in a very preterm baby whose heart was failing from the strain, in a 2023 case report. The defect, a tangle joining arteries and veins in the liver, shunts blood so fast that the heart overworks. Such cases are usually described in full-term babies, and many die.

This infant, born at 28 weeks, was diagnosed before birth, which let the team plan ahead. On his third day of life, doctors threaded a catheter in and partly blocked the tangle. Despite that early success and full medical support, the baby did not survive. The authors review how treatment choices hinge on the baby's size, the tangle's size, and symptom severity.
pmc-10703697:
A mild lymphoma can turn aggressive, and the change is written in the genome, including in stretches that code for nothing. The authors of a 2023 study sequence paired tumors from patients whose follicular lymphoma transformed into a fast-growing form. Many new changes cluster at regulatory DNA inside super-enhancer regions. One changed region controls a pair of genes, PAX5 and ZCCHC7. The second gene helps run a complex that trims ribosomal RNA.

During transformation the gene gains copies, swaps chromosomes, and falls under a hijacked enhancer, so its output rises. That shift garbles ribosomal RNA processing and rewires protein making in the cancer cell. The authors show how a noncoding change can drive malignant growth.
pmc-10703797:
Andres Calcabrini and co-authors report a 2023 outdoor test of a solar panel that can rewire itself. Partial shade drags down a whole panel when its cells are fixed in place. Their full size prototype has six blocks that can switch links to work around shade.

Over four months outside, the flexible panel made about a tenth more energy than a fixed panel under patchy shade. Under even light it made slightly less, since the switching gear wastes a bit of power. The team suggests a tweak to the switching rules. It would narrow the output range, easing converter design, at a small cost in shade tolerance.
pmc-10704697:
Chen, Wu, Zhou, Zhang, and Liu present a neural network that predicts whether a protein will dissolve, a key question in drug research and production, in a 2023 paper. Their model, HybridGCN, blends features from a large protein language model with classical physical properties of the protein, arranged as a graph.

A new fusion module weighs each feature's importance adaptively rather than treating them alike. The authors found that evolutionary features in particular complement what the deep model extracts. Tests and ablations show the hybrid reaches state-of-the-art accuracy on two public benchmarks, the eSOL and yeast datasets.
pmc-10706097:
Nataša Mlinar Reljić and co-authors present a 2023 review of online learning for nursing and midwifery students during the COVID-19 pandemic. Hands-on clinical training is the heart of these degrees, so moving classes online under lockdown posed a real problem. The team searched major health databases and judged the studies they found.

Thirteen studies made the final cut, and their findings grouped into benefits, challenges, and recommendations. Students valued flexible study and saved travel, and online teaching kept programs running when wards were closed. Problems included weak internet, poor equipment, cost, and clashes with work and family duties. The authors conclude e-learning is a workable stand-in during a crisis, provided schools fix access gaps and support clinical skills practice.
pmc-10707297:
Nan Liu and eight co-authors trace a pregnancy failure pathway that runs from placental cell recycling to the immune cells of the womb lining. Natural killer cells in the decidua must be educated into tolerance by trophoblasts, with the receptor CXCR4 marking the tolerant subset. Women with recurrent miscarriage have too few of those marked cells in early pregnancy.

Culturing the immune cells with trophoblast secretions raised their CXCR4 levels. Blocking trophoblast autophagy, the cells' internal recycling, broke that education and shifted the killer cells toward a harmful phenotype. The signal ran through an IGF2 and p53 route. Tissue from forty-two healthy pregnancies and twenty miscarriage patients grounded the experiments. The work nominates trophoblast autophagy as a guardian of pregnancy.
pmc-10707997:
Michal Fila and co-authors weigh the ketogenic diet as a way to prevent migraines in older adults. The diet is very low in carbohydrates and high in fat. It swaps glucose for ketone bodies as the brain's fuel. Migraines peak in midlife and grow rarer with age. Care in old age is tricky, since other illnesses and many drugs crowd in.

Some reports praise the diet for migraine relief. Others link high ketone levels to worse heart outcomes in older adults. Mouse work even hints at shorter life spans. The authors call the evidence thin and uneven. They want proper clinical trials before anyone recommends this diet to elderly migraine patients.
pmc-10708397:
Maria Bercea and six co-authors build hybrid hydrogels that mix a synthetic polymer with a natural protein, aiming at gels whose stiffness can be tuned on demand. The polymer is poly(vinyl alcohol), and the protein is bovine serum albumin. Such soft, water-rich materials are wanted for tissue engineering, printing bioinks, and wound dressings.

The team formed a chemical network first, using genipin and glutathione to link the mix in water. Freezing and thawing cycles then built a second, physical network in the polymer, while the protein formed its own bridges. The result is a tough, porous gel with pores of twenty to fifty micrometers. Its strength and springiness shift with the recipe and the linking steps, and it can heal itself after damage. The authors also studied how the gels take up water vapor, swell, and stick to surfaces.
pmc-10708597:
Eva Villegas and co-authors link what viewers look at in a game trailer to what they feel, in a 2023 study. Trailers sell games, yet makers rarely know which shots land. The team ran a three-step test with likely players of indie games. First came a read of how the group sees indie titles, then eye tracking during the trailer, then interviews and feeling questionnaires.

The eye data gave gaze trails, heat maps, and fix points, the spots where eyes rest. Some trailer zones drew no looks at all, a blind area that can warp what viewers expect. Fix points tied to sharp, distinct feelings, and the gaze trails traced the story each viewer built. Talk after viewing filled in the why. The authors offer the mixed method as a workbench: makers can spot strong and weak beats in a trailer and recut toward the feelings they want.
pmc-10709597:
Hiroki Koizumi, Yuichi Yamasaki, and Hideto Yanagihara report an unusual electrical effect in a magnetic oxide film in a 2023 paper. In the Hall effect, a current bends sideways under a magnetic influence. Known forms spread evenly across the plane, but this team found a version whose strength depends on which way the current runs within the plane.

The film is a spinel oxide grown as a thin layer. Its sideways response carried a four-fold pattern tied to current direction, added to the usual uniform part. Cooling the film in a magnetic field could even flip the pattern's sign. The authors trace the effect to an electron nematic state, where electrons favor one direction, born from a stretched magnetic order in the material.
pmc-10709897:
Alastair J Ludington and co-authors read sea snake genomes in a 2023 study. Sea snakes moved fully from land to sea within about the last fifteen million years. Despite that dramatic shift, they were a gap in gene level studies of how land animals adapt to the ocean.

Four new genomes were built for this work, three of them mapped at full chromosome scale. Comparisons with close land kin followed. Family trees hint that the main sea snake group split into species almost at once. Maps of gene order show internal shuffles that future work can target. A strict screen then hunted genes tied to life at sea.
pmc-10710297:
Ho and co-authors probe how pelvic surgery and ovarian hormones shape vaginal and bladder tissue. Surgery for prolapse often fails over time and harms quality of life. The rat model mimed surgical injury to the vagina and bladder. Four groups split by surgery and ovary removal. Tissue was checked ten weeks after the operation.

Ovary removal cut vaginal wall squeeze strength in both ovary groups. Bladder dome and base showed split squeeze patterns. Gene and protein tests tracked collagen and elastin shifts. Stains showed matching tissue changes under the microscope. The work suggests hormone loss, not surgery alone, drives much of the lasting weakness.
pmc-10710397:
Yongxiang Liao and co-authors uncover a new job for a plant enzyme best known for softening cell walls. The enzyme, a polygalacturonase named HCC1, turns out to steer the loss of chlorophyll, the green pigment whose breakdown marks leaf aging and fruit ripening. A mutant plant lacking the enzyme stayed greener but grew and yielded less.

In the mutant, enzyme activity, ethylene levels, and a wall-derived sugar acid all ran low, and its cell walls grew thicker. Adding back ethylene or the sugar acid raised ethylene and switched the gene on, and normal green loss resumed. Tests with knocked-out and restored lines confirmed the gene's role. The authors conclude that this wall enzyme feeds into the ethylene pathway, linking wall breakdown to the timing of chlorophyll loss in the plant.
pmc-10710797:
Monika Oliver and Christopher Patriquin reviewed care for a rare blood disease in 2023, setting out what works now and what is still missing. In this disease, the body's own defense system destroys red blood cells, causing anemia, blood clots, and organ strain. With basic care alone, about a third of patients die.

New drugs that block parts of the defense system have changed the outlook, raising blood counts and cutting clots and transfusions. Longer-acting and oral options now exist, and some help patients who stay anemic on older drugs. Gaps remain, such as care in pregnancy and guarding against infection. The authors back a shared world registry to track how the new drugs perform over time.
pmc-10710997:
Keiko Azuma and six co-authors track long-term sight outcomes across a family of retinal diseases sharing a thickened choroid. Their retrospective study was published in twenty twenty-three. The group ranges from quiet pigment changes to fluid leaks and new vessel growth.

Charts from a Tokyo hospital covered seven hundred and forty-one eyes of six hundred and thirty-eight patients seen from twenty eight to twenty twenty-one. Vision loss was tracked at several cut-offs over time. Eyes with central serous disease or vessel growth fared significantly worse than the milder types. The team then hunted factors tied to prognosis within the serous group. The data help doctors counsel patients on likely sight paths.
pmc-10711297:
Yan Zhang and co-authors measure the effect of a new tuberculosis control model on case rates in Xinjiang. Their 2023 study uses registered lung TB data from 14 prefectures from 2012 to 2021. Southern prefectures carried the highest rates across the span.

Overall rates fell over the decade, but the path bent sharply at the policy start. Rates rose through 2018, then plunged at near thirty percent a year. Time series models show a one-month jump right after rollout, likely from better case finding. The long-run trend then falls month by month. High-burden areas show the steepest monthly drops, with mid and low areas falling more gently. The split supports the model effect beyond detection alone.
pmc-10711497:
Camilo Brandao-de-Resende and a large team build a machine learning system to sort patients at a London eye emergency department, in a study from 2023. Many eye emergency visits are not urgent, clogging care for true emergencies. An automated triage suggestion could route people better.

The system trained on over eleven thousand past visits, learning to advise see immediately, within a week, or electively. In later visits it caught about ninety-five percent of emergencies, with better specificity than triage nurses on the same data. A Brazilian hospital test checked transfer abroad, and bias checks probed fairness. The authors aim to cut needless emergency attendances.
pmc-10712097:
Nai-Chung Nelson Chang and a large team track gene tests and blood counts in US veterans new on thiopurine drugs. Their past-look study appeared in twenty twenty-three. Such tests can head off drug harms. More than twenty thousand veterans who first took one of three such drugs from twenty ten to twenty twenty-one were read through VA health files.

Gene test shares rose from three in ten to near half by late twenty fourteen. Past a flag harm year, tests rose a bit then flat and a touch low. Most new users still got no test at all. The team call the stance one of fix past harm, not guard.
pmc-10712197:
Chao Wang and co-authors test a two-part cancer treatment in mice in this 2023 study. The target is triple-negative breast cancer, a form that lacks the usual drug targets. The team heated tumors gently with light-activated carbon particles, then added a drug that blocks PD-L1, a brake that tumors place on immune attack.

Gentle heating alone helped little, but it raised PD-L1 levels on both tumor cells and immune cells called macrophages. Adding the blocker then worked far better. The heat pushed macrophages toward an attack state, and the blocker freed them to act. When macrophages were removed, the combined treatment lost most of its effect. The authors call the pairing a way to turn tumor helpers against the tumor.
pmc-10713397:
Ping Hu and co-authors published a 2023 study on two tiny RNA molecules that may drive prostate cancer. MicroRNAs are short regulators that tune gene activity; when they misfire, cancers can grow and spread. Using data from 485 prostate cancer patients in a public atlas, the team screened microRNAs tied to survival. Two stood out: hsa-mir-503 and hsa-mir-1247.

Databases predicted which genes the pair controls. Then came lab validation. In a prostate cancer cell line, the researchers knocked the two molecules down and watched the cells. Migration and invasion, the moves that make cancer dangerous, were measured, as was programmed cell death. The knockdowns changed those behaviors, backing the statistical link. The authors propose the pair as candidate markers for prognosis and possible drug targets. The work follows a common arc, from atlas mining to bench proof, but the validation step is what lifts it above pure computation.
pmc-10714197:
Ravipas Aphikulvanich, Natapol Pornputtapong, and Duangdao Wichadakul adapt a molecule-making AI to new protein targets with no extra data. Their twenty twenty-three paper tackles a hard drug discovery problem. Some targets have too little data to train a model from scratch.

Their framework, Mol-Zero-GAN, tunes a trained generator by reshaping its weights with singular value math. A smart search method, Bayesian optimization, finds the best settings. The aim is drug-like molecules that are easy to make and bind well to the target. Readers see a zero-shot path to candidates for targets that data-poor fields often skip.
pmc-10714497:
Grzegorz Łabuz and four co-authors test how color fringing in the eye affects vision after cataract surgery. New lens designs try to fix this fringing, called chromatic aberration, but hard proof of benefit or harm is scarce. Their 2023 study worked with 37 patients who had received standard replacement lenses.

Each patient was tested in three states: natural vision, added fringing, and corrected fringing, using trial lenses with no power. Correcting the fringing sharpened contrast at all test sizes. Yet it also made vision fall off more sharply when focus shifted. Adding fringing blurred sharpness at best focus. The trade-offs matter for how future replacement lenses should be designed.
pmc-10716397:
Amina BiBi and co-authors test soil bacteria from Qatar for farm use in a 2023 study. Certain root-zone bacteria help plants grow and fight disease. The team gathered 55 isolates from the roots of ten local plant species. They screened them against two fungal crop pathogens in lab dishes.

Top isolates blocked fungal growth by about half in dish tests. Greenhouse trials then checked growth gains in tomato plants. One Bacillus strain gave the strongest boost. Two other strains helped seedlings beat disease and gain mass above and below ground. The work points to local strains as green aids for crop care in harsh soils.
pmc-10716997:
Molly Johnson and Karla Lawson survey caregivers of toddlers about water safety in a 2023 study. Drowning is the leading cause of death in this age group, and watchful, informed adults are the main defense.

Six hundred fifty caregivers answered an online survey on safety knowledge, supervision habits, and their child's skills. The average score was six correct out of ten knowledge questions. Knowledge tracked with education, CPR training, and the adult's own swimming ability. Toddlers could do about half of six standard water skills, and most had taken lessons. Worryingly, a third of caregivers thought lessons meant a child needed less watching. The authors call that belief a target for education.
pmc-10717397:
Yuan and co-authors follow three intertwined burdens of old age — frailty, failing cognition, and depression — as they move together over eight years in China. Most studies track one condition at a time. Using four waves of a national aging survey covering more than 6,100 older adults, the team modeled the three as trajectories. Four life paths emerged, from a robust group whose bodies held up while cognition slipped, to a group where all three worsened together.

That hardest path claimed 14 percent of the sample. It was tied to not working, no social activity, poor childhood finances, and poor adult health. Other paths carried their own signatures: childhood ill-health for one, low education and rural registration for another. The authors argue the three conditions should be screened and supported together, not in separate clinics. For China's aging society, the trajectory map shows where combined help would land earliest.
pmc-10717497:
Older people lose muscle and strength with age, which raises their risk of falling, and regular exercise is the main way to fight back. Karly Chan and co-authors lay out the plan for a trial that asks whether exercise classes delivered over the internet work as well as the same classes held in person. The trial will recruit older adults in Hong Kong who may have early muscle loss or a fall risk.

Participants from ten community centers will be split at random into an online group and a face-to-face group, both training three days a week for three months. Strength, physical function, attendance, mood, and social well-being will be measured over a full year, and some participants will join focus groups about the experience. The trial is already registered, and its results should guide how exercise can reach frail older people at home.
pmc-10717797:
Jiamei Wang, Zizhong Shi, and Xiangdong Hu study how safe pig farms in China are from animal disease, a steady threat to livestock farming. They surveyed farms in seven provinces, built a scoring system for farm safety steps, and used a rank sum ratio method to grade each farm. They then looked for the farm and farmer traits that track with higher scores.

More spending on safety steps went with higher scores. Male farmers, more schooling, and taking part in skills training each raised scores, and farms that joined cooperatives scored higher. Scores first fell and then rose as farm size grew, and more household members working on the farm also helped. The authors say raising farmer skills and investing more people, gear, and money in safety steps can lift farm safety and prevent animal disease.
pmc-10717897:
Morin and co-authors study what happens when patients themselves train nurses in Quebec primary care clinics on engaging patients better. A provincial guide had set out best nursing practice. A train-the-trainer project carried that guide into clinics.

Patients joined the teaching team as full trainers. They built lessons around the lived patient experience. Nurses' engagement habits were the target of change. Interviews and observation grounded the qualitative study. Practice varied widely between clinics before the project. The unusual format put patient voices at the front. Findings show how that voice shifts nurse attitudes. The model may travel to other care settings and small towns.
pmc-10718297:
Chemicals used to soften plastics turn up in nearly every body, and they can scramble hormone signals, which raises a sharp question for women hoping to conceive. Carrie Nobles and co-authors study that window before pregnancy in a 2023 paper. They draw on a trial that followed over a thousand women trying for a baby, with urine tests at the start.

Higher levels of three plastic-linked breakdown products went with lower odds of conceiving in each cycle. No steady link with pregnancy loss appeared. Blood markers told a matching story: more inflammation and cell stress, shifts in key hormones across the cycle. The authors name the months before conception as a sensitive window where cutting exposure may protect fertility.
pmc-10719197: Gian Andrea Lucidi and co-authors describe, in 2023, a surgical technique for rebuilding the posterior cruciate ligament in the knee. The operation is demanding because both attachment footprints must be found precisely. Many surgeons add one inner-side portal to guide the shinbone tunnel. Adding a second such portal as a working channel, the authors argue, makes footprint identification, stump clearing, and graft passage noticeably more straightforward.
pmc-10719297:
Erratic sleep, not just short sleep, tracks with poor health, and Elexis Price and co-authors mapped its spread across United States ages, in work from twenty twenty-three. Near ten thousand people aged six and up wore motion trackers for most of a week in a national survey. Swings in length, midpoint, weekend catch-up, and weekday-weekend shift were tallied.

Roughly half the group caught up an hour or more on weekends, and two in five swung an hour in length night to night. Youth and young adults swung most. Black participants swung most on every mark. The maps give sleep advice a firmer, fairer base.
pmc-10719397:
Zhenfang Zhang and Huan Liang model how to coordinate recycling of electric vehicle batteries when partners care about fairness and social duty, in a 2023 paper. Used power batteries need closed-loop handling. The chain pairs a manufacturer, a retailer, and a third-party collector. Spent batteries also serve second-life uses before final recycling. The authors build a game model of the chain. They vary social responsibility effort and fairness concern.

Fairness worry hurt the whole chain. It raised prices and lowered collection rates. Social responsibility effort helped the market grow. It also softened the collectors' sense of unfairness. A cost-sharing contract fixed the balance best. It spread benefits and lifted the recycling rate. Number tests confirmed the model's claims. The paper speaks to managers and policymakers in the battery trade. It shows contract design can align profit with green goals.
pmc-10720097:
Zhibao Ding, Jingai Zhu, Ye Ding, and Chun Zhu compared the other illnesses that accompany congenital heart disease in children and adults in a 2023 study. Drawing on two large intensive care databases, they counted how common extra conditions were in each age group. A pattern mining method then mapped which conditions travel together. Heart defects were far more often recorded in children than in adults in these data.

Children with heart defects almost always had at least one other condition, most often problems tied to the period around birth. Adults showed a lower but still high rate, led by circulation, hormone, and breathing diseases. The mixes differed sharply by age. The authors say care planning for heart defect patients should expect different companion illnesses in childhood and in adult life.
pmc-10720797:
Studier-Fischer and co-authors published a 2023 animal study on imaging blood flow in the small intestine during surgery. Poor blood flow in the gut can cause severe harm, yet surgeons lack a standard, objective way to measure it. The team worked with 54 pigs and compared four ways of judging flow. The four were a hyperspectral camera, the same camera aided by a dye called ICG, the surgeon's own eyes, and standard ICG imaging alone.

Each method suggested a different line where healthy gut should be cut from starved gut. Tissue checks six hours later showed early death changes in areas that standard ICG imaging had judged safe. The dye-aided camera marked the sharpest and most accurate border. The authors conclude that the combined method spots weak flow better than the other options tested.
pmc-10721997:
Lijun Song and co-authors study how brain wiring and brain activity drift apart in advanced kidney disease. Their 2023 study scanned forty patients with stage five disease who were not on dialysis, plus forty-seven healthy controls. Thinking decline is common and severe in this group, but its network basis is unclear.

Both structural and functional networks in patients showed weaker small-world organization and lower efficiency than in controls. The coupling between the two network types was also stronger in patients. Several network measures tracked memory test scores in the expected directions. The authors suggest that this mismatch between wiring and activity helps explain cognitive decline in late kidney disease.
pmc-10722197:
Pastushkova and co-authors study in 2023 how three days of dry immersion, a ground model of weightlessness, shifts blood proteins and the timing of the heart's electrical wave in healthy volunteers. Muscle pull feeds back on heart electricity, and uneven pull can desync the beat, a risk that matters for cosmonauts, among whom a common rhythm fault appears early in life. Blood protein profiles were set against measures of wave spread and recovery.

The team looked for links between protein change and the sync of excitation across the heart muscle. Risk markers named in the work include chamber enlargement, early extra beats, and set features of the traced wave. The study aims to flag who needs watch during flight like stress.
pmc-10722897:
Chinmaya Mishra, Rinus Verdonschot, Peter Hagoort, and Gabriel Skantze gave a social robot emotions generated live by a language model, in a 2023 paper. Robots that show fitting feelings connect better with people. The team reframed the robot's emotional choice as a recognition task over the conversation so far. A large language model read the dialogue and predicted the right emotion for the robot's next turn, which its face then displayed.

Forty-seven volunteers played a card sorting game with the robot under three conditions: model-driven feelings, no feelings, and mismatched feelings. The model's choices were reliable, and people could read them. Congruent expressions made the robot seem more human-like and appropriate, and players scored better at the game. The authors offer the method as a real-time, low-effort way to make service and companion robots emotionally literate.
pmc-10725297:
Hussain Ali John and four co-authors report a case of a smooth, diamond-shaped patch on the middle of the tongue. The condition, median rhomboid glossitis, removes the tiny bumps from a well-defined zone on the tongue's top surface. It usually causes no pain, though some patients feel mild itching. Specialists still argue over its roots: it is classed as a developmental disorder, yet many suspect a fungal cause instead.

The patient was a 55-year-old woman seen at a hospital in Wardha, India, with an oval, discolored area present since birth. The authors walk through how the lesion is recognized and how it differs from look-alike conditions. They stress the dentist's role in spotting the patch and in teaching patients what it means. Reassurance is often the main treatment, since the patch itself is harmless.
pmc-10725697:
Zilong Yin, Wanying Guo, and Yue Wang trace how teenage distress drains school engagement in a 2023 study. The link is well known; the machinery behind it less so. Social-emotional competence might carry part of the effect, and caring teachers might soften it.

Over eight thousand six hundred Chinese adolescents, surveyed as pandemic rules eased, completed scales for distress, competence, teacher care, and engagement. Distress predicted lower engagement, with competence mediating part of that path. Teacher care moderated both the direct and indirect links in the model. Schools get two levers: build students' social-emotional skills and train teachers to show care visibly.
pmc-10726397:
Ayano Yoshida and co-authors describe a rare, severe complication of a catheter-based mitral valve repair in a 2023 case report. The procedure clips the valve leaflets together edge to edge to stop leaks, avoiding open surgery in frail patients. Their patient was a ninety-two-year-old man with severe leakage and breathlessness, judged too risky for surgery.

During the clip placement, the team struggled to grip the shorter rear leaflet and repositioned the clip. Right after a firm grip was gained, his blood pressure crashed and fluid pooled around the heart. Review of the images showed the clip had sunk into the heart muscle as it closed, tearing the ventricle wall. The report warns teams about this failure mode when grasp length is tight.
pmc-10728997:
Yogi Fitriadi, Wahyu Danawati, and Adi Heru Sutomo present a 2023 protocol for a scoping review of community health worker programs against adult obesity. Obesity feeds diabetes, heart disease, and cancer, and trained local workers can carry prevention into neighborhoods in culturally fitting ways. The protocol sets out how the team will map such programs published from 2010 to 2022.

Six databases plus trial registries will be searched, with two reviewers screening and charting the studies independently. As a synthesis of published work, the review needs no ethics approval. The authors plan journal publication, conference talks, and a plain language summary of the map.
pmc-10731197:
Rui-Yao Wei and co-authors report a rare case of stomach damage from poor blood flow in a case report from two thousand twenty-three. Ischemic gastritis is uncommon, deadly, and often missed, since its signs mimic other gut diseases. A scope exam is the main way to catch it.

A woman aged sixty-eight with a brain aneurysm history arrived dizzy, with chest tightness and two days of lost consciousness. Scans showed widespread artery hardening, including the vessels feeding the gut. A scope found the whole stomach lining swollen, deep purple, and bleeding, worst at the top. Tissue study confirmed dying lining. The authors stress scope and tissue checks for the diagnosis.
pmc-10734297:
Chonradee Amnatsin and seven co-authors compare two ways of grinding graphite waste into fine powder in a 2023 paper. Graphite scrap can be recycled into carbon blocks, but milling it fine enough takes time. A bead mill promises the same fineness in a fraction of the hours.

Industrial bead milling cut the grinding from seventy-two hours to ten minutes. Particles from both methods looked alike, with only small differences in crystal dimensions. Blocks pressed from each powder shared nearly the same structure and density. Bead-milled blocks bent slightly stronger, with equal hardness and electrical resistance. Wear behavior rounded out the comparison. The study supports bead milling as a fast, quality-preserving route for graphite recycling.
pmc-10735397:
Zhuoer Lin and five co-authors compared dementia care across countries in a 2023 study. People with dementia who struggle with daily tasks need help, yet many get none. The team used matched survey data from 2012 to 2018 covering the United States, England, Europe, and China.

Three facts stood out everywhere. The share of people with dementia who had trouble with daily tasks kept rising. About one in five received no care at all for those limits. And that care gap did not shrink over the years in any country, rich or poor. For basic self-care tasks, about two in five went without help. Formal paid care was missing for at least three in five. The authors call the pattern alarming and steady. Growing old-age populations make closing the gap urgent.
pmc-10735497:
Lindsey Smith traces how rigged property values still shape who can get long-term care in old age. Decades of public and private action, from redlining onward, built racial gaps into home values. Home value quietly governs where care facilities can profitably open. Assisted living exists in about 30 percent of American communities overall.

But in counties where Black residents make up the largest share, access swings with the local Black-White mobility gap. About 31 percent have a facility where the gap is small, and under 15 percent where it is large. Smith proposes legal tools — building incentives, siting priorities, anti-displacement rules, community input, and affordability duties — to close the gap.
pmc-10735597:
Murad Taani and Mary Hook study the clinical nurse's role in asking older hospital patients what matters to them, in work published in 2023. The question anchors an age-friendly care framework built on four elements: what matters, medication, mentation, and mobility. Toolkits exist for all disciplines, yet nurse-specific evidence was thin.

A large Midwest health system rolled the framework out across five hospitals but saw no gain in nurse-sensitive patient experience scores. The authors describe a qualitative study now under way with nurse leaders and clinical nurses who ran the programme. It probes their knowledge, views, and lived experience of the approach. The findings should ground nurse-targeted training and better ways to partner with patients and caregivers.
pmc-10735797:
Jessie Ho-Yin Yau and co-authors study depression stigma among older Chinese adults in this 2023 paper. Older people can face a double burden: bias against aging and false beliefs about depression. The team asked whether civic activity, such as volunteer work after mental health training, builds knowledge that softens that stigma.

They surveyed one hundred forty-five older adults in Hong Kong who had taken a mental health first aid course and then volunteered. Volunteering linked to better knowledge of symptoms and facts. Knowing the facts, in turn, tied to lower stereotype, prejudice, and unfair treatment scores, while clinging to myths tied to higher stigma on every count. A path model fit the data well, and factual knowledge carried the main bridging effect between volunteering and lower stigma.
pmc-10735897:
Sara Bybee, Kexin Yu, and Rita Choula introduce a symposium on law itself as a driver of health in this 2023 paper. Health research often names social factors such as housing and care access. The speakers argue the deeper layer is political: the laws and policies that hand out resources unevenly and lock in disadvantage for groups with little power.

The session gathers talks on how statutes harm the health of people of color and older adults. One speaker reviews the host society's policy and advocacy work. A second shows how law can attack racial gaps in geographic access to care. A third covers housing laws that deepen health inequity for older and marginalized people. The authors aim to make policy talk plain and welcoming for researchers and practitioners who rarely deal with law, so that harmful rules can be spotted, tracked, and revised.
pmc-10736097:
Giselle Ferguson and co-authors probe how aging changes the sting of daily stress. Older adults often seem calmer under strain, credited to hard won emotion skills. Most past work compared age groups once, not the same people over time. This study followed over three hundred Bronx elders through repeated two week phone check bursts.

Stress clearly lifted negative mood at every level of the data. Yet the stress to mood slope did not shift with age, either across people or within them. What did rise with age was baseline negative mood on stress free moments. The authors urge designs that separate growing older from being older.
pmc-10736197:
Wei F Chen, Ying C Ku, Takumi Yamamoto, and Sonia K Pandey ask whether surgery can truly cure lymphedema, the stubborn swelling that follows lymph system damage, in this 2023 viewpoint paper. Modern microsurgery can reconnect lymph channels to veins or transplant lymph tissue, and these operations are now done worldwide. Whether they cure, rather than merely help, is still argued.

The authors define cure strictly: no symptoms and no further treatment, not even compression garments. By that bar, cure is real but rare in their practice since 2011, seen after all three main operations. Every cured case shared one trait: the swelling was still fluid based and reversible. Once fatty overgrowth set in, no operation reversed it. Improvement in cured patients began within two weeks and built over six months.
pmc-10736297:
Murphy and co-authors describe in 2023 an effort to link merit based payment measures to age friendly care for older adults. The age friendly frame rests on four ideas, mentation, mobility, medications, and what matters to the patient. A university center for older adults set out to weave those into daily workflows.

Record templates were standardized, intake software gained questions to spot eligible patients, and three forms of annual wellness visit were unified. Between mid 2020 and mid 2021, 297 health professionals finished online training modules. Post course surveys rated the content helpful with goals met. Visit rates are tracked yearly to judge uptake.
pmc-10736397:
Greta Jianjia Cheng, Sara Godina, Erica Fan, and Andrea Rosso linked neighbourhood wealth to memory change in two thousand twenty-three in older adults in Pittsburgh. Six hundred ten people aged seventy and above, Black and white, were followed for six years with yearly thinking tests. Neighbourhood status was built from census data on income, education, and jobs.

People in the poorest third of neighbourhoods started at about the same thinking level as those in the richest third. But their scores fell faster over time. The middle group showed no clear gap. Race did not change the pattern. The results say place shapes how fast the ageing mind declines.
pmc-10736497:
Shoko Miyagawa and Young Ah Seong study manual stool removal in home care in Japan, in work from two thousand twenty-three. The procedure, done by visiting nurses, clears hard stool by hand when patients cannot pass it. Seven skilled nurses were interviewed while a training simulator was being built.

Each nurse performed the task ten to thirty times a month. Patients included people with stroke or nerve damage, and those in the last stages of cancer. The skill is not taught in schools, nurses said, but learned on the job. Families struggle to assist, which is why routine nurse visits matter.
pmc-10736797:
Dawn Carr and co-authors follow older adults through the COVID-19 years in a 2023 study of anxiety and resilience. Data on the group were first gathered in 2018, before the virus appeared. Two years later, the team asked about virus-linked worries and anxiety signs. They asked whether mental toughness built up before the crisis softened its blow.

The study covers 453 adults living in their own homes. Virus worries did track with rising anxiety, even after earlier anxiety was counted. People with high earlier toughness gained less anxiety than those with low toughness. Toughness alone also linked to falling anxiety. The work suggests that building coping strength in calm times pays off in a crisis.
pmc-10736897:
Carol Musil and co-authors study grandmothers raising grandchildren in a 2023 paper. Such caregivers face strain that shows up in low mood and shaky family life. The team read their state through a known family stress model. A nationwide sample of 300 American grandmothers took part in an online study, reporting demands, coping, support, and how they sized up their load.
