One model explained much of the spread in how families felt they functioned. Feeling steady on one's feet, paying calm attention, and finding resources all served as coping paths in the model. Support from others added a further buffer. The results point to skills programs that build these inner tools, rather than aid that stops at money or services alone.
pmc-10737097:
Vadim Gladyshev wrote a 2023 study on the molecular strategies that set how long animals live. Lifespan varies hugely between species and somewhat within them, yet the general rules of that control were unclear. The team compared gene activity across many tissues in many mammal species. They looked for signatures tied to long life, and how those signatures relate to aging itself and to treatments that extend life.

Long-lived species shared a pattern: their signature genes were ancient and essential, and the pattern oddly aligned with changes seen in aging. Life-extending treatments pushed the other way, against aging patterns, acting on younger, changeable genes tied to energy use. The team also built a gene-based clock that tracks progress through a lifespan. It can measure how treatments shift that progress. The work separates what evolution does to grant long life from what medicine might do to extend it.
pmc-10737197:
Abigail Hansen, Kaarin Anstey, and six co-authors study how older Australians view driver help systems. These systems warn drivers or help steer and brake. The study, from twenty twenty-three, asks if age and gender shape trust and use. It was run with National Seniors Australia as an online survey.

More than thirteen hundred drivers aged sixty-five and up took part, and most said they use such systems. Older drivers trusted the systems more but found them harder to use. Women used the systems less than men yet trusted them more. The authors say ease of use may matter as much as trust for older drivers.
pmc-10737297:
Chenkai Wu and Qianli Xue present a set of talks on bouncing back after frailty. Their session, from twenty twenty-three, asks if frailty must mean decline to the end. Frailty leaves older people with low reserves and high risk from stress. Turning the state itself around has proved hard, and no single drug fixes it.

Four studies in the set hunt for traits that blunt frailty's harms. One finds a healthy daily routine helps most for those in poor social settings. Others weigh social ties, habits, and health marks. Frail people differ a lot from each other, the talks stress. Care built around the person may protect the most fragile best.
pmc-10737497:
Rahul Malhotra, Jeremy Lim-Soh, Pildoo Sung, and Ha-Linh Quach report a study from two thousand twenty-three on how families in Singapore share care for older adults. Most research watches only the main caregiver, leaving the wider family picture unclear. The team asked who gives which kind of help when several relatives are involved.

Primary caregivers of two hundred seventy-seven adults aged seventy-five and older with daily limits were interviewed. Three patterns emerged. In the largest, several relatives shared all three help types: daily tasks, health and social services, and emotional support. In another, families shared care but skipped formal services. In the third, the main caregiver did everything alone. Solo caregivers reported more depressive symptoms than those in fully shared care.
pmc-10737597:
Kevin Cahill, Michael Giandrea, Joseph Quinn, and Loretta Platts ask how much pay older workers will trade for flexible work in a 2023 study. As people near the end of their careers, they weigh wages against shorter or more flexible hours. Knowing the trade helps shape policy for longer working lives.

The team built work histories for thousands of older Americans from a long-running national study with thirty years of follow-up. They tracked how pay and hours changed as workers moved from career jobs to full exit. On average, a twenty percent cut in hours came with about a six percent drop in hourly pay, other things equal. The findings show workers do accept lower pay for flexibility, but the price is modest.
pmc-10737697:
Kate Leger and co-authors study in 2023 how daily stress, activity, and sleep intertwine in later life. Healthy habits are known to correlate with lower stress overall, but day-to-day links were less clear. One hundred eighty older adults reported mood and tensions every few hours over five to six days, wore activity trackers, and rated nightly sleep quality.

On less sedentary days with more light activity, people reported more stressors. More stressors meant worse mood the same day, though being active softened that hit. Sleep quality dipped the night after high-stressor days. The authors stress measuring all three in daily life.
pmc-10737797:
Yoon Chung Kim and co-authors study care coordination for people with dementia who live alone in a 2023 report. A third of older Americans with dementia live solo. Without a housemate to arrange care, risks like falls and malnutrition climb. A federal grant program has required solo-focused services since 2014.

The team read final reports from seventy-three funded projects. After exclusions, twenty-seven ran both solo-focused and coordination services. Most leads were community groups, with some health systems and universities. Services typically found clients, assessed needs, built care plans, and linked supports. Plans for keeping services alive after grants end are the core lesson for future programs.
pmc-10737997:
Arseniy Yashkin and five co-authors study a link between thyroid disease and Alzheimer's disease in a 2023 paper. Graves disease is the most common cause of an overactive thyroid in the United States, and it had been suspected to raise Alzheimer's risk, without agreement. The team used Medicare records for older adults from 1991 to 2017.

They matched more than fifteen thousand people with Graves disease to similar people without it. Those with the thyroid disease had about fifteen percent higher risk of a clinical Alzheimer's diagnosis. The link was stronger in men and in Black patients in their data. The authors suggest shared causes may connect the two diseases, and that thyroid care could help lower dementia burden.
pmc-10738097:
Surviving cancer is shaped by culture as much as by medicine, from family roles to trust in doctors. Candidus Nwakasi and co-authors studied Black and Latinx survivors and caregivers in the United States through a cultural model that sorts influences into identity, relationships, and empowerment. They interviewed nineteen survivors and ran five focus groups with twenty-seven caregivers.

Four themes emerged: how culture frames dealing with cancer, struggles over conflict and control, barriers to reaching care, and rethinking what survivorship means inside a community. The authors argue that these social and cultural forces help explain unequal quality of life after cancer, and that support programs ignoring them will keep missing the people they aim to serve.
pmc-10738297:
Kathy Xie, Lauren Winslow, Avshalom Caspi, and Terrie Moffitt trace the roots of body strength in old age back to the young child, in a 2023 study. Midlife is a prime time to invest in health, and early signs may foretell how the body will fare.

Their source is a birth cohort in New Zealand tracked from birth. Brain health was scored at age three with a nerve exam, thought tests, and a rating of mood and manner. Body strength was scored at age forty-five with walk speed, grip, balance, and chair stands. Children with weaker early scores had weaker bodies as adults, even with sex and home wealth weighed. The team reads body tests as a sign of whole-life health, not just of muscle and bone.
pmc-10738497:
Andrea Huseth-Zosel and Heather Fuller interview older adults in North Dakota about vaccine information in a 2023 paper. Older adults vaccinate at fairly high rates, yet how trust in information sources shapes their choices was less clear. The team spoke by phone with fifty-one adults aged sixty-five and over who had earlier taken a survey on vaccine behavior.

Three themes emerged from the talks. Some trust came automatically, from familiar people, expert roles like doctors, or sources seen as reliable. A second theme was confusion: sources contradicted each other or shifted positions, leaving people unsure whom to believe. A third covered how trust can be rebuilt, through openness, sincerity, and getting a second opinion. The authors point to these as levers for raising vaccination rates in this group.
pmc-10738597:
Janne Bromseth asks whether person-centered care in Norwegian elder services truly includes older LGBTIQ+ adults, whose identities the philosophy promises to affirm. Her 2023 paper draws on an interview study of queer perspectives on geriatric care in the Oslo area. Person-centered care is the ruling frame in these services, built on empathy and basic psychological needs.

Two sides were heard. Eleven older LGBQ adults, aged 61 to 78, recounted their care experiences across the life course. Staff from long-term, home, and day care joined focus groups and interviews. The paper weighs what staff actually know about these adults' lives and aging conditions, and where training has reached. It tests the philosophy against the experience of a minority it claims to cover.
pmc-10738697:
Feeling secure about money in old age is part of a good life. Yeon Ji Ryou, Mengya Wang, and Peter Martin ask what personality has to do with it, in a 2023 study. They drew 1,322 adults aged sixty-five and over from a national retirement study's 2020 round. Measures covered the five big personality traits, social support, and financial satisfaction.

Outgoing and conscientious elders reported more financial satisfaction. Anxious and agreeable ones reported less. Support cut both ways: warm support raised satisfaction, while strained, negative support lowered it. Joining social activities helped as well. Age, health, and marital status also mattered. The authors argue that money contentment in later life is partly a psychological and social product, not only a balance-sheet one.
pmc-10738797:
In Japan, near three in ten folk are past sixty-five, and more and more of them care for a spouse or kin as old as they are. Mineko Wada and Hideaki Hanaoka swept the past studies in 2023 to map that old-to-old care: its loads and its lifts. The sweep took in six stores of papers and kept the field studies of home care by the old for the old.

The loads are heavy: worn nerves, lost sleep, and a slide toward low mood, sharpest when the cared-for mind has faded. The lifts are habits more than goods: self-care steps and plain problem work, done day by day. Two gaps close the piece: what help truly cuts the load, and how the cared-for old themselves fare. The team call both asks urgent.
pmc-10738897:
Elise Valdes surveyed home health workers across the United States about how well their training prepared them for the job, in a 2023 study. More older adults want to age at home, which makes these workers a core part of care. The last large national survey of the group dated back to 2007. Valdes gathered just under one thousand five hundred workers, from aides to nurses, through an online form.

Hospice aides felt best prepared, with four in five rating their training as good. Nurses rated theirs lowest, with just over half feeling well prepared. Across skill topics, from patient care to dementia and end-of-life care, the same order held. Valdes warns that feeling unready can feed low job satisfaction and high turnover. The paper urges better training across all roles in the field, with the sharpest focus on nurses, who reported the weakest preparation despite their broad duties.
pmc-10738997:
Laila Scroggins, Qing Zhang, Kevin Koronowski, and Juan Palavicini report a 2023 study on broken body clocks and Alzheimer's disease. The team used a new mouse model that carries a human form of the tau protein. Half the mice lived under a steady light schedule, while the rest faced a shifting schedule like chronic jet lag.

The shifting schedule changed how the mice used fuel during fasting, with males hit harder than females. Males also gained fat mass and lost ground on a maze test of spatial memory. Females seemed shielded from the memory harm. The work links daily rhythm loss to sex-specific changes in body and brain.
pmc-10739097:
Xiaoang Li, Yiming Zhang, and Liping Duan study how butyrate-making gut bacteria slow gut aging inflammation. Their twenty twenty-three paper calls the process inflammaging, a slow burn tied to a thinning mix of gut microbes. Diverse gut flora help keep the bowel wall calm and stable.

Past work by the team showed these bacteria reversed age-linked gut swelling in old mice. The new work traces the path: the bacteria raise fatty acid sensor levels in the gut. One transporter, MCT-1, is suspected to carry the calming effect. Cell, organoid, and mouse gut models test the chain. A firmer mechanism could turn a probiotic hint into a targeted therapy.
pmc-10739297:
Shavonnye Rath and five co-authors tested a special form of heat care for pain in older adults, in a study from twenty twenty-three. The heat uses long light waves that mimic a dry sauna. Pain is common in later life and can lower quality of life and physical ability, so new options matter.

A small group of older adults took six half-hour sessions. Some got plain warm air, and others got warm air plus the special heat. Pain severity fell in the special heat group, and pain interference fell in the plain heat group. Overall, heat helped, but the special form was not clearly better. The authors call for more research.
pmc-10739497:
Carson De Fries and five co-authors published this study in 2023. It looks at end-of-life care planning among older Vietnamese American and Filipino American adults. The authors focus on the role family plays when people state their wishes for care at the end of life.

The team held three focus groups with twelve adults aged fifty-five and over. Most said they trusted their children most with their wishes, and most wanted to spend their last days at home. Some found these talks easier after past experience with aging relatives, while others met resistance. Cost, language gaps, and fear of burdening their children also held people back. The findings point to ways care can better fit these families.
pmc-10739997:
Galan-Gonzalez leads a large team improving light emitting transistors with a nanostructured channel, in work from twenty twenty-three. Hybrid light emitting field effect transistors combine switching and light emission in one device. They promise simple display pixels. But emission efficiency has held them back.

Shaping the transistor channel at the nanoscale changes how charge and light meet inside the device. The team reports improved emission efficiency from that design. Brighter, thriftier versions could make active matrix displays simpler to build. They could also make optical gear for data links simpler. In such gear, one part doing two jobs cuts build steps and cost.
pmc-10741197:
Ling Xu and co-authors wrote a 2023 scoping review on digital storytelling built from reminiscence with older adults. Looking back over one's life can support mental health in later years. Turning those memories into a digital storybook may deepen the benefit. The review asked how such projects are run, whether generations mix in them, and what outcomes follow.

Starting from 702 articles, screening narrowed the field to 35 full texts and finally 10 studies squarely on reminiscence-based digital storytelling. Only one study deliberately built intergenerational engagement into its design. Reported effects for older adults included personal meaning and emotional release, plus social connection. Outcomes for younger co-creators and audiences were also tracked. The authors map a young field and its gaps.
pmc-10741497:
Doucet, Brisebois, McKerral, and Agorastos study heart rhythm variation after concussion, in work from twenty twenty-three. A reliable body marker could help diagnose concussion and track recovery in athletes. Heart rate variability, the small gaps between beats, is one candidate.

Nearly one hundred seventy college athletes aged sixteen to twenty-two did baseline tests. Thirty who later got concussions were retested within three days and again before return to play. Surveys covered symptoms and mental health. Baseline results showed some sex gaps in rhythm measures. The team tracked how rhythm, sex, and symptoms moved together, to judge if a simple heart test can aid care.
pmc-10742397:
Ruperto González-Pérez and colleagues argue for molecule-level allergy testing when choosing mite immunotherapy, in a twenty twenty-three paper. Immunotherapy is the only treatment that changes the course of allergy, yet under ten percent of hay fever or asthma patients get it. The team profiled young patients' antibody responses to dust mite and storage mite parts at the molecule level.

Responses proved complex in every patient group, no matter the base condition. No one reacted only to the three classic mite molecules. Patients with asthma and skin disease carried higher levels to six mite parts, but no pattern marked one disease. The authors say products must match the local molecule mix that patients truly react to.
pmc-10742597:
Lizeth Katherine Tinoco Navarro and Cihlar review how biphasic systems in aerogels and xerogels can enhance titanium dioxide photocatalysts. Their review covers synthesis, methods, and how they work, for uses in cleaning the environment.

Its phases and mixed-phase junctions shape how well it works. The review covers the sol-gel route and variants such as low-heat hydrothermal making. It looks at how acid and base donors affect gelling, and which drying routes suit aerogel or xerogel forms. Topics include charge spread, carrier recombination, and helper chemicals. Doping and mixed structures are also treated as routes to stronger action.
pmc-10742797:
José Verdú-Soriano and co-authors test an olive-leaf hydrogel against a standard gel on hard-to-heal wounds. Chronic ulcers strain health systems, and proof that one dressing beats another is scarce. Their trial enrolled outpatients with pressure, vein, or diabetic foot ulcers that resisted care. Thirty-five patients got the extract gel and thirty-four the standard one.

Wound area shrank by about fifty-two percent under the new gel. The standard gel managed only about nineteen percent over the same span. Daily healing speed ran about ten times higher with the extract. The authors credit balance of acidity and oxidative stress in the wound bed. That action adds to the moisture and shield work of plain gels.
pmc-10742997:
Michael Keese leads a team of ten authors in 2023 in testing whether fat-derived stem cells can protect blood vessel lining cells starved of oxygen. Such stem cells are already being tried for poor circulation in the legs, but how they help is still being worked out.

The team added human fat-derived cells to vessel cells in the lab under low-oxygen stress, and also tested them in mice prone to artery disease with a blocked leg artery. The cells eased a damaging stress response inside the vessel cells, the terminal unfolded protein response. The findings help explain how a cell therapy might rescue tissue that lacks blood flow.
pmc-10743397:
Alexandra-Ioana Trandafir and co-authors review adrenal hormone excess and bone health in a 2023 paper. One adrenal disorder floods the body with a salt balancing hormone. Its effects on calcium handling and fracture risk deserved a fresh look. Two dozen human studies spanning decades met their screening rules.

Scans, bone markers, and a hormone of calcium control were tracked across studies. The calcium hormone ran higher in patients than in comparison groups. Many studies followed patients after surgery versus drug care. Bone density tools varied, which made cross study reading harder.
pmc-10743597:
Etindele Sosso and five co-authors sum up what is known about poor sleep and social rank in Latin America in this twenty twenty-three review. Poor sleep is a broad health risk, yet rank in pay, school, and work is often left out of sleep work. No past review had pulled the Latin American proof into one place.

Inside, twenty past studies made the final set, most of them from Brazil. Higher rank went with shorter sleep, while lower rank went with worse sleep and more day-time drowsiness. Low school years also went with more cases of not being able to fall asleep. The pooled share with sleep ills was near one in four across the studies.
pmc-10743897:
Federico Roggio and co-authors review what muscle tissue can tell about the spine curve of adolescence. Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis bends the spine without a known cause and affects one to three children in a hundred. Genes clearly matter; the LBX1 locus leads a long list of linked variants. Their 2023 narrative review searches three databases for the muscle side of the story. Sampling and biomarker choices across studies are compared.

Candidate protein markers emerge: Gi-protein alpha subunits, fibrillin-1 and fibrillin-2, plus sets of proteins expressed unevenly between sides. Hormonal theories run beside the genetic ones. Patient grouping by curve severity stays inconsistent, which thins every conclusion. The team calls muscle research young but promising for guiding earlier treatment.
pmc-10744097:
Dong Qu and three co-authors study how salicylic acid helps kiwifruit resist bacterial canker in a paper from 2023. The disease, caused by a Pseudomonas strain, threatens the kiwifruit industry. The acid is a plant defense signal known to boost resistance, but how it does so in this fruit was unclear. The team used advanced protein profiling to watch thousands of proteins shift after treatment and infection.

Infection switched on many defense paths, including a known signaling cascade and armor-building chemistry. Acid treatment pre-armed those same paths and kept them active during infection. The work gives a base for using the acid in orchards to control canker.
pmc-10744997:
Jose De La Flor and co-authors report a 2023 case of a rare kidney illness tied to a blood disorder. Some immune proteins turn solid in the cold and can inflame small vessels, harming the kidneys. That kidney pattern is rare and is linked here to a slow blood cancer that makes one protein in excess.

The patient was 52 years old and came in with body wide swelling, low blood counts, and heavy protein loss in the urine. Blood and urine tests showed a single band of one immune protein type. A kidney biopsy fit the cold protein pattern. A bone marrow test then confirmed the blood disorder. The case shows why a marrow check matters when this kidney pattern meets such protein signs.
pmc-10745297:
Margarida Liz Martins and co-authors adapt a scorecard for diets that are good for bodies and planet alike, then test it in Portugal, in this 2023 study. The SHED Index grades eating patterns on thirty items spanning health and sustainability. Three hundred forty-seven adults aged eighteen to sixty-five answered web questionnaires, and their food frequency reports let the team compare index scores against measured intake.

A higher score should track genuinely healthier, lighter-impact eating; the validation checks that it does. Countries cannot steer food policy toward sustainability without instruments that survive translation and culture. A checked Portuguese version gives researchers and officials there a common yardstick for surveys and programs.
pmc-10745397:
Zhang and co-authors pair two nanomaterials into an ink whose glow color shifts with heat, for anti-counterfeiting. Strong, hard-to-copy marks are a steady research focus. Their mix joins upconversion particles with perovskite quantum dots for two checking modes.

The upconversion particles grew brighter as they warmed, more so at smaller sizes. That odd gain was traced to less surface quenching of the glow. Quantum dots stuck to the particle surfaces and shared energy with them. As heat rose, the mix shifted from green to pink under infrared light. Under ultraviolet light, it faded from green to dark.
pmc-10745497:
Yu-Chan Wang and co-authors forge a new scaffold against the HIV integrase in a 2023 study. Integrase stitches viral DNA into human cells, a step HIV cannot skip. Five approved drugs block that stitch, but resistance mutations keep eroding them.

Docking-based virtual screens hunted fresh chemical starting points. Indole-2-carboxylic acid emerged as a strong new scaffold for the job. One derivative blocked the strand transfer step in lab tests. Its binding pose shows the indole core and acid group gripping the enzyme's metal heart. New scaffolds matter because resistant virus shrugs off familiar shapes.
pmc-10746097:
Jinjie Li and co-authors use Mendelian randomization to ask whether selenium levels actually cause, or protect against, osteoporosis. Past observational work pointed both ways, tangled by diet and lifestyle. Genes that nudge selenium levels act as natural randomizers, letting the team test causation cleanly.

Their 2023 study takes selenium-linked variants from genome studies of toenail and blood selenium, and osteoporosis and bone density outcomes from large databases. Three statistical methods agree: selenium level shows no causal effect on osteoporosis risk. Sensitivity checks find no hidden pleiotropy or single-variant leverage behind the null. The authors read the verdict as reliable within its tools: the selenium-bone link, whatever clinics observe, is not a simple cause.
pmc-10746397:
Phi-Hung Nguyen and co-authors present a 2023 study of apartment choice in Vietnam. Home building is booming in many growing countries. Providers need to know what buyers value most. The team builds a two-stage decision model with fuzzy math, which handles vague scores well. Expert views first set the key choice factors for Vietnamese buyers.

In stage two, the model ranks the top ten apartment providers. Scores use a spherical fuzzy form that gives raters more room to express doubt. The team checks the ranks against two older fuzzy ranking methods. Five rank-link measures test whether the orders agree. Builders get a ranked guide tied to real buyer factors. The checks show whether the new model adds trust or just adds steps. Such models help firms spend on the features buyers actually weigh when they pick a home.
pmc-10747097:
Yan Zeng and co-authors present a 2023 study comparing five major variants of the COVID-19 virus side by side in the lab. Each new variant spread faster and hit health harder than the last, so knowing their concrete traits matters for control. The team set the original strain against Beta, Delta, and three Omicron branches.

All six were grown in monkey kidney cells to compare replication speed. Leftover virus was tracked for seven days at fridge, room, and body temperatures to test environmental stability. Infection strength after varied incubation times was also measured. The older strains grew fastest in cells, with one Omicron branch outpacing its siblings. The paper profiles each variant's behavior.
pmc-10747197:
Raul Gonzalez-Castro and colleagues review a sperm protein, PLCZ1, that wakes the egg at fertilization. Once sperm and egg fuse, this protein sets off calcium pulses that start development. When it fails, eggs stay dormant, a leading cause of failed assisted fertilization in men.

Most knowledge comes from men and mice. The review asks what it means for cattle and horses. Horse sperm rich in the protein cleaves eggs better after injection procedures. Bull sperm, by contrast, struggles to trigger the pulses at all. In mice, injecting the protein rescues failed eggs fully. The authors call for standard tests and safety work before farm use.
pmc-10747397:
Xinlan Fan and co-authors design a tiny amplifier circuit in 2023 that runs on just half a volt. The circuit compares two input signals and boosts the gap between them, a common task in sensor and signal work. Low power matters for small devices, so the team built the chip in a modern process and added a chopping trick to cut offset and low hum.

The three-stage circuit reaches strong gain while using less than one microwatt. Tests show wide clean range, good rejection of shared noise, and low input noise. The authors note its supply voltage is among the lowest reported for this kind of circuit, which suits battery-run signal tasks.
pmc-10747597:
Ilaria Quaratesi and co-authors design a cleaner way to tan leather without chrome. Their 2023 study oxidizes sodium alginate, a seaweed extract, into a biodegradable tanning agent. A dusting of nano-hydroxyapatite, the mineral of bone, adds flame resistance. The process avoids chrome, aldehydes, and phenols, the usual toxic backbone of tanning.

Heat analysis showed the oxidized alginate binds and stabilizes collagen, leather's core protein. Magnetic resonance probed how water sits inside the treated matrix, and microscopy with elemental mapping traced the mineral through it. Standard industrial tests then measured the prototype's strength and fire behavior. Both additives proved workable stand-ins for the conventional chemistry. The authors frame the recipe as eco-design for a dirty industry.
pmc-10747997:
Thanakorn Phumkuea and four co-authors stack neural nets to read chest X-rays in a 2023 paper. A chest image is a fast first look when COVID-19 is suspected. Sorting COVID from other lung ills and from health in one pass is a stiff test for a single model.

Their system splits the job into two stages: first health versus sickness, then COVID versus other causes. Public image sets supplied the training scans. The stack reached accuracy and sensitivity near ninety-seven percent, clearly ahead of a single all-in-one net on the same sets. The authors pitch it as a triage aid for busy wards.
pmc-10748297:
Chewing areca nut drives mouth cancers across Asia, and its main active compound clearly does damage, yet one receptor story is missing. Hakan Gocol and co-authors run a two-stage evidence synthesis in a 2023 paper to find that gap.

The first pass mapped known mechanisms: runaway cell growth, invasion, scar-like fibrosis, immune imbalance, and DNA damage, through a web of named pathways. Receptors that the compound could bind, though, barely appeared in that map. A refined second search showed the compound prefers muscarinic receptors, which other work links to cancer. Those receptors switch on many of the same pathways. The authors propose this cholinergic axis as the missing link worth testing directly.
pmc-10749497:
Mariana Verdelho Machado argued in 2023 that treatment of fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction stands on the edge of a revolution. The condition, now called MASLD, is swelling toward the top cause of end-stage liver disease. Weight loss remains the most effective therapy, and its tools are escalating fast.

Care is shifting from lifestyle advice to surgery and endoscopy, and now to anti-obesity drugs that rival surgery's results. Patients whose livers are already scarred need liver-directed drugs on top. Machado predicts a disruption on the scale of the hepatitis C cure era a decade ago. The essay is a call to prepare clinics for combination, staged care. It frames the coming drugs as a paradigm shift, not an increment.
pmc-10750397:
Mingliang Wang and four co-authors build a tool to spot ADHD from brain scans in a 2023 paper. Resting brain activity changes over time, and those shifts can reveal what differs in this condition. Older methods that freeze connectivity into one snapshot miss the motion. Many learning methods also only compare neighboring moments, missing longer patterns.

Their network first builds changing connectivity maps from short segments of each scan, learned from data rather than fixed formulas. A second network then reads long-range patterns across those maps before a final diagnosis step. On a public dataset their method beat leading rivals. The authors say learned dynamic maps carry more signal than standard ones.
pmc-10751797:
Anthony Bogetti, Josephine Leung, and Lillian Chong present LPATH, a Python tool that sorts molecular simulation pathways into meaningful classes. Simulations of how a molecule changes state produce many routes of differing lengths, and comparing them by hand is tedious. LPATH borrows from linguistics: it discretizes the molecule's configurations into key states, spells each pathway as a string of visited states, and matches strings by similarity.

A two-stage machine learning step keeps the state clustering affordable in memory. Designed mainly for the WESTPA weighted-ensemble package but usable with ordinary simulations, the tool recovered physically sensible route classes and their probabilities for a classic test molecule's shape change. The authors release it as open analysis infrastructure for transition mechanism studies.
pmc-10751997:
Predicting how long a colorectal cancer patient will live guides hard treatment choices. Jyoti Verma and co-authors trained deep learning models to read that future from microscope slides. Their dataset held one hundred thousand image patches cut from stained tumor tissue. The patches spanned nine tissue types, from fat and mucus to cancer cells and the stroma around them.

Six network designs competed at the survival task. The best of them scored high on accuracy, precision, and recall. Visual maps showed which regions drove each prediction, opening the black box a little. The authors argue such models could support personalized treatment and reveal new prognostic signs in tissue. The study appeared in 2023 and drew on several centers.
pmc-10755597:
Zoe King and a large team of co-authors study what stops doctors and medical students from starting families. Their study is from two thousand twenty-three, based on a survey run in two thousand twenty-one. Long training, harsh hours, and a culture of delay hit people of all genders, not only those who can bear children.

More than two thousand people answered open-ended questions about their family plans. Most respondents were women, and most were doctors who had finished training. The team sorted the replies into themes, from personal worries up to the rules of whole institutions. People wished they had known sooner how training timelines clash with fertility. Advice to others and calls for policy change filled many replies. The study maps where support is missing.
pmc-10755697:
Shujuan Li and co-authors build a fingertip-like sensor that feels pressure with electricity and reads temperature with color. Wearable touch sensors often cram many sensing modes into one pixel, breeding interference and cost. Their design splits the jobs: a color-changing skin shows heat as a visible tint, so no electronics are spent on temperature.

Pressure falls to a capacitor whose middle layer is patterned with slanted pyramids at two scales, a geometry that sharpens sensitivity and stretches the working range. Because the temperature channel is purely visual, the two signals never corrupt each other. The authors pitch the recipe as a cheap route to multimodal sensors that factories could mass-produce for robots and wearables.
pmc-10755797:
Yingzi Bu and co-authors present a 2023 study of a gut focused drug for ulcerative colitis. The drug blocks a kinase family that drives gut swelling. Whole body use of such blockers can cause harm, so the team sought a form that acts in the gut and spares the rest.

Machine learning models first sorted draft compounds and guessed their strength. That screen let the team build just two leads for lab tests. One lead stayed in the gut channel, while its active child form built up in colon tissue with scant blood exposure. In mice with gut swelling, the lead beat rivals and cut a key signal mark. The authors say local activation trims the need for fine isoform aim.
pmc-10763497:
Whooping cough germ strains in South Africa are read gene by gene by Fahima Moosa and a large team in work dated 2023. Thirty-two germ samples from three watch programs across five years were sequenced whole. Type marks and vaccine-part genes got close reads. All samples were one type, and near all shared one gene set.

No vaccine-part loss or flaw turned up in the set. Closed genomes split into eight shapes, three of them common. Case rises, the team judges, stem from waning vaccine cover and the germ's own cycles, not new strains.
pmc-10763597:
M Dilip Kumar, Haritha Pottipalli Sathyanarayana, and Vignesh Kailasam review a teeth straightening device in a 2023 paper. The device, a functional mandibular advancer, pushes the lower jaw forward in growing patients whose upper teeth sit too far ahead. The team asked how well it works against no treatment or other fixed devices.

Six databases were searched for studies from 1945 to late November 2021. Only human studies of growing patients with the device and a comparison group were kept. Each study needed before and after images of the head or jaw. The pooled results weigh bone and tooth changes, to guide care for this common bite problem.
pmc-10764297:
Unmesh Khanvilkar and five co-authors compare three ways to seal a root canal at its tip. A poor seal lets bacteria leak in and can doom the treated tooth. Their 2023 lab study pits a glass-ionomer system, ActiV GP, against a resin system, Resilon with RealSeal, and the classic gutta-percha with AH Plus sealer. Extracted teeth were filled with each system and tested for leakage at the root end.

The head-to-head design gives dentists a direct ranking of sealing power under the same lab conditions. Newer systems promise a tighter bond to the canal wall than the classic fill. The authors frame the test as one piece of evidence for a choice dentists make daily. Lab sealing, they note, must still be matched with results in real patients.
pmc-10771797:
Jeremy Carter and co-authors test D-dimer as a rule-out test for acute aortic dissection. Their 2023 study deals with a dangerous tear in the aorta that is hard to diagnose and often fatal if missed.

Symptoms overlap with many other conditions, and the best imaging tests cannot be run on every suspect case. D-dimer, a blood marker, had little prior research for this use because the condition is rare. The team used a large research database covering dozens of United States health organizations and tens of millions of patients. They evaluated how sensitive an elevated D-dimer level is for the diagnosis, across a far larger cohort than earlier studies.
pmc-10775897:
Elizabeth Bearce and four co-authors laid out a protocol in two thousand twenty-three for imaging spine deformity in zebrafish with micro-computed tomography. Zebrafish are a growing model for spine growth and for scoliosis, a sideways curve of the spine. Fine three-dimensional scans let teams see and measure the whole skeleton in detail.

Their pipeline covers sample preparation, imaging, data handling, and processing, then guides analysis of single vertebrae and whole spine shape with free software. The steps build on an earlier study by the group, which readers are pointed to for full use details. Labs studying spine disease in fish can adopt the method directly.
pmc-10785997:
Kyriaki Katouni and six co-authors review the syndromes in which skull sutures fuse too early alongside problems across the body. In syndromic craniosynostosis the skull deformity travels with respiratory, neurological, cardiac, skeletal, and sensory abnormalities. The best known members include Apert, Crouzon, Pfeiffer, Muenke, and Saethre-Chotzen syndromes.

Each syndrome carries its own genetic signature, with mutations in genes such as FGFR, TWIST, and EFNB1 recurring through the family. Knowing the genetics aids diagnosis and feeds current drug research. Surgery remains the main treatment for the cranial deformity, with techniques advancing syndrome by syndrome. The authors press for personalized approaches, especially for the neurological and breathing complications that surgery alone cannot settle.
pmc-10801097:
Farzad Zakian Khorramabadi and co-authors examine Afghan refugees' access to health care under Iranian law, in a 2023 analysis. Health is a recognized human right that states owe without regard to nationality. Iran hosts a large Afghan population, documented and not.

Reading the statutes closely, the authors find the law can be read to cover all Afghan immigrants in the public system. Basic and primary care do reach everyone in practice. Fuller medical and rehabilitation care, though, runs on separate tracks for documented and undocumented people. The paper urges registration drives for the undocumented, which would lift their access as a direct legal side effect.
pmc-10801397:
Samson, Aromolaran, and Akingbade compare ways to model Lassa fever in Nigeria in a study whose head gives 2023 as its year. The fever is caused by a virus that is common in West Africa and hits working age adults hard. Sound models can help leaders plan steps to curb its spread.

Weekly data from January 2018 to December 2022 came from the national disease control center. Peak mean cases hit 56 in February, with nine deaths, and the first quarter led each year. For case counts, a mid level quantile model beat the best machine learning model on error. For deaths, a machine learning model won instead. The split result guides which tool fits which forecast task.
pmc-10808797:
Long and ten co-authors use gene tools to test if blood traits cause wild mood swings in sick old folks in this twenty twenty-four study. Such swings, named delirium, raise death risk and length of ward stays. Care and cure picks for them are still few and weak.

Inside, gene marks for one hundred twenty-nine blood traits were set next to a huge Finn gene bank. Two fat traits raised the odds of the swings in the gene checks. A third trait, a form of a known vitamin, cut the odds by a wide share. Wide scans showed the same three traits touch the risk of many other ills too. The team flags the vitamin form as a lead for new cure work.
pmc-10810997:
Lisha Shen and Jian Feng review what is known about NIN, a transcription factor at the center of nitrogen-fixing nodule symbiosis, in a review published in 2023. Legumes and actinorhizal plants form root nodules that house bacteria able to turn air-borne nitrogen into ammonia the plant can use. NIN is required for every stage of that partnership, and it is consistently missing from plant species that never form nodules.

The review gathers recent findings on the signals that switch NIN on and on what it controls during nodule formation. The authors also discuss what NIN's history says about how this symbiosis evolved, since the factor appears and disappears alongside the nodulating habit across plant lineages. The piece is a synthesis of recent work rather than a report of new experiments.
pmc-10822897:
Simon Wetzel and eight co-authors watch gut microbes shift around bowel surgery in Crohn's disease in this 2023 study. Bacteria clearly take part in the disease, but the role of gut fungi is murkier. The team tracked both kingdoms together in ten patients having part of the intestine removed.

Stool samples came the day before surgery and about five days after. Overall diversity of bacteria and fungi barely moved. Deeper analysis, though, found real abundance shifts and seventeen cross kingdom correlations. Network maps grouped the microbes into thirteen clusters of partners and rivals. Sex, age, body weight, habits, and surgical technique all left marks, and the shifts tracked hospital stay length and inflammation levels.
pmc-10824997:
Abid Ali and co-authors reported in 2024 the first records of two tick species in Pakistan, identified by shape and by DNA. One is a soft tick that infests birds such as swallows. The other is a hard tick found on small farm animals. The team collected 25 ticks from swallows' nests in one province and from small ruminants in another.

Fourteen ticks matched the bird soft tick and eleven matched the hard tick genus. DNA sequences from both closely matched known relatives abroad, including a hard tick species from China. Family trees built from the sequences supported those matches. The findings extend the known range of both ticks and add baseline data for tracking tick-borne disease in the region.
pmc-10834697:
Maiyo and co-authors record the medicinal plants used by people in Mosop, Nandi County in Kenya, in a study whose head is dated 2023. Healers answered open and guided questions about which plants they use, for what, and how they prepare them. Standard indices weighed how often each plant was cited and how much healers agreed.

Just over one hundred informants named more than two hundred and fifty plant species in seventy-four families. Almost all were native, with a few introduced species. Herbs and trees made up the largest shares, and leaves and roots were the parts used most. Boiling in water was the most common preparation. Agreement was highest for infections and parasites, including malaria and worms. The authors say the record validates wide local use and lays a base for drug research on these plants.
pmc-10834797:
Bin Zhu and co-authors train a smart model to flag high uric acid in people on low-dose aspirin, in a survey study from 2023. Uric acid highs feed gout and heart ills. Aspirin, though kind to the heart, can block uric acid loss, so its users need a watch.

The team drew on a United States health survey from 2011 to 2018 and kept 805 aspirin users, of whom 190 had the acid high. Six learn methods were screened; a boost tree build won. It scored well on train and test sets. A weigh tool then ranked which facts drove each call, so the model is not a black box. The team sees the build as a cheap flag for clinics: find the at-risk few in a crowd of aspirin users, then check and act.
pmc-10850397:
Shouming Li and co-authors published this tomato study in 2023. Cold damages tomatoes at every growth stage, so breeders need genes that help plants cope. The team screened 223 tomato varieties for cold response and compared their gene activity. One gene stood out: SUS3, from the sucrose synthase family, switched on under cold stress. The researchers then raised and lowered its activity in test plants.

Plants with extra SUS3 activity held up far better in the cold. They leaked less from their cells, built up more proline and soluble sugar, and kept protective enzymes working. Plants with the gene turned down suffered more membrane damage and more harmful oxygen radicals. The authors propose SUS3 as a direct target for breeding or engineering hardier tomato crops.
pmc-10866297:
Silvia Federici and colleagues overview blood vessel inflammation tied to inborn errors of immunity. Their 2024 review covers vasculitis and vasculopathy in these disorders. Autoinflammatory diseases flare without provocation in affected people. Fever and multi-system symptoms mark the attacks. Vessels of many sizes can be inflamed or damaged.

The review gathers evidence across the known genetic conditions. Target vessels and organ damage patterns vary widely. Some disorders show prominent vascular features early on. Others reveal them only in a subset of patients. Sorting immune errors by vessel involvement aids diagnosis. Treatment choices also hinge on the vessel pattern. The paper maps a rare but serious disease corner.
pmc-10869497:
Online surveys are cheap and easy, but language models now let cheats fill them in automatically, complete with plausible free-text answers. Benjamin Lebrun and co-authors test whether such AI-written responses can be caught. Human judges spotted the machine authorship with seventy-six percent accuracy — better than chance, yet far below what clean data would need.

Automatic AI detectors, by contrast, were completely unusable. The authors warn that researchers currently stay safe mainly because fraudsters lack interest, not because defences work. If fake submissions grow common, checking them could cost more than the survey saves, and simple attention checks will not rescue data quality. The fix, they argue, must come from the crowdsourcing platforms themselves, since neither human vigilance nor detector software can carry the load.
pmc-10880097:
Wei Li and co-authors ask why some women in labor skip a spine-based pain block. The study appeared in 2023. It covers over four hundred women at one birth hospital in Shanghai who gave birth without the block. Most had first said they wanted the block.

Five traits set apart the women who went without it. Past births, fear of back pain, past use of the block, views on labor pain, and late blood tests all played a role. The team's score model sorted the two groups with fair skill. They urge staff to spot women at risk early and teach them the facts, and to fix site rules that delay care.
pmc-10908297:
Sedera Radoniaina Rakotondrasoa and colleagues reviewed tuberculosis care outcomes in Madagascar in 2023. Records came from one hospital in the capital, Antananarivo. The cohort held over six hundred outpatients from one year. Treatment success, death, failure, and dropout were all tracked. Models adjusted for other factors when judging predictors. Most patients achieved treatment success overall. Death and dropout each claimed a small share. Failure was rare in this cohort.

Women succeeded in treatment more often than men. One lung form with negative smear tests fared far worse. That form predicted dropout and death most strongly. Disease outside the lungs also predicted death clearly. Center results still missed national and global targets. The authors urge faster diagnosis for the high-risk forms. Better patient education joins their call. Tight follow-up should target those likeliest to fare poorly. Registries made this risk picture possible, they note.
pmc-10909097:
Ahmedin and co-authors chart cancer of the hypopharynx across Kazakhstan, the first study of its kind for this rare throat cancer in the country. Using registry data from 2017 to 2021, they computed incidence rates by year, age, and region, and mapped the results. In all, 814 new cases were registered over the five years. The overall rate barely moved, easing from 0.898 to 0.895 per 100,000 people.

The flat headline hides moving parts. Population growth and an aging age structure pushed case numbers up, while the underlying risk of falling ill declined. Two western regions, Atyrau and West Kazakhstan, stood out with the highest rates on the map, well above the national average. The authors break their analysis down by sex as well. For health planners, the study shows where the burden concentrates and which forces drive it, a starting point for targeting screening and tobacco and alcohol control.
pmc-11110897:
Kathleen Egan, Kelly Gurka, Alexandria Macmadu, and Herb Linn study how seeing an overdose changes what drug users think of first responders, in a paper from 2023. Calling for help fast can save a life in an overdose. But bystanders may fear police or medics and hold back. The team interviewed people in West Virginia who use prescription opioids in risky ways.

The study kept fifty people who saw an overdose, called 911, and stayed until help arrived. Most said their view of responders improved after the event. A small share felt worse, and about a quarter felt no change. Income, being present during drug use, and prior worry all shaped the shift. The authors say good first contact matters. It can make people more willing to call next time.
pmc-11389697:
Rim Kallala, Yosra Gassara, Behaeddine Garrach, Soumaya Touzi, and Belhassen Harzallah tested two classic tooth proportion rules in a 2023 study from Tunisia. The golden proportion and the red proportion are ideas used to plan attractive smiles. Whether they fit North African teeth was unknown.

One hundred participants with full, intact front teeth had moulds taken at a dental clinic in Monastir. Widths and lengths of the upper front teeth were measured on casts with a digital caliper. Central incisors were the largest teeth. Ratios between tooth pairs matched neither rule, and men and women did not differ. Neither proportion applies among this Tunisian population, the authors conclude.
pmc-11532497:
Mahsa Khadem Sadigh and four co-authors study how solvents shift light traits of 1-indanone compounds, a group of bio molecules. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Solvent pull can change how such molecules soak and give off light, and how strong their bent-light response is. The team paired math models with light tests across solvent types.

Broad solvent pull ruled soak bands, while set bonds like hydrogen links ruled glow traits. Strong hydrogen bonds boosted the bent-light response. Low-grade bent response tracked high-grade response in the same way. The team says first-grade reads can flag high-grade worth, and these compounds may suit light tool design.
pmc-11533297:
Jingya Wang, Yijun Chen, Hongmin Zhang, and Jinghua Zhang survey rural doctors in China about plans to leave their jobs, in work from 2024. A state program trains doctors for rural posts with free tuition. Many of its graduates still plan to leave, even though ongoing training is seen as a way to keep them.

The survey reached more than thirteen hundred graduates working in rural posts in one province. It measured how strongly each doctor meant to leave and what factors predicted a high score. The study sits in the years after COVID-19, which strained rural care. Findings can guide steps that help keep trained doctors in villages.
pmc-11534897:
Jiao Deng and co-authors grew paired mini-tumors from a bowel cancer and its satellite deposit, in a 2024 study. Tumor deposits are a distinct form of spread in colorectal cancer, and no good lab models of them existed. The team built organoids, small self-organized tissue balls, from both the main tumor and a matched deposit of a forty-six-year-old patient.

Deposit-derived cells grew, invaded, and spread more aggressively than the main tumor's cells, and they carried more stem-like protein marks. They also resisted two standard chemotherapy drugs more strongly. Their gene activity pointed to ramped-up fat making, and blocking fat synthesis restored drug sensitivity. The authors offer the paired organoids as tools for studying spread and drug resistance, and fat metabolism as a target worth testing.
pmc-11534997:
Assefa Desalew and co-authors compare quality of life among children in eastern Ethiopia in a 2024 survey study. Some children live in areas that once housed leprosy settlements. Families there may face lasting hardship. The team asked whether these children report worse health related quality of life than children in other areas, and what factors link to better or worse scores.

The study covered 515 children aged 8 to 18 in two districts. Children and parents both answered a standard quality of life survey. By the children's own reports, scores were lower in the former settlement areas. About one in four children there had poor quality of life. Schooling, face washing, and freedom from tropical diseases linked to higher scores. A past tropical disease and a lack of hand washing facilities linked to lower scores.
pmc-11536897:
Xuyang Meng and nine co-authors linked a blood index of insulin resistance to death in hospital for heart patients, in a study from twenty twenty-four. The index blends fat and sugar measures from a routine blood draw. The question was whether it predicts in-hospital death for people with coronary artery disease, and whether the answer depends on their sugar status.

Patients were split into thirds by the index, and classed as normal, pre-diabetic, or diabetic. The highest third carried more than double the death risk of the lowest, after full adjustment. In subgroup checks, the link held clearly for diabetic patients. The authors offer the index as a cheap predictor, above all for those with diabetes.
pmc-11537697:
Sarah Malecki and three colleagues present a 2024 commentary on a care cliff in Canada. Children with complex genetic and developmental conditions now survive into adulthood, but the adult system has no equivalent of the team-based pediatric clinics that carried them. These patients are few, yet they consume a third of pediatric care spending, and their families absorb the gap when services vanish.

The authors propose transplanting the pediatric model: interprofessional adult clinics for the highest-need patients, easing pressure on families and family doctors. They also urge wider genetic testing for eligible adults still lacking a cause for their condition, and population data that follow genetic diseases across the lifespan. Better data, they argue, would let care anticipate rather than react.
pmc-11538497:
Paul Stammer and co-authors test whether fragments of a vessel-lining protein could flag dangerous aortic disease. The protein, VE-cadherin, glues the cells of the vessel wall together, and enzymes can snip off pieces that float in the blood when the wall is inflamed. The team grew human aortic lining cells, triggered the snipping, and measured fragment levels in patients.

In the dish, an inflammation signal set the cutting enzymes ADAM10 and ADAM17 to work and made the cell layer leakier. In blood samples, though, fragment levels in patients with torn or swollen aortas matched those in other patient groups. Those groups had neck artery narrowing or varicose veins. So the fragments do not single out aortic disease. Levels did rise and fall with the inflammation signal and with ADAM10 itself, most tightly in chronic tears, backing the mechanism if not the marker.
pmc-11539197:
Piero Agostinone and co-authors measure, in a 2024 study, how the knee's side ligaments stretch during a squat before and after cruciate ligament surgery. A torn front cruciate throws off the whole knee's mechanics. The partner ligaments share loads differently in its absence.

Sixteen patients, average age about twenty-five, performed single-leg squats under imaging. Length changes of the inner, outer, and rear ligaments were tracked. Magnetic resonance scans of the injured knee fed the analysis. Reconstruction aims to restore not one ligament but the ensemble's choreography. Knowing how the medial ligament's stretch pattern shifts could refine rehabilitation exercises after surgery.
pmc-11542497:
Yvette Hus and Osnat Segal review suicide among Indigenous youth in Canada in this 2024 paper. Suicide rates are high among Indigenous peoples worldwide. The review focuses on young people and young adults in Canada who face deep poverty and poor services.

The authors use ideas from transcultural psychiatry and a theory of suicide to frame the problem. Remote towns, a history of exclusion, and thin health and school resources all play a part. Low literacy and weak schooling feed hopelessness and raise risk. The paper also covers joint efforts by Indigenous groups and Canadian authorities. A literacy plan is proposed as one step toward change.
pmc-11548097:
Fangjie Wei and co-authors build an online inspection system for electric car seats, in an engineering paper from 2024. As electric cars spread, seat noise has become a prime source of cabin noise. Checking seats off the line by hand slows output and splits the checks into steps.

The system, built with LabVIEW software, tests seat noise and electrical functions at the same time on the line. Boards gather noise data while a controller runs the seat motor so its current can be read. A supervisor computer charts the data, judges it, and stores results for lookup. In real use, the line cycle time improved by 34.84 percent. Each seat took under 86 seconds to check, and faulty motors were caught fast.
pmc-11556797:
Cataract surgery is the world's most common operation, and busy clinics watch every minute of the workflow. Shetty and co-authors ran a time-and-motion study at two high-volume Indian eye hospitals. They compared the usual electronic record workflow with a digital one that links measurement devices, a planning tool, and the operating room. They timed each step for eighty-five surgeries and counted the data fields typed and the staff involved.

The digital workflow cut measurement time by about a quarter, planning time by more than half, and the procedure itself by about a fifth. Total surgery time fell from roughly 1,271 seconds to 887 seconds, with less spread between cases. Fewer fields had to be entered and fewer support staff were needed at both sites. The authors argue that full digital links can make cataract care faster and more standard.
pmc-11568097:
Hyun Sook Jin, Seung Hyun Oh, and Byung Soo Chang examine the metal and grime on needles used for semi-permanent makeup, in a study from 2024. Cosmetic tattooing is booming, and needle quality bears directly on skin safety. Microscopy can reveal what the eye misses.

A five-round shader needle was imaged by electron microscopy and its elements mapped by X-ray spectroscopy, comparing fresh and distorted tips. A good rounded tip measured about seven micrometers wide, while a deformed one was more than twice as thick. Rosette-shaped lead particles, four to five micrometers across, clung near welds and shafts. The authors blame grinding and polishing in manufacture and urge strict inspection.
pmc-11574097:
Shannon Marchal and co-authors review, in a 2024 paper, what space flight does to the human immune system. The defenses of the body were shaped on Earth over a long span of time. Space adds strain: more radiation, odd gravity, tight quarters, and stress far from home. Proof grows that crews show changed defenses, with more swelling signals in the body, old dormant viruses waking, and shifts in cell-based defense.

At the same time, germs in space can grow more harmful and harder to kill with drugs. Both shifts raise the risk on long trips. The authors doubt the body can adapt in the short spans of near-term missions. They argue the main risks must be met head on first, with shields, care plans, and close health checks for crews.
pmc-11574197:
Chiara Longo and four co-authors use network analysis to study thinking problems in Parkinson's disease. Some patients keep clear thinking while others develop mild cognitive impairment, and the team asked whether the links among mental skills shift as the condition sets in.

They gave a detailed test battery to 275 patients and split them into two groups: 171 with unimpaired thinking and 104 with mild impairment. Treating each test as a node in a network, they found the impaired group's network looked denser, with some links between skills weakened. The authors read this as a sign of reorganization, where the mind may work around failing links to keep functioning.
pmc-11574497:
Arne Jordan and seventeen co-authors report results from the CLIMATE pilot study in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Hot weather is growing more common, and people with chronic diseases face real risks from heat, so the study asked whether what patients do to protect themselves matches how they actually feel.

The team followed primary care patients through a warm season, combining local weather data with repeated online surveys on the hottest days. They linked heat levels and self-reported protective behavior, along with attitudes and confidence, to reported health complaints. The study tests whether asking patients what they do is a reliable guide for doctors planning heat advice, a question that matters more as heat waves reach cooler countries.
pmc-11574997:
Amanda Deaves and six co-authors review, in 2024 work, how students and teachers view new models for therapy training posts. In hand and body therapy, one-to-one posts rule, which caps how many posts schools can offer. New models, such as shared or group posts, must grow if the fields are to train enough staff.

Sixteen studies fed the review, which sorted views from both sides. Students told of growth in skill and self, gains from learning with peers, and strain from unclear roles and new settings. Teachers spoke of giving the right back-up, of pride in their role, and of joy in the peer mix. The team urges schools to plan support that meets those strains, so new models can widen post counts.
pmc-11576097:
Khairunnisa Che Ghazali and colleagues share lessons from operating on blocked bowels in patients with severe lung hypertension. Their case series from twenty twenty-four reports three patients. High lung pressure makes general anaesthesia very risky. Bowel obstruction still forces emergency decisions regardless.

One man with Eisenmenger syndrome had part of his colon removed. He died six days after the operation. A second Eisenmenger patient had a stoma-forming procedure. He died after a month of heart and lung complications. A third case completes the institutional experience reported. Anaesthetic and surgical strategies differed across the cases. The series aims to improve the next patient's odds.
pmc-11576597:
Dandan Xu and co-authors run a trial of remote exercise rehab in a 2024 paper. Heart patients often drop exercise programs over time, above all when stuck at home. The trial used a behavior model delivered through a chat app and wrist trackers to keep patients active after a stent procedure.

About one hundred forty-seven patients were split between the remote program and standard guidance. At one and three months, the remote group hit their exercise day and length goals far more often. Their drive, planning, and effort scores also ran higher, while anxiety about the process and outcome fell. Trends over time favored the program on most measures. The authors back the model for home-based heart rehab.
pmc-11576797:

pmc-11577097:

pmc-11577597:

pmc-11578497:

pmc-11579597:

pmc-11583897:

pmc-11585597:

pmc-11586397:

pmc-11587697:

pmc-11588397:

pmc-11588997:

pmc-11589597:

pmc-11591197:

pmc-11591697:

pmc-11591897:

pmc-11593597:

pmc-11606397:

pmc-11607797:

pmc-11608497:

pmc-11609697:
Tomáš Hanousek and co-authors free a vast look up library for forest light reads in a 2024 paper. Reading tree traits from sky light needs a rich match library. Past sets were thin in sites, times, and shapes.

Their set holds millions of leaf and canopy mixes for Central European broadleaf woods. Light reads span the visible to the short infrared in fine steps. Two files split mean scene light from sunlit leaf light alone. Sun angles vary across the set for real world match. Learning models can train on the set to read traits at scale.
pmc-11609997:
Yanli Wang and ten co-authors report a 2024 study of a new mutation in the MYO15A gene that caused sensorineural hearing loss. The gene is a common cause of severe deafness, in forms that start before or after a child learns to speak.

The variant was found in a Chinese Uighur family with inherited hearing loss that is not tied to other ills. To test its effect, the team made stem cells from the patient and from a kin member with no mutation. Those cells were grown into hair cell-like cells. The mutant cells stood apart in shape and work, which backs the variant as the cause.
pmc-11610297:
Richa Gupta and six colleagues train a gradient-boosted model to forecast how fast ALS will progress in a patient, in a 2024 paper. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis steals speech, movement, and breathing at rates that vary wildly between people. Clinicians need early warning of fast courses to plan care.

Fifty patients' clinical features, including speech, mobility, and breathing scores, fed an XGBoost regression aimed at the standard functional rating scale. The model's error was low on both training and held-out data, with near-perfect fit statistics on the test split. The authors present it as a practical tracking tool for clinics. The tiny sample invites caution, and they frame the work as a demonstration rather than a deployable instrument. Even so, the accuracy achieved on routine clinical features suggests progression carries more signal than clinicians usually extract.
pmc-11610697:
João Pedro Fontenelle and five colleagues published a 2024 genetics study of the eastern spruce budworm, a moth whose larvae defoliate North American boreal forests. Budworm outbreaks erupt across huge areas, changing forest ecology and hitting the timber economy. Outbreaks involve rapid growth in numbers and in the connections between populations.

The team characterized the genotypes of outbreaking populations in Quebec and neighboring regions over multiple years. Genetic data reveal whether outbreaks spread from a few source populations or ignite independently in many places. They also show how connectivity changes as an outbreak rises and falls. Such knowledge helps forecast where future outbreaks will move and how severely forests will be affected.
pmc-11611197:
Meng Lin and co-authors study what residents think of extra paid services from housing managers after the pandemic, in a paper from 2024. Managers have shifted toward add on services at the block level, such as health help, food and fun options, classes, and tailored aid. The team grounds the survey in two theories of choice and checks how views of basic service shape views of the add ons.

Residents showed much warmer views of add on services than before, above all for health, daily life perks, and classes. Contentment with basic service also lifted views of add ons by an inner path. The authors say trust built on core work opens the door to new income from extras that residents truly value.
pmc-11612297:
Katrina Jackson and co-authors link single-letter gene changes to how deadly strains of a fungal pathogen prove in mice. Their 2024 study concerns Cryptococcus neoformans, a yeast that attacks people with weak immunity. Doctors had noticed that one strain family tracks with worse patient outcomes, without knowing which gene differences drive it.

Pooling four genome studies pointed to shared gene regions tied to virulence. The team then tested a close family of clinical strains in mice and found four patterns, from extra-deadly to typical disease in or outside the brain. Pinpointing the variant sites behind those patterns gives drug and vaccine work a genetic map of fungal danger.
pmc-11612497:
Xueting Yang and co-authors study how families moved out of poverty in the mountains of southwest China settle into new homes, in a 2024 paper. A national program moved households from harsh Yi minority areas to new sites. Whether families thrive after the move shapes both their own futures and the land around the new sites.

Surveys feed a model of how outside shocks, coping skills, and outcomes link. Follow-up support policies prove to be the strongest help, lifting outcomes directly and by boosting learning and self-organization. Worry about risk pulls the other way, weakening the buffer families can fall back on. Village and town sites gain in different ways, and longer-settled families gain more from support. The work shows that help after the move matters as much as the move itself.
pmc-11613097:
Eight authors, led by Yanfang Liu, report a 2024 study of how a long non-coding RNA drives liver cancer growth. Tumors rewire their energy use, and that rewiring is now a target for new drugs. A snag is that energy enzymes work in normal cells too, so drugs can harm healthy tissue.

The RNA in focus is called LINC01419, and glucose switches it on in hepatocellular carcinoma cells. The team found that it speeds tumor growth and spread by reshaping sugar use in the cell. It works by binding a protein called YBX1. That binding steadies the message for PDK1, a key enzyme in the sugar pathway. With more of that enzyme, the cancer's glycolytic pathway runs harder. Because such RNAs can be specific to cancer, the authors see them as promising drug targets.
pmc-11613397:
Xuefei Zhang, Shan Gao, and Shuya Wei test, in a 2024 study, whether broad, whole-person nursing care improves outcomes for older patients with long-term heart failure. Such patients face weak hearts, low mood, and poor life quality at once. Records for 120 patients at one hospital were split by the nursing style they had received.

After care, both groups felt less anxious and low, but the broad-care group did better on mood scores. They also followed their drug plans more faithfully, at eighty-five percent versus seventy. Heart pumping and chamber sizes improved in both groups, more so under broad care. The authors back broad nursing as a way to lift both body and mind outcomes.
pmc-11613797:
Gaetano Gallo and co-authors present a 2024 protocol for the CHORMES trial, testing a natural drug preparation against acute haemorrhoid flare-ups. Haemorrhoidal disease burdens health systems and drags down quality of life. The drug, mesoglycan, is a mixture of natural sugar chains from animal tissue that thins clots and helps dissolve them, properties suited to a swollen, thrombosed flare.

The phase 2 trial runs double-blind at two Italian centres, so neither patients nor doctors know who gets the drug. Adults aged eighteen to seventy-five with mild to moderate internal disease, or an external clot, are assigned by chance to treatment or placebo. The protocol sets out the relief measures that will judge success.
pmc-11614497:
Skin cancers other than the deep pigment kind are the most common cancers in the world, and a layer-by-layer surgery clears them with care. Ahmad Berjawi, Namir Saade, and Zeina Tannous report cases of that surgery from a large center in Lebanon, in work from twenty twenty-four. Charts covered near one hundred patients and more than one hundred tumor cases.

Most patients were men, and most were over sixty years old. Tumors were small on the whole, and return rates were near zero for first-time tumors. Large tumors linked to male sex and to low- or mid-risk body zones. Side effects stayed rare. The report gives rare data from the region and backs the surgery as safe and strong there.
pmc-11614997:
Najdaghi and co-authors review tiny membrane bubbles released by cells and their roles in brain and nerve disorders. Such vesicles are shed by many cell types and float in blood, urine, and spinal fluid. Their 2024 review covers the history and traits of these particles, and what they may signal or do in the central nervous system.

Particles in spinal fluid may flag risk for conditions such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Their cargo shifts across disease stages, which could aid diagnosis and tracking. The review also weighs hard problems: isolating the particles cleanly, and their double edged roles in the brain. The authors give practical guidance for future studies of these particles as treatments.
pmc-11615097:
Tanner May and co-authors compare in 2024 two imaging methods for finding tooth and jaw structures in dogs. One method is standard dental X-ray, and the other is a newer layered imaging method. Both were used on sixteen dog cadaver heads, and scorers rated how well each method showed thirty five set structures, and at what quality.

Neither method won overall. Each was better for certain structures, and the view direction also mattered. The authors conclude that the newer method is a suitable tool for identifying specific structures in the dog skull. Readers in veterinary dentistry get a practical guide to when each approach is likely to help most.
pmc-11616297:
Di Huang and six co-authors grade the proof linking gum disease to illness in the rest of the body, in a 2024 paper. Many reviews have taken up the link, often on the same ground, and their worth varies. The team searched four big databases and kept reviews that treated gum disease as the exposure and body illness as the outcome.

Fifty-seven reviews made the cut, spanning 75 diseases. Two thirds of the outcomes tied to gum disease with clear signal, with head and neck cancer showing the highest odds. Yet the grading was grim: nearly three quarters of the reviews rated critically low in method quality, and only a tenth reached moderate. The link looks broad and real, the authors say, but the proof base needs better craft.
pmc-11618097:
Wang and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a deep learning tool that cleans noisy voltage imaging of brain cells. Voltage imaging films electrical activity, but signals are weak and noisy. Older cleaning methods assume rigid patterns for signal and noise. The team's method, CellMincer, learns from the data itself with no labels. It hides sparse pixels and predicts them from short time windows nearby.

Precomputed patterns of space and time correlation guide the cleaning. A physics-based simulator created realistic fake data for tuning. That guidance tripled the signal gain in their tests. On real data checked against direct electrical recordings, CellMincer recovered signals faithfully. It beat rival methods on signal strength and consistency. Workflows using it found neurons and activity peaks more reliably.
pmc-11618197:
Katewadee Boonyapakron and a large team engineered a heat-loving enzyme in two thousand twenty-four that breaks down xylan, a plant fibre, at near-boiling heat. Such enzymes serve food, feed, biofuel, and pulp work. Starting from an enzyme found in a bagasse pile's microbes, they added two changes by rational design.

The new enzyme works best at eighty-five degrees and lasts far longer at ninety, with a melting point above ninety-three. It turned xylan into prebiotic sugars with sharp selectivity and a tenfold yield gain over its parent. Simulations tied the gains to stronger internal bonds and a new kind of weak interaction that fires more often.
pmc-11618297:
Pathologists read tissue slides by eye, a slow craft that depends on scarce experts. Jiahui Yu and co-authors propose handing much of that labor to large AI models. Their task-driven framework pairs strong visual analysis with real-time control of the microscope itself. The system does not just label a finished scan. It adapts as it looks.

The team proved the concept on liver tissue slides stained for routine diagnosis. The framework handled the adaptive analysis end to end. The authors present it as a template for the next generation of microscopes: instruments that decide where to look and what to measure while the slide is still on the stage. That shift could make digital pathology faster and more consistent.
pmc-11618497:
Nelly Banda and seven co-authors trace how lead harm passes across mouse breeds, split by sex and by which parent was dosed. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Lead is known to hurt fertility, pregnancy, and child brain growth. Mice breathe leaded soil for weeks, then breed in four mixes of dosed and clean parents.

Conception falls with dose, worst when both parents are dosed. Testis gene reads pin the drop on oxidative stress. Pups of dosed parents fare worse in maze and balance tests, with harm that turns on which parent was dosed and on pup sex. A dosed father's harm lands hardest on daughters, with brain gene shifts to match.
pmc-11618597:
Wu and five co-authors hardened a coded radio system against fading in this paper from twenty twenty-four. Polar codes paired with OFDM, the multicarrier scheme behind modern wireless, suffer on multipath channels. Echoes make some subcarriers noisy and others clean, and errors arrive in bursts. Two fixes are proposed and simulated.

First, each subcarrier's channel quality is fed into the decoder's soft information. That tells the decoder which bits to trust less.
