Second, an interleaver shuffles the coded bits so bursts scatter into isolated errors. Together the two strategies beat the conventional setup by a wide margin. The authors call both essential for future polar-OFDM systems.
pmc-11619097:
Morgan Jibowu and co-authors map a common mosquito in Harris County, Texas, in work from two thousand twenty-four. The mosquito can spread West Nile virus, so health teams need to know where it clusters. The team used trap counts from two thousand twenty to two thousand twenty-two and mapped them by place.

High counts clustered in central Houston and the north-west of the county. Some of the oldest city areas stayed high across the years. Counts also rose in areas with more social hardship, which the authors link to the built setting. Maps like these can guide spraying and watch efforts.
pmc-11619297:
Ruoqi Zhang, Jiawei Chen, Mengru Wang, Zhengrong Chen, and Hongpeng Sun link dirty air to child hospital stays in Suzhou, China, in a 2024 study. Short bursts of bad air are known to stir lung illness in children. The team checked six years of local data to pin down which parts of the air did the harm.

Records held 13,408 children sent to hospital with lung illness from 2017 to 2022. Each child's bad days were matched with their own calm days to cut bias. Five air factors tracked with more stays, from fine dust to gases from fuel and smoke. School-age children and boys showed the strongest ties. The COVID years were checked as a side test.
pmc-11619497:
Philip Rosenthal, a medical researcher, reflects in a 2024 essay on a visit to refugee settlements in northern Uganda, near the war zone in South Sudan. He had traveled there to plan malaria research with Ugandan and American colleagues. What struck him was how calm and orderly daily life in the camp appeared.

Shops sold food and phone time, homes were kept neat, and fields were well tended. Families fleeing war were given care, shelter, and a chance to restart their lives. Rosenthal contrasts this quiet success with the strain seen in far richer countries. At the border post, though, new arrivals still looked anxious, carrying little and facing checks for illness.
pmc-11619797:
Diana Isabel Cáceres Rivera and co-authors check which signs truly define a nursing diagnosis of activity intolerance. Their 2024 study covers 111 hospital patients with acute coronary syndrome. The diagnosis is used when a patient's heart cannot meet the body's demands during effort.

Nurses rated each candidate sign with standard scales, working on their own. Three signs appeared in most patients: general weakness, discomfort on exertion, and changes on the heart tracing. Agreement between raters ran from fair to perfect. The authors say the check grounds the diagnosis in evidence. It should help nurses in coronary units shape care plans with more confidence in daily coronary care across the unit.
pmc-11621797:
Min Wang and four co-authors review gene-carrying printed scaffolds for cartilage repair in a 2024 paper. Damaged joint cartilage barely heals, leaving pain and stiffness. A scaffold that also delivers healing genes could coax long-term repair, keeping the genes in place, releasing them slowly, and losing few along the way.

The catch is shape: natural cartilage has a layered gradient the scaffold must imitate. Three-dimensional bioprinting can build that complexity layer by layer. The review gathers recent work combining gene-activated matrices with printed scaffolds for cartilage engineering. It weighs what has been shown in the lab, what remains unproven, and where the hard problems sit, from gene dosing to mechanical strength. The authors aim the summary at researchers designing the next generation of implants. Their closing message is that printing precision and gene delivery must mature together.
pmc-11622997:
Amri and colleagues analyze in 2024 how World Health Organization texts talk about health equity, and whether the talk matches the stated approach. They used critical discourse analysis on health promotion, social determinants, and urban health documents spanning several years. The organization usually compares groups when measuring equity. It names three approaches to equity, though the texts imply more.

Socioeconomic status got far more attention than other determinants. The authors warn that the mismatch favors short-term fixes over root causes. They argue attention to power explains why bolder approaches stay unspoken in texts governments must accept.
pmc-11623097:
Diabetes sharply raises the danger of peripheral artery disease, multiplying the risks of severe limb ischemia and amputation. Qiaoqiao Li and co-authors hunt for genes that cause the combined condition, using genetic methods that separate causation from mere linkage. They combined large genome studies of the disease with data on gene activity in blood.

Three genes passed their tests: DENND5B, C4A, and CYP21A2. A further analysis tied DENND5B and the disease to the same single genetic variant, strengthening the case that the gene helps drive the illness rather than just traveling with it. The authors present these genes as leads for understanding how diabetes damages leg arteries and as possible targets for future treatments.
pmc-11623197:
Muthuramalingam Sivakumar, Sudhaman Parthasarathy, and Thiyagarajan Padmapriya propose a scoring method in a 2024 paper on machine learning efficiency. Speed and memory matter when models must run on tight hardware or in real time, yet efficiency is often judged by feel. Their framework turns raw measures into one composite score.

Training time, prediction time, memory use, and resource load are gathered, scaled, and weighted by a structured ranking method. The framework was tried on medical image data and on crop prediction data. In the medical case it rewarded robustness; in farming, scalability. The authors offer the score as a shared yardstick for picking and tuning algorithms across fields with unlike demands.
pmc-11623797:
Michael Zouari and Zeev Shtudiner compared how Jewish and Muslim students in Israel choose their field of study. They combined surveys with a conjoint analysis, which forces trade-offs between factors such as pay, interest, and advice. The two groups weighed the choice differently. Muslim students scored higher on individualism and gave more weight to prior work experience and to teachers' influence. Jewish students put earning potential first.

The authors argue these gaps reflect culture, social setting, and economics acting together, not taste alone. They call for education policies and support systems that respond to each group's needs and aims. Inclusive mentoring and career guidance, for example, might stress different things for different students. The study adds evidence that field choice in mixed societies is socially patterned. The authors suggest future work should cover more ethnic groups and track how early choices shape later mobility.
pmc-11624597:
Ulrich Kaiser and four co-authors ask whether careful antibiotic use fits home-based end-of-life care. Their 2024 study works in German SAPV teams, who serve the sickest tenth of such patients at home. Most have cancer, and infections strike often. Drugs are often given with little proof they help.

Fifteen experts gave recorded interviews on the topic. They saw clear gains: safer drug choices and better days for patients. A steady program, though, looked hard to run in this setting. It would need backup from hospital systems and more staff training. Comfort-focused care and drug discipline can coexist, the experts suggest. Groundwork must come first, though, before rules can bite.
pmc-11624697:
Maud Muosieyiri and four colleagues tested whether Mozambique's expanded checklist finds more maternal near-miss cases than the World Health Organization's original tool. A near miss means a woman nearly died from pregnancy complications but survived; counting them exposes health system failures. Mozambique's abstraction tool adds clinical criteria to the WHO version. The cross-sectional study enrolled 2,057 women at two referral hospitals in Inhambane province during twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-two.

Both tools were applied to the same admissions, and sociodemographic effects on case identification were examined. Extra criteria only help if they catch real cases the standard tool misses, without flooding counts with false ones. Where records are paper-thin and staff scarce, the abstraction tool chosen shapes what the system can learn from its worst outcomes. This twenty twenty-four evaluation gives Mozambique evidence for keeping, trimming, or exporting its modification.
pmc-11625897:
Sofiah Hanis Ahmad Hisham and co-authors set out how anatomy education at Universiti Sains Malaysia changed in the COVID-19 pandemic, and after it. Their 2024 piece frames the crisis as a chance to build teaching that holds up more well.

Plans took in blended learning and tools made more strong by technology. They also took in practical sessions centred on students, and more strong formative assessment. Resources in digital form joined teaching in person. Those took in a virtual anatomy museum and quizzes on histology on the web. Practical classes were made anew, round joint work, teaching by peers, and skills in how to talk with others. Feedback that kept up at all times backed learning that went on. The team reports a better grasp of anatomical concepts. They also report better emotional well-being. Lessons from the pandemic now guide how they plan for breaks in teaching to come.
pmc-11628297:
Fujia Wu and co-authors test how warming changes seed sprouting in an invasive grass in a 2024 study. Spartina alterniflora is a salt marsh grass that has spread along China's coast across three climate zones. Its seeds sprout better after a spell of cold, called stratification. Warming is now changing how much cold seeds get in each zone.

Seeds came from nine sites and were sown in three shared gardens at distinct latitudes, with and without four months of cold storage. Cold storage made sprouting fast, full, and early, and warmth magnified those gains. The pattern split by origin. Seeds from cooler zones gained more from cold storage as gardens warmed. Seeds from the tropics gained less. The authors say cooler-zone plants may push north for the cold they need, while tropical spread south may stall.
pmc-11628597:
Yaoping Shi and co-authors test a drug pair for liver cancer that stopped responding in a 2024 trial report. A standard first-line drug often loses effect over time. Earlier lab work suggested adding a second drug could break that resistance in tumors rich in a certain growth receptor.

Thirty patients whose cancer progressed on the first drug joined the single-arm study. All had tumors with high levels of the target receptor. Nine patients saw confirmed partial shrinkage of their tumors. Side effects were common but familiar, led by fatigue, rash, and diarrhea. Appetite loss affected two fifths of the group. The early signal supports larger trials of the pairing in this selected patient group.
pmc-11628997:
Brazilian teenagers say they want to help guard each other's mental health, but they do not want the job dumped on them alone. Josimar Antônio de Alcântara Mendes and co-authors report a co-produced 2024 study with 46 adolescents aged fifteen to eighteen across Brazil. Interviews and focus groups, run with a youth collaborator, fed a thematic analysis.

Four themes emerged. The teens felt real duty toward friends and community, yet insisted adults must share the work. Their ideas ran from quiet, non-judgemental listening to school groups acting together. Many felt they lacked the skills and confidence to help well. Others said stigma and adults who brush them off keep them silent. The authors call for peer support training and true youth-adult partnerships that treat young people as partners, not mascots.
pmc-11629097:
Ling Wu and co-authors build a paired immune therapy for colon cancer in a 2024 paper. Checkpoint drugs help some cancers, but colon cancer gains little from them. Many colon tumors start with cuts to a gene called APC, which may shape their immune scene.

In mice bred to carry the cut gene, the team mapped immune cells in tumors. A checkpoint called VISTA stood out on those cells. A gene editor called METTL3 sat in the same path. Pairing drugs that hit this axis may wake immune attack in a tumor type that shrugs off current care. Tests in grafted tumors round out the mouse work.
pmc-11629197:
Wang and ten colleagues build an injectable gel that attacks bone cancer with copper and heat in twenty twenty-four. Osteosarcoma mainly strikes the young and often ends poorly. A newly found cell death type, cuproptosis, offers a fresh angle. Their gel combines copper ions with the drug vorinostat.

Copper targets the cell's energy cycle to trigger cuproptosis. Vorinostat blocks gene silencing enzymes and generates reactive oxygen. Together they raise a key protein that amplifies the copper effect. Light based heating adds a further attack. Injected into rat tumors, the gel partly erased the cancer without spread. The authors see a path toward clinical use of cuproptosis therapy.
pmc-11629497:
Tuning a machine learning model's settings can quietly cheat: search hard enough and the settings fit the test data's noise. Igor Tetko, Ruud van Deursen, and Guillaume Godin demonstrated in 2024 this trap in drug solubility prediction.

Re-examining seven datasets, they showed heavy tuning often failed to beat preset settings, while costing about ten thousand times more compute. Their own entrant, a transformer model reading molecule strings as language, beat graph-based rivals in twenty-six of twenty-eight comparisons, in a fraction of the time. Their moral: preset settings travel safer, and fair comparisons demand identical scoring measures.
pmc-11629697:
Babies born with a heart defect called tetralogy of Fallot need surgery that opens the path from the heart to the lungs. Akira Yamaguchi and co-authors, in a 2024 review, weigh four ways to rebuild that path. The classic patch can leave the lung valve leaking for years, so surgeons have tried ways to spare or rebuild the valve.

The team pooled thirty-four studies with close to nine thousand patients in a network review. The plain patch carried the highest leak risk over time. Sparing the valve cut deaths after surgery and time on a breathing machine. A patch with a new valve built in lowered leak risk both early and late. Length of intensive care and later deaths looked much the same across groups, so the choice turns on valve outcomes.
pmc-11630597:
Slob and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a cost study of a kidney drug in the Netherlands. The drug empagliflozin slowed chronic kidney disease in a large recent trial. Whether it is worth its price in Dutch care was unknown. The team built a simulation that follows patients through kidney disease stages. It compared standard care alone with standard care plus the drug. Inputs came from the trial, national cost data, and published sources.

Adding the drug saved money overall in their model. Patients also gained more than a year of life on average. Quality-adjusted life years rose by a similar margin. Checks that varied the inputs kept the same conclusion. The authors call the drug a dominant option, meaning better and cheaper. The result held regardless of diabetes status.
pmc-11630697:
Kai Cao, Xu-Yuan Quan, and Yan Hou review how patient-reported outcome tools are built and judged. Their 2024 paper sits inside patient-focused drug development, a movement that makes patients partners in research. Such tools let patients report symptoms and daily function in their own words. Regulators in the United States, China, and Europe now weigh these reports in drug decisions.

The review walks through the whole path of a tool: framing its concept, drafting questions, and testing them. It then covers how regulators review the tools and use them in approvals. In the United States, every qualified outcome tool so far is patient-reported. The authors lay out what developers must show for a tool to count. Their guide links careful tool design to sound regulatory choices.
pmc-11630997:
Ran Jia and four co-authors used gene data to test links between gut microbes, immune traits, and growths in the female genital tract, in a 2024 study. Such growths, called polyps, are common but their causes are murky. The team used a method that treats gene variants as natural experiments. Data came from large gene studies and a gut microbe consortium.

Twelve microbe groups and thirty-one immune traits showed causal links to the polyps. Four full paths ran from a microbe through an immune trait to the polyps. A ranking method placed five microbe groups and six immune traits at the top. The authors conclude gut microbes can sway polyp risk on their own. Immune cells appear to carry part of that effect. The findings suggest new leads for prevention research.
pmc-11631597:
Xinsheng Yan, Huali Fu, Wenjun Deng, Zhenlu Zhang, and Dong Wang present six cases of a bird-borne pneumonia that standard tests kept missing, in this 2024 case series. The disease, psittacosis, comes from a bacterium spread by birds and poultry. Its symptoms and scans look like many other lung infections, so doctors often cannot name it without a direct test for the germ.

All six patients arrived in the first half of 2023 with fever, cough, and chest tightness. Routine lab work and imaging failed to find the cause. A targeted gene sequencing test on lung wash fluid finally flagged the bacterium in each case. Treatment was adjusted at once, and every patient did well. The authors praise the test as fast, accurate, and fairly cheap.
pmc-11632097:
Madhav Chaturvedi and fifteen colleagues published a framework paper in two thousand twenty-four on testing for new infections during outbreaks. When a new germ spreads, tests must be built and checked fast. Yet disease levels and the germ itself keep changing, which makes accuracy hard to pin down.

Drawing on lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic, the authors propose one joined-up framework. It links three parts in a loop: measuring test accuracy, modelling for public health choices, and the effects of control measures. Each part feeds the others as the outbreak shifts. The authors argue this loop lets future testing platforms serve both patient care and public health better than working in separate steps.
pmc-11632397:
Suad Shamis and co-authors hunted for gene patterns tied to low oxygen in a hard-to-treat breast cancer in this 2024 study. The cancer type lacks the oestrogen receptor, so hormone drugs do not work on it. The team focused on a protein called CAIX, which rises when tumors lack oxygen.

They stained tumor samples from 191 patients and profiled the gene activity of the CAIX-high ones. High CAIX in the cell body marked patients more likely to see the cancer return. Gene tests flagged a small set of genes whose activity shifted with oxygen lack. Two of them work together on the matrix that holds cells in place. The results point to new markers for judging risk.
pmc-11632997:
Fangxu Yin and seven co-authors built web-based tools in 2024 to predict survival for thyroid cancer patients whose cancer has spread to the lungs. This group faces poor odds, and doctors need a clearer way to judge each patient's outlook when planning care.

The team drew on records for 679 patients from a large United States cancer database and checked their tools against 48 patients from two hospitals in China. They used a standard risk model to find which traits shaped survival, then built chart-like predictors for overall survival and for death from the cancer itself. Tests of accuracy and fit showed the tools scored well, and the web format lets doctors use them at the point of care.
pmc-11633297:
Liangliang Gao and co-authors test a way to stop the muscle jerks that a sleep drug can trigger. Etomidate puts patients under fast, but it often sets off myoclonus, a burst of jerking. The trial asked whether a small dose of a cousin drug, esketamine, given first could calm that side effect. One hundred adults set for surgery took part.

Half got the small dose and half got plain salt water, two minutes before the sleep drug. Jerks struck far fewer patients in the drug group, and the worst grades of jerking also fell. Blood pressure and heart rate stayed alike in both groups. Side effects such as dizziness were no more common with the added drug.
pmc-11633997:
Fange Meng and Xin Wen ask whether education can offset the drag of an aging population in China in a 2024 paper. Falling births and longer lives shrink the workforce and raise care burdens, threatening growth.

Both more schooling and better schooling softened the harm from aging, the authors find. Threshold tests sharpen the picture: once average schooling passes about ten point nine years, and once teacher density passes a set mark, education's protection grows stronger. The pattern held in China's east and west but not its center. In the north, only the amount of schooling helped, while in the south both amount and quality worked. Suggested policy: raise teacher numbers and lengthen free schooling.
pmc-11634597:
He Bai and co-authors link a gut-made compound in blood to mild memory loss in rural Chinese adults. Their 2024 study draws on a large health survey in one county, with more than fifteen hundred adults free of brain disease at the start. The compound, made when gut germs work on certain foods, was read in blood along with its three food-based sources. Memory state was scored with a known test made for low schooling levels.

About a third of the group showed mild loss. People in the top band for the compound and for each source faced higher odds of mild loss than those in low bands. Two sources showed a bent curve, where risk rose at both ends less than in the middle ranges.
pmc-11635997:
Mari Myhrstad and nine colleagues published a 2024 study hunting for early warning markers of type 2 diabetes in healthy people. Type 2 diabetes is spreading worldwide, driven by excess weight, inactivity, and poor diet. The gut microbiota, the community of microbes in the intestine, also influences how the body handles sugar.

Because the disease is preventable, early markers of risk are valuable. The researchers examined healthy individuals and explored how gut microbes, physical activity, and metabolic markers relate to each other. Their cross-sectional design takes a snapshot of all three at once. Patterns that stand out in healthy people could become biomarkers, simple measurable signs that flag who is drifting toward diabetes and might benefit from early lifestyle change.
pmc-11636497: Pontali and Centis argue, in a 2024 commentary, that curing tuberculosis often fails to end its harm. A finished drug course kills the germ, and that counts as cure by the book. Yet many survivors carry lung damage for months or years, a state called post-TB lung disease. Others live with limits in work and daily life. The piece discusses a study in the same issue that records adult survivors' own accounts, and presses care teams to follow survivors past the last dose.
pmc-11637397:
Swadesh Pal, Malay Banerjee, and Roderick Melnik built a math model in 2024 of how water, plants, and grazers shape patterns on dry land. Such patterns steer biodiversity and how well dry country weathers climate shocks. Their model links the soil surface itself to the living web above it.

Heavy rain in the model can flip the system suddenly, with real losses in plant yield. Energy lost as it climbs the food chain, and the way variety can raise or lower extinction risk, both shape the outcome. Water flow pushes the patterns toward stable stripes. The authors say the soil surface is no passive stage but an actor in pattern making. Their findings speak to land care under a changing climate.
pmc-11639897:
Innokenty Mokhosoev and three co-authors review the double-edged role of cytochrome P450 enzymes in cancer, in this 2024 paper. These liver enzymes process a huge range of chemicals, from drugs and hormones to substances that can start cancer. The same enzyme can detoxify one compound and activate another, which makes the family hard to summarize.

The review explains how different enzymes can push the same chemical toward a safer or a more toxic product, depending on the tissue and reaction. It gives special weight to hormone-driven cancers of the breast, ovary, womb lining, and prostate, where estrogen and testosterone breakdown products can feed tumors or protect against them. Inherited variants in the enzyme genes sort people into slow, normal, fast, and ultrafast processors, which shifts both cancer risk and drug response. Drugs that block or boost these enzymes also feed into treatment resistance.
pmc-11639997:
Graat and co-authors test in 2024 whether a phone app that lets pig farmers grade their own animals' welfare lifts welfare on free range and organic farms. The app gives instant feedback and compares each farm with peers. Twelve farmers used it for six checks over two years.

A researcher also graded the pigs in depth at the start and end. Overall welfare did not clearly rise with app use, though some single aspects hinted at gains. Farmers found the app easy and most of its parts useful. The study weighs self checks as a cheap spur for better care.
pmc-11640097:
Lisa Irina Körner and eleven co-authors refine the glow that guides brain tumor surgery, in this 2024 study. Before glioma surgery, patients drink a compound that makes tumor cells fluoresce pink under special light. The glow is reliable in the tumor's core but fades exactly where surgeons need it most: low-grade tumors and the infiltrating edge, where stray cells hide.

The glow's color carries information, the team shows. Tumor tissue emits at two nearby wavelengths, and the balance between them shifts with tumor grade and region. During operations on forty-three gliomas, samples from core and edge were collected and their emission spectra and glow lifetimes measured outside the body. The peak balance fell from high-grade to low-grade tissue and tracked the lifetime measurements. Reading the color, not the brightness, could one day tell the surgeon what kind of tissue the light is touching.
pmc-11640397:
Carla Abrahamian and co-authors review a cell channel called TPC2 that links fair hair to skin cancer risk. The channel sits in pigment cells, where it helps set melanin output and thus skin and hair color. Sun exposure is a top melanoma driver, and pigment level shapes that risk.

Several human variants make the channel overactive, and carriers tend toward blond hair and pale skin. Loss of channel function does the reverse: more melanin, plus weaker tumor traits such as growth and spread in lab models. The channel answers to many body signals and partner proteins. A partner called Rab7a boosts its action, a fresh finding the review stresses. The authors weigh whether tuning TPC2 could one day cut melanoma risk or slow its course.
pmc-11640897:
Hiramoto and Oikawa tested whether an extract of bitter melon, Momordica charantia, can slow melanoma in mice. Melanoma is aggressive and spreads readily, so new treatments are wanted. The plant extract had already suppressed cancer cell growth in dishes. The team injected mice with melanoma cells, fed them the extract daily for two weeks, and then examined their lungs, where the cancer had traveled.

Treated mice showed less tumor growth and invasion in the lungs. Inside the cancer cells, the extract raised a tumor-suppressing protein, lowered the PAX3 gene's product, and damped a growth signaling chain. Several other survival and growth factors fell as well. The authors conclude that the extract works mainly by suppressing PAX3, which then cuts the signals melanoma needs to grow and spread.
pmc-11640997:
Valiya Agisha and six co-authors study how a helpful fungus boosts phosphate use in a model plant in a 2024 paper. The fungus had shown promise as a biofertilizer, above all when phosphate is scarce in soil. The team grow Arabidopsis with the fungus under low phosphate and profile genes and proteins in roots and shoots.

Plants with the fungus grew better roots and took up more nutrients under scarcity. Genes for phosphate transport, root shape, and stress defense rose, while proteins tied to membrane reshaping and hormone signals also shifted. Two hormone pathways stood out as coordinators. The authors frame the work as a guide for greener farming.
pmc-11641197:
Five authors led by I-Chun Chen study brain guard cells in a mouse model of a grave child epilepsy. The disease, Dravet syndrome, stems from a fault in a nerve channel gene and resists most drugs. That same channel helps wake brain guard cells, called microglia, which prune cell links and eat dead cells. The team bred mice with the human-like fault and read their guard cells in depth.

Guard cells in the sick mice held far less of the channel than normal. At rest they leaned to a swollen, pro-harm state, yet under a germ cue they fired weakly. Their eating of dead cells fell sharply in tests. Brain reads showed too many young, raw links in one memory zone. The team links weak pruning to the wild circuits that drive seizures.
pmc-11641297:
Jose Bellver and co-authors map gut and reproductive tract microbes in infertile women with obesity. Past work linked microbes to both obesity and infertility, with mixed results. The team ran a study at many clinics, taking saliva and stool in person. Fluid from the vagina and womb was taken at the clinic, and microbe genes were read.

The gut ratio once proposed as an obesity mark did not differ by weight group. Some microbe groups were more common in one group than the other. Vaginal and womb samples looked much alike, backing the idea that womb microbes rise from below. A streptococcus-heavy womb profile was more common in women with obesity. The authors say the map may help explain poor outcomes in this group.
pmc-11641397:
Sophia Pavlova and co-authors built in 2024 matched stem cell lines to judge whether a small deletion in a heart gene actually causes disease. The deletion, in MYBPC3, turned up in a patient with a thickened heart muscle, its guilt unknown. They used gene editing to erase the deletion in the patient's own stem cells, and in earlier work had added it to a healthy donor's.

The corrected lines kept their stem character, normal chromosomes, and clean editing profiles. Grown into heart cells, both line pairs told the same story: cells carrying the deletion grew oversized, a hallmark of the disease. The authors say the variant is likely pathogenic. The paired lines now stand ready for drug and mechanism studies.
pmc-11641697:
Yuxuan Qian and co-authors present a 2024 study of a calcium pump gene family in pepper plants. Calcium is a key nutrient for pepper growth, and these pump genes move it across cell membranes. No full census of the family in the pepper genome had been made.

The team found eleven family genes with computer based methods. They mapped where the genes sit, how they relate to kin in other plants, and what control switches they carry. The proteins look stable and water shy, and all share the same set of motifs. Gene counts of parts vary a lot across the set. Activity tests showed each gene answers in its own time pattern to calcium dose. The authors offer the census as a base for breeding tougher peppers.
pmc-11641897:
Minyu Shou and co-authors catalog a family of genes in Salvia miltiorrhiza, a plant used in traditional Chinese medicine. The genes make enzymes that cut carotenoids, the pigments behind many plant colors. The cutting products help plants grow, respond to stress, and form useful compounds.

Scanning the plant's whole genome, the team found twenty-one of these genes, spread across five chromosomes. The genes fall into four subfamilies, and members of each share similar structures. Comparisons with other plants, including a small weed and rice, showed shared ancestry patterns. Most of the genes carry control switches tied to stress, light, and growth signals. Many switch on in specific tissues, and several in one subfamily respond to hormone and stress treatments. The authors say the survey lays groundwork for learning how this gene family shapes the plant's chemistry. That knowledge could later help breeders raise the plant's medicinal value.
pmc-11641997:
Tao Li and nine colleagues published a soil mechanics study in two thousand twenty-four on how grains rotate during shearing. The strength of sand and gravel matters for foundations and slopes. Grains both slide and roll when soil is sheared, and each motion eats energy differently.

The team recast irregular grains as regular shapes while keeping energy and density unchanged. They derived how rotation changes shear stress and energy use across the shearing process. Tests on jagged coral sand and smooth glass beads checked the theory. Early in shearing, most work went into rolling; later, sliding took over. Rolling energy reacted far more strongly to load than sliding energy. The findings refine strength rules for granular ground.
pmc-11642097:
Caroline Berchtold and others studied mismatched kidney transplants in two thousand twenty-four. Donor and receiver blood groups sometimes differ. Such transplants need stronger drugs to calm the immune system upfront. Long-term kidney function matches compatible transplants, though. The extra burden from side problems was never counted. Twenty years of records supplied matched pairs.

Each such case was paired with a matched one. Returns to hospital, infections, new diabetes, and tumors were set side by side. Survival and kidney function proved much the same overall. Rates of side problems showed no real gaps. Time back in hospital also matched between groups. The feared extra burden did not show up clearly. Careful centers can offer such transplants with far less worry.
pmc-11642197:
Javier Narvaez and co-authors published a real-world study in 2024 on antifibrotic drugs for lung scarring tied to rheumatoid arthritis. Trial data were scarce for this severe complication. The team followed twenty-seven patients on one of two drugs, tracking lung function, side effects, and how long treatment lasted. Typical follow-up ran about two years.

Before treatment, lung capacity and gas transfer had been sliding. After starting, capacity stabilized and even improved modestly at one and two years, while gas transfer held steady. Side effects hit most patients, mainly gut and liver troubles, and many needed dose cuts. About two thirds stayed on therapy at the end. The authors call the drugs helpful but hard to tolerate.
pmc-11642297:
Bingxin Jin and co-authors wrote a 2024 study on how gypsum content and hot curing affect a low-heat expansive cement. This cement cuts production emissions versus ordinary Portland cement and avoids the strength loss ordinary cement suffers in hot, humid service. Gypsum drives its expansion, so the dose matters.

Mixes with 8 to 20 percent gypsum were cured at 20, 50, and 80 degrees. Strength showed a critical gypsum dosage at room temperature, and that critical dose rose with heat and age. Heat helped high-gypsum mixes more than lean ones. More gypsum meant greater expansion that took longer to settle, while hotter curing shortened settling and lowered final expansion. Microscopy and thermal analyses traced the mechanisms. The results guide mix design for hot climates.
pmc-11642397:
Linji Chen and colleagues studied in 2024 how oxidative stress affects sperm quality in men from infertile couples with no obvious cause. Half of infertility involves male factors, yet many cases stay unexplained. Forty-one men gave semen and blood samples, and lifestyle was surveyed. Measures covered sperm count, movement, DNA damage, and stress markers in both semen and blood.

Higher body mass and higher stress markers in blood and semen each tied to lower sperm count. Semen stress levels and blood zinc tied to sperm movement. Zinc and a cholesterol measure tied to forward movement and DNA damage. Stress in blood and semen did not track together, which suggests body-wide and local stress act apart.
pmc-11642497:
Antonia Schuster and co-authors test a urine protein as an early warning for kidney donors. Living donors give a kidney and live on one, so spotting who may lose function matters. The protein DKK3 is tied to scarring inside the kidney and fast function loss in other settings.

Their 2024 study followed 117 donors seen between July 2022 and June 2023. Donors were split at a urine DKK3 value of 200: 89 below, 28 above. Before donation the groups' kidney function looked the same. Afterward, the high-DKK3 group's function ran clearly worse and fell faster over time. A simple urine test at checkups could flag donors who need closer watching, the authors suggest.
pmc-11642597:
Katarzyna Bergmann and co-authors study how sex and cardiometabolic risk factors affect high-sensitivity cardiac troponin levels in a healthy Polish population. Their 2024 study uses levels near the thresholds used to stratify cardiovascular risk.

Low but detectable troponin may signal risk in a primary prevention setting. The prospective study held 597 presumably healthy people, 313 women and 284 men. Both troponin I and T were measured, along with lipids, inflammatory and sugar markers, kidney function, and a natriuretic peptide. Subjects were split by a non-sex-specific troponin cutoff into risk groups. Sex-specific cutoffs for troponin I were also applied to see how classification changes.
pmc-11642697:
Małgorzata Mizerska-Wasiak and co-authors evaluate, in twenty twenty-four, a triple drug therapy for children with two related kidney diseases, IgA nephropathy and IgA vasculitis nephritis. Both deposit an antibody in the kidneys and cause blood and protein in urine. Sixty-eight children diagnosed by biopsy took part. Thirty-six got the triple therapy: azathioprine, prednisone, and enalapril, for one year, with a control biopsy. Thirty-two controls got enalapril alone. After a year, the triple therapy group showed a significant drop in proteinuria, cleared in nearly all, and in hematuria.

Proteinuria fell far more in the treated group than in controls, for both diseases. Biopsy scores for two damage features improved often in the treated group. The authors discuss which children need the stronger therapy.
pmc-11643197:
Roland Wohlgemuth wrote a review in 2024 on enzyme catalysis as a way to build value from renewable plant-based resources. Cultures used enzymes long before science explained them. Modern work can search, develop, and improve enzymes for set products. Their selectivity and range make them strong tools for efficient making of compounds, alone or in cascades.

The review covers enzyme use in green chemistry and industrial biotechnology. It draws on current supply challenges, the store of natural enzymes, and methods to engineer custom ones. Wohlgemuth argues that full use of enzyme power can shift products away from fossil inputs. It can also make manufacturing safer and cleaner.
pmc-11643397:
Roberta Puglisi and co-authors present in 2024 a glowing chemical sensor for amines in air and food. Amines come from industry and from living processes, and they pollute air and harm health. Some arise as amino acids break down in food and nature.

Their sensor is a zinc complex fitted with bright pyrenyl arms and a chiral bridge. Lab tests and computer models show it binds chosen amines strongly. That binding changes its glow, which allows detection. The authors present the design as a promising tool for spotting a broad range of amines in the environment.
pmc-11643597:
Xueru Wang and co-authors report a 2024 study of compounds from the herb Curculigo capitulata, a plant found in southern and southwestern China. Plants in this genus have shown effects linked to mood, so the team searched the herb for new active compounds. They also tested whether any of them protect nerve cells from harm.

The team isolated seven new compounds and nineteen known ones, and worked out the structure of each new find. In lab tests with a human nerve cell line, six compounds gave clear protection against cell death caused by glutamate, a common signal chemical. One compound acted through a known cell defense path involving the proteins Nrf2 and HO-1. The work points to plant compounds worth further study.
pmc-11643697:
Jongbeom Park and colleagues engineer a yeast to eat xylose from plant biomass. Their study from twenty twenty-four rewrites Komagataella phaffii metabolism. Plant hydrolysates hold plenty of glucose and xylose sugars. This industrial yeast could not use xylose effectively before.

Three pathway genes were added with tuned promoter strengths. A strong promoter drove the middle gene of the pathway. Weaker promoters balanced the first and third genes. The engineered strain grew far better on kenaf hydrolysate. Growth beat the native strain by a clear margin. This is the first xylose pathway reported in this yeast. Biofactories could make protein and chemicals from crop waste.
pmc-11643897:
Pereira, Tavernier, dos Santos Junior, and Vernilli published this study in twenty twenty-four on mold fluxes used in steel casting. Mold fluxes are powders that melt over liquid steel. They guide heat flow and help stop cracks from forming. The standard mixes contain fluorine, which raises health and environmental concerns. The team set out to design mixes that work without it.

The authors tested how four ingredients changed thickness, melting, and crystal growth in the flux. Four trial mixes were compared in the lab. One mix with a boron compound flowed well and formed few crystals. A fully fluorine-free mix proved too thick. The results show that fluxes without fluorine can match the old mixes, though plant trials are still needed.
pmc-11643997:
Fatma Abdel Samad, Mohammed Ali Jasim, Alaa Mahmoud, Yasmin Abd El-Salam, Hamza Qayyum, Retna Apsari, and Tarek Mohamed wrote a 2024 paper on titanium dioxide particles and light. Such particles are used in sunscreens, paints, and solar devices. Their response to strong light matters for switches and sensors driven by lasers.

The team made the particles by blasting a target with a laser under pure water. They then sized the particles with microscopes and light tests. The particles ran from about eight to nineteen nanometers across. Size depended on how long the blasting lasted. Using very short laser pulses, they measured how the particles refract and absorb light at several strengths. The results help judge this cheap material for light-based devices.
pmc-11644097:
Xi Liang and co-authors tested a vitamin plus probiotic pairing against alcohol-driven fatty liver in mice, in a 2024 paper. The pairing joined niacin with a gut bacterium strain called F1-7, of the species Bifidobacterium animalis. Seventy-five mice were split into five groups: healthy controls, alcohol-fed mice, and alcohol groups given niacin, the bacterium, or both. The trial ran eight weeks.

All treatments lowered blood fats and calmed inflammation to some degree, but the pairing worked best. It raised levels of a receptor, GPR109A, in liver and gut more than either part alone. It also restored gut microbe balance best and lifted levels of helpful gut acids the most. Certain microbe groups tracked those acid changes closely. The authors tie the benefit to the receptor, which steers fat building and burning in the liver. They propose the combination as a candidate therapy for alcoholic liver disease.
pmc-11644397:
Gong Cheng and co-authors review plant compounds in holly plants and their many uses, in a 2024 paper. Holly plants hold rich mixes of phenolic compounds and other active parts. Those parts show promise for health and for care of the body. Plant phenols as a whole are well studied, while holly phenols lag behind.

The review sums up five years of work on the main phenols in the most studied holly types. It then maps uses of plant phenols in drugs, food work, health goods, and beauty goods. The aim is to guide fuller study and wiser use of holly phenols. Clear gaps remain where holly trials are thin.
pmc-11644697:
Wenting Li and co-authors build a virtual sensor for what flows out of sewage plants. Their 2024 paper tackles effluent biological oxygen demand, a key pollution measure that is slow and costly to assay directly, by predicting it from easier plant data.

Their soft sensor first picks the most informative helper variables by a neighbor-based information measure. A bidirectional memory network then learns from process history across the plant's interacting tanks. The twist is self-repair: a density-based strategy rebuilds the model only when the incoming data truly drift, skipping useless updates. On a standard benchmark simulator the sensor beat traditional models on accuracy and avoided needless rebuilds under shifting conditions. The authors aim it at steadier plant compliance.
pmc-11644797:
Shaklein and seven co-authors model polymer burning with a mixture fraction method, in work from twenty twenty-four. Predicting how plastic burns is harder than gas burning. Heat and mass flow between the flame and the solid surface must be captured well.

The test case was flame spread over a surface of PMMA, a common clear polymer. The team built counterflow flame solutions with the flame close to the fuel surface to capture heat loss into the solid. Tabulated chemistry then rebuilt temperature and species fields across the full case. Comparing with past numeric studies checked the method. Better burn forecasts aid fire safety design for buildings and transport.
pmc-11644897:
Saima Kanwal and seven co-authors build a smart monitoring system for fish ponds, in a 2024 paper. Pond water quality shifts with the weather, and poor water kills fish. Farmers need live warnings and sound advice across species and regions.

Sensors linked to a small controller track acidity, temperature, and cloudiness around the clock. The team gathered 43,459 records covering ten fish species in varied ponds. Machine learning models learned to judge water states from these records. A decision tree model scored 99.8 percent accuracy on its tests. The system shares data through cloud services for remote control. The authors pitch it as climate smart fish farming.
pmc-11645097:
Caifeng Chen and co-authors study the layer beneath a tiny patch antenna used as a crack sensor. Their 2024 paper notes that such sensors are small and keen, which suits them for watching cracks grow in structures. Making them smaller is a main goal. The layer's traits play a key role in that shrink.

Raising one trait of the layer, its dielectric constant, cuts antenna size. But higher loss in the layer drains radiation and hurts efficiency. The team maps the trade-off to find the best mix. A thicker layer widens bandwidth and helps efficiency, yet thin layers are favored for overall form. Smaller antennas also proved more sensitive to crack growth. The paper gives design guidance for sensor builders.
pmc-11645897:
Sai te er Nu er lan and co-authors present a 2024 journal article comparing mutations in the two main lung cancer types to sharpen immunotherapy choices. The team sequenced 616 cancer genes in samples from 166 patients. Adenocarcinoma leaned on EGFR and a few partners beside the ever-present TP53; squamous tumors showed a different mix and higher overall mutation loads.

Squamous cancers also scored higher on mutation burden, PD-L1 staining, and tumor heterogeneity. Across both types, patients clearing two thresholds, high mutation burden and strong PD-L1, responded to immunotherapy every time in this series. The authors propose the paired markers as a better guide than either alone.
pmc-11646097:
Babies born very early face higher odds of heart and blood vessel disease later in life. Anja Meissner and five co-authors looked for early warning signs in the blood of such teenagers in a 2024 study. They compared 50 adolescents born before 30 weeks with 29 born on time. The team measured blood pressure over a full day, the stiffness of the main artery by scan, and several markers of inflammation.

The study asks whether those inflammation markers track with pressure and stiffness. It also asks whether the pattern differs by sex or by early growth. The authors hope such markers could flag at-risk teens early enough for prevention to help.
pmc-11646397:
Ramzan and co-authors make silver nanoparticles from ginger extract and test them against drug-resistant bacteria. Drug resistance is a growing threat, and plant-based methods offer one route to new tools. The team first checked what plant compounds the ginger extracts held.

They then formed the particles at room temperature and checked them with light, X-ray, and microscope tools. Tests confirmed the particles had formed as expected. The group next measured how well the particles killed resistant strains. HPLC tests found eight active plant compounds in the organic ginger extracts, which helps explain the results.
pmc-11646597:
Syphilis is surging worldwide, and vaccine makers need the bacterium's genome read straight from patients. Ligang Yang and co-authors collect samples from early syphilis cases in Guangzhou, China, in their 2024 study. They took ulcer swabs and blood from 17 people with primary syphilis and skin biopsies and blood from 51 with the secondary stage.

The bacterium's DNA showed up in nearly all ulcer swabs and skin biopsies and in over half the secondary-stage blood samples. Growing the germ in rabbits worked for more than two-thirds of samples, and paired genomes from patients and rabbits nearly matched. Most of the 51 distinct genomes fell in East Asian branches of the SS14 family. The authors back rabbit-grown isolates as a sound base for vaccine design.
pmc-11646897:
Maria Carella and co-authors untangle a heart scare that mimicked a heart attack. Their 2024 case deals with a seventy-five-year-old woman with advanced ovarian cancer and no past heart trouble. Her heart tracing showed a raised ST segment, the classic attack sign, and scans showed the ballooned heart tip of Takotsubo syndrome. Blood tests added a high injury marker. Yet her calcium ran severely low, a rare trigger for both the tracing and the ballooning.

Vessel imaging found no blocked arteries. Calcium dosing followed, the tracing swung to deep T-wave flips, and heart function healed fully within days as calcium normalized. The team urges checks for rare causes when cancer clouds the scene.
pmc-11647297:
Helen D'Couto and a large team simulate smoking's toll on people with HIV in South Africa. Their modelling study from twenty twenty-four projects lung cancer and stroke. HIV deaths fall as treatment spreads across the country. Tobacco diseases now claim a growing share of lives instead.

Eighteen lifetime cohorts varied by sex, age, and smoking status. A microsimulation followed each group through ageing and care lapses. Quitting at the start was modelled for former smokers. Cancer risk multipliers for smokers were large in the model. Results quantify how much cessation could avert future cases. HIV programmes may need tobacco treatment built in. Longevity gains from HIV care can be smoked away.
pmc-11647397:
Yordanos Sisay Asgedom and four co-authors split the wealth gap in neck-of-womb checks in sub-Saharan Africa. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Health poll files from the zone fed the work. Pooled check rates sat near one in ten women. A fair count showed a clear rich-lean in who gets checked.

Split math laid the gap most to wealth rank it self, school grade, home place, and news reach. The team urge work on school paths, news reach in homes, and the purse base, so the poor can reach checks at rates near the rich.
pmc-11648097:
Natasha S Crowcroft and nine co-authors review the world's stalled push to eliminate measles and rubella. Their 2024 paper notes that every World Health Organization region aims to eliminate measles, and most aim at rubella too. Progress this century has been real: over forty percent of countries are verified measles-free and over half have sustained rubella elimination. Yet the remaining road is the hardest.

The authors blame fundamental gaps in health systems, exposed whenever coverage slips, since measles spreads so fast that any weakness shows at once. Their prescription is a shift in strategy: build immunization into the center of primary health care at every level, rather than running it as a side campaign. New tools such as microarray patch vaccines could help. The tools to prevent every measles death already exist, they argue; the shared task is delivery.
pmc-11648797:
Christy Cassarly and co-authors lay out the design of a trial testing video-delivered speech therapy after stroke, in this 2024 paper. Aphasia, the language loss that follows stroke, responds to therapy that most patients never get in full. Distance and scarce providers block access across the United States.

The TERRA trial will enroll one hundred adults whose stroke came at least a year earlier. Half get therapy by video link, half in clinic, for thirty days split between meaning-based and sound-based work. Sessions run forty-five minutes daily at two South Carolina sites. The design tests whether remote care is no worse than in-person care. Raters judging outcomes will not know group assignments.
pmc-11649397:
Conghao Gai and nine co-authors study the halogen effect on serine-targeting covalent warheads in a 2024 paper. A warhead is the part of a drug that bonds for good to its target. Halogens, such as chlorine and bromine, can lift a drug's strength and how long it lasts in the body.

The team added halogens to a ring in one warhead family and read how the bond rate changed. The atoms shift the charge cloud of the ring, so each form hit the target enzyme at its own pace. Crystal shots prove the bonds form and show the shapes, to guide new drugs for gut harm from drugs.
pmc-11649497:
Sedation for a camera exam of the airways is the topic of a 2024 study by Xinyu Wu and co-authors. The team tested a balanced form of propofol sedation, where the main drug is mixed with others, against two standard mixes, to find a regimen that works well and stays safe.

In total, 418 patients were placed in four groups by the mix they received. The balanced groups used propofol on top of either of the two standard bases. Patients, doctors, and nurses all rated satisfaction, and the team also tracked waking times, drug doses, and side effects. Both balanced mixes raised satisfaction for all three rater groups compared with the standard mixes. The study points to a better default for this common procedure.
pmc-11649697:
Nersi Alaeddin and co-authors examine whether common stomach acid drugs are tied to brain health. Reports on proton pump inhibitors, cognition, and dementia conflict, and few studies looked at the brain's fine structure. The team used baseline data from the Rhineland Study, covering 7,465 adults with an average age of about 55. They compared drug users with non-users on thinking tests and brain scans.

Users, above all younger ones, scored worse on global cognition and working memory. Younger long-term users also showed worse total memory. Brain volume and one white matter measure showed no link to the drugs. A second measure, mean diffusivity, ran higher in users in regions tied to cognition, which hints at weaker white matter integrity. The authors stress that the design cannot prove cause. They call for more research into whether the drugs themselves, or the conditions behind their use, drive the pattern.
pmc-11650097:
Placing a breathing tube correctly is a core step in surgery care, and doctors need proof fast that the tube sits in the windpipe. Soma Ganesh Raja Neethirajan and co-authors compared two proof methods in this 2024 study. The standard proof reads carbon dioxide in the breath, shown as a wave trace. Bedside ultrasound offers a second way, by showing a flutter in the windpipe as the tube passes.

The study enrolled 104 patients set for planned surgery under general anesthesia. Staff timed both methods from the moment the face mask came off. For ultrasound, the clock stopped at the first sight of the flutter. For the gas method, it stopped after six steady wave traces. Ultrasound proved faster at confirming the tube. A faster check can shorten the risky gap in airway care.
pmc-11650597:
Alexandra Maier and co-authors dope hybrid nanoparticles with manganese to make magnetic heating therapy stronger. Their study appeared in 2024. The particles pair a palladium core, meant someday to carry a radioactive label, with an iron oxide shell that heats in an alternating magnetic field. Such heat, placed inside tumors, can pair with radiation or imaging. Adding manganese to the shell lattice raised magnetic saturation markedly.

Heating power rose up to 1.7 times over undoped particles. At higher manganese content, the metal gathered at the shell's rim, which further boosted heating at the tested field settings. The authors say the design keeps the extra functions of the hybrid while fixing its weak point, heat output. Stronger heating means lower doses could reach the same effect in future cancer treatment.
pmc-11650997:
Saskia Stein and co-authors report a 2024 study of a human antibody that fights the virus that causes COVID-19. Many drug antibodies lost power as the virus changed its outer spike. Changes cluster on parts of the spike, so the spot an antibody grips matters a lot. The team sought a spot that stays the same across variants.

The antibody came from patients who had recovered from infection. It blocked most tested variants, even recent Omicron forms, with strong grip on the spike. In hamsters it lowered virus levels in the lung and kept lung harm mild. An X-ray view showed it grips a site outside the known classes. The authors say such sites should guide future drug and vaccine design. Wide tests of new antibodies, they argue, will speed control of future outbreaks.
pmc-11651697:
Petros Perros and colleagues report a 2024 survey study of people living with an underactive thyroid. Between a tenth and a sixth of such patients still feel unwell even when blood tests look right. The team asked whether a distress-prone style of personality, called type D, helps explain that gap. Type D had been linked to heavier symptoms in other illnesses but not studied here.

The online survey drew more than thirty-nine hundred replies from many countries, with over thirty-five hundred valid. More than half of the respondents fit the type D pattern. That group also reported more anxiety, low mood, and body complaints. They were less satisfied with their care and felt the illness pressed harder on daily life. The authors suggest that how a patient is wired may shape how the illness feels, and care should take note.
pmc-11651797:
Keisuke Kadooka and seven co-authors investigated a shadow that appears in the deep veins of the brain during the first hours of a major stroke. On certain MRI scans, veins on the starved side stand out because the tissue is pulling extra oxygen from the blood. The team reviewed fifty patients whose main brain artery was blocked by a heart-born clot and treated with clot retrieval.

The sign did not track with the strength of backup blood flow, which surprised them. It did track with where the blockage sat: clots in the nearer segment of the artery, the part feeding deep structures, came with the sign far more often. Weighing three possible flow stories, the authors favor one in which ischemic blood drains outward from the deep nuclei through these veins, while admitting the mechanism remains an inference.
pmc-11653597:
Mohamad Saoud and a team of co-authors are featured in a 2024 journal cover summary of research on predicting how anticancer drugs work, using chemistry fingerprints and machine learning. Knowing a drug's mode of action guides combinations and repurposing, but finding it is slow. Their method reads the metabolic fingerprint a drug leaves inside cells.

The team profiled 38 drugs in prostate cancer cells with metabolomics, the large scale study of small molecules. A pattern recognition model learned to match fingerprints to known modes of action. It predicted modes accurately, including for new compounds such as natural products. The approach exposes intracellular mechanisms and transfers across cancer types. The summary highlights its promise for designing smarter drug combinations.
pmc-11653697:
Ngegbai and co-authors grade a system that tracks mothers' deaths in Sunyani, Ghana, in a 2024 study. Death rates for mothers have fallen in Ghana but stay high in rural areas. The tracking system aims to end deaths that could be stopped, yet its local strength was untested.

The team reviewed death records from 2017 to 2021 and spoke with health staff. Most staff could explain how the data guides action, and the report path was clear to most. Midwives were the largest group among those who took part. The study used a mix of counts and close reading of interviews. Findings like these help districts fix weak spots in how deaths are reported and reviewed.
pmc-11653797:
Chengxia Wang and four co-authors test continuous intraoperative neuromonitoring for spinal nerve root heat injury, in a 2024 pig study. Such a warning system could help guard nerves during work by automatic spine robots. The team used 32 nerve roots in four pigs, with sham, room temperature, and heat groups from 40 to 65 degrees.

Muscle signals stayed stable at 40 and 45 degrees, and tissue checks showed no clear injury after five minutes. At 50 degrees and above, signals fell and tissue damage appeared, faster at higher heat. The work supports using this monitoring method and gives time limits that rise sharply with temperature.
pmc-11653897:
Jan Novák and five co-authors present two cases of primary ciliary dyskinesia surfacing as male infertility, in a two thousand twenty-four case report with an overview of past work. The genetic disorder cripples the tiny motile cilia that clear airways and propel sperm.

Affected men usually carry normal sperm counts with zero motility, alongside lifelong respiratory troubles such as bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis, and ear infections. About half also have mirror-flipped internal organs, the Kartagener pattern. More than fifty causative gene mutations are known, and mechanisms beyond immotility can wreck assisted reproduction. The authors urge doctors and nurses to suspect the diagnosis from this symptom pattern and to include sperm DNA fragmentation testing in the work-up.
pmc-11653997:
Georgia Chisnall and co-authors review how well studies of childhood vaccination in the United Kingdom handle the idea of access. Shots for children have fallen for thirteen years in a row there, and calls grow to look past parent attitudes to how services can be reached. The team searched seven databases for work on parents' own experiences.

Forty-five studies made the cut. A third never spoke of access at all, even when their results touched it, and only a small share used a proper frame for it. Nearly all studies focused on access to information, while cost, distance, and supply drew little study. The authors urge that access be named and studied head-on.
pmc-11654197:
Jun-Sik Lim and five co-authors measure how fast African swine fever swept through South Korea's wild boar despite twenty-three hundred kilometers of fencing, and whether the fences mattered where it counted. From the national surveillance system they extracted over twenty-six hundred cases from the first detection in October twenty nineteen through September twenty twenty-two, resolving into four geographic clusters.

The wavefront averaged about half a kilometer per week, but the eastern cluster raced at nearly one kilometer weekly, a spread the authors attribute to boar density differences across habitats. Fencing significantly affected dispersal in only two of four clusters and slowed the wavefront in none. The heterogeneity itself is the finding: barrier strategies perform unevenly across terrain and host density.
pmc-11654297:
Jiao Tang and co-authors study a blood protein as a marker in a combined syndrome in a 2024 paper. The syndrome links heart disease, kidney disease, and metabolic risks such as diabetes and obesity. The protein is Klotho, tied to aging and mineral balance. The team asked whether its level in blood tracks how severe the syndrome is and who dies from it.

They drew on a national United States survey with close to ten thousand adults from 2007 to 2016. The link between the protein and syndrome risk bent rather than ran straight. Low levels tracked with higher risk of death from all causes and from heart causes. The pattern for all-cause death was U-shaped, and for heart death L-shaped. The authors say low Klotho flags both severity and danger well in this syndrome.
pmc-11654397:
Leonard Roth, Matthias Studer, Emilie Zuercher, and Isabelle Peytremann-Bridevaux proposed in 2024 a bootstrap check for regressions built on clustered life-course patterns. Sequence analysis groups similar life paths, such as work or health histories, into a typology. That typology is then used in regressions, but the sampling uncertainty in building it is usually ignored, which can mislead conclusions.

Their procedure draws many resamples of the data. For each resample, a new typology matching the original is built, and the regression is run again. The spread of results shows how firm the original finding is. The method is shown in the setting of state sequence analysis. Readers get a way to stress-test a common two-step analysis instead of trusting a single clustering as if it were exact.
pmc-11654697:
Dawit Lee, Sanghyub Lee, and Aaron Young wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four about a powered frame that helps people walk. Such lower-limb exoskeletons must adapt as ground and pace change. A fixed controller often fails to match what the wearer needs moment by moment.

Their system uses artificial intelligence to switch the type of help as walking mode changes. It also adjusts help with slope and times each push to the step cycle, all in real time. On a treadmill, the smart help cut the energy cost of walking more than standard help did. Tests outdoors showed good control and higher user preference. The system needs no separate mode classifier and works for new users at once.
pmc-11655297:
Finding which genes move together across millions of features is a basic step in biology data work, and it is slow. Shibin Long and co-authors introduce a Python package in 2024, pyNetCor, built for correlation analysis at that scale. It speeds both the full correlation matrix and the search for the strongest links.

A shortcut that interpolates values estimates significance quickly while keeping false discoveries in check, running more than one hundred ten times faster than existing methods in their tests. The package also trims memory use, the other usual bottleneck. The authors say the tool slots into common bioinformatics pipelines and can speed the hunt for patterns in multi-omics data, where datasets keep growing.
pmc-11655597:
Mira Burmeister-Rudolph studies, in twenty twenty-four, how migrant-led civil society groups mediate between low-wage labor migrants and state bodies in the Gulf states. Low-wage migrants face major rights abuses there despite labor laws and human rights pledges. India has built an official support frame for its estimated five and a half million low-wage workers in the Gulf, with emergency funds, repatriation help, and walk-in centers. In practice, many migrants cannot reach those rights.

Upper and middle-class Indian migrant groups step in as informal brokers to embassies and local state bodies. The article traces that gap to the migrants' historic marginalization and to the informal way citizen-state ties work in India. Data come from interviews and field observation of support networks.
pmc-11656197:
Witaya Sungkarat and co-authors study a curious leftover of vision in a 2024 paper on hemianopia. After damage to the visual pathway on one side of the brain, patients lose sight in half the visual field. Yet some still consciously perceive moving objects there, a puzzle called the Riddoch phenomenon.

One theory credits a direct wiring route from the thalamus to motion area V5 that skips the primary visual cortex. The study compared twenty patients with field loss against twenty-eight controls using field tests, brain scans, and tract tracing. It asked whether denser fibers on that bypass route track with preserved motion perception.
pmc-11656597:
Toxoplasma gondii infects a vast share of humanity and most warm-blooded animals, and the standard drugs against it are slow and often fail to clear the parasite for good. Lu Wang and co-authors test glabridin, a compound from liquorice root, as a fresh weapon. Their 2024 paper runs the compound through cell tests, microscopy, and mouse trials.

Glabridin barely harmed host cells yet blocked the parasite from entering cells and slowed its growth, more strongly the longer it acted. Treated parasites swelled with reactive oxygen, lost membrane voltage, and showed scrambled amino acid handling. In infected mice, a dose of 100 milligrams per kilogram lifted survival sharply. The authors name glabridin a strong candidate for new toxoplasmosis treatment.
pmc-11656997:
Daniel Barron and nine co-authors argue that pain should be sorted by function, not body part, in a 2024 paper. Clinics now triage, treat, and bill pain almost entirely by where it hurts. The team asked whether that habit matches how pain actually clusters across a population, using pattern-learning tools on more than thirty-four thousand people in the UK Biobank.

Four profiles emerged, cutting across medical specialties: pain interference, depression, medical pain, and anxiety. None of them lined up with the usual suspects of body part, pain intensity, sex, or body weight. Each profile instead tracked a distinct pattern of medicines, diagnoses, and life traits, mostly tied to chronic, changeable diseases. The authors say designing care around these profiles could serve chronic disease management better than the body part map.
pmc-11657297:
Sander Lagerveld and co-authors track bat migration across the sea in a 2024 study. Migratory bats cross barriers such as open water at higher risk, because long flights cost energy and weather can turn. How barriers shape their routes and timing was poorly known.

Forty four small bats were radio tagged on the English east coast in two springs and tracked to continental Europe by a wildlife receiver network. Bats detoured along the coast and shortened sea crossings by leaving the main direction. Males departed later than females. Females averaged set daily speeds, and wind use during overseas flights was measured.
pmc-11657397:
Lieke van den Brekel and co-authors study air pollution, stroke, and heart disease by ethnic group in the Netherlands in a 2024 paper. Pollution is a major risk factor and minority groups often face higher exposure. The team linked home address pollution levels to hospital and death records from 2014 to 2019. Each disease cohort held more than nine and a half million people aged thirty and older.

About one percent developed each disease during follow up. For stroke, links with two pollutants varied somewhat by ethnic group, with the lowest risk rise in one group and the highest in another. Heart disease results were partly unexpected, with higher exposure tied to lower rates in some checks. Readers see why group specific analysis matters for fair health policy.
pmc-11657497:
Wen-Yu Zhang and co-authors chart arsenic in rural drinking water in Inner Mongolia in a 2024 study. Monitoring spans a full decade, from 2013 to 2022. One stable supply point per township anchors the sampling. Finished and tap water were drawn in dry and rainy seasons.

Arsenic ran higher in the central-western region than in the east. Levels fell notably across the decade. Source type shaped the readings, tested by standard rank methods. A US health risk model then weighs what the levels mean for residents. The record gives officials a base for targeting treatment where arsenic lingers and for guarding rural water gains.
pmc-11657697:
Jieya Luo and four co-authors review, in 2024 work, flare hubs of the guard force as drug targets in stem cell grafts. Such grafts cure many blood ills, yet graft harm, germs, and graft loss still strike. The hubs in view wake on danger cues and pour out flare signals, at times to the point of cell death.

Calm hub fire guards health; wild fire wounds tissue. Graft steps stir the hubs at many points, from prep drugs to the graft's own clash with its host. The review walks each hub's build and wake paths in that light. It then sums which drugs mute the hubs and what gains trials hint at.
pmc-11657797:
Daniel Pratt and a large team set out a 2024 trial plan for talk therapy to prevent suicide in prison. Suicide is the leading cause of preventable death in prisons, and rates stay well above those outside. Talk therapy can ease suicidal thoughts, but men in prison at risk often have no access to proven programs.

The PROSPECT trial will recruit 360 men at risk across four prisons in the north of England. Half will get a cognitive behavioral suicide prevention program plus usual care, and half usual care alone. Main outcomes, suicidal thoughts and behavior, will be checked at six months. A side study will explore how the therapy works in the prison setting.
pmc-11657997:
Zandbergen and co-authors set out a phone-based screening trial for depression in a 2024 protocol paper. Catching major depression early by phone could cut its social burden. The trial runs in multi-ethnic Rotterdam with three arms. Two groups answer a standard nine-question screen every four weeks for a year; the third is not screened.

Referral rules differ by arm: one visit follows a single high score, the other needs three in a row. Nearly eighteen hundred participants will join. Quality of life at twelve months is the main outcome, with two-year follow-up and symptom tracking behind it. Results will feed a simulation of long-term benefits, harms, and costs. The authors say the findings can steer mental health policy in the Netherlands and beyond. The trial is registered, and the protocol is published ahead of results.
pmc-11658097:
Adanna Ezenwa-Ahanene, Adetokunbo Salawu, and Ayo Adebowale charted Lassa fever in Ebonyi State, Nigeria, in a 2024 study. The viral fever is common in Nigeria, and this south-eastern state carries a heavy load. The team read five years of state disease reports, from 2018 to 2022. Of 1,578 reported cases, three hundred were proved by lab tests.

Cases peaked in the first quarter of each year and fell over the study span. Two local areas stood out as hot spots. Farmers were far less likely to die of the fever than people out of work, a result the authors flag with care. Forecasts for the next year kept the same seasonal shape. The team urges stronger steps to curb the fever's spread.
pmc-11661197: Mathilde Haegeman, Douglas Lacomblez, and Antoine Loubet present a short teaching piece on imaging a rare brain emergency in a 2024 article. In cerebral fat macroembolism, fat blocks vessels in the brain. The symptoms are often vague and hard to pin to a cause, so standard scans can leave the diagnosis in doubt. Spectral tomography sorts tissue by how it absorbs X-rays at different energies. The authors present it as a valuable extra tool when this rare condition is suspected.
pmc-11663697:
Wen-yi Yang and co-authors test a nose spray against a classic sleeping pill for the sleepless night before surgery. Ninety patients with preoperative anxiety and insomnia were randomized three ways: intranasal dexmedetomidine plus dummy tablets, oral lorazepam plus salt spray, or double placebo, given the night before the operation.

The nose spray group fell asleep fastest, in a median of about nineteen minutes against thirty-four for lorazepam and fifty-seven for placebo. Total sleep matched lorazepam and crushed placebo, and patients woke easier and clearer than the lorazepam group. Satisfaction tied between the real drugs, and safety readouts stayed calm. The authors back the spray as a strong option for pre-surgery insomnia, especially where next-morning grogginess matters.
pmc-11663797:
Ford and co-authors examine how nicotine strength is shown on the front of vape packaging in the United Kingdom. The head dates the study to 2024, though the catalog lists 2025. Rules require buyers to be told that nicotine is present, yet many users misjudge product strength. Their study analyzes 156 packs sampled to represent the market in late 2022.

About eight in ten packs showed at least one nicotine descriptor on the front. Most packs gave a metric such as milligrams per milliliter, and a quarter gave a percentage. Over a third mentioned nicotine beyond the required warning. Rarer forms included strength icons, dose guidance, and cigarette equivalents. The authors say the mixed display may feed confusion about strength.
pmc-11663997:
Atiđa Selmani and co-authors tested how fluids like those in the human gut affect tiny selenium particles coated with polymers. Selenium is a nutrient the body needs in small amounts, and its nano form is absorbed better than other forms. That makes such particles a promising way to treat selenium shortage, as long as they survive the gut.

The team coated the particles with one of two polymers and tracked their size, shape, and make-up. They then exposed the particles to lab-made gut fluids and the main proteins found there. The fluids changed the particles' stability in ways that depend on the coating. Knowing how particles hold up in the gut helps designers make supplements that actually deliver their load.
pmc-11664097:
Yadong Wang and co-authors test in a 2024 study a gene editing tool against a fusion gene that drives bladder cancer. The fused gene joins two partners and appears in many tumor types. Cutting its message could stall tumor growth at the source.

The Cas13a system was aimed at the fusion message in two bladder cancer cell lines. It cut the target more deeply than a rival silencing method in head to head tests. Growth assays and organoid cultures both showed slowed cell division after the cut. Edited cells also formed fewer tumors when grown in mice in the study. The team frame the approach as a candidate new therapy for this cancer.
pmc-11664297:
Luke Glover and co-authors ran a quality project to cut the time staff need to gather gear for drawing blood or placing a vein line, in work published in 2024. Doctors at a hospital in England had flagged low stock and uneven trolley layouts across wards. Delays matter most in emergencies.

The team mapped the process, found root causes, and redesigned the trolley with clear markings and a fixed layout. Average gathering time fell from about one hundred forty seconds to eighteen seconds for both tasks. Feedback in a cardiac arrest drill was positive. Matching trolleys then began to spread across the hospital, though that wider roll out was not measured in the study.
pmc-11665797:
Haozheng Xu and Stamatia Giannarou build a vision system that tracks surgical tools even when they are partly hidden.
