Ding-Cheng Liu and colleagues test pharmacist led clinic care for lung cancer patients in Taiwan, in work from 2024. Targeted lung drugs often cause side effects that stop treatment and raise costs. Pharmacist teaching and symptom care in clinic visits may help patients stay on track through those effects.

Records covered patients who started one of three targeted drugs over five years. Forty patients used the pharmacy service, while close to one hundred did not. Skin side effects were logged more often in the service group, likely through closer checks. Monthly surprise clinic and emergency visits were clearly lower in that group. Emergency visit costs also fell, which supports the service value.
pmc-11700597:
Guarnido-Lopez and co-authors review computer vision tools for decisions in cattle production in a 2025 paper. Herd checks by hand are slow and prone to personal bias. Cameras plus deep learning can sort images, outline animals, spot objects, and pull out measures in an automatic way.

Such systems can estimate feed intake, body weight and gain, body shape scores, health status, and breeding performance. The review weighs where each tool helps beef and dairy work, in both barn and range settings. The stated goal for the field is farm ready systems that run live on site, turning pictures into same day choices.
pmc-11701297:
Milad Ahmadi Marzaleh and Marziyeh Hamyali Ainvand set out strategy for vector-borne diseases in a 2024 paper. These diseases pass to people through bites of insects and ticks, from mosquitoes to sandflies. They include malaria, dengue, Zika, and many more, and they threaten most of the world's people.

The authors argue that these diseases now rank among the top public health challenges, fed by travel, trade, and shifting climate. They lay out strategic steps: stronger watch systems, vector control, joint work across sectors, and care that reaches remote spots. Their stress falls on acting as a system, not disease by disease. The paper is a call to fund the unglamorous basics.
pmc-11703397:
Alexander Bouterse and co-authors used machine learning in a 2024 study to flag opioid risk after spine surgery. Spine work is a common source of pain drug orders, and some patients drift into long-term use. Such drugs play a role in about one in four opioid overdose deaths in the United States.

The team ran six learning methods on clinic data from three kinds of spine surgery. They hunted for patient traits that forecast heavy use of pain drugs after the operation. Knowing those traits at the start could help surgeons pick safer pain plans for high-risk patients. The work aims to cut long-term use without leaving real pain untreated.
pmc-11706297:
Halilibrahim Çiftçi and co-authors craft hybrid molecules aimed at lung and breast cancer, in a 2024 paper. Two growth receptors, EGFR and HER2, are often mutated or overproduced in these cancers, making them prime drug targets. The team built twenty hybrids joining naphthalene, pyrazoline, and thiazole parts and tested them on lung and breast cancer cell lines.

One compound, BTT-5, killed lung cancer cells at a lower dose than the comparison drug lapatinib and spared healthy blood cells by a wide margin. It pushed the cancer cells into programmed death and blocked EGFR by over half, with little action on HER2. Computer docking showed it gripping the receptor's pocket in its own way. The authors offer BTT-5 as a lead for lung cancer work.
pmc-11706597:
Wengui Yu and Michael Alexander review brain bleeding care and how future trials should be built, in this 2024 paper. Bleeding inside the brain makes up a tenth to a third of strokes and strikes some groups harder. Blood pressure loss and blood thinners are common causes.

Scans confirm the bleed fast, and vessel imaging hunts the source. Big bleeds, spread into fluid spaces, and early growth predict poor outcomes. Past surgery trials failed to prove clear gains. Drugs that curb bleed growth shrank hematomas yet did not lift outcomes. The authors weigh recent advances and press for sharper trial design.
pmc-11709397:
Tavia E Evans and co-authors study sex-specific brain shrinkage in Alzheimer disease in this 2025 paper. Sections of the hippocampus may each carry their own genetic wiring. Those sections could flag disease earlier than a single whole-brain score.

The study followed 1,051 people from a national cohort for up to eight years. Groups held healthy controls, people with mild impairment, and patients with Alzheimer disease. Scans every six months tracked each hippocampal subfield over time. Genetic risk scores were built with and without the famous APOE region. Plasma and spinal fluid protein data added more layers. Models then tested how genes, sex, and disease stage shape shrinkage rates.
pmc-11709497:
Anca Gabriela Frasineanu and Stephanie Gupton study the brain protein TRIM9 in Alzheimer disease in this 2025 paper. TRIM9 tags other proteins for handling and shapes neuron wiring during development. In adult brain it sits in the postsynaptic density, the receiving hub of synapses. That hub changes early in Alzheimer disease.

Mapping TRIM9 partners surfaced many synapse and Alzheimer linked proteins, including Tau. Cross checking against a disease mouse model showed a striking overlap. Nearly half the changed proteins in the model synapses touch the TRIM9 network. Adolescent mice lacking TRIM9 already show altered synapse composition. The work positions one ligase at a crossroads of development and degeneration.
pmc-11709597:
Carlos Cruchaga wrote a 2025 study that hunts for gene-driven targets in brain and blood data across many tissues. The method links genetic variants to protein and metabolite levels, then ties those to disease risk. Most past work looked only at nearby gene effects in blood or brain. This study widens the net to distant effects and multiple data types.

The team used spinal fluid from about 3,000 people and blood from African and European ancestry groups. They found thousands of variant links for proteins, many seen only in spinal fluid and not in blood. Metabolite links numbered in the hundreds, and many were new. Follow-up analyses tied 473 spinal fluid proteins to Alzheimer's risk. Forty proteins looked causal, and 42 may be druggable. The work names fresh leads for treatment research.
pmc-11709697:
Gabriela Raquel Paz Rivas and co-authors ask whether poor sleep goes with anxiety in adults who feel their memory slipping. Such subjective cognitive decline, with normal test scores, can be an early stage of decline, yet its causes vary widely. Their 2025 study draws on a south Brazilian cohort of adults over 65 with felt decline and no frank illness. Measures came from a set of short questionnaires on sleep, mood, anxiety, and daily activities.

At the 12-month check, 47 adults had complete data, most of them women with a median age of 71. Sleep scores tied to one thing only: the anxiety questionnaire. Worse sleep went with more anxiety, at a moderate strength. Sleep did not tie to felt decline scores from the adults or their informants, nor to test scores, age, or years of schooling. The team notes the small sample and calls for a wider study.
pmc-11709797:
Paresh Prajapati, Urim Geleta, and Wang-Xia Wang share a 2025 conference abstract on a tiny RNA that shapes talks between immune cells. The RNA, miR-223-3p, sits on the X chromosome and helps steer inflammation. The team paired brain microglia with macrophages from mice that lacked the RNA, in male and female mixes.

Macrophages missing the RNA showed sex-specific shifts in immune gene activity. Microglia grown with those macrophages switched on strong inflammatory genes, including IL1b and TNF. The pattern differed by the sex of the donor cells. The work suggests this small RNA helps tune brain inflammation in a sex-biased way.
pmc-11709897:
Brain immune cells grown from stem cells let researchers watch Alzheimer's biology in human tissue rather than mouse approximations. Berta Sanz Morello and co-authors built such a model in this 2025 paper. The cells are microglia, the brain's resident defenders, grown beside neurons from reprogrammed human cells. Both cell types carry disease-related mutations.

Microglia play both sides in the disease, clearing amyloid yet also pruning synapses. Two receptors, CD33 and TREM2, steer that balance and are flagged by genetic studies of patients. One common variant shortens the CD33 protein by skipping a segment. A human co-culture carrying these variants can test drugs against the real cellular players.
pmc-11709997:
Philip De Jager and co-authors map cell change across aged human brains in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 paper. The head names a single author, so the work is told without a team count. Past studies found many disease linked cell states, but when they act in the chain to disease was unknown.

The team built an atlas from more than one and a half million single nucleus profiles from the front cortex of hundreds of older people. Two fat linked microglial groups played apart roles: one tied to amyloid, the other pushed amyloid's effect toward tau. A star shaped support cell group linked tau to mind decline. Two paths of brain aging emerged, only one ending in dementia.
pmc-11710097:
An enzyme in the brain trims a precursor protein step by step, and the fragments it leaves are the stuff of the plaques seen in Alzheimer's disease. Xuefei Guo reads that trimming in a 2025 paper by freezing the enzyme with its work caught at four stages. Each stage shows the chain held in the same grip.

The chain crosses the membrane as a coil, links through a short bridge, then flattens into a strand that pairs with the enzyme's own strands. The cut lands just before that flat strand. After each cut the coil unwinds by one turn and slides forward, readying the next cut three links down. The cycle explains the steady step size seen in lab work and may hold for the enzyme's other targets as well.
pmc-11710197:
Courtney Glavis-Bloom and co-authors report a 2025 conference abstract on cognitive aging in marmosets. Aging hits people unevenly, and marmosets share many brain traits with humans while aging faster. The team built a touchscreen test battery to track thinking across the marmoset lifespan, then examined synapses under a microscope.

Older marmosets slowed in movement, drive, flexibility, and working memory, with wide gaps between animals. Aged brains lost synapses in a frontal region at rates like those in macaques. Yet impaired and unimpaired aged animals lost synapses to the same degree. The authors argue that synapse size scaling, not count alone, may set who declines.
pmc-11710297:
Lucineia Danielski and co-authors test vitamin D and a dementia drug on memory in rats without ovaries in a study from 2025. After menopause, falling estrogen raises the risk of brain decline. Vitamin D shortage, common in older people, adds its own threat. Donepezil, an Alzheimer's drug, props up a key brain chemical.

Adult and aged female rats had their ovaries removed to mimic menopause. Groups received vitamin D alone, donepezil alone, both, or neither. Memory tests then graded each recipe. The design separates the vitamin's solo effect from the pairing's. If the cheap vitamin helps, prevention gains a simple tool. The rat work maps the dose logic before any human trial.
pmc-11710397:
Daniel Whittaker and co-authors published this 2025 study on how time-restricted feeding reshapes the gut in Alzheimer's-model mice. Earlier work from the group showed that confining food to a six-hour daily window cleared amyloid, calmed gene activity in the brain, and rescued memory in these mice. Since gut bacteria feed into amyloid, inflammation, and daily rhythms, the gut was the next place to look.

Male and female APP23 mice ate freely or on the restricted schedule for three months. Stool and gut-end samples, taken around the clock, went through metabolite, gene, and transcript profiling. The team tracked how feeding time rewires the membership, chemistry, and daily oscillation of the microbiome, and how those shifts line up with the rescued brain. The study positions the gut as a working partner in the feeding effect, not a bystander.
pmc-11710497:
Carol Van Hulle and co-authors describe a 2025 study of past head injury in veterans and other adults. Mild head injury is common, and veterans face it more often than others. Past work is split on whether it leaves lasting marks tied to Alzheimer disease.

They drew on two groups, a trial group of veterans and a clinic group with some veterans. Staff recorded past mild injury, then tested spinal fluid, brain scans, and thinking scores. Veterans did report more past injury than others. Yet injury history showed no link to vessel harm signs, disease markers in fluid, or baseline thinking scores. The authors plan tests of injury weight and change over time.
pmc-11710697:
Marco Malaga and co-authors test a brief dementia screening tool in a 2025 paper on Quechua and Aymara patients. The tool, known as RUDAS, was built to work across cultures and languages. The team checked how well it sorted patients with and without cognitive problems in this group.

Their work is a second look at data from a large patient group in the GAPP study. The paper sets the test in a wider problem: aging raises dementia risk, yet native groups face language and access barriers to care. Readers learn how well a short, culture fair test performs where standard tests may fail.
pmc-11710797:
Davis C Woodworth and co-authors test a scan sign for LATE, a protein change of old age, in a 2025 study. LATE involves TDP-43 deposits and harms thinking, but no test can spot it in life. In a related younger-age disease, one side of the temporal lobe often shrinks more than the other. The team asked whether lopsided shrinkage of the hippocampus marks LATE.

They used scans and autopsy data from 104 people in The 90+ Study. Just over a third had LATE. As its stage rose, the two hippocampi grew more unequal and smaller overall. A model using the lopsided measure predicted mid-stage LATE far better than dementia status alone. The authors offer the sign as a new tool for spotting the condition.
pmc-11712097:
Yonah Joffe and seven colleagues report a case study, published in 2025, about a failed colonoscopy in a man with mild memory and thinking problems. A colonoscopy can find colon growths early and lower cancer risk, but it only works if the bowel is cleaned out well first. Known risk factors for poor cleaning include age and low health knowledge. The authors note that thinking problems before the exam have rarely been studied as a risk factor.

The patient, called CR, was sixty-nine and had a mild neurocognitive disorder with fast forgetting. His brain scan showed white matter changes, and he had a past history of confusion after surgery. His bowel cleaning scored four on a nine-point scale, which counts as too poor, so the exam failed. He was sent back for a second try.
pmc-11712297:
Damian Wheeler and co-authors count plaques and immune cells across whole mouse brains in a 2025 paper. New clearing methods make whole brains transparent for light sheet imaging. Flat slices, by contrast, sample only the spots a researcher picks. Whole brain counts suit drugs meant to act everywhere at once.

Their pipeline images a full brain at cell detail in under twenty minutes. Software spots each stained cell and maps it to a brain atlas. Plaques and immune cells can then be tallied region by region. The team aims the method at Alzheimer's model drug testing.
pmc-11712397:
Chanida Ruchisrisarod measured Alzheimer's-linked blood markers in people with long COVID, in a 2025 study. Many patients keep symptoms long after the first infection, including brain and mood complaints. The study asked whether their blood shows signs tied to brain damage and to the protein buildup of Alzheimer's disease.

The team enrolled 175 people and drew blood for virus antibodies, inflammation signals, and brain markers. Antibody patterns were much alike across groups, apart from one marker of past infection found almost only in patients. Inflammation signals ran high in both patients and controls. Patients whose amyloid test was positive showed a distinct set of signals, and a brain support cell marker stood out in patients overall. The author reads the pattern as a sign that brain injury may not fully resolve.
pmc-11712497:
The APOE4 gene variant is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease. The risk bites harder in women than in men. Hassan Mohammed, Jackie Coniglio, and Victor Luna test memory in mice carrying human APOE variants. Their task asks mice to tell two similar contexts apart, one with a foot shock and one safe. The skill depends on a brain region that grows new neurons in adulthood.

Basic fear learning showed no effect of sex or gene variant. The discrimination task told a different story. Female mice with the protective E2 variant outperformed E3 and E4 females. Males showed no gene effect at all. The authors link the gap to early disease symptoms.
pmc-11712597:
Krishna Kumar Gollepalli and co-authors described this 2025 work on a new brain scan tool for Alzheimer's disease. A receptor called GPR39 helps control zinc levels in the brain. When zinc balance fails, stress, swelling, and cell damage can follow, all signs linked to the disease. The team built the first tracer meant to show this receptor on PET scans.

The tracer is based on a drug that binds the receptor and can enter the brain. The team tested it in normal mice and in mice bred to build up amyloid, a protein tied to the disease. Scans and tissue checks after scanning showed how the tracer spread. A working tracer could later help test new drugs that target this receptor.
pmc-11712797:
Eiji Inoue and co-authors test a new antibody, E2025, against a brain receptor tied to Alzheimer disease in a 2025 paper. The receptor, EphA4, sits mostly in the brain and its activation is linked to nerve cell harm in several diseases. Loss of synapses is a hallmark of such diseases, and in Alzheimer disease plaques and tau tangles drive that loss.

E2025 bound strongly and only to EphA4, and it blocked its partner from binding. In rat nerve cells it changed how the receptor is cut, in a way tied to less harm. In mice bred to build tau tangles, checks of brain tissue showed less tau harm. The work backs E2025 as a candidate drug path.
pmc-11712897:
Suyeong Bae and Ickpyo Hong wrote a 2025 paper on the strain felt by people who care for a family member with dementia. The authors ask whether taking part in social life helps ease that strain, rather than only adding support from outside.

They drew on two large United States surveys from 2022 and studied 1,836 caregivers. Their model found that caregivers of people with dementia took part in social life less, and that less social time went with more strain in body and mood. The authors suggest that helping caregivers stay socially active could be a direct way to lower their burden.
pmc-11712997:
Linh N N Le, Evan Fletcher, Jinyi Qi, and Audrey P Fan predict future brain shrinkage from one baseline scan with deep learning in 2025. Shrinkage of the outer brain tracks decline in aging and disease. A U-shaped image network was trained to forecast shrinkage maps. Inputs were either a standard MRI scan or an amyloid PET scan. True maps came from paired scans over time.

Both input types yielded sound forecasts in a held out test set. Shrinkage ran higher in Alzheimer's patients than in mild cases, and higher there than in healthy peers. That ordering matched the true maps. Forecast averages did not differ clearly from truth in picked regions. The authors say one scan may suffice to project decline.
pmc-11713097:
Tyler Morris and co-authors describe a 2025 test of a music program led by a social robot for people with Alzheimer's disease or related dementia. The system, called MUSE, uses the robot Pepper to guide a group through a three-step music session. The team wanted to know how users themselves judged the system.

Fifteen people with mild to moderate dementia at care homes near Knoxville, Tennessee took part in workshops. They rated the robot and the session app above the midpoint on survey scales and praised the system in interviews. Many said the robot was hard to hear at times and the tablet screen was hard to see, giving clear targets for fixes.
pmc-11713197:
Carmensita Furlano and Pietro Gareri explore whether handwriting can betray the aging of the brain, in a 2025 paper. Graphology reads personality and physical state from the shapes and rhythm of writing. Writing is a brain-driven skill, so its decay might mirror decline in older people, healthy or with dementia. The authors, a graphologist and a geriatrician, set out to test the idea together on a small group.

Five volunteers aged sixty to eighty, three women and two men, took full medical and geriatric checks. Each wrote the same sentence about breathing in the scent of flowers. A blinded graphological reading scored features such as speed, pressure, rhythm, and direction. Four of the five writers showed the paper's listed signs of brain aging, such as slow, heavy, broken writing. The authors present the match as early support for handwriting checks in elder care.
pmc-11713297:
Julien Dubois and co-authors work on a new brain-based test for mild memory impairment in this 2025 paper. The test uses light sensors on the head to watch blood flow in the brain. The authors say primary care doctors miss many early cases, so a simple office test could help.

Twenty-one patients with mild impairment and twenty-four healthy older adults wore the device at rest and during tasks. The tasks covered word recall and holding patterns in mind at rising loads. The team pulled features from the light signals, body signals, and task scores. Their goal is a marker that can flag early decline more fairly than paper tests.
pmc-11713397:
Wai-Ying Yau and co-authors study in 2025 whether low physical activity speeds thinking decline in early Alzheimer disease by raising tau build up. Past work from the Harvard Aging Brain Study linked fewer daily steps to faster decline in older adults who carry amyloid but still think normally. Whether tau carries that effect was unknown.

Nearly three hundred such adults wore a waist pedometer for a week to set their activity level, then took thinking tests and brain scans over time. A smaller group also had tau scans across many brain regions. Models that account for age, sex, and schooling test how activity and amyloid together shape decline. The title finding is that tau growth in the temporal cortex carries the activity effect: less active adults built tau faster there, and that growth tracked their faster decline.
pmc-11713497:
Le Meur and co-authors test tiny drug carriers meant to fix body-clock problems in Alzheimer's disease, in this 2025 paper. About half of patients have sleep trouble, and a broken clock in the brain can speed the disease. Drugs for the clock often fail in patients because they cannot cross into the brain well.

The team packed melatonin into several kinds of nanoparticles, some coated to slip past the blood-brain barrier. They measured particle size, charge, drug load, and release speed. The best carriers were picked with a lab test that mimics the barrier. Timed release could one day restore daily rhythms in patients.
pmc-11713597:
Jiaqian Wu, Ye Na Han, Nicholas Cosford, and Lutz Tautz hunt for drug-like molecules that remove a brain enzyme tied to Alzheimer disease. The enzyme, called STEP, rises under the influence of amyloid and works against the strengthening of synapses, which the authors link to memory loss. Blocking or reducing it rescued thinking in mouse models, so the target is validated but hard to drug. Strong, selective fragments emerged. From the best binder they built degrader molecules that tag the enzyme for disposal. The degraders cleared the enzyme from human nerve-like cells, and one crossed into the brain and worked in living animals. The authors call them first-in-class tools against early synaptic failure.
pmc-11713697:
Joanna Philips and co-authors present a 2025 analysis of what patients and families want dementia research to study next. The Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute asked its stakeholders to name priorities for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. The exercise sits inside a wider push to promote older adults' health.

The institute has already invested 88 million dollars in fifteen comparative studies on these diseases. To find the gaps that remain, the team ran deep interviews and grouped the answers by theme. Stakeholders weighed in as the funder set one of its twelve topic themes. The analysis surfaces what caregivers and patients feel research keeps missing. Funders can use the themes to aim new awards where lived experience points.
pmc-11713797:
Julie Saugstad and co-authors check whether gene markers found in spinal fluid also work in blood in a 2025 Alzheimer's paper. The markers are microRNAs, tiny bits that help control genes. Spinal fluid tests found a set that separates patients from healthy adults. Blood is far easier to draw, so the team asks whether the same set shows up there.

First, the team checked whether blood levels stay steady within a person over three months. Then they matched spinal fluid and blood samples from the same donors on the same dates. The set of samples came from a national data project. If blood carries the same signal, screening for the disease could become much simpler.
pmc-11713897:
Leanne Howard and co-authors give guidance for running dementia drug trials from afar. Their 2025 consensus report weighs trials where patients stay home and staff work by phone, post, and web. Such trials could widen access and cut burden for drugs that lower dementia risk. Yet the dementia field lacked clear rules for running them well. A panel of experts in trial design, brain and mind care, and drug science shaped the guidance through rounds of comment.

Forty points span safety checks, drug shipping, outcome tests, and data capture for mid- and late-stage trials. The panel backs remote trials when sound safety checks are in place. The guide aims to be plain and usable for new trial teams.
pmc-11713997:
Guoqiao Wang and Kun Jin propose a new way to state a drug's benefit in Alzheimer's trials: one global rate of slowed progression, in a 2025 paper. Trials usually report a single score gap at the final visit, then turn it into a percent slowing that can confuse readers. Their method models that percent directly, across several outcome measures at once.

In simulated trials modeled on recent successes, the global rate gave more statistical power than a single-endpoint analysis, a global test, or a combined score. False alarm rates stayed in check for all methods. The authors say the rate is easier to explain to patients and can be computed with standard software in one step.
pmc-11714297:
Olivier Parent and co-authors map how white matter bright spots on brain scans differ in cause across disorders, in a 2025 paper. These hyperintensities signal small vessel disease and grow with age. Spots in different brain regions may not share the same biology. Treating them as one lump can mislead research.

The team built a framework to infer spot biology in living people. Data came from more than thirty thousand UK Biobank participants. Diffusion and susceptibility scans yielded fluid, fiber, myelin, and iron signals. Patterns for four disorders were charted across the brain. Regional signatures could sharpen diagnosis and trial design. The method turns a vague scan finding into a richer fingerprint.
pmc-11714597:
Kern and twelve co-authors report brain imaging results from the OVERTURE trial in Alzheimer's disease, published in two thousand twenty-five. The trial tested a home device that delivers light and sound pulsing at forty hertz for an hour a day, aiming to slow the disease.

Seventy-six patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's were randomized, with twice as many getting the real stimulation as the sham version, for six months. Brain scans showed the active group lost whole brain volume much more slowly, with about a sixty-nine percent reduction in shrinkage compared with sham. Benefits looked similar across age, disease stage, gene status, and amyloid level subgroups. The results support further testing of this non-drug approach.
pmc-11714697:
Lavinia Perquim and co-authors present a 2025 study linking blood marks on DNA to brain energy use in Alzheimer's disease. Chemical marks on DNA can turn genes up or down without changing the code itself. The team studied people with the disease and people with no loss of skills. All had a scan that shows how the brain burns sugar. Blood samples gave the DNA mark data for each person.

The team found hundreds of regions where the marks differed in a clear way. Many of those regions tracked with sugar use in parts of the brain. One region in a gene called ATE1 was tied to lower sugar use in memory areas. Another region was tied to higher use in some of the same areas. The work hints that blood marks may mirror what is happening inside the brain.
pmc-11714797:
A research team compares dementia risk factors in two care settings in Brazil in this 2025 study. Changeable risk factors, such as blood pressure, hearing, and lifestyle, are targets for public health, and the team asked how they look in primary care versus a specialist clinic.

Patients came from a government home care program and from tertiary memory clinics. The team gathered background data, risk profiles, thinking tests, and blood samples. Fifty-nine primary care patients and sixty-three clinic patients took part, with mean ages near seventy-two and seventy. Comparing the two groups shows where prevention efforts in everyday care could gain most.
pmc-11714897:
Andrew Burns, Igor Fortel, Barbara Bendlin, Liang Zhan, and Alex Leow measured the balance between excitation and inhibition in the brains of adults with and without thinking problems. A healthy brain sits near a critical balance point between go and stop signals. When that balance slips, it tracks risk factors for the most common dementia, such as a gene variant and sex.

The team analyzed nearly six hundred people aged forty-three to ninety-two, many scanned more than once. Three scan types were fused into maps of each person's brain wiring. Balance ratios were compared across gene status, amyloid build-up, age, sex, and clinical rating. Shifts in balance may be an early sign worth tracking.
pmc-11714997:
A blood test for Alzheimer's disease could change how whole countries count and catch the illness. Using a cutoff set in a separate, biomarker-confirmed group, they estimate how many participants likely have the disease's biology.

The estimate came to 16.9 percent, lower than the roughly 30 percent an amyloid-based method would suggest. Marker levels correlated modestly with one cognitive test and weakly with another. The authors say the blood marker may flag people at risk of symptoms, but larger studies must prove its worth for screening and risk sorting. The study appears in 2025.
pmc-11715097:
Primary progressive aphasia erodes language first, and its subtypes hint at different underlying diseases. Fifteen patients took the language battery, gave spinal fluid for Alzheimer's markers, and had amyloid PET scans that split them into positive and negative groups.

The positive group showed the expected fluid signature of Alzheimer's, with a lower amyloid ratio and higher phosphorylated tau. Their language profiles leaned toward the logopenic subtype and a related sensory aphasia. The negative group leaned toward non-fluent and semantic subtypes instead. With only fifteen patients the study is small, but the authors suggest the ordinary language test may help predict Alzheimer's pathology in this clinic population, guiding who needs confirmatory scans.
pmc-11715297:
Brains shrink with age in patterns that differ person to person, and one scan cannot show the pattern's shape. Cristina Sánchez and co-authors chart that shape over time in a 2025 study. They follow 79 healthy older adults through eight scans across about nine years.

A graph method sorts each person's shrinkage as one-site or many-site. Three groups emerged from the wiring of shrink sites. One group's sites moved in step, another's scattered, and a third sat between. Such maps could sharpen early reads of Alzheimer risk. They may also explain why disease paths vary so much.
pmc-11715497:
Jon Toledo and a large team of co-authors examined in 2025 how race, ethnicity, and neighborhood hardship relate to Alzheimer's markers in a United States trial cohort. Data on diverse groups remain scarce, though risk and care differ by background. The team studied 879 volunteers in an imaging sub-study of a lifestyle trial for at-risk older adults. Brain scans measured plaque, tau, and white matter damage.

Black participants showed lower white matter damage and lower tau in a key region than White peers. Participants rated with mild impairment were more often Black or Hispanic and carried more white matter damage. Higher plaque went with that rating in all groups except Black participants. Poorer neighborhoods tied to lower thinking scores but not to scan markers. The authors stress wide variety across groups.
pmc-11715697:
Alice Grazia and fourteen co-authors set out the plan for a study-within-a-study in this 2025 protocol paper. The scan's use in German care is being paid for under a coverage-with-evidence scheme while the data are gathered.

Using a standard framework for such checks, the team will measure whether patients and providers find the study acceptable, whether the right groups are reached, and whether sites follow the plan. Data will be gathered before and after, alongside the main trial. The aim is to learn not just whether the scan helps, but how the whole program works in real care.
pmc-11715797:
Yağmur Özbek and Görsev Yener read brain-wave sync to foresee dementia paths in a 2025 study. Mild cognitive impairment sits between normal aging and Alzheimer's disease. Each year a tenth or more of such patients convert to dementia.

Theta rhythm phase coherence during tasks had already flagged risk in earlier work. Here, thirty-three impaired patients were followed for two years. Fourteen progressed to Alzheimer's dementia while nineteen stayed stable. Their coherence values are compared with healthy seniors as the third group. A cheap scalp recording that sorts stable from progressive cases could guide early care.
pmc-11715897:
Jenni Lehtisalo and co-authors follow quality of life after a lifestyle program for older adults in a 2025 study. The Finnish FINGER trial mixed diet, exercise, and brain training to guard cognition. Life quality rose during the two-year program, especially physical function. Eleven more years test whether gains endure.

Over twelve hundred adults in their sixties and seventies were split between program and control. A standard thirty-six-item scale was filled at set points up to year eleven. Response thinned to about two in five by the end. Average scores slid with age in both groups. The study weighs how long a two-year push echoes in later life.
pmc-11715997:
Gabriel Colissi Martins and co-authors test star-cell transport effects on brain networks in a 2025 study. Glutamate is the brain's main go signal, cleared by star-shaped support cells. A tracer that binds a glutamate receptor lets scans read the system's state.

Rats were scanned before and after a drug that boosts the star cells' uptake pump. Earlier work found tracer binding rose in one deep relay zone only. The new read asks whether whole-network patterns shift even where single zones stay flat. Five rats give paired scans for the network comparison. The study links cell-level cleanup to system-level wiring.
pmc-11716097:
Rhoda Moise, Dingtian Cai, and a large team of co-authors study how stress in a person's life and family relates to Alzheimer's disease in groups often left out of research. Their 2025 study covers Black Americans, Hispanic and Latino participants, and Africans in a global cohort. Stress has become a known risk factor for the disease, but its weight across a life and a family was little studied.

The sample held 328 people. Regression models weighed the stress link while holding age, sex, group, and site steady. Stress was defined by a survey item on feeling tense, restless, or unable to sleep from a troubled mind. The study adds data from groups that bear a heavy load of the disease.
pmc-11716197:

Reserve is the idea that schooling, skilled work, and a larger brain help people cope with age-related damage. The team asked whether reserve also ties to the health of white matter, the brain's wiring. Their sample lived in the community and had no dementia.

The study covered 379 older adults, 287 thinking normally and 92 with mild impairment. Schooling years and job skill formed a score for mental reserve, while head-size-adjusted brain volume stood for brain reserve. Mental reserve was tied to better scores in every thinking area, most strongly for memory and attention. Brain reserve helped attention in the healthy group only. The wiring results were mixed, and the authors treat them with care.
pmc-11716297:
Gurveen Kaur Sandhu and thirteen co-authors probe how two blood markers shape the link between brain vessel damage and thinking, in a 2025 conference abstract. The markers are GFAP, a sign of astrocyte activation, and pTau-181, a tau fragment tied to Alzheimer's disease. Statistical moderation tests asked whether the markers change how strongly vessel damage predicts cognition. The setup combined thinking tests, automated lesion measurement, and single-molecule blood assays. The work extends a marker pair known from Alzheimer's research into vascular and mixed dementia, a setting where their interplay was not yet mapped.
pmc-11716397:
Maillard and co-authors study in 2025 a scan sign that may warn of future white spots in the brain before they grow. They followed 271 older adults who had brain scans about three years apart. White spots mark late harm from disease of the small blood vessels, a common partner of dementia in old age.

At the first scan, the team measured free water, a sign from a scan method, inside each spot and in normal looking tissue. They then sorted spots into those that stayed the same, those that grew, and new spots seen only later. High free water early on may flag tissue at risk, which could help doctors act before harm spreads.
pmc-11716497:
Shana Garza and co-authors study how a full day of blood pressure marks silent brain vessel wear, and whether the tie splits by sex, in a 2025 paper. High pressure and its swings are tied to stroke and to fade of thought.
