A higher day-long top pressure tied to both marks in men and in women. A swing mark tied to the scar mark in women alone. The team reads sex as a real thread in how pressure wears the small vessels of the brain.
pmc-11716597:
Anusha Bharadwaj and co-authors studied blood markers and thinking skills in aged common marmosets in 2025. Marmosets age fast, live only about ten to twelve years, and develop brain changes like those seen in Alzheimer's disease. The team drew blood from thirteen male and female animals and compared marker levels with test scores for mental decline and with brain findings after death.

One marker, called GFAP, was much higher in animals with poor thinking scores than in animals that scored well. The other markers in the blood test did not differ clearly between the two groups. No firm link was found between the blood markers and the brain damage seen in the tissue. The authors note that a larger study is under way to check these early results.
pmc-11716697:
Sarah Tom and co-authors published this 2025 study on pregnancy history and later brain health. Problems in pregnancy, such as early birth or high blood pressure, may leave marks that show up decades later. Few long-running studies hold both pregnancy records and late-life thinking tests. The team drew on a large cohort of older adults in one health system.

The study group included 444 women born in 1940 or later who had at least one pregnancy on record. Their thinking skills were tested at entry and every two years with a screening tool. The authors compared women with and without past pregnancy problems. The work tests whether a hard pregnancy predicts faster mental decline in old age.
pmc-11716797:
John K Maesaka, Louis J Imbriano, Grant Candace, and Nobuyuki Miyawaki published a study in 2025 on a newly described cause of salt loss through the kidneys in Alzheimer's disease. Low blood sodium is common in these patients, and the usual explanations did not fit many cases. The team traced the problem to a protein found in patient blood.

Earlier work showed that injecting patient plasma made rats pass more salt in urine. Comparing proteins in patient and healthy blood singled out one form of a haptoglobin-related protein as the active agent. Its effect strengthened as patients' mental scores fell toward zero. The authors argue many advanced patients slowly become dehydrated without anyone noticing.
pmc-11716897:
Min Chu, Li Liu, Binbin Nie, and Liyong Wu compare men and women with frontotemporal dementia in a 2025 study. The illness harms the front and side parts of the brain and changes conduct, speech, and thought. The team drew patients from their own center in China and from a shared study abroad, then lined up symptoms and brain scans by sex.

Women in the Chinese group had fewer school years, while men showed worse planning skills and more restless or false-belief symptoms. Women lost more gray matter, most in front brain areas, yet their brain fuel use held up better. A few shrinkage spots tracked with test scores in one sex only, a point the authors say care trials should weigh.
pmc-11726897:
Ioannis Tsamesidis and co-authors test whether wormwood extract can kill mouth cancer cells while sparing healthy ones. The herb, long used in drinks and folk care, is rich in a compound called artemisinin. Their 2024 study treats tongue cancer cells and healthy gum stem cells with the extract in the lab. It also charts what the extract holds.

Lab assays found high levels of artemisinin and a solid load of plant phenols. Healthy stem cells took the extract well and showed no harm. Cancer cells, by contrast, nearly all died within a day at a modest dose. Death signals inside those cells rose sharply. The authors call the results early but promising, and say the extract merits more study as a cancer aid.
pmc-11727797:
Eight authors read a dual block drug in nose growth care in a 2024 real-world study. The drug blocks two flare calls in long nose ill with polyps, a type-two flare state. Patients took skin shots for 42 weeks at the clinic in the study. Marks span polyp size, life grades, blood marks, and smell work.

All grade marks rose by firm spans at 42 weeks in the reads. Blood flare marks fell, with a short rise in one cell kind at week 16. Smell work and joy marks ran high in the set. The drug beat old care on most marks.
pmc-11727997:
Joanna Kosałka-Węgiel and co-authors profile the B cells circulating in lupus patients, comparing quiet periods with flares, in a 2024 study. Lupus is an autoimmune disease where B cells help produce antibodies that attack the body's own tissues. Which B cell families swell or shrink as the disease wakes was poorly mapped. The team studied thirty-five patients, twelve in flare and twenty-three in remission, all meeting current classification criteria.

Blood samples were sorted by flow cytometry into B cell subsets, from naive cells to memory and regulatory types. Activity scores tracked with the share of transitional and regulatory B cells. Other subsets tracked with complement levels, proteins consumed when the immune system attacks. The authors argue these patterns could help doctors read a patient's state and anticipate flares from a blood draw.
pmc-11728297:
Lyudmyla Antypenko and five co-authors present a 2024 study of fifteen related compounds tested against a drug resistant yeast. The yeast is the second most common Candida threat in clinics and often shrugs off the standard azole drugs. New chemical families are needed that can still stop it.

The team made two new compounds and characterized them with several spectral tools. All fifteen were tested on patient isolates of the yeast across a range of doses. Two stood out, stopping growth at doses about twenty times lower than weak peers. Computer docking, pattern models, and toxicity screens rounded out the checks on the best candidates.
pmc-11728397:
Gabriele Ruzijevaite, Enrika Acaite, and Egle Jagelaviciene review what vitamin C does for mouth and gum health in a 2024 paper. The vitamin is known for guarding cells and calming swelling, and dentists have eyed it as an add-on cure. The team searched three sources for trials from a five-year span.

Seventeen studies with over eight hundred patients met the bar. In most, gum scores such as bleeding and pocket depth were better with the vitamin than without. Some studies also found less pain, faster bone healing after tooth pulls, and gains for gum looks, the review reports.
pmc-11728497:
Jonatan Dorca-Arévalo, Antonio Santana-Ruiz, Benjamín Torrejón-Escribano, Mireia Martín-Satué, and Juan Blasi published this study in 2024. It watches how cells defend themselves against epsilon toxin, a pore-punching poison from a gut bacterium. The toxin attacks myelin, the insulation of nerves, and has been linked to multiple sclerosis.

The toxin needs a surface protein called MAL to strike. The team built a sensitive cell line displaying that protein, tagged so it glows. Under attack, the cells shed bubbles called extracellular vesicles, a trick for ejecting toxin pores from the membrane. The bubbles carried the receptor protein and clumps of the toxin. That cargo makes the vesicles a promising tool: studying them could reveal how the toxin binds, assembles, and might be blocked. The authors say the system offers a window on a toxin whose role in human disease is debated.
pmc-11728597:
A fast pine is the south land's chief tree wealth, and its groves bank sky gas in wood and soil alike. Daniel Bozo and co-authors weigh that bank in a 2024 study of ten groves at cut age. Sand and young ash soils span the set, from dry and poor to rich and wet; three plots per grove were dug a full stride deep.

Ash soil banked twice the sand's soil gas, and its whole grove bank ran high by near half. Grove yield tied hard to soil gas and to whole bank when soil kind was held in the sums. Shallow reads would miss the deep bank, the team warn. Soil fit yield models are their close plea.
pmc-11728797:
Yanping Li and co-authors fed a medicinal fungus to weaned pigs to find a safe, helpful dose, in a study published in 2024. Cordyceps militaris grows on insect larvae and is prized in traditional medicine, but animal dosing data were thin. Thirty pigs were split into five groups on diets with rising fungus doses for forty-two days. Growth, gut structure, blood chemistry, and organ health were tracked.

A low dose of one hundred milligrams per kilogram boosted daily weight gain and feed efficiency. It also improved gut lining structure and energy digestion, and raised antioxidant defenses in blood. Higher doses, up to forty times as much, did not help growth but also caused no harm across organs, blood counts, and tissue checks. The authors conclude the fungus is a safe feed supplement candidate, with benefits concentrated at the low dose.
pmc-11732497:
Michael Zarrella, Kolu Wynne, Basel Saadeh, and Gregory Gersten published a case report in twenty twenty-four on superior vena cava syndrome caused by the very pacemaker leads meant to help the patient. The great vein draining the head and neck narrows around implanted leads, producing venous congestion. Their patient also had sick sinus syndrome, the reason for the device.

Treatment combined invasive and conservative therapy. Balloon angioplasty reopened the vein, and the long-term fix was a leadless pacemaker, removing the offending hardware from the vein entirely. The authors walk through the diagnostic reasoning. As implanted devices multiply, device-caused versions of this once mostly cancer-linked syndrome are rising, and the case doubles as a management template.
pmc-11733397:
Kidney disease in India often arrives without diabetes attached, and Sharad Sheth presents four real cases to show how a diabetes drug can still help. Dapagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor approved in India for non-diabetic kidney disease as well, was given to four patients with differing profiles. After treatment, their kidney filtration rates and urinary protein levels moved the right way, and in every case the slide toward advanced disease slowed.

Sheth frames the series as real-world support for the drug's kidney-protective effects beyond blood sugar. The cases argue for treating the kidney risk itself, whatever the patient's diabetic status.
pmc-11733897:
Sebastiana Arroyo-Bote and Aina Antonelli-Sastre wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It surveys dentistry students at the University of Barcelona on how well they spot tooth decay in a real case, and whether senior students lean more conservative than juniors.

Cavities are the world's most common chronic disease, so detection skill matters. Students in years three, four, and five judged clinical and radiographic images from one patient. About seventy-two percent saw early decay or cavities in the photo, and every student caught them on the radiograph. On chewing surfaces, many chose gentle sealant treatment. On side surfaces, though, nearly all jumped straight to a drilled class II filling, even in early lesions. Eighty-five percent of answers leaned on minimal intervention concepts elsewhere. The authors see a training gap between diagnosis and restraint.
pmc-11736297:
Christine Weston and twelve co-authors surveyed Black and Latino adults on joining COVID-19 trials, in a 2024 study. Six hundred people across the Baltimore and Washington area responded in late twenty twenty-one. Both groups remain underrepresented in trials. About half said they were unwilling to join treatment or vaccine studies. Awareness and trust were the measures of interest.

Greater trust in trial information sources predicted willingness. So did simply knowing more about trials. The pattern held for both treatment and vaccine trials. Latino respondents facing more daily hardship were less willing on vaccines. Social needs competed with research participation there. The authors call for awareness campaigns built on trusted voices. Inclusion goals will fail without that groundwork, they argue. Community partnerships are the delivery vehicle proposed.
pmc-11741197:
Fahad Alshubaily and three co-authors report a rare fungal cause of an aortoenteric fistula in this 2024 case report. The fistula is an abnormal channel between the aorta and the gut, and it is often missed. Their patient was a sixty-five-year-old man with upper gut bleeding and black stools. Standard scopes found nothing conclusive. A CT scan suggested the fistula. He then vomited blood suddenly and went into hemorrhagic shock on the ward.

Emergency surgery controlled the bleeding. Surgeons replaced the aorta section with a graft, repaired the duodenum, and cleared whitish fungal debris. Culture of the aortic tissue grew Aspergillus, a mold. Fungal infection of a primary fistula of this kind is rare. The authors stress that the condition kills quickly when missed. Early surgery is the decisive step, they argue.
pmc-11770097:
A research team in China tested a combined rehab method for a leg nerve injury in this clinical study, published in 2024. The injury affects the common peroneal nerve and weakens movement and feeling in the lower leg. Drugs and surgery help only so much, so the team looked for a better option.

Thirty patients took part, split into two groups of fifteen. One group got electrical pulses to the muscles, while the other got the same pulses plus mirror therapy, where the healthy leg's image guides the hurt one. After four weeks, the combined group did better on surface feeling, nerve signal speed, and joint range of motion. The authors suggest the pairing is a useful new route for this kind of nerve damage.
pmc-11770797:
Fatma Dhaffouli and co-authors measured a calming immune protein, annexin A1, in kidney biopsies from patients with lupus nephritis, the kidney inflammation caused by systemic lupus. The protein helps resolve immune responses, and its behavior in this disease was unclear. Using antibody staining, the team compared tissue from twenty-four patients against eight healthy controls.

Patient biopsies showed significantly more annexin A1 in the glomeruli, the kidney's filtering knots. Stronger staining also tracked with the proliferative classes of the disease, in which kidney cells multiply aggressively, marking more severe illness. The authors suggest the protein could help pathologists distinguish severe from milder forms of lupus nephritis, while noting the small sample.
pmc-11776297:
Dana Al-Azzeh and Jasmin Lilian Diab review the mental health effects on children whose mothers migrate for work in a review whose text is dated 2024. Many women leave home countries to work as caregivers in richer nations, hoping to give their children a better future. Long separation, with patchy care in their place, leaves children exposed.

The review covers work across cultures. Children left behind face higher risk of depression and anxiety and trouble forming close bonds. Even after a mother returns, strained ties can last. Shared caregiving in some societies softens the harm, but not fully. The authors call for mental health support and policy shaped to local culture.
pmc-11794197:
Joyce Kamau and co-authors examine whether small farmers actually reach Kenya's school feeding market, in a 2024 study. Smallholders grow most of the country's food, and the Home Grown School Feeding Programme was designed to kill two birds. It feeds hungry primary school children and buys the food locally from those same farmers. The team surveyed hundreds of farmers, farmer groups, and teachers in three counties.

Only about a fifth of farmers and just over a third of farmer groups had managed to sell into the program, mostly maize and beans. The study also checked uptake of a mobile phone platform meant to smooth procurement. Barriers like paperwork, group organization, and payment delays keep the smallest growers outside a market built for them. The findings give program managers a concrete list of doors to unlock.
pmc-11803197:
Andrew Brownlow, Nicholas Davison, and Phillip Morin present the genome of the minke whale. Their genome note from twenty twenty-four deals with Balaenoptera acutorostrata. The assembly comes from a single female whale.

The full sequence runs to thousands of megabases in length. Most of it sits in twenty-two chromosome like scaffolds. The X sex chromosome is among those scaffolds. The mitochondrial genome was also assembled in full. The work comes from the Sanger Tree of Life effort. Such references aid whale biology and conservation study.  The whale species is a baleen whale.
pmc-11810897:
Jiahui Chang and co-authors study how exercise changes a protein mark in mouse muscle. The mark is called lactylation, a tag added to proteins after effort. Mice ran at a moderate pace for six weeks, while a second group rested. The team read genes, proteins, the marks on them, and small molecules in the muscle. The study was published in 2024.

The team found 159 mark sites on 78 proteins that shifted with exercise. Three marked proteins sit in the cell's power plant and help make energy. Their marks fell with exercise, while the proteins themselves rose in amount. Path checks point to energy making as the route most changed. Other routes, tied to fats and acids, also shifted and need more study.
pmc-11811497:
Rybakov and co-authors review in 2024 how to rebuild gene regulatory networks from single cell data. These networks are graph models of how genes switch each other on and off during growth and in response to change.

Older methods mined published studies, while current ones infer the networks from large omics data sets. Single cell data give very fine detail and let networks be drawn for each cell type and state. But the data are noisy and sparse, so they need special methods. The review covers tools that add data on factor binding sites and open chromatin to sharpen the inference. It also weighs what such networks can reveal about cell processes.
pmc-11816397:
Depression runs heavier in rural south India than in its cities, and Pooja Rai and co-authors split that gap into its parts, in work from twenty twenty-four. Two cohorts, one rural and one urban, held near five thousand five hundred adults past forty-five. A standard scale screened for depression.

Rural rates ran near fourteen percent against eight in the city. Even after full adjustment, rural living raised the odds by more than half. A split method weighed how much of the gap the measured traits explain and how much stays unexplained. The study tells planners where the rural burden sits, and how much of it simple traits cannot excuse.
pmc-11821597:
Marian Krawczyk, Kari Nyheim Solbrække, and Lisbeth Thoresen ask whether an idea from hospice care can illuminate life after cancer. The piece, published in 2024, starts from a gap: more people survive cancer than ever, yet the tangled suffering many feel after treatment ends is poorly understood. The authors borrow the concept of total pain, born in the hospice movement, and test it against interviews from a Norwegian project on rethinking survivorship.

They find the concept captures existential suffering while adding useful angles of its own. It treats the person as a whole and restores the body to the picture, respects the limits of what stories can express, and attends to relationships. Because it grew inside cancer care, it may also guide better services. Dying of cancer and surviving it differ, the authors argue, but total pain works as a compass for both.
pmc-11822597:
Patra leads a team measuring acute malnutrition in young children in tribal areas of India in a 2024 survey paper. Arm circumference offers a quick field test for wasting. Two tribal blocks in Maharashtra were surveyed through a child nutrition program.

Over a thousand children under five were measured. Severe acute malnutrition was uncommon, while moderate malnutrition affected about one child in ten. Girls carried higher rates of both forms than boys. Toddlers in their second year faced a much higher risk than infants. One block fared notably better than the other. A small share of children were critically malnourished. The authors urge block-level monitoring and program review. Sex gaps need targeted attention.
pmc-11839497:
Jiangyan Guo and co-authors report, in 2024, a rare case in which lung cancer spread to the uterus and its attachments. Lung adenocarcinoma is increasingly seen in women and often hides until it has spread. Spread to the womb and ovaries, though, is extremely uncommon, and uterine spread in particular is seldom documented.

The team reviews one patient's course, a microcapillary subtype confirmed by tissue appearance, immune staining, and molecular tests. They also survey the published literature on similar cases. The report aims to give clinicians a reference for recognizing and managing this unusual pattern of spread when it appears.
pmc-11881197:
Rukhsar Osman and co-authors report a 2024 quality improvement project on breastfeeding at a private hospital in Tanzania. Health guidance urges a first feed within an hour of birth and breast milk only for six months. Tanzanian rates fall short of those goals. The hospital team aimed to reach an eighty percent standard for both measures during the birth stay.

Working in plan-do-study-act cycles, they set a hospital policy, trained staff, and taught mothers before birth with videos. They added skin-to-skin contact after surgical births, new feeding charts, and daily lactation rounds. After three cycles, first-hour feeding rose from twenty-two to eighty-four percent. Milk-only feeding rose from forty-five to ninety percent. The authors credit the mix of policy, training, and daily support.
pmc-11881597:
Grant McGee Talkington and co-authors review what long COVID does to the brain, how doctors can image it, and what treatments might help, in a review the head dates to 2024. Long COVID leaves many survivors with insomnia, fatigue, mood trouble, and foggy thinking that linger for months. The team surveys how scans and brain-wave tests reveal subtle changes behind those symptoms.

They weigh several stories for the cause: the virus entering the brain, inflammation, a leaky brain barrier, signals from the gut, and damaged vessel linings that starve tissue of blood. The vessel story gets special weight as a shared root. The treatment survey runs from antivirals to anti-inflammatory drugs, with frank notes on thin proof. The authors aim the review at clinicians sorting a messy, multi-system illness.
pmc-11888697:
Ankita Pati and co-authors compare three ways to measure gum thickness. Their 2024 study sits in dentistry, where gum depth shapes choices for gum care and implants. A thick or thin gum can change how well treatment holds, so a sound measure matters.

The three methods are a CT scan of the jaw, a fine probe pushed through the gum, and sound-wave imaging. Each has its own trade-offs in accuracy, in how much it intrudes, and in daily use. The study finds the probe method to be the gold standard of the three. The authors weigh the scan and the sound method against that bar for clinic use in daily practice.
pmc-11967397:
Functional dyspepsia brings recurring upper-belly pain and fullness with no visible cause, and treatments often disappoint. Nayoung Kim reviews a suspect gaining ground: imbalance in the small intestine's microbes. Studies find more Streptococcus and fewer of several other genera in patients, plus frequent bacterial overgrowth in the small bowel.

Low-grade inflammation and a leaky duodenal lining may link the microbes to symptoms, working through gut-brain signaling in both directions. An antibiotic that stays in the gut, rifaximin, eases symptoms, especially in women. The 2024 review, published in Korean with an English summary, says the microbial case is strong but causality still needs proof.
pmc-11998097: Mikio Kataoka and Kuniaki Nagayama, two senior members of the Biophysical Society of Japan, reported in 2024 on attending the world biophysics congress in Kyoto in both 1978 and 2024. They compared the talks and posters at the two meetings, half a century apart, and traced how the field changed with the technology of each era. They close by looking ahead to the next stage of biophysics as a continuation of that trend.
pmc-12110497:
Bornface Chinene and Leon-say Mudadi survey pregnant women's knowledge and expectations about prenatal ultrasound in Harare, Zimbabwe. Their 2023 cross-sectional study questions three hundred eighty-five women at a private maternity hospital.

Most women agreed scans are important during pregnancy, yet nearly four fifths did not know scans can detect birth abnormalities. Knowledge about Down's syndrome was more common and rose slightly with education. Women's main expectations were confirming the delivery date and learning the baby's sex. Diagnosing abnormalities was the least expected purpose. Knowledge levels were lower than in similar studies elsewhere, so the authors call for more public education about what prenatal scanning can reveal.
pmc-12118297: Xu Wang and co-authors report the first BRIGHT symposium, held in Chongqing in June twenty twenty-four, and the declaration it produced for children's medicine. Teams showed work on generating and translating evidence for pediatric care, on building and judging clinical guidelines, and on applying artificial intelligence in the field. The meeting also built working ties across borders. The declaration aims to foster innovation in evidence-based practice and guidelines, raising the quality of care for children everywhere.
pmc-12269897:
Andre Sica de Campos and three co-authors look back at their own forecasts for sugarcane ethanol in Brazil in a 2024 study. A decade ago they had projected how the biofuel, and car travel with it, would evolve under responsible innovation pressures. Revisiting old forecasts is rare in their field, and they argue the habit is how engaged analysis improves.

The team tests those earlier expectations against what has in fact happened in Brazil’s fuel and car sectors. Several projected trends are confirmed by the later evidence. The exercise also shows where the discourse of responsible research and innovation matched or missed real power shifts. Their framework offers a way to grade foresight work honestly, a practice they urge on peers.
pmc-12375897:
Yashirdisai Sampasivam and co-authors review how agarwood, a prized fragrant resin, forms in Aquilaria trees, in work the text dates to 2024. The catalog lists 2025. The resin forms inside the wood as a defense against stress and infection, feeding perfume, religious, and medicine trades. Demand has pushed some Aquilaria species toward endangerment. Artificial induction exists, but the biology linking microbes, wood changes, and chemistry stays murky.

The review ties together wood structure shifts, the making of the resin's signature compounds, and signals from multi-layer molecular studies. Microbes living inside the tree, notably Fusarium, help trigger formation in both wild and induced settings. Stress signals and gene switches balance defense against growth. The authors argue that joining these threads is the path to agarwood production that does not fell wild forests.
pmc-12417297:
Hardy and a team including Ward describe co-design of a digital therapy for psychosis in twenty twenty-four. Digital tools may improve access to psychological therapy for people with psychosis. Tools must fit real needs, or they will not help in practice. The authors argue for inclusive co-design that starts from people's needs, not from a fixed solution.

They present a method that mixes agile exploration with clinical rules and regulation. The example is SloMo, a blended therapy for fear of harm from others. A mixed team, including people with lived experience, shaped its functions, look, and content. Cycles of widening and narrowing ideas were tested with stakeholders. The authors close with lessons on funding, rules, and keeping lived experience members involved.
pmc-12539497:
Alzheimer's disease is swelling with the age of the world: 43.8 million patients in 2016, a projected 152 million by 2050. Nobel Zong and co-authors argue in a 2024 perspective that the tide can still be turned. The molecular changes of the disease begin some twenty years before symptoms, leaving a long window for action.

The authors call for fast progress on four fronts: early detection and monitoring, targeted prevention, new therapeutics, and supporting policy. PET imaging gives powerful prognosis, while artificial intelligence offers cheap, wide-scale screening and fresh risk clues. Two newly approved antibodies already slow progression modestly, and gene therapy candidates promise durable protection. The piece is a call to use the window before the wave crests.
pmc-12661697:
Isabel Rodriguez and five co-authors gather views from Latino families to shape a new eating-disorder program, in this twenty twenty-five study. Teens in this community face stigma, language gaps, and few care options that fit their culture. Most existing programs were built for white, English-speaking families.

The team is adapting a brief workbook program so family doctors can offer it in primary care. Focus groups with teens and caregivers fed the first design steps. Their input guides language, food examples, and family roles in the new version. The study lays groundwork for care that Latino families can truly use.
pmc-12661797:
Anamaria Bancos and co-authors review tests for leftover leukemia in a 2025 paper. After treatment for acute myeloid leukemia, tiny traces of disease can remain and warn of relapse. Finding those traces guides later care, yet current tests are complex or hard to access in many places.

The review covers cell sorting, gene tests, and sequencing methods now in use, with their strengths and limits. Two newer options get close attention. One reads chemical marks on DNA that go awry in this cancer. The other uses laser scattering from blood or DNA samples to spot disease signs. The authors say both could widen access to precise checks once larger studies confirm them.
pmc-12661897:
Chen and co-authors trace a gene pathway that drives lung scarring after bacterial toxin exposure. The enzyme TET1 changes DNA marks on the KLF6 gene. That change raises KLF6 levels in lung vessel cells. High KLF6 then turns on the S1PR3 gene and its RhoA and ROCK signals. The chain pushes vessel cells toward scar-like traits and cell death.

Lowering TET1 eased those shifts in lab cells exposed to the toxin. Extra KLF6 undid the gain from lowering TET1. Lowering KLF6 shut down the RhoA and ROCK path as well. In mice, lowering TET1 reduced lung scarring from the toxin. The authors name this chain as a drug target for lung fibrosis.
pmc-12662697:
Qianqian Wang and co-authors report a 2025 case of closing a stomach defect after a full-thickness scope resection. Their patient was a 59-year-old man with a raised area in the lower stomach that reached the outer wall layer. Full removal left a long wound near the stomach outlet, where movement is strong and swelling made the view poor.

Standard clips could not finish the closure. The team first partly closed the wound with a three-arm clip, then fixed a thread at the wound edge with metal clips. Pulling the thread from outside drew the sides together and cleared the view, and more clips sealed the rest. Scope doctors get a step-by-step fix for closures that stall halfway.
pmc-12663197:
Yanju Cai and co-authors survey work flow and feelings among dialysis nurses in China, in work from 2025. Five hundred two nurses at fourteen blood cleaning centers in Fujian took part, and four hundred sixty gave valid replies. Flow at work means deep, smooth focus on the task. The feeling scale gauges how warmly nurses hold their work.

Feeling scores ran high, while flow scores sat mid-range. Flow split by age, hospital rank, years in the craft, and pay. Feeling split by more traits, from unit size to job title. The two scores rose together in a strong link. The authors say lifting feelings may deepen flow and drive.
pmc-12667697:
Rong Wang, Suqin Wang, and Jiapeng Qu test parasite effects on pika behavior and body state in a 2025 study. Plateau pikas are a keystone species on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau. Gut parasites commonly infect them in the wild. Whether infection shifts individual personality was unclear.

Thirty adult pikas were split into infected, control, and drug-treated groups. Boldness, exploration, and docility were measured across days. Thyroid hormones, metabolic rate, and stress hormone were also tracked. Infected pikas carried clearly higher parasite loads. At peak infection they grew bolder, more exploratory, and more docile. Thyroid hormones fell as parasite loads rose. Stress hormone and metabolic rate fluctuated by stage. The authors read this as a complex host adaptation strategy. Parasite load, they conclude, modulates both behavior and physiology in this mammal.
pmc-12673297:
Shutong Liu and co-authors report, in a 2025 real-world study, how a drug called surufatinib performed against advanced neuroendocrine tumors in China. These tumors grow from hormone-making cells, and the drug blocks both blood vessel growth and immune escape routes. It is approved in China for tumors that cannot be cut out. The team reviewed twenty-one patients treated at one hospital over two years.

Disease was held in check in about four fifths of the patients, while tumors shrank clearly in a smaller share. Median time without growth reached 9.7 months. Patients with the related, more aggressive carcinoma form answered the drug at a higher rate than those with the standard tumor type, though the small numbers blur that gap. Serious side effects struck about a quarter of patients, and no one died from the treatment.
pmc-12679197:
Jie Sun and Ping Wang study in 2025 how fatigue links with anxiety and low mood in people who live with chronic heart failure. The disease runs a long course, and tiredness is one of its most common burdens. Whether worry and low mood make that tiredness worse was not clear.

The study covered 162 patients who came to a heart clinic in Suzhou between May 2023 and May 2025. Staff rated each patient's fatigue with a 20 item scale that covers several sides of tiredness. Worry and low mood were rated with two standard self rating scales. The team also gathered basic facts on each patient to hunt for what drives fatigue. If mood worsens fatigue, then care that lifts mood could ease the most common complaint of these patients.
pmc-12685497:
An editorial in The Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific argues that stigma and missed diagnosis hide half the region's diabetes, in a 2025 comment. About seventy percent of people with diabetes are of working age, and shame at work can delay care seeking. A 2023 global study counts 248 million undiagnosed cases worldwide.

In the Western Pacific, roughly half of adults with diabetes are undiagnosed, the second worst regional rate. Delayed finding raises the risk of heart disease, kidney damage, and amputations. The piece blames silent symptoms, scarce screening, test cutoffs that fit Asian bodies poorly, and stigma itself, and urges a change of story.
pmc-12687297:
Jibin Kunjavara and colleagues survey nurses in Qatar on non-drug pain relief for children. Their study from twenty twenty-five covers tertiary public hospitals. Drug-free methods are a core part of good paediatric pain care. Top hospitals should model the best of those practices.

One hundred thirty-six nurses in emergency and inpatient units responded. Knowledge, attitudes, and reported practice were all measured. Demographic traits were tested against competence scores. Sampling was proportionate across the participating units. Data collection ran through autumn of twenty twenty-four. Gaps between knowing and doing can now be targeted. Training design benefits from knowing exactly where practice lags.
pmc-12690797:
Sharon Miracle Nayagam and co-authors search blood for signs of disc degeneration in a 2025 study. Back discs break down with a strong immune and inflammation component. Whether changes inside the disc echo into the general circulation was unknown.

Protein screening covered plasma and tissue from forty patients plus plasma from twenty healthy volunteers. Patients split into groups with and without a specific spine image change. Over seven hundred proteins appeared in patient plasma, with about five hundred shared with healthy samples. Immune complement proteins stood out, and most ran higher in patients. Two parts of the system ran lower instead. A blood signature of disc disease could ease diagnosis without invasive sampling.
pmc-12691197:
Meretukov and co-authors test large language models on non-English medical records in breast cancer care. Real-world evidence often sits locked in free-text electronic records, hard to use for research. Language models could turn that text into structured data sets, yet their reliability is still doubted by many.

The study focuses on hormone receptor-positive breast cancer cases. Records written in a non-English language add a further test of model skill. The team checked how faithfully the models extracted key facts. Trustworthy extraction would open vast record archives, in many languages, to outcome research.
pmc-12693297:
Rafael Campos Vieira and co-authors build a twin network that judges how alike two molecules are from charge maps and weak-contact art, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Charge images feed a vision net, while texture marks from density maps feed a second net. The two streams merge into one shared space trained to pull kin close.

Weak-contact data helps the model spot stand-in molecules that bind the same target in unlike shapes. Three drug sets test the system, covering leukemia, Alzheimer disease, and a cross-check set. The frame is pitched for screening, reuse of old drugs, and fresh candidate hunts. Readers get a similarity judge that reads more than raw shape.
pmc-12693797:
Giulia Bacilliere and four colleagues published an ecology study in two thousand twenty-five on a cold-loving moss in Italy. The moss Pohlia cruda grows in high, cold places across the far north and mountains. The team modelled where in Italy the moss could live as the climate warms.

They combined several distribution models and tested two paths for future greenhouse gas levels, for the years two thousand fifty and two thousand ninety. Under the middle path, suitable ground shrank by roughly a quarter to nearly a half. Under the highest-emissions path, losses ran deeper still. The authors say the work is the first of its kind for mosses in Italy. It gives planners a base for protecting mountain plant life.
pmc-12694297:
Giuseppe Trapani and co-authors coated plastics with a flame-slowing nanolayer in a 2025 study. Ethylene copolymers serve in cables and foams but burn readily. Bulk flame adds can spoil their traits, so a skin-thin guard is a neat swap.

The team cast thin films of the same copolymers loaded with layered double hydroxide flakes, in two flake shapes. The films were then laid as coats on plain stock. Burn tests in a cone calorimeter showed the coats cut the burn rate, even at a tiny flake share of the whole piece. The route suits goods that must stay light and flexible.
pmc-12695897: Elizabeth Germino and co-authors use a tracer scan to watch killer T cells enter mouse breast tumors in a 2025 study. The scan tags CD8 cells, the immune system's main tumor fighters, across the whole body without surgery. Radiation plus an immune drug were the treatments under watch. Tissue checks and scans agreed on the story. The combined treatment drew T cells in early, but unevenly across tumors. That patchy response could be seen on the images as it unfolded in living animals.
pmc-12699197:
Ye Tao and co-authors build, in twenty twenty-five, a chemical method to tell apart two Chinese herbal medicines that are often confused. Sinomenii caulis and Menispermi rhizoma come from the same plant family. Mix-ups risk wrong treatment. The team used liquid chromatography to build chemical fingerprints for each herb across batches. Fingerprints of the same herb matched well. One herb contained sinomenine; the other contained dauricine, two distinct marker compounds. A mass spectrometry step then produced a digital matrix of chemical components for each herb.

That matrix became the basis of a new identification method. It successfully separated the two herbs. Results on samples with varied adulteration levels followed a correlation trend, supporting the method for quality control.
pmc-12699297:
Sha Li and co-authors build a near-infrared fluorescent probe that reports two cancer-linked signals inside cells at once: glutathione levels and inner thickness, or viscosity. Both run high in cancer cells, and watching them together sharpens the picture. Their probe parks in the mitochondria, the cell's power plant.

Their 2025 study shows one part of the molecule snapping open on contact with glutathione for a bright turn-on, while a second part glows harder as thick fluid stalls its spinning. The probe picks glutathione out from a crowd of rivals, harms cells little, and tracks both signals as drugs push them up or down. Inflammation and cell death models show the dual read in action.
pmc-12699597:
Brianna McCoola and co-authors worked with young people to shape better health care in Queensland. Teens and young adults often fall into a gap between child and adult services. The team ran focus groups and a statewide survey to learn what needs fixing. Young patients, carers, and health staff all took part.

Nine focus groups and over a hundred survey replies fed into the plan. Most of the listed fixes were rated as needed and highly important. Two ground themes stood out. The system itself blocks smooth care, and no shared picture of good care for this age group exists. The team calls for standard principles and practices across the state.
pmc-12699897:
Ian Matandika and co-authors survey family caregivers in Malawi in a 2025 cross-sectional study. Relatives who nurse patients through palliative care carry physical, emotional, and social loads, and how much support they themselves receive shapes both their health and the patient's.

Three hundred eight caregivers at two rural hospitals answered standard questionnaires on perceived social support and psychological distress. Just over half felt supported, while about forty-two percent reported distress. Caregivers at one hospital fared better on support than the other. The authors link the two measures and argue that shoring up caregivers is part of good palliative care.
pmc-12700197:
Song Tian and co-authors trace how a plant pathogen disarms its host in this 2025 study. The water mold Phytophthora sends protein tools into plant cells to blunt defense. Two sibling tools proved key for infection strength, and a cut-down form of one binds a host protein long debated in the field.

That host protein weakens plant defense, so the pathogen gains by keeping it around. Two tagging enzymes pull it in opposed ways, one marking it for removal and one shielding it. The cut tool tips the balance toward shielding, so the protein survives and infection spreads. The team frames the trick as one more route by which these tools diversify.
pmc-12700897:
Imjoo Jung and Sunhee Lee study 3D printed shoe midsoles with a re-entrant inner pattern, a lattice that bends inward under load, in a 2025 paper. They printed the midsoles in two slice directions and three fill densities, then split each sole into toe, midfoot, and heel zones for testing.

Vertical prints proved about 1.5 times stiffer than horizontal ones. Both directions carried charge about equally, and denser fill conducted better. A 50 percent fill gave the best mix of electrical response and feel. Horizontal prints spread foot pressure over a wider area, which aids stability. The authors back flat-printed, half-filled midsoles for smart footwear that senses pressure while staying soft.
pmc-12700997:
Joel Hallgren and co-authors map the evolution of a bacterial order famous for a model species with a two-stage life cycle. Their 2025 study analyzes hundreds of Caulobacterales genomes, placing the lab workhorse Caulobacter crescentus in its wider family context. They chart where these bacteria live and how their shapes, development, and metabolism vary.

Close relatives of the model species have repeatedly and independently lost the two-form life cycle, a striking case of convergent simplification. Genes for harvesting light turned out to be widespread across the order. One new genus even carries the full kit for making food from light, a first for this group. The authors also trace the history of the protein that curves the model cell. The study reframes a textbook organism as one branch of a varied clan.
pmc-12703897:
Hyun-Jun Kim and co-authors target a signal protein behind muscle wasting in cancer in this 2025 study. The wasting, called cachexia, strikes patients with advanced cancer and claims many lives. No drug is approved to treat it.

Support cells inside tumors, once stirred by cancer cells, seem to feed the wasting. The team grew muscle fibers in dishes and bathed them in fluid from those support cells. A signal screen flagged the protein CXCL5. Blocking it in dishes and in mice eased the wasting. Gene data from the mice helped trace how the block works.
pmc-12704897:
Yinli Shi and co-authors scan United States drug safety reports for harms linked to filgotinib in a 2025 study. The drug calms the immune system and is used for inflammatory disease, but its full safety picture is still unclear.

They pulled reports from 2014 to 2024 in which the drug was the main suspect. Four math screens flagged signals across 17 body systems. Infections, gut problems, and muscle and joint problems were most common. Some flagged harms, such as a fast irregular heartbeat and lung clots, are not on the drug label. The authors stress that such signals are leads to check, and they offer the list as a guide for safer use.
pmc-12705197:
Alexandra Lapierre and a large team of co-authors study in 2025 access to pediatric trauma centres for injured children in Canada. Children with major trauma do better at such centres, but national access data were lacking. The team reviewed hospital admissions in nine provinces from 2016 to 2021.

Of 3,007 children with major trauma, about seventy-eight percent reached a pediatric trauma centre directly or by transfer. Access was higher for younger children and for the most severely injured. Adjusted access was lower in British Columbia, the Atlantic provinces, and Saskatchewan. Age and injury severity shaped subgroup patterns as well.
pmc-12705497:
Yuegang Li, Chengcheng Han, and Jianqiang Tang pool trials of immunotherapy added before surgery for a stubborn kind of rectal cancer. Tumors that repair DNA mismatches well, the pMMR or MSS type, usually shrug off immunotherapy. Yet pairing it with standard pre-surgery treatment might crack them. Their 2025 review searched six databases and conference sources through April 2025. Twenty-one trial cohorts fed the pooling. Outcomes include complete tumor disappearance under the microscope, clean surgical margins, organ preservation, and side effects.

If the pairing works even in this resistant type, many more patients could keep their rectum and skip its loss. The meta-analysis weighs early cohorts that single centers cannot judge alone. The authors grade both benefit and harm. Their question sits on a live frontier of rectal cancer care. The pooled numbers will steer the next trials.
pmc-12705697:
Tianli Li and co-authors find an ancient plant protein that calms a key stress enzyme family in two thousand twenty-five. The enzymes, called PP2C-As, steer how plants meet drought, salt, and germs. Known brakes on them need the hormone ABA, but other brakes were largely unknown.

The protein, FL7, grips many of the enzymes and mutes them without ABA, by a non-rival route. With the enzymes muted, plants gain salt tolerance and stronger defense. One end region of FL7 does the gripping. Kin of the protein trace back to algae kin of land plants, near a billion years deep, and the algal versions brake the enzymes too. The layer of control thus predates land plants.
pmc-12705797:
Lino Braadt and co-authors study lasting dizziness after stroke in a 2025 paper. Vertigo and dizziness are common after stroke but often overlooked. They can drag down quality of life long after other signs fade.

The team followed a hospital stroke cohort for a year. Of about 990 patients with full follow-up, 41 percent reported chronic vertigo or dizziness. Those symptoms cut quality of life across many domains, with presence in social life, movement, and memory hit hardest. New dizziness after stroke did not track with stroke severity. Yet those patients joined rehab more often. The authors call the symptom a marker of unmet recovery needs.
pmc-12705997:
Abdulrahman Al Ayidh and co-authors model base stations that feed on living cells for future 6G networks, in this 2025 paper. Dense 6G grids will gulp power, and grid supply would swell bills and carbon. Their stations harvest energy from microbe fuel cells and enzyme rigs.

The math tracks demand, conversion yield, and carbon under real-world wobble: sourness, heat, fuel saturation, and poisons. Simulated stations held energy self-rule, cutting grid draw and emissions hard. Hybrid storage smooths the swings that microbes cannot. The authors bridge telecom and lab biology in one frame. Field trials are the named next step.
pmc-12706097:
Sindhu Palla and co-authors track cotton growth from drone photos taken across the season. Their 2025 study flies small uncrewed aircraft over field trials run in 2016 and 2021. Color photos yield surface models, and plant height is pulled from those models at each flight.

Growth curves fit to the height series show how each cotton type grows over time. A five-part curve fit best, with very high fit scores and low error. Peak growth rate from the curve tied well to final yield in both years. The point where growth levels off rated plant maturity with 80 percent accuracy. The method can aid yield forecasts and timing of growth-control sprays.
pmc-12706197:
Xiaofeng Han and co-authors set out a trial plan in a 2025 protocol paper on knee recovery. Patients who have a torn knee ligament rebuilt, or a broken kneecap fixed, often face pain and swelling that slow healing. A layered, low-stretch bandage can press on the leg in a graded way and may control swelling better than standard care.

The planned trial will enrol 36 patients and split them evenly by chance. One group gets the bandage plus usual rehab, and the other gets usual rehab alone. Over 12 weeks, the team will track knee scores, swelling, pain, motion, leg strength, and balance. The plan aims to give strong evidence on whether the bandage helps across the full course of recovery.
pmc-12706697:
Nathalie Heidi Meyer and five colleagues published a neuroscience study in two thousand twenty-five on reliving memories. Feeling transported back into a past event depends on more than memory traces. Body-based signals at the moment of learning may set how vivid the reliving feels later.

In virtual reality, participants encoded scenes while the team varied hand-movement feedback and viewpoint between first and third person. Brain recordings captured coupling between the premotor cortex and the hippocampus. Stronger coupling tied body-congruency effects at encoding to richer reliving a week later. Weaker coupling broke that link. The authors say bodily self-awareness tunes memory through this circuit. The effect vanished under a control condition.
pmc-12707097:
Lina Julkunen and six co-authors study plaque microbes in older adults living in long-term care in a study from 2025. Nearly two hundred residents aged sixty-two and up had oral exams and plaque samples taken from each quarter of the mouth. Residents were grouped by oral disease burden: low, moderate, or high, based on clinical checks.

Overall microbe diversity was similar across groups, but the mix of species differed clearly. The high burden group carried more genera tied to oral and body-wide disease. Gum disease shaped the microbe mix more than tooth decay did. The authors read the shift as a move toward an unhealthy plaque community.
pmc-12709697:
Yufeng Zhang and co-authors test brain stimulation for walking and thinking in older adults in this 2025 study. Gait problems and mental decline threaten independence in old age. Two brain networks, one for attention and one for rest-state activity, shape both walking and cognition, so stimulating both at once might help.

In a crossover trial, 28 healthy older adults received real or sham stimulation, with electrode placement tuned by software. Walking was tested alone and while counting backward, alongside memory tasks. Real stimulation raised gait speed in both walking modes compared with sham. A memory task reaction time also fell. The authors suggest network-targeted stimulation may aid gait and cognition together.
pmc-12709797:
Ning Wang, Xue Wang, Xue Zhou, Guoyue Yang, and Qing Ye search for shared gene signatures. The signatures link COVID-19 with progression from liver cirrhosis to liver cancer. Their bioinformatics paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Cirrhosis is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, and COVID-19 hits such patients hard.

Comparing gene expression datasets, the team found seventy-eight genes changed in both conditions, mostly tied to the cell cycle. Network analysis singled out CDK1 as the hub gene. CDK1 levels predicted both COVID-19 and the cirrhosis-cancer cohort with excellent accuracy, and liver cancer patients with high CDK1 fared worse. Regulatory networks around the signature were also mapped, offering candidate targets for therapy.
pmc-12711197:
During sleep and rest, the hippocampus fires sharp-wave ripples, brief bursts tied to fixing memories. Robson Scheffer-Teixeira and Adriano Tort revisit a basic question about those bursts in a 2025 study: how widely do they synchronize? Newer reports had argued the two sides of the brain ripple out of step.

Their data come from probes laid along the full length of the CA1 region in rats. Ripples locked in phase within each hemisphere but not across the two, while their timing still matched everywhere. Cell firing followed the same pattern, and fast interneurons coupled more strongly than the main cells. The picture refines, rather than overturns, the older view of ripples as coordinated events.
pmc-12711597:
Muyao Qi and co-authors forecast where Europe's root-fungus partners will live as the climate warms. Their 2025 study models sixty common ectomycorrhizal fungi, the species that trade nutrients with tree roots and keep forests fed. Future ranges were projected under three social and emissions pathways, for mid- and late-century windows.

Both weather and host tree ranges feed the models, since a fungus can only follow its trees. Species sort into broadleaf specialists, conifer specialists, and generalists, and their fortunes differ by group. The team tracks shrinking or growing areas and the drift of each range's center, giving forest planners a fungus-level view of climate change.
pmc-12711897:
Taigang Zhang and co-authors built a worldwide inventory of floods bursting from glacier lakes and tied their rise to warming, in a 2025 study. When a lake held back by a moraine dam breaks, the flood can devastate mountain valleys, and whether such events are growing more common was unsettled. The team catalogued six hundred and nine moraine-dammed lake outburst floods from 1900 to 2020, from historical reports and landform evidence.

Reported floods crept upward with fluctuations before the 1970s, then accelerated sharply. The yearly rate roughly tripled, from about five per year in the 1980s to about fifteen per year in the 2010s. The long trend tracks global air temperature with a lag of about twenty years. The authors explain the delay as a response time: warming shrinks glaciers, grows lakes, and destabilizes slopes, and only then do dams fail.
pmc-12711997:
Zhenyu Zhang and co-authors published a 2025 study of a cell modification that a flu virus meets when it strikes. The modification, ADP-ribosylation, is a tag the cell hangs on its own proteins, and on those of the virus. The tag is hung by a family of cell enzymes, and it can be removed just as fast. The team asks what role it plays in a flu infection.

On infection, the tag count leapt up fast and wide, in a wave that curbed the spread of the virus. Mass spectrometry mapped nearly four thousand tag sites on nearly a thousand host proteins, and over a hundred on the viral proteins. Work tests show tags on the copying machinery of the virus blunt its activity. The lead shield protein of the virus fights back: it damps the tag wave. One enzyme of the family, PARP1, makes most of the wave.
pmc-12712297:
Mohammad Daher and co-authors present a 2025 review on sleep after shoulder surgery. Rotator cuff tears are common and often wreck sleep quality. Surgery to repair the cuff is known to help sleep. The open question is timing: when does the gain arrive? The team searched three databases through October 2024. Studies counted patients with disturbed sleep before surgery and at three months, six months, and one year after.

Sleep was scored by patient report or by validated scales. The title gives the headline: improvement lands at three months. That timing helps set patient expectations in clinic. People often judge surgery by pain and strength alone. A sleep timeline adds an outcome patients feel every night. The review pools past studies rather than running a new trial, so its strength is breadth across cohorts.
pmc-12713297:
Hongjing Guan and co-authors build a non-invasive prediction model for silent neurosyphilis in people living with HIV in a 2025 study. Guidelines urge screening all such patients, but the spinal tap test is invasive and often skipped.

Records covered over five hundred patients at one Nanjing hospital across a decade who had the tap. Training and test splits fed regression methods that picked key risk factors. Model checks covered accuracy, calibration, and clinical value curves. Subgroup checks by timing and treatment history tested reliability. A blood and history based score could flag who needs the tap most. The aim is fewer missed cases without tapping everyone.
pmc-12714097:
Shuo Yang and co-authors pool trials on blood thinners for a scarring lung disease in a 2025 analysis. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis stiffens the lungs, and clotting oddities travel with it. Whether anticoagulants help patients live longer was unclear and contested.

The search gathered three randomized trials and five prospective studies with 2,185 patients. Overall, blood thinners did not significantly change mortality. Once warfarin-only studies were set aside, other agents did extend survival. Lung capacity measures improved, and a clotting marker fell, while walking distance and gas transfer did not change. Adverse events, including bleeding, rose. The authors urge patient-level pooling to sort out which drugs help and which harm.
pmc-12714197:
Sneh Harsh and colleagues uncovered how adult fruit fly testes keep their male identity switched on. Stem cells in the testis need a factor called Chinmo to stay male; without it they convert toward the ovarian program through a female RNA-binding protein. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team shows the missing link is a pioneer factor called Zelda, which can open silent genes. In healthy cells, small RNAs keep the Zelda message locked away untranslated. When Chinmo is lost, those small RNAs fade and Zelda protein gets made.

Zelda proved both required and enough on its own to flip the cells toward the female program. It raises two target genes that feed the female pathway, and it also turns down the Chinmo gene itself, locking the switch. The same flip could be triggered in male fat tissue, hinting at a general guard mechanism.
pmc-12714797:
Shin Kameishi and co-authors review in 2025 whether drug treatment after a standard rectal cancer operation helps patients stay free of relapse. The operation removes the rectum's fatty envelope, and some teams also remove side lymph nodes. Their hospital skipped the node removal, and the benefit of follow-up drugs in that setting was unclear.

Records covered 117 patients treated over a decade. Three years after surgery, about seventy-four percent were free of relapse and about ninety-six percent were alive. No factor the team tested, from tumor site to drug mix, clearly forecast relapse on its own. The authors judge the drug course a sound partner to the operation.
pmc-12715197:
Kinga Bierwiaczonek and co-authors pool evidence on how migrants adjust to new societies in a 2025 analysis. Migration keeps rising worldwide, and what helps newcomers settle well is an urgent question. The team searched for the strongest social and situational factors tied to good adjustment.

Their pool covers over five thousand effects from more than a thousand studies. Participants include first-generation migrants, foreign students, business staff abroad, and refugees. Stress, above all stress from adapting and from discrimination, linked most strongly to poor adjustment. Feeling connected and not lonely linked most strongly to good adjustment. Learning the new culture mattered, but less than stress and social support.
pmc-12716497:
Tipanan Khunsri and co-authors study a helper T cell type that drives harmful antibodies in lupus in a 2025 paper. In lupus, helper cells in lymph nodes help B cells make antibodies against the body's own DNA. A blood form of those helpers that makes a signal called IL-17 is raised in active disease and tracks with worse illness, but how it drives B cells was unclear.

Forty people with lupus joined the study. Cell types were sorted by surface marks and inner signals with a flow method. The team linked the helper type to disease scores, anti DNA antibody levels, and swelling signals, and they tested how the helpers interact with B cells.
pmc-12716597:
Oumnia Bouaddi and a large team of co-authors study how migrants reach health care in Morocco, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Morocco sits between Africa and Europe and hosts many migrants in transit or settled. Care is free in emergencies and clinics, yet barriers persist.

The team spoke with migrants, community leaders, aid groups, and health workers in five cities. Fear of costs and wrong beliefs about rights shaped care seeking. Most found clinic care free and easy to reach. Still, office hurdles, language gaps, and drug costs blocked some. The authors list fixes drawn from all sides.
pmc-12717097:
Alexander Metcalf, John Chandler, and Max Birdsong map who owns wildlife habitat in Montana in a 2025 paper. Most habitat in the United States sits on private land, yet the wildlife on it belongs to the public trust. That split creates tension between landowner rights and public interests. Land records were hard to study at state scale until new data methods arrived.

The team analyzed records across Montana from 2004 to 2023. They found that 3,500 owners, each holding at least 3,600 acres, control sixty-three percent of private habitat. Companies and legal entities now outnumber families among owners, and land keeps splitting into smaller parcels. The trends reshape how agencies can work with owners to guard wildlife.
pmc-12717397:
Morgan Dillon and co-authors looked in 2025 for warning signs just before a common elbow injury in pro baseball. The injury tears a ligament on the inner elbow of pitchers. No past work had tracked the pitches thrown right before the tear. The team used the league's pitch-tracking system, which logs speed, spin, release point, arm angle, and how fast the ball speeds up.

They studied seven pitchers who tore the ligament on one pitch between 2020 and 2025. For each man, they built a model from his past four games and scored how far each new pitch strayed from his norm. They ran the same check on matched pitchers who stayed healthy. Every injury pitch scored as a clear outlier from that pitcher's own norm.
pmc-12718597:
Morris Gordon and four colleagues compare drugs for holding Crohn's disease quiet after surgery, in a twenty twenty-five review. About half of Crohn's patients need surgery, and many relapse after it. The team pooled thirty-four trials with 3,197 patients in a network analysis. Outcomes were symptom relapse, scope-seen relapse, and quitting from side effects.

One biologic drug, adalimumab, clearly cut symptom relapse against placebo, with fair-grade proof. Two older drug families may cut relapse slightly, on weaker proof. Another biologic probably cut scope-seen relapse. Most other options rested on very weak proof. The authors grade each claim so doctors can weigh certainty, not just effect size.
pmc-12719397:
Chalachew Yenew, Yehzibalem Azmeraw, and Almaw Genet Yeshiwas pooled studies in two thousand twenty-five on vision loss among diabetic patients in Ethiopia. Diabetes is rising fast there, and eye damage is a major complication. Their review combined results from many clinics to estimate overall burden, risk factors, and regional gaps.

About three in ten diabetic patients had visual impairment overall, but regional rates differed dramatically, from very low in one region to very high in another. Such gaps suggest unequal screening and care rather than biology alone. Ethiopian health planners gain a map showing where eye screening for diabetic patients needs urgent strengthening.
pmc-12719797:
Suresh Puttahonnappa and a large team reviewed anthrax in people and animals in India for a 2025 paper. Anthrax is a disease passed from animals to people, caused by a bacterium, and it keeps causing outbreaks in India. The team mapped where and when outbreaks happened between 1990 and 2022 and looked for links with the local environment.

They searched medical and government sources and kept forty four studies that met their rules. Those sources covered many human outbreaks with deaths, and far more animal outbreaks. Hot spots for human cases included West Bengal, Odisha, and Andhra Pradesh. Animal hot spots included Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal as well. The maps can help target watch and control work where risk is highest.
pmc-12719897:
Sydney Kelpin and co-authors set out the protocol for a trial of a digital program to cut harm and death around pregnancy, in a paper from 2025. The United States has the worst such rates among rich countries, above all in rural areas and among Black mothers. Most of these deaths can be prevented, yet strong programs are hard to spread. The team built a phone-based program that works at four levels at once.

Mothers and up to three of their supporters get an opening app session, then texts with deeper content. Providers get texts and flyers, and health workers stand by on a live chat. Ten clinics in Michigan will be split by lot between the program and usual care. Five hundred pregnant patients on Medicaid will take part. The trial tracks harm through one year after birth.
pmc-12719997:
Kim and An present a 2025 study on falls, mood, and life satisfaction in older Koreans. The team reused data from a 2023 national survey of older adults, covering 10,078 people. Average age was about seventy-four, and roughly two-thirds were women. Statistical tests traced how a past fall links to life satisfaction, with depressive symptoms as the middle step.

The middle step proved real: falls fed low mood, and low mood dragged satisfaction down. The indirect path was small but firmly measured. The authors urge steady fall-risk screening and mood checks for seniors. They also call for personal support plans that treat low mood directly, not just the fall risk itself.
pmc-12720297:
Elly De Vlieghere, Friedel Nollet, Helena Devos, and Barbara Cauwelier adapt a DNA extraction method for optical genome mapping in a 2025 paper. The mapping method spots large DNA changes in blood cancers, but it needs very long DNA strands, usually drawn from 1.5 million white blood cells. Such counts are not always reachable, as with sorted marrow cells in myeloma.

Their custom protocol starts from as few as 500,000 cells and still yields DNA of good quality and amount. The extract supports mapping runs that gather at least 1,500 billion base pairs of data. The change opens the method to samples that once fell short.
pmc-12720897:
Tuberculosis survives inside the very cells sent to kill it, partly by making those cells die on cue. Zulipikaer Abudureheman and co-authors traced the wiring in 2025: the bacterial protein ESAT-6, a main virulence factor, pushes macrophages toward programmed death, which helps the bacteria spread.

Working in a human macrophage cell line, the team showed the death signal runs through a chain of RNA regulators. ESAT-6 raises a long non-coding RNA, which soaks up a protective microRNA, which frees the inflammatory signal TNF-alpha to rise — and the cells die in step with the dose. Silencing the long RNA broke the chain and spared the cells. The authors propose this axis as a drug target: block it, and the macrophage may hold its ground against the bacillus.
pmc-12722297:
Mark Zupancic and ten co-authors track viral DNA in blood during treatment of throat cancers in a study from two thousand twenty-five. These HPV-driven cancers answer treatment better than others, but therapy is harsh and not always curative. A blood marker could personalize care.

Two hundred sixty-seven samples from eighty-three patients were tested across diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. About ninety-four percent of diagnostic samples carried the viral DNA. Levels fell in most patients within weeks of starting radiation. Roughly thirty percent cleared it fast; nearly all cleared it within months. Clearance speed varied with tumor site, patient traits, and treatment. No fresh recurrences had appeared yet. The authors want larger, longer studies of the marker.
pmc-12722597:
Ilaya Kumar and co-authors published this laboratory study in 2025. The team tested a preparation from the brahmi plant, long used in traditional medicine, on immune cells linked to lung cancer. They wanted to know if the plant extract could make dendritic cells better at fighting the disease.

Dendritic cells were grown from blood cells of a lung cancer patient and a healthy donor. After treatment, the cells matured more fully and woke up T cells, the immune system's attack cells. The extract also shifted gene activity toward a program that fights tumors and raised immune signals. The findings suggest the plant preparation may help immune-based cancer care, at least in the lab.
pmc-12722697:
Cardwell and co-authors test a worry raised by mouse studies: that antibiotics, by disturbing gut bacteria, might worsen breast cancer survival. Working with population cohorts of over 44,000 patients in England and Wales, they relate antibiotic prescriptions after diagnosis to deaths from breast cancer. The study uses a registered report format, with the plan fixed in advance.

Overall there is no clear link. Only the heaviest users, those with twelve or more prescriptions, show higher cancer deaths. That signal weakens when infections are accounted for, and it looks much the same for deaths from other causes. The authors read the pattern as likely leftover confounding rather than a true drug effect.
pmc-12722997:

pmc-12727797:

pmc-12729097:

pmc-12729297:

pmc-12729597:

pmc-12729697:

pmc-12729797:

pmc-12730197:

pmc-12730397:

pmc-12730497:

pmc-12730597:

pmc-12730797:

pmc-12732497:

pmc-12733197:

pmc-12733397:

pmc-12733897:

pmc-12744597:

pmc-12745197:
A blood sugar marker can drift from what a person's glucose alone would predict, and that drift may say something extra about the heart. Chuxin Lyu and co-authors test that idea in a 2025 study of patients hospitalized with heart failure. They split patients by how strongly the heart still squeezes and tracked who got worse during the stay.

Patients whose hearts squeezed weakest carried the highest drift values and worsened most often. Each step up in the drift score came with a strong rise in the risk of worsening, in a near straight line. The score also tracked with the weak-squeeze type itself. The authors offer the index as a cheap add-on for sorting heart failure patients by risk, drawn from tests wards already run.
pmc-12745397:
Weining Yang, Xuetao Jiang, Xue Luo, Xi Zhang, and Lu Yan studied side effects of a health policy in China's primary care in 2025. The policy joins physical activity promotion with basic health care under the Healthy China drive. Most past work judged the policy's design, not what happens when frontline staff carry it out.

Twenty in-depth interviews with primary care workers across China were coded step by step to build a theory from the ground up. Rollout proved uneven: staff read the policy in apart ways, faced tight resources and rules, and adapted with varied tactics. Side effects included token compliance, skewed resource use, and fragmented delivery. The authors model how those effects chain together during rollout.
pmc-12745797:
Yang Wang and a team of co-authors traced how colon cancer cells dodge immune attack in a 2025 study. A drug that blocks a cell protein called VCP makes the cells die in a swelling burst and shed tiny sacs. That death should rally immunity, yet paired immune care gained little, and the team hunted the brake.

The block slows the rot of a death switch protein, which then builds up. The pile pulls in a recycling crew that sends a shield protein, PD-L1, back to the cell surface in sacs. More shield at the gate mutes immune attack. Blocking the recycling crew in mice let the drug plus immune care work far better. The authors offer the pair as a new care plan.
pmc-12748097:
A gene-silencing enzyme, DNMT1, runs high in colorectal cancer and helps it grow and spread. Xiao-Mei Peng and co-authors map a feedback loop around it. The enzyme silences a second gene, TRAF6, by methylating its promoter. That second gene's protein normally tags DNMT1 for destruction, so silencing it lets DNMT1 pile up.

The drug decitabine breaks the loop, sending DNMT1 to the disposal pathway and freeing TRAF6. DNMT1 also shields a cancer-promoting partner, EZH2, from the same disposal route. Patient tissue checks confirmed the inverse pattern. The 2025 study reveals a self-reinforcing circuit and a drug that cuts it at two points.
pmc-12748297:
Nicola Veronese and co-authors issue a European expert consensus on infection control and vaccination in long-term care homes. Care home residents carry frailty, many diseases at once, and aging immune systems, which makes flu, pneumococcal pneumonia, COVID-19, RSV, whooping cough, and shingles all dangerous. Vaccines for each exist. Coverage inside care homes stays poor anyway.

The panel blames fragmented national rules, weak mandates, and plain neglect of adult immunization. In many places uptake is not even counted, so gaps stay invisible. Their 2025 document, from an interdisciplinary council on aging, sets out what facilities and policymakers should standardize. Geriatric care leaders get an agreed floor for protecting the frailest residents.
pmc-12748397:
Clear aligners can straighten teeth, but closing a gap after an extraction often tips the front teeth inward and the back teeth forward. Runa Yamaguchi-Higuchi and nine co-authors used computer models in 2025 to test whether small bone screws can stop that unwanted tipping.

The team built a three-dimensional model of the upper teeth with the first premolars removed, then varied the forces applied through the screws. A backward force near 300 centinewtons almost erased the molar's forward tip. Adding an upward force through front screws steadily reduced the front tooth's inward tip as well. The results give orthodontists concrete force levels to aim for when they combine aligners with mini-screws.
pmc-12748497:
Ho-Jin Kim and Hyo-Sang Park compare how two kinds of teeth aligners fit, in a 2025 study. Clear aligners straighten teeth, and their fit in the small gaps between teeth matters. The team compared aligners made by 3D printing with ones shaped by heat forming. Thirty aligners were made and set on an upper jaw model.

Fine X-ray scans measured gap size and wall thickness at two heights on each aligner. Printed aligners with a small built-in offset fit the gaps best. Heat-formed aligners grew much thinner during shaping. Printed ones, by contrast, grew thicker than planned. The fit edge held at both heights for the offset printed group. Dentists gain clear guidance on which build to pick.
pmc-12748597:
Chenxin Wang and co-authors map in 2025 how bone infection unfolds over time and place, to design better repair scaffolds. Bone infection, osteomyelitis, often returns after treatment, with failure rates above 25 percent. The team built a rabbit model of staph infection in the thigh bone.

Scans and tissue measures at two, four, and six weeks showed a steady march of damage. Spongy bone broke down first, then the hard shell lost its blood supply, then the joint end caved in. The shaft and the knob of the bone suffered in different patterns. The authors argue scaffolds should be graded, with structure matched to each zone, not one uniform design.
pmc-12748697:
Farzad Rezazadeh and co-authors study in 2025 how to monitor the making of ultra high performance concrete so that quality stays steady and waste falls. The material is very strong and durable, yet factory batches vary enough to produce costly off spec waste. The team took a whole chain view, from raw inputs to curing.

They used a data set of 150 batches, all varied in a planned way from one reference mix. Fluctuations in raw material quality, storage, dosing errors, mixer energy, and curing were tracked against the 28 day strength. Ten learning algorithms were compared; the best explained at least three quarters of the strength variation with small error. Naming the steps that swing strength most lets plants fix them first.
pmc-12748797:
Zhen Li and co-authors train in this 2025 study a deep learning model that spots throat cancer on MRI scans without contrast dye. Nasopharyngeal cancer checks usually need gadolinium dye, which carries deposit worries, time, and cost. Their model fuses plain scan types with distilled knowledge from richer data, trained on 854 cases.

On held-out hospital data it scored 0.95 area under the curve, and 0.86 on an outside set, beating plain-scan and virtual-contrast rivals. Thirteen readers from six hospitals, aided by the model on plain scans, matched dye-based reading. The authors pitch the tool as a safer, cheaper route to diagnosis and follow-up. Scan slots free up for other patients as well.
pmc-12748897:
Xiaojian Zhang and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a colour-changing device that pairs two conducting polymers to power itself while it tints. Electrochromic glass can dim light and heat on demand, but slow switching, weak contrast, and narrow colour range have held it back. The team combined a well-known blue-tinting polymer with a newer partner polymer of opposite type.

The pair delivered fifty-one percent optical contrast, switching in well under a second in both directions, with record colouring efficiency.
