Because the device harvests its own operating energy, the authors pitch it for self-powered smart windows. The same stack doubles as a miniature spectrometer, sensing light while it shades.
pmc-12749097:
Sakuya Ohnishi and ten co-authors report an unusual vision problem caused by a cyst near the brain's hormone hub, in a 2025 case report. Such cysts usually harm vision by pressing on the eye pathways. This patient, a woman aged fifty-five, lost patches of central vision in both eyes. Her cyst had not grown on scans.

Contrast scans showed brightening spreading from the cyst wall toward the crossing point of the eye nerves. That pattern suggested inflammation rather than pressure. Surgery through the nose drained the cyst. Her symptoms cleared fully afterward. Tissue checks confirmed immune cells in the cyst wall. Two years later, scans showed no return of the cyst. The authors urge early recognition of this inflammation route to protect vision.
pmc-12749597:
Francois Beauducel and six co-authors give a tool, called Jerk, that spots faint ground shifts before a volcano blows, in a 2025 paper. Peak watch nets give many signs, but no tool gave a clear live alert that chiefs could trust. Jerk reads very slow tilts and drifts from one lone shake gauge.

At one oft blown peak in the Indian Ocean, Jerk ran on its own for a decade. It warned in time for most of two dozen blows, from just ticks of time to hours ahead. Poorly watched peaks round the world may gain most from such a lean tool.
pmc-12749697:
Kazumitsu Maehara and Yasuyuki Ohkawa built a method that rebuilds the flow field of cell change from single-cell data, in a 2025 paper. Gene activity steers each cell's fate, and RNA reads can hint at where a cell is heading. Reading the bend of that motion, its acceleration, is far harder because the data are sparse and span thousands of genes.

Their framework, ddHodge, splits the flow into its basic parts: gradient, swirl, and spread. It recovers each part cleanly, even from biased, thin samples, and it yields acceleration as a second-order term. Applied to mouse embryo data, the method showed development running as a gradient flow over a landscape of potentials, a picture never before checked on real data. Spread values also marked each cell's potency, and the team named genes that drive it.
pmc-12750097:
Toka Amin and four co-authors present two patients who had both a slow blood cancer and lung cancer, in a 2025 case report. The blood disease, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, grows slowly but raises the odds of second cancers. Why the two diseases coincide in some people is unclear, and paired cases are seldom written up.

Both patients were heavy smokers who came in with breathing symptoms. One was a 77-year-old man and the other a 52-year-old woman. Scans showed lung masses, swollen chest glands, fluid around the lungs, and spread to other organs in both. Fluid tests and tissue work untangled which disease caused which finding. The authors use the pair to stress careful staging when two cancers share one chest.
pmc-12750797:
Sung Eun Choi, Daniel Nolte, and Ankur Pandya modeled in 2025 whether paying dentists bonuses for applying fluoride to children's teeth would be money well spent. They simulated 100,000 American children over ten years using national survey data. Scenarios varied the bonus size and how much fluoride coverage rose above the baseline of about a quarter of children.

Across most scenarios the bonuses looked cost-effective. One mid-range example prevented about 186 cavities and gained healthy life years at roughly 8,500 dollars each per ten thousand children. At coverage gains above roughly 27 percent, the program saved money outright. Benefits were larger in some subgroups. The authors offer the model as a guide for designing value-based dental incentives.
pmc-12750997:
Xirui Gou, William Privratsky, Wenhan Sun, Yuncong Liu, Hamed Abiri, and Qing Li published this study in 2025. It reports a chip-scale frequency comb, a device emitting a ladder of evenly spaced frequencies, built from light coupled to vibration. Such combs serve as rulers for measuring frequencies, but mechanical versions were stuck at narrow spans.

The team's resonator is a silicon carbide microdisk only two and a half micrometers across. Driven by a single milliwatt of light, radiation pressure pushes its vibration into phonon lasing, a coherent mechanical oscillation. The motion stamps forty-two locked harmonics onto the light, spaced about 1.65 gigahertz apart, spanning one to seventy gigahertz. Phase noise stayed very low and the frequencies held steady. The authors pitch the device for microwave photonics and precision measurement in a footprint smaller than a grain of sand.
pmc-12751397:
Jianfang Zhou, Yunlu Wang, and Lu Yang study how living arrangements relate to well-being in older Chinese adults. Their 2025 study uses a national survey from 2018 with six thousand five hundred thirty-five people aged sixty or more. Household forms in China have shifted from multi-generation homes toward couples alone and empty nests.

Living only with a spouse was the most common form, at about fifty-two percent. The team compared physical health, mental health, and self-rated health across arrangement types, with a focus on gender gaps. Several regression methods tested the links. The paper adds national-scale evidence to debates on whether new household forms help or harm health in later life.
pmc-12751597:
Seed weight decides much of a soybean crop's value, and its genetics are spread across many small-effect genes. Chunlei Zhang and co-authors map those genes in a 2025 study of a bred soybean population.

The team crossed a heavy-seeded parent with a light-seeded one and raised 325 inbred lines. A dense sequencing method placed nearly three thousand markers across the genome. Field trials in Harbin and Sanya, across three seasons, weighed the seeds of every line. Eleven significant regions on eight chromosomes turned up, jointly explaining about sixty-two percent of the weight differences. The strongest region sat on chromosome nineteen. Such maps help breeders stack favorable regions into new varieties.
pmc-12751697:
Beatriz Martins and co-authors study in 2025 how tiny vesicles released by stressed retinal pigment cells can break the outer blood retinal barrier. That cell layer sits under the light sensing cells and keeps the outer retina in balance. In age related macular degeneration, the layer sickens and may release vesicles whose cargo harms the barrier and speeds disease.

Pig cell cultures and eye cups were treated with stress signals or with vesicles from inflamed cells. Vesicles released from the top face of stressed cells damaged the cell layer in culture and in eye tissue. In mice, injected vesicles caused structural harm in the retina. The work names a path by which stressed cells spread damage.
pmc-12752897:
Ishika Sarkar and five co-authors compare two gels as add-ons to gum care for localised gum disease. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Gum disease is driven by many germs, and plain scaling and root planing may not fully curb it. Local gels placed in the pocket can help, from drug gels to plant-based ones.

Forty-six patients are split by lot after deep cleaning. One group gets a gel from orange peel extract, the other a chlorhexidine gel. At two months, both groups gain in pocket depth and attachment, with no clear gap between them. Germ counts fall in both. The plant gel looks as good as the drug gel, at lower cost.
pmc-12752997:
Shahzad Sadiq and five colleagues studied microRNA regulation in early-onset heart muscle thickening using a rat model. The hypertrophic heart rat develops primary cardiac hypertrophy without high blood pressure. The team profiled heart tissue from two-day-old pups of this strain and from normal heart rats. Microarray screening compared microRNAs and messenger RNAs between the groups. Selected candidates were checked again with a second laboratory method.

The young hypertrophic rats already showed a higher cardiac weight index and raised hypertrophy markers. Screening found 107 microRNAs expressed at different levels. Three of them, including miR-34a, were validated and linked to known hypertrophy pathways. The twenty twenty-five study points to early molecular switches that may drive inherited heart thickening before symptoms appear.
pmc-12753597:
Rentao Yu, Xinyu Lu, and Zhuangzhuang Yue mapped cell talk in bowel cancer in 2025. Tumors mix varied surface cells and immune T cells. Single-cell studies had listed many subsets of both. Where those subsets meet inside tumors stayed unclear. The team merged single-cell data with spatial gene maps. Samples came from dozens of bowel cancer patients. Tools traced cell family paths and signal exchanges. Spatial methods placed subsets back into tumor tissue.

Nine surface cell groups and eight T cell groups emerged. Each group carried its own gene pattern and damage load. One killer T cell group showed tumor-specific activation. It exchanged strong signals with surface cell groups. Three named signaling routes carried much of that traffic. Spatial maps found those T cells beside one surface group. The authors offer the atlas for precision care research. Named routes may serve as drug targets or markers.
pmc-12753697:
Chengfa Ren and co-authors survey dialysis patients about caring for their lifeline in a study from 2025. An arteriovenous fistula is the surgical vein link that dialysis machines plug into. Its health decides whether treatment runs smoothly. Patients themselves guard it daily, so their knowledge and habits matter.

Five hundred thirty-six patients at a Nanchang hospital answered a custom questionnaire in spring 2025. Knowledge scored near fifteen of twenty, attitude near forty-three of fifty, and practice near forty-one of fifty. The three rose together strongly: knowing more tracked with doing more. Modeling confirmed the chain from knowledge to attitude to action. Teaching patients fistula care may pay off in working access and fewer emergencies.
pmc-12753997:
Mingming Sui, Zhongpei Guan, and Peng Cui present a 2025 paper on tracking wheat height with reflected navigation signals. Satellites' signals bounce off fields, and their patterns carry crop information. Older methods lean on signal strength data that many receivers do not record. The team instead combined code and carrier phase readings from GPS and BeiDou satellites, testing six combinations in a field experiment in China. A growth model parameterized by accumulated warmth served as the reference curve.

The best combinations from each system tracked true height closely, with errors around eight centimeters. Fusing both systems cut the error by over a fifth against the best single system and by a third against the signal-strength method. The authors present their fusion strategy as a cheap, continuous tool for precision farming. It suits farms where signal-strength data are missing or unreliable.
pmc-12754997:
Kaitlyn Atkins and co-authors adapt a survey scale in 2025 to measure layered stigma among female sex workers in Namibia. People at high risk of HIV often face bias tied to more than one part of who they are at once. That layered bias can keep them away from prevention services, yet it has been little studied in southern Africa.

The team reworked older stigma measures with input from the women who would use them. The aim was a tool that fits this setting and gives scores that programs can act on. A sound scale lets health teams track whether bias falls as programs roll out. It also helps show which forms of bias bite hardest. Better measures are a first step toward care that welcomes the people who need it most.
pmc-12755897:
Huilin Liu and co-authors studied insulin resistance, muscle loss, and heart disease in older Chinese adults in a 2025 paper. Data came from a long-running national study of health and retirement. The team tracked new heart and vessel disease over a median of nine years.

Just over five thousand people aged forty-five and over took part, with five hundred fifty new cases. People with early muscle loss plus high insulin resistance faced far higher risk than others. Two combined indexes were the strongest single predictors, while two others showed the most consistent joint effects with muscle loss. The authors urge dual action on muscle and insulin.
pmc-12756797:
Zhai and six co-authors simulated gas movement in coal mine working faces in twenty twenty-five. Many Chinese mines hold dangerous gas that can build up underground. A Y-type ventilation layout with a retained side entry boosts coal recovery and eases gas at one corner, but may trap gas elsewhere.

Their two-dimensional model, built in COMSOL software, tracked gas over time in the worked-out area behind the face. They varied advance speed and the split of airflow between routes. Faster advance stirred more gas loose, raising peak levels. Nine meters per day looked best among the speeds tested. A balanced airflow split near one to one point five kept peaks lowest at both spots. Simulated values matched field data closely, supporting the model's use for ventilation planning.
pmc-12757297:
Vasileios Paschalis and co-authors use a split version of a proximity-labeling tool to catch the protein SRSF1 doing unexpected work in ribosome building. SRSF1 is best known as a splicing factor that helps cut and rejoin RNA messages. Clues placed it near a helicase involved in activating the spliceosome, hinting at wider duties.

The split-APEX method tags nearby proteins in living cells, letting the team map SRSF1's neighborhoods step by step through spliceosome assembly and beyond. The trail leads into ribosomal biogenesis, the cell's ribosome factory. Splicing helicases appear there too. Factors filed under splicing may moonlight in making the machines that read the spliced messages.
pmc-12757397:
Dan Niu and seven co-authors test a wrist entry point for heart artery treatment, in a 2025 trial. Patients with acute coronary syndrome often need a catheter threaded to the heart to open narrowed arteries. The usual path enters at the wrist; a newer path enters a bit farther along, at the back of the hand's artery.

Just over a hundred patients were split at random between the two paths. A day after treatment, the artery had closed off far less often in the new-path group, though the gap had faded by thirty days. The new path also needed a shorter pressing time to seal the entry point, while pain and bleeding were alike. The authors call the new route safe and effective for planned, non-emergency treatment.
pmc-12759297:
Stephan Zarich and co-authors set out the plan for a trial on walnuts and thinking after meals, in a paper from 2025. Some adults feel their memory and focus slipping, a state that raises the risk of dementia. What a person eats at one meal can sway how sharp they feel right after. Walnuts carry good fats and plant compounds tied to brain health.

The trial will enroll seventy-eight adults who report such slips. Each person will eat a walnut snack daily for one week and a chocolate-style snack for another week, in random order. A washout gap splits the two rounds. Thinking tests run before and after meal challenges and after each week. Blood, stool, and body measures round out the data. The protocol paper fixes the design before results come in.
pmc-12764297:
Kasem Seresirikachorn, Angela Zhu, and Ta Chen Chang review eye pressure checks for folks who seek sight fix surgery, in a 2025 review. Sight fix work has grown fast, but how it bends later glaucoma checks is still murky. Each fix type, lens or cornea based, needs its own watch plan.

The review walks through risk checks before surgery and watch steps after it. New tools have made finds and checks more sharp than in past years. High risk cases need close watch and the right pressure tool for their eye type. Clear steps aim to lift trust for surgeons who face such mixed cases.
pmc-12765297:
Liming Chen and co-authors test a plant compound, brevilin A, against gut inflammation in mice. Colitis, the inflamed colon seen in inflammatory bowel disease, was triggered with a chemical in the animals' water. Doses of the compound then eased the disease, and the team traced how.

Brevilin A reshaped the gut's microbe mix, favoring helpful Lactobacillus while thinning harmful kinds. It also shifted the chemicals those microbes make and turned down a key inflammation signal, TNF-alpha; forcing that signal back on erased the benefit. Stool transplants from treated mice passed part of the gain to untreated ones, proving the microbes carry part of the effect. The authors pitch the compound as a candidate drug worth clinical study.
pmc-12766597:
Matthew Lucy introduces a special issue on the future of dairy farming and dairy science, in work published in 2025. He notes how fast the field can change when new tools or new threats appear. One example is the rise of beef calves bred from dairy herds, and another is a bird flu virus that reached dairy cattle.

The issue holds eight invited reviews on fast moving topics. Three cover long standing subjects such as udder health, breeding, and genetics, while others take up new tools that could reshape the field. Lucy explains that the journal plans such reviews about every five years. The aim is to take stock of research as the industry keeps changing.
pmc-12766797:
Thomas Charles McHale, Terry Theuri, and Oleg Bilukha report in 2025 on low blood counts in women and children living in refugee camps around the world. Their study updates earlier work and covers the years from 2017 to 2024. Surveys run by the United Nations refugee agency and its partners supplied the data.

The surveys covered camps in East and Southern Africa, West and Central Africa, and South Asia. Staff measured a blood protein in non pregnant women and in children with a small hand held device. Low levels were graded as mild, moderate, or severe by world health rules. Knowing how common low blood counts are helps aid groups plan food and health care. It also shows where the problem is worst, so help can go there first.
pmc-12768297:
Neil McDougall gave the Royal Victoria Hospital annual oration in October twenty twenty-four, speaking mainly to students starting clinical training. His theme asks whether a disease can truly be eliminated. He traces hepatitis C, a virus first identified in nineteen eighty-nine, the year he graduated.

World leaders pledged in twenty sixteen to end viral hepatitis as a major threat by twenty thirty. At that time it was the only major infection with a rising death toll. Vaccines, safer care, and strong new drugs for hepatitis C gave grounds for hope. McDougall uses that story to probe what elimination means in practice. The speech blends career reflection with a hard look at global goals.
pmc-12768597:
Luiza Nascimento-Costa and co-authors ask why approved insulin drugs fail to reach Brazilian patients in a 2025 study. Modern insulin analogs entered the public health system on paper in 2017 and 2019. In practice, supply lagged badly, and patients kept suing for access. The team traced the gap using committee records, ministry purchases, and dispensing data from 2011 to 2022.

Rules say supply should begin within 180 days of approval. For short-acting analogs, the first dispensing came after 575 days, more than a year late. Long-acting versions also missed the mark. The study names the delay between decree and delivery as the core barrier. It shows how a favorable decision alone does not put medicine in patients' hands.
pmc-12768697:
Laís Lopes and co-authors describe a way to spot unmet medical needs inside a university hospital in a paper from 2025. Health technology assessment, or HTA, weighs whether a hospital should adopt a new tool or drug. Along the way, it can reveal needs that no current tool meets.

The team read every HTA report filed from 2018 to 2023 for adoption requests. They used a standard US definition of unmet need to flag cases. A priority system based on WHO and Brazilian health lists then ranked the themes. Sorted by field and patient group, the gaps form a research agenda. Hospitals can aim their research funds where patients lack options.
pmc-12768797:
Marcela Rousseau and Graciela Demirdjian report on a drug review unit in a 2025 paper from a large children's hospital in Argentina. Since 2019, the unit has had a sector that must judge every request to add a high cost or high risk drug. All requests follow a set path, starting with a check of relevance by a pharmacy and care committee.

The report reviews five years of that work. It counts output and reply times, the yearly cost per patient of the drugs judged, and the share of requests the sector advised against. It also tracks how often leaders accepted that advice and what happened to patients when drugs were added.
pmc-12769697:
Heng Wang and co-authors present a 2025 study of a plant compound that helps the body kill bacteria hiding inside cells. Such hidden germs shrug off many drugs, and host-directed cures are still scarce. The compound, called DEHD in short, blocked the growth of several germ types in lab tests. It also made standard antibiotics work better in mice.

Lab work showed the compound binds a protein called MDM2 and switches on a chain that keeps cell stomachs acidic. That acidity, plus a clean-up process in the cell, helps drugs reach the germs. In mice with lethal infections, deaths fell from nine in ten to one in ten when the compound joined drug care. The work names a new host pathway that drug hunters can aim at.
pmc-12771897:
Yidi Wang, Xianzhao Liu, and Jiaxi Liu study how farm carbon goals and food security move together across China in a 2025 paper. Farms must cut emissions and store more carbon while still feeding the country.

The team built score systems for both goals and measured how well they align in each grain region from 2000 to 2023. The match was stronger in the north than in the south. Their spatial model shows that gains in one region spill over to neighbors. Carbon taken up by major crops was the strongest driver of the joint gains. Heavy land share and heavy use of fertilizer and pesticides held the match back, both at home and next door.
pmc-12772197:
Joseph Collura and co-authors show a drug route that reverts Merkel cell carcinoma in a 2025 study. A virus drives most cases of this harsh skin cancer by forcing a viral protein that keeps cells growing.

Blocking a cell helper pair called CBP and p300 shut off that viral protein. Cancer cells then stopped dividing, raised a brake protein, and began to turn into nerve-like cells with small branches. Gene scans showed growth programs and Merkel cell marks switched down. A rare mixed tumor in a patient matched the treated cell pattern. The work offers a model where cancer can be flipped back and forth by drugs.
pmc-12772597:
Emilia Pietiläinen and co-authors compare the health, activity, and fitness of soldiers and civilian staff in the Finnish military, in a study from 2025. Two hundred sixty employees from six brigades wore activity trackers for two weeks and gave blood samples, body measures, and lifestyle answers. The question was whether uniform predicts a healthier profile.

After accounting for gender, soldiers and civilians looked much alike. Soldiers won only the muscle fitness test. Male soldiers averaged 0.9 hours of moderate-to-vigorous activity a day against 1.0 for male civilians, and sat more, 9.5 versus 8.9 hours. Cholesterol values were near-identical. The authors note that a desk-heavy military workplace may erase the expected soldier advantage, a warning for defense readiness.
pmc-12775097:
Liang Shi and co-authors compare two hormone-defined groups within aggressive breast cancer in a 2025 study. Tumors positive for the HER2 marker respond to targeted drugs, but not all patients gain equally. The team split cases by hormone receptor status and compared the groups across a national cancer database covering two decades. Over 30,000 patients had both markers positive, and about 12,000 had HER2 alone.

The hormone-positive group skewed younger and differed in tumor type mix. Gene expression and mutation data from public atlases added a molecular layer to the comparison. Survival patterns were also contrasted. The analysis aims to explain why the same targeted therapy lands differently across patients who share the headline marker.
pmc-12775697:
Xiaowei Chen and seven co-authors pool studies on whether tumor DNA floating in blood predicts outcomes in non-small cell lung cancer. Their systematic review and meta-analysis was published in twenty twenty-five.

The team searched seven sources for studies from twenty sixteen to mid twenty twenty-four that compared patients with and without detectable tumor DNA. Fifty-two studies qualified, with samples from a dozen to a few hundred patients. Pooled risks covered relapse-free survival, overall survival, and recurrence, at several treatment time points. Study quality was scored with a standard scale. Finding the DNA generally marked worse outlook. The summary helps doctors judge how much weight to give a blood test result.
pmc-12776197:
Jiyuan Zhu and co-authors compare the gene changes in breast cancer between men and women in a 2025 study. Male breast cancer is rare, often caught late, and treated by rules borrowed from the far more common female disease.

Tumor samples from twelve men and fourteen women went through targeted gene sequencing. Some mutated genes were shared, but the patterns differed. One gene's mutation rate differed sharply between the sexes, and two genes often gained extra copies in women yet never in men. Women's tumors carried more mutations overall. The men's private gene changes clustered in growth signaling pathways. The authors say the differences justify studying the male disease on its own terms.
pmc-12777397:
Heling Wu and co-authors reported a fungal allergy disease that mimicked lung cancer in two thousand twenty-five. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis occurs in people allergic to Aspergillus fungi, often with asthma. It can cause airway blockage, lung shadows, and fever that come and go.

Their patient was a thirty-nine-year-old woman with asthma and a productive cough. Scans showed solid lung lesions and enlarged lymph nodes, and a tumor marker in her blood was raised, all pointing to cancer. A biopsy plus other tests instead confirmed the fungal disease by standard criteria. Steroid treatment improved both her scans and the marker level. The authors urge doctors to consider this mimic before invasive steps.
pmc-12780097:
Leonardo Hernandez and nine co-authors map how many hospitals in the Americas sit in the path of natural hazards. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Quakes, storms, floods, slides, and volcanoes all threat care sites, but no shared map spanned the whole zone. The team built a matched list of hospitals with ER care and laid it on hazard maps.

More than twenty thousand hospitals in fifty-one lands were found. Near nine in ten face at least one hazard, with floods by far the most wide. More than four in ten sit in top-risk zones, and near four in ten face two or more hazards. Hot spots span Central America, the US east shore, and the Pacific rim.
pmc-12780597:
After liver cancer surgery, doctors disagree on whether extra treatment helps keep the cancer away. Jia-Jun Li and co-authors revisit one option, a procedure, PA-TACE, that delivers chemotherapy via the liver's artery after the tumor is removed. They compared about four hundred patients who did or did not receive it, and used matching to make the groups more alike. Both recurrence free survival and overall survival were tracked.

Patients who received the procedure lived longer, and their edge in staying recurrence free was borderline at first but clear after matching. The clearest benefit sat in patients whose tumors had invaded blood vessels: in that group the procedure cut recurrence risk by about two thirds and death risk by over half. Patients who did recur after the procedure had less aggressive tumors. The authors conclude the added treatment helps most patients with vessel invasion.
pmc-12780797:
Aija Laitinen and co-authors published this 2025 study on food education in Finnish primary schools. Schools can build healthy eating habits early, yet planned food teaching is often missing or patchy. The team asked the people who run schools what helps such teaching take root.

They interviewed twelve headteachers and five municipal education directors, all with experience from a project called Tasty School. The talks were sorted with a framework that spans national policy down to daily school life. Success, the leaders said, needs a school culture that treats food education as real work, woven into the curriculum with enough time set aside. The study maps the supports leaders see as decisive.
pmc-12781397:
Nida Buawangpong and eight co-authors report on medical students in Thailand who used a digital health app as part of their training. Their 2025 paper describes iCHANGE, an app that records and tracks six health behaviors plus lab results. The course put students in real contact with patients who had several long-term conditions at once.

Students monitored the patients' records, gave advice and health teaching, and worked under the eye of a care team, using the app's messaging and decision support tools. The researchers then ran six focus groups with twenty-six students. Three themes emerged: skill with digital health is now part of being a doctor. Digital tools bring real challenges in practice, and they still help in caring for patients with many conditions. The authors conclude that building such tools into the curriculum prepares students for the care they will soon give.
pmc-12781597:
Tao Wu and five co-authors build in 2025 a scoring system to foresee which patients keep hurting after a balloon procedure for trigeminal neuralgia. The procedure squeezes the nerve through a needle to stop severe facial pain, yet in some patients the pain fades only slowly.

Looking back at two hundred eighty-two patients, the team split them into a group used to build the score and a smaller group used to test it. They searched for factors that marked delayed relief and turned them into points. A reliable score would let surgeons warn patients early and plan follow-up with open eyes.
pmc-12782597:
Brian Milman and Samuel Parnell published a teaching case in 2025 for emergency medicine residents facing their board exams. The new certifying exam includes live cases where candidates must question, examine, and manage a patient out loud. Vomiting and belly pain bring many children to emergency rooms, and one dangerous cause is the bowel telescoping into itself, called intussusception.

Their mock case presents an irritable, vomiting eighteen-month-old, run over video with a faculty examiner. Learners must take a focused history, form a list of possible causes, and show how they would treat the telescoped bowel. A group debrief follows once everyone has played the case. Practice in the exact exam format, the authors argue, is the scarcest resource they can give.
pmc-12783797:
Thirteen authors reveal how shark derived binders block a key inflammation signal in this 2025 study. The signal, TNF-alpha, drives many immune diseases, and all current drugs against it also bind its membrane form, which can trigger reverse signals that suppress immunity and invite infection.

The team solved crystal structures of two shark variable antigen receptors bound to the soluble form of the signal, at two distinct sites. One binder grips a site found only on the soluble form, so it spares the membrane form. In activated T cells, the binders caused no reverse signaling, unlike current drugs. A selective blocker could be safer for high risk patients.
pmc-12784597:
Yu Yi, Yinghua Chen, and Yawen Luo ask whether aspirin helps the sickest liver cirrhosis patients live longer, in this 2025 study. Aspirin's promise in liver disease was shown mostly in outpatients. Mining a large intensive care database, the team matched three hundred thirty-four aspirin users with similar non-users.

Mortality at thirty and ninety days ran lower among users, as did deaths in hospital. Stay length in intensive care matched between groups. Bleeding data were missing, so the net benefit stays unproven, and most users took the low dose. The authors call for prospective trials.
pmc-12784997:
Matthew Ware and co-authors track shrinking nesting loggerhead turtles in northwest Florida in this 2025 paper. Body size shapes how many eggs a female lays, so size trends matter for recovery plans. Reports elsewhere hint that nesting turtles are getting smaller.

Seven years of night surveys on St George Island supplied the data. The average shell length sat near ninety-four centimeters across 232 turtles. About nine percent fell below the size agencies treat as adult. Each extra centimeter of shell added about one egg per clutch. Nests of the largest females faced higher wave wash-out odds, though. Size thus cuts both ways for hatchling output in this colony.
pmc-12785297:
Borja Suarez-Villadat and co-authors test in 2025 an adapted judo program for teenagers with Down syndrome. Young people with the condition often show weaker fitness and lower social well being, which can limit health and inclusion. Martial arts, adjusted to their needs, may help on both fronts at once.

The study used a comparison design with 43 teenagers. Nineteen formed a control group, while 24 trained in adapted judo for 24 weeks. The team measured fitness and social and mental outcomes before and after. Judo brings gripping, balance, and safe falling, plus the respect rituals of the mat. If the program lifts both body and mood, schools gain a cheap group activity with wide benefits. The authors report what changed in each group.
pmc-12785397:
Iqra Tabassum and co-authors give the first molecular profile of rare genetic diseases in the Punjabi population of Pakistan in a 2025 study. Genomic databases skew Western, leaving South Asian patients poorly served.

A provincial registry in Lahore enrolled families tested by modern sequencing over three years. One hundred sixty-seven families carried seventy-two distinct rare diseases. Niemann-Pick disease, a liver bile-flow disorder, and a sugar-storage disease led the list. Nearly nine in ten families reported cousin marriage, strongly tied to disease occurrence. Most families had low incomes despite high literacy, exposing care inequity. Over one hundred thirty variants across more than one hundred genes were classed for harm. Local data should sharpen diagnosis.
pmc-12785597:
Lijun Gao and co-authors build a quick strip test to check that deer meat is what the label claims. Their 2025 study targets sika deer meat, whose high price invites cheating with cheaper meats. The test reads DNA rather than looks or smell.

A gene segment found in the deer is copied many times over, then shown on a paper strip. True deer meat lights up two lines, while fake samples show only the control line. The strip caught DNA at levels ten times lower than the older gel method. It also found deer meat mixed in at a share of one percent. The team aims the tool at market checks on site.
pmc-12785797:
Salman Uddin and co-authors map in 2025 how a social amoeba's cells answer two different keep away signals at the level of proteins and their phosphate switches. Dictyostelium cells flee both a secreted protein called AprA and simple polyphosphate, but whether the two alarms ring the same circuitry was unknown.

Mass spectrometry censused the shifts. Each signal moved hundreds of proteins, yet the overlap was small, only a few dozen moving together and a handful pushed in opposite directions. Many targets sat in RNA handling and the ribosome, an unexpected address for a movement response. Phosphate switches flipped on motility proteins as expected. Two shared switches stood out: both signals dimmed the same pair of regulators, and mutant cells missing either one ignored both repellents. The verdict is two partly separate escape programs that converge on a few common nodes, which the authors nominate as the core of chemorepulsion.
pmc-12785897:
Buev and coauthors study a gene that helps build the tail of sperm cells. Sperm must grow a long tail to swim well. Faults in the gene NSUN7 link to weak sperm and male infertility. The team asks what the gene does at each growth stage.

They used mice that lack the gene and sorted sperm at each stage. Protein checks covered young round cells, stretched cells, and mature sperm. The gene was most full in round cells, when the tail forms. Without it, key tail and sheath proteins shifted in amount. The work helps explain how tail faults arise.
pmc-12785997:
Latika Giri and co-authors test in 2025 an AI reader for chest X-rays that works without the internet. Radiologists are scarce in poorer countries, and chest films are the world's most common scan. Their network was trained on public sets, then tuned on local films from a Nepal hospital.

The system screens one patient for 14 diseases at once, using front and side views. On a held-out test set it scored well overall, catching about two thirds of disease while almost never raising false alarms. Colored boxes marked each finding, even when several diseases shared one chest. It also ran inside the hospital's image system and offline. The authors offer it as a triage aid where specialists are few.
pmc-12786497:
Xavier Laurent, Damien Dodelin, Nicolas Graveleau, and Nicolas Bouguennec tested how blocked sight changes jumps after knee ligament repair. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, deals with patients after ACL reconstruction. Many keep movement flaws in hard tasks like the one leg drop jump. At six months, they lean on sight to make up for weak body sense. That lean can bend their form.

Patients still in rehab jumped under three sight states: plain sight, low blur, and high blur, through special eyewear. Past work used two leg jumps; this one tests the one leg form that strains the knee most. Readers in sports rehab learn if sight loss unmasks flaws that plain tests miss.
pmc-12786697:
Georgiana-Florina Badea and four co-authors wrote a 2025 study on new fire protection coatings made from phosphate cement and perlite. Passive fire protection slows heat reaching steel, buying time in a blaze. The team built cements from dolomite, a common mineral, heated alone or with fly ash at two temperatures.

Heating at 750 degrees yielded a mix suited to cement making; adding fly ash and heating to 1,200 degrees formed new hard compounds. Mixed with a phosphate solution and borax, the powders set into cements whose strength and mineral makeup were measured. Coated steel plates then faced direct flame for up to 60 minutes. Perlite, a light volcanic rock, was added to some mixes. The coatings slowed the steel's heating and stuck well to its surface.
pmc-12786797:
Poliana Bellei and four co-authors turn oyster shell waste into building material in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Piles of discarded shells are a disposal problem in coastal areas. Lime mortars, used on old brick buildings, may take shell as an ingredient. The team made mortars with natural hydraulic lime. In one mix, shell powder replaced part of the lime. In another, crushed shell replaced part of the sand.

They tested the mortars in molds and spread on solid bricks like those in historic walls. Heat and humidity cycles mimicked aging. The shell mixes were then compared with a plain control mortar. The authors report on strength, physical traits, and durability. The work points to greener repair materials for heritage buildings.
pmc-12787097:
Chaoyu Li and co-authors study how a magnetic field during plating changes the corrosion resistance of nickel-titanium nitride coatings. The coatings were deposited on Q235 steel by electrodeposition with magnetic help at three field strengths. The team checked surface shape, titanium content, crystal structure, hardness, and sticking strength, then tested how each coating stood up to corrosion.

The middle field strength, 0.7 tesla, gave the best coating on nearly every measure. Its surface and thickness beat those made at 0.3 and 1.1 tesla. It held more titanium, stuck more firmly, and reached the highest hardness. Its nickel grains were finer, and in corrosion tests it showed the highest corrosion potential with the lowest corrosion current. No clear pits formed on its surface, and its weight loss in testing was the lowest. The results suggest a middle-strength field is the sweet spot for this coating method.
pmc-12787397:
Cristiana Gijiu, Daniel Dinculescu, and Raluca Isopescu used computer models to tune a membrane process in a 2025 study. The process pulls water from ethanol through a plastic film, a step in making pure fuel alcohol. Near a key mix point, the two liquids are hard to split by boiling.

The team varied feed mix, heat, and pressure on the far side of the film, under a planned design. Settings near one hundred degrees and a low pressure suited both a wetter and a drier feed. Recovery stayed above ninety-nine percent in those runs. For the drier feed, good trade-offs between purity and yield could also be had at lower heat. The study maps where the process works best.
pmc-12789497:
Xu and coauthors ask if doctor mothers have better pregnancy outcomes in China. Obstetric doctors serve as both providers and patients in pregnancy. Their medical knowledge may shape habits and outcomes. Data on that group in China have been sparse.

The study ran at a large women hospital in Zhejiang. It held 100 doctor mothers who gave birth from 2012 to 2022. Two hundred matched non-doctor mothers gave the contrast set. Outcomes held surgery births, urgent surgery, and birth weight. Newborn scores and pregnancy harms were also logged. Results test if expertise alone improves outcomes.
pmc-12795397:
Swings in blood sugar, not just its average height, may wear on the growing brain of a child with type 1 diabetes. Malik Asfand Yar and co-authors test that idea in a 2025 study at a teaching hospital in Pakistan. Records for a group of children covered two years of sugar readings alongside standard tests of thinking.

Children whose long-term sugar marker swung widely scored lower on overall intelligence, working memory, processing speed, and self-control tasks than steady children. The swing measure was the single strongest predictor of lower scores, ahead of average sugar. Frequent low-sugar episodes added their own drag. The authors argue that smoothing the ride, not merely lowering the average, should be a stated goal of care for these children.
pmc-12799297:
Ohta, Ryu, and Ichinose pool proof on hard-to-treat low platelets in lupus. Low platelets are a common and grave sign in lupus. Some patients stay low despite standard drug care. Three targeted drugs have been used in small studies.

The team searched for all studies of those three drugs in lupus. Each study covered adults with proven lupus and stubborn low platelets. Pooled rates showed how often platelets rose with each drug. Harms and dose facts were also weighed in the pool. Clear pooled proof can guide doctors in rare, tough cases. The review sets a base for larger trials.
pmc-12801497:
Lusheng Wang and co-authors test an old antibacterial drug, clofoctol, against triple negative breast cancer in a 2025 study. This cancer form lacks the targets most breast drugs aim at, so reused drugs are prized. Computer screening first pointed to the pathways the drug might hit; cell and mouse tests then checked the guesses.

Clofoctol slowed the cancer cells' growth and spread and pushed them into arrest and death. It wrecked their power plants, spilling stress signals and a death trigger. The damage also woke an immune alarm pathway inside the cells. Tumors in mice shrank as well, the team reports, with safety checks alongside.
pmc-12801597:
Jiahui Zou and co-authors compare four diets for a fatty liver disease tied to metabolism. Their 2025 analysis pools trials of the Mediterranean diet, fasting plans, the DASH diet, and a low-fat diet. The disease is a broad public health concern, and food is a main tool to treat it. The team searched six sources for trials up to October 2025.

Fasting plans ranked best for weight loss and for trimming waist size. The Mediterranean diet ranked best for liver health, with drops in liver fat and in blood fats. Stronger fasting plans seemed to drive larger gains than time-limited eating alone. The authors advise tailoring the diet to each patient's main needs. They also note that long, high-grade trials are still needed.
pmc-12801797:
Jin Fan and co-authors review diagnosis and care for myalgic encephalomyelitis, also called chronic fatigue syndrome, in a 2025 paper. The illness has drawn more attention as cases rise and overlap with long COVID grows. The review gathers current rules for diagnosis, ideas on causes, and care options.

Diagnosis still rests on symptoms, since no firm lab marker exists. Faulty immune control, cell power problems, and brain inflammation sit at the centre of current thinking. Drug options target those routes, while non-drug care includes pacing and some traditional methods. Talking therapy may ease symptoms but does not cure, and graded exercise can harm and is ruled out. The authors call for marker-based tests and combined care plans.
pmc-12801997:
Jie Kang and nine co-authors present SimGBS, a 2025 tool for simulating genotyping-by-sequencing data at large scale. The method, called GBS, reads DNA at scattered points and is a cheap way to genotype many samples, but its low depth leaves some gene variants unread. New analysis methods must handle that uncertainty, and testing them needs realistic fake data. SimGBS builds such data from any real or simulated genome.

Users can shape populations by changing size over generations or by feeding in a family tree. Enzyme choice, read depth, and other settings are adjustable. The tool outputs both the true genotypes and raw sequence files, so pipelines can be tested end to end. It simulated 172 samples in under two hours while matching the messiness of real data.
pmc-12804697:
Yuhui Qiao and co-authors show how sodium overload kills cells by wrecking energy production in mitochondria, in a research paper from 2025. Sodium influx is a key event in ischemia, salt stress, and organ failure. A channel called TRPM4, when held open by a chemical trigger, floods the cell with sodium and causes a necrosis form named NECSO.

Extra sodium enters mitochondria and pushes calcium out through an exchanger. That shift blocks energy pathways, including the main fuel cycle. Energy failure then stops the sodium-potassium pump, ion gradients collapse, and the cell swells and bursts. The chain may underlie diseases where sodium runs high.
pmc-12804897:
Karolina Cysewska and six co-authors report a 2025 method to set nanodiamonds into a conductive polymer coat for stent use. The polymer is polypyrrole, and the base is a fast-rusting iron alloy that the coat must shield while it does its work in the body.

An electric deposition step drives the charged nanodiamonds into the growing film. A salt coat calms the alloy face so the film can form. Light and X-ray tests prove the diamonds sit in the film. Scan images show how the settings shape the coat, and first rust tests show its pace can be tuned.
pmc-12804997:
Kai Peng and six co-authors published an environmental modeling study in twenty twenty-five on forecasting plant cover in drylands from rainfall and evaporation data. In arid regions water rules vegetation, but greenness responds with a lag that simple models miss. The team built a hybrid deep learning model pairing convolutional and memory networks.

A drought index first sorted the study area into aridity types, giving the model varied training cases. The convolutional part reads spatial patterns in the water data; the recurrent part follows long time dependencies. The model distinguished how heavy rain contributes far more to anomalies in arid than semi-arid zones. Dynamic change indices tracked cover over time, supporting land management under a drying climate.
pmc-12805697:
Zhuo Feng builds a theory of how green technology spreads across countries when each nation acts with strategy. Nations invest in clean research, and what one learns leaks to others through a network. Acting alone, each nation spends too little, since it cannot claim the full gain of its work and can ride on the work of others.

The model mixes game theory, growth theory, and network maps to show these forces at work. Lone action delays the shift to clean tech and lets pollution run longer. Joint action does far better. Computer runs show that a world mix of carbon pricing and green research support can come close to the joint result.
pmc-12808397:
Fatma Alshehri and a large team report a 2026 study of infections caused by the bacterium Klebsiella pneumoniae. This germ can cause lung infections and other serious illness. Some strains are far more aggressive than the common form, and the team compared the two kinds.

They screened 600 samples and found the germ in about 17 percent. The aggressive form made up just over half of the finds. It ruled in infections outside the lungs, while the common form ruled in lung cases. Lung cases were mostly adults with breathing symptoms. Cases elsewhere hit children and older adults more, often with fever.
pmc-12808997:
Faliq Abdullah and co-authors review twenty years of a rare childhood disorder at one Welsh center, in a 2025 paper. Langerhans cell histiocytosis makes bone-marrow-derived cells pile up where they should not. It most often strikes the skeleton, and its lumps can look like cancer or infection on scans. That disguise makes diagnosis tricky. The team gathered every case treated locally between 2005 and 2025.

The series held 35 children. Records and imaging were mined for age, sex, disease sites, scan features, and outcomes. Cases were sorted as single-site, multi-site, or whole-body disease. Tissue tests, where available, checked for the standard marker proteins of the disorder. The authors lay out the patterns of bone lesions and the treatments used, giving doctors a clearer picture of how this rare disease behaves over the long run.
pmc-12809897:
Mengyuan Sui, Mingxing Zhou, and Yang Yang study emotional labor among college teachers in China in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Emotional labor means managing feelings as part of the job, by faking a display, forcing a real change, or showing what one truly feels. The team links these styles to mental health.

The survey covered nine hundred twelve vocational college teachers. Faking feelings was tied to more mental health problems, while the other two styles were tied to fewer. A strong sense of professional identity carried part of these effects. Good relations with students softened the links. Effects also varied by sex, age, and income. The authors draw lessons for easing strain on faculty.
pmc-12812497:
Car crashes are a leading cause of injury in pregnancy, yet most mothers and babies come through well. Avis Chan and co-authors review 157 pregnant patients seen at a level one trauma center within a day of a crash, from 2015 to 2021. They record crash details, injuries, and outcomes for mother and fetus.

Most patients were in their mid-20s and in the second trimester, and nearly all wore seat belts. About 85 percent had no or minor injuries. Only two patients needed belly surgery. Crash speed was the clear driver of harm: faster crashes meant more inner injury, more skin tears, and longer stays. Airbag deployment tracked with speed but did not itself predict injury. The authors say speed, not the safety gear, should guide how hard clinicians look for hidden harm.
pmc-12812697:
Lina Qiu, Ahmad Alhaskawi, and Safwat Adel Abdo Moqbel review worn joint illness as a whole-joint ill in a 2025 paper. The old view blamed cartilage wear alone. The field now sees stress, swelling, weight strain, and cell aging meet across bone, lining, fat pad, and muscle to drive the ill.

The review maps each tissue's part, plus fresh paths such as one iron-tied cell death and nerve-and-vessel growth. It grades the full care shelf, from drills and drugs to shots, surgery, and cell cures. Gene maps, scan marks, and AI tools point to care shaped to each patient. Early, cause-based care is the push.
pmc-12812897:
Ralph Cooper, James Simpkins, and Charles Breckenridge present a review published in 2025 on how the weed killer atrazine affects female hormones, working from rat studies toward human cancer questions. In rats, high doses derail the brain signal that triggers ovulation, leaving hormone levels that encourage mammary tumors as the animals age.

The reviewers stress the mismatch with human aging: rat tumors ride on high estrogen late in life, while menopause in women means estrogen loss. Lab tests showed the chemical family does not bind estrogen receptors, and high doses may even oppose estrogen. Human epidemiology, finally, showed no consistent link between exposure and breast, ovarian, or uterine cancer. The authors conclude the rat mechanism translates poorly to women.
pmc-12813297:
Nakazawa and co-authors report hidden fractures at the start of dialysis in a kidney patient. The patient was a 55-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease. Fractures appeared within two months of starting dialysis. X-ray and CT scans missed the breaks entirely. MRI found fractures in heels, foot bones, and pelvis.

Blood tests showed high parathyroid hormone and low zinc. Care paired hormone drugs, active vitamin D, and zinc. Symptoms cleared over 17 months of treatment. The authors urge early MRI for odd pain at dialysis start. Low zinc, they suggest, may add to bone fragility.
pmc-12815797:
Nari Kim and co-authors hunt for breast cancer subtypes ruled by regulatory T cells, in a study published in 2025. These T cells damp the immune attack inside a tumor, and tumors rich in them resist standard immune drugs. Sorting such tumors out could guide who gets immune therapy.

The team merged four layers of molecular data, from gene activity to proteins, across tumor samples. One cluster stood out for heavy regulatory T cell presence and strong immune dampening, and the same pattern appeared in a second cohort. Computer models of tumor and immune dynamics predicted that pairing a Treg-targeted drug with checkpoint blockade would beat either alone. Tests in mice with a suppressive breast tumor bore that out.
pmc-12816997:
Lufuno J Badzhi, Timothy C Hardcastle, and Pumersha Naidoo compare bedside exams with scans in spinal trauma in a 2025 study. At a large South African hospital, they reviewed six years of charts for 290 patients who had CT or MRI scans after spine injury. Neck injuries were the most common.

They measured how well the clinical exam predicted what scans showed, using standard accuracy statistics. If exams match scans closely in some patterns, extra imaging might safely wait or be skipped; where they diverge, scans stay essential. The answer matters most where scanners are scarce and trauma loads are heavy, as in much of the region.
pmc-12817697:
Bekalu Yirga and Mikias Negash tested whether simple blood measures can predict outlook in chronic heart failure in 2025. Their study ran at a large hospital in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Blood tests are cheap and widely done, so a clear link to disease severity would help clinics with few funds.

The team enrolled 206 adults with heart failure and took a small venous blood sample from each. A lab machine measured blood values, and the team compared them across the standard classes of symptom severity. They also used curve analysis to judge how well chosen values flagged poor outlook. Readers get local data from Ethiopia on a low-cost approach to risk checks. Such work can guide which cheap tests deserve a place in routine heart failure care.
pmc-12819397:
Shahar Ben-Zeev and Itzhak Lior build an earthquake early warning system on fiber-optic cables, using physics rather than trained patterns, in this 2025 paper. Distributed acoustic sensing turns existing fibers into thousands of vibration sensors. Most warning systems need long local calibration; a physics-based one can deploy fast.

Detection and location run on delay-and-sum beamforming, stacking the cable's signals in the time domain. Magnitude and predicted shaking come from analytical formulas built on the Brune source model, which links a quake's spectrum to its size. The team demonstrates magnitude estimation and ground-motion prediction on local earthquakes and shows the computation is fast enough for real time. Because every module rests on wave-propagation physics, the system skips the phase of gathering local earthquake data that data-driven rivals require.
pmc-12819597:
Saeed Alqahtani grades dental students' crown shaping with a part-by-part rubric to test grader fairness, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Forty-five fourth-year students shaped one front tooth for a metal-ceramic crown under set rules. Four trained judges scored eight traits blind, each on a small scale.

Judges agreed well to near perfectly across traits. No judge scored higher or lower than peers in the stats. Top scores went to edge form and gum care, while cut depth and taper lagged. The author calls the rubric clear, fair, and rich in feedback. Readers in skills teaching get proof that fine rubrics calm grader drift.
pmc-12819897:
Ana Gago-Veiga and co-authors build and validate a questionnaire that asks migraine patients, in Spanish, how satisfied they truly are with their care. Satisfaction steers whether patients stay on preventive therapy, yet general surveys miss migraine's specifics: attack treatment, prevention, daily interference, and the care team's attentiveness. The MISAT-Q was designed to cover all of it.

Headache units across Spain recruited treated migraine patients for a cross-sectional validation study between 2023 and 2024. A thirty-five-item draft was tested for reliability and validity against patient experience. A fit-for-purpose instrument lets clinics audit themselves through patients' eyes and lets trials count contentment as an outcome beside attack counts.
pmc-12821197:
COVID-19 in children has softened season by season, and Polish doctors set out to document the change. Dobrowolska and eight co-authors review all children hospitalized with the infection across Polish centers in two seasons, 2023/24 and 2024/25. The study covers 366 children. About three quarters in both seasons were under two years old, boys outnumbered girls, and over a quarter had other illnesses.

Children arrived with lower oxygen levels in the first season, and unstable cases were more common then. Oxygen treatment was used significantly more in that season too. Severe cases clustered in babies under one year, most with existing conditions. By the second season the course ran milder overall. The authors urge special vigilance for the youngest children and those with other illnesses, in whom the disease can still turn fast.
pmc-12821297:
Ruoshui Liu, Thomas Kowal, Caden Chow, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It compares how the two best-known compounds in cannabis, THC and CBD, change gene activity across many species and body tissues.

The team gathered 105 public datasets from humans, monkeys, mice, and rats, covering both gene chip and gene sequencing studies. They tracked which genes switched up or down after exposure to each compound. CBD produced more gene changes and more affected pathways than THC. Its effects also grouped more neatly by species and by how the dose was given. Pathways tied to zinc balance, calming inflammation, and cell stress stood out for CBD. The paper gives a broad map for judging claims about each compound's effects.
pmc-12821597:
Setor Kunutsor and Jari Laukkanen report a 2025 study that compares three body measures as flags for multiple heart and metabolic diseases in older adults. One measure, the cardiometabolic index, blends a fat ratio with waist to height. The team set it against body mass index and waist size alone.

Data came from 3,348 adults in an English aging study, free of the target diseases at the 2008 to 2009 wave. Over 12 to 15 years, 197 people developed two or more of the conditions. All three measures rose in a straight line with risk. Waist size showed the strongest link, while the new index matched body mass index in effect size.
pmc-12821797:
Kamlesh Meena and Sanatan Nayak map how Indian families fall into distress financing when someone needs hospital care. Distress financing means paying through borrowing, selling assets, or other desperate routes rather than income or savings. Even as out-of-pocket spending trends down, the practice remains widespread. The team analyzed a national survey of nearly 114,000 households from 2017 and 2018.

Reliance on desperate payment ran highest among Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe households and those with less income and schooling. Four states stood out for the heaviest incidence, especially in their countryside. Insurance did not erase the problem: insured rural households still resorted to distress routes at notable rates. The statistical model confirmed social group, income, education, job, household size, and coverage as predictors. The authors call the persistence of distress financing a core failure that policy has yet to close.
pmc-12821997:
Hongzhan Liu and colleagues catalogue a family of stress genes in barley, in this genome-wide study from twenty twenty-five. The genes, called DREB, help plants answer drought and salty soil, two threats that cut barley yields. In barley itself, though, the family had not been fully mapped.

The scan found thirty-nine DREB genes spread across all the barley chromosomes, with some copied in pairs. Their control regions carry switches that answer stress, cold, and hormones, and small RNAs were predicted to tune sixteen of them. Lab tests then showed the genes switching on at varied levels in roots, stems, and leaves under stress. Comparisons with four other species showed parts of the family kept in step through evolution. The authors say the map gives breeders and engineers a parts list for building barley that holds up better in dry, salty fields.
pmc-12822097:
SangKu Yi and co-authors present a 2025 study of how growth broth shapes a bacterial delivery machine. Some bacteria fire proteins into host cells through a syringe-like device. Teams have rebuilt that device as a programmable tool, but broth effects on its work had never been mapped in a set way.

The team built a switchable form of the device in Salmonella, with a glow tag on one base part. The device shipped its cargo well across dose levels in a lean broth. In a rich broth, more switch signal did not mean more shipping, and part levels fell at high dose. Gene reads showed build messages still rose, so the block sat later, in protein making or folding. Stress genes rose as ribosome genes fell.
pmc-12822297:
Yanqing Ren and co-authors lay out a trial combining exercise and brain stimulation for frail, forgetful older adults. Muscle loss and mild cognitive impairment reinforce each other through inflammation and a disturbed muscle-brain axis. Exercise supports brain plasticity from the body side, while magnetic pulses boost it.

Fifty-one older adults with both conditions will be assigned by lot for sixteen weeks to exercise plus real stimulation, exercise plus sham, or control. Training mixes a traditional Chinese routine with resistance training; the pulses target the frontal cortex. Muscle fitness, thinking, and well-being are taken at the start, middle, and end.
pmc-12823597:
Keeping a car stable in a fast swerve is a hard control problem, and older methods falter in complex cases. Mu Lin and co-authors pair a digital twin of the vehicle with a predictive controller in this 2025 study. The twin, a detailed live model fed by real data, helps the controller plan torque and steering moves ahead of time.

In joint simulations, the paired system cut lateral stability error by 62.5 percent and yaw rate error by 57.1 percent against older methods. The gain comes from the twin updating the controller's picture of the car in real time. The authors present the setup as a base for safer smart vehicles. It also supports work on self-driving systems that must react in emergencies.
pmc-12824397:
Feng Han and Bo Mo tackle a forecasting job for spacecraft: guessing how much useful life is left in electronic gear before it fails. Their method blends a neural network with the physical laws of wear, so the model learns from data while respecting known rules. Such blended models can drift when working conditions change and old learning is lost.

The pair add continual learning, letting the model absorb new wear patterns online without forgetting old ones. Tested on a NASA data set of power devices, their method cut forecast error to about a quarter of a standard network's error. Updates took under a second per cycle. The authors say the speed and steadiness suit power gear in harsh space settings.
pmc-12827097:
Lin Wang and co-authors predict hidden lymph node spread in thyroid cancer in a study dated 2025. Cancers arising near the thyroid's bridge, the isthmus, spread to the opposite central neck nodes in about a third of cases, far above other tumors. Surgeons need to know that risk before choosing how much neck to clear.

From 1,672 patients, the team focused on 397 near-isthmus cases and split them into training and validation sets. Two selection methods narrowed the field to five predictors, including scan assessment and growth beyond the gland. Seven machine learning models competed on accuracy, and an explanation method ranked each factor's push on individual predictions.
pmc-12827497:
Fansheng Zhang and co-authors track hip function after lower spine fusion in a study published in 2025. Fusing the spine to the pelvis can stiffen the chain that walking depends on. The team used three-dimensional gait analysis to measure the cost.

Thirty patients at one hospital in Guizhou were followed for over a year. Half had spine-to-sacrum fusion; half had spine-to-pelvis work. Pain, disability, and clinical scores were logged at each visit. Against healthy controls, fused patients walked with shorter steps and strides. Hip swing angles and ranges shrank, and body sway patterns shifted. The data give surgeons a concrete picture of what fusion takes from the hip, and what rehab must target.
pmc-12828997:
Yue Huang, Dejin Gao, and Wanchen Dou published a 2025 study on blood clotting around the time of epilepsy surgery. Some epilepsy does not yield to drugs, and surgery is a key option for such cases. Bleeding after the operation is a real risk for some patients.

Anti-seizure drugs stay part of care through the surgery window. Some of these drugs can weaken the blood's clotting power. The team summed up clotting measures for patients across the surgical period. They compared results for two common drugs, sodium valproate and levetiracetam. Knowing which drug strains clotting less can help teams plan safer surgery and drug schedules.
pmc-12830697:
Yuting Deng and co-authors test a modified heart and metabolic index as a screening tool for cardiovascular disease, in a 2025 paper. The index joins insulin resistance and central obesity in one composite number. Its link to new heart disease had not been well explored, so the team ran a large cohort study in China.

Data came from a national aging study with baseline in 2011 and follow up in 2020. Of more than six thousand adults aged forty five or more, about thirteen hundred developed heart disease. Higher index values were an independent risk factor, with a bent, J shaped curve. The authors also compare its predictive power with a known sugar and fat index.
pmc-12830797:
Zuzana Pegrimocova and Michal Ritz use Raman spectroscopy to estimate mineral content in rocks in a 2025 paper. Knowing the silicate content of sedimentary rocks usually takes slow lab analysis. Raman scattering reads the way molecules vibrate, from a laser beam, and could give a rapid option.

The team ran clay shale and claystone samples under a laser at 633 nm. Strong fluorescence and bands that overlap made the spectra hard to read, so they used a multivariate regression method to fit estimates. A fast tool that does not destroy the sample would help screen many samples in the field and the lab.
pmc-12830897:
Kedan Gu and co-authors program cancer-fighting macrophages inside the body, no cell factory required. Their 2025 study targets cancer spread within the belly, where therapy options run thin, by delivering messenger RNA in fat particles tuned to reach macrophages.

The particles carry blueprints for chimeric antigen receptors, and the team screened thirty-six receptor designs to find the strongest. The winning build paired two signaling parts and switched macrophages into an attack state that also rallied wider immunity. Combined with checkpoint therapy it worked better still. Single-cell readouts showed the treated cells warming a cold tumor environment and growing a reserve pool of fighter T cells. The authors map the feedback loops the design triggers, for better and worse.
pmc-12831397:
Szymon Baluszek and colleagues show that mutations in the TP53 gene mark, and may drive, how chordomas turn from manageable to aggressive. Chordomas are rare bone tumors; their dedifferentiated and poorly differentiated variants carry a far worse outlook than conventional ones. The team read matched primary and recurrent samples from a patient whose tumor changed, plus more aggressive cases and a large conventional cohort built with published cases.

The returned tumor had newly gained harmful TP53 and BRCA1 mutations, and lost a chromosomal region holding the TBXT locus. Across cohorts, TP53 mutations showed up in most aggressive cases but only about one percent of ordinary chordomas. In recurrent samples, the mutations were missing from the matched primaries, proving they arose as the tumor grew. A routine sequencing panel could thus flag ordinary chordomas at risk of changing.
pmc-12831497:
Matthew Darmadi and four colleagues published a quality improvement study in two thousand twenty-five on residents' knowledge of fatty liver disease and metabolic syndrome. The liver condition, now called MASLD, is the world's commonest liver disease, yet training covers it thinly. A targeted lecture series was the intervention.

Internal medicine residents attended a structured session on obesity, metabolic syndrome, and the internist's role, held across January and February two thousand twenty-five. Pre- and post-surveys measured confidence in screening and treatment plus quiz knowledge, compared with paired statistics. Prior training was self-described in open answers. The authors set out to prove a single lecture can close practical gaps. Detailed score changes fill the report.
pmc-12832097:
Marino, Izhar, Israel, Jean, and Watson ask which health and social factors track with leg amputation after a severe injury. Trauma is the second most common cause of amputation, yet most past work looks at chronic illness instead. Their 2025 study uses records from a major United States trauma center.

The team compared 63 amputation cases from 2017 to 2022 with 129 similar fracture cases where the leg was saved. Diabetes, high blood pressure, bone infection, kidney disease, and alcohol in the body at arrival all tracked with higher amputation rates. Head injury, by contrast, tracked with lower rates. Substance use also tracked with high energy crashes. The study is limited to one center, so wider checks are still needed. The study is limited to one center, so wider checks are still needed.
pmc-12834997:
Chou-Yi Hsu and co-authors solve a two-dimensional quantum oscillator bent by a magnetic field and an inverse-square pull. Their 2025 study treats a textbook system with two twists: a field across one axis and a potential that spikes near the origin on the other. The equations separate cleanly, giving exact energy levels and wave patterns built from classic polynomial families.

With the solution in hand, the team computes information measures in both position and momentum views, then the heat-side quantities, energy, entropy, and free energy, from the partition function. The magnetic field is shown to sharpen the information content, one of several parameter effects mapped in the paper.
pmc-12836897:
Paula Jaimes-Buitron and co-authors track psychiatric drug use in young people with autism in a 2025 study. Two drug families dominate care: one used for agitation and behavior, the other for mood and anxiety. How often patients start each kind, and how often they switch, was unclear.

Insurance records covered nearly twenty five thousand people aged two to twenty six across a decade. Almost two thirds had a prescription from one of the two families. Switching was nearly twice as common after starting the behavior drugs as after starting the mood drugs. Over the decade, switching away from one behavior drug fell while switching from the other rose. The patterns can guide prescribing choices.
pmc-12837097:
Havva Karadeniz and Hatun Erkuran ask anesthesia students how they would face a medical error in a 2025 qualitative study. These students will soon work in operating rooms, where mistakes can harm patients fast. Thirty-three students from one program answered a made-up error scenario in depth interviews during late 2022 and early 2023. Their words were coded for feelings and likely actions.

Feelings split into hard ones, like fear, and useful ones, like resolve. Likely actions split into desired and undesired kinds, from honest reporting to hiding the slip. Knowing which instincts students bring lets teachers train disclosure and coping before the first real error, when habits set hard.
pmc-12837297:
Shujie Chen, Mei-I Cheng, Shira Elqayam, and Mark Scase explore work family conflict in contemporary China in a 2025 interview study. Most research on this conflict is Western, so its lived shape under Chinese cultural values, such as filial piety, may differ in ways that matter for coping.

Sixteen employees were interviewed, yielding hundreds of significant statements grouped into themes. Many described the conflict as a minor life problem and leaned on avoidance coping. Family support eased strain yet added obligation. Contrasts with Western findings are drawn, and culturally specific factors are proposed for future studies.
pmc-12837597:
Lv and coauthors review smart tech aids for protective gear training. Errors in putting on and taking off gear can expose health staff. Smart systems can watch each step and flag faults fast. No full review of that training use had been made.

The team searched four databases plus grey sources and citations. Studies ran from 2000 to late 2025 in the search. Kept studies used smart aids for gear training of staff or students. Just five studies, all from 2022 to 2025, fit the rules. Most came from China in that small pool. The team maps tool types and training gains.
pmc-12838497:
Talani Mhelembe, Shaun Ramroop, and Faustin Habyarimana ask not just what drives childhood anemia in Nigeria, but where in the hemoglobin distribution each driver bites hardest. Standard regression averages effects away; quantile regression follows them across low, middle, and high hemoglobin levels. Data pooled a twenty twenty-one malaria survey with a national household dataset.

Children aged six to fifty-nine months were analyzed against altitude, age, region, housing materials, wealth, mosquito net use, sex, recent fever, and malaria status. Effects differed across the distribution: poor housing materials, among other factors, weighed differently on the most anemic children than on healthier ones. The authors offer the segmented picture to target interventions where anemia is deepest.
pmc-12839097:
Ransheng Huang and three co-authors review brain network research on Parkinson's disease in this 2025 paper. Brain scans now let doctors see the disease as a disorder of whole networks, not single spots. The review asks which networks lie behind each of the four main motor symptoms. It also asks which networks change under deep brain stimulation, a treatment that sends electric pulses into the brain.

The team sorted studies by symptom: tremor, balance and gait problems, freezing of gait, and stiffness with slow movement. All four symptoms shared faults in the sensorimotor network, yet each had its own pattern. Tremor involved a wide loop through the cortex, thalamus, and cerebellum. Freezing of gait involved midbrain regions. Stimulation seemed to work by changing the motor cortex through its connections. The authors say such maps could guide finer target and setting choices.
pmc-12841097:
Hyerin Lee, Yujin Jeong, Nayeon Lee, Inhye Lee, and Jin Hyun Lee published a 2025 review on injectable hydrogels for medical and aesthetic uses, with a focus on how they flow. These gels are pushed through a needle as liquids, then set into place inside the body. That trick allows targeted delivery and slow release of active agents with little invasion.

The review centers on rheology, the science of flow and deformation. Measures like viscosity, stiffness, and yield stress predict whether a gel injects cleanly, heals after shear, and holds its shape. Shear thinning and recovery after flow are key behaviors. The authors link these numbers back to the gel's molecular links and crosslinking. The frame helps designers match a gel's flow profile to its job.
pmc-12844397:
Rui Wang and co-authors present, in a 2025 study, a device that harvests energy from the vibration of a rotating vehicle wheel. Low frequency vibration during driving is plentiful, but hard to recover with good efficiency. Their harvester uses piezoelectric parts, which make voltage when bent, set as two side by side cantilever beams with added masses.

The masses tune the device to sing at low frequencies met on the road. A special switching circuit grabs the charge at peak voltage. That active timing beats the losses of a classic diode bridge, which wastes small voltages below its turn on point. The team modeled the device and ran linked physics simulations to map its modes and stress. Tests then varied the beam thickness ratio and mass weight to see how power output changed.
pmc-12844797:
Verma, Wu, and Shah measured swallowed antibody absorption in this study from twenty twenty-five. Monoclonal antibodies are usually injected, and interest in pill forms runs high. Yet no one had pinned down how much of a swallowed antibody reaches the blood. The team dosed mice and rats with a humanized antibody that binds nothing in rodents.

Blood levels were tracked for fourteen days and set against injection data. Only about two hundredths of one percent of the dose reached circulation. That is roughly one molecule in five thousand. Rats and mice absorbed at the same rate, with slightly different totals. The authors say this is the first absolute figure for an antibody. Whether it generalizes to people remains open.
pmc-12846497:
Robert MacTavish and co-authors estimate how well COVID-19 vaccines protected older Canadians in this 2025 study.
