Adults over fifty faced high risk of severe illness, so tracking real-world protection matters for policy. The team used the screening method, which compares vaccination rates among severe cases with rates in the wider population.

The study covered more than one hundred thousand severe cases from 2021 to 2023. Protection stayed moderate to high during the Delta and early Omicron periods. Extra booster doses held steady protection later on, and recent or mixed-brand boosters worked best. The authors say the method gives near real-time estimates that can guide vaccine planning.
pmc-12847597:
Wenjun Hao and six co-authors report a rare case of lung cancer that spread to bone and destroyed a woman's hip and pelvis, in a 2025 case report. Lung cancer often spreads, and bone is a common site, yet full loss of a hip joint is very rare. The woman, aged fifty-six, had over a year of hip pain and growing trouble walking. Scans showed wide bone loss and many nodules in both lungs.

A biopsy of the hip bone showed the growth came from lung adenocarcinoma, a common lung cancer type. The disease had spread too widely for surgery, so care was conservative. A targeted drug was given, but the patient died a week later. The authors stress early checks when bone pain stays vague. They urge joint work by imaging, tissue tests, and cancer teams in such cases.
pmc-12847697:
Clivia Lisowski and co-authors show that a high salt diet shrinks melanoma in mice without help from the immune system. Their paper from 2025 runs against the usual story, which credits salt buildup in tissue for stronger anti tumor immunity. In skin and lung tumors here, neither salt buildup nor immune cells drove the effect.

Tumor cells from salt fed mice raised a metabolic brake protein, which shut down cell metabolism even with food at hand. A master switch of pigment cell fate also rose, turning on pigment making and halting the cell cycle. In effect, the diet pushed the cancer cells back toward a normal pigment cell state. The authors read the effect as tumor specific.
pmc-12847997:
Maja Linke and Michael Ramscar ask in 2025 why kids learn some words prior to others, and what their speech shows of the mind maps back of that path. Low space maps of kids' speech by age form the base. Three age bands of child talk face grown talk from film sub texts.

Speech in each band fits short lived gram mars that spread facts in the best flow, not mere broke rules. Word kind ties re sort as years pass, with the map of word sense zones in flux. Two use words, which hold more than one job, bridge the sorts. Lack of exact word sense may aid both learn and talk.
pmc-12848097:
Deferiprone is a drug that removes excess iron from the body, and tracking its level in patients matters for safe dosing. Nima Sheikh Abdollahzadeh Mamaghani and co-authors build a simple fluorescent probe that measures the drug in exhaled breath condensate, the fluid collected from breath. The probe needs no added label, which keeps the test cheap and simple.

Their system pairs a porous crystal material called UiO-66 with ferric ions. The drug binds the iron, and the resulting complex dims the crystal's glow in proportion to drug amount. The probe detected levels down to 0.005 milligrams per liter and worked reliably on patient breath samples. The authors present it as a practical tool for monitoring therapy.
pmc-12848297:
Raphaela Wehr and five co-authors study how fat tissue clears its dead cells in this 2025 paper. Dead fat cells are too large for macrophages, the immune cells that normally eat dead tissue. Instead, the macrophages gather around each dead cell and dissolve it from outside, spilling digestive enzymes onto it. This process is called lysosomal exocytosis. The team used mouse fat tissue kept alive in dishes for seven days to test drugs that speed or slow the process.

Over the week, ring shaped clusters formed around dead cells and enzyme release rose. Rapamycin, a drug that lifts a brake on the process, sped clearance and cut inflammation. Two blocking drugs did the reverse, harming lysosome function and raising inflammatory signals. The authors name this clearance path a drug target for calming fat inflammation, which feeds insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.
pmc-12849497:
Tianyuyi Feng and co-authors studied shifting brain connectivity in white matter disease in a 2025 paper. White matter bright spots on scans mark small vessel disease. Their load tracks with thinking decline. The team asked how moment-to-moment brain links change with severity.

Eighty-five patients from a Shanghai hospital took part. Thinking tests and both structural and resting scans were collected. Patients split into mild and severe groups by a rating scale. A sliding window method traced the moving links. Cluster analysis then named the recurring states. Findings tie connection timing to cognitive scores.
pmc-12849597:
Madhav Chaturvedi and co-authors review guidance for reporting epidemic models in a 2025 scoping review. Math models steer real policy during outbreaks, yet missing reporting rules make many studies hard to judge or trust. The team searched medical and preprint sources for guidance on writing or grading such models, including nearby fields like health economics.

They sorted the advice into thirty-one subtopics under seven broad themes, from fitness for purpose and model structure to uncertainty and openness. Double screening kept the selection careful. The review is a first step toward dedicated reporting rules and quality tools for infectious disease modeling. Clearer standards should help decision makers tell solid models from shaky ones.
pmc-12852097:
Saeid Afshari, Ali Soltani, and Mohammad Amin Amiri published a 2025 study mining Australian road death data for patterns that policy can use. The authors combined forecasting with causal modeling, two lenses that answer different questions: what comes next, and what drives the toll.

Four forecasting methods were compared across horizons. One technique led for short term prediction, while a multivariate model won for medium and long range outlooks. A panel model then weighed the circumstances of fatal crashes. Older age groups, remote and outer regional roads, nighttime, and high speed settings all raised fatal risk. Younger adults and single vehicle crashes carried lower fatality likelihood, a counterintuitive pair the authors report plainly. The results aim at targeted interventions and smarter infrastructure planning.
pmc-12852697:
Amir Hossein Molaei, Matin Shahin, and Mohammad Simjoo published a study in 2025 on how salt levels shape foam used to steer fluids in oil reservoirs. Foam can improve sweep in layered rock, but its behavior with leftover oil at pore scale was unclear. The team used a two-layer lab model of porous rock. They compared low and high salt water with a common surfactant.

Without oil, low salt gave fine, stable foam and better sweep. With oil present, the picture flipped. High salt made coarse emulsion drops that blocked the fast paths and pushed flow into the slow layer. Final oil recovery was higher at high salt. The authors say tuning salt can balance foam strength and emulsion blocking.
pmc-12853797:
Xiangzhi Qin and co-authors test a simple ratio as a forecast tool for cancer at the join of the food pipe and stomach, in a study from 2025. This cancer is rising in much of the world. Spread to nearby lymph nodes is a strong sign of how a patient will fare after surgery.

The ratio compares how many removed nodes held cancer with how many nodes were removed in all. The team looked back at 257 patients who had full stomach surgery with node removal. They split the group at a ratio of one fifth and compared traits and survival between the low and high groups. Standard accuracy curves were used to check how well the ratio sorts patients by outlook after surgery.
pmc-12853897:
Yihan Zhang and co-authors studied how replanting changes the way grapevines take up nitrogen, in a 2025 study. Vines set into old vineyard soil often grow stunted, a problem called replant disease. Nitrogen feeds growth, yet its handling after replanting was little known.

Total nitrogen fell in both roots and leaves of replanted vines. Roots drew in less nitrate but more ammonium, and more of the tagged ammonium stayed in the roots. The team found twelve ammonium transporter genes in the vine genome, and their activity rose and fell over time after replanting. Two genes stood out, and one was proven to move ammonium across cell walls. The authors conclude that replanted vines shift their diet toward ammonium.
pmc-12854697:
Natalia Chalupczak, Matilde Iorizzo, and Shari Lipner audit teen hair marketing in this two thousand twenty-five study. Hair products are promoted to adolescents online, but ad tactics and skin risks were unknown. The authors coded the first one hundred TikTok and fifty Instagram posts under teen hair care hashtags from October twenty twenty-five. Posts were classified by promoter, strategy, product category, claims, hair type, and ingredients.

Influencers created about forty-five percent of posts and brands about nineteen percent, while dermatologists made under three percent. Colorful packaging and natural or clean labeling were the top strategies; shiny hair and damage repair the top claims. Eighty-two percent of products contained allergens or irritants like fragrance, sulfates, silicones, or parabens, and only six percent targeted afro-ethnic hair. The authors urge dermatologists to ask teens about hair routines and to push for oversight of influencer ads.
pmc-12854797:
Ji-Sook Park, Hyeon-Mi Bae, and Jung-Eun Yim score the diets of older adults in a rural Korean community in a 2025 study. Korea is aging fast, and country elders face poor diet quality and chronic disease risk.

Seventy-nine residents of one county, average age about 76, gave day-long food recalls and filled a diet quality questionnaire. Their average score, 55, sat below the urban national figure. Women over 75 ate less energy, protein, and several vitamins than men of the same age. Higher diet scores came with more fiber and several vitamins. The authors say rural elders need targeted nutrition support, shaped by age and sex.
pmc-12855897:
Factories and clinics need cheap sensors that sniff out harmful gases like carbon monoxide and methane. Poundoss Chellamuthu and co-authors compare three metal oxide sensors in a 2025 study. A soap-like helper shapes the oxides into fine grains, and a soft plastic layer pairs with each to form a junction.

The tin oxide pairing led the pack, with response near 92 percent for carbon monoxide. It answered in about ten seconds and reset in five. All sensors held a steady, repeat pattern over a full day of cycles. Lab checks tied the lead to fine grains and wide surface area. The design points to low-cost, real-time gas alarms.
pmc-12857897:
Mubashir Zafar and co-authors study social media use and body image shame among university students in Hail, Saudi Arabia, in a 2025 paper. Heavy social media use among students has raised concern about body image. Idealized bodies on platforms like Instagram and TikTok can distort how young people see themselves.

The study explores the association between use and body image shame in this student population. It aims to clarify how these dynamics affect mental health and well-being. Findings from a Saudi campus add regional evidence to a debate often based on Western samples alone.
pmc-12858797:
Enrui Zhang and Dan Wang present a 2025 study on the ethics of AI recommendation systems, read through a Marxist lens. Systems that learn from clicks shape what consumers buy. The authors argue that these systems can deepen a sense of alienation and unfairness when predicted tastes drift away from real needs.

Their framework joins graph neural networks with a context-aware transformer model. Tests used two public datasets of user and movie ratings, one with rich context details. The team built an index that measures the gap between predicted ratings and actual situational needs. Fairness constraints were then added to the training. The combined model cut the alienation index by twenty-nine percent in their experiments.
pmc-12859897:
Hamod Alqahtani grades four leading AI chatbots on exam questions about dental occlusion, in a 2025 study. Chatbots now help dental students study and revise. Occlusion, how teeth meet, is a core subject with precise facts. Whether chatbots answer such questions accurately was untested. Wrong answers could quietly mislead learners.

Each chatbot faced the same textbook question set twice. Accuracy, self-consistency, and agreement between models were scored. One model led the pack in the reported results. Gaps between rounds exposed shaky spots in every system. Educators gain a benchmark for advising students on AI help. The study also shows how to audit chatbots in other dental subjects.
pmc-12859997:
Mohammad Almari, Stephen O'Neill, and Zia Sadique present a 2025 study of the money cost of early COVID-19 deaths in Kuwait. The count covers all confirmed deaths from 2020 to 2022. Years of life lost came to about 68,000, with three fifths among non-Kuwaiti residents. The team priced the loss three ways: a value-of-life gauge, a lost-earnings gauge, and a friction gauge that counts only the gap till a worker is replaced.

Non-Kuwaiti men died mostly in working years, while Kuwaiti deaths clustered in old age. That split shapes the price under each gauge. Kuwait's two-tier job market, citizens in state posts and migrants in exposed front-line jobs, drives the pattern. Pricing early death helps states weigh protection for the most exposed groups.
pmc-12860097:
Wanjun Lan and twelve co-authors describe in 2025 a platform that builds predictable, high-yield CHO cell lines for making therapeutic proteins. Drug makers usually insert genes at random spots in hamster ovary cells, then screen many clones to find a good producer. Targeted insertion at proven sites promises speed and consistency.

Using AI screening and robots, the team placed marker genes at chosen sites, then swapped in production genes. Some lines topped 15 grams per liter of product. Clone performance matched the pools they came from, and output and quality held steady over 26 passages. Predictable cell lines could shorten the path from gene to medicine factory.
pmc-12865997:
Imran Paruk, Kamal Govind, Fraser Pirie, and Ayesha Motala chart hungry bone syndrome after neck gland surgery at a South African center, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Records span one hundred seventeen patients over twenty years. The syndrome means lasting low calcium once the overactive gland is out.

About a fifth of patients developed it, and they stayed near twenty days versus four for the rest. Cases ran younger and leaner, with worse bone disease. High gland hormone and bone enzyme reads before surgery flagged risk sharply. Bone cyst disease and top hormone reads stood as lone predictors. Early spotting can shape care around surgery. Readers get clear risk marks for a long-stay trap.
pmc-12866497:
Liyong Zhang and co-authors build a tool to flag which liver abscess patients are likely to suffer a return of the infection. The abscess type studied is caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae, the lead source of such infections in China and the wider region. Drugs and drainage have cut deaths, yet relapse stays a stubborn problem.

The team read records for four hundred eighty-six patients treated over nine years at one hospital. Cases were split into a training group and a check group. Stepwise tests sorted which traits truly tracked relapse. The best traits were combined into a scoring model, drawn as a nomogram chart for bedside use. Curve checks judged how well the scores sorted future cases and how sound the risk calls were. A simple chart like this can steer follow-up care toward the patients most at risk.
pmc-12866597:
Sari Soutukorva and co-authors survey how Finnish college staff rest from work and move their bodies in a 2025 study. Staff in higher schools face heavy loads, strain, and a real risk of burning out. How they bounce back, and whether sport helps, was not well known.

More than fifteen hundred staff in a trade group took an online poll early in 2025. It asked how drained they felt, how much they moved, and whether they take active breaks in the day. The results map rest habits across a whole field. School chiefs can use the map to plan breaks and sport perks that staff will use.
pmc-12867197:
Mohammad Rezaei and co-authors hunt for gene markers of breast cancer in a 2025 study. Breast cancer is one of the most common cancers in women. The team looked at long RNA strands that do not build proteins, since these strands can steer gene activity and may serve as test markers.

Computer searches first mapped links between genes, small RNAs, and the long strands. Lab tests then checked 50 tumour samples against 50 control samples. Two long strands and one growth gene all showed lower levels in tumours. A small RNA that may drive cancer sat higher and seemed to press all three down. The authors say the two long strands could aid diagnosis and outlook calls, tied to a known growth pathway.
pmc-12872797:
Rong Zhou and ten co-authors compare six mountain shrubs in a paper whose text is dated 2025. Shrubs anchor dry ecosystems in the Qilian Mountains of China. Their shape and leaf function together set how much carbon they store. The team measured both sides for six typical species.

Heights, stem widths, root lengths, and biomass splits were recorded. Leaf gas exchange tracked photosynthesis through the day. One pea family shrub grew tallest and heaviest overall. A honeysuckle species rooted deepest, past forty centimeters. Daily photosynthesis curves came in single and double peaked forms. Species sorted into distinct survival strategies from the combined data. The morphology plus physiology view explains desert adaptation better than either alone. Planting choices for restoration can use the ranking.
pmc-12876197:
Min Xu and co-authors compare what clear aligners and fixed braces each do to the mouth's microbes and chemistry. Both straighten teeth, but brackets trap plaque while removable trays let patients brush freely. Their prospective study randomizes twenty-four matched orthodontic patients, half to each appliance.

Saliva, plaque, and gum fluid are sampled at the start, three months, and six months. Technicians score gum health, sequence the microbes, and measure a marker of oxidative DNA damage in both fluids. Plaque scores rose faster in the fixed group early on. The team also tests whether microbial shifts track the oxidative marker and the gum scores. Orthodontists get a biological comparison where marketing usually substitutes for measurement.
pmc-12913797:
Santos leads a large team identifying mastitis microbes in Brazilian dairy cows, in work from twenty twenty-five. Mastitis, udder infection, is among the costliest diseases in dairy herds. Its causes vary by region and farm system, and fast naming guides treatment.

Samples from cows with clinical and silent mastitis in northern Minas Gerais were typed with mass spectrometry fingerprinting. The method is rapid and reliable compared with classic culture steps. Special attention went to uncommon and emerging species with possible public health relevance. A full local map of causes helps vets target therapy and tighten herd biosecurity.
pmc-12926097:
Qin and Chen compare stimulator infection control in China and the United States. Brain and spine stimulators face infection rates of 3 to 7 percent worldwide. Their MCS frame splits the issue into mechanism, clinical care, and system. Evidence ran from 2020 to 2025 for both lands. Sterilization picks differ sharply between the systems.

The U.S. leans on ethylene oxide, while China favors peroxide plasma. Outcomes look equal despite that split. China uses ten times more antibiotics, and MRSA runs higher there. Long prophylaxis persists in China past proof for 24-hour use. Neither system wins across all three frame levels.
pmc-12964197:
Cristiane Aparecida Favoretto and co-authors introduce a journal Research Topic on the brain basis of substance use disorders in this 2026 editorial. Addiction remains a major public health burden, shaped by genes, life history, and surroundings together. The editors gather reviews and studies that probe the brain circuits, risk factors, and related conditions behind these disorders, and they summarize what each piece adds.

One review covers a cannabis-related receptor that steers reward and impulse control, varying by age and brain region. Another examines a stress-linked peptide and its sex-specific patterns across mental illness and addiction. The editors note that blocking some targets has caused harsh mood side effects in past trials, which tempers hope. They frame the collection as a step toward treatments matched to each patient's biology.
pmc-12980097:
Konstantin Protasov and co-authors followed 101 men after lung cancer surgery in a 2025 study to test whether silent heart injury foretells death within a year. Such injury, spotted by a rise in a heart protein after surgery, is a known bad sign after many operations. Its weight after lung removal was unclear.

Heart injury appeared in over a third of the patients in the first days after surgery. Within a year, more than a quarter of the men had died. After weighing other factors, the injury nearly tripled the risk of death. A heart strain marker before surgery and advanced cancer stage also predicted death, while later chemotherapy and aspirin use went with lower risk. The authors urge heart checks around lung surgery.
pmc-12982397:
Sanchari Kundu and three co-authors test whether spraying the compound putrescine on leaves helps a hybrid poplar tree withstand salty soil, in a study published in 2025. Putrescine is a polyamine that plants use in growth and stress responses, but its effect on salt tolerance in trees was largely unknown. The team grew the poplar clone NM6 in a greenhouse, watered roots with two salt levels, and sprayed the foliage on several days.

Sprayed plants grew better under the milder salt level, gaining about 20 percent more height and 15 percent more stem thickness than unsprayed plants. Sugar levels in the leaves also rose, with fructose about 37 percent higher on day six. The benefit was weaker at the stronger salt dose. The authors link the protection to better water balance and energy supply in the leaves.
pmc-13011597:
Ling-Zhi Li and six co-authors study how exercise training modulates receptor expression in the peripheral arteries of hypertensive rats. Three receptor types steer how tightly vessel walls contract. One rat strain is bred prone to high blood pressure, and a normotensive strain serves as the comparison. Rats ran treadmill training for 16 weeks or stayed sedentary. Tissue came from the renal artery, the thoracic aorta, and the caudal artery.

Blood pressure fell significantly in the hypertensive rats that trained. One receptor type, P2X1, held the top expression spot overall and in the tail artery, while alpha1D peaked in the aorta. Hypertensive rats showed lower expression of all three receptors than the comparison strain. Training moved alpha1D most: in the tail artery of trained hypertensive rats it rose while the others fell. The team links receptor distribution to vessel diameter and hypertension.
pmc-13014897:
A virus carried by ticks, named Yezo virus, was first found in two fever patients in Hokkaido, Japan, in 2021. Nathan Markarian and Levon Abrahamyan reviewed what is known about it in 2025. Later cases appeared in China, and the virus turned up in ticks taken from migratory birds in Japan, hinting it can travel.

Patients showed fever with low platelet and white cell counts. Big gaps remain in how the virus causes disease, spreads, and can be prevented, and warming climates plus land clearing are widening tick range. The review maps the virus's biology, cases, and care options, and urges joint human-animal-environment surveillance to prepare for wider spread.
pmc-13037597:
Discarded potato chips, the malformed ones pulled before packaging, are energy-rich feed if their value can be proven. Yesica Arteaga Wences and co-authors fed them to forty-eight finishing lambs in 2025, replacing cracked corn at five and ten percent of the ration over sixty-three days. They tracked growth, carcass traits, and internal fat.

Intake, daily gain, and feed efficiency held steady at both levels, and the chips' measured energy matched the diet's design, coming out about six and a half percent above corn's. Inner fat depots did grow with chip level, a caution the authors flag given the chips' high fat content. Within those limits, a waste stream became a sound feed.
pmc-13064897:
Lutz Nitschke and co-authors, writing for a German safety commission, set out a lab method for measuring a solvent chemical in workplace air. The method paper was published in 2025. The chemical, known as mesityl oxide, has a set limit for safe exposure over a shift.

Air is pulled through a tube of silica gel at a steady rate, for two hours to check shift exposure or fifteen minutes for short peaks. The trapped chemical is then washed out with a solvent and measured by a standard liquid-based lab method. The method covers a range from one tenth of the limit to twice it, with recovery near full and modest error. Safety staff can use it to check that workplaces stay within the rules.
pmc-13106697:
Nahid Khademi and Fariba Asghari audit Iran's HIV care rules against the ethics they should embody, in this 2025 study. HIV care lives or dies on trust: patients who fear exposure or unfair treatment vanish from the system. The authors critically reviewed national care guidelines and the country's Anti-Stigma and Discrimination Bylaw, sorting every provision by bioethical principle.

Some ground is covered well: informed consent, confidentiality, and privacy all appear, with one gap around childcare consent. The misses cluster where decisions get hard. Capacity assessment, substitute decision-making, the right to refuse treatment, and when a diagnosis may be disclosed go unaddressed. The bylaw, meanwhile, says nothing specific about fair care for the very groups most exposed: people who inject drugs, female sex workers, men who have sex with men, and health workers themselves. Their call is for dedicated, tailored ethical guidelines.
pmc-13113597:
Katarzyna Pogoda and co-authors review antibody-based upkeep therapy for advanced breast cancer in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. The cancer type is HER2-positive, meaning the tumor carries extra copies of a growth signal protein. Care has shifted from endless chemotherapy to a fixed burst, then antibody drugs alone to hold the disease.

Trials back the shift: dual antibody therapy with a taxane set the pattern, and later trials added targeted pills to the antibody base. One add-on stretched time without disease growth while life quality held, despite more blood side effects. Another pairing also delayed growth. The authors frame upkeep choice around tumor traits and past therapy.
pmc-13114497:
Sabine Drossard, Maria Christina Stefanescu, and Andrea Schmedding give a 2026 nationwide analysis of training in pediatric surgery in Germany, called Mind the Gap. Care for sick children is spread across many sites in that land, and training shapes vary a lot from site to site. Yet the craft needs a high count of operations in training.

Set rules name more than twenty classes of procedure, each with a target count a trainee must reach. Fears have grown that the standard training span no longer lets them get there. The study maps how cases are split across sites and what each resident truly sees.
pmc-13116097:
Five researchers in Turkey rank OECD health systems with an integrated scoring frame in a 2026 paper. Health spending rises and populations age, so fair cross country comparison matters. Past studies often leaned on one outcome or one ranking method with hand set weights, which makes rankings fragile.

The study covers twenty-seven countries on measures like life expectancy and avoidable, infant, and maternal deaths. An objective method sets the weights from the data itself, and two ranking methods score the countries in parallel. The two rankings agreed closely, which the authors read as robustness. Wide gaps between top and bottom systems still stand out, giving policymakers a steadier comparison base.
pmc-13117897:
Henrik Stelling and co-authors published a study in 2026 on chat models reading heart tracings. A heart tracing is a core test in heart care, but reading it well takes training. New models that take both text and images claim skill at such tasks. The team tested whether that skill holds up here.

They showed thirteen standard tracings to five large models, five times each. That gave more than two thousand graded answers on rhythm, axis, and wave shapes. Overall accuracy ran from about fifty-two to sixty-five percent. One measure, the width of a wave complex, scored best; wave-shape reads scored worst. Heart rate guesses were off by fifteen to forty-seven beats per minute. Models also disagreed with themselves across runs. The authors say the tools are not yet safe for clinic use.
pmc-13121997:
Arkiath Veettil Raveendran is first author on a 2026 article proposing a simple screening tool for obstructive sleep apnea. In this condition, the airway partly or fully collapses in sleep, causing snoring, broken rest, and daytime sleepiness. It is common yet under-recognized, with most cases undiagnosed, and it raises risks from high blood pressure to car accidents.

Existing screening tools can be cumbersome, so the authors built a three-question tool meant to be quick and user-friendly for clinicians. A self-assessment version is intended for the general public. The article sets out the tool and the case for it, aiming at earlier identification of people at risk so treatment can start sooner.
pmc-13124797:
Joseph Mitchell and co-authors searched a world database of drug side effect reports in 2026 for reports tied to the environment. Drugs can reach water and soil, but reporting of harm from such exposure has no standard route.

The database held more than thirty-eight million reports in total, back to 1967. Only 713 carried an environment related term, though counts have risen steadily since the first such report in 2001. Reports spanned many drug groups and often came with terms for symptoms in exposed people. A large share came from non health professionals. The authors call for a clear framework to guide reporting and study of these effects in future.
pmc-13126597:
Rachel Culbreth, Monica Swahn, Jane Palmier, and Rogers Kasirye test a quality of life index for young women in Kampala in a 2025 paper. Little research covers well-being in urban slum youth. Two pilot studies of daily diaries supplied the data. Sixty young women across three slum areas took part.

The index scored living conditions, relationships, and independence. Scores held steady across the two pilot rounds. That steadiness marks the index as reliable for use. Real gaps showed between the three neighborhoods, though. One area, Bwaise, scored higher on most domains. Dwelling satisfaction peaked in a different area, Makindye. Aid should target each slum's own gaps, they say.
pmc-13128397:
Alice Boughrum and co-authors wrote a 2026 essay on how United States policy can better help people who live with dementia. About 7.2 million older adults in the country live with the illness, and most live at home, not in care homes. They lean on family, friends, and home-based help to stay in their own homes.

Medicaid pays for most home-based help, but each state chooses how much of that help to fund. The essay says this patchwork leaves many people with dementia without the food aid, rides, day care, and rest breaks for family carers that they need. The authors set out ways Medicaid could widen access and make help more even across states. Their aim is care that lets people stay at home longer and with more dignity.
pmc-13134997:
Emanuele Maria Cipollini and co-authors treat nose scars with a fractional laser. Their 2026 study reviews eight patients whose scars followed skin cancer removal and flap repair on the nose. Such scars can pucker into a trap-door shape that mars looks and function.

Two laser sessions, two months apart, were given to each patient. Scores from patients and observers both improved across thickness, color, and softness. Three-dimensional surface scans showed the scar dip shrink by about a quarter on average. Redness and swelling after each session cleared within a week. The authors call the method safe and effective for these scars, in a small group.
pmc-13135497:
Pedersen leads a team studying whether dynamic balance predicts horizontal hop performance, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Volunteers were healthy adults in Denmark with no muscle or joint conditions. Tests were done on the right leg.

Balance was measured with the Y-Balance test, which sums reach in three directions. Hop performance used a single-leg hop for distance, and hip strength was measured with a fixed device. Better balance was linked to better hop distance. The link held for people with hip strength both below and above the group average. The authors offer the data as a reference for work with injured groups.
pmc-13135597:
Chronic pain grips forty to eighty percent of people with cirrhosis, yet nearly every painkiller carries extra danger in a failing liver. Lisa Deng and Jessica Rubin review the options. Most guidance rests on how the body handles each drug plus expert opinion, since trials in this population are scarce.

Opioid use has fallen lately, but safer substitutes have not risen to fill the gap. Non-drug approaches are barely studied here at all. Shared drivers like alcohol use, poor sleep, and mood disorders offer double-duty targets that may ease pain and slow liver decline together. The 2026 review argues for tailored, mixed plans and more research.
pmc-13136197:
Eau Liang Teow and eleven colleagues chart five-year recovery after knee replacement in a Singapore cohort, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Patient-reported outcomes are well documented in Western populations. Asian long-term data were scarce. The registry held nearly five thousand osteoarthritis cases.

Average symptom scores improved hugely by five years. The greatest gains landed within the first six months. Older patients, especially past seventy-five, improved less reliably long-term. Having any comorbidity also lowered the odds of improvement. Ethnicity shaped pain and stiffness trajectories at some intervals. The authors identify who benefits most and who lags. Such interval-specific predictors can guide follow-up care after surgery.
pmc-13141097:
Mohammed Rajah and Yakubu Yakubu listen to nurses handling central lines in a Ghanaian hospital in this two thousand twenty-six study. Central venous catheters are lifelines and infection risks, and protocols presume resources. Thirteen ICU and critical care nurses at a low-resource major hospital gave in-depth interviews, sorted by themes. Four themes emerged: system constraints, protocol feasibility, capability building, and psychosocial impact.

Nurses felt sure in routine tasks but told of supplies, infrastructure, and workload shaping what care was possible. Infection prevention rules needed fixes when supplies ran short. They wanted hands-on training, oversight, and mentoring, and a voice in choices, while telling of burnout, fear of complications, and thin emotional support. The authors conclude good line management in such settings depends on hospital support, staffing, and growth, not personal skill alone, with clear meaning for patient safety and global infection prevention.
pmc-13141197:
Greta Hulej and colleagues published a 2026 study of an antibody drug in lupus patients with blood problems. Lupus can lower red cells, platelets, and white cells. Those drops add danger and fatigue. The drug belimumab is used for active skin and joint disease. Italian referral centers pooled their records.

Patients were followed for up to four years. Checks ran every six months. Entry required clearly abnormal blood counts. The analysis asked whether counts recovered on treatment. Real-world cohorts include patients trials often exclude. Evidence here can guide doctors treating blood involvement. Longer follow-up strengthens confidence in any gains.
pmc-13143197:
Janett Chavez Sosa and co-authors link heavy AI reliance with distress in medical students in a 2026 study. One hundred eighty-seven students at a Peruvian university took surveys in 2025. Scales graded dependence on generative AI plus stress, worry, and low mood. Adjusted models weighed age, sex, income, and study year.

Higher AI dependence tracked with higher worry and low mood scores. Each added dependence point linked to about five percent higher worry scores. The stress link ran positive but weak. Fifth year students showed more worry than sixth year peers. The authors urge schools to teach balanced AI use and pair digital skills with mental health support.
pmc-13143497:
Yair Shachar offers five tips for learning plastic surgery with help from AI tools, in an article from 2026. Plastic surgery is a broad field that keeps changing with new technology. Hands-on work stays the core of training, but a wide base of book knowledge is also needed.

Language models can now explain topics in a tailored way, sort complex data, and stage practice problems. Yet many trainees still lean on textbooks and long journal papers alone. The tips start with using AI as a thinking partner, not a search box, by framing sharp, context-rich prompts. A second tip tells the model to base answers on formal guidelines. A third urges comparing techniques across sources to build judgment.
pmc-13144297:
Thyl Snoeck, Frédéric Paillaugue, and Steven Provyn compared breathing through the nose and the mouth for effects on blood vessel function, in a 2026 crossover study. Forty-five healthy young men each completed both breathing protocols in random order, with rest between. Vessel behavior was read non-invasively by finger plethysmography and by ultrasound of the arm artery before and after cuff release.

Nasal breathing lengthened pulse propagation time by about six percent and cut the reflection index, both signs of more relaxed vessels. The arm artery also widened measurably during nasal breathing, by about four and a half percent, an effect mouth breathing did not produce. The authors conclude that breathing route alone shifts vascular tone at rest in healthy young adults. They call the difference physiologically relevant and worth probing in patients, while noting the study group was narrow: young, male, and healthy.
pmc-13144397:
Lyons and a large team tracked brain changes after a first psilocybin dose in a 2026 study. The drug is known for strong short term effects and hints of long gains in mood and thought. Whether it leaves lasting marks on brain build and wiring was still open, so the team scanned healthy first time users before and after one high dose.

Twenty eight people took a high dose or a near zero dose in a blind swap design. A month on, the high dose group showed more flexible thought, more insight, and better well being. Scans found looser wiring in tracts from the front brain, tied to a less split brain network. A burst of signal variety in the first hours foretold who felt better a month later.
pmc-13144797:
Svetlana Lorenzano, Stefano Strano, and Danilo Toni report a multicenter trial on finding hidden heart rhythm faults after stroke, in a 2026 conference abstract. A quivering heart rhythm is a major cause of stroke, yet it often comes and goes without symptoms. Short checks miss many cases, and the worth of long monitoring after some stroke types was unclear.

The trial enrolled 317 patients aged sixty or more after a first stroke from artery disease or small vessels. Half got an implanted recorder plus standard care. At one year the recorder group had four times the detection rate, and the gap held at three years. Most episodes were silent and brief. More recorder patients started blood thinners, though repeat stroke rates are still being weighed.
pmc-13144897:
Vonhof and co-authors test a computer-designed, multi-drug treatment for stroke in mice, in a 2026 conference report. Decades of single-drug trials have failed to protect the brain after stroke. So the team mapped the network of proteins involved in the disease. They picked a drug combination meant to hit several targets at once.

Mice received the treatment after a brain artery was briefly blocked. Their blood-brain barrier stayed stronger, with more of the proteins that seal vessel walls. Harmful activation of immune and support cells in the brain also eased in the days after the stroke. The authors present network-based drug selection as a promising route forward.
pmc-13145097:
Axel Wolsink and nine colleagues lay out the Dutch trial of early keyhole surgery for bleeding inside the brain. Such bleeding makes up a sizable share of strokes in Western Europe and kills or disables many. Signs grow that removing the blood early, through small openings, may help. The trial tests that idea head-on.

Six hundred adults with a spontaneous bleed in the upper brain will join. Half get scope-guided surgery within eight hours, plus standard care. Half get standard care alone. Patients with bleeds from aneurysms, malformed vessels, or tumors are left out. The main measure is function at six months, scored by blinded assessors. Safety and technical success count as secondary aims. The result should settle whether early surgery earns a place in routine care.
pmc-13145197:
Wenjin Yang and co-authors pooled patient data on stroke treatment in 2026. Patients with a blocked large brain vessel can get a clot-busting drug by vein before a procedure that pulls the clot out. Whether starting severity changes the drug's benefit or its bleeding risk was unclear.

The pool held two thousand three hundred thirteen patients from six trials, all treated at centers that can do the procedure. Analysis found no clear sign that starting severity changed the drug's effect on function. Among severe cases, bleeding risk did not vary by time window either. The results suggest the drug step can be judged on other grounds than severity alone.
pmc-13145497:
Teuni Ten Brink and co-authors describe a 2026 conference study on doing thinking checks online after a bleed around the brain. Such bleeds often leave lasting thinking harm that clinics miss. A web test set done at home could catch it early with little burden.

One hundred fifty patients from a Dutch group study get an email link six months after the bleed. The test set takes about an hour and covers focus, memory, speed, and planning. Eighty-six patients had finished the full set when the abstract was written, and data work was still going. The team will link scores to complaints, life quality, and return to work to judge the tool's worth.
pmc-13145697:
Some strokes have no found cause, and a hidden heart rhythm fault is a prime suspect. Jannicke Koldéus-Falch and co-authors studied women with such strokes in this 2026 conference abstract, drawn from two university hospitals. One center gave patients an implanted heart monitor, while the other used standard follow-up care.

Among 475 women, the monitor found the rhythm fault in thirty-six percent, against nine percent without it. Blood thinners could then be given with more safety. Death and major bleeding looked lower with the monitor in some analyses, but repeat stroke rates did not clearly differ. Age and a blood marker each predicted poor outcomes on their own. The authors support the monitor's role in preventing further strokes in this group.
pmc-13146097:
Julian Schwartze and Hlaing Ni report a single tricky case in this 2026 conference abstract. A fifty-one-year-old man arrived at a British hospital with signs that looked like a major stroke from a blocked brain artery. About one in six treated stroke cases turns out to be a mimic, and this case shows why that share is so high.

Scans found no blockage or bleeding, and the man's weakness cleared within a day after clot treatment and phosphate replacement. His blood phosphate had fallen to a very low level. Days later the weakness returned when phosphate dipped again, and cleared once levels rose. Extended tests found no other cause, and the pain drug naproxen was named a possible culprit. The authors urge doctors to weigh low phosphate when stroke signs come with clean scans.
pmc-13146197:
Po-Lin Chen and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on how stroke severity should set the start day for blood thinning pills after stroke from a heart rhythm fault. Starting too early can risk bleeding, and the safe edge inside two days was disputed. The team split patients by severity score.

Records covered more than five hundred patients. In mild stroke, starting within two days looked as safe as starting later. In mid-to-severe stroke, early starts tied to far more repeat strokes or deaths within ninety days. Curve checks put the safest start for severe cases at about five to six days. The authors urge severity-based timing rather than one rule for all.
pmc-13146297:
Leonardo Bruno and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on neck vessel ultrasound screening for stroke prevention in Kinshasa. Stroke strikes hard in Sub-Saharan Africa, and prevention must work with scarce means. The ISA-AFRICA project tested a two-step screen in the city.

More than three hundred people passed a first community risk triage. About a third, judged high risk, went on to full checks with vessel ultrasound. The scan found artery buildup in near four of ten checked patients. A few had severe narrowing or rough, risky plaques, and none had ever been scanned before. High blood pressure was near universal in the checked group. New clot drugs were started for some based on the finds.
pmc-13146397:
Emma Patchwood and nine co-authors train mixed NHS staff to run online group therapy for stroke survivors, in a 2026 study abstract. Many survivors face unmet emotional needs, especially those with language loss or minority backgrounds. The program, WAterS-2, uses acceptance and commitment therapy in groups.

Psychologists trained staff of varied professions and lived experience to lead the groups. Nineteen survivors joined across four sites, about half with aphasia. Nearly nine in ten finished, with no safety problems. Survivors valued peer connection and calming practices, though some therapy metaphors were hard with aphasia. Staff grew in skill and confidence. The study shows inclusive online groups can work in routine services.
pmc-13146597:
Magdalena Bucher and co-authors report a 2026 conference study on whether standard heart tracing measures add warning power for a hidden rhythm fault after stroke. A clinical score already estimates the chance of finding the fault on short monitoring. The team tested tracing measures from the MonDAFIS study beside that score.

More than sixteen hundred patients had hand-measured arrival tracings. The score alone tracked with fault finds in hospital and over two years. No tracing measure improved in-hospital forecasts past the score. For two-year finds, a widened main tracing wave and a longer early wave each added signal. Joined tracing picks lifted sorting a modest amount, and the authors suggest they can help choose who gets long monitoring.
pmc-13146697:
Olga Ciobanu-Caraus and seven co-authors re-score a major stroke trial with a ranking method that puts survival first, in this 2026 conference abstract. The TENSION trial tested clot retrieval, endovascular thrombectomy, in patients whose strokes came with unusually large areas of already-damaged brain. Traditional scoring compresses recovery into one disability scale and can blunt real differences.

The win ratio method instead compares every treated patient against every control patient in matched pairs. The ranking asks who did better on death first, then disability at twelve months, then serious side effects, then quality of life. Of 253 patients, the treated group won decisively: a win ratio of 1.61, meaning treatment came out ahead in about sixty percent of pairs, with most of the margin coming from survival. For trialists, the re-analysis argues that hierarchical scoring can rescue information standard endpoints leave behind.
pmc-13147097:
Omnia Samy El-Sayed and nine co-authors report a 2026 conference review on liver tests and bleeding strokes. Blood levels of liver enzymes are easy to measure, and past studies hinted they might track the risk of a stroke caused by bleeding in the brain. The findings, though, pointed in mixed directions.

The team searched four major databases and pooled twenty-three studies covering over two million people. Higher levels of two enzymes were tied to clearly higher risk of bleeding stroke. A third enzyme showed a smaller but real link, while a fourth showed none that held up. The pooled result gives doctors a sharper picture of which cheap blood tests carry warning value. The authors present the work as a step toward using routine liver panels in stroke risk checks.
pmc-13147797:
Karan Pongpanit, Mariane Bertagnolli and their co-authors evaluate activity questionnaires for postpartum women in rehab, listed for 2026. Staying active aids recovery after birth, but no self-report tool was built for this group, so choosing one is hard.

Women a few months after birth wore a fitness tracker for two weeks while filling in three recall questionnaires. A short international questionnaire tracked daily steps and distance most closely by a clear margin. The other two tools matched only their own sport sub-scores, not total activity. Still, those tools captured household and caregiving work well, which matters greatly in this life stage, the authors note.
pmc-13148097:
Ayisha Arishi, Khalid Alamry, and Mahmoud Hussein review benzoxazine plastics as shields against stray radio waves. Gadgets crowd the air with waves that jam each next kit, so shields are a growth need. This resin kind brings heat grit, strength, low water soak, and firm shape to the job. The review stacks fresh work on resin blends fed with nano fillers.

Carbon tubes, fibres, flake metals, and clays each get a worth pass in the tale. Fed blends gain wave block, heat hold, and wear life in one build. Dress-worn and army shields join board kits as use fields in the read. Green resin feeds and low-heat cures close the gaps list.
pmc-13148697:
Forecasting how a disease will progress is hard because long-term patient records are scarce, while diagnostic records are plentiful. The authors test whether training a model first on diagnosis can sharpen later forecasts. Their targets were joint worsening in knee arthritis over four years, mental decline in Alzheimer's disease over two years, and a breast cancer diagnosis within five years. Plain retraining caused a known failure: the model forgot its diagnostic skill, a patient safety concern.

Their fix adds experience replay, mixing old diagnostic cases into the new training. Pretraining lifted forecast scores on all three diseases, for example on outside knee data and breast cancer records. The replay version matched forecast scores of single-task models while keeping diagnostic accuracy close to a dedicated diagnostic model. Simpler combined training lost much of that diagnostic skill.
pmc-13150697:
Zegang Zhang and co-authors build a cobalt nanoparticle catalyst on carbon made from chitosan, for a green route to alkylated ketones, in a 2026 paper. The target reaction uses the borrowing hydrogen strategy, where an alcohol lends hydrogen and takes it back. A good solid catalyst for this route is hard to make. Their design anchors tiny cobalt particles on nitrogen-doped porous carbon spheres.

The carrier comes from modified chitosan, a natural polymer from shell waste. Its many pores and nitrogen and oxygen groups hold the cobalt evenly. The bond pattern at the surface tunes the active sites' electronic state. The catalyst shows high activity in the target reaction, beating most reported systems, liquid or solid. It offers a reusable path for this class of synthesis.
pmc-13151297:
Susanne Olofsdotter and five colleagues build and evaluate a free diagnostic interview for young psychiatric patients, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Standardized interviews anchor accurate diagnosis in child psychiatry. Many tools in use are locked behind licenses or platforms, or sit in legal ambiguity.

Their instrument, the EPSI-C, runs electronically in its form. It follows the DSM-5 diagnostic manual in its content. Twenty-two modules cover the common disorders of childhood and adolescence. Clinicians can run the full battery of modules if they wish. They can also run targeted subsets for the case at hand. The study evaluated content validity, as judged by experts in the field. It also checked the internal consistency of the responses it drew. To make the tool open access, and free of any one platform, is the point. Clinics and researchers priced out of commercial instruments gain a structured diagnostic option.
pmc-13152697:
Chen Ling and co-authors present a new spine surgery technique in a 2026 paper. In three-column osteotomy for adult spinal deformity, a feared slip called sagittal translation can occur at the cut site. Their technique corrects the cut site first with short rods, then aligns the whole spine with long rods.

The team reviewed 101 patients with at least two years of follow-up. Sixty-five had the new technique and 36 had the standard multi-rod method. The new group had shorter operations and less blood loss. Deformity correction was similar in both groups. The slip rate was far lower with the new method, and nerve injury was also less common.
pmc-13152997:
Anna Chatzi wrote a 2026 commentary on a Korean nursing placement that puts students on real community health projects. The placement was built in steps: aims tied to national health priorities, a seven step project learning design, and a survey based review. Students reported high satisfaction.

Chatzi links the case to wider shifts in nursing training, from hospital apprenticeships to degree study and more self directed roles. Today's wards bring sicker patients, fast tech change, and staff pressure, so courses must keep moving. Project work, she argues, builds the critical skills modern nurses need. The commentary is a discussion piece, inviting schools to weigh this model for their own programmes.
pmc-13153397:
Eman Abbas and co-authors turn okra into nutrient rich crackers in 2026. Okra pods, seeds, and slime carry vitamins, protein, and helpful plant compounds. Even the waste parts hold value that is often thrown away. The team tested cracker recipes that swap part of the wheat flour for okra flour.

They tried fresh, boiled, and waste okra flours at two swap levels. Lab checks measured moisture, protein, and other nutrients in each batch. Fresh okra flour gave the highest protein share among the variants. Waste flour still added fiber and nutrients to the snack. The work shows a tasty route to cut waste and raise food value.
pmc-13155397:
Chunyan Deng and nine co-authors survey women in rural western China about low mood around birth, in a study from 2026. Care for this type of depression is little used, even though it can harm mothers and babies. The team compares Han women, Zhuang women, and women from other minority groups.

More than one thousand pregnant or new mothers in Yunnan took part in 2022. About one in eight showed signs of depression, yet very few had used mental health care. About a quarter had never heard of depression, and more than half did not know where to get help. What shaped plans to seek help differed by ethnic group.
pmc-13155497:
Amanda Leonberg-Yoo and co-authors followed living kidney donors in 2026 to track pain and opioid use after surgery. Donors give a kidney while healthy, so their comfort and safe drug use matter a great deal. The team used an auto text-message system to poll donors from discharge to day twenty-eight. The study ran at one large center in Pennsylvania, for donors treated from 2021 to 2023.

Seventy-five donors took part, about seven in ten of those asked. Pain scores sat at a mid level on day four and fell to near one by day twenty-one. Felt control of pain hit the top of the scale by day fourteen. By then, few donors still used opioids. The team urges leaner default drug orders at discharge.
pmc-13156297:
Tianjun Ma and co-authors polish the rough face of a solar cell layer with laser light to lift tandem cell output. Their 2026 paper deals with all-perovskite tandem cells, which stack two light-catching layers. The lower layer, rich in lead and tin, tends to form a rough, flawed face. That face wastes charge and blocks smooth flow to the next layer. A fast UV laser smooths the face with no touch, and a screened surface agent then rebuilds it.

The rebuilt face pulled charge out better and slowed stray ion drift. Single and tandem cells built without solvent steps reached high output, with strong staying power in use. The authors frame the trick as a broad fix for tandem design.
pmc-13156397:
Ji-Yong Sung and Kihwan Hwang review glioblastoma, the most common and deadly primary brain tumor in adults, in work from twenty twenty-six. Median survival sits near fifteen months despite full care. New world rules sort the tumor by key gene marks, which sharpen diagnosis.

Standard care joins surgery, radiation, a chemo drug, and electric field therapy, but gains have plateaued. Immune therapy, strong in other tumors, helps little here. The review blames the tumor's mix of unlike regions and its fast change over time. New maps of space and time show how parts hide from immunity and resist care. Future plans pair immune care with precise drug delivery and close tracking.
pmc-13156997:
Jenni Pettay and co-authors study in this 2026 paper how marriage and widowhood shaped survival in past Finland. Church books from 1730 to 1910 gave them 11,892 people aged forty to ninety, whose marital state and social class they tracked over time. Modern studies show a sharp death risk right after a spouse dies; the team asked whether the same held in a world of large households.

The short-term widowhood effect was large here too, though the long-term effect ran smaller and weaker in women. Remarriage restored survival to first-marriage levels. The never-married fared no worse than the married, which hints that communal living cushioned single life in that era.
pmc-13157497:
HIV spreads inside tissues, not in bare dishes, and the tissue itself may fight back in an unnoticed way. Samy Sid Ahmed and co-authors show in a 2026 study that collagen, the body's main scaffold protein, both dulls the virus and exposes it to immune alarms.

Brief contact with collagen fibers cut the infectivity of many virus strains by weakening their ability to fuse with cells. The same contact reshaped the virus's surface protein so it gripped an immune sensor more tightly. Immune cells then swallowed the particles into compartments holding a second sensor, triggering strong alarm signals. The authors frame the scaffold as an active arm of innate defense, not passive scenery.
pmc-13157697:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease slowly strangles airflow, and standard inhalers do little to stop the decline. The second shrinks overinflated lung tissue through a bronchoscope, with no surgery. The third uses stem cells in hopes of repair. For each, they weigh mechanism, trial evidence, patient selection, benefits, risks, and cost.

As a narrative review, the article leans on key trials and major studies rather than new data. The comparison lays out where each approach shines and where it falls short. Biologics suit narrow patient groups, the scope procedure suits others, and stem cell work remains the least proven. The authors aim to guide treatment choices in the clinic. They also map the research steps each strategy still needs.
pmc-13157797:
Ebaa Al Ozairi and co-authors set out a trial plan for weight-loss treatment in people who have both obesity and type 1 diabetes. Their twenty twenty-six protocol centers on tirzepatide, a gut hormone drug. In Kuwait, more than a quarter of type 1 patients also live with obesity.

Past trials showed strong weight loss with mild side effects, mostly in type 2 diabetes. Far less is known about safety when insulin use is lifelong, as in type 1. The single-center trial will test the drug under close watch. Readers get the full design, who can join, and what outcomes will count as success or risk.
pmc-13162197:
Conlon, Preston, and Zupan survey how confident Australian speech therapists feel in tools that help people speak, in a study from twenty twenty-six. These tools range from picture boards to speech devices. They need skills that differ from other therapy work. A new national disability scheme has also reshaped how therapists work in this area.

Two hundred three therapists filled a survey, and sixteen gave deep interviews. Those with early training in the tools felt more confident. So did city-based staff, senior staff, and those with many tool users as clients. Therapy tasks scored highest, while assessment tasks scored lowest. Barriers spanned training access, fast tech change, workplace limits, and views of key stakeholders.
pmc-13163397:
Linyue Zhang and co-authors design ultrasound views aimed squarely at the heart's papillary muscles, in a 2026 study. Those small muscles anchor the mitral valve and drive its mechanics, but standard echo views show them poorly. The team built targeted views and validated them in stages. Pig hearts provided the anatomical truth for one comparison.

Healthy adults were scanned with both old and new views in the next stages. The targeted views matched anatomy better and measured the muscles more reliably. A large healthy group then set normal reference ranges for size, position, and function. Patients with a leaking mitral valve were compared against those norms. Better muscle pictures should sharpen valve disease assessment.
pmc-13163497:
Bryant Nguyen and co-authors review how artificial intelligence could fix sepsis care's two weak points: bundle compliance and fluid dosing. Their 2026 review covers SEP-1, the United States quality bundle for early sepsis management, whose completion stays modest and uneven across hospitals. At the same time, the bundle's fixed fluid volumes are contested as care shifts toward individualized, physiology-guided dosing.

The authors survey AI tools matched to each gap. Early warning systems, language-processing models that read charts, and telehealth platforms sped up antibiotics and bundle steps when embedded in real workflows. Reinforcement learning and causal models promise patient-specific fluid strategies, though most evidence is still retrospective. The review weighs what is proven in process gains against what remains promise in personalization.
pmc-13167397:
Yong-Ho Cho, Myoung-Ho Lee, and Yong-Jun Cha reviewed trials in 2026 on robot assisted training for arm recovery after stroke. The training pairs a robot with task based practice, and the question was whether it improves arm use and daily life.

The team searched five databases for randomised trials from 2014 to 2025 and kept ten studies. Robot training steadily improved arm movement, above all when added to standard therapy or paired with tools such as mild electric stimulation. Gains in daily life tasks were less even, confirmed in only three studies. Results depended on the type of robot help, the stage after stroke, and how well the tools were combined.
pmc-13169497:
Ulrich Anglas and nine co-authors study long life in worms in 2026. A mild flaw in the worms' cell power plants, from a mutation called isp-1, stretches lifespan and stress resistance. Signals from the power plants to the nucleus seem to switch on resilience genes, but the wiring was unclear.

Removing a kinase called MAK-2 erased the lifespan and stress gains in the mutant worms, yet left normal worms untouched. A parallel kinase path proved needed as well. Gene reads showed many mutant-driven gene shifts depend on MAK-2, above all in immunity and stress genes. The kinase thus relays the power plant's signal.
pmc-13170597:
Jakub Polinski and co-authors set side by side the sight results for three types of intraocular lens used in cataract surgery. Their 2026 cohort study covers a boosted monofocal lens, a non-diffractive extended depth-of-field lens, and a standard monofocal lens used as the control.

Patients had surgery on both eyes, aimed at clear sight at a distance. Results were checked more than three months after surgery. Corrected distance acuity was much the same in all groups. The extended depth-of-field lens gave better acuity at mid range and at near range. It also gave more freedom from glasses for near work, but it gave lower contrast sensitivity. The boosted monofocal lens beat the standard lens at mid range only. Scores that patients gave also split, in how much sight problems got in their way.
pmc-13170797:
Antonio Frolli and co-authors revisit the rare pairing of mastocytosis with lymphoma. Their 2026 letter deals with a blood illness where mast cells build up in organs. About twenty to thirty percent of patients have a second blood cancer. Most such cancers are of the myeloid type. Those pairings carry a far worse outlook than slow forms alone.

Pairings with lymphoma, by contrast, are exceedingly rare. Past reports are mostly single cases. They cover types such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia and marginal zone lymphoma. Little is known about traits, treatment, or outlook for these patients. The team looked back at patients at their centers with both illnesses. They describe clinical and lab traits, the spread of lymphoma types, and the order in which the two appeared.
pmc-13172397:
Ehab Abdelrahman and Sawsan Alashqar present a study the catalog lists under 2026. Brilliant green dye is a water pollutant that can harm genes and cells. It resists natural breakdown and can hurt organs in people. The team made two new mixed materials to pull the dye from water. Both were cooked by a gel route at two heat levels, 600 and 800 degrees.

Tests showed the grain sizes of the two materials and proved their element mix. Images showed round, even grains across each sample. Heat changed the phase mix inside the materials, which can shift how well they grab dye. Water treatment teams get fresh candidate materials with full lab records. pmc-13172597:
Niko Kaciroti and co-authors rerun a blood pressure trial with learning tools in a 2026 paper. The trial paired one base drug with either of two partners. The calcium-blocker partner gave better heart protection, perhaps beyond pressure control alone.

Using a forest method built for survival data, the team ranked risk factors in each arm. Six factors weighed less under the winning pair. Pressure at six months counted about a third less there than in the other arm. That gap backs the claim that the pair guards the heart by more than pressure drops. The work shows how learning tools can mine old trials for new clues.
pmc-13172997:
Carlton Moore and co-authors describe a summer programme that introduces undergraduates to data science careers in health research, in a 2026 report. The seven-week course mixes classes in data skills and health equity with a research placement, clinic shadowing, and career networking. Students came from varied majors.

Two cohorts of five students each finished the course in 2024 and 2025. Demand was strong, with forty applications for five places in the second year. Surveys showed clear gains in confidence across data research, equity research, and science identity. Students rated the placement, mentoring, and contact with researchers most highly, and overall satisfaction was high. The team will track students over time to see if they enter the field.
pmc-13173497:
Zhu and a large team reconstructed wetland methane emissions over several decades in twenty twenty-six. Methane is a strong warming gas, and wetlands are a major natural source. Yet records of wetland methane are short and patchy, unlike carbon dioxide records, making long trends hard to assess.

Their method guides machine learning with field data, warming experiments, and chemical knowledge. They focused on the eleven longest-running monitoring sites in the AmeriFlux network. Trends varied by site, with rises up to fourteen percent per decade from two thousand to twenty twenty-four. The rises weakened from high to low latitudes, pointing to the exposure of northern wetlands. The authors offer their records as benchmarks for checking ecosystem models.
pmc-13175197:
Kunying Zhao and thirteen co-authors tested whether chromosome-cap length predicts thinking problems after stroke in a 2026 cohort study. Telomeres in white blood cells mark biological aging and have been tied to cognition. The team drew on a large Chinese stroke registry, measuring telomere length from genome data and building a genetic risk score from eighteen variants.

Among 923 patients checked a year after stroke, about one in five had cognitive impairment. Neither telomere length nor the genetic score predicted impairment overall. Exploratory splits hinted that effects might differ by age and stroke subtype, but the authors treat those as leads only. The result tempers hopes that this aging marker can flag at-risk stroke survivors.
pmc-13176897:
Braulio Silva and co-authors report a 2026 study of biodiversity in a large watershed in Ontario, Canada, where farmland is widespread. The team used environmental DNA metabarcoding, which identifies species from DNA traces in water samples. They sampled 18 watercourses in summer and fall 2023, along a gradient from forested to agricultural land, focusing on organisms that live on stream beds.

It also resolved many organisms that the older data had left unidentified. Community patterns separated more clearly by land use in the DNA data. The strongest contrast was between farm-dominated and forested sites. Water conductivity, turbidity, and pH were linked to these patterns. The authors argue that this finer resolution is needed to track how human activity changes stream communities.
pmc-13177997:

In all, more than 8.8 million links were found, across 24 types of tie. Both blood ties and other ties were counted. Child service sets had the best cover. Older people in Victoria were a noted gap.
pmc-13178597:
Nur Fariha Mahmuda and co-authors built a green-made cleaning material in 2026 for stripping toxic hexavalent chromium from water. The pollutant pours out of tanneries and endangers health. The authors offer the composite for wastewater duty.
pmc-13178797:
Patricia Hrasnova and a large team map what is known about tiny sacs found in human milk in a 2026 review. The sacs carry signals from mother to child and may one day serve as drugs. The team combed two databases and sorted the finds into one shared picture of the field so far.

pmc-13180797:
Bhaskar Gupta and co-authors update the picture of reactions in leprosy, sudden inflammatory flare-ups that can strike before, during, or after treatment. pmc-13180897:

The authors present it as a lighter, faster screen for clinic use. Less handling by staff is part of the appeal.
pmc-13181597:
Mohammad Mehdi Asgari and co-authors compare ways to thaw frozen carp fillets, and find ultrasound thawing kindest to the fish, in a study from 2026. Ultrasound thawing held pH best and cut protein clumping, shrinking protein particle size by about 49 percent. Cooking loss fell by about 10 percent against water thawing. pmc-13183597:

pmc-13184597:

pmc-13185697:

pmc-13186197:

They fitted thigh sensors to 479 people aged seventy-five, eighty, or eighty-five, recording sit-to-stand moves for up to a week. Groups were split by self-rated walking fatigue, tested fatigue, and daily function.

Everyone's stand speed dipped late in the day, but the dip ran deeper in the high-fatigue groups from mid-afternoon on. Those with function limits dipped most in the evening hours. The authors propose the evening fade, caught by a wearable, as an early flag for fatigue and decline.
pmc-13187597:

pmc-13188997:
Citric acid is a workhorse of plant metabolism, and roots both make it and leak it into soil. The acid mopped up reactive oxygen, in part by switching on protective enzymes, and shifting that balance at the junction alone triggered anchor roots. pmc-13189497:
Alishba Khan and co-authors reported a rare and tragic presentation of Ewing sarcoma, a cancer of bone and soft tissue. A middle-aged patient arrived with two weeks of right-sided chest pain and breathlessness. Scans showed the right chest cavity fully clouded, with a soft-tissue growth on the pleura and fluid around it. The patient had beaten pelvic Ewing sarcoma in youth with drug and radiation treatment, and the new illness proved to be its return.

While doctors awaited biopsy, the patient declined quickly and moved to end-of-life care. A postmortem found a large bleed into the chest lining, the spontaneous haemothorax of the title, with collapsed lung, and tissue tests confirmed recurrent sarcoma. pmc-13190097:
Wei Li, Jing Zhao, Die Liu, Bo Pang, Jun Wang, and Qingliang Shao chart two decades of research on treating bronchiolitis in children. The United States led output, then China and the United Kingdom. Five theme clusters stood out, from risk-based care to virus-specific drugs. Hot topics in recent years include prevention and oxygen therapy. The paper gives the field a map of its own growth and its next frontiers.
pmc-13190297:

Working across five large cohorts, the team found variant-linked protein changes present before amyloid buildup and steady across age and disease stage. Proteins tied to the protective variant clustered in cell upkeep and anti-inflammatory paths. The risk variant showed a narrow set of upstream drivers plus broad signs of vessel, immune, and protein-handling trouble. The contrast names targets for variant-specific treatment.
pmc-13191097:

pmc-13193997:

pmc-13194297:

After seven days, staining showed nerve cells made up the largest share, with two glial types also present, plus a group of cells the stains did not label. One glial type varied widely in shape. The team also tested how the culture reacts to inflammation, giving labs a fuller model for cord studies.
pmc-13194497:
Igbayilola Yusuff Dimeji and four co-authors sum how gene tags rule first cell growth in the womb. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-six. Such tags switch genes with no change to the code self. This first span is a soft spot: poor food, ill health, or strain in the mom can mar the re-set and shape growth. Those so met bear high life risk of sugar ill, heart ill, and food ills. Marks that dodge the wipe are a key open ask, the team say.
pmc-13195297:

The trial screened patients twice daily at a mid sized Norwegian hospital to catch cases early. A multiplex molecular panel, which hunts many germs' DNA in one run, was compared head to head with culture. The endpoints were germ yield, time to answer, antibiotic choices, and the measured rate of the infection itself. The authors expected the panel to find more germs, faster.
pmc-13195597:

The team interviewed twenty-one sexual minority adults using recovery services in the Northeast. Three needs dominated: programs that are structured and reachable, spaces that feel safe across intersecting identities, and an end to stigma and bias inside the rooms. Participants offered concrete fixes, including dedicated programming of their own. Centers that act on such advice could close a real gap in recovery support.
pmc-13195797:

Off steroids, the rash kept returning over months with weaker responses each time.

pmc-13196797:

Old care fixed sight with lenses or replaced the tissue, but did not stop the slide.

pmc-13197397:

At top power the laser cuts deep with no harm to underlying cartilage. Pulses remove cholesteatoma yet leave ossicles intact. The results suggest laser ablation could preserve hearing structures during ear surgery.
pmc-13197697:

pmc-13198797:
