After matching, the study compared 139 patients on the pathway with 139 on standard care from the year before. The pathway group's main outcome, time in hospital, came out significantly shorter. The team also tracked pain, drug use, costs, anxiety, depression, quality of life, and complications across the two groups. Their design lets readers judge the pathway on body and mind together, a fuller test than most surgery studies attempt.
pmc-13225597:
Malik and co-authors present a 2026 review pooling trials of triple versus dual pill therapy for type 2 diabetes. The triple mix joins metformin with two newer drug families, SGLT-2 and DPP-4 blockers. Eight randomized trials with 2,606 patients were gathered from four databases under standard review rules. Blood sugar, fasting glucose, weight, target reach, and side effects were the measures.

Triple therapy cut the long-term sugar marker HbA1c by a firm margin over dual therapy, the pooled result showed. Random-effects models guarded against study-to-study spread. The authors weigh whether the extra drug's gain justifies its place before insulin enters the picture for patients failing two drugs.
pmc-13226097:
Jae-Weon Kim and co-authors presented an authorship framework for global cancer trials in a 2026 article. As gynecologic oncology trials span many countries, old credit models built on single institutions strain to fit cooperative work. The Asia Pacific trials group they belong to covers wide ethnic and health system diversity, which also sharpens what trial results mean worldwide.

Their framework ties authorship to scientific contribution, patient enrollment, and collaborative representation, aligned with international editor standards. Its defining choice: credit is allocated at group level rather than institution level. The system is public on the group's website. The authors present it as a working model for fair credit in multinational research.
pmc-13226597:
Wu and colleagues present a Chinese expert consensus on the first step in lowering cholesterol. Lowering LDL cholesterol, the panel stresses, is the most effective known way to cut heart and vessel disease caused by clogged arteries. Past studies show that active early treatment lifts the share of patients who reach their LDL goal and improves outcomes.

The consensus weighs which starting strategy fits which patient, rather than leaving the first move to habit. Choices at the start matter because delay lets risk build while doses stay too low. For Chinese clinicians, the document sets a shared, evidence-based opening play for a very common and deadly risk factor.
pmc-13228097:
Haibo Zhang, Dawei Wang, Jiebin Li, and Jing Zhang test a 2026 simple blood score as a predictor of death in acute pancreatitis, using the large MIMIC-IV intensive-care database. The albumin-bilirubin score combines two routine liver-related blood values and needs no special equipment. Records of 1,953 patients were split into three bands by score, and survival at thirty days and one year was compared.

Each unit rise in the score came with a clearly higher risk of death at both horizons. Survival curves separated significantly, and the risk relationship bent upward sharply beyond a turning point in the score's range. Links ran stronger in patients who had not received certain antibiotics or early ventilation. The authors support the score for early risk sorting.
pmc-13229397:
Connor G Wright and colleagues report a 2026 twelve-month feasibility study of a smartphone app supporting HIV prevention in women in New York's South Bronx, an area of high HIV burden. Daily preventive pills, called PrEP, remain underused by cisgender and transgender women. Forty participants received the pills, home HIV test kits for themselves and partners, and an app sending daily reminders and logging doses taken.

Most enrollees had never used PrEP before, and two thirds did not believe themselves at risk, even though nine in ten reported at least one recent risk behaviour. Interviews every three months tracked sexual behaviour and how acceptable the app felt. The study's purpose was practical: can this population use and stick with app-supported prevention over a full year?
pmc-13229797:
Lamei Zhao and co-authors study the immune profile of a horseshoe bat in this 2026 paper. The species Rhinolophus pusillus carries several coronaviruses linked to SARS at once. How it hosts them without clear illness is not well understood.

The team built gene activity maps from many tissues of two bat species. They compared those maps with public data from other mammals tied to zoonotic disease. The focal bat showed high baseline activity in innate antiviral defense genes. Network work found tissue modules and long non-coding RNA links that shape this state. The pattern may explain its tolerance of many viruses.
pmc-13229997:
Serdar Baler and co-authors raise an overlooked hazard of earthquake recovery: radon gas building up in ground floor gyms. Published in 2026, the paper joins three fields that rarely meet. Quakes crack rock and soil, letting radon rise faster into ground contact buildings. Gyms sit exactly there, and the people inside breathe far harder than at rest.

The authors argue the dose math breaks: reference levels assume ordinary breathing, so a post quake gym at plausible radon levels delivers far more internal radiation than the number suggests. Baseline indoor levels of fifty to three hundred units could plausibly jump to five hundred or a thousand after a quake. They call this a disproportionate lung cancer risk for active people, hiding in plain sight.
pmc-13230297:
Philipp Ernst and colleagues explore in 2026 whether living in a high-radon area shapes lung cancer type or stage in central Germany. Registry records covered eight hundred ninety-three cases from ninety-six communities in Thuringia between 2018 and 2022. Communities were split by soil radon levels and rock-based radon potential.

Overall lung cancer rates did not differ between high and low radon communities after age and sex adjustment. One common cancer type appeared somewhat more often in high radon areas in simple comparisons. Among small cell cancers, widespread disease at diagnosis was also more frequent there in simple comparisons. Both patterns faded after correcting for many tests, and smoking data were missing. The authors treat the clues as ideas for deeper study, not proof.
pmc-13230997:
Namrata Gaikwad and colleagues report in 2026 a rare case where bowel slipped through a caesarean wound and mimicked skin infection. A thirty-nine-year-old woman returned three days after her planned caesarean birth with belly pain, vomiting, and spreading redness near the scar. The wound looked clean and she had no fever, so staff first treated the picture as cellulitis.

Scans instead showed small bowel herniating through a gap beside the scar, with early blockage signs. Surgery freed and returned the bowel, which stayed healthy, so no section had to be removed. She went home four days later without problems. Only four similar cases were found in print, and later care in those cases often meant dead bowel.
pmc-13231697:
Iden Amiri and Aya Barzelay-Wollman report in 2026 a sixty-five-year-old whose pulling vitreous gel freed itself after a deep scuba dive. The gel in his left eye had partly detached and tugged on the central retina, slowly blurring his sight. Such traction clears on its own in only a small share of cases, and surgery is the usual answer when sight worsens.

After a dive to sixty meters, he noticed a sudden shower of floaters, then sharper vision. Eye scans confirmed the gel had fully released with no tear or lasting damage to the retina. Sharp pressure swings during the dive may have finished the separation. The link is only a timing clue, so pressure effects on this condition deserve formal study.
pmc-13233497:
Yan-Xiang Tang and co-authors report a striking case of advanced ovarian cancer that vanished under a new targeted drug. The patient, a 40-year-old woman, had stage IV high-grade serous cancer without BRCA mutations. Her cancer resisted chemotherapy, surgery, and several maintenance drugs in quick succession. Testing showed her tumor strongly expressed a surface protein called NaPi2b.

She began YL205, an antibody-drug conjugate that aims at that protein and carries a topoisomerase inhibitor payload. After 24 weeks, scans showed a complete response and her tumor marker fell to normal. The response held through 48 weeks of treatment. Side effects stayed mild, limited to manageable low white cell counts. The authors say this is the first complete response seen with the agent. They argue such conjugates can bypass resistance left by earlier drug classes, supporting biomarker-matched care in heavily treated patients.
pmc-13233597:
Jonathan Jie Lee and Daniel M. Blumberger published a 2026 review on managing treatment-resistant depression, where standard antidepressants have failed. The authors describe a pattern of drug exhaustion: each successive drug step in the landmark STAR*D trial remitted fewer patients, while relapse grew more likely. Current Canadian guidelines therefore favor adding a second agent, such as aripiprazole, after one or two adequate trials rather than endless switching.

Magnetic brain stimulation gets a long look as an option that targets brain networks, not chemical messengers. Head-to-head evidence cited in the review shows repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation beating medication switching on response and remission, and matching antipsychotic add-ons without their body-wide risks. The article helps clinicians sequence these options when first-line drugs fall short.
pmc-13234397:
Esther Wortmann and colleagues reported in 2026 on how bile acids made by gut microbes shape the lining of the colon. One such acid, deoxycholic acid, rises with long-term high-fat diets and has been linked to colorectal cancer. The team colonized germ-free mice with a defined set of bacteria that included a species able to produce that acid. Human biopsy material from patients with polyps or cancer provided a comparison.

Single-cell sequencing of mouse colon cells showed more bile-acid-sensitive surface cells after exposure. Stem cells, mucus-producing cells, and rapidly dividing cells became fewer in number. A gene tied to energy control rose, while the main mucus gene fell, matching patterns seen in human growths. In separate patients, drugs that bind bile acids were linked to more cell growth in colon biopsies. The findings clarify how microbial bile acids may influence cancer risk.
pmc-13234497:
Min Liang and colleagues combined in 2026 results from trials of online health support for people caring for a relative with dementia. Family caregivers often face heavy stress and depressive symptoms while providing unpaid care. The review gathered randomized trials from eight databases and trial registries. Interventions were interactive digital programs compared with usual care or inactive controls.

Thirty-five trials with more than three thousand caregivers entered the main analysis. Digital support produced a small but statistically clear reduction in caregiver burden. Depressive symptoms also eased modestly across the trials that measured them. Results varied a great deal between studies, so real-world benefit will differ by setting. Shorter programs, human-supported programs, and mobile delivery showed larger point estimates in subgroup checks. Caregiver age may shape how much benefit a program delivers.
pmc-13234597:
Nicolas Gautron and a large team reported in 2026 on making a key cancer drug building block in engineered yeast. Etoposide is a powerful chemotherapy medicine first derived from mayapple plants. Supply stays tight because plants contain little precursor and climate pressure limits harvests. The team rebuilt part of the plant pathway inside yeast cells.

Starting from a compound called yatein, the yeast produced an advanced intermediate used to make etoposide. Repeated strain changes improved how carbon flowed through the pathway and sped production. Bioreactor material was purified and then converted chemically into etoposide itself. Sourcing resilient plants rich in the starting compound forms a parallel supply route. The hybrid plan mixes plant sourcing, yeast factories, and chemistry to secure the medicine.
pmc-13235497:
Xinyu Liu and colleagues followed in 2026 British adults with prediabetes to see how social position shapes progression to diabetes. More than thirty-four thousand UK Biobank participants with prediabetes were tracked for a median of over thirteen years. Education, employment, and income defined social groups through a statistical clustering method. A lifestyle score combined smoking, diet, sleep, body mass, and sitting time.

Nearly seven thousand participants developed diabetes during follow-up in the cohort. Diabetes risk rose stepwise from the highest to the lowest social group in the analysis. Lifestyle factors explained about one third of the extra risk tied to lower social position. Body mass stood out as the largest single contributor among the lifestyle components examined. The authors estimate substantial fractions of cases could be prevented through lifestyle and social improvements, guiding fairer intervention design.
pmc-13237397:
Twelve authors led by Nada Elbuluk re-cut a drug trial in skin disease to see who gains most from a new pill. The pill blocks a single kinase, TYK2, and is drunk once a day for plaque psoriasis. Their base trial ran twelve weeks against a dummy pill in mid-to-grave cases. This fresh cut splits gains by age, sex, weight, race, past drug use, and start scores, and by body zone.

Both dose arms beat the dummy pill on clear-skin marks in near all splits. Gains held across head, trunk, and limb zones and across each scale part of the rash. Life-quality wins tracked skin wins in the same arms. The spread of gain backs the pill for a wide range of patients, not a lucky few.
pmc-13237797:
Buist and colleagues assess custom-made implants for rebuilding long bones with a segment missing. Gaps in the thigh or shin bone, left by tumour removal or severe injury, are hard to bridge while sparing the nearby joint. Implants designed for one patient, built from three-dimensional scans by additive manufacturing, promise an exact fit where stock parts fail.

The study reviews how such implants performed in joint-sparing reconstructions. Fit alone is not success; the implant must bear weight for years and knit to living bone at its ends. Their experience helps surgeons judge when a bespoke implant is worth its cost and planning time.
pmc-13237997:
Frederik Heumüller and team reviewed 1,628 patients who had bypass surgery within 48 hours of a heart attack at one center between 2001 and 2023. Their focus was the 77 who suffered neurological injury around surgery. Most injuries were clot-related strokes, with a smaller share from oxygen deprivation. The injured patients were compared with the rest on risk factors and outcomes.

Injury patients more often smoked, had badly weakened heart pumping beforehand, and had needed resuscitation before surgery, and their operations ran longer. Thirty-day mortality was roughly double theirs, at about 21 percent against about 11 percent. Nearly all injury patients stayed in intensive care beyond two days. Peripheral artery disease and pre-surgery resuscitation independently predicted early death among the injured.
pmc-13238797:
Yuan and colleagues report lung nodules that turned out to be rheumatoid disease, not cancer. Rheumatoid arthritis mainly attacks joints, yet the lungs are its commonest target outside them. Their patient, a man of seventy-four with a smoking history, was being treated for rheumatoid arthritis when scans found many nodules in both lungs, around their edges and linings.

In a smoker of his age, that picture screams cancer until proven otherwise. The nodules were rheumatoid ones, a rare form of the disease in the lung. Documenting the case helps chest doctors keep this possibility alive before ordering drastic treatment, and shows why a biopsy can change everything.
pmc-13238997:
Michael Nuss, Tobias Schrimpf, and Carsten Strohmann determine the crystal structure of a lithium compound and compare it with its parent ether, in a 2026 paper. Two solvent partners keep the lithium ion alone rather than clustered, giving it a squashed tetrahedral surrounding. Such organolithium reagents are workhorses for taking protons off molecules in synthesis. The structure was solved at 100 kelvin, with disorder in one solvent partner and in trapped pentane handled by standard tricks.

The parent compound, diphenyl ether, was re-measured under the same cold conditions for a clean comparison. Putting the two side by side shows what swapping a hydrogen for lithium does to the ring system. The authors present the pair as a reference for how metalation reshapes an aromatic frame.
pmc-13239097:
Megersa Regassa and colleagues reported in 2026 two young adults in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, whose obstructed stomach outlets hid an incidental finding: pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis, gas-filled cysts in the bowel wall. Both patients had long histories of early fullness, pain after meals, reflux, vomiting, and marked weight loss from chronic duodenal narrowing. Surgery bypassed the blockage with a stomach-to-intestine connection.

During the operations, surgeons spotted the gas cysts scattered on the small intestine's outer surface, with no dead bowel, perforation, or peritonitis. They left the cysts alone, and both patients recovered smoothly with symptoms gone and weight regained. The authors argue the cysts arose from chronic mucosal damage and pressure build-up behind the obstruction. Recognizing the pattern, they say, prevents needless bowel removal.
pmc-13239997:
Shu-Yu Wu and a large team investigate a hawthorn flavonoid against high uric acid in a 2026 study. Vitexin, one of seventeen flavonoids they identified in hawthorn extract, was flagged by computer screening as the compound most worth testing for hyperuricemia, the condition behind gout.

Docking simulations suggested vitexin binds two proteins in a pathway controlling urate export. In mice with raised uric acid, treatment cut blood levels by blocking two production enzymes in the liver and by restoring export pumps in kidney and gut almost to normal. Liver, kidney, and intestinal injury eased, and oxidative stress and inflammation fell. The authors propose vitexin as a multi-target natural candidate.
pmc-13240397:
Zahra Jaafari and co-authors model why type 2 diabetes rates differ between countries in a 2026 ecological study. Using Global Burden of Disease data from 1990 to 2021, they nested yearly observations inside countries and separated lifestyle factors from development and health spending indicators.

High body mass index and the passage of time were tied to rising incidence in both models they built. Physical inactivity flipped direction between models, showing how sensitive ecological results are to assumptions. Development level consistently pointed the other way, with higher development linked to lower incidence once other factors were held. Diet low in fibre showed no stable link. Prevention, the authors argue, must join personal and structural levers.
pmc-13240497:
Lianying Chang and team argue for shaping acupuncture to each patient's biology in a 2026 review. Pain varies a lot between people, and so does relief from acupuncture. The method is used for chronic muscle pain, migraine, and cancer pain, yet trials that report only average effects may hide who gains most.

Gene studies, mostly small candidate-gene work, link variants in pain and brain signalling genes such as COMT and OPRM1 with unlike responses. Blood and tissue profiling after care shows molecular shifts. The authors split such shifts from markers that can flag response in advance. Small samples and mixed protocols limit how firm the claims can be, but the base for response-split trials is set out.
pmc-13241397:
van Wissen and colleagues at Leiden priced long-term exercise therapy for severely limited axial spondyloarthritis patients. Their randomized trial tracked two hundred fourteen Dutch participants for one year. Half got personalized exercise therapy; half got usual care. Costs and quality-adjusted life years were weighed from a societal angle.

Therapy patients averaged forty-one sessions, and uptake reached ninety-three percent. Extra physiotherapy costs were largely offset by savings elsewhere in care. Quality-of-life gains were tiny and statistically uncertain, as was the cost difference. The verdict: no clear economic winner, so cost alone should not block access.
pmc-13241497:
Maetzler's team at Kiel asked where on the body motion sensors best capture activity in early Parkinson's. 25 newly diagnosed, still untreated patients wore motion sensors for two weeks. Devices sat on the ankle, wrist, and lower back at once. Diaries turned daily doings into energy units for comparison.

Wrist and lower back sensors tracked diary motion about as well across effort levels. The ankle sensor lagged clearly behind both. Tremor hurt readings across the board, with the lower back coping slightly best. Maetzler's rare drug-free group gives trial planners concrete sensor placement guidance. None had started Parkinson's drugs.
pmc-13241697:
Amo-Tachie at Ghana describes a ninety-year-old whose standard heart failure dose turned toxic. The man had taken a small daily carvedilol dose as told for six months. Twice in one week he reached emergency care with dangerous low blood sugar. The first episode triggered a seizure; the second dulled his mind.

Pill counts proved he never overdosed, and scoring rated carvedilol the likely culprit. Stopping the drug and giving glucagon by vein restored him fast. He left care on day three with better kidney function. Amo-Tachie warns that aging livers and kidneys let standard doses build up without warning.
pmc-13241797:
Tianran Zhang and co-authors lay out a trial plan comparing real and virtual nature for adults with and without ADHD, in this 2026 protocol. Nature contact aids focus and mood, and virtual reality can mimic it cheaply. Whether the mimic works the same in the brain is unknown.

Eighty adults, half with ADHD, will be assigned to sit in real nature or a VR version for twenty minutes. Brain waves are recorded during exposure. Then come game-like tests of flexible thinking, mood and restoration surveys, and app check-ins over eight weeks. The team will trace how effects fade or hold, and who benefits most.
pmc-13241997:
Ahmad Alhabashi and co-authors publish a 2026 retrospective study of teeth crowned after crown lengthening surgery in Dubai. Crown lengthening exposes more tooth so a crown can grip, rescuing teeth that might otherwise be pulled. Long-term complication data for this pathway are valuable for treatment planning.

Records covered well over a hundred restored teeth treated over a decade at a dental hospital. Survival stayed very high at both five and ten years. Among surviving teeth, gum-related complications were the most common, followed by root and restoration problems. Patients who attended the dentist regularly had fewer complications. The authors conclude the approach preserves compromised teeth reliably, supporting its place when prognosis looks uncertain.
pmc-13242197:
Laura Roelans and co-authors offer a 2026 review proposing a mechanism for the puzzling toxicity of the fungicide fludioxonil. The chemical protects stored seeds and crops, and it breaks down quickly outdoors. Reports of harm to wildlife and possible human effects have been inconsistent, with no proven explanation.

The reviewers gathered literature from over a decade and searched for shared threads. The fungicide degrades into a breakdown product classed among perfluoroalkyl substances. That product carries a chemical group able to bind permanently to glutathione, the cell main antioxidant shield. Draining that shield would raise oxidative stress, matching the scattered toxicity reports. The authors warn the mechanism matters for aquatic life near farms and for human health assessments.
pmc-13242997:
Xunwei Deng and co-authors publish a 2026 study of a blood protein called fetuin-B in stroke caused by large-artery plaque. They compared patients with this stroke type against matched healthy controls, then asked whether the protein also predicts poor recovery. Blood was drawn after stroke onset and measured with a standard assay.

Fetuin-B levels were clearly higher in patients and rose alongside cholesterol, blood sugar control markers, and inflammation markers. Higher levels independently tracked with having the stroke and with poor functional outcome. Adding the protein to a basic prediction model improved accuracy for both questions. The relationship with stroke presence curved, while the outcome link ran roughly straight. The authors propose fetuin-B as an added risk marker.
pmc-13243197:
Hassan Ahangar and co-authors describe a woman whose breathlessness led to a rare form of high blood pressure in the lungs that surgery can cure. Their case report appeared in Clinical Case Reports in 2026. The thirty-seven-year-old patient arrived with worsening breathlessness, back pain, and cough. Scans showed an enlarged right side of the heart, very high lung pressures, and wide gaps between air flow and blood flow in the lungs.

Surgeons cleared the blocked lung arteries in a major operation, and her pressures soon improved a great deal. Only later did an unnoticed early pregnancy come to light, ending in miscarriage at fourteen weeks. The strain pregnancy puts on blood flow may have unmasked her illness, the authors suggest. The case warns doctors to think of this diagnosis in women of childbearing age with unexplained breathlessness.
pmc-13243297:
Paolo Squillaci and co-authors build carbon electrodes that turn a plant-derived chemical into useful products in 2026 work. The starting chemical is furfural, a building block made from farm waste. Their electrodes use ordered porous carbon formed around a silica mold, with one version carrying gold particles.

Tests in a small flow cell compared the carbons under acid and alkaline conditions. The glycerol-based carbon worked best, converting furfural to a valued ring compound with high efficiency. The gold version instead favored a different product at higher voltage. The team links the win to surface area, pore shape, and graphitic character. Such tailored carbons could help replace fossil feedstocks in chemical production.
pmc-13243497:
Min Seo Lee and seven co-authors traced how the body handles a designer stimulant in a 2026 paper. Eutylone is a synthetic cathinone turning up in toxicology cases, often alongside other drugs. Knowing how it is broken down, and what it does to drug-processing enzymes, matters for surveillance and risk calls.

Testing blood and liver material from four species, the team found twenty breakdown products and wide species gaps: rat liver cleared the drug fast, human liver only moderately. One human enzyme, CYP2D6, did most of one key step, and eutylone itself jammed that enzyme over time. That jamming could raise levels of other drugs a user takes, a concrete interaction risk.
pmc-13243597:
Yuan Wang, Hao Xu, and Wenliang Lu test rebuilding a whole heart in 3D from a few ultrasound views in a 2026 study. Sparse echo views are cheap and safe, but stitching them into a full shape needs knowing where each view sat.

Simulated views were cut from CT scans, which serve as truth. Views alone rebuilt hearts poorly. With exact pose data, four standard views scored high overlap. Even stray views with rough pose beat no pose by a wide margin. Chamber volume reads confirmed the edge. Pose tracking looks like the key upgrade for echo based heart models.
pmc-13245797:
Zaizen, Koga, and Tsutsumi studied skin biopsies from patients with dermatomyositis, an autoimmune disease that attacks muscle and skin, in this 2026 PLOS One paper. They stained samples from twenty-two patients and thirteen controls to map where complement proteins, antibodies, and a viral-sensor protein called MDA5 sit in the skin layers.

Patient skin carried clearly more complement C3c and two antibody types, IgM and IgA, in the upper dermis where the inflammation occurs, a pattern pointing to immune-complex injury. MDA5 appeared in the outer skin of everyone, but in patients it also showed up strongly in inflammatory cells and tiny blood vessels deeper in the skin. The map helps explain how the skin damage develops.
pmc-13247197:
Qinqing Chen, Fangfang Xi, and Min Lv test a teaching blend for medical residents in a 2026 study. Their method pairs mind mapping with virtual patient simulation during obstetrics and gynecology rotations. Clinical reasoning is the skill at stake, since residents must link book knowledge to live care.

Records covered 80 second-year residents trained from 2023 to 2024, split into two equal groups. Both groups learned the same cases from the same teachers. The mind mapping group scored no higher on theory tests. It did score higher on history taking, reasoning, and specialty skills, and reported greater satisfaction. The authors credit the maps with organizing complex cases without adding mental strain.
pmc-13247297:
Huang and co-authors measured how canal building unmasks crabs in this 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. Two fiddler crab species living side by side in estuaries rely on matching the mudflat's color to hide from predators. The team photographed crabs in engineered canal habitats and in natural mudflats nearby, scoring body-to-background color matching with a vision-based metric.

Both species matched their background significantly worse inside canals, where construction had changed the substrate's color and light properties, while brightness and pattern measures shifted less. The authors warn that this sensory disruption could raise predation on the crabs and ripple through estuary food webs. Habitat engineering, they argue, should be judged on visual ecology too, not structure alone.
pmc-13247797:
Samson, Maximo, and Nelson combined brain chemistry and brain-network imaging in people experiencing psychosis for the first time, in this 2026 Psychological Medicine study. Sixty-seven patients who had never taken antipsychotics and one hundred ten healthy controls underwent spectroscopy measuring GABA, the brain's main inhibitory messenger, in the anterior cingulate cortex. They also had resting-state scans of connectivity in four major networks.

Patients had significantly lower cingulate GABA. Connectivity differed between groups in several networks. The key result was an interaction: in healthy brains, more GABA tracked with stronger connectivity in parts of the executive control and salience networks. In patients the relationship flipped negative. The authors argue that disturbed inhibition is woven into the network dysfunction of early psychosis, not a side note, and that the mechanism deserves direct study.
pmc-13248897:
Bounyarith, Braun, and Kucyi tested a brain scanner that asks questions at the right moment, in a 2026 proof-of-concept study. People resting in a scanner have spontaneous thoughts, but random prompts catch brain activity only roughly. Their method watched two brain regions live and triggered a thought probe whenever either region flared.

Sixty volunteers took part, and after strict exclusions about forty to fifty remained per test. Probes fired by the posteromedial cortex, a daydreaming hub, indeed caught moments of low attention to the outside world. The insula hypothesis did not hold up. The authors say the method works and can sharpen studies of wandering minds.
pmc-13249197:
Walter and co-authors screened newly arrived asylum seekers for diphtheria in Heidelberg, Germany, in a 2026 study. Europe had seen a rise in diphtheria among displaced people during 2022 and 2023. Between August and October 2024 the team swabbed throats and wounds from a random sample of one thousand seventy-three arrivals and checked blood samples for immunity.

No toxin-producing diphtheria bacteria turned up at all. Wounds told a different story: nearly half of the inflamed wounds carried MRSA, a drug-resistant staph. About thirty-eight percent of participants lacked protective diphtheria antibodies, though almost everyone accepted vaccination when offered. The authors urge early testing, wound care, and vaccination at arrival.
pmc-13249697:
Ntais and Greek colleagues measured how well brain blood vessels flex in multiple sclerosis, in a 2026 study. Ninety patients with the relapsing-remitting form and forty-five matched healthy volunteers held their breath while ultrasound tracked blood flow speed in the brain, a stand-in for carbon dioxide response. Thinking tests and a standard disability scale completed the picture.

Patients' vessels reacted notably less than controls'. Weaker reactivity tracked with greater disability and with slower mental processing speed, and both links survived adjustment for other factors. The authors propose vessel reactivity as a measurable contributor to MS disability that routine scans miss, worth tracking alongside the usual immune markers.
pmc-13249797:
Papayanis and co-authors use a blood type clue to trace where a leukemia began, in a 2026 case report. A man with primary myelofibrosis, a bone marrow scarring disease, received a stem cell transplant from his brother, whose blood type differed from his own. Afterward his blood type switched to his brother's, a sign the donor marrow had taken over blood production.

Ten months later he relapsed with acute myeloid leukemia, yet his blood type stayed his brother's. That persistence argues the leukemia grew from relatively mature donor-lineage precursor cells, not from the deepest stem cells. The authors present the case as rare evidence about which cell stage drives this feared transformation.
pmc-13249897:
Huang and colleagues found that a mitochondrial cleaning machine needs an iron-sulfur cluster to work, in a 2026 Nature Communications study. Cancer cells must clear misfolded proteins from their mitochondria. If they fail, the proteins pile up and poison the cell. The team studied CLPX, one part of the cell's mitochondrial shredder.

CLPX carries a cluster of iron and sulfur atoms. It can only join its partner protein and cut up waste when that cluster is in place. Starving cells of iron broke the shredder. So did starving them of cysteine, a building block for the clusters. The cell then switched to digesting whole mitochondria instead. The authors map this weak point as a possible target in cancer cells that lean on the system.
pmc-13249997:
Ran Wang and co-authors present a spider-web-inspired battery material in this 2026 paper. Flexible zinc-ion batteries are safer than lithium ones, but their zinc electrodes fail early as spiky deposits grow and side reactions eat away at the surface.

The team built a layered gel that fills the battery, copying a web's mix of sticky spots and open paths for ions. Zinc ions moved through it quickly and evenly. In tests, zinc electrodes lasted 4,600 hours, over six months, and full flexible cells ran more than 10,000 charge cycles. The design could suit wearable devices that need long-lived, bendable power.
pmc-13250397:
Vasef and colleagues describe a teenager whose missing periods led doctors to a hidden chromosome condition and advanced ovarian cancer. Their 2026 Clinical Case Reports paper concerns a sixteen-year-old girl with Swyer syndrome, where a person with XY chromosomes develops as female with non-working gonads. Such gonads carry a high risk of cancer.

Hormone tests showed that her ovaries were not functioning, and chromosome testing confirmed the XY pattern. Scans found several pelvic masses, and surgery confirmed dysgerminoma in both ovaries with spread to nearby lymph nodes, staged as IIIC. She was referred for chemotherapy after the surgery. The authors stress that absent periods with this hormone pattern demand chromosome testing, so that cancer is not found late.
pmc-13250497:
Abha Pokharel and Surya Kathayat wrote a 2026 scoping review on blockchain-based self-sovereign identity in health care. Self-sovereign identity lets people hold and share their own digital credentials instead of relying on one central database. The review asks where this approach has been tried in medicine and how ready it is for real clinics.

The authors screened work published through August 2025 and included thirty-seven studies in their map of the field. Most described early designs or prototypes rather than systems running in hospitals today. Common uses were checking identity, managing credentials, and sharing health records with patient consent. pmc-13251197:

pmc-13253197:

pmc-13253997:

pmc-13254097:

pmc-13254697:

pmc-13255297:

pmc-13255897:

pmc-13256497:

pmc-13256597:

pmc-13257097:

pmc-13257797:

pmc-13257897:

pmc-13257997:

pmc-13259197:

pmc-13259297:

pmc-13260097:

pmc-13262097:

pmc-13263397:

pmc-13263797:

pmc-13264297:

pmc-13264797:

pmc-13266097:

pmc-13266397:

pmc-13266797:

pmc-13267297:

pmc-13267697:

pmc-13268397:

pmc-13269597:

pmc-13269897:

pmc-13270997:

pmc-13272197:

pmc-13272397:

pmc-13272997:

pmc-13273497:

pmc-13273797:

pmc-13274597:

pmc-13274897:

pmc-13275497:

pmc-13275897:

pmc-13276597:

pmc-13277397:

pmc-13278497:

pmc-13278797:

pmc-13278897:

pmc-13278997:

pmc-13279697:

pmc-13280097:

pmc-13281297:

pmc-13281597:

pmc-13281897:

pmc-13282397:

pmc-13282897:

pmc-13282997:

pmc-13284297:

pmc-13284597:

pmc-13284697:

pmc-13284897:

pmc-13285497:

The weak grip between C1q and antibody tails drives cell killing, and sugar tags on the tail tune it, yet standard tests blur the mix. Their column method pairs a single-chain C1q trap with mass reading.

A salt swap in the wash fluid cut sticky false binding that had plagued weak-grip work. The setup echoed the known grip ranking of human antibody classes. High-mannose sugars clearly weakened grip, while added galactose helped a touch. The authors say makers can now compare antibody batches fairly, sugar by sugar.
pmc-13285697:
Complete tooth loss in China is compared with the wider Group of Twenty in a 2026 analysis led by Yilin Zhang and colleagues. The work uses Global Burden of Disease 2023 data to track edentulism, the loss of all natural teeth, from 1990 onward. It asks what drives change in the burden and where that burden may head next.

Joinpoint regression tracks trends over time, while a decomposition step splits change into population growth, aging, and shifts in rates. Forecast models then project the burden through 2038. The authors report that China's rates fell only slightly, and that aging drove most of its rising burden. Across the G20, population growth mattered most instead. The contrast supports oral care aimed at older adults, linked with wider care for aging patients.
pmc-13286797:
Qing Yan and colleagues gather trial evidence on traditional Chinese exercise for people with Parkinson's disease, focusing on thinking, sleep, and quality of life. Their 2026 review and meta-analysis covers fifteen randomized trials found in five databases up to March 2025. Gentle practices such as Tai Chi and health Qigong are widely used, yet their non-motor benefits needed a summary.

Pooled results showed clear gains in cognition and sleep quality, plus a moderate gain in quality of life. Programs lasting at least twelve weeks with at least three hours weekly looked most favorable. Tai Chi helped thinking and daily life most, while Qigong led for sleep. People ill for five years or more seemed to gain extra. The authors advise cautious reading of the subgroup patterns.
pmc-13287097:
Shimrit Daches and colleagues probe when bodily vigilance feeds fear of cancer's return in a 2026 survey study. Somatosensory amplification, the habit of reading faint body signals as alarming, seems a natural fuel for recurrence fear, yet direct tests are scarce. Questionnaires from 116 adult survivors, averaging 47 years old, measured that tendency, emotion regulation difficulties, and recurrence fear, with anxiety and time since treatment held in account.

Neither tendency alone predicted the fear on its own. The combination told the story: bodily vigilance tracked stronger recurrence fear among survivors with low or average regulation difficulty. At high regulation difficulty, the link vanished, as if the noise floor already sat at maximum. The authors suggest screening for both traits in survivorship care to spot whose body watching is most likely to spiral into fear.
pmc-13287297:
Klaus Oberauer, Philipp Musfeld, and Frederik Aust ran six simulation studies in 2026 comparing two ways to estimate a Bayes factor, a measure used to weigh one statistical model against another. One route bridges between models. The other reads a density ratio from a single fitted model.

With many simulation draws, both routes gave accurate answers across wide conditions. Bridging grew slow and shaky as models gained parameters. The density ratio stayed fast and steady at larger sizes, though careless density smoothing could bias it. The authors give practical guidance on matching method to model size and on checking density estimates before trusting the result.
pmc-13287797:
Ahmed A Tayel and co-authors made a smart fish coating in 2026 from hibiscus pigment, zinc oxide particles made by green methods, and chitosan particles. The pigment flips colour as acidity changes, turning from red in acid toward green and yellow in alkaline fluid, which signals spoilage.

Dipped Nile perch fillets kept in a fridge stayed fresh up to six days longer than untreated fish. The coating also fought two common bacteria and showed strong antioxidant action in lab tests. As storage went on, the coating shifted from red to green, giving shoppers and handlers a visible freshness cue. The authors pitch the mix as eco-friendly packaging.
pmc-13287997:
Ping Yi and co-authors engineer a hydrogel from pig dental pulp to regrow tooth pulp, in a 2026 study. Keeping inflamed pulp alive helps a tooth survive for the long term. The team removed cells from pig pulp tissue, leaving its natural matrix behind as an injectable gel. That matrix kept many pulp-specific proteins and growth signals. Lab tests checked how immune and blood vessel cells responded to the gel.

The gel switched on a growth pathway in immune cells and pushed them toward a calming state. In shared culture dishes, it helped vessel cells activate and pulp stem cells mature toward dentin-making cells. In rats, capping exposed pulp with the gel produced a solid dentin bridge with new blood vessels. The surrounding tissue showed a repair-friendly immune profile. The authors see the gel as a candidate material for vital pulp therapy in clinics.
pmc-13288697:
Okello Ncube, Methembe Yotamu Khozah, and Wilfred Njabulo Nunu lay out a 2026 research protocol on disaster planning in Bulawayo Province, Zimbabwe. Their question is whether gender and sexual minority residents appear at all in plans for climate-driven disasters, a topic barely studied in sub-Saharan Africa.

Working through a local sexual rights center, the team plans to recruit 165 participants for structured questionnaires, focus groups, and interviews with key informants, running from April to December 2026. Ethics approval is already in place, with written consent required. Results will travel through journals, conferences, policy briefs to the local government ministry, and feedback sessions with the community partner.
pmc-13288997:
Elnora Abdurakhmanova and colleagues detail plans for a 2026 review of neck size as a liver test. Fatty liver disease is common yet often missed. Neck width is quick and cheap to measure. It tracks upper-body fat and heart risk. Past studies give mixed results.

The team will search four large databases. They will keep adult studies from 2010 to 2025. Liver disease must be shown by scan or biopsy. Two reviewers will pick and grade each study. Pooled hit and miss rates are the main goal. The team will also probe why results differ. Findings could support a simple first screen.
pmc-13289397:
Saumya susan Zacharia and Raji Thomas report a 2026 record review on medical problems during rehab after severe brain injury in India. Recovery needs work on body, thinking, and social life, yet complications during inpatient rehab were poorly described in Indian settings. Many such problems can be prevented with early spotting and care, the authors note.

Records covered 100 adults admitted for rehab from August 2017 to August 2019 with severe injury scores. Men made up 81 percent, road crashes caused 81 percent of injuries, and mean age was 35 years in the group. Fully 87 percent had at least one complication during rehab overall. Behavior and thinking issues led at 35 percent, followed by abnormal bone growth in soft tissue.
pmc-13289497:
Xinxin Zhong and co-authors build a prediction model in a 2026 study for drug resistant tuberculosis in people who also have diabetes. Having both diseases raises the risk that standard drugs will fail. Early warning tools for this group have been lacking, so the team set out to build one that doctors can also understand.

The study used records for two hundred forty five patients from two centers and tested seven learning methods. A random forest model did best, though it still missed a fair share of cases. Five factors stood out, led by the gap between first symptoms and diagnosis. The authors frame the tool as a triage aid that flags high risk patients for closer checks, not as a stand alone test.
pmc-13290697:
A skin disease wore two different faces on one patient, Sandesh Shah and colleagues report in a case report from 2026 on Hailey-Hailey disease. The inherited blistering condition usually raises eroded plaques in skin folds, but atypical forms can imitate other blistering disorders.

Their patient, a 38-year-old man, had recurring itchy lesions in flexural areas that worsened with heat and sweat. His neck and armpits showed the classic eroded plaques, while the groin and other folds carried bumpy, follicular lesions with heavy leftover pigmentation instead. A biopsy showed the split skin layers and 'dilapidated brick wall' pattern typical of the disease, and matching clinic with microscope settled the diagnosis. Shah and colleagues remind clinicians that this papular variant exists and that correlation between the two views is what resolves it.
pmc-13290897:
One disease, three patterns: machine learning splits chronic traumatic encephalopathy into distinct variants, Fatima Tuz-Zahra and colleagues report in a brain study from 2026. CTE, the degeneration tied to repeated head injury, shows patchy tau buildup that varies widely between people, and the team asked whether that variation hides order.

Applying a subtype-and-stage algorithm to tau density measured across 26 brain regions, in a sample of 207 CTE cases alongside 75 controls, produced three progression patterns. One was cortex-heavy and fast, matching classic descriptions. A second spared the cortex but hit the hippocampus hard and moved slower. A third, in older cases, came bundled with other pathologies and extra tau in related regions. Daily-function scores tracked tau burden only in the cortex-heavy group. The authors say the variants should sharpen diagnosis criteria and the search for in-life tests.
pmc-13290997:
Whether removing more lymph nodes helps women with endometrial cancer live longer is weighed in a 2026 meta-analysis led by Yunlong Fan. The comparison sets combined pelvic and para-aortic node removal against pelvic removal alone or no node removal, with attention to groups split by recurrence risk.

Searches through December 2025 gathered 14 studies covering 25,432 patients, only one of them a randomized trial. Raw comparisons gave mixed answers, a pattern the authors link to sicker patients more often receiving wider surgery. After statistical adjustment for such differences, wider removal was linked with better overall survival than no removal. The risk-split results are offered as help for tailoring a major surgical choice to each patient’s likely course.
pmc-13291097:
A handheld skin checker called SkinConnect is validated for measuring skin hydration in a 2026 device study led by Frédéric Flament. Built for shop-floor skincare advice, the compact device also reads skin color and surface texture, and the team tested whether its hydration readings repeat well and match a standard laboratory instrument.

Forty-four adults, half women and half men, were measured in triplicate at six body sites at hourly gaps, before and after a hydrating cream went on one forearm. Nearly all of the roughly 4,665 readings were usable, repeat readings held close together, and two devices agreed well with each other. Agreement with the standard Corneometer was weaker at low hydration, yet the device clearly caught the cream-driven rise in moisture.
pmc-13291297:
A plant sugar from a prized Chinese herb may soothe skin. Xuan Li leads a 2026 study of Bletilla striata tubers. The plant has long use in folk medicine. Its sugar chains were poorly mapped until now.

One pure fraction, called BSP60, was pulled from the tubers. Its backbone links mannose and glucose units in turn. Some mannose units carry small acetyl tags. The syrup flows thin under force yet forms a springy web. It beat a common skin acid at mopping up harmful radicals. In immune cells, it cut three swelling signals. Such traits suit creams and wound care research.
pmc-13291597:
Fish carry an oxygen-immune link that land animals lost. Zhipeng Zhan leads a 2026 study of this teleost-specific axis. Water holds little oxygen yet teems with germs. Fish must tune inflammation under low oxygen.

An oxygen sensor called FIH switches on immune pathways. It works by pushing aside a brake protein. That frees a key immune factor to act. Zebrafish lacking the sensor gene fought infection worse. Structure studies show why land vertebrates lack the link. Domain swaps proved the interface is water-specific. The axis may guide fish farm health as waters warm.
pmc-13291797:
Chris Sara Mathew, Manjush Karthika, and Khalid Ansari offer a 2026 integrative review on mouth care as a way to prevent pneumonia in critically ill adults. Ventilator-linked pneumonia and other hospital-acquired pneumonia remain frequent and serious in intensive care. The reviewers searched three databases for work from 2005 to 2025 linking oral health with pneumonia prevention.

From 935 records, 20 studies survived screening and entered the final synthesis. The reviewers grouped the evidence around the oral-lung pathway, current bedside practice, specific cleaning methods, record keeping, and staffing hurdles. They conclude that structured oral care lowers ventilator pneumonia rates and propose a practical, dentistry-informed care bundle. Practice today, they note, stays uneven and poorly specified.
pmc-13292297:
Linli Zhang and co-authors grade a 2026 overview of reviews on magnetic brain stimulation for arm recovery after stroke. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation is widely reviewed, but nobody had checked how trustworthy those reviews are. The team searched nine databases and grey literature through April 2024, scoring reviews with AMSTAR-2 and PRISMA 2020 and grading evidence strength with GRADE.

Seventeen reviews qualified. Only 13 outcome measures rated high; 47 rated moderate, 91 low, and 71 very low in their tally. Sloppy methods and incomplete reporting, more than publication year or bias, drove the downgrades. The authors conclude that stimulation probably aids arm movement, yet the evidence base needs stricter standards, fuller reporting, and MRI biomarkers to sort out mixed results.
pmc-13292797:
Gal Tsaban and colleagues built a computer model, reported in 2026, that uses heart tracings to estimate the risk of death within one year. Care in hospital and emergency settings often lacks clear risk tools, and repeated tracings may hold extra clues.

Records covered 13,417 adults over age 50 treated between 2014 and 2019, of whom 4,372 died within one year. A model using three tracings over time reached 0.84 on the area-under-curve scale, a value the authors treat as strong. Adding most clinic details beyond age and sex did not help. The authors propose the tool could sort patients for closer follow-up.
pmc-13293397:
Samuel Anyaso-Samuel leads a 2026 national survey study on how United States adults rate their own grasp of statistics. Skill with numbers shapes daily choices, from health news to money, yet self-views on this skill are rarely mapped.

In a representative survey, 62% of adults said they had little to no idea what statistics or terms like p-values mean, a share the authors report. Yet 90% said they would use reported statistics at least sometimes if they grasped them better. More schooling linked to higher self-ratings, while older groups rated lower. The authors urge wider statistics teaching in and out of school.
pmc-13293697:
Antonio Tonutti leads a 2026 registry study of systemic sclerosis patients who lack the classic tiny-vessel pattern under the nailfold. That pattern aids diagnosis, yet a small share of patients never show it, and their illness course was unclear.

Among 1689 Italian registry patients with nailfold data, 90 lacked the pattern, which is 5.3% of the group, a share the authors report. They were older at onset and more often had the form without skin thickening. Vessel harms like fingertip scars and calcium deposits were less common, and skin scores stayed lower over five years. Lung transfer capacity also held up better over time.
pmc-13293997:
Jie Lei and co-authors engineer a vaccine-like treatment for stubborn bone infections, in a 2026 study. Chronic infection with drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus creates a suppressed immune pocket where bacteria persist and bone cannot heal. Ideal therapy would first rally antibacterial immunity and later calm inflammation so repair can proceed. The team screened vesicles shed by a probiotic bacterium for exactly that two-stage behavior.

The vesicles carried a rich supply of a metabolic molecule called NAD+, and tuning the culture conditions boosted that cargo further. Early on, the engineered vesicles woke up dendritic cells and built strong antibody protection, clearing nearly all bacteria in animal challenges, including repeat attacks. Later, delivered NAD+ reprogrammed inflammatory macrophages at the defect site, and bone repair ran about ten times faster. The design treats infection and healing as one sequence.
pmc-13294097:
Jinfa Gu heads a 2026 pooled review of trials on beta-alanine supplements for exercise in women. Most prior evidence came from men or mixed groups, leaving female effects unclear. Five databases were searched through April 30, 2026, for randomized trials against placebo or control, with bias and certainty graded by standard tools.

Twelve reports from 11 trials covered 312 women. Time to exhaustion favored the supplement in pooled results across eight studies with 187 women. Other outcomes, including oxygen uptake, peak power, and body fat, stayed imprecise. Certainty was very low for every outcome after downgrades, so the authors urge caution and better trials.
pmc-13294197:
Chenxi Deng and Bingnan Guo measure whether China's low-carbon city pilot program also cleaned the air, in a 2026 study. The program sits inside the country's dual carbon goals for peaking and then cutting emissions.

Panel data from two hundred eighty-two cities over fifteen years fed a staggered comparison design. Pilot cities gained clear air quality improvements, and the finding survived repeated robustness checks. The gains ran through two channels: greener, more efficient economies and upgraded industry mixes. Effects were stronger in big, energy-hungry, and well-funded cities, but weaker where infrastructure was already advanced. The authors recommend tailored strategies and urge firms to green their operations voluntarily.
pmc-13294297:
James Yu and Peter C. Schalock review harms from cosmetic products in a 2026 invited narrative review. Daily cosmetic use is near universal, and new launches keep coming, so side effects deserve stocktaking. A broad PubMed search gathered case reports, series, trials, and population studies on reactions tied to product use.

Contact dermatitis dominates, affecting about 1–5% of the general population in the cited range. Other harms include breathing sensitization, light-triggered reactions, workplace exposures, and pregnancy and nursing concerns. Long-term and combined exposure effects stay poorly understood. The authors call for stronger safety oversight as the market grows.
pmc-13294497:
Shogo Nagaoka and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six geodesy study mapping ground strain around a plate boundary in central Japan. The region mixes a major tectonic line, a known strain belt, and volcanic terrain. Thick vegetation and mountains blunt ground surveys there.

Satellite radar data spanning nearly a decade were fused with a dense positioning network. Private stations filled gaps in the official grid. The combined map resolved sharply concentrated strain along the northern tectonic line. Parts of the known strain belt also stood out tightly. Finer strain maps sharpen earthquake hazard reading in complex country.
pmc-13294797:
Stefan Linsler and co-authors examine how storage timing affects lab-grown meningioma cells in a 2026 study. Tumour tissue is often kept overnight before culture work begins, but whether that delay changes growth was poorly known. Ten samples were taken from patients operated on at Saarland University during 2022.

Cultures started on the surgery day and cultures started a day later both grew at rates of at least 80 percent, with no clear difference between them. Genetic checks found chromosome losses matching the original tumours, even after freezing. Sixteen of 17 frozen specimens also grew again after six months in liquid nitrogen storage.
pmc-13294897:
Karl Thomas Jackson, Robert H. Lomax, and Fatemeh Parnianchi tune a sponge-like crystal to catch dyes from water, in a 2026 study of the metal-organic framework UiO-66. Such frameworks are built from metal clusters and organic links, and adding acid during synthesis changes both particle size and the number of missing-link defects. The team brewed three batches with rising acid doses and challenged each with three dyes: methyl orange, methylene blue, and curcumin.

More acid grew bigger particles, from about 190 to 450 nanometers, and steadily lowered how much dye each batch absorbed. Surface area and defect counts rose then fell across the series, so the relationship was not a simple line. Methyl orange was captured best and methylene blue worst, and uptake patterns fit a model of varied surface sites. Changing cooking time changed nothing, giving makers a clean dial for performance.
pmc-13294997:
Yi-Fen Li and colleagues compare factors linked to vaginal precancer lesions across age groups in a 2026 study. Vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia is an early change that can precede vaginal cancer. Whether test results and nearby lesions mean the same thing in younger and older women was unclear.

Records covered 212 women who had colposcopy and vaginal biopsy between 2020 and 2024, split at age 50. Lesion presence linked with younger age, while older women more often showed high-grade cell test results. In women aged 50 and above, lesion grade rose alongside grades of past or current cervical and vulvar lesions, supporting age-specific screening plans.
pmc-13295697:
Hwajin Yang and co-authors set out a framework for how stress feeds heavy social media use, in a 2026 study. They call it Stress-Induced Digital Escapism. The idea runs in steps: outer demands stir bad feelings, bad feelings push weak ways of coping, and weak coping builds a wish to escape into feeds. Survey data from 238 people let the team test the chain.

The chain held. Outer demands linked to heavy use only through the steps in between: dark stress reactions, poor ways of handling feelings with others, such as venting and seeking comfort, and escape wishes. Checks against flipped models backed the order the team proposed. The framework gives one account of how stress turns scrolling into a habit that is hard to drop.
pmc-13295797:
Xiaodong Zhu and colleagues survey animal science students on welfare views and career plans in a 2026 study. Students in animal-related degrees may carry welfare teaching into both attitudes and job choices. Questionnaires went to undergraduates at Northeast Agricultural University in China.

How students first met welfare ideas tracked with how they judged animal treatment overall. Gender, pet-keeping experience, and career intention each linked significantly with welfare perceptions in the answers. Many students had received welfare teaching far later than they wished. The authors propose a staged system, starting with life and human-animal lessons in primary school and adding hands-on courses at university.
pmc-13296297:
Carlos Javier Lainez Reyes and co-authors compare heart rhythm patterns in miniature cows and Holstein cattle in a 2026 field study. Miniature breeds are gaining interest for small farms, yet little is known about how their smaller size affects heart regulation. Beat-to-beat variation was recorded with a wearable sensor placed on each animal.

Miniature cows showed slower heart rates and stronger variation between beats than the Holsteins. The gap between the groups grew wider in mature animals. The authors urge caution, because the herds lived on different farms and only the Holsteins were producing milk. Even so, the readings give a useful starting baseline for later controlled work on heart health in small cattle.
pmc-13296897:
Hasan Zeybek and Tugrul Hosbul study hepatitis B patients whose virus levels sit below the measuring limit in a 2026 retrospective paper. Such faint traces appear in treated chronic infection and in occult infection, where surface antigen tests read negative. Records of 390 patients with very low viral loads were examined alongside antibody markers.

Low-level virus was commoner in men and in patients aged fifty or older. Among occult cases, two antibody markers appeared far more often, and both stayed linked to occult infection after adjustment. A third antibody pulled in the opposite direction. One marker of reduced replication clearly did not mean full suppression. The authors ask for prospective validation.
pmc-13297297:
Mashal Fatima, Faraz Akram, and Imran Khan Niazi test whether the complexity of brain-wave signals can flag harmful brain change in substance use, in a 2026 study. Three hundred fifty people took part, split evenly among six substance groups and one control group with no such diagnosis. Resting brain signals were recorded with a small eight-channel headset.

Four measures of signal complexity all ran lower in the substance groups than in controls. Losses were largest over the front and centre of the scalp, zones tied to planning and movement. A simple classifier sorted the seven groups with very high accuracy, near ninety-eight percent. Cheap, portable brain-wave checks could suit intake screening and progress checks during recovery care.
pmc-13297597:
Norma Olvera and colleagues examine how anxiety and sleep quality travel with binge eating in Hispanic and African American early adolescents, in a 2026 study. These groups face higher obesity rates than white peers, and binge eating feeds that risk. Three hundred fifteen boys and girls, most of them carrying excess weight, answered surveys and had height, weight, and body fat measured.

Higher binge eating scores went with higher anxiety and with poorer sleep, in both boys and girls alike. The links held after accounting for age, ethnic group, sex, and body fat. Together the measured factors explained about a sixth of the spread in binge eating. Programmes against binge eating should screen for anxiety and sleep trouble, the authors urge.
pmc-13297997:
Javier Jurado and co-authors revisit how methane partial oxidation proceeds on a platinum catalyst, in a 2026 kinetic modelling study. Reaction schemes for many catalysts remain unsettled because accurate data are scarce. An earlier model failed to reproduce the available experiments, so the team proposed a revised scheme.

Data came from past packed-bed reactor runs across a high temperature range. Nonlinear parameter estimation, careful starting values, and sensitivity plus stats checks produced the new parameter set. The revised model predicted the experimental data closely. Readers in catalysis get both a corrected scheme and a worked example of how model fitting choices affect kinetic findings.
pmc-13298797:
Kensuke Kitsugi and colleagues examine bleeding after percutaneous liver biopsy in patients who stopped blood-thinning medicines under Japanese endoscopy guidelines, in a 2026 retrospective study. Bleeding is the main risk of the procedure, and rules for managing such drugs were unclear. Records covered 630 biopsy cases, including 64 patients on antithrombotic therapy.

Bleeding rates did not differ significantly between patients who had therapy withdrawn and those never on it, even after matched comparisons for tumour and non-tumour biopsies. No treated patient needed surgery or vessel blocking for bleeding, and one clot event followed withdrawal. Low platelet count, not therapy itself, predicted bleeding.
pmc-13298997:
Adedolapo V Adejumo reports a severe calcium channel blocker overdose case in a 2026 medical paper. Such poisoning is rare yet can cause dangerously slow heart rate, shock, and body-chemistry upset. The patient developed low blood pressure that resisted standard treatment, which illustrates the difficulty of critical care itself in these cases.

Current treatment combines several drug tactics, including high-dose insulin with glucose control, intravenous calcium, glucagon, and lipid rescue therapy. Advanced haemodynamic support may also be needed. Because these medicines are widely prescribed for heart and blood pressure problems, the author argues clinicians should understand overdose consequences and spot it early.
pmc-13299097:
Predicting how drugs interact inside the body is a network problem, and Zhongyi Chai with co-authors attack it with a graph neural network in a 2026 paper. Their framework, PHARMNet, learns from multi-relational biomedical graphs, while a companion strategy injects ontology knowledge and uncertainty estimates.

Relation-specific convolutions and memory-augmented attention let the model trace hidden dependencies between drugs, targets, and diseases, and the ontology-guided layer steadies predictions when data are sparse or noisy. Across drug interaction benchmarks the system reported an AUC of 0.873 and an F1-score of 0.831, which the authors describe as state-of-the-art performance with better interpretability than earlier tools.
pmc-13299997:
Liyang Xiao, Kai Siang Chan, Isaac Chan, and Aung Myint Oo pool evidence on curative oesophagus removal in patients aged eighty and above, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Eighteen studies covering more than seventy thousand oesophageal cancer patients compared octogenarians with younger patients on survival, deaths, and complications after surgery.

Overall survival was clearly worse in the older group, and hospital, thirty-day, and ninety-day mortality all ran higher. Overall complications were also more frequent, although specific problems such as leakage and chest infection occurred at similar rates. Complete tumour clearance was somewhat less common in octogenarians. The role of keyhole surgery in this age group needs study.
pmc-13300397:
G Caluori and co-authors study how tissue type shapes pulsed field ablation lesions in ventricles, in a 2026 preclinical paper. The technique is proven in atrial fibrillation, but its behavior inside scarred ventricular muscle is poorly known. The team created a sheep model of healed heart attack damage with embolization coils. They then delivered focal pulsed field energy, and they followed the lesions with magnetic resonance imaging and tissue staining at one month.

Lesions stayed durable in both scar and healthy tissue. Temperature feedback at the catheter, used as a contact estimate, responded very differently by tissue type. Healthy tissue lesion depth grew with dose only up to two applications. Treated areas shrank as they healed, losing little depth across the wall. Collagen patterns let the team pick out mature ablation lesions inside old scar, which they offer as a guide for future dosing.
pmc-13300697:
Sending COPD patients home from hospital is a risky handover, and Sanja Dimic-Janjic leads a 2026 survey of how Serbian physicians handle it. One hundred doctors involved in COPD care, recruited through the Respiratory Society of Serbia, described their discharge routines. A SWOT analysis framed the answers about gaps, barriers, and appetite for structured discharge summaries.

Practice varied widely and stayed largely unstandardized, even though most doctors knew the recommended principles. Respondents nonetheless showed strong willingness to adopt structured discharge tools, which they rarely used in daily work. The team reads the blockage as organizational rather than motivational, and points to standardization, coordination, and patient teaching as improvement targets.
pmc-13300797:
Rogue circles of DNA floating outside chromosomes may forecast how a cancer will behave, Filip Gajewski and colleagues argue in a 2026 review. These extrachromosomal elements carry heavy loads of growth genes such as EGFR, MYC, MDM2, and CDK4. Detection routes covered include FISH, whole-genome sequencing, and reconstruction software across many tumor types.

Because the circles lack centromeres, daughter cells inherit uneven shares, which speeds tumor diversity and drug resistance. Surveys find them often in glioblastoma, liposarcoma, and HER2-positive breast cancer, and their presence tracks with poorer outcomes. The authors back ecDNA as a risk marker, while warning that no standard, scalable test yet exists for routine care.
pmc-13300897:
E G Ferro and a large co-author team compare stroke risk between pulsed field and radiofrequency ablation for atrial fibrillation in a 2026 registry study from a high-volume American center. Recalls of some pulsed field catheters had raised brain safety worries. So the team examined 3,566 consecutive ablations from 2022 to 2025. Suspected strokes were judged by three blinded neurologists, and statistical weighting balanced the groups.

Only nine stroke or mini-stroke events occurred within thirty days, yet the split was uneven: about half a percent after pulsed field treatment against a tenth of a percent after radiofrequency. The gap persisted after weighting, at both seven and thirty days. Other complications, including nerve injury, coronary spasm, and fluid compression of the heart, ran similar between methods, and no esophageal fistulas occurred. The authors urge confirmatory studies and protocol changes to trim the cerebrovascular risk.
pmc-13301197:
S Kotoulas and co-authors examine flecainide's effect on complex ventricular ectopy in the prospective UNIFLECA study, reported in 2026. The subanalysis covered ninety-seven patients with extra beats and no structural heart disease who had declined catheter ablation and started slow release flecainide. Around the clock rhythm recordings before and after treatment tracked not beat counts but paired beats and short runs of tachycardia, the patterns that signal an unstable substrate.

Paired beats were present in about fifty-nine percent of patients at baseline and fell on treatment, with resolution in twenty-seven percent. Short tachycardia runs dropped by roughly two thirds in patient count, and over half of those affected were fully suppressed, while a few simplified into paired beats. About twenty-nine percent of patients achieved full or partial clearing of complex patterns. The authors support flecainide as a safe, effective option for this group.
pmc-13301297:
Christos Ch. Andrianos and co-authors grade brain gliomas from MRI scans without first outlining the tumor, in a 2026 methods study. Their network was itself designed by an automated architecture search over a three dimensional backbone, then strengthened with residual links and attention blocks. Training and validation used preoperative scans from 1,194 patients across four public cohorts, with a fifth collection held out for external testing.

The model separated low grade from high grade tumors with about eighty-eight percent accuracy internally, dropping to roughly seventy-five percent on the unseen cohort, still ahead of benchmark networks. Heat map analysis showed it looking at the tumor region despite never being taught outlines, checked against available hand drawn masks. The same machinery predicted a key mutation with about ninety percent accuracy and handled multi grade sorting respectably. The authors pitch segmentation free grading as a lighter path to computer aided diagnosis.
pmc-13301397:
Yiyu Zhang, Xiajing Yao, and Dechao Li watch translators' eyes to learn which language model statistics predict their reading in a 2026 eye tracking study. Twenty-six native Chinese translators worked both directions between English and Chinese, translating from scratch and post editing machine output, yielding 104 recorded sessions. The team pitted two model families against the gaze data: a language model and a machine translation system, each supplying surprise scores and attention features.

Time spent reading the target text was explained best by the language model's surprise at each word, a monolingual signal. Source reading leaned on the translation model's attention, with language model surprise a second. How long production took drew on both systems' translation surprise. Translation direction mattered more than the translate versus post edit distinction. The authors conclude that inside a bilingual task, the reading clock runs on monolingual predictability, while production adds the cross language machinery.
pmc-13301497:
Wojciech Karolak and co-authors extend minimally invasive valve surgery to operations on valves in a 2026 case series. Ten patients with combined aortic and mitral disease were treated through a five to seven centimeter chest incision, with heart lung bypass run from the leg vessels. Nine received double valve work and one a triple valve procedure, all without spreading ribs or disturbing the internal mammary artery.
