Typical scan signs are laid out for crush injury, outlet squeeze, sudden nerve swelling illness, immune nerve ills, and tumor spread. Core anatomy, step by step scan routes, and how to read size and texture signs come first, then per illness patterns and set scan plans. Proof grades for each use close the guide, which aims to lift daily clinic uptake.
pmc-13320497:
Jonathan Mertens and six co-authors present a 2026 study linking liver fat to insulin resistance in people with type 1 diabetes. Fatty liver disease tied to metabolism is common generally, but in type 1 diabetes, where insulin is absent rather than resisted, the connection was murky. Both conditions travel together more than chance suggests.

The team studied 39 adults who had lived with type 1 diabetes for about 27 years. A glucose clamp test, the gold standard, measured how well the body used insulin. Liver fat was read by magnetic resonance, and stiffness by an ultrasound based scan. Participants were split evenly by fatty liver status. Higher liver fat tracked with stronger resistance, independent of other factors.
pmc-13320697:
Praveen Barrodia and colleagues show in a 2026 study how fasting helps the small intestine heal after damage. Fasting reshapes gut germs, yet how those shifts aid recovery was poorly understood. The team traced a chain from one helpful germ to gene control inside gut cells in mice.

Fasting raised levels of the germ Akkermansia muciniphila, which makes a compound called propionate. That compound changed histone marks and gene activity in gut cells, expanding a pool of hardy persister cells that rebuild the lining after radiation harm. The chain suggests diet or germ based treatments could ease gut side effects of cancer radiation therapy.
pmc-13320997:
Arathi Shenoy and colleagues compare mouth germs and drug resistance genes in a 2026 study of severe gum disease with and without type 2 diabetes. Diabetes weakens defence against infection and may foster resistance, while gum disease and diabetes each worsen the other. The team studied 68 patients, half with diabetes and half without.

Plaque from under the gum line was tested for the red complex germ group and for two resistance genes, blaTEM and nim. Gum pocket depth and attachment loss were worse in patients with diabetes. The nim gene appeared only in the diabetes group, in 26.5 percent of them, while blaTEM rates matched across groups. Germ detection itself did not differ clearly.
pmc-13321497:
Wang and co-authors study why chrysanthemum plants cope poorly with cold. They focus on PLATZ genes, a family of plant regulators tied to stress response. A genome-wide search in Chrysanthemum morifolium found 41 CmPLATZ genes.

The team mapped where each gene sits, how the genes relate to each other, and which switch on in cold weather. They also checked gene activity in 11 plant lines with strong or weak cold tolerance. The work names key genes that may help breeders grow hardier stock for cold regions and large-scale farms in the near future.
pmc-13321897:
Majid Hussein Thadeo and George Msema Bwire checked how quickly HIV patients in Dar es Salaam move to backup drug treatment after their first regimen fails. World health guidance says the switch should happen within ninety days of a confirmed high viral load, since delays let the virus gain resistance. The pair reviewed records from three clinics in the Ilala District covering patients treated since 2019.

Of the patients with complete records, about 73 percent switched within the ninety-day window, while 27 percent waited longer. The most common backup regimen combined tenofovir, emtricitabine, and atazanavir with ritonavir. No patient trait or clinic factor explained the delays, and the authors call the gap a shortfall against the recommended timeline.
pmc-13322197:
Jiaojiao Wu and colleagues extend, in 2026, a family of artificial molecules that mimic DNA to fool DNA-binding proteins. These folded aromatic chains carry negative charges like DNA and can bind some proteins even more tightly than DNA itself. Until now they repeated a single building block, so they carried little sequence information, like a stretch of one base pair repeated.

The team designed four new monomer units meant to display varied chemistry in the groove that proteins read. Sixteen sequences were assembled on solid supports. Spectroscopic, crystallographic and modelling studies showed three monomers behaved as planned and loosened the molecules' conformational dynamics, while the fourth behaved in a more complex way. The modified mimics still bound a bacterial DNA-organising protein, opening routes toward mimics aimed at sequence-reading proteins.
pmc-13322397:
Justine Chan and colleagues review national heart attack registries in rich countries in a 2026 scoping review. Quality registries gather routine care data to monitor and lift standards for acute coronary syndrome patients. No standard method for building such platforms exists, so the team mapped how established national registries are designed.

Searches found national registries in 24 countries, of which nine stay currently active. Entry rules varied, centring on suspected or confirmed heart attack or acute coronary syndrome. Main outcomes were death and major heart events in hospital and at 30 days or one year, drawn mostly from discharge and administrative records. Shared aims sit beside wide design variety.
pmc-13323497:
Yan Li, Chao Sun, Yanqiu Wu and Xue Tian build a CT-based model to size breathing tubes for babies under one year, in a 2026 study. The work took place at Peking University People's Hospital. Tube choice in infants is delicate, since the airway is small and still growing.

Records covered infants who had chest CT scans before anaesthesia checks between 2020 and 2022. Scans spanned the cricoid cartilage. The team measured the narrowest cricoid opening. They also measured the gap from cricoid to the airway split. Regression then found which clinical factors predicted those sizes. Age, prematurity and growth measures all played a part. Two models resulted, aimed at personal tube size and depth choices.
pmc-13324497:
Guillaume Lamé and co-authors study how CT navigation gear changed teamwork in spine surgery in a 2026 qualitative study at one hospital. The imaging system guides complex operations but takes up much room.

Twenty surgeons, anesthesiologists, and nurses gave interviews, and the team mapped answers with the SEIPS work system model. Everyone valued better surgical results, yet the bulky unit cramped movement around the patient. Teams needed extra talks on positioning and airway access, and nurses had to learn image capture to protect sterile fields. Steady staff gained skill over time, but high nurse turnover made training hard to keep up. The authors urge planning for people and workflow, not just the device.
pmc-13324697:
Alaina M Bever and co-authors estimate how much chronic disease better habits could prevent, whatever a person weighs, in a 2026 cohort study. Body mass index often stands in for lifestyle, which can mislead people in both directions.

Three long-running United States cohorts followed 142,041 adults, most of them women, with an average starting age of 50 years. Activity and diet quality were scored and tracked over time. People in the top tenth for both habits had 46 percent lower chronic disease risk with lifelong habits and 34 percent lower with midlife change. The team estimates 34 percent of cases, about 1.1 million a year, could be preventable with sustained habits.
pmc-13325597:
Qian Dong and colleagues published a cancer study in 2026 comparing two forms of melanoma. Acral melanoma grows on palms, soles, and under nails. It responds far worse to immunotherapy than ordinary skin melanoma. The team used single-cell profiling to find out why.

They combined data from acral tumors, skin tumors, and normal skin. Acral tumors held a more suppressive environment around the cancer. Certain support cells there secreted collagen and sat beside abnormal blood vessels. Low oxygen and vessel problems lined up with the poor drug response. Lab tests and tissue imaging confirmed the main patterns. The authors point to this oxygen, vessel, and immune chain as a treatment target.
pmc-13325797:
Yu Zhao and colleagues studied premenstrual symptoms in young Chinese women in two thousand twenty-six. About one in three women face premenstrual disorders. Symptoms burden daily life and mental health. The team combined genetic and lifestyle information. Genetic risk scores came from large depression studies. Surveys covered drinking, resilience, childhood adversity, and body weight.

College students formed the study group. A standard calendar tool rated their symptoms. The analysis tested each factor alone and together. It also checked whether genes and life factors interact. Such combined risk marking could guide monitoring. Women at highest burden could get earlier support.
pmc-13325997:
Meng Li and co-authors pool studies on oral frailty in older adults, in a 2026 review. Oral frailty means decline in mouth function, such as chewing and swallowing, and it links to wider frailty and poor quality of life. How common it is, and what raises the risk, had not been pulled together.

Sixteen studies with just over thirteen thousand people were combined. About a third of older adults had oral frailty, though rates varied widely by country, study design, and the tool used to measure it. The measuring tool explained much of that spread. Risk was higher with physical frailty, older age, fewer than twenty remaining teeth, and female sex. The authors urge clinics and community services to spot high-risk older adults early. They suggest combined responses: mouth checks, nutrition support, frailty care, and targeted oral health teaching.
pmc-13326097:
Han Yan and co-authors build a tailored vaccine against melanoma from the shells of tumor cells killed in a fiery way, mixed with shells of immune cells. Tumor vaccines can rally the immune system, but weak signals, poor reach to lymph nodes, and weak display of those signals hold them back.

The fiery death makes tumor signals more rousing. A loaded compound then switches on a self eating path in the immune cells, which helps them mature and show the signals to killer cells. The mix gathered in lymph nodes after a shot under the skin. It curbed tumor growth in mice, both before and after tumors were planted.
pmc-13326297:
Losing control over cannabis use is a core mark of addiction, yet it is rarely measured. Erin Courtice, Nicolle Fox, Christian Hendershot, and Jeffrey Wardell validate a scale built for that trait. They followed 147 young adults who used cannabis and alcohol regularly. Phone surveys ran daily in three 21-day bursts, six months apart. The scale was given before each burst. Daily reports captured trouble limiting use, amounts used, and consequences.

One subscale predicted daily difficulty limiting use, which in turn predicted heavier consumption. Another predicted consequences through the same daily struggle. The scale showed no link to alcohol outcomes once cannabis was accounted for. The authors offer it as a valid tool for cannabis research.
pmc-13326397:
Mohammed Alshehri and six colleagues review eye surgery outcomes for retinal detachment caused by diabetes in young type 1 patients, a harder surgical problem than in type 2 disease. Their Riyadh cohort covers 339 eyes treated with vitrectomy between 2014 and 2022. They also propose a staging system classifying detachments by membrane extent, membrane attachment, and retinal breaks.

Complex detachments were the most common presentation, and accidental retinal breaks occurred in nearly forty percent of operations. Retinas reattached in about ninety-one percent of eyes overall, and vision improved in about sixty-nine percent. Eyes managed without internal tamponade, or with gas rather than silicone oil, saw the best visual success. Outer retinal integrity on scans helped predict visual recovery.
pmc-13326997:
Bird flu jumping from wild birds into poultry barns is a costly threat in British Columbia, Canada. Riley Oremush and co-authors search for the weather and bird patterns that raise that risk in a 2026 study.

The team focused on farm cases from the 2022 outbreak that were judged to be fresh entries of the virus, not spread between farms. They compared weather and wild bird counts in case weeks with control weeks for the same farms. More rain and falling peak humidity went with higher odds of a fresh infection. Wild bird patterns were tested in separate models. Knowing the risky weeks could help farms tighten defenses when conditions favor the virus.
pmc-13327397:
Sandeep Grover and colleagues present a 2026 bibliometric study of the Indian Journal of Psychiatry covering 2009 to 2024. Drawing on the Scopus database, they tracked how the journal's output, citations, and teamwork changed over sixteen years. The final set held 2,357 publications.

Yearly output grew at an average rate of 9.16 percent, and the impact factor climbed from 0.384 in 2010 to a peak of 3.1 in 2022, while Indian authors supplied 88.63 percent of papers. Single-author work fell from 28.65 percent to 9.9 percent as joint papers took over. Depression and schizophrenia led the topics, with a clear response to the COVID-19 crisis, and papers from some other countries drew more citations each.
pmc-13327597:
Jijuan Ding and co-authors report that tiny protists hold steady under chemical stress in wastewater sludge in a 2026 study. Using DNA profiling, they tracked protists under an antibiotic, ciprofloxacin, an antibacterial agent, triclosan, and copper ions, alone and combined. Protists are often ignored next to bacteria in treatment systems.

Protists kept a stable share of the community, between 6.35 percent and 7.88 percent relative to bacteria in the reported range, with hunter types most common, and copper even raised their numbers. The antibiotic alone changed little, and stress strengthened mostly friendly links between protists and bacteria. Their toughness may help whole treatment communities ride out pollution shocks.
pmc-13327897:
Shuhua Zhuo and co-authors ask when extra surgery should follow incomplete endoscopic removal of early colorectal cancer in a 2026 study. Added surgery is standard after a noncurative scope resection, but the best interval was unclear. The review covered 112 patients who had laparoscopic surgery after scope treatment between August 2019 and August 2024.

Waiting time showed no link to how hard the surgery was or to lymph node spread, and no ideal timing point emerged. Longer waits did raise the odds of leftover tumor, with an odds ratio of 1.09 per unit of time in their model. Vessel invasion and a raised tumor marker predicted node spread instead, guiding who needs surgery most urgently.
pmc-13328097:
Wei Wang and co-authors review measures for bringing TMS-EEG into clinical use in a 2026 article. Pairing magnetic brain stimulation with EEG reads cortical reactivity at millisecond speed, yet findings scatter across analysis styles and people, slowing translation. The review gathers time-domain responses, whole-scalp power measures, and rhythm-based indices.

Early response parts such as N15 and P30 carry set meanings, global and local field power sum up spread of responses, and phase coherence indices capture rhythm resetting after each pulse. Work in Alzheimer's disease, depression, epilepsy, and stroke shows the promise, while artifacts, personal variation, and missing standards remain the brakes. Shared protocols would let clinics compare results fairly.
pmc-13328497:
Jiahui Li and co-authors explore a new cell death route in minimal change disease in a 2026 analysis. The disease is the top cause of primary nephrotic syndrome, and disulfidptosis, death from disulfide stress collapsing the cell skeleton, had never been mapped in it. Public gene datasets were mined with four learning methods.

Four hub genes, FLNC, GYS1, INF2, and MYH11, built a diagnostic chart reaching an AUC of 0.839 in exploratory testing, and clustering on them split patients into two molecular groups with distinct pathways and immune traits. Lab staining confirmed MYH11 runs high in patient tissue. The system is a starting map only, the authors stress, needing proof in larger groups.
pmc-13328897:
Kun Hwang reflects in a 2026 essay on a visit to the Chipyong-ni Battle Memorial and what its stories mean for military medicine. Chipyong-ni was a key Korean War battle for United Nations forces. Hwang focuses on three officers, most of all Ralph Monclar, who had been a three-star general in France yet served in Korea as a lieutenant colonel.

At age 58, Monclar led troops in harsh combat despite his former rank. Hwang links that choice to his own path: 38 months as a junior officer from 1983 to 1986, then training in plastic surgery and 30 years in academic medicine. Service past personal glory, and care for soldiers, form the core lesson Hwang draws.
pmc-13329797:
Diane Berry and team found signs that predict dementia in older people with essential tremor. Their 2026 prospective study tracked thinking skills in 350 cases, mean age 79.5 years, for up to 7.5 years, with mean follow-up of 4.7 years in all. Older people with essential tremor face a higher dementia risk, yet little was known about which traits raise that risk.

Older age and worse thinking at the start each predicted dementia. Weaker daily function, worse gait, lower balance confidence, and more low-mood signs at the start also predicted dementia, all with strong significance. Neither steady nor grouped tremor onset age predicted dementia, against the earlier view of older onset age as a risk factor. The team gives the fullest review to date by traits studied and cohort size, flagging low mood as a treatable factor that offers ways to cut dementia risk.
pmc-13329897:
Dinesh Baral and a large team study how film thickness affects germanium-tin layers for infrared devices in a 2026 report. Such alloys can be tuned for light sensing and can work with silicon, but high tin content brings strain and defects. Five samples with about 15 percent tin were grown by molecular beam methods at varied thickness.

X-ray maps tracked strain easing as thickness grew. Light output tests suggested fewer harmful defects as films thickened, up to a point. Near 150 nm thickness, tin began to separate out, marking a limit in the reported data. The authors define a useful growth window from 35 to 150 nm for relaxed, low-defect layers at this tin level. Thickness control is central, they argue.
pmc-13329997:
Evgeni S. Penev, Ksenia V. Bets, Jincheng Lei, and Boris I. Yakobson simulate how sulphur changes iron particle clumping in nanotube growth in a 2026 study. Large-scale nanotube making uses floating iron catalysts plus a sulphur helper, yet the helper's early role is poorly known. The team built a machine-learned atomic model and ran collision tests.

Sulphur cut sticking for small iron clusters but raised it strongly for larger ones, the simulations showed. The flip came from shape softness: sulphur on the surface lets clusters flex on impact, soaking up energy and holding together. That flex effect may explain mixed past lab reports on sulphur help, the authors suggest. Reactor design could use size-aware sulphur dosing.
pmc-13330097:
Liwei Sun and co-authors built in 2026 imaging-based models to predict whether invasive breast cancer will spread, using texture patterns inside tumors. They studied 1,097 patients across three centers. Features came from mammograms and MRI scans, plus measures of how uneven the tumor interior looks. Separate models targeted any distant spread and spread to bone.

The combined model performed best for both outcomes and separated high-risk from low-risk patients cleanly. The main risk score carried the most weight in explanations. Interior unevenness mattered more for bone spread than for spread overall. Distance, shape, and topology features were influential throughout. The authors suggest such models could sharpen prognosis using scans patients already receive.
pmc-13330297:
Awa Sadikh Badiane and co-authors report a single case of malignant Brenner tumor, a rare cancer of the ovary with erratic behavior. Care for it lacks firm rules, and long term data on risk matched treatment are scarce. Their 2026 report pairs the case with a review of current evidence.

A woman aged 54 had a right ovary mass found by chance during a screening visit. Tests showed an early stage tumor with a high growth index. Her team chose wide surgery plus platinum based chemotherapy, tuned to her risk. She had only mild nerve pain in the hands and feet. Eight years on, she stays free of disease, with clean scans and normal markers.
pmc-13333097:
Prabhleen Brar and colleagues report a 2026 case of severe front-tooth injury caused during removal of an extra tooth, repaired by a mixed-field team. Injury during mesiodens extraction can badly damage neighboring teeth and their support, notably when imaging and surgical planning fall short. A 28-year-old woman presented with grade II looseness of four upper front teeth six months after mesiodens extraction. Clinical exams and cone-beam CT showed extensive root destruction and loss of supporting bone around those teeth.

The team chose a tooth-preserving course: root canal therapy with mineral trioxide aggregate filling, surgical apicectomy, fiber-reinforced composite splinting, and final zirconia prosthetic rebuilding. Follow-up at twelve months showed satisfactory healing and reduced looseness. The case stresses careful imaging and planning before mesiodens surgery, and it shows that even extensive iatrogenic damage can sometimes be salvaged without extraction.
pmc-13333597:
Hui Zheng and a large team of co-authors carried out a 2026 prospective cohort study of an integrated labor-delivery-recovery-postpartum unit at a busy tertiary hospital in China. They asked whether keeping low-risk mothers in one unit through birth improves outcomes.

A total of 542 low-risk women with full-term single pregnancies chose either the integrated unit or traditional delivery care. Groups were compared with matching, regression, Bayesian analysis, and machine learning. The integrated group had shorter labors, at 7.3 hours against 9.8 hours in traditional care, and far fewer cesarean births and newborn transfers. Mothers also reported feeling calm and relaxed more often, which supports wider use of this model for low-risk births.
pmc-13333697:
Giuseppe Scardina and co-authors examined how biological maturity relates to athletic performance in young soccer players in a 2026 study. Players of the same age can differ widely in physical development, and the team asked whether that gap shows across a full test battery.

Forty-four male players aged about 13, from under-13 to under-16 squads, completed jump, sprint, and endurance testing. Maturity status was estimated with the modified Mirwald equation, sorting players into pre, circa, and post peak height velocity groups. The post group beat both other groups on every measure, including jump height, 10 and 30 meter sprints, leg power, and VO2max, with large effect sizes throughout. The authors recommend that academies factor maturity into fitness profiling and training design.
pmc-13333897:
Digital twins are live virtual copies of real systems, and linking them across firms and fields raises safety worries. Mrim M Alnfiai, Reemiah Muneer Alotaibi, and Faiz Abdullah Alotaibi present TwinGuard-Sec in a 2026 paper. The framework aims to give twin networks shared rules for safety and privacy on fast 6G links.

One layer uses smart models to spot threats and checks identity without exposing private data. A second layer keeps a shared ledger that all domains can read. In a test bed of 50 nodes across five fields, threat spotting rose to 95 percent accuracy. Delay fell to 147 milliseconds, and privacy scores rose as well. The authors offer the design as a base for safe twin networks.
pmc-13334397:
Börge Schmidt and co-authors asked whether selenium status explains lingering fatigue after COVID-19 in a 2026 community study. Inflammation during post-acute illness can suppress selenoprotein production, so the team tested selenium, selenoprotein P, and autoantibodies against it.

The cross-sectional study covered 750 adults checked about 21.9 months after a PCR-proven infection, and 23.1 percent reported lasting fatigue. Low serum selenium showed in 63.7 percent of participants and low selenoprotein P in 89.6 percent, while autoantibodies were rare at 3.9 percent. Taken singly, none of the three markers tied strongly to fatigue. The pairing of low selenium with raised autoantibodies, though rare, showed the notable signal, suggesting joint pathways deserve a closer look.
pmc-13334697:
Zhihua Zheng and co-authors asked why exercise links to lower depression in college students in a 2026 cross-sectional study guided by Acceptance and Commitment Therapy. They tested mindfulness and experiential avoidance as the steps in between.

Students came from 11 physical education classes at a single university in Jiangsu, China, and 308 valid questionnaires were kept from 320 invited. Scales scored activity, mindful attention, psychological inflexibility, and depressive symptoms, with gender accounted for. About 20.78 percent of students showed at least mild depressive symptoms. Exercise was tied to fewer symptoms and to higher mindfulness, and the serial pathway through mindfulness and then avoidance-related scores carried much of the association. The results suggest motion helps mood partly by training present-moment attention.
pmc-13336597:
Danielle Lee, Nicholas J. Norton, and Adam P. Dale assess newer microbe-finding tools in a 2026 review for patients with weak immune systems. Standard lab tests can miss odd or mixed infections in these hosts. Gene sequencing methods scan broadly without needing a guess first about which germ is present.

Case reports show sequencing caught unusual infections that routine tests missed at first. Larger studies found higher detection rates than standard methods, though fungi such as Aspergillus and some slow bacteria remain hard to spot. Gains for patients vary, and cost, complex workflows, and data skills limit wider use. The authors call for clearer proof of benefit and shared work standards.
pmc-13336897:
Marilyn Esclance DMello and colleagues match battery fluid to framework cathodes in a 2026 study of lithium batteries. Their cathodes are porous covalent frameworks decorated with TEMPO radicals, which store charge at high voltage near 3.6–3.7 V against lithium in cell tests. How the salt anion in the fluid shapes that storage was little known.

Five lithium salts were compared head to head. LiDFOB gave the best balance of capacity, speed, and cycle life, thanks to helpful anion-linked storage and surface behavior. Binder-free paper electrodes carried up to 80 wt.% active material at loadings of 40 mg per square centimeter while holding about 1.3 mAh per square centimeter in the reported cells. Matching parts, not just picking stars, lifts organic batteries.
pmc-13337097:
Zexuan Hong leads a 2026 team building a virus toolkit that homes to one neuron type in Parkinson's research. D1 receptor neurons of the striatum drive the direct movement pathway and fall quiet in Parkinson's disease. Selective tools to reach them were lacking.

Screening a capsid library found virus variants with far better backward access along D1 neuron axons from the substantia nigra. Engineered enhancers then drove strong, specific gene activity in those neurons in both mice and a macaque. Using the kit to modulate the direct pathway produced pathway-specific behaviors and rescued movement deficits in a Parkinson's mouse model. Precise access tools serve both basic circuit science and future therapy design.
pmc-13337397:
Hyuk Kim and co-authors compare death risks between two fatty liver definitions in a 2026 nationwide Korean study. MASLD ties liver fat to metabolic problems, while MetALD adds heavier alcohol intake. The sample held 7,783 adults aged 20–79 years from national surveys between 2007 and 2015, weighted to represent about 7.6 million adults, with deaths tracked to November 2023.

Both conditions raised overall mortality versus controls, significantly so for MetALD with a hazard ratio of 2.085 in the reported model. Cancer deaths rose in both groups, while heart deaths did not differ clearly. In MetALD, heavy drinking and smoking independently predicted death; for MASLD, being female and having higher income linked to lower death risk. Splitting the definitions reveals distinct risk profiles worth separate management.
pmc-13337497:
Xiaofeng Jing and co-authors build a gallstone risk model from health checks in Western China in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Among 17,768 subjects, 1,673 had gallstones and 16,095 formed the control group. The team picked factors with a selection method, then raced a logistic model against a random forest, checking separation, accuracy, and clinical benefit.

The random forest won, reaching an AUC of 0.747 with specificity of 0.91 and sensitivity of 0.86 in the validation check. Its risk estimates matched observed outcomes well, and benefit analysis favored it across useful thresholds. Confirmed risk factors included bile acid levels, smoking, diabetes, and blood lipid and protein measures named in the model. Moderate but usable separation could support earlier lifestyle counseling.
pmc-13337697:
Ce Gou and co-authors review treatments for oral lichen planus in a 2026 article. The condition causes long-lasting mouth inflammation with pain and burning, and it tends to return. Its causes are mixed, so no single clear treatment path exists.

Drawing on 46 articles from 2020 to 2025, the review covers drug options first. Those include steroids, calcineurin blockers, hydroxychloroquine, hyaluronic acid, and mTOR blockers. It also covers non-drug options such as platelet concentrates from the patient's own blood and light-based therapy. The authors propose combined drug plans and alternatives, aiming to guide trials toward care fitted to each patient.
pmc-13337897:
Tingjie Liu and a large team survey health literacy in model healthy communities in a 2026 study. Residents of two such communities in Xiaoshan District, Hangzhou, were sampled at random. The question was whether community building links to stronger skills for finding and using health information.

A total of 263 residents answered, and the overall literacy rate reached 65.78 percent as reported. That rate sat above the local 2024 figure of 53.18 percent cited for comparison. Gains appeared for lifestyle, skills, and disease prevention areas, while first aid and basic care areas slipped. Marriage, chronic illness, age, and self-rated health each linked to literacy level.
pmc-13338197:
Nikolaos Gkantidis and four co-authors test if face shape ties to self-seen traits in young adults. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Six hundred thirteen folks aged past twenty to mid thirties, of like purse and school ground, had 3D face shots and filled set trait forms the same day. Shape was told by more than one thousand points, and fits ran split by sex.

Self-worth tied to face shape in women but not in men. No other trait or mind mark tied to shape in a way that held. The team read the split as born of growth or world roots, and bound the claim to this folk set.
pmc-13339297:
Yiu and co-authors count what Australia saved when cheaper biosimilar versions of three blockbuster arthritis drugs joined its national subsidy scheme. Biologic drugs are among the costliest lines in any health budget, and copycat biologics promise relief. Using public scheme data from 2015 to 2025, the team compared actual spending with a modeled world where the biosimilars never arrived, taking the scheme's own price-cut rules into account.

The biosimilars saved an estimated 562 million Australian dollars over the decade. One drug, etanercept, delivered most of the savings, helped by early entry. Adalimumab saved less than its huge use would suggest because its copies arrived late. Most savings came from rheumatoid arthritis care. The authors' lesson travels beyond Australia: in a regulated pricing system, when a biosimilar enters matters as much as how good it is. Timing and price rules together decide the public payoff.
pmc-13340097:
Morgan De Kleine and colleagues lifted prenatal care in 2026 at Kijabe Hospital in Kenya, where death rates for mothers and babies rank among the world's highest. Most such deaths can be prevented by better prenatal care. A chart audit found large gaps at the first prenatal visit. The project aimed to lift good prenatal care for new patients to 75 percent within eight weeks.

Two tools drove four two week cycles of change. One was a standard intake form built from 32 World Health Organization and Kenya Ministry rules. The other was a risk calculator sorting patients into low, moderate, or high risk. Good care rose from 21 to 77 percent, and standard care scores rose from 42 to 83 percent. The cheap form can be adapted elsewhere, with birth outcome studies still needed.
pmc-13340197:
Maria Stefania Latrofa and colleagues test a dual Leishmania PCR assay across three machines in a 2026 study. Leishmania infantum causes dog and human disease widely, while a reptile-associated species now appears in mammals too. Samples came from sand flies, lizards, and dogs.

A portable chip device, a standard lab system, and droplet digital PCR each ran the same minicircle DNA assay. Detection limits and specificity were checked on cultures plus 120 sand fly guts, 29 lizards, and 101 dogs in the reported sample counts. Comparing platforms shows whether field-ready tools match lab accuracy for surveillance where both species overlap.
pmc-13340497:
Meral and colleagues check a Turkish tool that flags poor food intake risk in children with cancer. Poor intake can raise harm and slow care. The team ran the check in a children's cancer unit. They set it against two trusted checks. One was a scan tool for child cancer. One was a full hands-on review of each child. Close to half the children met the bar for poor nutrition.

The new tool matched both trusted checks well. At some cut points it caught all at-risk children. At others it missed some. Meral calls the tool simple and fit for daily use. More work should test how staff and families take to it.
pmc-13341497:
Where fat sits matters more than how much, argue Anke LiuLi and research partners in a 2026 review of adipose tissue distribution. Subcutaneous, visceral, brown, and beige depots differ in cell makeup, hormone output, and metabolic behavior, and fat lodged in organs adds further risk.

Visceral and ectopic fat track closely with insulin resistance, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease, while lower-body subcutaneous fat can act as a safer storage buffer. Patterning reflects genes, development, sex, age, diet, activity, sleep, and stress. Treatments differ too: lifestyle change and GLP-1 drugs trim visceral fat, thiazolidinediones repartition lipids, and cold-based approaches stir heat-producing fat.
pmc-13342397:
Salomé Abdellaoui and colleagues tracked Janus kinase drugs in 2026 in rheumatoid arthritis in routine care, with prescribing shifts after October 2022 safety warnings. The look back study at one centre took in all consecutive patients starting a first Janus kinase drug, tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib, or filgotinib, from April 2018 to November 2023.

Drug staying power by Kaplan Meier curves was the main endpoint. Disease scores at six and twelve months and reasons for stopping were secondary endpoints. Among 120 patients, 85 percent were women with mean age 57 and mean disease span 19 years. Pre versus post warning starters show how safety warnings reshaped prescribing.
pmc-13342497:

pmc-13377197:
Md Alhaz Uddin and co-authors use machine learning to predict the strength of concrete mixed with steel slag in a 2026 study. Electric arc furnaces leave mountains of slag, and reusing it in concrete eases a growing waste problem. Slag's odd physical traits make strength hard to guess, so the team built models instead of running endless lab batches.

They assembled 730 samples with mix details and measured strength. Five models were tested, including hybrids that stack two methods. A boosting model scored highest on test data, with a hybrid close behind. Explanation tools showed curing time and cement content drive strength most. The authors say such models can cut costly trial mixes and support greener concrete design.
pmc-13377397:
Puteri Nur Athirah Megat Mohamad Aminuddin and co-authors tell of brain TB with a nerve palsy in a 2026 case report. A man aged 22 from Bangladesh had fever, head pain, mind shifts, and a droop of one eye with a wide pupil. Scans showed fluid on the brain and small dead zones.

Spinal fluid held high protein but plain sugar, and all germ tests came back blank. The team still called it brain TB, on tale, scans, and risk, and began germ drugs plus high steroids. His signs got much better on drugs alone, with no need for a brain drain. The case backs bold calls when tests lag.
pmc-13377697:
Jia-chun Tao and colleagues survey neuromuscular reversal and monitoring practice among anaesthesiologists in China in a 2026 study. Residual muscle blockade after surgery raises lung complications, yet monitoring and reversal use were poorly mapped. An online questionnaire with 25 questions, distributed through an anaesthesia forum and WeChat for 30 days with one response per IP address, yielded 3,168 valid responses.

Rocuronium and cisatracurium were the most used blockers. Only about 40 percent routinely gave reversal drugs, mostly neostigmine, with sugammadex used by only about 19 percent. Quantitative monitoring was routine for only 1.6 percent, while 98 percent relied on clinical signs alone. Higher education and senior rank predicted better practice. The survey exposes a wide gap between guidelines and routine practice.
pmc-13379397:
Gokulkumar Sivanantham and co-authors describe a 2026 study turning jackfruit seed peel, a waste material, into a useful plant-based filler. The peel comes from the fruit of Artocarpus heterophyllus. The team extracted microcrystalline cellulose, a fine powder widely used in medicines and materials, from that peel.

Extraction used alkali treatment, acid breakdown, and bleaching to strip away lignin and other plant parts. A battery of tests then checked the product's structure, purity, heat stability, and particle size. The cellulose proved highly ordered in structure, with a crystallinity measure above seventy percent in the results reported. The work suggests farm waste can supply a renewable filler for greener materials.
pmc-13380797:
Huanchang Yan and a large team present a 2026 analysis of a giant cluster in an HIV transmission network in Guangzhou, China. Large clusters hold a large share of people living with HIV, but their size makes targeted action hard. The team developed a way to split a giant cluster into smaller communities for precise intervention.

Using network data from 2008 to 2020, they split one component of 681 members into 34 communities with dense links inside and few outside. Every link between communities ran through central members of one community, which family-tree analysis identified as the likely source of the whole component. People with similar traits tended to cluster, flagging possible outbreak pockets.
pmc-13381997:
Eusebi Chiner and colleagues wrote a 2026 review of how older patients stick with airway pressure treatment for sleep apnea, where the airway collapses repeatedly during sleep. The condition becomes much more common with age. The standard treatment blows air gently to keep the airway open, but only works if patients keep using it.

Good use is usually defined as at least four hours on most nights, with best results at six to eight hours. Many patients stop early, and long-term abandonment is common. Among older adults who start, though, use can match or beat younger patients. The review describes a pattern where use rises into the late seventies and then falls, and discusses the barriers involved.
pmc-13382697:
Genevieve Crotty and Wasim Awal describe a 2026 case of a dangerous bulge in a stomach artery treated by injecting clotting agent through the skin, guided by scans. Such pseudoaneurysms are a rare complication of long-standing pancreas inflammation, where digestive juices erode nearby artery walls. Their patient was a man of 65 with chronic pancreatitis.

The usual treatment threads a catheter through the arteries to block the bulge, but his vessel layout made that unsafe. Instead, doctors injected thrombin directly through the skin under scan guidance. The bulge clotted and resolved on follow-up imaging. The case offers an alternative route when standard access fails, with imaging central throughout.
pmc-13383197:
Fangman Chen's team built a nanozyme whose power switches on under sound waves for precise cancer therapy, in a 2026 study. Natural force-sensitive enzymes tune cell chemistry under force, but artificial nanozymes with strict time and place control were rare. The team embedded force-responsive ferrocene units in a flexible frame to create the MRNZ device.

Acoustic shear reshaped the units, lowering electron density and steric crowding at iron sites and boosting peroxide-like activity. Controlled low-dose oxygen signals then acted as messengers to rewire cell chemistry and toughen stem cells against oxidative stress. Loading glucose oxidase inside hollow MRNZ added a second enzyme layer, pointing toward sound-triggered paired therapy.
pmc-13385897:
Helena Bilandžija, Kenneth Renner, Helena Ćetković, and William Jeffery study why cave animals lose their pigment. Their 2026 paper asks what mechanisms and evolutionary forces drive albinism that evolved again and again in caves.

Across annelids, mollusks, and vertebrates, melanin loss always came from disruption of the first step in the pathway that makes melanin. Yet cells able to make melanin are retained, in patterns like those of surface relatives, and they aid immune responses during tissue repair. With the model cavefish Astyanax mexicanus, the team tests whether albinism is neutral drift or adaptation, and finds melanin synthesis carries a real energetic cost.
pmc-13386797:
Zhongnan Xiao's team tested AI-based retinal screening in teachers and a retinal density marker for myopia, in a 2026 prospective study. AI fundus imaging enables large-scale retinal screening, but use in worker groups was limited. The team screened 648 Beijing teachers with fundus photography and systemic exams, using AI to quantify fundus tessellated density and other retinal measures, then testing links with refractive error and work factors.

Mean refractive error sat near minus two and a half diopters. Density varied across the macula, highest in the nasal quadrant. Density, near work at 30 centimeters, and eye structure measures each linked independently with refractive error. Near work beyond one hour at 30 centimeters tracked with higher density. Density showed moderate power to flag high myopia, at about 78 percent area under the curve, and linked with immune-inflammatory indices. The marker is observational and needs longitudinal validation.
pmc-13388097:
Ashton Bailey, Ryan Gibson, and Kristine Griffett review clock-receptor drugs against inflammatory brain disease in dogs in a 2026 article. Meningoencephalitis of unknown origin is a presumed autoimmune condition and a major treatment challenge in veterinary neurology. Evidence ties helper T cells of the TH17 type and their messenger IL-17A to the inflammation.

Compounds that activate REV-ERB receptors suppressed TH17 growth and eased disease in autoimmune models, with favorable safety signs. Those receptors also steer circadian rhythm and metabolism, widening their immune footprint. The authors map a path for testing such drugs as add-ons to standard immune suppression in dogs.
pmc-13389897:
Hatem Mousa Taha and Khaled Hatem Taha present, in 2026, a 63-year-old Palestinian man with Morvan syndrome whose blood tests stayed negative for the usual antibodies. He showed the full pattern of the disease: constant muscle twitching, extreme sleeplessness, fast heart rate, heavy sweating, and major weight loss.

Muscle recordings across twelve muscles showed the characteristic rapid discharges of this condition, while brain imaging, spinal fluid tests, and cancer screening found nothing. Validated tests confirmed no CASPR2 or LGI1 antibodies in blood or spinal fluid. Working in a resource-limited setting, the team built the diagnosis from the clinical pattern and electrical proof. Neurologists gain a worked example of treating a rare autoimmune condition without antibody confirmation.
pmc-13390197:
Runzi Yang's team tracked eight men with Kimura's disease of the eye socket, a rare chronic immune illness that usually strikes young Asian men in the head and neck. Orbital spread is rare and its long-term course was poorly mapped, so the team looked over cases at one centre from 2010 to 2025.

Patients averaged about twenty-one years old. Painless eyelid swelling was the top first sign, and eyelid and tear-gland tissue were most often hit, with dense eosinophil buildup on lab checks. Surgery plus body-wide steroids formed the main treatment, and the series maps return patterns that doctors can use to plan follow-up.
pmc-13390297:
Natalia E Jiménez's team compared seven automated tools for building draft genome-scale metabolism-linked models in multicellular eukaryotes, a task most tools were not designed for. They applied AuReMe, CarveMe, merlin, ModelSEED, Pathway Tools, RAVEN, and Reconstructor to a mosquito, a hamster ovary cell line, and a brown alga.

No tool excelled at both model functionality and eukaryotic traits such as compartmentalisation and organism-specific metabolism, with methods trading one strength against the other on network size, consistency, annotation, and speed. The comparison gives teams a practical guide for matching a reconstruction tool to their organism and goal.
pmc-13391697:
Trent Kite and colleagues systematically review, in 2026, artificial intelligence tools that predict recurrence in high-grade gliomas. These aggressive brain tumours almost always return, and no definitive treatment exists despite standard therapy.

Following standard review guidelines, the team searched PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science for studies using machine learning to forecast recurrence, then pooled key accuracy measures with a random-effects model. Neuro-oncology readers gain a combined verdict on how well algorithms currently predict return, which could support individualised therapy timing, plus a clear view of the variation between studies that tempers enthusiasm.
pmc-13394097:
Amanda Sandoval Karamian and co-authors scan white matter in newborns with genetic epilepsy in a 2026 paper. Seizures during the brain's fastest wiring period may bend development itself. Babies whose epilepsy comes from genes, with normal standard scans, offer a clean test of whether seizures alone alter wiring. The study compared nineteen such babies with thirty-nine healthy ones in a top-level intensive care unit.

A diffusion scan measured how water moves along nerve tracts. The epilepsy group showed higher direction scores and lower spread scores across wide tract areas. Those signs suggest the wiring differs even before standard scans can see it. Early wiring checks may one day flag which babies need the closest developmental follow-up.
pmc-13394397:
Hagita, Murashima, and Ohkuma use, in 2026, united-atom molecular dynamics simulations to watch strain-induced crystallization in polyisoprene, the polymer in natural rubber. Stretching rubber past a threshold makes tiny crystals form inside it, and those nanocrystallites toughen the material like extra cross-links. Experiments confirm the crystals exist, but their birth and distribution at the molecular scale have stayed murky, which the simulations were built to clarify.

The simulations captured nanocrystallites forming spontaneously from an oriented, stretched melt, verified against computed two-dimensional scattering patterns. Small crystals born during rapid stretching then either grew or melted away during the following still period at constant temperature. Crucially, whether a crystallite survived correlated better with how aligned the polymer segments were at the start than with the overall strain level alone. The authors argue that designing tough soft materials should focus on controlling segment orientation, not just stretch.
pmc-13394697:
Philippe Genereux and a large team model, in 2026, the costs of early valve placement in symptom-free aortic stenosis. The valve narrows with age, and risk climbs once symptoms start. Their model compared a tube-placed valve, TAVI, with watchful waiting across nine European countries. Inputs came from the EARLY TAVR trial and past studies, tracked over a whole lifetime.

Early TAVI came out ahead in every country in the model. It saved money and added healthy years of life in each setting. Gains in quality-weighted years were modest but steady. The authors credit the timing of costs, since waiting still ends in valve work. They back early spotting and prompt care.
pmc-13394897:
Wang and team examine, in 2026, whether ovarian function and fertility recover after anti-NMDAR encephalitis. The disease is an autoimmune brain illness that mainly strikes women of reproductive age and often involves ovarian teratomas, a type of tumor. Their cohort covered 106 women treated at one hospital between 2015 and 2024, tracking hormone levels, menstrual function, and pregnancies, with a separate look at the 23 tumor cases.

Tumor-associated cases were sicker at presentation, needing intensive care and mechanical ventilation more often than other patients. During the acute illness, 38 percent of all patients showed suppression of the hormone axis controlling the ovaries, usually as missed periods. Recovery was the rule afterward: hormone levels improved significantly during convalescence in the followed patients. Pregnancy rates ended up comparable, at 80 percent in the teratoma group and 83.3 percent without tumors, reassuring data for counseling young survivors.
pmc-13395397:
Pengchao Yang and colleagues trace, in 2026, a stress path that drives bone loss during swelling diseases. A cell stress arm named IRE1-XBP1s ran hot in bone-eating cell precursors in inflamed mice. Blocking it cut the making of bone-eating cells and eased bone loss in dishes and animals. Gene reads showed the arm switches on a serotonin carrier gene.

Serotonin, the carrier's cargo, blocked a self-cleaning process that restrains those cells. A common antidepressant that blocks the carrier also slowed cell making. A compound named 3MA softened serotonin's effects. In cells from patients with inflamed bone disease, blocking the axis helped too. The authors name a new drug target.
pmc-13396097:
Emma Valima and others study cell-fate rewiring by chromatin SUMO tags in a 2026 paper. How this protein tag shapes cell give was unclear, so the team tracked CEBPA-led flip of blood cancer B cells into guard-cell-like cells.

Joined chromatin, access, RNA, and protein maps showed a live rise in SUMO2 and SUMO3 tags at CEBPA-bound spots in early rewiring. The helper NCOA3 showed a sharp rise in SUMO tie and shared CEBPA and SUMO-bound spots. The work bares a SUMO-backed control layer in cell fate flips, with hints for steering cell kinds on demand.
pmc-13396197:
Matos and team describe, in 2026, a newly found pegivirus causing encephalitis in red-legged partridges, a game bird farmed across Europe. Pegiviruses are usually seen as harmless, so brain disease linked to one is unexpected. Gene sequencing of brain tissue from outbreak flocks identified the virus, named ParPgV, and microscopy showed encephalitic lesions, dying neurons, and viral particles inside neurons.

Two distinct strains circulated, sharing 83.78 percent identity across their genomes. Field checks found widespread spread from hens to their chicks across many flocks. Experimental infection of red-legged partridges, grey partridges, and lab chickens confirmed the virus targets the nervous system, and infected red-legged partridges developed cerebellar atrophy visible on MRI scans. Finding negative-strand RNA, the copying intermediate, proved the virus was actively copying itself in each host species tested.
pmc-13396297:
Roger Plaza-Clar and others weigh two seed-growth tests for Parkinson-type illness across labs in a 2026 multi-site study. This seed test spots Parkinson-type illness, and test brews may sort Lewy-body illness from glial-inclusion illness, but head-to-head test proof was thin.

In a tight two-by-two plan, two brew kinds each ran at two free labs. Spine fluid came from 60 people, with system atrophy cases plus Parkinson and Lewy dementia cases in the mix. The study scores match and illness sorting across brews and sites. Doctors gain a firm base for picking and reading these seed tests.
pmc-13396397:
Cai and team name, in 2026, the ion channel TMEM63B as a regulator of placental development acting through nucleocytoplasmic transport, the shuttling between nucleus and cytoplasm. The channel senses osmotic and mechanical cues. In trophoblast cells, the placenta's building blocks, it stabilizes transport machinery that moves cell cycle regulators in and out of the nucleus as conditions change.

Losing the channel weakened the Ran protein and its export complex with XPO1, trapping the cell cycle brake p21 inside the nucleus and stalling trophoblast growth. In mice, homozygous knockout pups survived at only 5 percent after birth, far below the 25 percent expected from Mendelian inheritance, and placenta-specific knockouts survived at 12 percent in the reported litters. The resulting placental dysfunction caused perinatal death. The authors frame TMEM63B as a pivotal link between mechanical sensing, nuclear transport, and healthy placental growth.
pmc-13396997:
Kshitiz Pandey and co-authors survey how artificial intelligence could personalize nerve-based treatments for heart disease, in a 2026 review. Cardiac neuromodulation covers techniques that rebalance the autonomic nerves, from stimulating the vagus nerve to silencing overactive kidney nerves, all aimed at hearts driven by faulty nerve balance.

Big trials of these methods have repeatedly missed their main goals, with many patients simply not responding. The authors blame blunt dosing, stimulation that spills onto the wrong fibers, and wide differences in nerve patterns between patients. Learning algorithms that read a patient's signals and tune stimulation to match are offered as the route from mixed trial history to clinic.
pmc-13397097:
Meihui Huang and co-authors gathered the meta-analyses on exercise for people on hemodialysis and graded the whole pile, in a 2026 umbrella review. Dialysis patients are often urged to exercise, yet the reviews behind that advice are scattered and of uneven quality.

Eleven meta-analyses, drawn from four databases through January 2026, were scored for method quality and evidence strength. Aerobic exercise improved dialysis adequacy, peak oxygen use, walking distance by about 65 meters, systolic pressure, inflammation, and depression scores. Resistance training helped walking and physical quality of life. Effects the reviews claimed for other outcomes, such as diastolic pressure, did not hold up.
pmc-13397197:
JaeWoo Park and co-authors printed microscopic OLED pixels in one inkjet pass, with each pixel walling itself off as it dries, in a 2026 paper. Inkjet printing promises large light-emitting displays without masks or vacuum steps, yet keeping micron-sized pixels even has been a stubborn problem.

Two solvents, chloroform-like trichloromethane and dichloroethane, were blended so that as the drop dries, the glowing material separates sideways from a displaced polymer underlayer and settles into its own compartment. Microscopy and chemical mapping confirmed the self-sorting. A single programmed solvent step replacing several lithography steps could cut the cost of fine-pitch display making.
pmc-13397597:
Augustin Murhabazi Bashombwa and others gauge hospital readiness for road crash care in Central Africa in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Well-ready hospitals with enough staff and supplies are vital for crash care, yet readiness along major road routes was uncharted.

Fifty-three hospitals along crash-prone routes in Cameroon and South Kivu province in DR Congo were surveyed face-to-face with managers on rules, staff and stuff, buildings, and training needs. Thirty hospitals were in Cameroon and 23 in South Kivu. The study bares gaps that ministries must close to save crash victims.
pmc-13397697:
Abdullah Al Habib and others name drivers of patient contentment in a Bangladesh primary health clinic in a 2026 study. Patient contentment signals health care quality and readiness, chiefly in low- and middle-income primary care, yet proof from Bangladesh public clinics was thin.

Among 508 patients visiting Savar Upazila Health Complex in April and May 2025, contentment was gauged with the short-form Patient Satisfaction Questionnaire, with social, patient, and clinic factors gathered by set interview. Stock and machine learning reads matched each other in finding telling patterns. Clinic chiefs gain locally grounded levers for lifting primary care.
pmc-13397897:
Sonu Koirala and colleagues characterized an enzyme that may help honey bees cope with pesticides and oxidative stress. Their 2026 paper centers on AmGSTO1, an omega-class glutathione transferase from the European honey bee, a vital crop pollinator often exposed to farm chemicals. How bee detoxification enzymes work at the structural level had remained incompletely understood.

The enzyme was most active in fat tissue from nurse bees and forager bees, and X-ray crystallography revealed its glutathione-bound structure with a characteristic active-site cysteine. Lab assays showed antioxidant activity against several damaging chemicals and binding to farm chemicals without breaking them down, suggesting the enzyme traps toxins rather than digesting them. The work adds a concrete defense mechanism to bee health research, though protection in whole colonies still needs direct testing.
pmc-13398097:
Suze J Te Hennepe, Eline M Voorendonk and Ad de Jongh ask whether autism traits blunt the gains of intensive trauma therapy. Their 2026 pre-post study covers 175 adults with post-traumatic stress disorder, a condition that often travels with raised autism spectrum traits. Hard evidence on whether those traits change therapy response had been scarce.

The programme packed prolonged exposure, EMDR therapy, teaching sessions and physical activity into an intensive course. Based on a 50-item questionnaire, 70 patients fell into a high-trait group and 105 into a low-trait group. Clinician-rated symptom scores were taken before and after, and the analysis tested whether change over time differed by group, a result therapists can use when planning care for mixed presentations.
pmc-13398397:
Christopher Sparks and co-authors build and test an electronic phenotype, an algorithm that finds chronic kidney disease in hospital records at scale. Their 2026 study uses four years of encounter and laboratory data from a large Australian tertiary hospital, excluding transplant recipients and dialysis patients.

The algorithm flagged 17,908 likely cases from a hospital cohort of 342,146 people, about 5.2 percent, using diagnosis codes, reduced filtration rates, or protein in urine lasting at least three months. Blinded chart review of 200 records showed diagnosis codes were the most sensitive single route, while filtration and protein criteria were highly specific. Coding for kidney disease rose steeply with disease stage. The authors conclude that adding laboratory data finds new, often early, cases with high confidence, though overall sensitivity remains limited compared with codes alone.
pmc-13398497:
Guilin Wang and colleagues compare two ways of watching kidney risk during ureteroscopy, the scope procedure that clears urinary stones. Their 2026 review weighs pressure inside the kidney against how much irrigation fluid the body absorbs. Both drive bacteria and toxins into the blood, the route to the dreaded post-procedure infection called urosepsis.

Pressure acts as the instant push behind backflow, while absorption tallies pressure, time and tissue leakiness into one outcome. Sheaths with pressure sensors and scopes with built-in gauges now give live pressure readings in theatre. The authors argue that watching one measure alone undersells risk, and sketch how paired monitoring could catch danger sooner.
pmc-13398697:
Kadeem A Knight and Cherian J Cherian present a teenager whose pancreas was cut in two by what looked like minor trauma. Their 2026 case report follows an 18-year-old woman who arrived ten days after a blunt blow to the belly, with worsening upper abdominal pain and vomiting. Pancreas injuries are rare, hidden deep in the body, and notorious for late discovery.

Imaging showed a grade IV injury: a clean break at the pancreatic neck with the main duct torn. Surgeons removed the tail of the pancreas and the spleen, and she healed without complications or later hormone or enzyme failure. The authors back decisive surgery when high-grade injury tears the duct, rather than watchful waiting.
pmc-13399197:
Izabela Feres de Oliveira and co-authors compared two tendon graft choices for rebuilding a torn anterior cruciate ligament, in a 2026 Brazilian study. Surgeons can take the graft from the hamstring tendons or from the peroneus longus tendon in the lower leg. The team asked whether a patient's age, height, and weight predict the length and thickness of the harvested graft.

Thirty patients were split between the two graft types, and the surgeons measured each graft before implantation. Hamstring grafts came out longer, averaging 28.8 centimeters against 25.8 for the peroneus longus grafts in the reported comparison. Peroneus grafts were thicker, at about 9.33 millimeters against 8.47 for the hamstring option. Body measurements did not reliably predict hamstring graft size, though younger and taller patients tended to yield longer peroneus grafts. The authors say such patterns can help surgeons plan which graft to harvest.
pmc-13399297:
Luise Longo Angeloni leads a large Brazilian team reporting whole-genome sequencing results for patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, in a 2026 paper. This genetic disorder, caused by faults in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17, produces skin markings, eye signs, bone problems, and a raised risk of tumors. Clinical diagnosis can be hard in young children, whose only sign may be a few café-au-lait spots.

The work sits inside the Brazilian Rare Genomes Project, a public-private effort bringing genome sequencing into the public health system. Standard sequencing already finds the responsible variant in most diagnosed patients, yet mosaic cases and structural rearrangements can hide from it. Whole-genome sequencing can also surface novel NF1 variants, incidental findings unrelated to the reason for testing, and occasional dual diagnoses. The authors present their cohort as evidence for what genome-wide testing adds beyond targeted panels in this disorder.
pmc-13399797:
Harrison Volaski and five co-authors test a grapefruit as a training model for keyhole joint surgery, in a 2026 study. Trainees must learn to steer a camera and tools inside a joint while fluid flows through it. The model pairs a grapefruit with active fluid control to mimic that setting. Twenty-nine surgeons and trainees, split into novice, mid-level, and expert groups, each did five set tasks on the model.

Scores rose with experience, from a median near the low twenties for novices to a perfect top score for experts. Experts also finished far faster and handled the fluid best. Senior surgeons who rated the model's realism backed it as well. The authors call the cheap fruit model a valid first step for skill drills. It could widen access to early training where costly simulators are scarce.
pmc-13400197:
Isaiah Hipel and colleagues compared long-term care nurses' quality of work life before the pandemic and deep inside it, in a 2026 repeated analysis from Canada. The team used Translating Research in Elder Care program surveys from 39 urban homes, fielded in February 2020 and again in December 2021, with 389 and 430 nurses responding. They modeled the change with two-level regression.

The pandemic sample worked more hours and reported worse core outcomes: emotional exhaustion, the central burnout component, rose clearly, and mental health declined by a small but real margin. Then the surprise: cynicism, burnout's detachment component, fell significantly during the pandemic rather than rising. Job satisfaction and physical health did not change significantly. Their practical conclusion targets workload management and mental health support for this workforce.
pmc-13400297:
Ghazaleh Tabatabai and team report the dose-escalation phase of a trial giving nivolumab directly into the brain fluid for leptomeningeal cancer spread. Their 2026 phase 1 work addresses cancer that has spread to the membranes around brain and spinal cord, a stage with high unmet need. Intravenous immune therapy reaches this compartment poorly, so intraventricular delivery was tested.

Thirty patients enrolled, 24 received at least one dose, and 18 completed safety checks across doses from 20 to 50 milligrams, with one dose-limiting toxicity at 40 milligrams. The primary safety endpoint was met, and 50 milligrams was chosen for the ongoing expansion phase. Median life span was 6.6 months, with quality of life stable. The trial establishes safety and feasibility, while efficacy awaits the larger expansion cohort.
pmc-13400697:
Mekonnen Sisay Shiferaw, Klaartje Somers and Zaklina Kovacevic review, in 2026, how the cancer gene MYCN reshapes the surroundings of neuroblastoma, a childhood solid tumor. Amplified MYCN drives the highest-risk disease, yet the gene itself is hard to drug directly. Attention has shifted to the metabolic and stromal dependencies it creates.

Single-cell and spatial studies show the tumor neighborhood is highly mixed, with immune and support cells interacting in complex ways. Cancer-associated fibroblasts, which build matrix and modulate immunity, remain poorly defined in this tumor and blur with tumor cell programs. The authors weigh fibroblast states, from inflammatory to contractile, and their roles in growth, immune exclusion and treatment response.
pmc-13400997:
Aibek E Mirrakhimov reports, in 2026, a rare benign heart tumor growing inside the left ventricle away from any valve, paired with a review of similar cases. Papillary fibroelastomas usually sprout from valve surfaces. Although harmless under the microscope, they are mobile and can throw off clots that cause stroke or heart attack.

The patient, a 64-year-old woman being evaluated for irregular heart rhythms, had a small mobile mass attached to the lower inner wall of the ventricle. Surgeons removed it on bypass and pathology confirmed the diagnosis. The accompanying review found varied presentations and attachment sites in published cases, with a strong preference for surgical removal of mobile non-valve lesions.
pmc-13401297:
Oliver Chinonso Mbaoma, Stephanie Margarete Thomas, Andrew J Macdonald, and Carl Beierkuhnlein wrote a 2026 primer on Europe's native mosquito species that can transmit disease, a group often overshadowed by invasive species. Transmission risk from mosquito-borne pathogens is rising at higher latitudes as climate and environments change.

The authors gather current evidence on native species proven able to carry pathogens in Europe. They cover where each species lives, which habitats it prefers, how it seeks hosts, which hosts it bites, how it survives winter, and how well it transmits disease. They also discuss habitat shifts, hybridization across habitat gradients, and the finding of non-endemic pathogens in field-caught secondary vector species, all of which shape future risk.
pmc-13401397:
Chao Han, Yifei Wang, and Shuai Guo wrote a 2026 letter about a study by Zhang and colleagues on kidney injury linked to polymyxin B, a last-resort antibiotic, in 325 Chinese patients. The original study found kidney injury in about a third of patients and named risk factors including other kidney-toxic drugs and the loading dose.

The letter's first concern is measurement: injury was defined only from blood creatinine changes under KDIGO criteria, ignoring urine output. In intensive care patients, who made up nearly 88 percent of the cohort, low urine output often signals injury earlier and more sensitively than creatinine. Leaving it out likely understated injury rates, especially early on. The writers add that nearly half the patients already had kidney disease, which makes the creatinine threshold for stage 1 injury harder to reach and further biases the count.
pmc-13401597:
Mohamed Elbadry and a large multi-site team report 2026 findings on familial Mediterranean fever in Egypt. It is an inherited autoinflammatory disease of recurring fever and membrane swelling caused by MEFV gene mutations. Attacks usually bring short bursts of abdominal pain, chest pain, and joint inflammation, and long-term amyloidosis can be prevented with colchicine.

The study enrolled 280 patients suspected of the disease at clinics of several centres, all with repeated fever and belly pain episodes pointing to the condition. Diagnosis rested on the Eurofever/PRINTO criteria plus gene proof of MEFV mutations, and patients not meeting criteria were excluded. The final group held 173 females and 107 males aged from two to sixty years. The authors chart the clinical picture, background traits, and mutation patterns of the disease in Egyptian patients.
pmc-13401797:
Alastair Kilpatrick and co-authors trace a student competition that writes science into Wikipedia in this 2026 paper. The ISCB competition, running since 2012, has drawn hundreds of students and postdocs into editing computational biology articles. Early years ran English only. Later editions added other languages and team entries.

The paper weighs how the contest now fits into teaching, and why keeping volunteers engaged stays hard. It looks ahead to large language models reshaping how scientific content gets made. Diversity and regional outreach also matter for closing knowledge gaps. The authors frame the contest as open science training for the next generation.
pmc-13401897:
Vishal Kumar and colleagues report early results of a modern nailing technique for fractures of the tibial plateau, the knee's load-bearing surface, in a 2026 prospective study. These joint fractures are tricky: traditional plates can damage the soft tissues they cross, while the Expert Tibia Nail fixes from inside the bone with multidirectional locking.

At a medical college hospital in Jabalpur between May 2022 and June 2024, 36 patients were treated with the nail. Most were men, about 81 percent, with a mean age just under 42 years. Road traffic accidents caused three-quarters of the injuries, and falls the rest. The main outcome was the Knee Society Score at six months, with simple fractures, Schatzker types one to four, pre-planned for comparison against complex types five and six. Time to weight-bearing, X-ray healing, and complications completed the picture.
pmc-13402297:
Aitian Li and team showed that a matrix protein made by tumor macrophages stiffens tumors and dampens anti-cancer defense in mice. Their 2026 work focuses on non-small-cell lung cancer, where tumor-linked macrophages and tissue stiffness both blunt immune care. Whether macrophages themselves raise stiffness, and how stiffness feeds back on them, had been unclear.

Single-cell data from human lung tumors tied macrophages to an immune-dampening niche and marked them as a main source of fibronectin. Removing that protein from macrophages in mice softened tumors, raised lymphocyte entry, strengthened anti-tumor defense, and aided checkpoint blockade. pmc-13402397:
Saki Fukushima and co-authors study how weekend style schedule shifts desync the liver clock in middle aged mice in a 2026 paper. Social jet lag misaligns the body clock with social time. Heat and hormone tests on liver slices showed distinct gene sets, altered by the shifts.
pmc-13402497:
Sirvan Elmas Dal reports a patient who developed air inside the skull and meningitis after oxygen-ozone injections given for low back pain. Such injections into the muscles beside the spine are widely used and usually tolerated well. pmc-13402597:
Xiong Xiao and colleagues modeled how vegetation and two-dimensional building patterns affect surface temperature in Osaka, Japan. Their 2026 study uses Landsat 9 data from August 2024 and OpenStreetMap building footprints at 100-meter resolution, without reliable 3D height data. The associations are statistical, not causal.
pmc-13402797:

pmc-13402897:

pmc-13402997:

pmc-13403597:
Bekir Rovčanin and colleagues reported in 2026 a fluid-filled brain tumor that looked exactly like a deadly cancer on scans. An 84-year-old woman struggled to find words when she spoke. MRI showed a 3-centimeter mass in her left temporal lobe with a dead-looking center.

Her speech cleared after full removal. Ten years of yearly scans showed no return. Only three similar cases turned up in their literature search.
pmc-13403897:

pmc-13404097:
Shengqiang Mao and team mapped how lung adenocarcinoma grows from early lesions to invasive cancer at single-cell and spatial detail. pmc-13405097:
Maryam Janbozorgi and colleagues run a 2026 pilot study on exercise timing and bone genes in diabetic mice. Diabetes weakens bone by lowering the activity of bone-building cells and quieting stem-cell genes. The study asks whether morning or evening training changes that picture.

Eighteen male mice formed healthy, diabetic and diabetic-exercise groups, with diabetes induced by diet and a low-dose drug. Exercising mice ran for eight weeks, five times weekly, in either the light or dark phase at moderate intensity. Diabetic mice showed higher glucose and insulin resistance and lower expression of the four target genes. Bone gene activity was measured by qRT-PCR alongside blood tests and top running speed.
pmc-13405397:
Shurong Pan and colleagues introduce WAVE, a 2026 method that learns from unlabelled heart tracings. Deep learning reads electrocardiograms well but needs many labelled examples, which are costly to produce. Their framework first learns the structure of the signal itself from raw recordings.

Separate branches capture each lead's character, shared projections join leads from the same wall, and a dual alignment task teaches links within and across walls. Tests show WAVE beating rival pretraining methods across settings, and holding up when only a few labelled tracings are available. Removing parts of the design confirmed each piece adds value.
pmc-13406497:
Xueqing Wang and colleagues compare how children with dyslexia and ADHD handle their own mistakes, in a 2026 study of 148 children. Four groups took part: dyslexia only, ADHD only, both conditions and typical peers, each with a combined inhibition task. Error monitoring was tracked through behaviour after wrong answers.

The two disorders split apart in the reported findings. Dyslexia tied to weaker error detection, shown by less slowing after mistakes. ADHD tied to weaker error regulation, shown by lower accuracy on the next try. Slowing after errors predicted reading character recognition but not ADHD severity. The authors suggest the split helps explain why the conditions often co-occur.
pmc-13407197:
Spine tuberculosis in the chest and lower back can look much like other spine infections on scans. The authors, a six-name team writing in 2026, built a scoring aid from plain blood tests to tell the two apart. The catalog lists the title in Chinese; the head gives the English form used here. Cases came from more than one center, split into a tuberculosis group and a group with other spine germs. Forty lab marks were screened by a strict pick method, then a leaner set fed the final score.

The score is drawn as a chart where each mark adds points toward the call. Curve tests in the build group and a held-back group weighed how well the chart splits the two ills. Fit checks and gain curves backed the chart for clinic use. The team offer it as a cheap first screen where scans alone leave doubt.
pmc-13407597:
Arvind Rajamani and team weighed a mixed-reality simulator for bedside heart ultrasound training among novice intensive care trainees. Their 2026 feasibility work in two Indian intensive care units takes on spatial grasp and image capture hurdles for beginners learning bedside ultrasound. An ultraportable mixed-reality simulator could add to patient-based teaching without burdening patients.

Simulator set-up took 92 seconds, all trainees liked its design and image realism, and ten felt it improved spatial grasp. Simulator-first trainees got usable images faster, at 8.1 versus 9.7 minutes. Hurdles included headset fit for glasses wearers, battery life, and alignment. The work backs simulator add-ons for novice training.
pmc-13407797:
Hui Zhang and team joined metabolomics and transcriptomics to find metabolic markers of early-onset colorectal cancer. Their 2026 work weighs tissue from 15 early-onset cases, 15 later-onset cases, and 15 nearby normal samples, plus gene data from 25 early-onset and 35 later-onset cases. A 10-metabolite random forest model told early-onset cancer apart with a cross-validated AUC of 0.916. Gene net study tied a module to Lynch syndrome, microsatellite instability, and PIK3CA mutations, while citrate cycle and central carbon metabolism routes were enriched at both levels. The work names four candidate genes and metabolites for early detection research.
pmc-13408197:
Jordane Goulas and co-authors examine in 2026 how a damage-tolerant DNA-copying enzyme gets switched into its most active form. The enzyme, polymerase zeta, copies across lesions that stall normal replication, and its main subunit is unusually large in vertebrates. pmc-13408497:

pmc-13408597:

Early in pregnancy their immune cells over-responded to an adrenaline-like stimulus, and by the third trimester inflammatory cytokine production ran higher. pmc-13408697:
Liang Shi, Boqiang Liu, and a large team report in 2026 a paradox: the immune system's first patrol against liver cancer can train the cancer to become worse. pmc-13408797:

Models with all three inputs did best, above all with photon doses at survival fractions of 0.1 and 0.2, suggesting a standard dose input in that range. pmc-13408997:

In lab aged human cells, the drug delayed recovery and triggered arrhythmias. Blocking steps in one signaling chain reduced the arrhythmias, and a drug that boosts a protective potassium current also helped. pmc-13409097:

Four themes organised the deeper analysis, covering life with the condition beyond the trial, the procedures themselves, and the support surrounding them.
