pmc-13410397:
Ting Cao and colleagues describe in 2026 a way the material around cells can steer them without ever touching them. That surrounding mesh, the extracellular matrix, gives cells support and signals, normally by direct contact. The team used a three-dimensional cavity setup to test influence at a distance.

pmc-13410797:

Diabetic mice treated with gel plus ultrasound closed wounds faster, with more nerves, vessels, and better-arranged collagen. Gene checks pointed to cell energy systems as a shared driver. In rabbit ears, the treatment also softened thick scar growth, hinting at cleaner healing.
pmc-13411097:

pmc-13411297:

pmc-13411897:

pmc-13411997:

pmc-13413197:

pmc-13414697:

pmc-13415297:

pmc-13415497:

pmc-13416697:

pmc-13417097:

pmc-13417297:

pmc-13418497:

pmc-13418697:

pmc-13420297:

pmc-13420497:

pmc-13421297:

pmc-13421497:

pmc-13421597:

pmc-13422297:

pmc-13422797:

pmc-13423297:

pmc-13423397:
Amber M. Franz and eight colleagues report a quality improvement project speeding the trip from ward to operating room for child inpatients at a large academic children's hospital. Half a million child inpatients have surgery each year in the United States, and slow, unreliable transfers were causing costly operating room delays at their centre.

Using the Institute for Healthcare Improvement model, the team ran repeated test cycles improving communication between ward, operating room, and preparation staff. Mean time from the call for the patient to finished preparation tasks fell from 48.2 to 43.7 minutes, a 9.3% gain, and process variation narrowed after the second cycle. Control charts showed the improvement held, giving other hospitals a template.
pmc-13423497:
Nobuaki Hoshino leads a ten-author nationwide Japanese study of how perianal inflammatory lesions, fistulas and abscesses around the anus, affect Crohn's disease patients who develop anorectal cancer. Such lesions mirror disease activity and may seed cancer, yet their effect on surgical results and survival was unclear.

Data from 43 hospitals, gathered between 1983 and 2020, covered 173 patients who had major pelvic surgery for the cancer; 135 had the lesions and 38 did not. Complication rates after surgery were nearly identical, near 46% in both groups. Survival diverged sharply, though: five-year overall survival reached 73.3% without lesions against 46.8% with them. The lesions, the authors conclude, mark a poorer outlook rather than a harder operation.
pmc-13423997:
Joshua Potman and five colleagues measure syntaxin-4, a protein that helps insulin granules fuse with the beta cell surface, in human pancreas samples across the course of type 1 diabetes. Whether this release machinery fades in surviving beta cells, worsening insulin output, had been unclear.

Staining of donated tissue compared four groups: autoantibody-negative and autoantibody-positive donors without diabetes, new-onset cases, and long-term cases. Staining varied between donors but ran similar in the two non-diabetic groups and lower at diagnosis. Among long-term donors, levels held up in the first year or so after diagnosis, then fell in those with four to seven years of disease. The pattern suggests the release machinery erodes gradually.
pmc-13424297:
Yan Zhang leads a fourteen-author team building paired-atom catalysts that turn nitric oxide pollution into ammonia using electricity. Single-site catalysts grip the molecule by only one end, which limits activation of this strongly polar gas. The team's design pairs a copper atom with a titanium atom on titanium oxide, exploiting titanium's pull on nitrogen and copper's pull on oxygen.

The pair gripped nitric oxide side-on with both ends at once, a geometry single-metal pairs could not reach. Performance reached an ammonia yield of 189.9 micromoles per hour per square centimetre with 93.7% of the current doing useful work. Live measurements and theory confirmed the side-on mechanism, a template for activating other polar molecules.
pmc-13424797:
Nishimura and colleagues compared in 2026 three ways to remove the bladder in high-grade bladder cancer: open surgery, keyhole surgery, and robot-assisted surgery. Quality was scored with trifecta and pentafecta bundles, sets of three and five goals covering margins, complications, and recovery. The team studied 192 patients treated between 2006 and 2023 and reweighted the groups statistically to balance their starting differences.

Nishimura found robot-assisted surgery came out best on most measures. It produced no positive soft tissue margins, against a small rate in open surgery, and far fewer major complications within 90 days. Problems tied to the urine diversion were also much rarer, and blood loss was a fraction of the open group's. Keyhole surgery did not beat open surgery on the big outcomes. Local pelvic return within a year was alike across all three approaches, the authors note.
pmc-13425097:
Yi-Hsuan Chiang, Sarah Winter, and Manjunatha Kalavala report a 2026 case linking cutaneous leishmaniasis with guselkumab treatment for psoriasis. Their patient, a 72-year-old White man, had two painless but itchy plaques on his left arm for three months despite topical care. His plaque psoriasis had stayed stable for five years on guselkumab, an antibody against interleukin-23.

Biopsy confirmed leishmaniasis and showed amastigotes lined along histiocyte edges, a pattern called the marquee sign. Tissue PCR identified the organism, giving readers a new reported association to consider when persistent plaques appear during biologic therapy. The case is a good prompt for care teams to ask about travel and past trips when new plaques do not heal as they should.
pmc-13425897:
Eyad Jamileh and a large multinational group reviewed cardiovascular screening programs in low- and middle-income countries in a 2026 systematic review. Heart and vessel disease kills more people than any other cause and falls hardest on lower-income settings, where screening reach and follow-through remain uncertain. Following PRISMA guidance, the team searched databases through November 2025 for observational and interventional studies of screening for cardiovascular or major metabolic risks.

Outcomes covered how accurately tests performed, how many new cases screening found, and whether people reached care afterward. The synthesis helps governments judge which screening designs actually connect detection with treatment.
pmc-13426097:
Cancino-Fuentes and colleagues showed in 2026 that magnetoelectric nanoparticles let weak steady magnetic fields switch on brain networks in a dish, at field strengths that alone do nothing. Steering brain activity without wires or surgery is a major goal, but current methods lack fine spatial and time control. The particles pair a magnetic core with a shell that turns squeezing into voltage, so a magnetic field makes each particle a tiny local electric source.

The team made the particles, modeled their electric fields, and tested them on living slices of rat cortex. Weak fields changed nothing by themselves. With particles present, the same fields sped up the tissue's rhythm and raised its excitability. The authors argue the particles lower the threshold for magnetic brain control.
pmc-13426197:
Ibrahim A. Bakari and colleagues describe a neck ultrasound pitfall in a 2026 case of lipoplastic lymphadenopathy imitating cancer. A 25-year-old woman had a slowly enlarging swelling at the back of her neck plus low-grade fever. Ultrasound showed several enlarged cervical nodes that had lost their normal fatty center and looked heterogeneous, features suggestive of malignancy, so excisional biopsy followed.

Tissue examination found reactive follicles with fat replacement of lymphoid tissue and no cancer, confirming this benign condition. The authors stress that imaging alone cannot separate benign mimics from malignant nodes, and biopsy remains decisive. The lump had grown bit by bit, with no pain at first, which shows why scans alone can mislead when nodes swell in the neck.
pmc-13426497:
Anna Majapuro-Hirvonen, Brent Rutland, and Jasmin Bosshard reviewed infusion devices for under-skin immunoglobulin therapy in a 2026 structured literature review searching PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar in January 2026. Spring-driven mechanical pumps were compared with electronic systems in patients with immune deficiency or chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy. Focus fell on local infusion-site reactions and reliable dose delivery.

Because direct delivery measures were inconsistently reported, the reviewers used end-of-study immunoglobulin G levels as a stand-in for successful delivery, aggregating data descriptively with bias appraisal. Home therapy patients and clinicians gain a device comparison where head-to-head trials are lacking. Home use puts the stress on ease and trust in the pump, since no nurse stands by to fix a jam or a leak at the time it fails.
pmc-13426897:
Rosenbaum and colleagues published a 2026 survey on video therapy after the pandemic in Germany. Video sessions kept care going when offices closed for distancing rules. The team surveyed licensed outpatient therapists in 2020 and again in 2024. Their final 2024 group held 296 therapists, with 117 answering both times.

About seven in ten therapists still used video sessions in 2024. Use sat far above the pre-pandemic level but below the crisis peak. Before the pandemic, only about four in a hundred had used video at all. At the peak, more than eight in ten reported using it. The authors call video a lasting but selective part of care. Video care now sits as a steady extra, not a full replacement.
pmc-13427097:
Catherine Varner asks how to keep Canada's emergency physicians from leaving in a 2026 commentary on new longitudinal survey findings. Among respondents first surveyed five years earlier, some no longer practiced emergency medicine at all and an additional 48 percent had cut their hours. Burnout and depersonalization stayed high without resolving after the pandemic, while national data show admitted patients waiting longer in emergency departments again in 2025 and nearly eight percent leaving unseen.

Physicians described helplessness and resignation inside overcrowded departments where timely, safe care feels impossible. Varner argues system fixes, not resilience training, must answer attrition on this scale. Staff who feel they can not give safe care in time are the ones most apt to quit, and that link runs through each round of the poll.
pmc-13427497:
Elise C. Bixby, Christine Banks, Lauren H. Redler, and Jennifer J. Beck tackle billing codes for shoulder joint surgery in young athletes in a 2026 coding guide. Lower limb problems dominate pediatric sports practice. Adolescent upper limb injuries and overuse still fall squarely in scope. Coding for the shoulder blade and collarbone joints is less familiar than coding for instability. Worked hypothetical cases walk through posterior shoulder impingement in a 17-year-old pitcher and other scenarios across the glenohumeral, acromioclavicular, and sternoclavicular joints.

Clarifications tie each code choice to what the operative report must document. Accurate coding protects reimbursement and audit standing for procedures surgeons perform less often.
pmc-13427997:
Sai Sanikommu and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, early trials of engineered immune cells against brain tumors in children and young adults. CAR-T therapy retrains a patient's own T cells to hunt a chosen target, and it works well in blood cancers. Solid brain tumors are a harder test. The review gathered eight early phase trials covering 74 patients, of whom 63 received cell infusions.

Targets included markers named B7-H3, GD2, and HER2, given into the fluid spaces of the brain, into a vein, or both. All patients had heavy prior treatment, and many tumors had returned. No deaths were caused by the therapy itself. Immune side effects were common yet reversible with steroids and related drugs. About two thirds of judged patients at least held their disease stable, while clear shrinkage stayed rare.
pmc-13428097:
Alberto Zambudio Munuera and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, cystinuria, an inherited condition that makes hard kidney stones return again and again. A gene fault stops the kidneys from reabsorbing cystine, an amino acid that then crystallizes. Fresh registry data from 269 European patients show how far real care falls short of targets. Only about 16 percent hit the goal range for urine acidity, and about 39 percent formed a new stone within a year.

The review covers genetic testing, a newer assay that measures how much cystine urine can hold, and gentler surgical lasers for breaking stones. It also weighs N-acetylcysteine, a familiar drug with a sound chemical rationale but no solid trial proof yet in this disease. Many patients stop the current sulfur drugs because of side effects, which keeps the search for add-on options active.
pmc-13429697:
ZuoJun Huang and colleagues quiet a gene called CLYBL to ease lung harm in sepsis, where wild inflammation and a upset body chemistry kill air-sac cells. In a mouse model of gut sepsis, CLYBL rose a lot in lung tissue and in gut macrophages, the clean-up cells of the immune system.

Tiny balls coated to look like platelets, the blood cells that plug cuts, carried gene-quieting RNA into cells, and the gene was cut back hard in lab and mouse tests. With CLYBL quiet, a calm-down chemical called itaconate built up, harsh macrophage action eased, and air-sac linings held firm, so fewer cells died. Lung doctors get a new gene target and a smart carrier aimed at septic lungs.
pmc-13429897:
Daniells Erazo leads a large French team reporting, in a 2026 study, real-world results for tofersen in a genetic form of ALS. Tofersen is an injected genetic drug for patients whose ALS stems from a faulty SOD1 gene. Nineteen centers in the national ALS network contributed 46 treated patients. Each patient's decline rate before treatment was compared with the year after starting, and blood levels of a nerve damage marker were tracked.

Average monthly decline on the standard function scale more than halved over twelve months. The damage marker in blood fell by about two thirds over the same span. Against a matched historical group, survival ran longer for treated patients and adjusted death risk dropped to about a third. Retrospective data cannot prove cause, yet the direction matches the drug's design. Registries like this one test whether trial promise survives ordinary care.
pmc-13430797:
Jennifer L. Ridgeway and colleagues study champions and early adopters of shared decision making for heart-disease prevention, a practice urged but rarely routine. Enthusiastic, skilled champions may pull peers along, yet their real influence was little described.

A conversation aid for cardiovascular risk reduction was built into electronic records in three United States health systems. Eight of fifteen affiliated clinics used a champion strategy, with adopters defined by at least two tool uses and superusers by at least twenty. Adoption and penetration were tracked across early, active, and maintenance phases. Implementers get a human map of how a decision tool spreads clinic by clinic.
pmc-13431497:
Peter K Vogt wrote a 2026 essay that traces where cancer genes came from and where the field now heads. Bird viruses form the root of the story. Work that began with the first found sarcoma virus grew into lab tests that could count cancer-driving strength in grown cells.

Bird retroviruses gave the young field rare tools, and those tools led to finds of viral and cell cancer genes, cell surface ports, and hidden infection tests. Work on mammal viruses soon joined in, and some genes found that way now anchor drugs that hit cancer with aim. The essay limits its scope to genes that drive growth when switched on, and it skips the brake genes that guard cells. Vogt closes by urging wider views as new tools reshape the field.
pmc-13432797:
Li and colleagues test isobavachin, a plant flavonoid, as a guard for the kidney and heart against high uric acid, the state behind gout. Uric acid lowers with the compound in past work, but organ protection needed proof. Their 2026 study combines network pharmacology, which predicts drug targets from databases, with docking models. It adds tests in kidney and heart cells bathed in uric acid, and a mouse model of long term high uric acid.

The screens pointed to NF-κB, an inflammation switch, and cell tests confirmed the compound calmed that pathway and protected cell types. In mice, treatment improved kidney tissue damage and cut collagen scarring by blocking a cell shape shift that drives fibrosis, meaning scar buildup. Heart injury, thickening, and scarring also eased. The anti inflammatory effect ran through two gates at once: quieting NF-κB and stopping assembly of the NLRP3 inflammasome, an inflammation trigger complex.
pmc-13432897:
Sidra Ghafoor and co-authors sprayed a building-block amino acid on maize leaves in 2026 to test whether the spray shields the crop from salt strain. Salt cuts growth and yield for maize across wide farm belts. Pots split by salt load and by spray strength, with plain water and no-spray sets for fair checks.

Salt slashed shoot and root weight and drained leaf greens. The strongest spray clawed back much of the loss, lifting weights and greens past the plain sets. Salt also raised two harm marks in leaves, while the strong spray cut both back down. Guard enzymes and a guard compound all ran hotter under the strong spray. The authors pitch leaf sprays of this kind as a cheap, scale-ready shield for salt-hit fields.
pmc-13433597:
Fatemah I Ammar and co-authors looked back in 2026 at 133 patients at a Saudi center. Each patient had blood plasma swapped as care for nerve diseases. The team asked whether daily function rose after the swaps. The swap clears antibodies and like plasma freight that drive harm. Charts spanned care from 2015 to 2022 across a wide disease list.

A standard daily-life scale read each patient before care and three months after the last swap. Scores rose with firm proof for six named diseases, from joint-nerve and muscle-nerve faults to brain swelling of immune kind. A mixed tail group showed no firm gain. Deaths ran under seven in a hundred, with none laid on the swaps. The authors back swaps for picked diseases, with the chart base as the cap.
pmc-13433997:
Ján Bíňovský and co-authors froze a tail-gripping virus of staph germs in 2026 to watch its base plate flex and fire the tail's squeeze. Such viruses punch germ walls with a spring tail to pour their genes in. Cold frames show the plate as core, wedges, and arms that bear grip proteins and tripod stacks.

On host touch, grip proteins swing and reshape. Tripod shifts free the core spike and weld parts, which bare wall-chewing zones of hub proteins. Arm moves run through wedges to the tail's starter ring. The ring swells, the sheath snaps to half length, and the tube drives a short span into the cell. Kin viruses of thick-wall germs likely share the play, the authors say.
pmc-13434597:
Hana Popelka and Daniel Klionsky untangle this 2026 puzzle in the cell's self-eating machinery. Autophagy runs two tagging systems that share one activating enzyme, Atg7. Yet one tag is made in far greater amounts than the other, and how the enzyme favors it was unknown. Working with yeast proteins in purified form, the team compared the two tag proteins directly.

The floppy head region of the scarcer tag turned out to guard its own tail and brake its attachment to Atg7, throttling its flow. The abundant tag's folded head does the opposite, gripping the enzyme eagerly and promoting the process. Swapping these heads rebalances the systems. The findings explain a long-standing imbalance and refine the wiring diagram of cellular cleanup.
pmc-13434797:
Ruikang Yan and a large team blend ranking math with machine learning to firm up transport safety choices in 2026. Multi factor choices for policy often wobble when judges weigh factors by feel. Their model pairs a refined ranking method with a learning step that cuts noise.

The learning step squeezes data onto axes that best split groups apart. Cleaner data then lets a grouping method find crisp patterns. A case study across Asia Pacific economies shows steady, scalable results. Planners get a tool that shows its work while it ranks. Resource choices gain a firmer footing.
pmc-13436097:
Jivraj and colleagues investigate Britain's coastal health puzzle in this 2026 study: seaside towns record some of England's worst health outcomes, yet living near the sea is also claimed to protect health. Using two national birth cohorts, people born in 1958 and 1970 and followed into midlife, they tested whether coastal residence itself predicts multimorbidity, meaning two or more chronic conditions.

The analysis covered 13,691 respondents from the earlier cohort and 14,683 from the later one. Growing up on the coast showed no link to midlife multimorbidity, but living coastally in midlife carried 1.21 times higher odds of later multimorbidity in the 1958 cohort, an association that faded once neighborhood deprivation entered the model. People who moved away from the coast were healthier than those who moved in, pointing to selective migration concentrating disadvantage in coastal towns.
pmc-13436497:
Christopher Slobogin argues that expert testimony about risk, common at sentencing, commitment hearings and some detention hearings, should face the same evidence rules as other expert proof. Courts often let claims about dangerousness in with little check. He sets four tests such testimony must pass before a factfinder hears it.

The opinion must be material: logically relevant, backed by findings that generalize, and sound in its method. It must be probative, meaning accurate, with expert claims held to a higher bar. It must add value beyond what the factfinder already has. And it must be presented in a way that limits misuse or misreading.
pmc-13438397:
Olufisayo Olakotan and colleagues evaluated STORK, a parent education program built to cut infant death risks in England's Midlands, a region with high rates and stark ethnic gaps. The program teaches parents of early-born babies, backed by a phone app holding the lessons. Their 2026 study interviewed sixteen parents and three facilitators at a Leicester hospital group between June and December 2024.

Parents said the training left them surer and readier, above all on emergency response, safe sleep, and infection control. They asked for teaching that is hands-on, early, and flexible around fragile babies. Facilitators agreed on the program's value and named its strains: thin resources, and content needing shaping for the region's many cultures. The authors argue parent education earns its place only when it fits family life and language. Their findings sketch how to spread such programs without losing families most at risk.
pmc-13439697:
Bauer and colleagues engineer mice that produce mostly daughters or mostly sons. Their 2026 paper borrows machinery from the t-haplotype, a selfish genetic element in mice that rigs its own inheritance. The team built a selfless version of its central responder element that disables the sperm carrying it, and placed it on the X or Y chromosome.

When the element sits on one sex chromosome, the sperm carrying that chromosome are knocked out, so offspring are predominantly the other sex and mostly non-transgenic. The authors stress what the design avoids: earlier sex-ratio methods compromised animal health, cut fertility, or required fully transgenic breeding stock. Because undesired-sex offspring in livestock are often culled, a cleaner genetic route could matter commercially. The authors describe the mouse results as a groundbreaking proof of principle for animal breeding.
pmc-13439997:
Pierre-Luc Fournier and colleagues ask whether rules and paperwork help or hinder nurses' agility at work, surveying Canadian nurses in 2026. Agile staff adapt quickly in a shifting system, and patients benefit when they can. Standardised processes might support adaptation by clarifying work, or choke it like red tape does. Survey answers from 2,173 nurses fed a statistical model linking standardisation, administrative burden, agility, and judged quality of care.

Care quality rose with nurses' agility, both inward-facing and outward-facing kinds. Standardisation fed agility rather than blocking it. Administrative burden did the opposite, dragging agility down. The authors separate enabling structure from coercive bureaucracy: clear shared processes free nurses to adapt, while form-filling for its own sake ties their hands. Cutting pointless paperwork is their practical takeaway for managers.
pmc-13441397:
Samuel Kienzle and co-authors study phase-dependent optimization of bioprocesses in a 2026 paper. A single fixed set of process settings often misses how cells respond to their environment over time. The team tests shifting settings within one run, a design of dynamic experiments approach, against keeping settings fixed throughout.

Using a monoclonal antibody production scenario, they compare the two approaches head to head. Static optimization lands near the center of the design space. Phase-dependent optimization instead shifts temperature and dissolved oxygen between growth, transition, and production phases, matching what cells need at each stage. The study shows why timing of exposure matters for both performance and product quality in fed-batch production.
pmc-13442397:
Bartłomiej Ptaszek and colleagues ask whether whole-body cold sessions change balance in a 2026 study of 12 healthy young women. Each woman stood on a force plate before and after ten cold chamber sessions. Tests used one leg or both legs, with eyes open or shut, to vary how hard balance had to work.

Some sway measures shifted after the cold series, most clearly path length and sway speed in the hardest stance, one leg with eyes shut. Load spread across the feet also changed in a few tests. The authors read the shifts as a sign that cold can tune the sense of body place, yet they stress the small group and lack of a control arm. Firm claims must wait for larger trials with random group splits.
pmc-13442597:
Choi and colleagues compare exercise patterns and high blood pressure across social groups in South Korea. Weekend warriors pack their weekly activity into one or two days, while regular exercisers spread it out. Their 2026 study analyzes 28,039 adults from a national health survey run from 2018 to 2023. It sorts people as inactive, partly active, weekend warriors, or regularly active, and splits results by schooling and household income.

Every active pattern tied to lower odds of high blood pressure than inactivity, and weekend warriors showed the lowest odds of the active groups in adjusted models. Schooling did not change the weekend warrior link. Income did: the tie between weekend activity and lower pressure ran stronger in lower income adults. The authors note the survey is a snapshot, so long term studies should test whether packed weekend exercise truly protects across income levels.
pmc-13442897:
María Estefanía Peña Giraldo and colleagues report brain vein clot removal with a stent tool in a 2026 case paper. A 32-year-old woman with migraine and pill birth control woke with a sudden headache, confusion, and right-side weakness. Scans showed wide clots in the top brain vein and in side veins on both sides.

Her stroke score rose from 3 points to 7 points as seizures hit. On day one, doctors threaded tools through her jugular vein, mixing suction with a NeVa stent puller. Six passes left the top vein near-fully open, with flow restored and no harm from the work. She left after 12 days with strong limb marks. At 34 days her function score sat at zero, which marks no lasting deficit.
pmc-13442997:
Tiantian Pan and colleagues test a growth-versus-safety trade in 22 Eucalyptus species in a 2026 study. Trees must move water fast to grow, yet wide pipes risk air blocks in drought. Young trees grew under controlled terms for six to ten months, with drought stress used to grade each species' pipe safety mark, called P50.

Fast growers showed weaker pipe safety and wider vessels that carry more water. Slow growers built thick walls and dense narrow vessels, which guard flow at a cost to speed. Home climate tracked both traits, since dry or cold homes bred safer pipes and slower growth. A world vote count of 34 prior studies gave weak, context-tied backing for the trade. No study in that count showed fast growth and strong safety together.
pmc-13443097:
Ashleigh Iwikau and colleagues show how migrant fish carry the seeds of fast form change in Galaxias fishes in a 2026 study. Some lines gave up sea trips and settled in fresh water, a shift that remakes salt handling, muscle, motion, and breeding. Gene, body, and behavior checks covered eight landlocked groups and their migrant kin.

Most strong shift genes sat clumped on one chromosome, a packed kit of co-adapted parts. Migrant groups held jackpot fish that carry the whole kit intact, at high shares. Fresh splits cut off by landslides in New Zealand shifted form fast, fed by those carriers. The authors call the kit a clear case of modular change, where one packed gene block lets whole trait sets flip in a few generations.
pmc-13443197:
Itziar Cenzano and colleagues track marrow wall and stem cells as a blood state slides toward myeloma in a 2026 study. The early state, MGUS, can sit quiet for years before cancer blooms. Mouse models that copy the slide gave single-cell reads for vessel lining cells and marrow stem cells.

Lining cells took a stress cast at the MGUS stage, before new vessels sprouted in full cancer. Stem cells lost their bone-making power early, and that loss held through the slide. A joint interferon program marked one model but missed its fiercer twin. A three-drug mix hushed that program, helped lining cells adapt, and revived bone power in stem cells. Patient checks found the same mark enriched across stages.
pmc-13443797:
Tingting Wen and coauthors propose a 2026 diagnostic framework linking three-dimensional city form to urban vitality, a link that simple density measures capture poorly. Using building footprints and heights for central Jinan, China, the team built multifractal metrics and a vitality index from population, venues, and road data. The link was then modeled with XGBoost and SHAP explanations.

The heterogeneity index emerged as a top predictor of vitality and stayed highly ranked across alternative settings, adding signal beyond standard shape measures. A segmented analysis found a stable sensitive zone near an index value of 1.82. The mismatch gauge flags places where built form and lived activity diverge, giving regeneration planners a quantitative triage tool rather than a causal claim.
pmc-13444497:
Capucine Habay and colleagues compare clot makeup in cancer-linked strokes against twin stroke types in a 2026 study. Cancer can spark strokes and can hide behind a first stroke. Their pool held nine cancer stroke patients, three with heart valve clot growths, plus matched peers with heart-source or artery-source strokes, 16 in each peer arm.

Pulled clots faced lab melt tests with a standard clot drug. Cancer clots held their weight at a median mark of 92 percent after the drug bath, against 9 percent for artery clots. Melt resistance rose with platelet and von Willebrand marks and fell as red cell share rose. A white clot subgroup, pale and red-cell poor, held all three valve cases. The authors tie clot build to drug failure risk.
pmc-13445197:
Xin Cheng and colleagues present a lab protocol that makes fear memories spread to safe settings in mice without making the core memory stronger, published in 2026. Over-broad fear memory is a hallmark of anxiety and low mood, yet standard methods blur it together with memory strength. Their design pulls the two apart so each can be studied on its own.

Mice receive two rounds of fear training in chambers that differ in shape, light, feel, and smell. Training in two distinct settings, rather than the same one twice, brings lasting stress-like behavior along with the broadened fear. The protocol then lays out memory tests and behavior checks, giving labs a shared way to probe how sharp fear turns wide and heavy.
pmc-13445497:
Lisa Schoof and colleagues ask how much yearly MRI scanning adds for people with multiple sclerosis who take the drug ocrelizumab, in a 2026 cohort study from Amsterdam. Guidelines urge a scan each year, yet disease activity on this drug runs low, and scans burden patients and clinics alike. The team counted how often follow-up scans showed fresh activity.

The group held 342 patients with at least two scans during treatment, giving 1,639 scans in all. Activity appeared in under two in a hundred scans, touching fewer than seven in a hundred patients, over a median of about four years on the drug. The number of scans needed to find one active case climbed steeply after two years. Yearly scans in patients without symptoms never led to a change in treatment.
pmc-13445697:
You-Tong Lin and colleagues test whether a chemical mark on RNA, carried in tiny blood particles, can flag colorectal cancer and its stage, in a 2026 study. The particles, shed by cells into blood, offer a liquid biopsy path that avoids tissue sampling. The mark, called m6A, is the most common edit on RNA inside cells.

Blood came from seventy-six patients and thirty healthy donors, with tumor tissue pairs for part of the group. Patients carried more particles and more particle RNA than donors. The mark's level sorted patients from donors with good accuracy and ran higher in late-stage than early-stage disease. High levels also marked worse survival, while the same mark in tumor tissue gave no such signal, which sets the blood test apart.
pmc-13446297:
Saime Güzelsoy Sagiroglu and colleagues put forward a brain inflammation idea for stuttering, testing immune signals in the blood of children who stutter, in a 2026 study. Stuttering disrupts speech flow with repeats, stretches, and blocks, and its roots mix genes with brain wiring. No past work had tied it to immune activity in this way, the authors say.

Blood levels of three signal proteins, interleukin-1, interleukin-8, and tumor necrosis factor alpha, ran higher in stuttering children than in peers. Those proteins drive inflammation across the body and can reach the brain. The team reads the gap as a first clue that immune processes may take part in how stuttering arises, and they call for deeper study of the link.
pmc-13446597:
Hang Yang and colleagues review microRNA396, a tiny RNA that reins in plant growth genes, in a 2026 paper. Its targets, the GRF family, steer leaf shape, root tips, flowers, seed size, and regrowth after damage. The pair forms one of the most conserved control modules in the plant kingdom.

Fresh work casts the small RNA as more than a growth brake: it tunes how plants meet drought, salt, and germs, bending its grip by setting and stage. The review maps where its gene copies sit across species, what switches the RNA itself on, and how crops might gain from fine edits to the module. The prize is plants that hold yield while standing stress, a balance breeders chase.
pmc-13448197:
Eloísa Felipe Fumero leads a team describing a prospective cohort protocol on vaccine responses in immunocompromised patients in 2026 work. People with blood and other cancers face the highest risk from flu and COVID viruses, yet their vaccine responses are often weak and mostly tracked through antibodies alone. Cell-based immunity, especially T cells, may be induced more reliably in this group and deserves equal attention.

Enrolled patients will have binding and neutralising antibodies measured with standard assays, while cell responses are probed with functional tests including flow cytometry and spot assays. Early versus late booster timing is a central comparison. Disease state, treatment and personal factors will be linked to response patterns. Recruitment began in spring 2025, with the platform intended to extend later to the newly approved RSV vaccine and beyond.
pmc-13448897:
Junya Matsumoto and co-authors investigate in 2026 a proposed brain-based subgroup within schizophrenia marked by enlarged fluid spaces in the brain and cognitive impairment. Earlier large studies suggested this EVCI subgroup as a step toward diagnoses grounded in biology rather than symptoms alone. Prior reports linked it to electroencephalogram abnormalities, rare genetic copy number changes, white matter spots, and treatment resistance, with favorable response to clozapine in some cases.

The present study compares cognitive profiles directly. Gene tests on the tissue matched the tuberculosis complex, the family that includes the cattle form of the disease. Sequencing checks backed the match. This infection can pass between animals and people. So the team urges attention to how it entered the herd, and how to stop it spreading.
pmc-13493797:
Jonathan Ericson and others model heat buildup during light-cured polymer printing in space, where weightlessness removes natural heat flow. In 2026, the study joins lab tests with data from the International Space Station and a looping flight campaign. The merged data confirm that weakened heat flow worsens heat buildup and defects such as bubbling and warping. Future long missions need on-demand making.

The model joins heat transfer, light uptake, and changing matter traits, matching lab heat readings. Applied to space tests, it recreated bubbling in one store-bought resin while pointing to flaw-free results for optical glues. Builders can use it to choose resins, contact, and settings that prevent excess heat.
pmc-13493997:
Du and colleagues explore a cell therapy for aortic dissection, a life-threatening tear in the wall of the body's main artery. Surgery and stents fix the tear mechanically but do little to heal the wall itself. Their 2026 study first noted that human dissection tissue, especially near the tear, accumulates cells resembling endothelial progenitor cells, the circulating repair cells that help reline blood vessels. The team then transplanted such cells into mice with an experimental form of the disease.

The transplanted cells homed to the injured aorta rather than spreading evenly. Treated mice showed less widening of the vessel, a more completely restored inner lining, and better preserved wall structure under the microscope. The benefits appeared in the early phase after injury, which is when dissection patients are most vulnerable.
pmc-13494597:
Preeti Lamba commented in 2026 on a study of live birth after transfer of chromosomally normal embryos. Lindner and co-authors compared women's own eggs with donor eggs in patients over 35, using only embryos screened as euploid. By holding chromosome status fixed, the study asks whether aging hurts reproduction beyond the well-known rise in abnormal embryos.

Live birth rates fell with age in own-egg cycles, suggesting normal chromosomes do not fully restore fertility. Donor-egg outcomes stayed steadier, pointing to egg quality itself: aging mitochondria, spindle faults, and chemical marks on genes may blunt development. Lamba praises the large multicenter cohort but warns the backward-looking design leaves confounders, from embryo grading to lab methods that changed over time.
pmc-13495197:
Hasan Burak Isleyen and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, whether the heart's end-systolic volume beats ejection fraction at flagging kidney strain around the time of a heart scan. Ejection fraction, the share of blood the heart pumps out, bends with heart shape and load. End-systolic volume, the blood left after a beat, may show harmful remodeling directly.

The team linked over a thousand heart scans from a large hospital database to kidney blood tests in the day around each scan. An injury marker appeared in about eight percent of studies, and in most it showed before the scan, not after. The volume measure kept a link with the marker after severity was counted, while ejection fraction did not, though both sorted cases weakly. The authors read the signal as a mark of illness present, not a forecast, and call any edge over the standard measure modest.
pmc-13495297:
Na Liu and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, next-generation biomedical nanorobots, tiny active machines meant to move, sense, and act inside the body. Older nano carriers drift passively, which limits aim and timing. New designs use chemical, magnetic, or sound power to swim and steer, built from hard, soft, mixed, or living materials.

The review covers sensing of the surroundings, group behavior modeled on swarms, and AI-guided control. Promising uses span targeted drug delivery, tissue repair, and combined diagnosis with treatment in hard-to-reach spots. The road to clinic stays steep: body reactions, long-term safety, mass production, and unclear rules all block the way. The authors set priorities such as bodies that dissolve after use, shared test standards, and links with imaging and digital medicine, so the field can move from lab promise toward safe care.
pmc-13495597:
Dragan Nikolić and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a preoperative score that estimates a patient's risk of varicose veins returning after open surgery. Recurrence strikes a fifth to three fifths of patients within five years, yet no simple validated score existed to size up risk beforehand. The team reviewed operations at one center across two decades, tracking over ten thousand legs with full five-year follow-up.

One in four legs saw veins return within five years, and most of those patients had another procedure. Six features known before surgery carried the prediction, including reflux in a front branch vein and faulty perforator veins, and the team compressed them into a simple whole-number score. Checks within the data supported the score's stability. The authors offer it for counseling patients and planning follow-up, while noting it still needs testing at other centers.
pmc-13499397:
Dandan Geng and colleagues explore in 2026 why some small meat ducks grow just as well on less feed. Their yardstick is residual feed intake, a measure capturing efficiency beyond growth rate alone. From 500 day-old ducks, 420 healthy birds were housed singly from day 21 to day 42 to record intake. Efficient and inefficient groups were then compared across blood chemistry, gut microbes, gut chemicals, and brain gene activity.

Efficient ducks ate less and converted feed better, with lower blood fat levels, while gaining the same weight as inefficient peers. Their gut communities leaned toward groups skilled at breaking down complex carbohydrates and making energy-related compounds, and their gut chemical profiles differed in fat and bile-related molecules. Brain tissue in the hypothalamus, a feeding control centre, showed altered genes for appetite signals and serotonin production, linking gut and brain in one efficiency picture.
pmc-13499697: Hywel Williams and co-authors discuss how to build trustworthy AI for climate services at scale. Demand for climate data and advice is growing fast, and generative AI could widen access. Two prototype systems show how AI can open climate data, aid choices, and cut staff load. The authors flag worries about duty, output quality, and trust in such systems. They tie sound build habits to three aims: that outputs matter to users, ring true, and carry fair standing.
pmc-13499797:
Ebraam Kamel leads a team that tests a drug and its break down part. Their work from twenty twenty-six deals with gliclazide, used for type two diabetes. The part forms when the drug sits in base fluid.

The team used light based tests that need no split step first. Two math tricks pulled apart the mixed light signals. Tests were done in ethanol, a safe and green fluid. Checks met world guide rules for truth and repeat results. Scores for green and fit for use are also given. The tests offer a cheap, clean way to check drug quality.
pmc-13500397:
Akari Tachibana and others fix PCR primers that failed to detect the cattle disease agent Mycoplasma mycoides subtype mycoides. In 2026, the study traces the failure to misfits between manual-suggested primers and target codes in a tamed strain, then designs fixed primers and tests them with cutting enzyme analysis. Catchy cattle lung illness is a severe, must-report breathing disease.

The new primers copied target regions well from Mycoplasma mycoides strains, and cutting patterns told apart the cattle subtype from the goat subtype capri. Reliable finding strengthens readiness for future outbreaks, including in countries like Japan where the disease has been wiped out but could re-enter through farm animal trade.
pmc-13500497:
Érika M Pereira and colleagues survey in 2026 Brazilian eye doctors about barriers to treating young children and their appetite for digital training. Children's eye care is understudied and hard to access in Brazil, so the team sent a ten-question online survey through the national ophthalmology council between September and November 2022. Of 496 invited doctors, 315 completed the survey, most with over a decade in practice, and answers were analysed descriptively.

About a third of respondents did not treat children under five, mainly citing insufficient paediatric training or the long consultations children need in their reported reasons. The remaining two thirds did see young children. Interest in an online paediatric training tool ran high across the whole sample, including among doctors already treating children. The authors propose digital platforms as a way to widen specialist access in underserved regions.
pmc-13500897:
Zhang and colleagues scanned the brains of children with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. They asked whether social problems track with how evenly, rather than how strongly, the amygdala connects to the brain. Their 2026 study compared three groups of children: fifty-three with the disorder plus social dysfunction, seventy-one with ADHD alone, and seventy-two healthy controls. They measured average and time-varying connectivity of amygdala subregions.

Zhang found no group gaps in static connectivity. The socially impaired group showed greater moment-to-moment variability in connections between the basolateral amygdala and both a visual area and a frontal control area. The pattern followed a gradient across the three groups. The link between that variability and social drive scores depended on group, while attention symptoms showed no such link. The authors propose shaky amygdala-visual coordination as a neural feature marking impaired children within the disorder.
pmc-13501597:
Seoyoung Baek and colleagues examined what first aid nursing officers in South Korean military clinics need to learn. Their 2026 mixed-methods study built a full list of first aid tasks for these clinics. The team reviewed past work and records of emergency room visits. They also held focus groups and ran a nationwide survey of nursing officers.

The study found 79 first aid tasks in all. Most were direct nursing duties, and the rest dealt with emergency management. Two methods for ranking needs agreed on 16 high-priority tasks. Those tasks covered brain, chest, and spinal injuries, shock, burns, bleeding, and drowning. The authors call for structured training built for the military clinic setting.
pmc-13501897:
Gu and colleagues tested whether a ratio of two routine blood tests predicts death in patients hospitalized with acute worsening of chronic heart failure. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 342 patients at a Chinese hospital followed for a median of sixteen months. The ratio divides an inflammation marker, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, by albumin, a protein that falls with poor nutrition and illness.

Gu found ninety-five patients died during follow-up, and higher ratios were independently tied to death: each standard-deviation rise carried about forty percent higher risk. The high-ratio group faced roughly three quarters higher risk than the low group. Survival curves separated clearly, and the association held across subgroups and sensitivity analyses, though the ratio's own predictive accuracy was modest. Because both inputs are cheap, the authors propose the ratio as a practical add-on for flagging high-risk patients for monitoring.
pmc-13501997:
Maria Dolores Salinas and co-authors report a 2026 study on blocking a cell cleanup path to slow glioblastoma, the most aggressive brain cancer. Vessel wall cells near the tumor are pushed by tumor cells to overrun one cleanup route. That shift helps the tumor hold cell contacts and dodges immune attack.

The team dosed mice with a peptide known to calm the same overrun path in immune cells. The peptide reset the vessel cells, broke their contacts with tumor cells, and turned their output toxic to the tumor. One secreted protein, tau, stood out as a main part of that output. The work names tau release as a key lever in the tumor surroundings.
pmc-13502397:
Tianshu Liu, Yiting Cai, and Baiqin Zhao report a lung surgery patient whose lingering chest fluid leak came from an injury outside the usual dissection zone. Their case report appeared in two thousand twenty-six. The fluid was chyle, leaked from the thoracic duct. Such leaks after lung resection are rare and usually follow direct duct injury.

The patient had a thoracoscopic removal of part of the right upper lobe, with lymph node clearing. Drainage and a low-fat diet failed to stop the leak. A second operation found the true culprit: a surgical stapler had overreached while dividing lung tissue. Its line had nicked the neighboring duct. The authors call the mechanism unreported until now. They urge surgeons to watch staple lines near the duct.
pmc-13502797:
Willow Pastard and five co-authors called in 2026 for kinder, patient-first wording in skin care and research. Words in medical records shape how doctors treat patients. Doubting quotes around reported symptoms appear more often in notes on women than on men. Stigma tied to skin conditions can also push patients to skip care they need.

Patients now read their own records more often, so they meet this wording face to face. The authors say bias in notes can be measured, not just felt, and families can push for clearer text. They urge the skin field to keep building and using shared guides for fair wording. The aim is care where women feel believed and stay engaged.
pmc-13503097:
Xudong Li and colleagues built a gradient gel that helps broken bones rebuild themselves. Big bone defects cannot heal alone. Their gel starts from a shrimp-shell-derived polymer, carboxymethyl chitosan, laced with tiny mineral particles laid out in a gradient.

In dishes, the mineral gel pushed bone stem cells to grow and mature, switching on key bone genes. In rats with thigh bone defects, implants sparked more new bone and better inner structure, with a one percent mineral load working best. A scaffold that fades as bone grows could one day spare patients a second surgery.
pmc-13503397:
Vitor Almeida and co-authors assign the NMR signals of a tick protein's active domain in a 2026 paper. Amblyomin-X, from a Brazilian tick, blocks a blood clotting factor and interests drug developers. How it grips its target is poorly understood, and signal assignment is the first step of NMR structure work.

Multidimensional spectra yielded nearly complete backbone assignments and most side-chain ones. The signal spread showed a well-folded protein in solution, and shift-based analysis matched the expected Kunitz fold. With the map drawn, the team can now locate exactly where the clotting factor binds. Assignment papers are quiet infrastructure for structural biology.
pmc-13503697:
S. Alsalmi presents a 2026 simulation study of clear shields that block gamma rays. Such shields serve in medical scans and nuclear medicine, where staff must see through the barrier. The design stacks layers whose atoms grow heavier across the stack, a plan called graded-Z.

The stack joins a bismuth-rich glass, a lutetium garnet layer, and silica. Computer runs with the Geant4 tool kit tested rays from low to high energy and matched the stack to a standard glass of the same weight per area. The stack blocked more rays and cut the depth needed to halve a beam. Light given off by the layers and the paths of rays were also tracked. One flaw stood out: at high energy, more rays leaked straight through.
pmc-13503797:
Bryce G. Inman leads a team that mapped the thickness of mucus in three dimensions without disturbing it, in a 2026 study. Bacteria live in mucus on sea particles, plants, and animals, and the gel's texture shapes what they do. Older methods tear the gel and blur those spatial links.

Their tool uses dye molecules that spin less freely in thick gel, read under a microscope that scans in depth. Maps showed mucus from two algae types with distinct builds, one packed and one patchy, each with its own pattern of bacterial settlement. A jellyfish wore a mucus coat that may hold its own microbes while keeping them off its skin. The method gives a physical frame for flows of food and carbon.
pmc-13504797:
Jingjing Li leads a team weighing long-term ovarian risks of birth control pills in women with polycystic ovary syndrome, in a 2026 study. The syndrome is a common hormone disorder, and the pill is a mainstay treatment. Whether years of pill use wear down the ovary's egg reserve was unclear.

The team joined clinic data for 336 patients with a sweep of more than three thousand adverse event reports. Longer pill use tracked with higher risk of early ovarian failure. Past metformin use, a common companion drug, tracked with lower odds of ovarian decline. Computer models suggested the pill touches ovary-harm pathways, while metformin may block some of those contacts. The authors call for forward-looking trials before practice changes.
pmc-13504897:
Vivek Nambiar and co-authors measure in 2026 the toll of stroke on tea-garden communities in Assam, northeast India. These tea-tribe residents face poverty, thin access to formal care, and distinct customs, and their stroke burden had gone largely uncounted. Health workers surveyed households door to door across five estates from mid 2024 to mid 2025.

Suspected cases were screened by symptoms and confirmed by a senior neurologist over teleconsult, with scans where possible. The study counts diagnosed stroke, maps the physical and mental disabilities it leaves, and charts gaps in care. Survey factors were also combined into a simple scoring rule for spotting prevalent stroke.
pmc-13504997:
Ho and colleagues develop a spit-based screening test for periodontitis, the gum disease that loosens teeth, built from a questionnaire plus saliva chemistry fed into machine learning. Clinic probing is accurate but needs a dentist, so early disease slips by. Their 2026 study recruited 77 adults and classified them by examination as healthy, gingivitis, or periodontitis. It measured six inflammatory saliva markers and trained three model types on different combinations of answers, background data, and chemistry.

A random forest model pairing the questionnaire with saliva markers performed best. It separated periodontitis from the rest with solid accuracy on the standard discrimination measure, and it had the highest precision among the models tried. Plain statistics and a simpler Bayes model trailed behind in the ten-fold validation. Adding background demographics on top of chemistry did not help further, which keeps the test lean.
pmc-13506097:
Shaista Salman Guraya and colleagues examined what speaking up really means inside a multicultural academic health system. Hospitals urge staff to voice safety concerns, yet the behaviour stays rare despite years of training programmes. The team ran a critical discourse analysis of interviews with seventeen healthcare professionals from varied backgrounds.

Four ways of defining voice emerged, backed by eight patterns of reasoning that justified speaking or staying silent. Loyalty, conscience, professional duty, and emotional honesty all appeared, and a local practice of using personal connections, called wasta, worked as social capital rather than corruption. Only one pattern, strongest among residents, framed speaking up as self-destruction that threatened a career. The authors argue voice is a situated judgement shaped by hierarchy and relationships, not a skill that training alone can install.
pmc-13506597:
J G Chen and colleagues pool, in a 2026 review, evidence on whether excess body weight worsens short-term results after keyhole surgery for rectal cancer. Their search found 26 studies with 7172 patients that compared people classed as overweight or obese with lighter patients. All operations used small-incision or robot-assisted methods rather than open surgery.

Patients with excess weight had more switches to open surgery, longer operating times, more problems after surgery, and more readmissions to hospital. Stay length, blood loss, wound infection, and joint leaks showed no clear gap. The authors call for careful risk checks and preparation before surgery for this higher-risk group.
pmc-13507097:
Hui Yin leads a 2026 field study in Chengdu, China, on how sky view factor, the share of sky visible from ground level, shapes comfort in streets and parks. Teams paired climate sensors with surveys of 1692 walkers in both settings under matched weather. Heat comfort was judged with a felt-temperature scale that blends heat, wind, and sun.

Walkers felt neutral at higher felt temperatures in streets than in parks. In streets, surface brightness drove heat comfort most, while sky view led in parks. Higher sky view linked to more fine dust in street canyons yet cleaner air in the park. Design rules must fit each setting rather than follow one formula.
pmc-13507197:
Natalya Khodeneva and colleagues test, in 2026 work, whether inherited variants in the MC1R gene change how anti-inflammatory melanocortin drugs work. The gene also shapes hair and skin color, and red-hair variants weaken its function. Drugs targeting this receptor are in trials for arthritis, scleroderma, and bowel disease, yet gene effects on response were unknown.

Thirty variants were checked for signaling strength, and nine drugs were tested on blood from healthy volunteers. Loss of function formed a gradient, not a yes-or-no split, and each drug felt variants differently, from loss to gain of effect. Most drugs worked less well when variants were present. Gene screening should join future melanocortin drug trials.
pmc-13507297:
Elizabeth Appel, S Amin Enderami, Elaina J Sutley, and Admin Husic measure, in 2026 work, how flood exposure maps onto neighborhoods graded by a 1930s federal lending agency. That agency stamped districts from best to hazardous, a practice called redlining that entrenched segregation. Fine-scale flood models and population mapping covered 202 neighborhoods' worth of graded districts in 202 cities.

Hazardous-graded areas bore outsized flood burdens in about three quarters of cities, following a clean gradient across grades. A larger share of hazardous-grade residents face the hundred-year flood than best-grade residents face the thousand-year flood. Gaps persisted far from rivers and coasts, pointing to drainage and infrastructure deficits. Century-old lending maps still predict who gets wet.
pmc-13508297:
Jiaxin Li and four co-authors identify a protein called FSTL4 as a driver of aggressive lung cancer, in work published in 2026. Non-small cell lung cancer remains hard to treat, and fresh drivers are needed as drug targets. Gene data and local tumor samples showed FSTL4 levels run high in cancer tissue compared with normal lung. High levels marked shorter survival on their own.

Turning FSTL4 down in cancer cells slowed growth and movement, stalled the cell cycle, and triggered cell death. Normal lung cells were spared, an encouraging safety sign. Raising FSTL4 had the opposite effect. The protein works through a growth signaling chain and binds helper switch proteins to do so. Blocking the chain erased the effect of silencing in patient cells. In mice, silencing FSTL4 sharply slowed tumor growth, backing it as a treatment target.
pmc-13508397:
Yaqin Yan and five co-authors show how disturbed gut microbes worsen a lung disease of premature babies, using a newborn mouse model, in 2026 work. The disease, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, is driven in the model by high oxygen in the first two weeks of life. High oxygen stunted lung air sac growth, broke the gut barrier, and shifted gut microbes off balance. Lung inflammation rose, and a signaling chain tied to a cell-shape change program switched on. The team then tested gut transplants and a pathway blocker.

Antibiotics early in life made every harm worse. Transplanting gut microbes from healthy-air mice repaired the gut barrier, calmed the signaling chain, and reversed the cell-shape program. A drug that blocks the same chain copied those protective effects closely. The findings build a gut-lung link with named steps, giving drug hunters concrete targets for protecting premature lungs.
pmc-13509697:
A soft exosuit that pulls the hip with cables usually helps in one plane, but real hips move in three. Avinash Pramod and co-authors ask whether moving the cable anchors can redistribute the help in a 2026 study. A geometric model with empirical corrections predicts the three-dimensional torque from any anchor layout.

The team tested twelve anchor configurations across seventeen joint angles on a hip-thigh phantom, two hundred four cases in all. Shifting anchors did systematically steer torque among the sagittal, frontal, and transverse planes. The model tracked the trends well, best for the twisting component, with errors growing when cables wrapped more. The authors offer anchor placement as a design dial for suits that assist the whole hip, not just its swing.
pmc-13510097:
Kajsa Gustafsson and co-authors study bone infection in foals in a 2026 veterinary paper. Blood-borne bone infection can cripple or kill young horses, and CT scans are now used to find it. Which scan features truly forecast survival, and whether readers agree on them, was unclear.

Scans of fifty-six foals at three referral centers were read blind by three observers. About two-thirds of foals left the hospital alive, and most with follow-up lived long term. Joint involvement and a long fuzzy edge around the lesion each cut the odds of discharge. Spread to several sites cut long-term survival. Readers agreed only weakly to moderately on most features, so the authors call for clearer shared rules.
pmc-13512297:
Mustafa Özdemir and co-authors test whether a simple blood ratio before weight loss surgery predicts pain afterward. Their 2026 study reviews eighty one adults who had a sleeve gastrectomy at one center. The ratio compares two white cell types and tracks body wide inflammation. Immature white cell share was tested alongside it. Pain was scored on an eleven point scale in recovery, at one day, and at three months.

The ratio correlated with pain at every time point. The link was strongest at three months. After adjustment, it stayed an independent predictor of early pain, with odds ratios of 6.1 and 8.1. A cut off of 1.73 best flagged moderate to severe recovery pain. The immature cell measures showed no link to any pain outcome. The authors suggest the cheap blood test could help plan pain control for these patients.
pmc-13513897:
Mohamed Ezzaitouni and three co-authors wrote this 2026 review on farming insects the way engineers tune a process: by programming what they eat and which microbes they carry. Edible insects are rising as sustainable protein, and their nutritional makeup is unusually plastic. The review synthesizes how feed inputs, from farm by-products to algae, reshape gut microbial communities and metabolic pathways in the black soldier fly, mealworm, and house cricket.

Fat chemistry gets the spotlight, since fatty acid profiles drive the insects' value for human food and animal feed alike. The authors propose treating the insect as a programmable biological system and sketch precision feeding plus microbiome-guided interventions to hit nutritional targets on purpose. They also name the gaps honestly: prediction lags practice, and systems-level models are scarce. The direction, they argue, is from empirical feeding toward designed biomass inside a circular bioeconomy.
pmc-13513997:
Rocky E. Stroud and co-authors describe who joined a large case-control study of psychosis genetics across four African countries, in 2026 work. About 1.3 million people in sub-Saharan Africa live with psychotic disorders, yet research rooted in these populations stays scarce. The study recruited 42,953 participants in Ethiopia, Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda between 2018 and 2023 to hunt genetic and environmental risk factors.

Men made up about fifty-seven percent overall, with national shares running from under half in Uganda to two thirds in Ethiopia. Schizophrenia and unspecified psychosis dominated case diagnoses in Ethiopia, while bipolar and manic presentations led in Uganda. Every demographic and clinical measure, from body illness to substance use, differed by country and by case status. The authors say the spread warns against treating African psychosis cohorts as one block in genetic analysis.
pmc-13514497:
Mikołaj Basza and seven co-authors evaluate, in a 2026 retrospective study, home spirometry with remote monitoring for people who have received a lung transplant. The programme group sent breathing measurements from home devices to the transplant centre, while two comparison groups used home spirometry without remote review or attended only routine centre visits.

The remote group completed nearly five thousand breathing tests over about eight months on average, keeping to the schedule roughly three-fifths of the time, and most measurements met technical standards. Their hospital stays, planned and urgent combined, ran markedly shorter than stays for the routine-care group, and urgent stays alone showed the same pattern. Basza's team reads remote spirometry as workable and linked to lighter hospital use. They stress that the comparison was not randomised, so a larger prospective trial is needed before firm claims.
pmc-13516497:
Jihyun Hwang, Maria Dulay, Bruce Schaar, and Joseph DeSimone present a review, published in 2026. It covers vacuum-assisted microneedle devices for sampling dermal interstitial fluid. This is the liquid between skin cells. It carries many of the same health markers as blood. Collecting enough of it painlessly is hard. The authors reframe the problem as engineering a pressure gradient.

They compare two designs. One draws fluid through tiny pores left after microneedles are removed. It feeds bench analyses of many markers. The other keeps hollow microneedles in the skin for continuous collection. The review weighs the strengths of each design. Liquid biopsy and wearable health monitoring development are the targets.
pmc-13516997:
Alejandro Perez-Mendoza and co-authors measure a key voltage trait of platinum films at tiny scales in work dated two thousand twenty-six. The trait, the potential of zero charge, marks where a surface holds no net charge. It shapes ion layout and reaction ease at the surface, and it varies with grain direction and atomic steps.

A scanning method that probes through a fine pipette had been stuck at wide tips, since the signal near that point is faint. The team shows it can work with tips well under a micron wide on a platinum film of one crystal face. Values matched large-scale results. Prep voltage, acidity, and gas cover all shifted the reading, and shifts tracked with hydrogen reaction ease.
pmc-13517297: Cao-Sang Truong and five colleagues publish a correction notice for their 2023 study of far UV-C germicidal light in the journal Viruses. The notice rewrites several sentences. One change drops a misleading claim about 254 nm light: it harms skin and eyes. Another anchors safety to an international standard: cell survival near eighty percent under 207 nm light sits well above the harm threshold, while 254 nm light pushed survival below it. A figure caption is corrected too, clarifying the dose behind each virus reduction and where exposure time replaces energy values.
pmc-13518097:
Ayaka Ichise and co-authors reported a 2026 case of brain stimulation after focused ultrasound for Parkinson's disease. A man developed tremor and slowness at fifty and joined a trial of ultrasound lesioning of the subthalamic nucleus, a no-incision treatment needing no hardware. The lesion at age 53 nearly erased his tremor, but symptoms slowly returned, and a second ultrasound target was treated a year later.

Tremor persisted in several forms. Four years on, scans showed the old ultrasound lesion still present. The team then implanted a deep brain stimulator in the same right-side nucleus. Little was known about how stimulator and old lesion interact, since the electrical traits of healed ultrasound lesions are barely described. The case adds rare evidence for sequencing the two treatments.
pmc-13518797:
Aleksandra Pidde leads a twelve-author team showing in 2026 that a worm's gentle touch neurons also sense the surface it crawls on. Movement depends on friction between body and ground, plus the body's own force sensing. How those forces shape nerve activity in a freely moving animal was largely unknown.

Working with the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, the team combined calcium imaging, traction force microscopy, simulations, and control theory. Friction force and crawling speed emerged as the main drivers of touch neuron activity. Worms with a broken MEC-4 channel moved sluggishly and regulated body posture poorly. Touch receptors, the authors argue, tune movement to save energy.
pmc-13518997:
Weibin Wu and colleagues tested whether choline, a nutrient, can protect pregnant sheep whose poor late-pregnancy diet inflames the gut. Published in 2026, the study focused on highly fertile Hu sheep, which often eat too little in late gestation, and on the gut microbes and bile acids that help govern intestinal inflammation. Drug options in pregnancy are narrow, so a safe food-based approach carries special appeal.

Choline eased colon inflammation, restored the gut lining barrier, and calmed immune activity in the intestine. It reshaped the colon microbe community, boosting a bacterium that raises bile-processing enzyme activity and steadies bile acid balance, and it restored levels of a key bile acid called DCA. That acid then quieted inflammation through a cell signal pathway involving Nur77 and NF-kB. The work supports choline as a pregnancy-compatible nutritional strategy, while noting results remain early.
pmc-13519497:
Nilima Jain and colleagues compared saliva defenses in reflux patients against healthy controls to explain tooth erosion. Published in 2026, the study tested 120 people, sixty with gastroesophageal reflux disease and sixty without, scoring tooth wear with a standard erosion index. Reflux sends stomach acid into the mouth, where it can dissolve tooth mineral over time.

Reflux patients showed clearly lower saliva acidity balance and weaker buffering power, alongside more frequent and more severe erosion. Saliva normally dilutes acid, neutralizes it, and shields enamel with minerals and a protein film, so weakened saliva leaves teeth exposed. The authors urge early reflux diagnosis and preventive dental care to slow erosion. Readers learn why a stomach condition deserves a dental plan.
pmc-13519897:
Maria Raju and six co-authors study a chiral cobalt complex in water with near resonant Raman optical activity, and pair the tests with density functional theory. Chiral metal complexes matter in catalysis and drug chemistry, and their spectra reveal their structure in water. Spectra are taken with light at 532 nanometers, near an electronic resonance.

A strong background part from the solution is gauged and corrected to extract the true spectra. They simulate Raman, optical activity, absorption, and circular dichroism spectra for four conformers under two solvation models. Both models capture main trends, while the density based one matches vibrational traits better, above all for amine and methylene modes. The work shows such spectra in water can be matched from first principles.
pmc-13519997:
He Huang and co-authors test a vitamin K2 cream against skin aging, in a 2026 study. Aging skin loses energy as its mitochondria, the cell's power plants, falter under stress. The team asked whether menaquinone-7, a form of vitamin K2, can recharge those power plants in skin cells.

In lab dishes, stressed skin cells treated with the compound held more energy stores and healthier power-plant signals. A human trial then enrolled 30 women, each using the active cream on one side of the face and neck and a plain cream on the other. That split design lets each woman serve as her own control. The study pairs cell-level proof with a careful human test of a topical anti-aging claim.
pmc-13520197:
Alicia Sanchez-Sanz and Sergio Baranzini review the gut microbiome in multiple sclerosis in a 2026 article. The disease inflames and damages nerve insulation in the central nervous system. Genes and environment shape its risk, and gut microbes have emerged as a key, changeable factor.

pmc-13520297:
Yao Yang and colleagues offer in 2026 a review and combined analysis of what shapes professional identity among nursing interns in China. Professional identity here means how strongly interns see themselves as nurses, which the authors link to staying in the profession.

Twelve factors entered the pooled analysis, while thirty more were summed up in words. The review gives mentors a ranked set of supports to strengthen during placements.
pmc-13520397:
Mark J. Butler and colleagues test in 2026 whether a phone-delivered, personalised walking programme is workable for middle-aged and older health workers. The programme bundles five habit-building techniques, such as goal setting and self-monitoring, to make daily walking automatic.

Forty-four staff aged 45 to 75 years wore activity trackers through a two-week baseline and a ten-week programme phase. Daily prompts supported a personal walking plan, while satisfaction ratings were gathered at the end. pmc-13520497:
Christina Stamou and co-authors show how an aging solvent quietly changed the outcome of a chemistry experiment, in a 2026 case study. With old solvent, the products picked up chlorine atoms that no starting material contained, giving two unexpected complexes in low yield. pmc-13520697:
Beena G. pmc-13520797:

pmc-13521897:

pmc-13522497:
Nguyen and co-authors profiled a 2026 dataset of gene activity in human fat tissue, comparing brown fat that burns fuel for heat with white fat that stores it. pmc-13522797:

The authors argue the design overcomes a key barrier for selective gene therapy and virus-based cancer treatment.
pmc-13522897:
Uterine cancer resists current treatment, and Zhang and a large team build tiny delivery bubbles to attack it through a rust-like cell death called ferroptosis. pmc-13523297:
Hafsa Zafar leads a randomized trial of a lipid-based food supplement in underweight women with preeclampsia in Pakistan in a 2026 study. Differences in systolic pressure also appeared by six months in the reported results. The authors present supplementation as a way to improve metabolic status in this high-risk group, with follow-up continuing after birth.
pmc-13523897:
Wang and Wang review blood clotting care around heart pump surgery, in this 2024 paper. Four patients with end-stage heart failure got a left ventricular assist device at one Chinese hospital in late 2023. Such surgery carries high clot and bleeding risk.

pmc-13524097:

pmc-13524197:

pmc-13524897:

pmc-13524997:

It highlights sex-specific points, such as pregnancy and device sizing, that generic guidance can miss. The authors close with steps to improve lifetime care for this group.
pmc-13525797:

pmc-13526397:

pmc-13526697:

pmc-13526797:

pmc-13527497:

pmc-13528097:

pmc-13528697:

pmc-13529697:

pmc-13529797:

pmc-13530097:

pmc-13530197:

pmc-13530297:

pmc-13530397:

pmc-13530497:

pmc-13530797:

pmc-13530997:

For twelve cancers that drive two-thirds of cancer deaths, the test caught an estimated sixty-four in a hundred cases across stages. pmc-13531197:

pmc-13532297:

pmc-13532497:

pmc-13533197:

pmc-13533497:

pmc-13533597:

pmc-13534197:

pmc-13534497:

pmc-13534597:

pmc-13535397:

pmc-13535997:

pmc-13536697:

pmc-13536797:

pmc-13537597:

pmc-13538297:

pmc-13538397:

pmc-13538497:

pmc-13538697:

pmc-13538897:
Tamil Selvi Sundaram and colleagues surveyed milk whey as a dairy route to serum-free meat growing. pmc-13539197:

The team also checked the mark against how patients felt a month later. A clear target can guide tailored prep before surgery.
pmc-13539697:

pmc-13539797:
Carla Girling and a large team of co-authors set out, in a 2026 protocol, how they will study the rollout of intensive remote help for breathing support in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Findings should show what helps or hinders services in adopting the new support model.
pmc-13539897:
The authors report a 64-year-old man whose retinal detachment grew for six months from a tear that early images showed. He came in with floaters and good vision. Wide-field images, reviewed later, revealed a horseshoe-shaped retinal tear with a small detachment creeping toward the center, missed at first. pmc-13540897:
Omar Keritam and a large team assess whether specialised care improves survival in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, in a study published in 2026. pmc-13541197:

pmc-13541797:

Slices grew for four days in two media. One medium was ordinary, the other fattening. Each ran with or without the cytokine. Gene activity shifted toward inflammation and scarring. Adding the cytokine intensified those features.
pmc-13541997:

Sediments carried heavy loads of the banned insecticide DDT and its kin, and the eggs carried its breakdown product along with circuit-board chemicals. pmc-13542397:
Ryo Mitoma and co-authors (2026) measured brain responses to sound in people with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Within the patient group, stronger and better-synced responses went with better attention. Other thinking scores showed no such link. pmc-13542697:

The rare genetic disorder grows benign tumors in many organs, and classic skin and brain signs usually bring diagnosis in childhood. Some patients slip through to adulthood with odd presentations, as here.

Imaging showed kidney tumors on both sides, a lung condition tied to the syndrome, brain lesions, and womb muscle tumors of a linked type. She met the current international criteria for a definite diagnosis. The case warns clinicians to think syndromic.
pmc-13543497:

pmc-13543597:

pmc-13543797:

pmc-13543997:

The authors say the ion effect gives food makers a dial for gel strength and water hold.
pmc-13544197:

pmc-13544697:

pmc-13545597:

pmc-13546997:

pmc-13547497:

pmc-13547597:

pmc-13547697:

pmc-13548497:

pmc-13548697:

pmc-13548997:

pmc-13549097:

pmc-13549197:

pmc-13549697:

pmc-13549797:

pmc-13549897:

pmc-13550097:

pmc-13550397:

pmc-13550497:

pmc-13550597:

pmc-13550697:

pmc-13550897:
