pmc-13551297:
Niccolo Simoni and Daniel Hashemi ask what a base layer does to a lead sheet material in work dated 2026. pmc-13551497:

pmc-13551597:

pmc-13551697:

pmc-13551897:

pmc-13552097:

pmc-13552297:

pmc-13569897:
Kasey Irwin, Janet Kelly, and Frank Donnelly study, in a 2026 Australian mixed-methods project, how operating room staff are included when operating rooms are designed. Clinicians prized safety, ergonomics, and workflow, whereas designers focused on rules and technical demands. Support access, layout, and body fit topped the shared safety list. pmc-13569997:
Yunnong Luo and co-authors test a simple blood ratio as a flag for muscle loss in older adults. Their twenty twenty-six paper studies sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength with age. The ratio joins uric acid with HDL cholesterol, the so-called good cholesterol.

Two large surveys, from the United States and South Korea, gave the data. The team weighed the ratio against muscle loss risk in both groups. Readers get both the link and a tested screening aid.
pmc-13570197:

The team sent a questionnaire to podiatrists and podiatric surgeons endorsed to prescribe these medicines.

pmc-13570497:

Referrals to the specialty rose from none to about nine in ten. Eye protection was high in both groups. The authors say preset orders can steady guideline-based care.
pmc-13570897:
Masato Terai and Junko Yamashita ask whether readers picture the color of an object a sentence only implies, in work from twenty twenty-six. Embodied theories say language taps sensory memory. A bear in the woods implies brown, while a bear at the North Pole implies white.

Typical colors got faster answers in both sentence types and both context orders. Context did not sway the effect toward the implied atypical color. pmc-13571297:
Garcia and five co-authors trace Portugal's cancer registry from local lists to a national data resource, in a 2026 paper. Registration began in scattered towns in 1976 and reached full coverage in 2007. Law created the unified national registry in 2017.

The national system added over 30 clinical variables beyond the old core set. In 2022 data, core facts were fully complete and lab confirmation hit 97.8 percent. The authors urge automation to cut the lag.
pmc-13571397:
Stephan and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a rare coronary fistula, an abnormal channel from a heart artery into a heart chamber. A 57-year-old man with two weeks of chest pain on effort had a fully blocked main artery, the left anterior descending.

The fistula ran from the first diagonal branch into the left ventricle, and its branches fed blood around the blockage into the territory the blocked artery should serve. That backup flow likely limited damage and kept the heart muscle working. Doctors reopened the blocked artery with a drug-coated stent and widened the fistula branch with a balloon. pmc-13571697:

pmc-13572497:

Adaptability sharpened the first step: for students high in adaptability, self-aware thought lifted attention more strongly. The authors offer the model as a guide for programs that aim to lift student engagement.
pmc-13572997:
Piyaporn Chokevittaya and co-authors test a combined steroid and antihistamine nasal spray in real-world clinic patients whose rhinitis is not driven by allergy, in a 2026 study. The spray is approved for allergic rhinitis, but evidence for the nonallergic form was thin. pmc-13573197:
Lisa E. Kilpatrick, with two colleagues, led a 2026 study of standard nut flours meant to steady allergy testing. pmc-13573297:
Yong Jun Choi and five co-authors compared the tumor surroundings of lung cancer in smokers and never-smokers, in a 2026 study. pmc-13573397:

Ninety studies were included from searches running to April twenty twenty-five. Colorectal and pancreatic cancers were studied most often. Haemoglobin and a blood sugar marker were the most investigated tests for those cancers respectively. Most studies examined associations between trends and cancer, while fewer built prediction models using trends. Additional themes covered combining trends with other information. The authors identify research gaps for future detection approaches.
pmc-13573697:
Yi Deng and four co-authors explore a two-faced protein that can guard cells or harm them, in a 2026 review. That frame may guide drug work that avoids blunt blocking.
pmc-13573797:
Wu and co-authors reviewed antibody drugs for asthma in children and teenagers, in a paper published in 2026. These biologics target the allergic arm of the immune system and have widened options for hard-to-control asthma. Trials in young patients are few, and no trial has pitted the drugs directly against each other. They also graded how certain those indirect estimates are, and tracked side effects both mild and serious. Families and doctors must choose among these costly drugs with thin evidence. pmc-13574697:
Ying Zhang and co-authors test a Chinese herbal capsule on rats with memory loss caused by poor blood flow to the brain. The capsule, Compound Congrong Yizhi, is already sold in China for such disorders. Earlier work looked at its chemistry, but not at how it reshapes brain networks. pmc-13574797:

Screening methods distilled the many candidate measures down to a core set. Three model types, from forest ensembles to plain regression, were trained on those variables. Accuracy, calibration, and clinical usefulness were all graded. Six indicators stood out as tied to response in the training data.
pmc-13574897:
Rodríguez Sánchez and co-authors show biopsy-true labels beat bulk labels in scan models in a 2026 study. Radiogenomics predicts tumor genes from scans, sparing some biopsies. Most studies stamp one biopsy's result onto every lesion in a patient.

pmc-13574997:
Hean Wu Kang and co-authors review, in a 2026 study, outcomes after a full release of part of the triceps muscle during reverse shoulder replacement. The release aims to stop the implant from catching and to free motion, yet surgeons rarely do it for fear of weak arms or joint slips. The team checked strength and motion two years after surgery.

Eighty patients, with an average age near seventy-one, were included. Arm strength at two years matched the level before surgery. Motion and pain and function scores all improved clearly. pmc-13575097:
Debarati Dutta and Priya G present a blockchain system for tracking medicines through the supply chain in 2026. Fake and poor-quality drugs remain a serious risk, with weak tracing across makers, shippers, and sellers. Their framework, called drugledger, pairs blockchain records with decentralised file storage.

Smart contracts assign roles to each party and log each step, from product registration and manufacture to transfers and final checks of authenticity. Unique digital identifiers let users verify a product's history. The prototype ran on Ethereum-compatible test setups, and repeated runs showed steady computing costs for core steps. pmc-13575197:

pmc-13575497:
Mei-Sing Ong and co-authors ask in 2026 how young joint pain patients and their parents view smart tool aid in care choice. Such tools shift ward choice fast, yet young care views on them are scarce read. The group here was a keen, well read set.

Four talk groups drew eight patients and ten parents in all. All liked the tools' fit to the child, yet all held that tools must aid, not swap, the healer's call. Fears ran to healer over trust, weak guard of child data, and skew in the math. Clear facts on how the tools fare were the price of trust.
pmc-13575897:

pmc-13575997:

pmc-13576097:

pmc-13576197:

pmc-13577197:

pmc-13577397:
Adugna Olani and co-authors watched health workers give vaccines in East Wollega, Ethiopia, to grade their skill, in a 2026 study. pmc-13577997:

pmc-13578097:

pmc-13578397:

pmc-13578497:

pmc-13579097:

pmc-13579597:

pmc-13579697:

Uses span disease tales, drug harm screens, and graft hopes for sick hearts. Joint tools with gene snips and smart grades lift their truth still more. Batch shifts, thin vessels, and young cell states curb trust for now. Donor yes, gene data guards, and bank rules need clear frames.

pmc-13579897:

pmc-13579997:

pmc-13580597:
Kristian Carlson and a large team use limb bone strength to ask how much early human relatives climbed trees, in a research paper from 2026. Bone shafts record the loads a body puts on them during life. In living apes, the balance of arm and leg strength tracks how much they climb.

pmc-13581197:

pmc-13581497:

pmc-13581897:

pmc-13582097:

pmc-13582497:

pmc-13583097:

pmc-13583497:

pmc-13600897:

pmc-13601597:

pmc-13602497:

pmc-13602897:

pmc-13603697:

pmc-13603797:

pmc-13604797:

pmc-13604997:

pmc-13605497:

pmc-13605697:

pmc-13605897:

pmc-13606597:

pmc-13606797:

pmc-13606897:

pmc-13607197:

pmc-13607897:

pmc-13608697:

pmc-13609097:

pmc-13609597:

pmc-13609897:

pmc-13610297:

pmc-13610597:

pmc-13610797:

pmc-13611197:

pmc-13611297:

pmc-13611397:

pmc-13611997:

pmc-13612397:

pmc-13613397:

pmc-13613797:

pmc-13613897:

pmc-13614097:

pmc-13614197:

pmc-13615097:

pmc-13615997:

pmc-13616097:

pmc-13617197:

pmc-13619897:

pmc-13621497:

pmc-13622897:

pmc-13623297:

pmc-13623497:

pmc-13623597:

pmc-13623797:

pmc-13630497:

pmc-13630597:

pmc-13631297:

pmc-13631897:

pmc-13631997:

pmc-13632697:

For six weeks, bacterial loads in lung, spleen, and liver looked alike across ages.

Two weeks into treatment, though, older mice cleared lung bacteria more slowly. Their spleens held more of an unusual killer T cell type, and protein scans of helper T cells showed disturbed mitochondrial machinery. The team suggests fixing this age-linked metabolic fault could speed cure in older patients.
pmc-13633097:
Ling Liang and colleagues review why fruits differ so much in color, tracing the many mechanisms behind anthocyanin buildup across species and cultivars in a 2026 synthesis. Anthocyanins, the water-soluble pigments behind red, purple, and blue hues, sway buyer choice and market value, and they also help plants attract pollinators and resist stress. The review gathers evidence on how pigment production, transport, and regulation vary between fruits.

Differences arise from mutations in biosynthesis, transport, and control genes, layered with epigenetic, post-transcriptional, and post-translational regulation. Those natural variants offer concrete targets for breeding or biotechnology aimed at fruit color. Breeders get a map that moves beyond single-gene stories. Color emerges from a network of controls, so screening natural variation across that network is the fastest route to new hues with nutritional appeal.
pmc-13634197:
Fevers that resist explanation for weeks send doctors hunting through infections, immune diseases, and cancers. Soufiane Abdouh and co-authors report a case where the answer sat in the gut. A thirty-three-year-old woman spent a month with fever, muscle pain, and a racing heart before entering the hospital.

Standard hunts found nothing, but her blood showed anemia and high inflammation markers. That hint led to a blood test for celiac disease, which came back positive. A biopsy of her small intestine showed the flattened lining typical of the condition, at Marsh stage IIIa. The 2026 case urges doctors to add celiac disease to the fever hunt.
pmc-13638297:
Victoria Gudiño and a large team of co-authors hunt, in a 2026 study, for what drives a painful complication of Crohn's disease. In about a fifth of patients, tunnels called fistulas form near the anus, and why they form is unknown. The team took rectal biopsies from thirty-one patients, with and without the complication, and read the tissue cell by cell.

The rectal lining of patients with fistulas carried a distinct cellular pattern, separate from gut inflammation itself. A signal called TL1A, switched on in helper T cells, seemed to drive it. Downstream, two messengers reshaped the tissue: one pushed support cells to grow and release tissue-cutting enzymes, and the other imprinted a signature on the surface cells. The work names new drug targets.
pmc-13639097:
Castellani and co-authors deliver a tiny tumor-fighting RNA into the stem-like cells of the deadliest brain tumor. This tumor is the most common and aggressive in adults, with median survival of fifteen to eighteen months. Its stem-like cells drive spread into nearby brain and regrowth after treatment.

The RNA they deliver normally holds tumors back, and its loss marks worse disease. Getting it into the right cells is the hard part. The team guided it with a short binding molecule that homes to the stem-like cells. In their models the delivery curbed the cells' invasion and slowed tumor growth. A guided RNA could one day pair with standard care. The work joins two tools: a homing guide and a natural brake.
pmc-13639697:
Kawai and colleagues examined in 2026 whether heart and brain vessel disease changes how two hormone-blocking drugs perform in castration-resistant prostate cancer, a stage where standard hormone therapy has failed. The earlier ENABLE trial had found enzalutamide and abiraterone broadly equal, but patients with cardio-cerebrovascular disease are often excluded or feared harder to treat. This randomized study deliberately enrolled them and compared outcomes by disease status and drug.

Thirty-six patients had such disease, most often prior brain infarction, against 142 without. Survival measures, including time to marker progression, scan progression, and overall and cancer-specific survival, did not differ significantly between the groups, and neither drug beat the other inside either group. Side effect rates were also comparable throughout. The authors conclude both drugs remain feasible choices for patients with this history, a group clinicians often hesitate over.
pmc-13642897:
Siddhi S. Desai and thirteen colleagues present a 2026 metabolomics study linking flame-retardant chemicals called PBDEs with preterm birth in an Atlanta cohort of African American mothers. This group faces both higher exposure to these pollutants and higher preterm birth rates.

Serum from 177 pregnant participants, drawn early in pregnancy between 2014 and 2019, was measured for three PBDE compounds and scanned with high-resolution metabolomics. Forty-six participants delivered early. Twenty-six confirmed metabolites tied exposure or early birth to thiamine use, sulfur amino acid handling, fat transport, and membrane lipids. The authors read this as disturbed stress, inflammation, and energy pathways.
pmc-13642997:
Ting Cui and nine colleagues present a 2026 study of a blood protein, ADAMTS18, as an early forecast of recovery after ischemic stroke. The protein helps protect blood vessels and injured brain tissue, but its clinical value at admission was untested.

Using the Chengdu Stroke Registry, the team measured the protein within two days of arrival in 194 patients. Those with lower levels fared worse at three months, and the link held after adjustment for other factors. Adding the measure to standard prediction models sharpened their accuracy noticeably. The authors suggest admission testing could guide counseling and discharge planning.
pmc-13643297:
Rosa L. Sava and Michael J. Gebhardt present a study of why the regulator protein CsrA is essential for the hospital pathogen Acinetobacter baumannii in rich media but not in lean conditions. CsrA normally reins in gene activity after genes are read, and losing it proves lethal in settings like human serum.

Suppressor hunting led the team to Lrp, a broad transcription regulator, and to a small gene cluster handling D-alanine, a building block of the cell wall. Without CsrA, two cluster genes overproduce and poison the cell, weakening its envelope and raising sensitivity to wall-targeting antibiotics. The pair of regulators balances the pathway together.
pmc-13645997:
Antonin Fuzeau and sixteen colleagues test a simpler way to measure blood clots inside the heart's main pumping chamber after a heart attack, in a 2026 study. Such clots can break loose and cause strokes, yet measuring their size on heart scans has lacked a standard method. The team reanalyzed heart scan data from a trial of heart attack patients, taken five days after treatment. Twenty-five of 161 patients had a clot, measured with a formula based on three lengths.

Repeated readings by the same and different readers matched closely, which makes it dependable for routine use. Clot shape barely changed the size estimate. Four fifths of clots had vanished by three months, and no feature of the clot predicted which ones would persist. No clot-related events occurred over one year of follow-up. The authors offer the simple formula as a shared yardstick for future studies.
pmc-13646197:
Diana Patalwala and nine colleagues review the imaging toolkit for watching blood flow in the brains of living rodents, the main lab models of Alzheimer's disease. Disrupted brain blood flow is now seen as an early feature of the disease. But comparing studies is hard, since each method trades resolution against depth, speed, and access.

Two-photon microscopy sees single capillaries but only shallowly, and it is invasive. Speckle imaging and optical coherence tomography cover surfaces. MRI and PET scan the whole brain coarsely. The authors single out ultrafast ultrasound localization microscopy, which tracks single microbubbles for flow maps of very high resolution. They see it as the technique best placed to standardize imaging of small vessels over time.
pmc-13646497:
Kana Tominaga and Naoomi Tominaga study a membrane repair protein in immune cells called macrophages. The protein is famous for patching torn muscle fibers using calcium signals. Its work in immune cells is far less known.

The pair link the protein to stronger inflammatory replies by macrophages. Those replies run through a calcium-tied signaling path that switches on inflammation genes. In cell models, the protein's activity also tracked with poorer growth of new muscle cells. That pairing hints at a trade-off: the same protein that patches muscle may fan inflammation that slows its rebuilding. The findings widen the protein's known stage from muscle to immunity. They may matter for muscle-wasting diseases where both repair and inflammation fail.
pmc-13647997:
Ashish Singh and eight colleagues review custom three-dimensionally printed implants for severe bone loss around the hip socket during revision hip replacement surgery. Such loss, including Paprosky type III defects and pelvic discontinuity, can defeat grafts, metal augments, and cup-cage constructs that cannot match complex shapes.

Drawing on searches of three databases plus two cases from their own institution, the review reports implant survival near ninety-six percent at three to six years in selected series. Printed implants fit the defect, restore the hip centre, and improve bone contact, though evidence rests mostly on retrospective series. The authors call for prospective trials with longer follow-up.
pmc-13648297:
Mehrdad Mark Mofid defends a glue safety study in a 2026 reply letter. Critics had questioned his work on formaldehyde fumes from a skin glue used in surgery, and on the risk of allergy from skin contact. The letter thanks them and then answers point by point with lab and rule details.

He notes that two lab runs agreed closely, that chamber tests cover two hours rather than a full work shift, and that his no decay case sets an upper bound. He also splits a safety screen value from true harm doses drawn from patch test studies. Three of the critics claims are called wrong on benchmarks and airflow rules.
pmc-13649397:
Anna Nagórka-Bolek and nine colleagues compared lung function in hobby marathon runners with men from the general public in the Pomerania region of Poland. The team tested 31 runners and 82 other men, all aged 35 to 66, with standard breathing tests.

The runners blew out much more air than the control group, both in total lung size and in the air forced out in one second. The share of air expelled in that first second was much the same in both groups. Rates of blocked airway disease also matched. Body size gaps between the groups did not explain the lung gaps. The authors urge care in reading the results, since the group was small and the design took one snapshot in time.
pmc-13649597:
Copy number variants, where chunks of DNA are missing or duplicated, contribute to schizophrenia risk, but most studies have covered European ancestry groups. The authors present a large study in East Asian populations, with 20,903 patients and 23,258 controls. They ask how much these rare variants add to risk there, and how the pattern compares across populations.

Patients carried a clearly higher burden of rare variants than controls. Nine genomic regions reached strong significance in the East Asian sample, and combining with European data gave fourteen, eight of them new. Genes in these regions tolerate damage poorly, which fits a real role in the illness. Some new variants were far more common in East Asian carriers, which shows why diverse samples matter.
pmc-13649697:
Bhuvana M and Durgaprasad P model a hybrid nanofluid, a liquid spiked with two kinds of nano grit, as it flows over a cone in a porous bed. Their math lets heat lag behind, as thick fluids do, and adds a spring-like fluid trait plus a magnetic field. Such fluids are pitched for sharp heat control in gear and care.

Sweeps of the math show the bed's drag term rules skin drag and heat pass most. Its grip on waste heat stays strong too, and cross-links grow as lift swells. A neural net trained on the math then calls all three outputs with high scores and low error. The authors sell the trio of math, sweeps, and nets as a fast design bench.
pmc-13649897:
Romana Wass and co-authors lay out a plan for a national lung cancer screening program in Austria, in a 2026 position paper. Lung cancer is a top cause of cancer death in the country and is often found late, when cure is unlikely. Trials abroad show that screening with low-dose CT scans cuts deaths and finds more early, curable cases.

Four Austrian medical societies — radiology, lung medicine, family medicine, and chest surgery — jointly wrote the paper. It sets out who should be screened, how scans should be run, and how results should be handled, based on the trial evidence. A shared framework from all the involved fields gives the health ministry a ready base for policy.
pmc-13650297:
Huan Lv and five colleagues build a tool to estimate, before surgery, which patients with advanced esophageal cancer will develop lung complications afterward. These patients first receive drug treatment to shrink the tumor, then undergo removal of the esophagus, and lung problems are a leading source of suffering after that operation.

The team reviewed 232 patients treated during 2023 and 2024, of whom just under a third developed lung complications. Five facts known before surgery went into the model: smoking history raised the odds, while high blood pressure, immune-based drug treatment, inhaled medication, and breathing exercises each lowered them. The model sorted patients with acceptable accuracy and held up under internal checking. Presented as a scoring chart, it is meant to guide preparation for surgery, though the authors say outside testing must come before routine use.
pmc-13651497:
Soo Min Cho, Young Eun Kim, and Eui-Hwan Choi present a 2026 review on cohesin, the ring-shaped protein complex that holds sister chromosomes together and folds DNA into loops. Textbooks say stem cells use only the everyday mitotic form of the complex, while a variant form serves only in making eggs and sperm. New evidence breaks that tidy split.

The review gathers studies showing the reproductive variant's parts are also switched on in embryonic stem cells, where they join core subunits and sit at distinct DNA sites. The authors compare the two forms' makeup, timing, and removal, and ask how the variant shapes gene control and guards the genome during fast stem cell division. The boundary between the two systems looks porous.
pmc-13652097:
Putsarat Insin, Trinya Chaiwongsa, and Nisa Prueksaritanond ran a clinical trial on whether vitamin B12 can prevent nerve damage caused by chemotherapy. Their patients were women with gynecological cancer treated at Rajavithi Hospital. Nerve damage in the hands and feet is a common and lasting side effect of the drugs these patients receive.

Forty patients were split evenly between a B12 group and a placebo group, with neither side knowing who got what. The vitamin was taken by mouth from the start of chemotherapy until four weeks after the last cycle. Nerve damage appeared in 5 percent of the B12 group and 20 percent of the placebo group. Quality of life scores and side effects were much the same in both groups. The authors suggest B12 as a safe preventive option for these patients.
pmc-13652297:
Jagadish N and co-authors build a deep learning system that grades tumor severity and malignancy across several scan types. Early, accurate sorting of tumors guides treatment, but standard reads can miss early-stage disease or delay action. The team gathered mammograms, MRI, and CT images from public sources, covering varied tumor types and stages.

Their pipeline first cleans images and boosts contrast to isolate suspect regions. A hybrid network then extracts both fine local detail and broad global patterns from each image. A final classifier, tuned to punish the most dangerous mistakes most heavily, assigns severity and malignancy labels with explanations attached. The system reached about ninety-eight percent accuracy in tests, beating standard machine learning and deep learning rivals.
pmc-13652397:
Muñoz and co-authors present three cases of a bullet that traveled inside a vein after a gunshot wound. The bullet can ride the blood flow to a distant site, where it may block flow or harm tissue. It follows mostly low-speed, small-caliber wounds.

The three patients were treated at several centers with a hybrid plan. Doctors first caught the bullet with catheter tools from inside the vein. In each case the bullet was too wide to pull out that way, so a vein opening finished the job. All three patients did well, with no problems from the procedure. Finding a wandering bullet takes suspicion and the right scans. The series adds practical steps to a thin record on this rare event.
pmc-13654097:
Yi Ding and co-authors test a way to predict how brightly the aorta will light up during a heart CT scan, in a 2026 study. Clear vessel images need the right amount of contrast dye in the blood at the right moment. Fixed dosing rules ignore body differences, so brightness varies a lot between patients.

A test-bolus method first injects a small dose and watches its peak brightness. The team checked how well that peak predicts the final scan brightness in fifty patients at one center. They also split results by body mass and heart output to see where the link holds best. A firm link would let scanners tailor the main dose to each patient, cutting dim or blown-out scans.
pmc-13654497:
Ji-Young Yun and co-authors show how a fat-building pathway in mice calms the inflammation that comes with obesity. Inflammation in fat stores drives poor insulin control. The pathway builds plasmalogens, a class of fats, and its first step is run by the enzyme GNPAT. Their 2026 study fed mice a high-fat diet, with or without alkyl glycerol, a raw material that feeds the pathway.

Mice on the supplement kept better insulin control and had calmer fat, with no change in weight. Their fat held fewer inflammatory M1 macrophages, and key plasmalogen types lost to the diet came back. Mice born with half the enzyme fared worse on the rich diet. In cell tests, extra enzyme hushed a signal chain, PKCδ to STAT1, that fires those cells up. In human fat from people with diabetes, the enzyme ran low. Boosting the fat pathway may aid care.
pmc-13655397:
Lung researchers in China find a grip protein that helps drive airway reshaping in asthma. In asthma, the airway wall thickens and stiffens over time, a change called remodeling. A growth signal on airway skin cells is known to drive that change by flipping cells to a scar-like state. What sets the level of that signal dock was not clear. The team pinned it on cadherin-26, a grip protein rich in airway skin.

Levels of the protein in patient airway samples tracked with wall base thickness. Mice that lacked its gene showed far less airway twitch and reshaping under dust mite stress. In lab airway cells, cutting the protein blocked the scar-like flip, while adding it sped the flip. The protein holds the growth dock steady on the cell surface. Blocking that grip is a fresh drug idea.
pmc-13655897:
Shi, Yang, Ban, Li, and Zhu study a cancer that grows where the food pipe meets the stomach. They focus on one subtype, set by where the tumor's center sits. Treatment for this cancer is still debated, above all the value of drug and radiation treatment given before surgery.

The team drew patient records from a large United States cancer database. They compared survival across treatment paths and across stages of disease. A key aim was to see whether early and advanced cases gain the same benefit from pre-surgery treatment. They also asked whether extra treatment after surgery adds value. From the data, they built a chart that estimates survival for a new patient. Such a chart can help doctors tailor talks about likely outcomes.
pmc-13657597:
Safal Bogati, Bishal Pradhan, and Naresh Kharbuja report the case of a twenty-year-old woman, six weeks pregnant, who arrived after three days of vomiting, then seizures and headache. Scans showed a clot in the large vein along the top of the brain, with several damaged patches and some bleeding. Such clots in the first weeks of pregnancy are rare, since they usually strike late in pregnancy or after birth.

Blood thinners were started at once, but the clot was large and weakness persisted, so doctors threaded a device into the vein and pulled the clot out. The removed clot measured twenty-five centimetres, the vessel reopened, and she recovered fully within two weeks. After counselling, the pregnancy was later ended by her choice.
pmc-13659897:
Mohammad Bagher Shamsodini Moghadam and co-authors report a teenager whose neck scan revealed a doubled right vertebral artery by pure chance. She was being checked for possible lupus and vessel inflammation. A blood pressure gap between her arms raised the alarm.

CT angiography was ordered to hunt for vasculitis. Instead it showed two limbs of the artery arising together. Both sprang from the same subclavian source vessel. One limb ran behind the carotid on an odd path. No narrowing, clot, or tear accompanied the variant. She had no symptoms from the doubled vessel. Such variants matter when surgeons plan neck work. The case adds a rare finding to the record.
pmc-13661297:
Maryam Shojaei-Asl and Mohsen Moradian build a single atom catalyst in a 2026 study. Single atom catalysts offer even active sites and strong performance for chemical making. The team fixed single zinc atoms into a nitrogen rich porous carbon. That support keeps the atoms stable and selective during reactions.

The catalyst drove a one pot reaction that builds ring compounds used in drugs. Twelve target products were made from simple starting materials. Best results came in methanol at room temperature over half a day. Yields reached near total conversion for the best cases, and side reactions stayed low.
pmc-13668397:
Nurses now work amid records software, data tools, and artificial intelligence, so the skills they need keep shifting. Ursula Hübner and co-authors updated in 2026 a global framework that spells out the informatics skills nurses should learn.

The update rested on a survey of 117 experts worldwide, four regional workshops, and twenty-one teaching case studies. It keeps five role tracks, from bedside nursing to IT management in nursing. Each track shows its own skill pattern: bedside roles stress patient topics and legal basics, while IT roles stress deep computing skills. The framework urges that AI topics appear in every track, alongside lasting themes like safety and record use.
pmc-13668697:
Tara Barron and co-authors find a calm-seizure drug slows a mid-line brain tumor in kids by hush work at nerve links. The study appeared in 2026. Such drugs are stock care for tumor sick folks. Past fate reads on them clash, blurred by tumor kind and drug class.

Ward reads showed kids with this tumor kind who took the drug lived long, a gain not seen in a side tumor kind. In beast runs the drug cut growth and stretched life for this kind alone. The tumor feeds on hush nerve links that the twin kind lacks. The drug dims those link calls in the tumor, not in sound cells.
pmc-13668897:
Jitka Bolchová and a large registry team published this 2026 study on babies born with cytomegalovirus infection. The infection is the most common one passed before birth and a leading cause of hearing loss and developmental harm in children. Care and screening have changed over the past decade, and the team asked whether outcomes changed with them.

Using an international registry, they compared 1,653 children diagnosed from 2011 to 2024, split at 2017 when European expert guidance appeared. The later group held 1,087 children against 566 in the earlier one. Children were found through pregnancy care, symptoms at birth, hearing checks, and newborn screening. The study tracks how presentation, treatment, and results shifted across the two eras.
pmc-13669797:
Tim Chambers and colleagues published a 2026 study of water fluoridation in New Zealand. They tracked tooth decay in four-year-olds nationwide. Data spanned more than a decade of preschool checks. Each child was linked to local water records. Fluoridation exposure covered the check year and three prior years.

The dataset held over six hundred thousand children. About one in seven had early childhood decay. Simple comparisons first looked misleading. Adjusted models accounted for ethnicity and deprivation. They also allowed effects to differ between groups. The study gives current national evidence for a debated policy. Local councils can weigh real numbers, not slogans.
pmc-13670397:
Guava leaves yield an essential oil with reported healing properties, but Tarsila da Silva and co-authors show in a 2026 study that handling before distillation changes what ends up in the bottle. They compared oil from fresh and frozen leaves, ground by hand or by machine.

Oil from fresh leaves ground in a mixer carried the richest mix of the heavy scent compounds, led by beta-caryophyllene and alpha-humulene. That oil was also gentlest on test cells and reduced nitric oxide and reactive oxygen inside them. It killed Candida albicans and the drug-resistant Candida auris, while the pure lead compound only slowed the fungi. The message for producers is practical: preprocessing is part of the recipe, not a detail.
pmc-13670997:
Nine researchers, led by Sébastien Bihorel, reply in 2026 to comments on their study of aflibercept, a drug injected into the eye for retinal diseases. The exchange concerns how long the drug stays active in the eye and how that shapes the gap between doses.

The authors note that their model tracked how the drug clears from the eye. It predicted that the higher 8 mg dose holds its level about six weeks longer than the 2 mg dose. They describe follow-up analyses linking faster clearance and greater retinal thickness to shorter dosing gaps in trial patients. They welcome wider modeling that ties drug levels to treatment results.
pmc-13671097:
A seven-year-old girl with early puberty and a growing belly is the subject of a 2026 case report by Sanaa Bouramdane and co-authors. Scans showed a large mass in her abdomen, and tissue tests pointed to a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, a rare ovarian growth. This one released estrogen, which is unusual for its type.

The team first shrank the tumor with chemotherapy, then removed it with surgery that spared the girl's fertility. Lab work confirmed the diagnosis, and the tumor's stage reflected a break in its outer layer found before surgery. One more round of chemotherapy followed, hormone levels returned to normal, and the girl stayed free of disease after 27 months. The case shows why tissue proof matters when a child's symptoms point in more than one direction.
pmc-13672697:
Facundo Van Isseldyk replies in 2026 to comments on his group's study of a spine operation meant to cut postoperative burning leg pain. The exchange turns on definitions: the paper had defined the pain syndrome as starting three to seven days after surgery, yet one patient's symptoms began on day two.

Van Isseldyk confirms the mismatch from the source data and reclassifies that patient as not having the syndrome. With the correction, the rates become seven of 46 patients in one group against one of 54 in the other, still a clear and significant gap. He also accepts that the study compared outcomes rather than proving the two techniques equal. The reply is a worked example of authors correcting their own record in print.
pmc-13673097:
Farhad Dadgar and Mehdi Rostami wrote a 2026 letter to the editor on a review of COVID-19 vaccine boosters. The review they read weighed same-type and mixed-type booster shots. Its authors held that a mixed shot may give an edge in immune response, as immunity fades and new variants come.

The letter writers praise the topic but urge care in how the results are used. The trials pooled in the review vary a lot in clinic and method. Same and mixed boosters are not one treatment each, but many mixes of first shots, platforms, gaps, and age groups, they note.
pmc-13674497:
Lauren Aubrey and co-authors establish dairy goats as a stand in for cows in bird flu mammary research. Published in 2026, the study answers a logistics problem: the H5N1 virus now infects dairy cattle and sheds in milk, but cow work in high containment is slow, costly, and space hungry. Goats offer the same target organ in a smaller frame.

Two virus genotypes placed in the udder caused acute mastitis, falling milk yield, and heavy shedding into milk, mirroring the cow disease. A killed virus vaccine given by injection raised antibodies in blood and milk, softened illness, cut shedding, and protected yield. The authors offer the goat model for pathogenesis studies and control design at workable scale.
pmc-13676197:
Steven Persaud and co-authors examine, in a 2026 study, pay gaps in shoulder replacement surgery tied to patients' insurance status. Patients covered by both Medicare and Medicaid tend to carry heavier medical and social burdens. The team asked whether surgeons whose panels hold more of these patients get paid less.

Working from a public 2023 federal file on doctors' payments, the authors found surgeons who perform this operation. They linked each surgeon's share of dual-covered patients with standard Medicare pay rates. The title gives the core finding: a higher share went with lower pay, despite greater patient complexity. Results like these fuel debate about whether pay formulas punish doctors who serve the poorest patients.
pmc-13676397:
Julia Dietzsch, Yitzhak Tor, and Claudia Höbartner create a glowing stand-in for one of RNA's letters, letting researchers watch RNA at work. Labels that shine under light are prized for tracking RNA's shape and changes, but many labels distort the molecule. The stand-in used here mimics the letter G closely and is known for its brightness.

The team reports the first chemical synthesis of the building block needed to insert this letter into RNA by machine. Tests showed the substitute behaves like the real letter and does not warp the strand. Its glow shifts with the local setting, which turns it into a sensor. The authors used it to follow an enzyme-like DNA strand cutting RNA in real time. They present the labeled letter as a gentle, precise probe for RNA modification studies.
pmc-13676497:
Dongdong Zhang, Ning Ning, and Lin Chen wrote this 2026 study comparing robotic and keyhole surgery for stomach cancer at a Chinese center new to robots. Both methods remove the stomach through small cuts; the robot adds wristed tools and a steadier view. The team matched forty-five robot patients with eighty-eight keyhole patients of similar risk to compare early results.

The counts of lymph nodes removed, the key quality measure, came out even. Robot patients left hospital about two days sooner, and their removed nodes held fewer cancer-positive ones, though that gap may reflect case mix. Operating times ran similar by the program's late phase, after an early learning dip visible in the trend charts. The authors call the robot approach safe and comparable in skilled hands, while asking for fuller follow-up data.
pmc-13676997:
Xin Ni, Cailu Xiao, Gongbing Zhou, and Jingzi Zhang review catalysts for a biomass upgrade. Their review from twenty twenty-six deals with levulinic acid from biomass. Its product, GVL, bridges biomass to value chemicals.

Ruthenium catalysts work well for this conversion step. They start carbonyl groups well and pick GVL with care. They also suit many hydrogen sources, from gas to alcohols. The review sums up tuning at many scales of design. Acid sites, support form, and particle size are all covered. A workflow for use of these tricks is proposed.
pmc-13677397:
Rejina Gurung and co-authors test a quality improvement package for care during childbirth across eight hospitals in Nepal, in a trial report from 2026. Good care at birth saves mothers and newborns, but earlier efforts to spread improvement methods in Nepal gave mixed results. The package worked at two levels: hospital governance and frontline clinical habits.

Hospitals adopted the package one by one in a stepped design over twenty-one months, each with a two-month start window. More than one hundred thousand women were enrolled across control and intervention periods. Local teams tracked deaths around birth and staff performance. Results were computed hospital by hospital, comparing event rates before and after the switch. The design lets each hospital serve as its own control.
pmc-13678497:
Miao Su and co-authors test a faster way to age an unripe citrus fruit used in both food and medicine in China. Aging raises the level of helpful plant compounds in the fruit and softens its taste, but the natural process is slow. The team aged the fruit in rooms where heat and damp air were held steady.

Three groups were checked over time for looks, water content, drink color, and key compounds such as naringin. One steady setting, warm air with high moisture, gave the best gains. Levels of the target compounds rose, and a broad scan of small molecules showed shifts that help explain the change in quality.
pmc-13680097:
Eamonn Tweedy and co-authors report a live test, in 2026, of a warning tool for a children's intensive care unit. The tool, P-WIN, scores each child's risk of a sharp decline every 30 minutes from health record data. Decline events include revival from a stopped heart, use of a heart-lung machine, or an unplanned breathing tube. Tools like this are rarely checked as they run in real wards, which is the gap the team set out to fill.

Among 1,005 young patients, 99 decline events hit 62 children in three months. The tool caught 73 percent of events one to 24 hours ahead. The team also weighed false alarms per day and how the tool stacks up next to the ward's past warning tool and staff huddles.
pmc-13680497:
Viruses that kill cancer can also hit sound cells, which caps their use as drugs. Eileen Theune and co-authors fit one such virus with a cap in a 2026 study. The cap keeps the virus mute till it meets enzymes that run rich in tumours, which snip the cap off.

The team armed the capped virus with a gene that fires immune attack. Shot into the blood of mice with colon tumours, it wiped set tumours out with no broad harm. It left a long immune mark and slowed lung spread too. Paired with a known immune drug, it did still better. Tumours showed strong killer cell waves and a near wipe of guard cells. The cap route may make virus care both safer and stronger.
pmc-13680597:
Zhu and co-authors examine how a week of heat stress reshapes the liver of a farmed fish, in a 2026 study.
